en: [1] Therein begins the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*) (now begins the commentary).
Resplendent with the various flickering rays of the excellent jewels set in the crowns of the gods and asuras bowing down to attain perfection;
that divine and singular medicine which pacifies the great fear of obstacles to spiritual welfare.
May that pair of lotus feet of the elephant-faced one be of great benefit for our attainment of the desired goal. || 1 ||
Salutation to that Supreme Brahman, from whom arise the creation, sustenance, dissolution, and liberation of the entire universe.
He who, being immeasurable, becomes Brahmā, Hari, and the Three-eyed One in his efforts for the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe—
him, whose nature is pure awakening, fearlessness, and blissful existence, [I salute].
We worship the Self, which is non-dual, infinite, and unborn. || 3 ||

I bow to that Yājñavalkya, the foremost among the hosts of yogis, who, having obtained the Śukla-yajus from the Sun, was honored by the multitude of sages, so that the understanding of Dharma may be celebrated by him. (4)
He, who was filled with wonder at his devotion by the enemy of Smara (Śiva), surpassed Vācaspati in intellect, the host of enemies in valor, the sun in purity,
and the earth in forbearance— he, the ornament of the Jīmūta lineage, [attained] great [success] as proclaimed by the Lord of Yogins.
In this treatise, he composes an exposition that follows the principles of sentence-structure and is esteemed by the virtuous.

[2] Commencing this work connected with the Dharma, he speaks in order to remove the suspicion of invalidity—which arises because it shares the common characteristic of being a human composition—and which acts as an obstacle for great people regarding its study, retention, and so forth:
"Oṃ! Having worshipped Yājñavalkya, the Lord of Yogins, the sages said:
'Tell us, in their entirety, the duties of those belonging to the castes (varṇas), the stages of life (āśramas), and others. (1)

The yogī is one who possesses self-restraint (*saṃyama*). Furthermore, in that regard, Īśvara is endowed with qualities such as *aṇimā*. That these qualities constitute the grounds for the application of the term "Īśvara" is understood from the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Aṇimā, laghimā, mahimā, and prāpti;
likewise prākāmya, īśitva, and supreme vaśitva."
O tiger among men, there one attains these eight divine qualities, including the power to resolve at will, which indicate supreme nirvāṇa.
The quality of lightness (*laghimā*) is subtler than the subtlest because of its swiftness;
greatness (*mahimā*) consists in being worthy of worship by all; and attainment (*prāpti*) is that for which there is nothing unattainable for him.
Because he pervades all things, he possesses the power of irresistible will (*prākāmya*); because he is the Lord, he possesses lordship (*īśitva*);
and because of his mastery, the yogi possesses the seventh quality known as self-control (*vaśitā*).
Wherever there is the power of abiding at will, and wherever there is the power of determining the fulfillment of desires— by these causes, the eightfold sovereignty of the yogi has been described.
"The form that indicates liberation belongs to one whose mind is set on supreme nirvāṇa. Thus [it is said].

Thus, this word *īśvara* refers primarily to one who possesses qualities such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and the rest. Consequently, the term *yogīśvara* is a *karmadhāraya* compound in its primary sense, meaning "this person is both a yogin and an *īśvara*. It is not, however, a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound meaning "the lord of yogins," because that would entail the fault of implying a secondary metaphorical sense (*lakṣaṇā*) for the genitive case, and it would result in the redundancy of employing the word *yogīśvara*. For in that case, what is being stated by Yājñavalkya regarding the yogins would not be their sovereignty characterized by *aṇimā* and so forth; rather, it would be his ownership over yogins such as Sanaka and others. And that [ownership] is irrelevant to the present context. But in the *karmadhāraya* interpretation, the author's intention is understood to be the sovereignty consisting of *aṇimā* and the rest, which has yoga as its cause. Furthermore, by the word *yogin*, ignorance, attachment, and aversion—which are antagonistic to yoga—are implicitly excluded. And it has been stated in the Purāṇa that yoga possesses the power to eliminate those [defects].
"One should burn away defects by means of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sins by means of concentrations (dhāraṇā).
One should burn away attachments by means of withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and non-divine qualities by means of meditation (dhyāna). Thus it is said.

By the word *Īśvara*, his status as a knower of the Vedas and Vedāntas exactly as they are, as well as his supreme compassion, are indicated; thus, since the authority of the work composed by him is established, how could any suspicion of its lack of authority arise? *Yājñavalkya* is the offspring of Yajñavalkya. Having "honored" means having paid respect. The sages—the great seers (*maharṣis*)—said, "Tell us, enlighten us, in their entirety—that is, without remainder—concerning the duties (*dharmas*) of the castes (*varṇas*) and so forth. The "castes" are the Brāhmaṇas and others. Although the word *āśrama* (stage of life) refers to the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder, and so on, nevertheless, because the duties belonging to those stages would not otherwise exist, the word *āśrama* here indicates the *āśramins* (those belonging to the stages). Therefore Vasiṣṭha says: "The four stages of life are the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the wandering mendicant. Those who are distinct from being merely a caste or merely an *āśramin*—that is, those specific forms which are the subjects of the duties to be described—are here called "others" (*itare*). These specific forms are as follows: first, in the rule for begging alms before one's elders, there is the state of being a Brāhmaṇa combined with studentship (*brahmacarya*); likewise, in the rule for begging alms from the middle of the assembly and so on, that same state is required in relation to Kṣatriyas and others; in the rule for marriage, there is passion for a woman and the status of a *snātaka*; in the rule for approaching a wife, there is the state of having a wife during her fertile period or the state of having a wife through sexual union; among the duties of women, there is femininity, sometimes the state of being a wife, sometimes the state of having a husband away, and sometimes widowhood; in the rule for purifying liquids, there is the quality of being the substance to be purified; in prohibitions, however, there is the possession of the full capacity to engage in the prohibited action; in the rule for *śrāddha* rites, there is the state of having a deceased father while living through the uninterrupted time of the *śrāddha*; in the rule for bathing the Vināyakas, there is being afflicted by Vināyaka; in the rule for the sacrifice to the planets, there is the desire for prosperity (*śrī*) and so forth; in the rule for royal duties, there is the consecration of a Kṣatriya; in the rule for cremation and so forth, there is being a sapinda relative of the deceased; in the rule for duties in times of distress, there is the state of being destitute; in the rule for old age, there is the presence of wrinkles and grey hair, and the state of having a grandson born; in the rule for the wandering mendicant, there is the state of possessing detachment from worldly existence after having studied the Vedas, produced a son, and performed sacrifices; in the rule for penance, there is the state of being sinful, and so on. Those who are qualified by these are the "others. "Castes, stages of life, and others" is the compound *varṇāśrametarāḥ*. Regarding this, the prohibition of the designation of a pronoun (*sarvanāman*) by the rule "dvandve ca" applies to the word *itarāḥ*. Dharma is that which is to be known through the scriptures and which brings about the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). Adharma is the prohibition of auxiliary parts of a sacrifice. The word "in their entirety" (*aśeṣataḥ*) expresses the completeness of the general intention regarding dharma, in relation to the act of proclaiming the faultless and exhaustive meaning of the scripture to be described. For if this were intended to mean "without remainder," then the *homa* offerings and other rites mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* would not need to be performed for the initiation (*upanayana*) and so forth. There are three general types of dharma conditioned by the limiting adjuncts of caste, stage of life, and others. Since he was requested to "tell the dharmas," the primary motive for the composition of the *Dharma-saṃhitā* is primarily the knowledge of the duties inherent in the students. Consequently, that alone is the motive for the students' study. Indeed, their study cannot be without a motive. Therefore, the study of the Dharmaśāstra is motivated precisely by the knowledge of its nature as a Dharmaśāstra. Even in this verse composed by Yājñavalkya, the expression "having honored Yājñavalkya" and the use of the first person in the subsequent verse, "the Lord of Yogins said" (*yogīndro 'bravīt*), are not improper. For the usage "Manu said" is seen in the text of Manu, and "Baudhāyana said" in the text of Baudhāyana. Nor should it be argued that "Manu said" is the speech of Bhṛgu and not of Manu himself; for it is only at a later time that Manu speaks thus.
"This Bhṛgu will proclaim this scripture to you in its entirety; for this sage has learned all of this from me in its fullness. Thus [he spoke].

"Adhijage" means he studied. Regarding this *Saṃhitā*, the traditional memory (*smṛti*) of the commentators alone is the authority that Yājñavalkya is its author. Nor should it be argued that they remember only the meaning as being Yājñavalkya’s; for while uniqueness belongs to the author in relation to a book, it does not belong to him in relation to the meaning, since that meaning has been perceived by other sages as well. Furthermore, designation based on uniqueness is not possible when there is commonality, for designations are indeed made on the basis of uniqueness. || 1 ||
Remaining in Mithilā, that lord of yogis meditated for a moment and spoke to the sages:

That sage, having been requested to "speak the Dharmas," and being especially tranquil due to his residence in Mithilā, reflected for a moment upon the meaning of the scripture to be spoken and the fitness of the sages for hearing it; then, having so considered, he spoke the Dharmas that were to be taught. To indicate that the authorship of the treatise belongs to Yājñavalkya, the word *saḥ* ("he") was used, rather than *aham* ("I"). From the word *aham*, the understanding would not necessarily be of Yājñavalkya; however, from the word *saḥ*, which denotes the subject under discussion, the mind immediately apprehends Yājñavalkya as the one currently in context, and thus he employed that very term. Furthermore, because of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with *abravīt*, the third person alone is appropriate, and not the first person *abruvam*.
In this regard, since the practice of dharma is preceded by the selection of a location, he speaks of the place even before the discourse on dharma:
"In that land where the black antelope roams, there you shall learn the dharmas. (2)

[5] The word *kṛṣṇa* signifies the *hariṇa* (the black antelope). This is because we observe its usage in such expressions as "the black antelope skin" (*kṛṣṇājina*) and "the black antelope horn" (*kṛṣṇaviṣāṇa*), as well as in the phrase "as long as the black antelope roams. In whatever region that animal would roam by its very nature, there—O sages—understand (*nibodhata*, i.e., *nibudhyadhvam*) the duties (*dharmān*), both those prescribed by the Śruti and those by the Smṛti, as being those to be performed. The word "antelope" (*mṛga*) is used so that there may be no understanding of a different meaning from the word *kṛṣṇa*. Furthermore, it should be understood that a region characterized by the black antelope serves as a subsidiary factor for the performance of dharma when regions such as Brahmāvarta are unavailable. Thus says Manu:
The region between the Sarasvatī and the Dṛṣadvatī, those two rivers of the sky,
that land created by the gods is called Brahmāvarta.
Kurukṣetra, Matsya, Pañcāla, and those born in Śūrasena—
this is indeed the land of the Brahman-sages (brahmarṣideśa), immediately following Brahmāvarta.
The region situated between the Himavat and Vindhya mountains, extending eastward from Vinaśana and westward from Prayāga, is proclaimed as Madhyadeśa.
From the eastern ocean to the western ocean,
the region between those two very mountains is proclaimed as Āryāvarta.
That land where the black antelope roams by its own nature is to be known as fit for sacrifice; beyond that is the land of the Mlecchas.
And here, each preceding region is superior to each succeeding one. As it is said in the Purāṇa:
"Brahmāvarta is the supreme land; the land of the Ṛṣis is next;
the Madhyadeśa is inferior to that; and Āryāvarta is next after that."
And Viṣṇu says:
"One should know that country to be the land of the Mlecchas in which the established order of the four castes does not exist; beyond that is Āryāvarta."

Thus he states another definition of Āryāvarta. Consequently, that place where the system of the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*) does not exist and the black antelope (*kṛṣṇamṛga*) is not found is a land of barbarians (*mlecchadeśa*); other than that is a land of Dharma (*dharmadeśa*). Therefore, when the four regions beginning with Brahmāvarta cannot be reached, one should reside in a place where the four castes are established and the black antelope roams, for those desiring Dharma. In the absence of such a place, one may reside in a region possessing the system of the four castes or inhabited by the black antelope. From the mention of "Dharma" in the phrase "learn the Dharmas," it should be understood that there is no specific restriction regarding the avoidance of unrighteousness (*adharma*) in the choice of location. [6] Manu states the favor shown toward the livelihood of a *śūdra*:
"Twice-born men should diligently seek refuge in these countries;
however, a Śūdra, distressed for a livelihood, may dwell in any [place].
Thus, since the practice of Dharma must be preceded by knowledge, he first states the means for the knowledge of Dharma.
The Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, the Dharmaśāstras, and the auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) of the Vedas—these fourteen are the seats of knowledge and of dharma. (3)

The Purāṇas are those beginning with the *Brahma-purāṇa*. Logic (*nyāya*) is that which is accompanied by sound reasoning. Hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*) is the investigation of Vedic statements. The Treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*) are the legal codes (*smṛti*) of Manu and others. The four Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, together with their six auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) such as grammar and so forth, constitute these fourteen bases of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*). They are the causes of knowledge, and through knowledge, they are the cause of Dharma; for it is only knowledge produced from these that serves as the cause of Dharma. Consequently, it is established that knowledge arising from practical manuals (*prayogapaddhati*) and the like is not a cause of Dharma. Thus, there are these fourteen bases of knowledge.
The Vedānta is the fifteenth, and the Vidyā is the sixteenth.

Thus, in the *Brahma Purāṇa*, the mention of both the Vedas and the *vidyās* is intended to refer to the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) that serve as means to liberation; therefore, it was not mentioned here [in this context] because it would be of no use. "Vedānta" refers to the *Śārīraka*. "Vidyā" refers to the secret doctrines (*rahasya*) such as the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and others. As for the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "The limbs, the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya, the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra—these are the fourteen sciences (*vidyās*)."
Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and Gāndharvaveda— these three,
together with Arthaśāstra as the fourth, constitute those eighteen branches of knowledge.

That [definition] intends only the status of being a field of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), not the status of being a field of Dharma (*dharmasthāna*), because Āyurveda and the others lack the status of being fields of Dharma. Otherwise, apart from the mention of "fourteen," there would be no inclusion of the Atharvaveda. (3)
Now, in order to distinguish the treatises on Dharma from those that merely appear to be so, he names their authors:
Manu, Atri, Viṣṇu, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Uśanas, and Aṅgiras;
Yama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Kātyāyana, and Bṛhaspati; || 4 ||
Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Dakṣa, Gautama, Śātātapa, and Vasiṣṭha are the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.

The *prayojakas* are the authors (*praṇetāraḥ*). The rest is self-evident. On this point, Gautama employed the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the passage: "Smṛti refers to the Dharmaśāstras. Their authors are Manu, Viṣṇu, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Atri, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Āpastamba, Gautama, Saṃvarta, Ātreya, Kātyāyana, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śātātapa, Pracetas, Yājñavalkya, and others. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), those who composed texts rooted in the Veda are included here. And thus says Manu: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as well as the Smṛti and the conduct of those who know it."

For this very reason, the remaining Vedic syntactic remainder (*vākyaikaśeṣa*) is "Aṅgiras"; it is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*) in the neuter gender, ending in the singular number. For this same reason, in the *Guhyeśvara-vākya* of the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*, only thirty-six Smṛtis are mentioned:
"The Smṛtis beginning with Manu that have been proclaimed as thirty-six—I shall state their passages to you in order and in brief."

And these thirty-six authors are enumerated in another Smṛti: Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Dakṣa, Aṅgiras, Trita, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Āpastamba, Vasiṣṭha, Kātyāyana, Parāśara, Vyāsa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Saṃvarta, Gautama, Śātātapa, Hārīta, Yājñavalkya, Pracetas, Budha, Devala, Soma, Jamadagni, Viśvāmitra, Prajāpati, Nārada, Paiṭhīnasi, Pitāmaha, Baudhāyana, Chāgaleya, Jābāli, Cyavana, Marīci, and Kaśyapa. Likewise, the Vṛddhamanu and others should be understood as being the very same authors as Manu and the rest, distinguished by differences of age and so forth; for they are non-contradictory, they supplement the Śruti and Smṛti, they are accepted by the learned (śiṣṭas), and they are the words of authoritative persons (āptas). Furthermore, the Caturviṃśatimata-pariśiṣṭa and other such works are to be known as Dharmaśāstra itself. (4–5)

Now, having cited the example of *dāna* (giving), he states that a scripture which, being independent of other scriptures, is unable to convey its complete meaning, is an authority regarding *dharma* only when it depends upon other scriptures:
"When wealth, accompanied by faith, is given at the proper place, at the proper time, and by the proper means to a worthy recipient—that is the complete definition of *dharma*. (6)

In a place such as Kurukṣetra, at a time such as an eclipse, by means of the prescribed procedure (*itikartavyatā*), with the substance (*dravya*) such as a cow, accompanied by faith (*śraddhā*)—that is, the conviction that "it is so"—and given to a worthy recipient (*pātra*) whose characteristics will be described hereafter, being given with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*) characterized by indifference to fame and the like, and being relinquished until the acceptance by the recipient; this entire sentence which establishes these points is to be understood as the definition of Dharma and the authority for Dharma (*dharme pramāṇa*) for a Dharma endowed with all its constituent means and possessing these specific details. However, the definition of Dharma does not apply to a Dharma that is merely joined with every single [possible] mode. Thus says Śaṅkha: "Place, time, means, substance, faith, and the recipient—when all these are present, there is the arising of Dharma; this is common and proper. Otherwise, it is the reverse. "Common" means it is the same as giving (*dāna*). "Proper" refers to other Dharmas such as sacrifice (*yāga*). "Otherwise" means in the absence of completeness. "The reverse" means the non-arising of Dharma. When one has the capacity, all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) must be performed. But when lacking capacity, optional rites (*kāmya*) should be abandoned; however, what is mandatory (*āvaśyaka*) must be performed according to one's ability. As for the statement of Kātyāyana: [The text continues with the citation of Kātyāyana’s verse.]
Whether the ritual procedure prescribed in one's own *gṛhya* text is extensive or brief, when that much of the meaning of the scripture has been performed by him, everything is considered performed.

Thus, that [rule] refers to the subject matter of one's own scripture which expresses its meaning independently. However, regarding matters that require dependence upon other scriptures within one's own tradition, he himself has stated:
"Whatever is not recited in one's own branch (śākhā), provided it is not contradictory, should be performed by the learned, just like the Agnihotra and other rites."
[9] Now he states the authorities for Dharma:
Revelation (śruti), Tradition (smṛti), the conduct of the virtuous (sadācāra), and what is pleasing to oneself.
Desire born of right resolve is remembered as this root of Dharma. || 7 ||

Scripture (*śruti*) and the rest are each a root of *dharma*, that is, a cause for the determination of *dharma*. In the verse beginning "Purāṇa, Nyāya," etc., the status of being a root of *dharma* was stated generally for both *śruti* and *smṛti*; here, however, their status as roots is specified individually. By implication, this means that the other branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) serve as supports for knowledge. *Smṛti* does not support the Vedas like grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and the others do, but rather infers them; hence it is mentioned separately. As for conduct (*ācāra*) and so forth, the fact that they are again stated here to be roots of *dharma* does not constitute redundancy. *Śruti* is the Veda. *Smṛti* is a scripture rooted in the Veda concerning *dharma*. "Good conduct" (*sadācāra*) is the conduct of the cultured (*śiṣṭa*). "What is pleasing to oneself" (*svasya... priyam*) means what brings satisfaction to one's own mind. Here, by the word "self" (*ātman*), the mind is indicated; by the word "pleasing" (*priya*), satisfaction is meant. Thus, "satisfaction of the mind" (*manastuṣṭi*) here refers to the cessation of the desire to act. "Resolve" (*saṃkalpa*) is a mental activity directed toward a proper scriptural subject, thinking, "By this, I shall accomplish this. The "desire born thereof" (*tajjaḥ kāmaḥ*) is the desire to perform *dharma*. All of this is the root cause in the determination of *dharma*. By the term "dharma," its determination is indicated. In that regard, *śruti* is the root of the determination of the *agnihotra* and so forth; *smṛti* is the root of the determination of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*) and so forth; good conduct is the root of the determination of the *holākā* sacrifice and so forth; and the satisfaction of the mind is the root of the determination of those actions which are enjoined as being limited by mental satisfaction. For example: [Example omitted in source] The meaning is that all of this is the root cause in the determination of *dharma*. Through *dharma*, its determination is indicated. Among these, *śruti* is the root of the determination of the *agnihotra* and so forth; *smṛti* is the root of the determination of the duties of the castes and stages of life and so forth; good conduct is the root of the determination of the *holākā* and so forth; and the satisfaction of the mind is the root of the determination of that action which is enjoined by way of being delimited by the satisfaction of the mind. As, for example: [Example omitted in source] The meaning is that all of this is the root cause in the determination of *dharma*. Through *dharma*, its determination is indicated. Among these, *śruti* is the root of the determination of the *agn
"In whatever action he has performed that causes unease of mind, he should perform penance (tapas) for that until it becomes a source of satisfaction. Thus [it is said].

Desire born of a specific resolve regarding a particular time is, for example: "As soon as one brings him [the student] with faith, at that very moment one should establish the sacred fires," or "And likewise, a desire directed toward the *śrāddha* ceremony."—Vyāsa.
By those desiring the purity of Dharma, nothing other than the gods is sought as the pure cause of Dharma; any other is proclaimed to be mixed.
Purity means being unmixed; that is to say, the purity of the Dharma, which is the determination of Dharma. "Pure" means faultless; "mixed" means suspected of having defects.
Therefore, that Dharma which is understood from the Veda is supreme;
however, that which is recorded in the Purāṇas and other such texts should be known as inferior.
One should diligently practice that which was ordained of old by the sages who were the foremost knowers of the meaning of the Vedas, and one should avoid what is forbidden therein.
For those who know the meaningfulness of the Veda’s content have prescribed that dharma out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds; one should not call that dharma into question.
Even if there might be ignorance regarding a meaning of the Veda that one has understood by oneself,
what doubt could there be among the wise concerning that which has been determined by the seers?
Know that whatever else there might be besides these which expresses the Dharma is even further removed; delusion is considered its basis.

One should not investigate it, nor should one treat it as authoritative on the basis of mere convention. Whatever else besides these [scriptures] such as the *Dharmaśāstras* is of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), that is to be rejected.

Now, one might object: "The scriptures of the Śaivas, Pāśupatas, Pañcarātras, and so forth, are indeed non-human (*apauruṣeya*); therefore, in the practice and observance of them, there is only prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and no fault whatsoever, because they are the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
This is not so.
Having sipped water (ācamana), one who belongs to the two [higher] stages of life (āśrama) should first perform the Brāhmī Sandhyā;
the other, however, whose soul is dispassionate, should turn away from worldly affairs.
One may perform either the Brāhmī or, by necessity, the Śaivī [form of worship];
internally it is Śaiva, externally it is Kaula, while in worldly conduct it is Vaidika.
One should remain having extracted the essence, just like a coconut fruit.

Thus, because the Śaiva and other traditions are shown by such statements as those of Svāyambhuva to possess the defect of rendering Vedic rites fruitless by failing to produce worldly satisfaction, they cannot be established as the cause of supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) for the elders learned in the three Vedas, who are solely devoted to the performance of duties prescribed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. Nor is there any harm to them in not following the Śaiva and other scriptures; for their purpose is served by the duties of their respective stages of life (*āśrama-karma*) as declared in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, such as "One should offer the *Agnihotra* as long as one lives" and "One should always offer the *Agnihotra* at the beginning and end of day and night," and not by others, since transgressing the meaning of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* results in sin (*pratyavāya*). Thus says the *Śruti*: "He who extinguishes the sacred fire is indeed a slayer of the heroes of the gods. The *Smṛti* also [says the same].

"A Brāhmaṇa who, out of desire, neglects the sacred fires of the Agnihotra, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for one month; for that is equal to the killing of a hero. Nor should it be argued that the fault is established merely by the non-performance [of the rite].
Those who hate the scriptures of Śiva and those who revile the Vedas stand there in suffering, their mouths filled with molten tin.
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are supreme authorities;
one should not examine them by means of logical reasoning.

Thus, because the *Devīpurāṇa* and the *Yogayājñavalkya* are considered irreproachable and their contents are not to be scrutinized as potential fallacious reasons (*hetu*), that [work] is remembered as being beyond reproach. Nor should it be argued that there is some fault in its performance on this account; for, according to the maxim "as far as the word extends, so far the scriptural injunction," one ought not to perform the adoption of what is deficient or excessive based on mere personal conjecture. Furthermore, since it is impossible to perform the practice of all irreproachable scriptures, and because the *Śrāddha* rite spoken of by the Goddess is exceedingly censured for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*), the Vedic *Śrāddha* ritual is not [performed] even by those who are uninitiated.
Regarding those who have been initiated, the procedure for both [the teacher and the disciple] is that which leads to their departure.
Because one who follows the Śaiva scriptures incurs defects such as falling into hell by performing Vedic rites, [it is said]:
"Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed;
death in one's own duty is better than the success of another's duty."

By such statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts, although the excellence of even a partial practice is shown, there is still no attainment of the state of steadfastness in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) because the practices of the various scriptures (*āgama*), though not defective, possess mutually contradictory meanings. Thus, the Śaivas—who maintain a doctrine of a distinct God (*bhedaiśvaravāda*)—hold that God is the presiding cause of both primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the individual soul (*puruṣa*), being merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), and that primordial matter, the soul, and God are distinct from one another. The Sāṃkhyas are proponents of a non-theistic doctrine (*nirīśvaravāda*). The Pātañjala Yogins, however, hold a theistic view (*seśvaravāda*), asserting that God is a specific soul (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) who is the creator of the worlds, untouched by afflictions, karma, its results, or latent impressions, and omniscient due to His knowledge of all scriptures. The Pāñcarātras, on the other hand, regard God through a non-dual perspective (*advaitabhāva*), holding that the Lord Vāsudeva is the supreme primordial nature (*paramā prakṛti*) existing as the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*) through the distinctions of the peaceful, the emergent, the manifest, and the indefinable. The Pāśupatas, moreover, accept only the doctrine of a distinct God, maintaining that the five categories—effect, cause, yoga, ritual, and the end of suffering—were taught by the Lord Paśupati for the purpose of liberating bound souls (*paśu*) from their fetters (*pāśa*). Thus, because the knowledge of all these scriptures is unsettled, doubt cannot be removed if everything is accepted; consequently, the attainment of knowledge is indeed difficult to achieve. If one were to accept them selectively, the consequence would be madness. Now, one might object: "Just as the authority of the Śaiva and other traditions rests solely on their being irreproachable, so too should the Veda be authoritative, since there is no difference in its being remembered as irreproachable. True; yet, as stated in the passage beginning with "by molten tin," the authority of the Veda is based solely on its irreproachability, which is exactly like that of the Śaiva and other scriptures.
The Vedic scripture is the eternal eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings; it is inconceivable and immeasurable—such is the established principle.

By such statements, Manu and others have declared that the Veda alone is the supreme means for accomplishing goals pertaining to both this world and the next, and not the scriptures of the Śaivas and others. On the contrary, [it is said]: "Indeed, for the sake of deluding those who have strayed from the path of the Veda, I first presented the scripture known as Siddhānta."
When one who is a *paśu* (bound soul), abiding in a state of non-animality (*apaśubhāva*), becomes fallen (*patita*),
then the *Pāśupata* scripture, which deludes the universe, is known.
For they shall be deluded by me alone, O twice-born one;
in the Kali age, men seeking their own desires will compose various scriptures.
That which consists of one hundred thousand breaths in its measure is indeed the Pāśupata yoga; from it, the various divisions of the Pāśupatas arise.
Whatever else arises here from this [practice], such as the path of the Vedas and so forth,
should be known as a minor action— fierce and devoid of purity.

By such statements in the *Varāha Purāṇa*, through the words of Rudra addressed to Agastya, its very nature as a deceiver (*vipralambhaka*) by means of deluding others is established. Because it deludes all people, the Śaiva and other [systems] are indeed deceptive. Furthermore, in that same [text], there is the speech of Janārdana addressed to Śrī Rudra:
"I shall quickly create this delusion which will bewilder people;
and you, O mighty-armed Rudra, compose treatises of delusion (*mohaśāstra*)."
Having shown little effort, display a great result;
for deceivers employ magical illusions and contradictory practices.
"O Maheśvara, having shown yourself to all people, quickly delude them.
For this very reason, Manu says: "Whatever things there are that arise and pass away..."
"Because they are of recent origin, they are fruitless and false.

For this very reason, Āpastamba stated the lack of authority regarding the conduct prescribed in the Śaiva and other scriptures: "[13] 'The Vedas are the authority'—this is the settled conclusion. In that regard, those things which are heard in connection with rice, barley, cattle, clarified butter, milk, sacrificial pots, and vessels, and which are to be performed loudly or softly; conduct that contradicts these is considered unauthoritative. Now, one might object: "In the absence of Vedic mantras, indeed, by that which is declared in the Pañcarātra..."
Those men who proceed according to right conduct shall attain me.
A five-night [observance] is prescribed for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas;
it shall not even come to the range of the ears of Śūdras and others.

Because the *Varāha Purāṇa* records the Pāñcarātra as a substitute for the Veda through the words of the Blessed One, the Pāñcarātra is non-different from the Veda. True, it is non-different; however, there is a distinction due to a difference in subject matter. For instance, because this statement refers to *vrātyas* who have not performed penance due to some stroke of fate, it does not rely on Brahmins and others whose conduct is unimpaired. This being so, the word "unavailability" (*alābha*) in this context becomes logical, since such *vrātyas* lack access to the Veda. And thus says the *Mānava* [Smṛti]:

"A Brāhmaṇa must never, even in times of distress, enter into spiritual or matrimonial alliances with those who have not been purified according to the rules. If this were so, then the eligibility of the twice-born for the *Pāñcarātra* would indeed be undermined. Therefore, because this statement refers specifically to *vrātyas* who have failed to perform penance due to the force of their circumstances, there is a distinction between the Veda and the *Pañcarātra*. For this very reason, the mention in the *Yogayājñavalkya* of the *Pañcarātra* alongside the *Pāśupata* and other systems as a "siddhānta" (established doctrine) serves only to create the impression that it is outside the Vedic fold.
However, the *praṇava* alone should be known as the means for yoga,
both by others who have mastered the seven philosophical systems and likewise by those who know Brahman.
By the followers of Hiraṇyagarbha, the Kapilas, the Apāntaratamasas,
as well as the Sānatkumāras who are most devoted to Brahman, and also by the Pāśupatas.
"By these seven systems of tenets, including the Pāñcarātras as well.
Thus, it is indeed because the Pāñcarātra is irreproachable that its authority is established, not because it is something to be practiced.

Now, one might object: just as the Veda and other scriptures proceed by being directed toward certain specific [classes of] people, so too let there be Śaiva and other scriptures directed toward those belonging to the Śaiva and other castes.
No;
one for whom the ritual procedure beginning with the impregnation and ending with the cremation ground has been prescribed by means of mantras—
only such a person is to be known as qualified for this scripture, and no one else whatsoever.

Since Manu and others have demonstrated in their own treatises that the qualification [for study] belongs only to the twice-born (*dvija*), [the qualification] does not belong to Śaiva-brāhmaṇas and the like in the Śaiva and other scriptures.
Well then, let it be that the *śūdra* is qualified in the Śaiva and other scriptures.

No, because that is not accepted in the *Smṛti* and other scriptures. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a "Śaiva" by birth for whom a scripture such as the Śaiva would exist; rather, when the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to Pāṇini 4.3.101 (*tena proktam*), the scripture taught by Śiva is called "Śaiva. Then again, from the word "Śaiva," when the suffix *aṇ* is produced according to Pāṇini 4.2.59 (*tad adhīte tad veda*) and subsequently elided according to Pāṇini 4.2.64 (*proktāl luk*), one who knows or studies the Śaiva [scripture] is called a "Śaiva. The same applies to the Pāśupata and others. Since the Śaiva and other scriptures have thus proceeded without depending on any specific individuals by nature, they become like a painting in the sky. And this being so, their practice must certainly be abandoned. Nor should it be argued that their practice occurs simply because they are established in irreproachable scriptures; for mere irreproachability does not grant them the capacity to compel the performance of their own meaning in the same way as the *Śruti*.
Whatever scriptures are outside the Veda and whatever false views there may be—
all those are declared to be fruitless, for they are said to be composed of darkness.

Because [the practice] has been prohibited by Manu and others through such statements as "the performance of that leads to fruitlessness in the hereafter," therefore, in rites such as the worship of the gods, only the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) well-known from the *Narasiṃha Purāṇa* and other such texts is to be adopted, and no other. This should be understood to apply to initiation (*dīkṣā*) as well; for in the initiation well-known in the Purāṇas, there is no purification of caste (*jātiśodhana*). However, in the Śaiva and other Āgamas, it is said:
"First is the stationary caste (*sthāvarā jāti*), then the reptile caste is considered [second];
the bird caste is the third, and the fourth is the animal caste."
The fifth is the species of cattle, and the sixth is remembered as the lowest-born;
the seventh is the Śūdra caste, and likewise the eighth is the Vaiśya caste.
The ninth is the Kṣatriya caste, while the tenth is designated as the Brahmin;
these castes are to be purified by Jātīśa or by Śiva.

Because of the observation of such purification through these and other passages, there arises the contingency that one would lack the qualification for Vedic rituals. Vedic ritual activity proceeds only with reference to those possessing caste (*jāti*), as in: "A Brāhmaṇa should establish the sacred fires," "A king should sacrifice with the Rājasūya," and "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma. How then could that [Vedic ritual] exist upon the cessation of caste? [15] Likewise, even regarding the *Pratiṣṭhā* (consecration) rites, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) stated in the Purāṇas and similar sources is what should be adopted, and no other. This is because they alone are recognized in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* as the authoritative source for mixed dharmas. And so says the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*:
The eighteen Purāṇas, as well as the life-story of Rāma,
the Viṣṇudharma and other scriptures, and the Śivadharma, O Bhārata.
"And the fifth Veda is that which is remembered as the Mahābhārata of Kṛṣṇa;
and the Saura [Vedas], O Indra among kings, born of Dharma and spoken by Manu—O Lord of the Earth, the wise call these by the name 'Jaya'. Thus it is said.

In that regard as well, Smṛti texts such as "O King, one should drink *surā* with the exception of *madya*" are to be understood as applying to eras other than the Kali Yuga; for [the following are forbidden in Kali]:
long-term celibacy, the carrying of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), marriage with a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*) or the same ancestry (*sapiṇḍa*), and likewise the killing of a cow.
Human sacrifice, horse sacrifice, and liquor must be avoided by the twice-born in the Kali age.

Because liquor and other such substances have been declared in general as things to be avoided in the *Brahma Purāṇa* and elsewhere by such passages; by this, the offerings to Caṇḍikā and others are also explained. Furthermore, regarding the rule for collyrium in the *Kālikā Purāṇa*: "Having placed [the ingredients] in a hollowed skull-cup and likewise in great clarified butter, the wise man should collect the soot during an eclipse of the moon or the sun."
One should anoint one's eyes with that; thus, one may bring even Indra under one's control.

This and other such passages—such as, "Now, one desiring to kill an enemy should kindle a fire with wood from a cremation ground and offer a thousand oblations mixed with poison and blood; he kills the enemy immediately," or "One practicing *abhicāra* (malevolent magic) should sacrifice with a hawk"—are indeed unrighteous (*adharma*). This is because subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and similar acts are prohibited here and there, just like violence (*hiṃsā*). Thus, Manu has included subjugation among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), stating: "Violence, [the use of] medicinal herbs, living off women, *abhicāra*, and *mūlakarma* [black magic]. Furthermore, in the *Devīpurāṇa*:
He who knows the left and the right and has mastered the meaning of the Mātṛveda shall be the most excellent installer of the goddesses and the Mothers (Mātṛkās).
One skilled in the meaning of the Pāñcarātra, proficient in the Mātṛtantras,
a householder of Viṣṇu who is always praiseworthy, and a celibate student who bestows peace— [these are recommended].
One who knows the teaching of Śiva and understands the purpose of the host of planets and mothers is declared a *sthāpaka* (consecrator) in the cult of Śiva,
whether he be a householder or a celibate student. One who understands the meaning of the Sun is an auspicious *sthāpaka* and worshipper in the cult of the Sun.
Thus, even this is not a mark of the practice of the Brāhma scriptures; for the practice of that [other path] is prohibited in the *Matsyapurāṇa*. And so says the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"O twice-born ones, hear in brief the characteristics of the Sthāpaka (the consecrator):
he must be endowed with all limbs and be proficient in the Vedic mantras."
One who knows the Purāṇas, understands the Dharma, is free from hypocrisy and greed,
possesses an auspicious form, and was born in a region frequented by black antelopes.
Constantly devoted to purity and right conduct, free from desire for the families of heretics, he was impartial toward both enemy and friend, and beloved by Brahmā, Upendra, and Hara.
The preceptor should always be one who knows the truth regarding the purpose of reasoning and refutation, who has mastered the science of architecture (vāstu-śāstra),
and who is free from all defects.
"Those who worship the images, those of the same kind, as well as those of noble birth and those who are upright. Thus it is said.

As it is stated in the *Pāñcarātra-saṃhitā*: "Fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) are to be known, namely: the *Ṛgveda*, the *Yajurveda*, the *Sāmaveda*, the *Atharvaveda*, the *Itihāsa-purāṇa*, *Nyāya*, *Mīmāṃsā*, *Śikṣā*, *Kalpa*, *Vyākaraṇa*, *Nirukta*, *Jyotiṣāmayana*, and *Chandovicitir*. Even in this regard, there is no lack of qualification; rather, there is indeed qualification. Thus, just as the knowledge of the three Vedas (*trayi*) and so forth is to be accepted, so too here only the knowledge of the *Vāma*, *Dakṣiṇa*, and other *Āmnāyas* is to be accepted. And so says the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
For one should contemplate the established doctrines for the sake of self-knowledge;
if a twice-born man studies them merely as such, he becomes an outcast from the Veda.

[17] Merely studying while abandoning one's own duty and practicing the duty of another—such is the performance of that [act]: "He who, having utterly cast aside his own duty, takes pleasure in the duty of another, is a thief with eyes like those of a cakora bird; he is a Śūdra, though appearing like the moon."

This is because [such practices] are censured in the *Skanda Purāṇa* and other texts, as indicated by the phrase "and so forth. Furthermore, knowledge of the left-hand (*vāmamārga*), right-hand (*dakṣiṇamārga*), and other paths is for the purpose of adopting certain auxiliary elements that are required by one's own scripture and are not in contradiction with what is stated therein. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Even when there is dependence [on another source], the authority is the very fact of dependence;
one should act according to another source only to the extent that it is required, and not otherwise, lest there be an infinite regress."
"But there must be the abandonment of what is contradictory. For this very reason, with the intent of avoiding the confusion of *dharma*, the *Mahābhārata* states among the duties of kings:
"The duties of the four castes must be protected by the ruler of the earth;
for the protection against the confusion of *dharma* is the eternal *dharma*."

Nor should it be argued that the knowledge of the Vāma and Dakṣiṇa traditions by the *sthāpaka* (consecrator) and others—who are authors of works such as the *Svadharmapratiṣṭhā-tantra*—is necessarily preceded by their receiving initiation according to those [traditions], because this is not accepted in the *Smṛti* and other scriptures; and because, as previously stated, the status of being a *sthāpaka* and so forth is not established as being restricted to the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other scriptures [alone]. This is because the person in question has a mind refined by the study of many branches of learning (*vidyāsthāna*) through personal examination of the Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, and other scriptures, including their commentaries and observations; and because, through a complete understanding gained with ease, he is capable of performing the mere maintenance of his own consecration rituals and tantras. Furthermore, regarding the words of the Lord addressed to Dakṣa in the *Mahābhārata* and elsewhere:
Furthermore, O observer of noble vows, I grant you another boon; accept this renowned one.
With a cheerful countenance, listen now with a single-minded focus.
Having extracted it from the Veda with its six limbs, from Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and by means of power,
[he performed] extensive and well-performed austerity, difficult for gods and dānavas to practice.
It is unprecedented, auspicious on all sides, facing every direction, and imperishable;
it is endowed with five topics, profound, and beyond the reproach of the unwise.

[18] This other stage of life (āśrama) is remembered as being contrary to the duties (dharma) established for the castes and stages of life, yet in some respects equal to them; it is determined by those who have reached the end of a hundred [years].
In former times, I previously brought forth the Pāśupata yoga;
the abundant fruit that results from its correct practice is this.
And let that be yours, O highly fortunate one; let the fever of your mind be abandoned.

Thus, this is not a mark (*liṅga*) indicating that those belonging to the stages of life (*āśramin*) must practice the *Pāśupata* scripture, because what is intended here is merely the equality of their results. For there are indeed statements in the *Pāśupata* and other Āgamas such as, "One shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma. Yet, by this much alone, their eligibility for that [Vedic sacrifice] is not established. Nor is the *Atharvaśiras Upaniṣad*—which states, "This is the vow: one should touch the limbs with ashes; therefore, this is the Pāśupata vow for the sake of liberation from the bonds of the bound"—a mark indicating that one must practice the meaning of the *Pāśupata* scripture, since only the rule of touching the limbs with ashes is heard here. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the scriptures intend for those in the stages of life to find the *Pāśupata* and other systems objectionable simply because the Smṛtis prescribe bathing with one's clothes on (*sacaila-snāna*) upon touching a *Pāśupata*. For we observe that even after touching bricks piled in a sacrificial altar (*cit*) consecrated by numerous mantras during the Soma sacrifice and other rites, bathing is required. Some maintain that our intellects, being limited to the scope of the Śāstras, cannot fathom the question of whether the sacrificial altar is untouchable due to its impurity or because it is highly venerable like the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) to Rudra. However, in reality, just as...
Even a Brahmin who is learned in the four Vedas, if he has not been initiated into the sacrifice of Śiva, should be considered a Śūdra; no instruction of the [Śaiva] teaching should be given to him.

By such statements as these, the Śaivas and others treat those who lack initiation—even if they are elders learned in the three Vedas—with the same loathing shown toward those of inferior caste. Likewise:
"If one sees Kāpālikas, Pāśupatas, or Śaivas together with craftsmen, one should look at the sun; if one touches them, one should perform a ritual bath."

Because of this observation in another *smṛti*, the elders learned in the three Vedas consider those who have entered the Śaiva and other systems—such as the Śaivas—to be as defiled in their sight and touch as those of the lowest castes (*antyāvasāyin*). This alone is logical, for the scripture is thus. Therefore, one’s practice should be undertaken only after careful consideration of the reasoning found in the *Purāṇas* and other such texts. Nor should one suspect a single purpose with the external scriptures (*bāhyāgama*) merely because of some commonality in what is to be practiced according to them. Even where there is a semblance of similarity to what is practiced in external scriptures—as in:
"whether she be formless or possessed of form, fortunate or unfortunate..."—[the conclusion remains the same].
Whether she be virtuous or even unvirtuous, one should not feel loathing for her limbs.

And so forth. Even in that regard, one should understand according to the perspective stated in the *Devīpurāṇa* and other texts that these rules apply only to one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*). Therefore, it is established that while the *Śva-sūtra* and others are authoritative as being beyond reproach, they are not to be accepted in their entirety for performance; rather, they may be adopted in some part as auxiliary (*aṅga*) elements when they are to be practiced. Furthermore, it is proven that whatever is of human origin is not only non-performable, but is also to be rejected because it lacks authority (*apramāṇa*). For this very reason, the Teachers have said: "That scripture which is composed by men is not to be performed."
That should be known as invalid, for it originates from human intellect.
Enough with this digression.

It has been stated that right conduct (*sadācāra*) is the conduct of the refined (*śiṣṭācāra*). Regarding that, Baudhāyana describes the nature of the refined: "The refined are indeed those who are free from envy, devoid of egoism, possessing only as much grain as fits in a jar;
they are not covetous, and are exempt from hypocrisy, greed, delusion, and anger."
And by whomsoever the Veda, along with its supplements, has been attained through righteous means.
"The remaining [virtuous] ones are those who know how to infer that [dharma], for whom the Vedas and direct perception are the means [of knowledge].
The phrase "those whose grain is stored in jars" (*kumbhīdhānyāḥ*) is intended as an illustration of the contraction of one's livelihood.
One should augment the Veda with the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*.

According to this statement of Manu, the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and so forth are supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*) to the Veda; and because of their inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) and the other auxiliary sciences are also included. Those who know them are "knowers of Smṛti," for Smṛti is indeed the means of inference (*anumāna*)—the inferential mark (*liṅga*)—for that Veda. Those whose accepted view is that Śruti is the cause of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) are described as such. Both the words of Smṛti and established custom (*ācāra*) are considered "direct perception" (*pratyakṣa*) because they lead to direct perception [of the Veda]. Thinking that in regions such as Brahmāvarta, custom is predominantly rooted in the Veda, Manu said: "In whatever country a certain custom has come down through tradition..."
"That which pertains to the social classes (varṇas) along with those in between is called right conduct (sadācāra). Thus [it is said].

However, this is not because one should think that *sadācāra* (right conduct) exists only in Brahmāvarta. For if that were the case, even conduct in Brahmāvarta rooted in greed and other such motives would become authoritative regarding *dharma*, and conduct in other regions, even if rooted in the Veda, would not be so. Vasiṣṭha also says: "In Āryāvarta—east of the Ādarśa mountain, west of the Kālaka forest, north of the Pāriyātra mountains, and south of the Himavat and north of the Vindhya—all those *dharmas* and all those practices (*ācāras*) are to be accepted; but others are not, as they are contrary to the law (*pratiloma-dharmāṇaḥ*). Here too, the word "all" (*sarva*) is intended in the sense of "most. The phrase "but others are not, as they are contrary to the law" means that not all *dharmas* and practices of other regions are to be accepted. This is because, among them, practices are for the most part preceded by greed and other such motives, while only some are preceded by the Śruti; thus, their meaning should be understood accordingly. Otherwise, since conduct in other regions that is not possible [there] might be rooted in greed and the like, such conduct would be without foundation (*nirmūla*). — Manu.
But when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, Śruti alone is more authoritative;
however, when there is no conflict, the Smārta rite should always be performed according to the Vaikhanasa tradition.

Vasiṣṭha says: "Dharma is that which is ordained by Śruti and Smṛti; in their absence, the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭa) is the authority. Now, if Śruti and Smṛti have authority only regarding dharma, how then can the authority of those Śruti and Smṛti texts whose primary focus is the knowledge of the Self (ātmajñāna) be maintained as dharma? For the knowledge of the Self is not dharma, because it is not something to be performed. It is known through the ascertainment of the meaning of such statements as "That thou art" (tattvam asi), and it is not performed after ascertaining the meaning of the statement in the manner of a sacrifice or other ritual acts. Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "Of the acts of sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and Vedic study..."
But this is the supreme dharma: the vision of the Self through yoga. (8)

Among the duties such as sacrifice (*ijyā*) and the like, which consist of the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance), this is the supreme, primary duty: namely, the vision of the Self (*ātma-darśana*) through yoga, that is, through meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This word "Self" (*ātman*) refers here to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and not to the individual soul (*jīvātman*), because the latter is attained even without sacrifice and without meditative absorption. In the passage, "The Self, indeed, is to be seen," there is the injunction of origin (*utpatti-vidhi*). In the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," there is the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-vidhi*). For here, by the word "Supreme" (*para*), the Supreme Self is denoted; and its attainment consists in the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) abiding as one with That. In this context, the knowledge of Brahman mentioned in the term "knower of Brahman" is the instrument. As for the scriptural statement, "They desire to know [Brahman] by means of sacrifice, by giving, by austerity, and by fasting," the mention of "by sacrifice" and so forth is intended to indicate all the obligatory and occasional duties (*nitya-naimittika-dharma*) pertaining to the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*). Therefore, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa says: [21]
He is propitiated by one who performs the duties prescribed for his own caste;
therefore, wise men should exert effort to attain him.
O Great Sage, both knowledge and action have been declared as the causes for attaining that.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Just as food mixed with honey, or honey combined with food,
even so austerity and knowledge joined together are indeed a remedy."

Having considered this and other such points, he said: "Sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence... (Gītā 16.1). *Ācāra* (conduct) refers to that matter which, based on actions already prompted by worldly attachment (*rāga*), is enjoined by the scripture for the sake of a person's prosperity (*abhyudaya*). For example: "One should eat food facing the east, remaining silent," and so forth. *Dama* (self-restraint) is the subduing of the mind. *Ahiṃsā* (non-violence) is the cessation of violence prompted by attachment. *Dāna* (giving) is the relinquishing of one's own ownership and the transfer of ownership to another. *Svādhyāya* is Vedic study. The word *karman* (action) is intended to include all other enjoined duties besides those performed for the sake of desire (*kāmya*). (8)

The vision of the Self that arises through yoga is not accomplished merely by ascertaining the meaning of the scriptural texts; rather, it results from hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative concentration (*nididhyāsana*). Nevertheless, since even for a learned person qualified for ritual action, a decision regarding a doubt about *dharma* may depend upon an assembly due to some cause or other, he first describes that assembly:

"An assembly (*parṣad*) consists of four who know the Vedic law, or even those who possess the three Vedas (*traividya*); what they declare shall be the *dharma*. Or [there may be] a single person who is the best among those who know the inner self (*adhyātma*). (9)

The *veda* is well known. *Dharma* refers to the treatises on law (*dharmaśāstra*). Those who know their meaning—four persons who act as speakers for the determination of *dharma*—are called an assembly (*parṣad*). The three Vedas are the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas; by this term here, the three Brāhmaṇas who study them are indicated. Manu says: "This very assembly, consisting of at least three members, is declared [to be authoritative]. "One who knows the *Ṛgveda*, one who knows the *Yajurveda*, and one who knows the *Sāmaveda*:
this should be known as the minimum assembly for the resolution of doubts regarding *dharma*."

Alternatively, even if there is only one person who is the best among those who know the inner self (*adhyātma*), whatever matter he declares according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is indeed the Dharma. The term *adhyātma* refers to a treatise (*śāstra*) that proceeds with reference to the self (*ātman*). Among many such knowers, one who possesses superior knowledge is the "best knower of the inner self" (*adhyātmavit-tama*). The status of being an assembly (*pariṣat*) belongs primarily to Brāhmaṇas alone. As Manu says:

"If it should be asked how it ought to be regarding matters of Dharma not mentioned in the traditional texts (*anāmnāta*), whatever the learned Brāhmaṇas (*śiṣṭa*) declare, that shall be the Dharma, free from doubt."
[22] "Regarding those not mentioned" means those whose status is not determined solely from the recitation of the texts. Aṅgiras states:

"One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), a reciter of the Dharma, and three elders belonging to the [four] stages of life—this is an assembly of at least ten members."

Those best of the twice-born among all four castes who have mastered [the Vedas] in their proper order, together with the Upāṅgas, are traditionally known as "possessors of the fourfold knowledge" (cāturvidya).
That twice-born man who knows the authoritative standard for these three— the Dharma, the assembly, and the rite of penance— shall be a true investigator.
One who is well-established in grammar, Vedic meter, and ritual procedure,
and who is skilled in the science of astronomy, is called a Nirukta and an expert in the auxiliary sciences (aṅgavid).
One who has completed the ceremonial bath after studying the Vedas and their branches, who is true to his word, has conquered his senses,
and is learned in many treatises on dharma, is called a reciter of dharma.
After the stage of the student life (brahmacarya), the three elder stages of life (āśrama) shall declare his duty; these have been proclaimed by me.
But Manu says: "One learned in the three Vedas, a logician, a dialectician, an etymologist, a reciter of the Dharma,
and the first three orders of life— this assembly, consisting of at least ten such members, [is authoritative]."

Thus he says: one who knows the reason (*hetuka*) is one who knows inference (*anumānajña*). One who possesses *tarka* is a *tarkī*. When an attribution of validity has been made to a point of doubt, the conviction that "there must be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here" because a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) is observed is *tarka*. And it has been stated by that same [author] that such [tarka] should be accepted when it does not contradict the Veda: "He who investigates the instruction on Dharma given by the seers (*ārṣa*) with *tarka* that does not contradict the Veda and the scriptures, he—and no other—knows Dharma."

The *ārṣa* consists of the *smṛtis*, *purāṇas*, and so forth; the *upadeśa* is the Veda. By means of reasoning (*tarka*) that contradicts those [scriptures]—that is, by reasoning devoid of the Veda and other such sources, and characterized as previously described—the process of *anusaṃdhāna* is the establishment [of the truth]. "The elders" refers to householders and others who possess the status of being aged. Regarding the phrase "at least ten," this means no fewer than ten. As Aṅgiras states: "Whether four or even three Brahmins who know the Vedas and maintain the sacred fires, when assembled together, are designated as a *parṣad* (an assembly)."
[23] Those who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet are masters of the Vedas alone—
these five, being knowers of the Vedic scriptures, are declared to constitute what is known as an "assembly" (parṣad).
But those Brahmins who know the Dharma, who are discerning regarding what ought and ought not to be done,
and who are formulators of penances— these seven are proclaimed [as authorities].
One should constitute the assembly with twenty-one members who have mastered the Vedas and the principles of logic, and who are likewise skilled in the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (vedāṅgas).
Even a single person among ascetics who possess true austerity, whose minds are endowed with knowledge and realization, and who have performed the head-observance, may constitute an assembly.
But those three who were previously mentioned by me as abiding on the path of the wandering mendicant (yāyāvara) should be known as an assembly that removes all sins.

"But this [penance] is for minor offenses; for middling ones, it is middling; and for those to be purified from mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*), it is indeed performed hundreds of times. This refers to the *sirovrata*, well-known from the scriptures on asceticism. The meaning is that even a single person may perform the rite if he is capable of acting as the assembly (*pariṣad*). A *yāyāvara* is a specific type of householder. "Those to be purified from mortal sins" (*mahāpātaki-śodhya*) refers to those who are both great sinners and require purification. (9)
He speaks of the castes (*varṇa*) and the twice-born (*dvija*) who are entitled to expound the Dharma:
"The castes are Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra; however, the first three are twice-born.

Each of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra receives the designation of a caste (*varṇa*). But the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya should each be known by the designation of twice-born (*dvija*).
For them, the rites beginning with conception and ending with the cremation ground are indeed performed with mantras.

For those twice-born men, the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with the funeral ceremonies (*pretakarma*) must be performed with mantras. Regarding the Śūdra, however, Yama states that the sequence of sacraments continues only as far as what has been prescribed, ending with the *upanayana*:
"A Śūdra also should be consecrated in this same manner, though without mantras;
Prajāpati did not endow him with any Vedic verse."

Having created him, he did not initiate him; therefore, the meaning is that he is not to be initiated. As the Śruti says: "He created the Brāhmaṇa by means of the Gāyatrī, the Rājanya by means of the Triṣṭubh, the Vaiśya by means of the Jagatī, but the Śūdra by no metre at all. He is known to be one who is not to be consecrated. "Not to be consecrated" means not to be initiated. The *Brahma-purāṇa* states: "Let even a Śūdra always receive the sacrament of marriage alone. By the word "alone," there is an exclusion of mantras or of the previous sacraments. In that case, there is an option, because those [mantras] are also prescribed. Jātūkarṇya says:
The two duties of the twice-born, in brief, are considered to be *iṣṭā* (sacrificial rites) and *pūrta* (charitable works). A *śūdra* may be entitled to the Vedic *pūrta-dharma*.
The Mahābhārata:
The ritual of the single fire and the oblation offered in the three fires,
as well as the gift given within the sacrificial altar— this is designated as *iṣṭa*.
The construction of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, as well as temples for the deities, the gift of food, and groves— this is designated as *pūrta*.
The mention of "the giving and receiving of food" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for [gifts] that are not auxiliary parts of a sacrifice (*ayajñāṅga*). Thus says Jātūkarṇya:
"That gift which is given during an eclipse of a planet, at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkramaṇa*), on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and so forth, is designated as *pūrta*. (10)

Now, with two and a half verses, he prescribes the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception), whose specific forms are established in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, in connection with their particular times:

*Garbhādhāna* [should be performed] during the fertile period (*ṛtu*); *puṃsavana* before the movement [of the fetus]; *sīmantonnayana* in the sixth or eighth month; and these [other rites], including *jātakarman*, in the [first] month [after birth]. (11)

On the eleventh day the naming ceremony is performed; in the fourth month the first outing; in the sixth month the first feeding of solid food; and the tonsure ceremony should be carried out according to family custom.
In this way, the sin arising from the seed and the womb is pacified.

The *garbhādhāna* (conception rite) is so called because by this ritual the embryo (*garbha*) is deposited; that it should be performed during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) is established from other sources. Likewise, prior to the extraction of the embryo, there is the rite for a male child called *puṃsavana*. In the sixth or eighth month of pregnancy, the *sīmanta* (parting of the hair), also known as *sīmantonnayana*, takes place. When these have occurred, the *jātakarma* (birth rite) is performed. On the eleventh day, the naming (*nāmadheya*) occurs—this is the understood remainder. The count of days beginning with the eleventh is calculated from birth, since that is the subject under discussion. In the fourth month, the *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing) occurs, which is the going outside to see the sun and the moon. In the sixth month, the *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food) takes place. Regarding the *cūḍā* (tonsure): in whichever year and according to whatever number of locks of hair are prescribed for performance in one's family, it must be done without transgressing that; "one should have the hair-arrangements made according to family custom" is well-known from the *Gṛhya-sūtras*. When these sacraments (*saṃskāras*) have been thus performed, the sin (*enaḥ*), the impurity arising from the seed and the womb, is pacified. "Seed" (*bīja*) refers to the semen and blood; "womb" (*garbha*) refers to the body situated within the belly, by which the dwelling in the womb is indicated. Here, "sin" (*enaḥ*) means impurity (*aprāyatyam*), produced from the mother’s consumption of food and so forth. And this is intended for all four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), not restricted to the twice-born (*dvijāti*) alone; for if that were the case, it would have had to be stated after prescribing the initiation (*upanayana*). Thus says Devala:
Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by many constituent parts,
so too does the status of a Brahmin arise through purificatory rites performed according to the prescribed rules.
For this very reason, Manu, having prescribed initiation with reference to the twice-born,
says: "By means of the oblations for the embryo, the birth-rite, the tonsure, and the tying of the girdle of muñja grass,
the sin pertaining to the seed and the sin pertaining to the womb are wiped away from the twice-born."

Thus, it is established that these sacraments (*saṃskāras*), when performed for the pacification of sin, are to be carried out after the *puṃsavana* by one who stands in the place of the father—such as a paternal uncle—in the absence of the father. In this context, specific times such as the *ṛtu* (the period following menstruation) and so forth are merely restated (*anūdyante*) as they are in the case of the *garbhādhāna* and other rites; they do not exclude other times prescribed by scripture, but rather serve to indicate them. In this regard, other scriptural authorities are seen to specify particular details. Among them, Hārīta states: "The wives of the twice-born are consecrated once and for all by the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony."
Whatever womb they are born from, all of that shall become consecrated.

Regarding the *Sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), the *Baijavāpa-gṛhya-sūtra* states: "During the waxing fortnight, when the moon is conjoined with a masculine lunar mansion. Devala says: "A woman who has been consecrated once is considered consecrated for all her subsequent pregnancies."

For this very reason, Pāraskara states: "Now, the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) is performed like the *puṃsavana* during the first pregnancy. Thus, he prescribes the *sīmantonnayana* for the first pregnancy; however, the *puṃsavana* should be repeated with each subsequent pregnancy. Next, regarding the *puṃsavana* and *anavalobhana*, the *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-sūtra* says: "The *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, and *anavalobhana* are taught in the *Upaniṣad*. If one has not studied that section, then in the third pregnancy, during the month of the third month, under the asterism of Tiṣya (*Puṣya*), she who has fasted should have two beans, two grains, and a barley grain placed into a handful of curds from a cow whose calf is of the same color as herself. He should cause her to eat them with a handful of curds. Having asked, 'What are you drinking? What are you drinking? she should reply three times, 'It is the *puṃsavana*. In this manner, she should consume three handfuls. Then, in the shadow of a circular shed, he administers an unfading herb into her right nostril. Having offered oblations of the *sthālīpāka* belonging to Hetuka and Prajāpati with the two mantras beginning with *prajāvat* and *jīvaputra*, he should touch her heart region with the mantra: 'What is placed within your heart, O fair-browed one, within Prajāpati— I consider myself to know it within; may I not bring the sin of a grandson upon my son. 'The mantra beginning with *apaśyaṃ tvā manasā dīdhyānaḥ* is the *prajāvat* mantra. The mantras beginning with *agnir aitu prathamaḥ* are the *jīvaputra* mantras. Sāṅkhyāyana states: 'In the third month, the *sīmantonnayana* is performed under Tiṣya or Śravaṇa. Regarding the *jātakarman* (birth-rite), there is a specific detail mentioned in the *Brahma-purāṇa*.
Since both the gods and the ancestors come on the day a son is born to the twice-born, that day is always auspicious and meritorious, and worthy of honor.
Therein one should give gold, land, a cow, a horse, a chariot,
an umbrella, a goat, a garland, sesame seeds, a house, and much wealth.
"And one should also give cooked food to Brāhmaṇas on the occasion of a birth-śrāddha.

This [rite] is neither before the cutting of the umbilical cord nor after it. Thus says Hārīta: "When a son is born, because of the joy of the ancestors, that day is meritorious; therefore, having invited Brāhmaṇas, one should offer *svadhā* to the ancestors with vessels full of sesame seeds and containing gold. And for Prajāpati [the offering is made] before the cutting of the umbilical cord; they perform these rites for the sake of sanctity. Once the cord is cut, there is impurity. [This is also supported] by the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"On an auspicious day, during the three-fold [periods] of the *mṛdu*, *dhruva*, *cara*, and *kṣipra* [nakṣatras], and on a favorable weekday..."
When Jupiter or Venus is in a quadrant, both one's occupation and one's name are determined.
The *bhāni* are the lunar mansions. Regarding the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*,
O King, some desire the naming ceremony on the tenth day,
others on the twelfth day, and still others when the month has been completed.
"Others, however, say it should be on the eighteenth day,
at an auspicious lunar date, at a favorable moment (muhūrta), and under a constellation endowed with excellent qualities."

The *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa* states: "The naming ceremony (*nāmadhyakaraṇa*) is performed when ten nights, a hundred nights, or a year have passed since birth; however, the rite of naming is ordained once the period of impurity (*aśauca*) has elapsed. This is not a restrictive rule, because it contradicts such statements as "the naming is on the tenth day. Therefore, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, this arrangement is relative to one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. Thus, passages such as "one should perform it on the eleventh or twelfth day" refer to the intended meaning itself and are not merely indicative of the end of the period of impurity. Consequently, the rite should be performed even during impurity. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Having raised her on the tenth day—meaning on the tenth lunar day or the tenth day from birth—one should perform the naming on that very day after offering an oblation into the fire, honoring the ancestors (based on the Vedic text: 'there the ancestors are present'), and feeding the Brahmins. Or, another elder of the family should give a name consisting of two or four syllables for males, beginning and ending with a sonant (*ghoṣavat*), containing a semi-vowel (*antaḥstha*), and ending in *ī* for females. When the name is thus given, the family becomes pure. Having first raised the woman who has recently given birth from her bed, "on the tenth day" means on the tenth lunar date or the tenth day. "Increasing the rice-balls" (*piṇḍavardhana*) refers to worship; its nature is as follows: the Brahmin first offers an oblation, honors the ancestors, and worships them with an *abhyudaya-śrāddha*. Regarding the phonemes: the third letters of the *ka*-group and so forth, along with *ya*, *ra*, *la*, *va*, and *ha*, are sonants (*ghoṣavat*). Among these, the four semi-vowels (*antaḥstha*) beginning with *ya* should be placed in the middle of the name. The remaining sonants should be at the beginning of the name. Baijavāpa says: "The father gives the name—one syllable, two syllables, three syllables, four syllables, or unlimited syllables. It should be a primary derivative (*kṛta*), not a secondary derivative (*taddhita*). For a female, it should end in *ī*. Yama [says the same].
One should cause the name of a Brāhmaṇa to end in Śarman or Deva, that of a Kṣatriya in Varman or Trātṛ,
that of a Vaiśya in Bhūti or Datta, and that of a Śūdra in Dāsa.

These are the suffixes applied to names that are compounds. Manu states the rule regarding the first member of the compound: "The name of a Brāhmaṇa should be auspicious; that of a Kṣatriya should be endowed with power;
that of a Vaiśya should be connected with wealth; but that of a Śūdra should be contemptible."
Likewise: for women, [speech] that is easy to pronounce, not harsh, clear in meaning, captivating, auspicious, ending in long vowels, and containing words of benediction.
Regarding the departure [from the womb], there is a specific rule stated by Yama:
"Then, in the third month, the seeing of the sun must be performed. Thus says Vṛddha-Śātātapa.
Before the performance of the tonsure ceremony he is a *bāla* (child); before the first feeding of solid food he is a *śiśu* (infant);
but he should be known as a *kumāra* (youth) until the tying of the girdle of muñja grass.
Sprinkling with water is prescribed for an infant, while sipping water (ācamana) is traditionally taught for a young child;
however, upon contact with a woman in her menses or similar impurities, the boys must bathe.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, a child who eats the remnants of his mother and father shall be happy. Thus says Dakṣa.
A child from the moment of birth until eight years have passed should be known as equal to a fetus, manifested merely by its outward appearance.
Regarding what may or may not be eaten, what may or may not be drunk, what may or may not be spoken, and likewise regarding falsehood:
at this time, there shall be no fault so long as he has not been initiated.
