This approval of eating what is not to be eaten and drinking what is not to be drunk refers only to the case of the leavings of one's mother and father; it does not refer to food or drink that causes loss of caste (*jāti-bhraṃśakara*) and so forth, for that would entail the consequence of being ineligible for the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) and other rites. Indeed, it is frequently seen in the Smṛtis that initiation and other such rites are based on an unimpaired caste and so forth, as in: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn. [From] the Purāṇa: "In the fourth month, the infant’s viewing of the moon should be performed."
On the twelfth day, O Indra among kings, the ceremony of the child's formal exit from the house was performed.
O Lord, it should be performed in the fourth month; such is the opinion of others.
Yama states the specific rule regarding the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana):
"Then, the annaprāśana should be performed according to the prescribed rite in the sixth month,
or it should be performed in the eighth month, or whenever an auspicious occasion is desired by the family."

Śaṅkha says: "The first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) takes place in the first year, or in the half-year, according to some. Laugākṣi says: "The first feeding of solid food takes place in the sixth month, or when the teeth have appeared. Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"In front of the deity, while the child is seated on the lap of the nurse and has been adorned, food should be given to him in a golden vessel."
One should have the child, facing eastward, consume honey, clarified butter, and gold;
once he has consumed them, the nurse should release the boy from her lap.
Then, having arranged all the artisan's tools, as well as the treatises and weapons, in front of the deity, one should examine their characteristics.
Whatever vessel the child first touches, he shall then take that for himself;
by that alone shall the livelihood of that child be sustained.
[29] On the day of one's own birth, everyone, having bathed with auspicious waters,
should especially worship the guru, the gods, the sacred fire, and the brahmins.
The ancestors, as well as the god Prajāpati, [dwell] under one's own constellation;
therefore, a great festival should be performed with diligence every year.
The worship of the ancestors is the *śrāddha*. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"When the moon is situated in one's birth asterism (*janmanakṣatra*), one who has diligently performed a head-bath must perform the worship of Soma, as well as that of the asterism and of oneself."
One should diligently perform the *śrāddha* ceremony, the satiation of the fire and the Brahmins,
the worship of the gods, and especially that of Keśava;
and the person should remain adorned with all ornaments and dressed in washed garments.
And the teeth, hair, and nails should be kept clean and well-trimmed.
Regarding the caulakaraṇa (the tonsure ceremony), Yama states a specific rule:
"Likewise, when a year has been completed, the cūḍākarma is prescribed;
or it should be performed in the second or third [year], according to the injunction of the Śruti."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The *cūḍākarma* (tonsure ceremony) takes place in the third year, or in the fifth. Laugākṣi says: "When the greater part of the third year has passed, one should have the *cūḍās* performed. For the Vasiṣṭhas, the worship [of the hair] is on the right side; for the Atris and Kaśyapas, it is on both sides. The Bhṛgus are shaven; the Aṅgirases have five tufts (*pañcacūḍā*); the Vājas have a single tuft for the sake of auspiciousness. Others have a crest-lock (*śikhin*), or follow the custom of their own family. This should be done during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day or on a festival (*parvan*). Here, *kapūjā* means *cūḍā*. *Vāji* refers to a row of hair. Vyāsa says:
"It should not be performed even under the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) in which the man was born."
O Bhārata, one should not perform [these rites] during the months of Bhādrapada and Āśvina, nor during the months sacred to Agni.
One should avoid all cruel [planets] as well as the corrupt stars;
one should perform all those [rites] which have been declared in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa).
One should avoid the days of Saturn, the Sun, and the Moon, as well as the night; one should also avoid the first lunar day (pratipad), the "empty" days (riktās), and the Viṣṭi yoga.
One should perform [the rites] under Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, Citrā, Tiṣya, Punarvasu,
Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, Jyeṣṭhā, Mṛgaśiras, and Hasta.
One should perform the morning shaving during auspicious *aṃśakas*, in the *kendra* houses, and under favorable *karaṇas*; this increases longevity and strength.
The three stars beginning with Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, the three stars beginning with Śravaṇā, the asterisms of Pūṣan, Aśvinī, Indra (Jyeṣṭhā), Bṛhaspati (Puṣya),
and Punarvasu are beneficial for the rite of shaving, whether performed at sunrise or during the day.
And if they are joined with the lord of the stars (the Moon) and the auspicious lunar mansions, [it is favorable]. 11–12.
These rites for women are performed silently, but their marriage ceremony is accompanied by mantras.

For these rites, beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*), are for women without mantras; however, the marriage ceremony is with mantras. Since the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* are referred to here, and since their constituent parts (*aṅga*) are also taught therein, it should be understood that the silence (*tūṣṇīmbhāva*) applies to the rites along with their ancillaries. Therefore, Manu says:
"This entire cycle of rites for women must be performed without mantras, for the sake of purifying the body, at the proper time and in the proper order."

The *āvṛt* is the ritual action; it is complete with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*). By the statement "in due order," he shows that the non-transgression of the sequence must be observed regarding the consecrations (*saṃskāras*). If there is a transgression of that, one should cause the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) to be performed. Regarding the lapse of time, Kātyāyana says:
"In the case of a reversal of the deities during the *homa* offerings, what should be done?
Having offered the entire expiation, one should offer again in the proper sequence."

If the ritual preparations should be interrupted or if one's own time should somehow be lost, O King, that very rite must be performed after making an oblation; otherwise, it would cause one to fall into the lower realms.

Laukāxi stated that the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) consists of [the oblations] with the seven [verses] beginning with *manojyotiḥ*. Gobhila, in the section on the tonsure ceremony (*caula*), says: "For women, however, the procedure is the same as this, but the oblation is performed silently, without a mantra. Mārkaṇḍeya states:
"Now, when the fifth year has arrived and Janārdana is not yet [fully] protected, one should avoid the sixth lunar day (*ṣaṣṭhī*), the first (*pratipad*), and likewise the eighth (*aṣṭamī*)."
On the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight when it is empty (the new moon), as well as on Sundays and Tuesdays—
having thus determined the auspicious time— one should cause the commencement of learning to take place.
[31] Having worshipped Hari, the goddess Lakṣmī, and Sarasvatī,
as well as the authors of the sūtras of one's own science, and especially one's own science;
One should offer clarified butter into the fire using the names of these very deities;
furthermore, the worship of the best of the twice-born should be performed with sacrificial gifts.
Seated facing east, the teacher should first cause the pupil— who faces the western direction and has been well-honored with the blessings of the twice-born— to recite.
From that time forward, one should avoid those occasions on which study is prohibited:
both the eighth days of the lunar fortnight, as well as the two days at the end of each fortnight.
In cases of impurity, during a procession of the senses (Indrayātrā), during an earthquake, at the sight of Rāhu,
during the Vyatīpāta yoga, and likewise upon the fall of a meteor, one must observe a fast for a full day and night.
Another Smṛti states:
One should teach the boy the Mātṛkā-nyāsa and arithmetic. || 13 ||

The initiation ceremony (upanayana) for a Brāhmaṇa takes place in the eighth year from conception or in the eighth year [after birth]; for Kṣatriyas, in the eleventh year plus one; for Vaiśyas, in the twelfth; or according to family custom. 14.

The act of leading toward (*upanayana*) is the activity of the initiator directed toward the one to be led; and this is indeed distinct from the mere act of leading (*upanayana*). For this very reason, the wise one says:
"In the eighth year from conception, in the spring, a Brāhmaṇa should cause himself to be led [toward the teacher]."

Relying on this very procedure, Śaunaka prescribes the mantra: "Placing the knee [on the ground] and clasping [the teacher's feet], say: 'Recite, sir! Recite the Sāvitrī, sir! The term *garbhāṣṭama* means the eighth from conception; that is, the year associated with the embryo (*garbha*) is considered the [first] year, and it is the eighth in relation to that. The ablative case (*pañcamī*) is used here by ellipsis (*lyablope*), meaning "after [the completion of] the eighth. This same time for the initiation (*upanayana*) is stated by Śaunaka: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year, or in the eighth year from conception; a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth. Now follow the optional times for initiation. Regarding this, Manu says:
For a Brahmin desiring the glory of sacred knowledge, initiation should take place in the fifth year;
for a Kshatriya seeking power, in the sixth; and for a Vaishya seeking worldly prosperity, in the eighth.

*Īhā* means effort or exertion. [32] Gautama states: "The initiation (*upanayana*) takes place in the eighth, fifth, or ninth year. For optional initiations based on the number of years from conception, the eighth year is the obligatory time, while the ninth and fifth years are optional. Āpastamba states: "In the seventh year, one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); in the eighth, one desiring long life; in the ninth, one desiring splendor (*tejas*); in the tenth, one desiring food and so forth; in the eleventh, one desiring sensory power (*indriya*); in the twelfth, one desiring cattle. Here, the phrase "one should initiate" (*upanayīta*) is to be supplied from the *Purāṇa*: "When the moon has set, when Venus has gone down, and when the sun is without its rays..."
The initiation ceremony (upanayana) should not be performed during a period of suspended Vedic study (anadhyāya) or when there is a seizing of the throat (galagraha).
The Sun situated in the first portion of a zodiac sign is without degrees (niraṃśa). The fourth, seventh, ninth, and thirteenth lunar days are *galagrahas*.
In the three [nakṣatras] beginning with Hasta, as well as Puṣya, Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, and Aśvinī, one should worship Viṣṇu.
On an auspicious lunar day endowed with the strength of the Moon, the rite of initiation (*upanāyana*) for the twice-born should be performed.

Gobhila states: "On the day that the *māṇavaka* is to fast, they feed him early in the morning on that very day; they have him groomed; they cause him to bathe and adorn him; and they clothe him in a new, unwashed garment. "Early in the morning" (*prage*) means at dawn. Śaṅkha says: "The food for the three [stages] on the day of initiation consists respectively of milk, barley-gruel, and curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*); ten Brahmins should be fed at each of the sacraments beginning with the *garbhādhāna*. As Kātyāyana says:
"At all [sacraments] beginning with the *garbhādhāna*, one should feed ten Brahmins. (14)
Having initiated the pupil with the Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛti) at the beginning, the teacher should teach him the Veda and instruct him in the rules of purification and conduct. 15.

Having brought the student near by means of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana-karman*) according to the prescribed rule, the teacher (*ācārya*) should teach him the Veda preceded by the *vyāhṛtis* and cause him to grasp the rules of purification and conduct (*śaucācāra*). By the mention of the "teacher," it is understood that the father himself should perform the initiation and other rites; however, in the absence of his fitness, there may be another teacher. Furthermore, through initiation, a specific relationship consisting of a particular proximity is established between the student and the teacher, rather than mere physical proximity of place. Āpastamba states the qualities of the initiator: "He indeed enters from darkness into darkness who initiates one who is ignorant, and he too who is ignorant. Therefore, one should seek an instructor who is endowed with noble lineage and learning, and who is composed. The meaning is that even he who initiates an ignorant person enters into darkness. Initiation has the *gāyatrī* and other meters as its primary elements. As Kātyāyana says: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa with the *gāyatrī*, a Kṣatriya with the *triṣṭubh*, and a Vaiśya with the *jagatī*; or for all of them, the *gāyatrī*. The word "should recite" (*anubrūyāt*) is to be supplied. Laugākṣi says: "For a Brāhmaṇa: *tat savitur vareṇyam*; for a Kṣatriya: *tāṃ savituḥ*; for a Vaiśya: *viśvā rūpāṇi*. Having uttered *oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, he recites the *sāvitrī* three times—verse by quarter, then by half-verse, and finally the whole verse at the end. Manu states the number of *mahāvyāhṛtis*.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *Sāvitrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.

The "mouth" (mukha) refers to the beginning. Consequently, it is not the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛtis*) alone that are to be employed at the commencement of teaching; rather, it is the *praṇava* and the *gāyatrī*. And this applies to the very first commencement of instruction, not to every single day, because of the designation "the mouth. Furthermore, Manu has stated the nature of the triad consisting of the *praṇava* and the Great Utterances: "Prajāpati drew forth the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m* from the three Vedas, as well as [the words] *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*."
He also speaks specifically regarding the Gāyatrī:
[34] "From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the first quarter of this Sāvitrī verse beginning with 'tat'."
Likewise:
When about to be instructed, the teacher, always free from sloth, should say, "Recite, sir! and he should conclude with, "May there be a pause."
But when about to be taught, having sipped water according to the scriptures and being unwearied,
he should be instructed with his hands joined in the *brahmāñjali*, wearing light clothing, and with his senses subdued.
He himself stated the *brahmāñjali*:
"Having joined the two hands together, one should study; for that is remembered as the *brahmāñjali*. (15)
First, he describes the conduct preceding purification:
"During the day and at the twilights, with the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) worn over the ear and facing north, one should void urine and feces; however, if it is at night, one should face south. (16)

During the day and at the two twilights, one should void urine and feces facing north; at night, facing south. Having placed the sacred thread over the left (or right) ear, one should discharge urine and feces. Manu says:
"Having concealed oneself with wood, a leaf, a clod of earth, or grass, one should perform the act, restraining speech, being pure, with the body covered and the head veiled."

The meaning is that one should void excrement after covering the ground with wood and other materials. "With limbs covered" means having the body wrapped; "veiled" means having the head covered. Yama says: "One should perform the discharge of feces and urine after covering the head and having spread the earth with sacrificially unfit and dry grass."
Facing west in the forenoon, facing east in the afternoon,
facing north at midday, and facing south during the night.
Manu says: In shade or in darkness, by night or by day, a twice-born man may perform [the purification] facing any direction that is comfortable to him, as well as when there is danger to life.
Aṅgiras:
Having risen during the last watch of the night, having sipped water,
and having covered the ground with grass and veiled his head with a cloth.
Restraining his speech with effort and avoiding spitting or exhaling, he should void urine and feces in a clean place with a concentrated mind. (16)

[35] He states the rule for purification: Having risen with his penis held [in hand], he should perform purification without sloth, using earth and drawn-up water, so as to remove both odor and residue. (17)

Just as no contact with impurity occurs, so one should rise, holding the penis with the left hand, sit down in another place, and—being untiring—perform purification that removes the odor of filth and eliminates both smell and stain using water drawn from a *kamaṇḍalu* or similar vessel and with earth. Bhāradvāja says:
"Then, having removed the feces and urine with wood, clods of earth, grass, or the like, one should perform purification according to the rule, firmly supporting the penis."
The penis is the sign [of the organ]. This is from the Purāṇa.
Devala says that cleansing with the left hand using non-sacrificial materials such as vīraṇa grass and the like [is prescribed].
One should not release the penis oneself during urination or defecation until purification is complete—
so says Vivasvat.
Having left a space of one cubit in water, one should perform purification without drawing out the water.
But afterwards one should purify the bathing place; otherwise, one will not become pure.
Yama says: A Brahmin should not take earth from a riverbank that contains sand;
likewise, he should not take earth from the outside edge of a step-well or a pond.
One should take [the water] from within the water, beyond the wrist.
From the Purāṇa:
One should not take earth from an anthill, from that dug up by mice, from within water, nor from what remains after cleansing, nor from a house, nor that which originates from a smear.
[And that which is inhabited by living creatures, or dug up by a plow, not from mud.
[The prohibition against earth containing internal water or clay refers to sources other than ponds, wells, and the like. Bhāradvāja says:
Not from saline soil, nor from a cremation ground, nor earth from a mouse-hole.
One should never take [fire] from a path, nor from water, nor ever from a wall.
Devala says:
One who knows the Dharma should not employ the right hand for cleansing below the navel;
likewise, one should not cleanse above the navel with the left hand.
Śātātapa says:
At the waning of the moon, mouthfuls of food the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit are prescribed;
likewise for all sacrificial oblations and for the clay used for purification.
[36] One application on the penis, three on the left hand, and two on each of the two hands is declared to be the purification for urination; however, it shall be double in the case of semen.
Manu says:
One application of earth should be made to the penis, three to the anus, ten to the left hand,
and seven to both hands by one desiring purification.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Dakṣa says:
The first clay is prescribed to be the measure of half a handful;
the second and the third are proclaimed to be half of that [measure] each.
Even so, if the disappearance of the odor and the stain does not occur, then more earth should be taken, either by measure or by number. Regarding this, Aṅgiras says:
"The first [application] should be known as one handful (prasṛti); the second, however, half of that;
the third application of earth should be known as filling the palm to three parts."
Vasiṣṭha says: Five applications of clay at the anus, ten on each of the two hands, and seven on both together.
Śaṅkha says: Seven applications of clay are prescribed for the urethra, two for the penis;
twenty are to be known for one hand, and fourteen for both hands.

The anus is for urination; this refers to the case of a *brahmacārin*. Hārīta says: "One should wash the left hand ten times, the back six times, both hands seven times, and the feet three times. Vṛddhapārāśara says:
"He who, while seated, is unable to perform the purification after voiding feces or urine, shall always perform half of his prescribed purification."
[Even when the odor and the stain have been removed, the number must be completed as half-measures. As Dakṣa says:
"One who desires purity through cleansing must not perform it with deficiency or excess;
one becomes liable for penance if a prescribed rite is transgressed."
If, after purification has been performed according to the prescribed rule, a foul odor does not depart,
Manu says regarding that case:
"As long as the odor caused by contact with impurity and the stain produced by it do not go away..."
In all purifications of objects, earth and water should be employed accordingly.
But regarding the absence of mental satisfaction, Devala says:
"As long as one does not consider oneself pure, purification is prescribed.
This is from the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
However, it is prescribed that at the beginning and end of purifications, one should wash with water for the sake of removing all residual smears and for the purification of one's inner disposition.
From the Ādipurāṇa:
"The wise have declared that for women and Śūdras, purification is half [of what is prescribed];
for the night, it is half of the daytime purification; and on the road, one quarter is ordained."
One who is distressed should act according to his ability; one who is capable should act as prescribed.
Seated with his knees together in a clean place, facing north or east,
a twice-born man should always perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet) using the Brāhma-tīrtha.

In a clean place, having sat down facing either the east or the north with his hands between his knees, a twice-born man should always sip water using the *brāhma* *tīrtha* (the part of the hand between the thumb and forefinger). Gautama states: "Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), having washed his hands up to the wrists, being silent, and touching his heart, he should sip water three or four times. He should also sprinkle his feet and touch the apertures of the body; he should apply [water] to the apertures of the head and to the crown of the head. This is stated in another *Smṛti* following the word "he should sip" (*ācāmet*).
Placing his hands within his elbows, facing either east or north,
and without letting his heels touch the water, he should perform the rite with water that is in its natural state.
[Vṛddhapārāśara says:
Having performed purification at the elbows and knees, and having washed his feet and hands with earth and water,
the twice-born man, sitting with his topknot tied, should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having placed the sacred thread over the left shoulder, one should remain restrained in speech, mind, and body.
Devala says: First, standing facing the east, one should slowly wash the feet;
or facing north for rites pertaining to the gods, and facing south for those pertaining to the ancestors.
Having tied his topknot and put on two clean, bright garments,
he should remain silent and composed, neither becoming angry nor looking about.
Neither while walking nor lying down, neither while stumbling nor touching [anything],
neither while laughing nor even while speaking, nor while looking at oneself.
[38] Without touching the hair, the waist-knot, the lower body, or even the ground;
if he touches these again, he should wash his hand.
Having thus washed his two feet separately with water up to the knees,
and his hands up to the wrists, he should afterwards sit down restrained.
Then, one should drink water three times from the first vessel in the south,
evenly, silently, without spilling, with the knees not raised above the water level, and without bubbles.

Neither moving nor shaking [the hand], the base of the wrist is the root of the *brahmatīrtha*. The first sacred site (*tīrtha*) is the *brāhmatīrtha*; the meaning is "from the right side of the right hand. Bhāradvāja states: "Having taken water with his hand whose fingers are joined, the twice-born should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) with the remainder [of the water] after releasing the thumb and the little finger."
Having taken up water only enough to submerge a masha bean, one should drink it three times,
having first extended the hand in the shape of a cow's ear.
Hārīta says:
If that lowest of men, while standing on dry ground, sips water while still wearing wet clothes,
the *preta*s indeed drink the water dripping from his body.
One should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) daily, facing either east or north,
whether standing in water, standing on dry land, or situated in both.
One who stands in water is authorized for water-related tasks, and one who stands on land for land-based activities;
however, one who stands in both places is authorized for the duties of both.
Gobhila says:
Having sipped water while standing in the water with [the knees] above it, one does not incur fault; likewise, a wise person should neither sip water nor remain standing with [the knees] below them.

The *Likhita* states: "One should sip water (*ācāmet*) that has been drawn up, examined, free from salt, not boiled, free from bubbles, and not poured by a Śūdra, an impure person, or with only one hand. The word "with water" (*adbhiḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. Āpastamba says: "Having sipped water from water that has reached the ground, one becomes pure. Or, one may cause someone who is pure to sip water for him. One should not sip water from the streams of rain, nor from water in a fissure in the earth. In the continuation of the rule "one should sip water," Vasiṣṭha states: "[Water] even from a fissure [is acceptable] if it is sufficient for the satiation of a cow; provided it is not corrupted by smell or taste, and does not come from an impure source. A *pradara* is a hole or fissure in the ground. Pracetas says:
One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) three or four times with water that is neither hot nor cold, purified by the cloth and the eye, which reaches the heart, and is free of froth. 1.18.
In this context, he states the characteristics of the *brahmatīrtha* and other sacred sites (*tīrtha*) as well:
"The base of the little finger, the base of the ring finger, the base of the thumb, and the tip of the hand are, in order, the *prājāpatya*, *pitrya*, *brahma*, and *daiva* sacred sites. (1.19)

One should know that the base of the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*) is the *prajāpati-tīrtha*, the base of the forefinger (*pradeśinī*) is the *pitṛ-tīrtha*, the base of the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) is the *brahma-tīrtha*, and the tip of the hand is the *deva-tīrtha*. The little finger is the shortest finger; the *deśinī* is the index finger; and the thumb is well known. Hārīta states: "One should sip water with the *brahma-tīrtha*. One should perform the pouring of oblations (*āvapana*), the fire sacrifice (*homa*), and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with the *prājāpatya-tīrtha*. Cleansing (*mārjana*), sipping water (*ācamana*), the offering of bali, and eating should be done with the *daiva-tīrtha*. Rites for the ancestors (*pitṛ-artha*) should be performed with the *pitrya-tīrtha*, and the acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) with the *āgneya-tīrtha*. The *āgneya-tīrtha* is in the middle of the palm. *Āvapana* means the pouring out [of grain]. This refers to the cleansing of the hair, not its sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), according to the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*.
A wise man should perform the offering of rice-balls and water for the Nāndīmukhas through the Prājāpatya tīrtha, as well as whatever else pertains to Prajāpati.
In the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa: "O Indra among kings, a wise man should always perform the ritual touching of the water-pot and the consumption of curd at the Soma-tīrtha."
One should likewise perform the oblation of parched grain and the milking of the cow according to the Prājāpatya rite.
Yogayājñavalkya states: The Brāhma [tīrtha] is at the base of the thumb; the Daiva is at the tips of the fingers;
the Prājāpatya is at the base [of the little finger]; and the Saumya is established in the middle.
"In the middle" means in the center of the palm. || 1.19 ||
Having sipped water three times and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch the apertures with water.
Having drunk water three times and wiped the mouth twice, one should touch the openings with water. Devala says:
"Likewise, one should wipe the mouth twice with the base of the thumb."
One should never wipe [the face] with the fingertips or with the back of the hands.
But with water that is in its natural state, free from foam and bubbles. || 1.20 ||
The twice-born are purified by [water] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; women and Śūdras are purified when it has touched the extremities even once. (1.21)

Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are purified by waters that are unaltered—that is, free from foam and bubbles—and which reach respectively the heart, the throat, and the palate. Women and Śūdras, however, are purified when the water touches the inner corners of the mouth once with both lips. Furthermore, the water for sipping should be such that it reaches the heart. Dakṣa says: "Having washed his hands and feet, he should drink water three times after looking at it;
then, using the base of the thumb, he should wipe his mouth twice."
"Without hair" means that the lips are covered. Yama says:
"Purification by water alone has been declared by the wise for those who do not look [at the water] at night;
likewise for the sick, and for those who drink hot water, with hot water."

Those who have undergone initiation (dīkṣita) drink [the water] warm. It should be old. Having formed the right hand into the shape of a cow's ear, one should drink the water three times after looking at it, and wipe the mouth twice.
First, having sprinkled water on the head, one should touch the face with three [verses];
then, by touching the apertures according to the prescribed rule, one becomes pure.
The meaning is "with three fingers. Manu says:
"One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should touch the cavities with water, as well as the self and the head."
The skillful one should first touch the mouth with the three middle fingers,
and immediately thereafter, the two nostrils with the thumb and the index finger.
One should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger;
the ears with the little finger and the thumb; the navel with the thumb alone; the heart by touching it with the palm; and the head with all the fingers.
And by touching his arms with the tip [of the grass], a man then becomes pure.

The thumb, the forefinger, the ring finger, and the little finger; the palm is the center of the hand. Having repeatedly touched all the locations of the streams [of the body], one becomes purified. "A Brahmin should always sip water," so said the blessed Bhṛgu.
One should touch the navel with the thumb joined to the little finger;
then the chest with the palms and fingers, and finally the head with all five fingers.
Having touched his shoulders with the tips of his fingers and touched water while composed in mind,
and having recollected Padmanābha, the brahmin becomes thoroughly purified.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "O mighty-armed one, the thumb is said to be Agni; the forefinger is Vāyu;
likewise, the ring finger is Sūrya; and the little finger is remembered as Candramas."
But Prajāpati, O best of the Bharatas, is to be known as the middle one.
Yama says:
A wise man should not touch water until he has touched it with his left hand; "water" is the word understood in the remainder of the verse.
For on the left are the twelve Ādityas, and Varuṇa, the lord of the thirty-three gods.
Vyāsa says:
A twice-born man may perform the sipping of water (ācamana) even while standing, provided he uses water that has not been drawn up;
likewise, if he is ill, he may do so even while lying down, as may one who is looking about or frightened.
Another Smṛti states:
"One may sip water using copper, stone, coconut, lotus, bamboo, bottle-gourd, leather, or even a clean vessel; he is always pure."

The meaning of the word *api* (also) is that it is not only with water from an irreproachable hand; thus says Baudhāyana: "One should not sip water with the remainder after washing the feet. If one should sip, one should do so after pouring it out upon the ground. One should not sip water that has bubbles, nor that which has foam, nor that which is hot, nor alkaline, nor discolored, nor turbid. One should not sip while laughing, nor talking, nor standing, nor looking around, nor bent over, nor bowing down, nor with the topknot untied, nor with the waistband unfastened, nor with the knees exposed, nor with the head wrapped, nor with the girdle tied, nor in haste, nor without the sacred thread, nor with legs spread apart, but silently, drinking three times as much water as reaches the heart. Devala says:
A twice-born man should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while wearing shoes, standing in water, with his hair loose,
wearing a turban, or having his head wrapped in a cloth.

Āpastamba: "One should not sip water while it is falling in streams. Yama: "The twice-born who sips water that has been touched by the hand or the nails clearly drinks liquor; such is the word of Yama."
And likewise, from the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Having covered his neck or his head, or even while standing on a street or in a marketplace,
one becomes impure even after sipping water (ācamana) if he has not performed the purification of his feet."
Marīci: One who stands on sandals, one who is not composed, one who is impure, or one whose mind is not restrained—
having performed the ritual sipping (upaspṛśya), O twice-born ones, he shall indeed become pure.
Even while remaining seated after eating, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), but never at any other time.

Pracetas states: "One should not sip water while wearing an inner garment, nor while without a garment, nor while shedding tears, nor while performing the *ācamana* rite. Āpastamba says: "One should not perform useless acts with the remnants of water used for the sacred fire; or one may sip water after having poured it upon the ground. Viṣṇu states:
"No Brāhmaṇa should touch water while touching [impure things], laughing, or talking, nor upon seeing a dog or a *caṇḍāla*, nor while his hand is not purified by a ring of *kuśa* grass (*apavitra*)."
All of that [water] becomes impure for him, as does his act of sipping water.
Yama says:
If one sips water with the right hand while the *darbha* grass remains in the left hand, that water becomes blood; having drunk it, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (1.20–21)
He now describes the midday twilight ritual, along with its constituent parts such as bathing, which is prescribed in due order for one who has been initiated:
"Bathing with mantras addressed to the waters, sprinkling [with water], restraint of the breath (prāṇāyāma), worship of the Sun, and the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī. (1.22)

Bathing (*snāna*) means immersion; it is performed with the deities of the waters using mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Sprinkling (*mārjana*) is the sprinkling of one's own head. Breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*), and the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* are to be performed daily at midday. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*): "Immersion in the waters like a staff. Kātyāyana says:
"For the sake of protection, having encircled oneself with water on all sides, one should perform the sprinkling of the head with *kuśa* grass and drops of water."
Regarding that, Yājñavalkya in the *Yogayājñavalkya* states the seer and other details for the verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*:
"Sindhudvīpa is the seer; the metre is Gāyatrī;
the deity is declared to be the Waters; and the application is for the act of sprinkling."

Vyāsa states: One should cast eight droplets upward for the destruction of that which is above, and downward for the destruction of that which is below. The ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) should be performed with each quarter-verse of the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. Among these, one should cast [the water] downward onto the ground with the verse *yasya kṣayāya jinvatha*. Likewise, [he says]:

"Sprinkling (mārjana) is performed in the midst of water, whereas breath control (prāṇāyāma) may be done anywhere; that is to say, either in water or on land. Now follows the consecration of the purifier (pavitrakaraṇa). Regarding this, Kātyāyana says:
"It should be made of kuśa grass, without an inner core, with a tip, consisting of two blades, and indeed [without a knot]."
It should be known as being the size of a span, the purifier wherever it may be found.
This very same characteristic of the *kapiñjalī* plant has been declared for the purpose of clarifying the clarified butter (*ājya*); it is indeed just this much.
Some authorities declare that the *piñjalī* consists of a single fresh *kauśī* sprig,
whether moist or dry, or one whose flowers have withered.
Mārkaṇḍeya says: A Brāhmaṇa’s purifier consists of four blades of *darbha* grass;
for each subsequent social class (*varṇa*), it is prescribed to be reduced by one blade, respectively.
Rites for pacification (śāntika) are performed with three blades of darbha grass, and likewise rites for nourishment (pauṣṭika) with five;
all rites pertaining to the gods (daiva) and the ancestors (pitrya) are prescribed with seven tufts of darbha grass.
One should know those darbha blades that are placed within the *nīvī* and those that are made into the *brahmasūtra* as sacred; as is the body, so is the *kuśa*.
During recitation, burnt offerings, giving gifts, Vedic study, and the libation to the ancestors,
one should ensure that the hand is never empty, using gold, silver, or *kuśa* grass.
[44] In recitation, fire-offerings, giving, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors,
a wise man should perform the actions with both hands provided with the *pavitra* grass, using the *savya* (left) and *apasavya* (right) positions.
One should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with that sacred thread which has a knot;
rather, one should remember the sage (ṛṣi), the meter (chandas), the deity (daivata), and the rule for its application (viniyoga-vidhi).
Having recited the syllable *oṃ* and the *gāyatrī*, one should then tie the topknot;
having sipped water again, one should touch the heart, the navel, and the two shoulders.
Likewise,
one should then mutter the Vyāhṛtis beginning with the Praṇava and the Sāvitrī;
having thus consecrated the water, one should perform the Sandhyā worship.

He states the nature of *prāṇāyāma*: "One should recite the *gāyatrī* together with its head [the *śiras*], preceded by the *vyāhṛtis* and joined with the *praṇava* at each [verse]; this, performed three times, is the restraint of breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). (1.23)

The *gāyatrī* is "tat savituḥ" (RV 3.62.10), because it is traditionally taught in the *Taittirīyaka Āraṇyaka* as the mantra for *prāṇāyāma*. One should recite it three times together with the *śiras*, beginning with "oṃ āpo jyotiḥ," preceded by the *vyāhṛtis* and joined with the *praṇava* at each instance. This is *prāṇasaṃyama*; the meaning is that it is *prāṇāyāma*. That which has the seven *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ* and ending with *satyam* as its preceding part is "preceded by those. The *praṇava* for each mantra is "per-mantra-praṇava. The mantras consist of the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and the *śiras*. The *praṇava* that occurs at the end of the *śiras* is indeed included within the end of the mantra itself. Thus says Saṃvarta.
A twice-born man should daily recite the seven vyāhṛtis joined with the syllable Om,
and the Sāvitrī together with its head, three times with his mind.
Manu says:
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma.

Bṛhaspati: Having assumed a firm posture, having restrained the senses, and likewise having remembered the Ṛṣi and other [components of the mantra], one should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma) while keeping the eyes closed and observing silence.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"The syllable *Oṃ* is the supreme Brahman, the leader among all mantras;
it was produced from the mouth of Prajāpati, who had attained perfection through austerity in the past."
[45] Therefore, the *brahmārṣa* of that [meter] is the Self-existent One (*svayaṃbhū*);
its metre is said to be *gāyatrī*, and its deity is Agni.
In the beginning, one should employ it in all various single rites;
this is declared to be its application, and it is described as being white in color.
Brahmā is proclaimed as the seer of all the vyāhṛtis;
thereafter, one should correctly demonstrate the meters belonging to them.
The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti [are the meters];
Indra and the Viśvedevas are declared to be the deities.
And the application [of this mantra] in the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma) has been declared.
Likewise,
that [Gāyatrī] whose deity is Savitṛ, whose mouth is Agni, which has three feet,
whose seer is Viśvāmitra, and whose metre is Gāyatrī, is preeminent.
The Gāyatrī is indeed all this: in its application (viniyoga), in the initiation (upanaya), and likewise in the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma); it is the Brāhmaṇa and the Brāhmaṇas.
Indeed, many other [forms] of the Gāyatrī are proclaimed in the Vedas;
however, this mantra which is specifically celebrated is "Oṃ āpo jyotiḥ."
For that Prajāpati, the Ṛṣi is the Yajus mantra devoid of meters;
Brahmā, Agni, Vāyu, and Sūrya are declared to be the deities.
The application of the vital breath (prāṇa) in the vehicle of speech has thus been illustrated.

Prāṇāyāma is to be known as having three characteristics: inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka). As it is said: "Inhalation drawn through the nose is called pūraka; retention is when the breath is motionless; and exhalation is when it is being released."
One should meditate, by means of inhalation alone, upon the Great-Souled One, who resembles the dark blue of a blue lotus and is established at the region of the navel, possessing four arms.

During the retention of breath (kumbhaka), one should meditate upon the lotus-seated Brahmā, the Grandfather, whose entire body is fair-complexioned and who has four faces, located in the region of the heart.
Through the exhaling breath (recaka), one should know Maheśvara, the Lord situated in the forehead—
resembling pure crystal, stainless, and the destroyer of sins.
[46] Likewise, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) during all three junctions of the day;
having performed the restraint of the vital breath, one should sip water for purification even if already pure.
Because one is internally distressed [by impurity], therefore the ritual rinsing (ācamana) is prescribed.
Having said, "May Agni protect me in the evening," and "May Sūrya protect me in the morning," one should drink [the water].
"May the waters purify me from the midst of the fire," and then one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

"Āpaḥ punantu": Sindhudvīpa is the seer (ṛṣi), Brahmanaspati is the deity, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter. "Sūryaś ca mā": Agni is the seer, and Sūrya, Manyu, and the Lords (patayaḥ) are the deities. "Agniś ca mā": Viṣṇu is the seer, and Agni is the deity. Having touched the consecrated water, one should perform the sprinkling (mārjana) upon the head with Darbha grass while reciting the hymn beginning with "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," through the mouth of Brahmā.

The *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* constitute the mouth of Brahman. Having touched water with that [formula], one should perform the sprinkling (*mārjana*) upon the head with *darbha* grass using that water, reciting the hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā"—this is the meaning. Regarding this hymn "āpo hi ṣṭhā," Ambarīṣa Sindhudvīpa is the seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Waters (*āpas*) are the deity. For the ninth verse, Agni is the deity for the latter half. For the first seven verses, the meter is *gāyatrī*; for the two following, it is *anuṣṭubh*. Their application (*viniyoga*) is in the rite of sprinkling. Kātyāyana says: "Having risen, one should cast three handfuls of water toward the sun."

The triad consists of the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī*. Then, one should worship the Sun with mantras dedicated to the deity Sūrya that have been studied in one's own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā*). Thereafter, one should mutter the *sāvitrī*. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"One should invoke Gāyatrī, the destroyer of all sins:
'Come, O Goddess, granter of boons; be present before me during my recitation.'"
Because you protect one who sings, you are therefore known as Gāyatrī.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states: She is described as being white in complexion, likewise dressed in silken garments,
and adorned with holy unguents and ornaments that are white.
Residing within the solar orb and dwelling in the world of Brahmā,
the auspicious Goddess holds a rosary and is seated upon a lotus throne.
Having invoked [the deity] according to the rule with the mantra "Ojas tvam asi," and having indeed invoked,
worshipped, and paid homage, the sacrificer should dismiss [the deity].
[47] Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, and likewise *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*,
with the *gāyatrī* and the *praṇava* at the end— this indeed is declared to be the recitation (*japa*).
Yama said: One should constantly recite the Gāyatrī, the goddess who has a thousand as her maximum, a hundred as her middle, and ten as her minimum, which destroys all sins.
In continuation of the phrase "one should perform," Yājñavalkya says:
"Recitation performed at home is said to have a single-fold merit; by a river, it is three-fold;
in a cow-pen, it is a hundred-fold; and in a fire-sanctuary, it is more than a hundred-fold."
In all the fields of the perfected ones (*siddhakṣetra*) and in the presence of the deity,
[the merit] is infinite in the presence of Śiva, even compared to hundreds of thousands of millions.
Likewise,
if standing, one should perform the recitation while gazing at the sun with a concentrated mind;
otherwise, one should face the east, following the sequence to be described hereafter.
Seated thus on a beautiful seat covered with kusha grass whose tips point eastward— a seat that is neither too high nor too low— with darbha grass in hand and well-restrained senses.
A rosary should indeed be made from crystal, *indrākṣa*, *rudrākṣa*, or *putrajīva* seeds; each subsequent one is superior to the preceding.
The increase [of merit] when recitation is performed becomes more than ten millionfold, especially with a rosary; therefore, each subsequent one is superior to the last.
In the absence of a rosary, however, one should always perform the recitation with a focused mind, using either a knot of *kuśa* grass or the hand.

Śaṅkha says: "Seated upon a grass mat (*bṛsī*) or one covered with *kuśa* grass, with his hands joined as a support (*hastopayāma*), holding *kuśa* blades as a purifier (*pavitra*) in his hand, facing north or toward the sun, and taking up a rosary (*akṣamālā*) while meditating on the deity, he should perform the recitation (*japa*). A *bṛsī* is a seat. 'Covered with *kuśa*' means spread over with *kuśa*. He should make the rosary from any one of the following: gold, gems, pearls, crystal, lotus seeds, *indrākṣa*, or *putrajīvaka* seeds; or it may be made from knots of *kuśa* grass, or with the hands joined as a support. In no other way does a twice-born man burn away his sin through recitation."
Just as one is liberated from all sins by the recitation of the Sāvitrī, so it is said in the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"One should meditate on the mantra with the mind; one should not move the tongue or the lips."
One should not shake the head or neck, nor should one display the teeth.
Neither walking, nor laughing, nor looking to the side;
neither leaning against anything, nor talking, nor likewise with his head covered.
One should not recite while stepping with one foot upon the other, nor while remaining in such a posture,
nor with an unconcentrated mind, nor while making others hear it.
A wise person should not perform recitations and other rites while standing on dry ground with wet clothes;
except when observing a formal vow, one should not perform them with wet garments nor with only a single garment.
One should not recite [the mantra] with a thread that is worn out, dyed blue, or soiled;
[otherwise] the hosts of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, siddhas, and vidyādharas [will be disturbed].
Because they carry [the merit] away by force, one should therefore keep it secret;
likewise, one should not speak during the time of recitation, nor during vows, fire-offerings, and the like.
But if a most excellent twice-born man should arrive while one is occupied with these very tasks,
one should then salute that brahmin and inquire after his well-being and security.
Being attentive and focused,

one should remain silent while reciting [the mantra]. Upon seeing outcasts (caṇḍāla), those who have fallen from their caste (patita), or others of that sort, one should touch water, speak to them, and having bathed, recite it again.
Having touched water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana); "having addressed" means having conversed.
Having sipped water and being constantly pure, one should recite hymns to the Sun according to one's enthusiasm, and the Pāvamānī verses according to one's ability, upon seeing anything impure.
For one engaged in whispered recitation, it becomes a hundredfold;
mental recitation is said to be a thousandfold, for it is indeed equal to meditative concentration.
Loud recitation (*śaṃsya*) is [performed] audibly;
however, where there is merely the movement of the lips, that is whispered (*upāṃśu*), as is the case when reciting on a journey.
Having rendered the tongue free from conceptualization, one should indeed contemplate that which is mental (*mānasa*).
A wise man should not perform recitation aloud, especially that of the Sāvitrī mantra. Thus [ends verse 1.23].
He describes the evening twilight worship:

"Having restrained his breath and sprinkled himself with water while reciting the three verses addressed to the waters, he should sit facing west, muttering the Sāvitrī until the appearance of the stars. (1.24)

[49] Having restrained his breath according to the rule and having sprinkled himself with water while reciting the three-verse hymn beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, he should sit facing west by a river or similar body of water, muttering the *Sāvitrī* as before until the appearance of the stars. "Appearance" (*udaya*) means being fit for sight; regarding the instruction "he should wait upon" (*upāsīta*), Śaunaka states: "From when half the solar disc has set until the appearance of the stars. Regarding the mantra *agniś ca mā manyuś ca*, Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Agni, Manyu, and the Lords of Wrath (*manyupati*) are the deities (*devatā*). The *Prakṛti* is the meter (*chandaḥ*). A specific rule for the upward throwing of water has been stated by Vyāsa.
Taking water with both hands and consecrating it with the Gāyatrī mantra,
one should stand facing the sun and cast it upward three times during the two twilights.

The rest is the same as for the midday twilight (*madhyandina-saṃdhyā*). At the conclusion of the evening twilight recitation (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā-japa*), there is the worship of the night (*rātry-upasthāna*). Baudhāyana says: "He worships the night with two verses addressed to Varuṇa beginning with *imaṃ me*. *imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhī havam adyā ca mṛḍaya | tvām avasyur ācake || tat tvā yāmi brāhmaṇā vandamānas tad āśāste yajamāno havirbhiḥ | aheṣamāno varuṇeha bodhy uruśaṃsa mā na āyuḥ pra moṣīḥ ||* Śunaḥśepa is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Night is the deity (*devatā*). The first verse is in the *gāyatrī* meter; the second is in the *triṣṭubh* meter. (1.24)
He states the rule for the morning twilight worship:
"One should thus stand during the morning twilight before sunrise until the appearance of the sun."

The terms *prāṇāyāma*, *prokṣaṇa*, and *gāyatrījapa* are included by the word *evaṃ*. Facing east, one should remain standing during the morning *saṃdhyā*, reciting the *Sāvitrī*, until the time of the sun’s appearance. In the expression *saṃdhyām*, the accusative case is used according to Pāṇini 2.3.5 (*kālādhvanor atyantasaṃyoge*). Therefore, the entire duration of the *saṃdhyā* period must be spent in recitation. Furthermore, in this context, the recitation itself is the primary injunction to be performed, in order to avoid contradicting the Vedic revelation that "one should recite the *Gāyatrī* preceded by *Oṃ*"; whereas bathing and sitting are merely its ancillaries. Thus, the phrase "sitting while reciting" means that one should recite while seated. — Saṃvarta.
One should perform the morning twilight devotion along with the stars according to the prescribed rule;
and the western twilight devotion together with the sun until half of it has set.
Yogayājñavalkya states: "The decrease and increase of the days occur constantly in their respective order;
however, the twilight (saṃdhyā) is traditionally held to last for exactly one muhūrta during both decrease and increase."
That which is the western twilight should be known as Sarasvatī;
Gāyatrī becomes red, and Sāvitrī has white leaves.
The Kṛṣṇā Sarasvatī is to be known as the three junctions (saṃdhyā);
one should perform the twilight worship at the junction, neither when the sun has set nor when it has risen.
The knower of the Self, being twice-born, must always perform the three twilight devotions;
and both twilights must be performed by Brahmins even while at home.
And from this statement, it is understood that the midday *saṃdhyā* should not be performed at home. Vasiṣṭha says:
"But the *saṃdhyā* performed at home is said to have one-fold merit; in a cow-pen, it is ten-fold;
by a hundred-thousand-fold on a river; and infinite in the presence of Viṣṇu."
Śātātapa says: "The twilight prayer performed outside purifies one from falsehood, the smell of liquor, sexual intercourse during the day,
and even the food of a Śūdra."

The twilight prayer performed outside [a village] is ten times more meritorious; at places such as pits and springs it is a hundred times more meritorious; at a renowned sacred ford (tīrtha) it is a thousand times more meritorious; and in the waters of the Jāhnavī it is ten thousand times more meritorious.
Manu says:
By muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during both twilights, a Brahmin becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas.
This syllable is the *praṇava*, it is *Yama*. Whatever evil deed is committed during the day by action, mind, or speech,
one destroys that by sitting for the evening twilight prayer (*saṃdhyā*) and through breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*).
Whatever evil has been committed during the night by deed, thought, or speech,
one dispels it by performing the morning twilight devotion (pūrvā saṃdhyā) with breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
But those who constantly perform the twilight devotions with firm vows,
having shaken off their sins, go to the eternal world of Brahmā.
Because of their long observance of the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), the sages attained long life,
as well as honor, fame, renown, and spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
From the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
"Attendance at the two twilights is required at all times by those on earth,
except in cases of birth-impurity, ritual impurity from death, confusion, illness, or fear."
Pulastya said: One should perform the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), the sacrifice (iṣṭi), the cooked oblation (caru), and the fire offering (homa) as long as one lives;
even during periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka), one must not abandon the rite of the twilight prayers.
A twice-born man should recite the mantras mentally, without performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Yama says:
"Those who have not observed the preceding morning [twilight worship], and those who have passed the following evening [twilight worship],"
Those Brahmins who do not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) are declared to be Śūdras.
Dakṣa says:
That Brāhmaṇa, especially, who does not perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), becomes a Śūdra even while alive;
after death, he is born as a dog.
One who neglects the twilight prayers is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other work he may perform, he shall not partake of its fruit.
Then one should perform the fire-ritual during both twilights.

After the appearance of the stars and after the sight of the sun—during the time of twilight, when that very moment has arrived—one should perform the oblation of fuel-sticks (*samiddhoma*) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. From the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*:
"Having brought fuel-sticks from afar, one should place them upon the house;
evening and morning, one should offer them into the fire without weariness."

The word "from afar" (*dūrāt*) is intended as an indication of a place that is not enclosed. Furthermore, the deity here is one known from the words of the mantra. From the statement "one should offer" (*juhuyāt*), the fire-ritual consisting of oblations and so forth is understood. By the two words "evening" and "morning," night and day are indicated. Baijavāpa says: "Before sunset, having gone toward the northern direction, one should fetch fuel-sticks from the forest without causing injury. Dry sticks if one desires spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); moist ones if one desires food; both kinds if one desires both. Kātyāyana says: "In no case should a fuel-stick be thicker than the thumb."
It must not be stripped of its bark, nor infested with insects, nor split open.
The sacrificial ladle should not be longer than a span nor shorter; likewise, it should have two prongs.
It should neither have leaves nor be devoid of potency for those wise ones performing oblations.
Those that are shattered, split, short, crooked, or likewise possessed of a hole should not be taken up; even if endowed with good qualities, they cause the destruction of the success of the rite.
From the Vāyupurāṇa:
"Fuel-sticks should be made of *pālāśa* wood; if those are unavailable, they should be of *khādira* wood.
If those are unavailable, they may be of *śamī*, *rohitaka*, or *aśvattha*; and if even those are unavailable, of *arka* or *vetasa*. [52]
Kātyāyana states: Where an action is prescribed but the limb of the agent is not specified,
it should be understood that the right hand is the instrument for those actions.

In those rites such as recitation and fire-offerings where no restriction of direction exists, three directions are prescribed: the eastern (aindrī), the northern (saumyā), and the unconquered (aparājitā).
Whether sitting, standing, or bowing, where no such rule is specified,
that [act] should be performed while sitting, not while bowing or standing.
Śātātapa says: A Brahmin must never salute Kṣatriyas and others,
even if they are endowed with knowledge, ritual action, and virtues, and are deeply learned in the scriptures.
"The Veda declares that a Brāhmaṇa should pronounce blessings for all social classes;
however, among those of the same class, the formal salutation (abhivādana) must indeed be performed by equals toward equals."
Aṅgiras:
Those twice-born who offer blessings when a Śūdra passes by without bowing go to hell;
the Śūdra goes to hell as well, and the Brāhmaṇa immediately after him.
Yama said: That happiness which exists in the three worlds, free from disease and calamity,
in which all desires are contained— that is designated as "Svasti."
Likewise,
it is said that a Kṣatriya kills [the merit of] three yugas, a Vaiśya kills four yugas,
and a Śūdra kills twenty-one yugas of a Brāhmaṇa.
From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Viṣṇu is addressed as 'abhī' (fear not), and Śaṅkara says 'vādayāmi' (I shall cause [you] to sound);
those two alone are honored by him who performs the salutation."
Wherever no specific rule regarding the right or left side and so forth is found, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder in all such rites. (1.25)
He states the procedure for salutation:

"Then one should salute the elders, saying, 'I am so-and-so. Having performed the fire-ritual, one should salute those who are senior, saying, 'I am so-and-so. In place of the word 'so-and-so,' one should utter one's name in the nominative case; or likewise, by saying, 'Salute me. Thus says Manu.
After offering a salutation to an elder, a Brahmin who is performing the greeting should proclaim his own name, saying: "I am so-and-so by name."

One should cause the word *bhoḥ* to follow at the end of one's own name when performing a salutation. Thus, the formula becomes: "I, named Caitra, salute you, sir (*bhoḥ*). And he (the author) himself explains how the response to a salutation should be made by the person who has been saluted: "A Brahmin, when saluted, should be addressed with the words, 'May you be long-lived, O gentle one (*saumya*').'"
And the letter *a* should be uttered within this name, with the preceding syllable protracted.

And here, the letter *a* is mentioned for the purpose of indicating the final vowel situated at the end of the name used in salutation (*abhivādana*). Consequently, whatever vowel is the last one must be protracted (*pluta*), according to the rule: "the preceding syllable (*pūrvākṣara*) is to be made protracted. That which has a preceding syllable is "preceded by a syllable" (*pūrvākṣara*); that which precedes it is what exists within the name used in salutation. And by implication, this is a consonant, for a consonant alone precedes a vowel. Therefore, because of the inclusion of the qualification "preceded by a syllable," the vowel together with its accompanying consonant is to be protracted. It is thus determined that a new *a* is not prescribed at the end of the name. Accordingly, Vasiṣṭha says: "In a vocative, the final vowel is protracted; likewise, a non-pragṛhya diphthong (*saṃdhyakṣara*) undergoes the change to *āy*, *ai*, or *au*. The vowel at the end of a name ending in a vocative case is protracted, meaning it becomes three morae (*trimātra*). Likewise, for a diphthong—namely those in the form of *e* or *o*—that is not designated as *pragṛhya*, the change to *āi* (for *e*) or *āu* (for *o*) is to be applied. If it is in the form of *o* or *au*, then the change to *āu* is to be performed. Examples here are: *āyuṣmān bhava saumya yajñadatta3*, *bhadraśarmā3*, *yajñabhūtā3i*, *citragā3u*. It has been stated: "Saluting one who is senior. When it is asked, "By how much time does one become senior?", Manu says: [Manu 2.120–121] "One hundred years of a Brāhmaṇa's life are divided into four parts. The first part is for study; the remaining three are for bestowing gifts, performing sacrifices, and practicing austerities. "One who has completed his studies and is endowed with self-restraint is called a *snātaka* by the wise; he should always remain devoted to the six duties. [Manu 2.124] "A Brāhmaṇa who salutes first an unlearned person of the same caste, or one who is younger, falls from his own status; he does not fall from it if he salutes one who is superior. [Manu 2.125] "One should not salute a person who does not return the salutation, nor one who is ignorant of the rules of salutation, nor one who is impure, nor one who is a woman, nor one who is a Śūdra. [Manu 2.126] "A Kṣatriya should be saluted by a Brāhmaṇa who knows the rules, but the Brāhmaṇa need not salute a Kṣatriya; the same applies to a Vaiśya; and a Śūdra is never to be saluted by any twice-born person. [Manu 2.127] "A Brāhmaṇa who does not salute an elder of his own caste when meeting him on the road incurs the sin of killing an embryo for every step he takes. [Manu 2.128] "Upon meeting a person of equal caste and age, one should say 'I am so-and-so' after having first greeted him with the word 'well-being' (*kuśala*). [Manu 2.129] "To a Brāhmaṇa who is not a teacher, one should say 'I am so-and-so' while extending the hand; to a Kṣatriya, one should say the same while holding the bowstring. [Manu 2.130] "To a Vaiśya, one should say 'I am so-and-so' while pointing with the hand; to a Śūdra, one should say it while merely raising the hand. [Manu 2.131] "To women other than one's mother, sister, or teacher's wife, and to young girls, one should say 'I am so-and-so' while keeping the right hand extended. [Manu 2.132] "To one's maternal uncle, the father-in-law, a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, a father's sister, a mother's brother, and a teacher, one should always say 'I am so-and-so' while rising to greet them. [Manu 2.133] "To one's maternal grandfather, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a father-in-law, a king, and an accomplished student (*snātaka*), one should rise and say 'I am so-and-so' even if they are younger. [Manu 2.134] "To these six—one's maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the king, a maternal aunt, a paternal aunt, and a maternal grandfather—one should rise to greet them even if they are younger. [Manu 2.135] "One should rise to greet a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, and a paternal aunt; however, one need not rise for a maternal aunt, a paternal aunt, or a maternal grandfather. [Manu 2.136] "Among all these, the mother is the most venerable; next to her is the father; next to the father is the teacher; and next to the teacher is the Brahman itself. [Manu 2.147] "One should not cross over a person who is saluting, nor a cow, nor a king, nor a Brāhmaṇa carrying fuel-sticks, nor a bride being led to her husband's home. [Manu 2.148] "When one meets a person who is saluting, one should say 'I am so-and-so'; and upon meeting a person who is not saluting, one should say 'I am well' (*kuśalam*). [Manu 2.149] "To a Kṣatriya, one should say 'Are you well? (*anāmaya*); to a Vaiśya, 'Have you prospered? (*kṣemam*); and to a Śūdra, 'Are you free from disease? (*ārogyam*). [Manu 2.150] "To a Brāhmaṇa, one should say 'May you live long! (*āyuṣmān bhava*); to a Kṣatriya, 'May you be victorious! (*vijayī bhava*); to a Vaiśya, 'May you prosper! (*vardhasva*); and to a Śūdra, 'May you be healthy! (*ārogyavān bhava*). [Manu 2.151] "An old man, one who is ill, a pregnant woman, a bride, a king, and a person carrying a load—these six should be given way by a chariot. [Manu 2.152] "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, one who is ill, a person carrying a load, and a king—these eight should be given way by a cart. [Manu 2.153] "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, one who is ill, a person carrying a load, and a king—these eight should be given way by a horse-carriage. [Manu 2.154] "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, one who is ill, a person carrying a load, and a king—these eight should be given way by a palanquin. [Manu 2.155] "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, one who is ill, a person carrying a load, and a king—these eight should be given way by a boat. [Manu 2.156] "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, one who is ill, a person carrying a load, and a king—these eight should be given way by a carriage drawn by a beast of burden. [Manu 2.157] "A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, a woman, one
Friendship with fellow citizens is established by ten years; that with those skilled in the arts, by five years;
that with Vedic scholars, by three years; and even by a very short time among one's own kin.

Among city-dwellers, one who is ten years older becomes a senior friend (*pūrva-sakha*), while one more than that is a superior elder (*jyāyān*). Among those who possess artistic skills—such as craftsmen, singers, and the like—one five years older is a friend, and one more than that is a senior elder. Here, "fewer" is relative to three years. Among those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one three years older is a friend, and one more than that is a senior elder. Furthermore, the gradation between them depends upon the gradation of their qualities. The word "api" (also/even) has the sense of "eva" (only/exclusively). Thus Manu spoke regarding women and men who are ignorant of the proper forms of returning a greeting.
To those who do not know how to respond to one's name,
as well as to all women, a wise man should simply say, "I am he."

Āpastamba: "A Śrotriya who has been a teacher for three years is worthy of salutation. Furthermore, when a difference in lineage is known, one should salute the more senior. Likewise: "One desiring heaven and long life should salute other seniors living in the same village even before the morning meal. A Brāhmaṇa should salute by extending his right arm level with his ear; a Kṣatriya level with his chest; a Vaiśya level with his waist; and a Śūdra with his hands joined low. One should not salute a teacher who is on uneven ground; rather, having climbed up to him, one should salute. In all cases, however, the salutation is performed after rising. One who is impure (aprayata) should not be saluted. Likewise: "And one who is impure should not return the salutation of one who is pure. Women of equal age should be saluted with the head bowed and the hands lowered. All women, as well as Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, should be saluted by name; some say that one's mother, the wife of a preceptor, and one's own wife should not be saluted by name. Sāṃkhyāyana: "One should salute the teacher day by day, and upon meeting, the Śrotriya teachers. Manu: [follows].
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge,
one should first pay homage to the person from whom that knowledge was received.
When the teacher’s own teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward one's own teacher;
nor, unless permitted by his teacher, should one salute one's own teachers.
Without being dismissed or permitted [to leave], he should attend upon his own maternal uncles and others, as well as his teacher, with a concentrated mind for the sake of Vedic study. 1.26.

And one should salute the teacher. Although saluting the teacher is already established by virtue of his seniority, this separate statement is intended to provide an alternative to the ritual clasping of the feet (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) mentioned in other treatises. Regarding this ritual clasping, Manu says: "The ritual clasping of the teacher must be performed with crossed hands:
the left [hand] should be touched with the left [hand], and the right [hand] with the right."

The meaning is that one should touch the left and right feet of the guru with the left and right hands respectively. Having touched the ears for the sake of concentrating the mind, [one should touch] below those knees as far as the feet. Gautama states: "The clasping of the guru's feet occurs in the morning, during the recitation of the *brahma*, and at the beginning and end [of study]. *Brahma* refers to the Veda; *anuvacana* means teaching. "At the beginning and end" means at the commencement and conclusion. Āpastamba says: "But when the sun has risen, having met the teacher, there is the clasping of feet; this salutation (*abhivādana*) always includes the clasping of feet, according to some. Here, "guru" refers to either the teacher (*ācārya*) or the father. Atri [states]:
Raising his right hand, he should offer salutation according to his desire;
however, toward a *śrotriya* and a teacher, he should perform the clasping of the feet with joined palms.

Now the subject at hand is stated: one should also attend upon and serve the teacher for the sake of attaining the sacred study (*svādhyāya*). The word "the teacher" is understood from the previous context. Being concentrated means having a mind focused on nothing else. (1.26)
When summoned, he should study, and he should report whatever he has obtained to him.

When summoned by the teacher, he should recite; and what he has acquired, he should report to the teacher. Regarding the act of clasping [the teacher's feet], Gautama says: "Having been permitted, the disciple should sit to the south, facing east, or facing north. This should be done every day at the commencement of study. However, on the first day of study, having grasped the left foot with his hand, excluding the thumb, he should say, 'Recite, sir! In that context, there is the touching of the eyes, mind, and vital breaths (*prāṇa*) with *darbha* grass; three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), each consisting of fifteen measures (*mātrā*); and sitting on a seat of grass blades pointing eastward. Then follow the seven *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ*, ending with *satya*. The 'vital breaths' (*prāṇaḥ*) refers to the apertures of the head. A short syllable is a 'measure' (*mātrā*); by it, time is indicated. 'Kūla' means the tip."
And one should always act for his benefit through the actions of mind, speech, and body. || 1.27 ||

One should always act for the benefit of this teacher, in accordance with his long-term welfare, through mental, verbal, and physical activities. One should never act contrary to the teacher’s wishes by means of speech. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include the statements mentioned in other treatises. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Restraining the body, speech, intellect, senses, and mind, one should stand facing the east, gazing at the face of the teacher."
[56] He should always have his hand uplifted, be of virtuous conduct, and well-restrained;
and when told, "Be seated," he should sit facing the teacher.
He should always wear inferior food, clothing, and ornaments, and he should always sleep on the ground; while lying down, he should not engage in answering a call or conversing.
A "pratiśravaṇa" (promise) is an acceptance.
One should not make a promise while sitting, nor while eating, nor while standing, nor while facing away;
one should stand when the other is seated, and go toward them when they are walking away.
Going forward to meet those who are approaching, running after those who are running behind,
facing those who face eastward, and going near to those who are at a distance.
Having prostrated before him while he is lying down, one should likewise remain under his command; furthermore, in the presence of the guru at all times, one's bed and seat must be low.
In the presence of the guru, one should not sit as one pleases;
nor should one utter his name alone, even in his absence.
One should not imitate the gait, speech, or gestures of the guru; nor should one remain where censure or even slander of the guru is being uttered.
In that case, one should cover one's ears or depart elsewhere;
one should not worship him from a distance, nor when he is angry, nor while in the presence of a woman.
And while standing on a vehicle or a seat, one should descend and then salute him.
In this context, he mentions those who should be taught by the teacher:

"Grateful, non-malicious, intelligent, pure, indicative of auspiciousness, virtuous, capable, trustworthy, and those who provide for one's own welfare—these, according to the Dharma, are the ones to be taught. (1.28)

One who is grateful is mindful of a benefactor. One who is not envious is free from offense. One who is intelligent possesses retentive memory (*dhāraṇā*). One who is pure is self-restrained. One who indicates auspiciousness possesses favorable marks. In the reading *kalyāṇasūyakāḥ*, however, *kalya* means healthy, and *anasūyaka* means free from envy. An *āpta* is one who does not deceive. A *sva* is a kinsman. One who provides wealth is a giver of money for the teacher’s needs; in the reading *jñānavittadā*, however, a *jñānada* is a giver of books that serve as a cause for knowledge. These are to be taught by the teacher according to the law (*dharma*), without transgressing the law. Regarding one who provides wealth, teaching him is not unrighteous, because providing for his livelihood is prescribed. Teaching on the basis of a prior agreement for wages is forbidden. Manu, moreover, mentions even the teacher’s son.
"The son of the teacher, one who is obedient, a giver of knowledge, righteous, pure, capable, wealthy, trustworthy, a kinsman, and virtuous— these ten are to be taught according to the Dharma.
As for that which was stated by him [the same author]:
Where neither virtue nor wealth are found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve,
there knowledge should not be imparted, just as one would keep seed hidden from salty soil.

Thus, this refers to one who, despite having the capacity, does not perform acts of giving and service for the sake of practicing the Dharma, provided that the person to be taught lacks other virtues. 1.28.
In response to what has been brought forward, he says:
"He should carry the staff, the deerskin, the sacred thread, and the girdle.

The staff and the others are to be carried for their specific purposes. Among these, the purpose of the staff is support, warding off cattle and the like, penetrating darkness, entering water, and so forth. For the deerskin, the sacred thread, and the girdle, the purpose is transcendental (*adṛṣṭa*). Therefore, these must be worn constantly. The *upavīta* is the *brahmasūtra*. (Manu).
According to the Dharma, a Brāhmaṇa deserves staffs made of Bilva or Palāśa wood; a Kṣatriya, of Vaṭa or Khadira; and a Vaiśya, of Pippala or Udumbara.
Yama: But if even all of these are unavailable, then [the wood of] all [trees] fit for sacrifice [may be used].
Manu:
All those [teeth] should be straight, free from blemishes, pleasant to behold,
not causing distress to people, possessed of their enamel, and undamaged by fire.
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline;
that of a Kṣatriya should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the tip of the nose.
Likewise, students of the Veda should wear,
in their respective order, the skins of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat, as well as garments made of hemp, flax, and wool.

The meaning is that the Brāhmaṇas and the other classes should respectively wear, clothe themselves in, or make upper garments (*uttarīya*) out of the skins of the black antelope, the spotted deer, and the goat. Thus says Pāraskara: [58] "The upper garment of a Brāhmaṇa is the skin of the *aiṇeya* (black antelope); that of a Rājanya is the *raurava* (spotted deer); that of a Vaiśya is the skin of a goat or a cow; or for all, the skin of a cow. Yama says: "For all, the *raurava*, linen, silk, and woolen [skins serve as] lower garments (*adhovāsas*) by virtue of their suitability; others do not.
