Gautama, however, states that for all religious students (*brahmacārin*), there is an option between white cotton cloth and others such as linen: "For all, the garment is white cotton cloth, unaltered. "Unaltered" means white. Vasiṣṭha says: "The Brāhmaṇa’s garment is white or unwashed (*ahata*); the Kṣatriya’s is cotton or madder-dyed linen; the Vaiśya’s is yellow or silk; or for all, an undyed woven cloth. Or, even the linen and so forth may be white and unwashed. Manu [says]:
The sacrificial thread of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of cotton, twisted upward and triple-stranded;
that of a Kṣatriya should be made of hempen threads, and that of a Vaiśya of woolen threads.
Bhṛgu says: "The three threads should be wound upwards and then wound downwards;
the sacred thread (upavīta) should thus be triple-stranded, and for it, a single knot is prescribed."

"Trivṛt" means consisting of nine threads. And that which is wound around the back and the navel, reaching as far as the hips— that should be worn as the *upavīta* (sacred thread), neither too low nor too high.
One should always wear the sacred thread and always have one's topknot tied;
whatever is performed without the topknot or without the sacred thread is as if it were not done at all.
The sacred thread (upavīta) of a student is single, while for the other two [stages of life], it is traditionally held to be two.
Baudhāyana: "The sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) should be made of kuśa grass or sūtra, and should be threefold (trivṛt) in each strand. Manu:
"The girdle (mekhalā) of a Brahmin should be made of kuśa grass, threefold, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya should be a bowstring made of muñja grass; and that of a Vaiśya should be made of hempen threads."
If muñja grass is unavailable, however, it should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass;
it should have three strands and be tied with one, three, or five knots.

The intention is that the knots should be made according to one's *ṛṣi* lineage. Paiṭhīnasi states: "A girdle made of muñja grass or of *aśmantaka* wood is for a Brāhmaṇa. Baudhāyana says: "Then he winds a threefold girdle of muñja grass around him three times from left to right. Manu says:
"Whatever skin, whatever thread, whatever girdle, whatever staff, and whatever garment is prescribed for each, those same items are to be used by him during his vows as well. [59]
The vows are those beginning with the Sāvitrī.

Having placed the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread, and the water-pot into the water when they have become damaged, one should take others with the appropriate mantras. Thus it is said.
He should go for alms among blameless Brahmins for the sake of his own subsistence. 1.29.

He should practice the collection of alms obtained from blameless Brahmins who are beyond reproach and so forth. *Bhaikṣa* is the food begged; the aggregate of such portions is *baikṣa*. These means of subsistence (*ātmavṛttayaḥ*) are for his own livelihood alone, not for another person other than his teacher. However, the teacher shall certainly consume the alms-food offered by the pupil. As Āpastamba says: "Alms-food is commended as a sacrificial oblation (*havis*). In that regard, the teacher is for the sake of the deity and for the sake of the *Āhavanīya* fire. Having fed him [the pupil], he eats what remains; that which is the remnant of the *havis*, that indeed is it."—Manu.
He should fetch a water-pot, flowers, cow-dung, earth, and *kuśa* grass—
as much as required— and he should go out for alms every day.
A student, being self-restrained, should daily fetch alms from the houses of those who are not deficient in Vedic study and sacrifices, who are praised for their own duties.
One should not beg for alms from the family of one's teacher, nor from the families of one's paternal or maternal relatives.
But as for that which says:
"He should first beg alms from his mother, or his sister, or his own maternal aunt— whichever of these would not treat him with contempt."

Thus, since this refers to the occasion of begging for alms as part of the initiation (*upanayana*), it is not in conflict with the rule "one should not beg from the family of one's teacher," because the present rule concerns the obligatory daily begging.
However, if houses are unavailable, one should avoid each preceding house in turn;
or, if those previously mentioned [eligible houses] are impossible to find, one may wander through the entire village.
"O mighty-armed one, with the exception of the last," thus spoke the Lord, the all-pervading one.

The last is the Śūdra. Having restrained his speech and being self-controlled, he should also avoid meat. O joy of the Kurus, he should go about for alms from members of all four castes; if nothing is obtained, he may do so [from others].
"In the absence [of these]"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "among those of the three castes. || 1.29 ||
In the beginning, middle, and end [of the Vedas], the practice of begging alms is indicated by the word *bhavat* for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas respectively. 1.30.

[60] The phrase *baikṣaprāktana* (preceded by *bhikṣā*) is indicated by the term *bhaikṣacaryā*. At the beginning, middle, and end of that [phrase], it should be employed for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya respectively, joined with the word *bhavat* ending in the feminine vocative case. Thus it is established: "O Lady, give alms" (*bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi*) for a Brāhmaṇa; "O Sir, give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*) for a Kṣatriya; and "O Sir, give alms" (*bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi*) for a Vaiśya. Regarding the first alms-round, the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states:
One should first beg for alms from one's mother, or a sister, or one's own maternal aunt— whichever will not treat him with contempt.
She should place gold, silver, and jewels into his bowl.
And another Smṛti states:
"For the sake of the alms-offering, the father who has performed the initiation ceremony should then provide a golden vessel for the Madhuparka, or a silver one held in the left hand."
Yama says: Alms, salt, and condiments that are given directly from hand to hand cause the eater to fall into impurity, and the giver does not go to heaven.
Manu says:
Having taken up his desired staff and having worshipped the sun, he should circumambulate the fire from left to right and go about for alms according to the prescribed rule. (1.30)
Having performed his fire-ritual, he should eat while maintaining silence, with the permission of his guru, preceded by the *āpośāna* rite, honoring the food and not disparaging it. (1.31)

One who has performed the fire-rite (*agnikārya*) is called *kṛtāgnikāryaḥ*. *Vāgyataḥ* means observing silence. Having performed the *āpośāna* rite, honoring and revering the food, and not disparaging or criticizing it, he should eat with the permission of his teacher, saying "Eat," according to the teacher's consent. The *āpośāna* rite refers to the ritual action prescribed at the time of initiation (*upanayana*) regarding the *āpośāna* command. Here, the fire-rite consists of offering a portion of the alms-food (*bhaikṣa*) into the fire. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says: "Having offered the oblation (*havis*), having satiated the fire, and having placed a fuel-stick (*samidh*) upon it, one should consecrate the food three times, reciting: 'The food which I eat as nectar for the gods; the food which I eat in many forms. Having performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* fire-rite, he should eat, permitted by the teacher and remaining silent. Likewise, Āpastamba says: "Having offered into the fire a portion of the consecrated alms-food, he should eat. [61] Therefore, when the teacher is absent, this fire-rite is to be performed; however, when the teacher is present, the teacher himself should be fed in place of the fire-rite. This was stated by that same author in the passage beginning with "honored with the oblation. On this point, Manu says:
Having collected that food without guile, he should eat as much as required after offering it to his teacher; being pure, he should face the east and consume it after sipping water.
One who eats facing east gains long life; facing south, one gains fame;
facing west, one gains prosperity; and facing north, one eats the truth.

The meaning of this is as follows: that which one eats facing the east is conducive to longevity (*āyuṣya*); it is beneficial for life. Likewise, it is conducive to fame (*yaśasya*). He who eats facing the west attains prosperity (*śrī*); he who, however, faces the north attains *ṛta*, truth, or sacrifice (*yajña*). Thus, facing the east for the eater is both obligatory and optional (for specific desires). One should not give the leavings (*ucchiṣṭa*) to anyone, nor eat them, nor [eat] in between [meals].
Nor should one practice overeating, nor go anywhere while still impure from food.
Saṃvarta says:
"The eating of food by humans in the evening and in the morning is ordained by the gods;
one should not eat in between, for this rule is equal to the Agnihotra sacrifice."
Vasiṣṭha says: Eight mouthfuls are the food for a Muhūrta; sixteen for a forest-dweller;
twenty-two for a householder; and an unlimited amount for a student.

Āpastamba: "Having eaten, one should wash [the vessel] oneself without using mantras, and one should not leave any residue; if unable to do so, one should bury it in the ground, or cast it into water, or hand it over to an Ārya, or give it to a Śūdra through an intermediary. (1.31)

Established in the vow of celibacy, one should not eat the food of a single person except in times of distress. A student, when not in distress, must not eat the food of one person; however, a Brāhmaṇa may eat at a Śrāddha feast at his pleasure, provided he does not violate his vow. 1.32.

If a Brahmin who is a student (brahmacārī) is requested [to attend], he may eat food from a single house even when not in distress; and if he should eat at a śrāddha, he should eat while avoiding honey, meat, and other things that would cause an obstacle to his vow. 1.32.
He states the rules for the religious student (*brahmacārin*):
"One should avoid honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, fermented liquids, women, injury to living beings, gazing at the sun, vulgar speech, and slander. (1.33)

A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should avoid honey and the like. This includes honey and meat, even if they are fit for the food of refined people (*śiṣṭa*). *Añjana* refers to collyrium (*kajjala*). *Ucchiṣṭa* refers to the leavings of oneself or another, excluding one’s teacher (*guru*). Thus Vasiṣṭha [6.2] states: "The leavings of anyone other than one's teacher are not to be eaten; nor are one’s own leavings, nor what has been defiled by the leavings of others. *Śukta* refers to harsh speech or food that has become sour over time. By the word "woman" (*strī*), both looking at her and physical contact with her are indicated. As Gautama says: "Looking at a woman or touching her when there is a suspicion of sexual intercourse. *Prāṇihiṃsana* is the killing of living beings. *Bhāskarālokana* (looking at the sun) is well known. *Aślīla* is speech unfit for an assembly. *Parivāda* is slandering others; here, the object of avoidance is the act of avoiding such slander. *Saṃkalpa* is understood as that which is denoted by terms such as "vow" (*vrata*) and "observance" (*niyama*). For this very reason it is said: "Even while performing a vow at a *śrāddha*, without causing distress. Manu, however, says:
A student living with his teacher must observe these rules,
fully restraining the collection of his senses for the sake of increasing his own austerity.
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including other duties of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) mentioned in other Smṛtis. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Having bathed daily and being pure, he should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of fuel on the fire."
He should avoid honey and meat, perfumes, garlands, savory flavors, and women;
as well as oil massage, collyrium for the eyes, and the use of shoes and umbrellas.
Sensual desire, anger, and greed; dancing, singing, and instrumental music; gambling, idle chatter, slander, and likewise falsehood—these he should avoid.
He should avoid looking at women and causing injury to others;
he should always sleep alone and never spill his semen.
For by emitting semen out of lust, one indeed destroys his vow.
Practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*). This is self-restraint (*yama*): one who has conquered the senses, conquered laziness, conquered anger, and conquered the self.
Likewise,
He should avoid a high bed, a couch, and a tooth-cleansing stick;
he should sleep alone on *kuśa* grass and never let his semen be spilled.

Gautama says: "One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium for the eyes, ointments, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, playing musical instruments, bathing [for pleasure], brushing the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear. In the presence of the teacher, one should avoid covering the neck, crossing the arms, and stretching out the feet; likewise, spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. One should also avoid looking at women, touching them, having suspicions regarding sexual intercourse, gambling, serving the low-born, taking what is not given, violence, and [associating with] the teacher’s wife, his son, and those initiated by him. One should also avoid harsh words and intoxicants. A Brāhmaṇa must avoid these constantly. In this context, "bathing" refers to bathing for the sake of enjoyment. "Fear" refers to fear toward others. "Covering the neck" means wearing coverings around the neck. "Crossing the arms" (avasaktikā) means binding the hands above the knees. "Cracking the knuckles" (avaspheṭana) means cracking the fingers or other limbs. "Serving the low-born" (hīnasevā) refers to cleaning urine, feces, and so forth; even in the case of the teacher, one should avoid such service, based on the observation: "One should wash the limbs of the teacher even if they are smeared with impurity. "Harsh words" are speech that causes distress to others. "Intoxicants" (madya) are well known. The connection is that the student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) should avoid these. Regarding the phrase "a Brāhmaṇa [must avoid] intoxicants constantly": because of the word "constantly," intoxicants are to be avoided by a Brāhmaṇa even in the Kṛta and other ages. However, for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, it is only in the Kali age. As stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: [text follows].
Practicing celibacy for a long period, carrying a water-pot,
marrying a woman of the same lineage (sagotra) or of the same ancestry (sapiṇḍa), and likewise killing a cow.
"In the Kali age, human sacrifice, horse sacrifice, and liquor must be avoided by the twice-born.
This means that at all times, constantly, even a Brāhmaṇa who is not a student (*abrahmacārī*) must avoid liquor. Likewise:
"Sleeping on a low bed or seat, rising before [others], and retiring to bed after [others]."
His speech is unimpeded everywhere, except in the case of a mortal sin.

Sleeping on the ground and similar practices are to be observed out of regard for the guru. Āpastamba says: "One should avoid self-praise and the disparagement of others. Likewise: "When there is no contact with the guru, one should wash those limbs that have been smeared with impurities, ensuring that one's appearance is unassuming; the sense is that one should wash them so as not to be conspicuous. Āpastamba further states: "One should not look at a naked woman. One should not smell plants or trees after cutting them. One should not smile; if one must smile, one should do so covering the mouth—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Covering the mouth means closing it while smiling; such is the Brāhmaṇa. Hārīta says: "One should avoid mounting horses, elephants, chariots, or special sacred trees (caitya-vṛkṣa); gathering fruit, joining joints, crawling through narrow passages, descending into wells, crossing great rivers or oceans, and other acts of great risk. Manu [says]:
Whether he be shaven-headed, or wear matted locks, or have his hair tied in a topknot—
never should the sun set or rise while he remains within a village.
"Whether constantly urged by his teacher or even without being urged, he should apply himself to his studies and to the welfare of his teacher. (1.33)
In order to explain the duty of the student regarding those who are to be honored, he first states the characteristics of those worthy of honor:
"He is a guru who, having performed the [initiatory] rites, imparts the Veda to him."

The purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with *garbhādhāna* and ending with *upanayana*—he who performs these for another is the *guru* of that person. This alone is the definition of a *guru*. In this context, there is another injunction: "He gives the Veda to him. The suffix *-ktvā* (in the word *dattvā*) restates the sequence of performing the rites such as *niṣeka* and giving the Veda, which is already established by the sense of the passage. However, in reality, these are two distinct sentences. Otherwise, a Kṣatriya or others would not possess the status of *guru* toward their own son, because they do not give the Veda [to him]. Yet, the status of *guru* toward one's own son is desired even for Kṣatriyas and others. Furthermore, otherwise, if a son of a Kṣatriya or other caste were to have intercourse with his father’s wife, he would not incur the sin of violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpaga*), as the father would not be his *guru*. For this very reason, Manu states that the performance of rites such as *garbhādhāna*, independent of the giving of the Veda, is the defining characteristic of a *guru*.
That Brahmin who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and sustains [the child] with food, is called a guru.

In this context as well, the provision of food, which follows naturally from propriety, is restated rather than being prescribed as a defining characteristic of a *guru*. Furthermore, the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" is for the sake of illustration and not for the purpose of restriction; for if it were so, a Kṣatriya or others would not be considered a *guru*. By the inclusion of the phrase "according to rule," he shows that even one who performs only the *niṣeka* (conception rite) may be a *guru*, since only that much is prescribed for him. The same applies to Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas. From the statement that "he gives [the gift] when the *puṃsavana* and other rites have been performed," it is understood that, provided it is possible, the Brāhmaṇa father himself becomes the *ācārya*. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
Having thus duly refined the boy by means of the staff and other such measures,
the father should diligently teach him the Veda as well as the scriptures of Manu and others.

Thus, he declares that the authority belongs to the father alone. The mention of the definition is intended to show that the status of "guru" for those other than the father is merely figurative. Devala says:
"The teacher, the father, the elder brother, the king, the maternal uncle, the father-in-law, the protector, the maternal grandfather, and the paternal grandfather."
The eldest of one's caste, the paternal uncle—these are remembered as teachers among males;
likewise, the mother, the maternal grandmother, the wife of the teacher, and the uterine sisters of both one's father and mother.
The mother-in-law, the paternal grandmother, the elder sister, and the nurse—these are the female elders.
Thus has this group of elders been described, divided twofold according to the maternal and paternal sides.

Thus, that [term] should be understood as a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). And in this regard, the result is that one must behave toward them as toward a guru. For this very reason, he speaks of "following" (*anuvartana*):

"Following these [elders] through the actions of mind, speech, and body. The wife of the guru is the "guru's wife. The expression "from the mother's side and from the father's side" is intended to indicate the majority of cases, since such [wives] do not exist for kings and others. Manu also spoke with the intention of referring merely to those who are worthy of honor.
One should know that person to be a teacher in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever assists one with their learning, whether it be little or much.
Having initiated him and having imparted the Veda, he is called an Ācārya. || 1.34 ||

He who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda is called an *ācārya*. By the word "Veda" here, other branches of knowledge (*vidyā*) are also included. Thus says Manu: "The twice-born teacher who, having initiated his pupil, teaches him the entire Veda along with its secret portions (*rahasya*), is designated as an *ācārya*."

By the word *kalpa*, the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) such as grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), as well as Mīmāṃsā and Nyāyavistara, are here intended. *Kalpa* determines the meaning of the Veda. And so Vyāsa says:
"A twice-born man should not allow himself to be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Veda;
for one who rests content with the mere recitation sinks like a cow in the mud."
The meaning is that he is one who has mastered only the literal recitation, being ignorant of the underlying sense. || 1.34 ||
Regarding the *upādhyāya*: he who teaches a single portion of the meaning of the Veda is his *upādhyāya*. Manu says: "But [he who teaches] a single portion of the Veda, or even the Vedāṅgas..."
He who teaches for the sake of his livelihood is called an *upādhyāya*.
The officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) is called the "performer of the sacrifice" (*yajñakṛt*).
He who, having been hired by the one entitled to perform the sacrifice for the sake of accomplishing his own sacrifice, becomes the performer of that sacrifice, is called his *ṛtvij*. Manu says:

He who, being chosen by someone, performs for him the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), the cooked sacrifices (pākayajñas), and the sacrifices beginning with the Agniṣṭoma— such a person is here called his officiating priest (ṛtvij).

And that [appointment] is of three kinds. As Hārīta says: "The *kṣīrahotṛ*, the *āhāryavṛta*, and the *viśeṣavṛta*. He states their definitions: "He who takes over someone's sacred fires (*agni*) is his *kṣīrahotṛ*. The meaning of this is: among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) connected with the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), whoever serves as the priest for the fire-oblation (*agnihotra*) is the *kṣīrahotṛ*. Thus says Āśvalāyana: "One may offer the oblation himself on the festival days (*parvan*), while one of the officiating priests performs it at other times. "In the absence of such a person, whomsoever else one chooses for the sake of the obligatory rite is the *āhāryavṛta*. Then, whomsoever else one chooses for successive sacrifices (*kratu*) is the *viśeṣavṛta*. The definition of the officiating priest here is incidental, as it is of no use to the religious student (*brahmacārin*).
"These are to be honored according to seniority":

these elders and others are to be honored—that is, revered—according to seniority, meaning without overstepping the order of precedence, they are to be honored by salutations, clasping the feet, and so forth, each succeeding one being more venerable than the preceding.
Of these, the mother is the most venerable. || 1.35 ||

The meaning is that among these—beginning with the teacher and others—the mother alone deserves the highest degree of reverence. Gautama, however, speaks of the reverence due to the mother and the teacher: "The teacher is the best among gurus; some say the mother. In this context, the word *guru* is used figuratively (*aupacārika*). As stated in the Purāṇa: "In this world, according to dharma, there are two gurus for a man: his father and his mother. Of these two, the father is superior, because of the perceived primacy of the seed."
The absence of these two is better: a teacher who is fully discerning;
for all these [students] are independent, yet always dependent upon others.
In matters of instruction, distribution, or sale, they are considered masters.

This being the case, when there is a conflict between the commands of the father, the mother, and the teacher regarding matters of contradictory purpose, the father’s command is weightier; in his absence, that of the mother; and in her absence, that of the teacher. Furthermore, Manu states that the teacher’s command is even weightier than the father’s command:
"Between the biological progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is weightier;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both in this world and after death."
The teacher is the giver of the Veda. 1.35.
He states the duration of the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*):
"The studentship for each Veda is twelve years or five;
some say it lasts until [the text] has been mastered."
The student life (*brahmacarya*) has been described; it must be observed for twelve years, five years, or until the mastery of the Veda for each Veda and each recensional branch (*śākhā*). Manu says:
"The vow of the three Vedas (*traividyaka-vrata*) consists of a thirty-six-year course of study under a guru;
or half of that, or a quarter, or even until the [Veda] is grasped."

In the case of one who masters half the Veda, it is six years; in the case of one who masters a quarter, it is three years; this constitutes the period of celibate studentship (*brahmacarya*) for a single Veda. Yama says:
"Even a guru—if he is arrogant, ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done, or has set out upon a wrong path—his abandonment is ordained."
And the tonsure ceremony (keśānta) takes place in the sixteenth year. || 1.36 ||

In the sixteenth year, the sacrament called Keśānta (the tonsure) must be performed for a Brāhmaṇa; for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, however, it is as stated by Manu: "The Keśānta is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in the sixteenth year, for a member of the royal caste (Kṣatriya) in the twenty-second, and for a Vaiśya two years after that."

This number of years begins from birth; had it been intended to begin from conception, he would have said "the sixteenth from conception," as in the expression "the eighth from conception. However, since only the number is mentioned, birth alone is the limit, as in the phrase "in the eighth year. (1.36)
The time for the initiation ceremony for the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya classes extends beyond the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth year respectively. (1.37)

The time for the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Brāhmaṇa is from birth until the sixteenth year; the meaning is that beyond this point, that time no longer exists. Likewise, it is until the twenty-second year for a Kṣatriya and until the twenty-fourth for a Vaiśya. This prefix *ā* is used in the sense of inclusive limit (*abhividhi*). As Vyāsa has said:
"The period for initiation extends up to the sixteenth year for one [the Brāhmaṇa];
for another [the Kṣatriya], it extends up to the twenty-second; and for the other [the Vaiśya], it extends up to the twenty-fourth."
If this [prescribed] time has passed for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, they become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vrātyas, and are censured by the righteous. || 1.37 ||

He states what happens for those whose time for initiation has passed: "Beyond this point, all three of these, if not initiated at the proper time, become fallen from the Sāvitrī, outcasts (vrātyas), except by means of the Vrātyastoma sacrifice. (1.38)

The twice-born who have not been initiated become ineligible for all religious duties after sixteen, twenty-two, and twenty-four years respectively, unless they perform the sacrifice known as the *vrātyastoma*. They are designated as *vrātyas*, meaning those who have fallen from the *sāvitrī*. The *vrātyastoma* is a sacrificial rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*) for *vrātyas*. Having performed their atonement through that sacrifice, or through the *auhālaka-vrata* and other such observances, and having been initiated, they become eligible for religious duties and fit for social interaction with others. As Manu says: "One must never, even in times of distress, [perform rites] with these [twice-born] who have not been purified according to the rule."
O Brāhmaṇa, he may enter into matrimonial alliances with other Brāhmaṇas.

From the statement "by those who are unpurified," it is understood that there is no fault in social interaction with those who have performed penance. Here, however, in the reading "excluded from all dharmas," the word *dharma* refers to the duties of the twice-born (*dvijāti*), and not to the duties of the [specific] castes (*varṇa*), because the status of being a caste (*varṇatva*) has not been lost for the *vrātyas*. (1.38)
In this regard, he states the reason for their exclusion from the dharma of the twice-born:

"Since they are born first from the mother and a second time from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are therefore remembered as the twice-born (dvija). (1.39)

Brāhmaṇas and the other [castes] are born first from their mothers; secondly, from the tying of the girdle of muñja grass. Therefore, these are remembered as "twice-born" (dvija) by Manu and others. Here, the word "secondly" is an adverbial modifier of the action. Consequently, because they have not been initiated, the vrātyas are not twice-born. For this reason, it is stated that they lack the entitlement to the duties of the twice-born. || 1.39 ||
For the twice-born, the Veda alone is the supreme means for attaining the highest good, whether through sacrifices, austerities, or indeed auspicious deeds.

Among sacrifices—such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*)—and among austerities—such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances—as well as among other actions that yield auspicious fruits, the Veda alone is supreme, most excellent, and the bringer of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). The determination of the Veda’s superiority over actions such as sacrifice might appear untenable; therefore, by the word "Veda," the study of the Veda is indicated. Its status as supreme among sacrifices and the like is appropriate, both because it brings about the highest good and because it makes known that which leads to the highest good. Thus says Manu: "Indeed, he performs the highest austerity even unto the tips of his nails."
That twice-born man who, even while wearing a garland, studies his own Veda daily to the best of his ability;
The syntactical connection is: "He performs supreme austerity even unto the tips of his nails. Likewise:
"One should constantly recite the Veda itself at the proper times without weariness; for they declare that to be his supreme duty; any other is called a secondary duty. (1.40)
Here he states the reason:
"The twice-born who studies the Ṛgveda verses daily shall satisfy the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. (1.41)
The twice-born who studies the Rigvedic verses every day satisfies the gods with honey and milk, and the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. 1.41.
The twice-born who studies the Yajus mantras every day according to his ability gratifies the gods with clarified butter and nectar, and the ancestors with ghee and honey. (1.42)
He who studies the Yajus formulas according to his ability gratifies the gods with clarified butter and nectar, and the ancestors with ghee and honey. 1.42.
He who recites this every day shall satisfy the gods with Soma and clarified butter;
and he shall provide satisfaction for the ancestors with honey and ghee.
He who recites the Sāman hymns every day shall satisfy the gods with soma and clarified butter, and the ancestors with honey and ghee.
[70] He who studies daily according to his ability the dialogues (vākovākya), the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsī verses, the Gāthās, the Itihāsas, and likewise the sciences (vidyā); || 1.45 ||
He provides the gods with a satiating meal of meat, milk-rice,
and honey, and likewise satisfies the ancestors with honey and clarified butter.

*Vākovākya* is a portion of the Veda consisting of questions and counter-questions. *Purāṇa* is well known. *Nārāśaṃsīs* are the three verses beginning with "This, O people, hear" (*idaṃ janā upaśruta*), studied among the supplementary texts (*khila*) of the Ṛgveda. *Gāthās* are the songs of Indra and others. *Itihāsas* are the *Mahābhārata* and similar works. *Vidyās* are the sciences such as the *Madhuvidyā*. He who studies these daily according to his ability performs the satiation of the gods with honeyed rice-porridge and milk, and the gratification of the ancestors with honey and clarified butter. (1.45–46)
Being satisfied, they satisfy him with all auspicious fruits of action.
Those gods and others, being satisfied in the manner described, satisfy the one who has offered libations with all desired fruits.
Whatever sacrifice he may study, he shall obtain the fruit of each of them. (1.47)
A *kratu* is that portion of the Veda which sets forth a ritual sacrifice; he who studies it obtains the fruit of that sacrifice. || 1.47 ||
The twice-born who is constantly devoted to the private recitation of the Veda enjoys here the fruit of three earths filled with wealth and of the highest austerity.

A twice-born man who constantly practices the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) of the Veda obtains the fruit of that supreme austerity which consists of the gift of the entire earth filled with wealth, performed three times over. The direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) regarding [the rewards for] honey, milk, and so forth, is the very root of this. Since that [revelation] serves as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) for the injunction to study the Veda as a sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), the injunction for the *brahmayajña* must be inferred here; for without it, the explanatory praise would be purposeless. And since that injunction applies even to the religious student (*brahmacārin*), the passage begins in the section concerning him: "Restrained, near water, having resorted to the daily rule."
"Having gone to the forest, one should study even the Sāvitrī with a concentrated mind.
Therefore, one who is incapable [of reciting the entire Veda] should perform the Brahmayajña with the Sāvitrī; one who is capable [should do so] with the Ṛg-verses and so forth. 1.48.

Indeed, there are two kinds of religious students (*brahmacārin*): the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*) and the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*). Among them, the duties of the temporary student have been stated; now he speaks of the lifelong student: [71] The lifelong student shall dwell in the presence of his teacher;
in his absence, in the teacher's son, in his wife, or even in the sacred fire (7.49).

The *upakurvāṇaka* student may dwell in whichever stage of life he desires. If, therein, he should desire the stage of lifelong studentship (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*), then he becomes a lifelong student. "Niṣṭhā" means the fall of the body; he is a lifelong student who has made a resolve to observe studentship until that limit. He shall continue to live in the presence of his teacher and not perform the return ceremony (*samāvartana*). In the absence of the teacher, he lives with the teacher's son; in his absence, with the teacher's wife; and in her absence, with the sacred fire. (1.49)
Regarding the fruit obtained by one dwelling there, he says:
"Practicing this discipline for the sake of the body, having conquered the senses, one attains the world of Brahmā and is not born here again. (1.50)

By means of this aforementioned practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), one who perfects the body—that is, the embodied self—making it fit for the attainment of Brahman, becomes a master with conquered senses and reaches the world of the Four-Faced One (Brahmā); he is not born again in this cycle of transmigration. For one who is a devotee of Brahman, the fruit characterized by non-returning occurs; it does not belong to mere ritual action alone. As it is said in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad* concerning the stages of life (*āśramas*): "All these attain worlds of merit; he who is established in Brahman attains immortality. The meaning of this is: all these four classes of practitioners belonging to the branches of Brahman, though they be in the various stages of life, attain worlds of merit. Among them, he who is "established in Brahman"—that is, fixed in Brahman—attains immortality, which is characterized by non-returning. Hārīta says: "The student (*brahmacārī*) is of two kinds: the temporary (*upakurvāṇa*) and the lifelong (*naiṣṭhika*). Of these, the temporary has been explained. If he should pursue the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhā*), he should remain with his teacher until the fall of the body. In the absence of the teacher, he should serve the teacher’s wife; in her absence, the teacher’s son; and in the absence of the teacher’s son, he should attend upon the sacred fire itself. Having gathered sacrificial fuel-sticks, he should serve the fire through sweeping, smearing, kindling, stirring, adding fuel, circumambulation, standing near, offering oblations, chanting hymns, and prostrations. He should not step over the fire, nor drag it with his feet, nor blow on it with his mouth, nor hold both fire and water simultaneously. When he has not yet digested his food or is impure from eating, he should not add fuel, nor should he pass between the fires. He should not spit. Day after day, he should kindle the fire with various offerings of cooked rice and oblations dedicated to Agni. Having taken leave, he may go out, and having returned, he should report his actions. With his mind fixed on that, at the end of the body's dissolution, he attains union (*sāyujya*) with Brahman. Vasiṣṭha says: "A student should attend to the stage of life until liberation from the body. When the teacher has died, he should attend to the fire, restrained in speech, eating at the fourth, sixth, or eighth meal-time, dependent on the teacher for alms, wearing matted hair—either in a single lock or in several—and likewise approaching the water three times a day. Devala says: "Eating once a day, bathing once in the water, performing the *agnihotra* twice daily, and the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*). He must avoid: breaking the skin, hair, nails, or skin; using perfumes, garlands, oils, ointments, dress, ornaments, umbrellas, shoes, or vehicles; jumping, swimming, running, medical treatment, astrology, architecture, auspicious rites, nourishing rites, pacifying rites, association with musicians, making binding agreements, crafts, painting, writing, manual labor, house-building, fields, goods, wealth, grain, household utensils, weapons, gambling, legal disputes, giving commands, play, joking, affectionate dalliance, deception, causing wonder, mockery, quarrels, arrogance, lamentation, weeping, enemas, nasal drops, rubbing the feet, and so forth. Rising before the teacher, retiring later, performing prostrations and carrying out instructions, serving him in desired ways, constant attendance, and honoring him; in his absence, following this same conduct toward his son or wife, until death. If, in an emergency, the teacher happens to be a Kṣatriya or another caste, there should be no permanent residence with him. The same applies even to a Brāhmaṇa who does not perform the teaching of the Vedas. As Manu says: *(Note: The provided text ends here, so the final citation from Manu is not included in the translation.)*
A student who desires the highest goal should not dwell for life with a teacher who is not a Brāhmaṇa, nor with a Brāhmaṇa who has not mastered the Vedas.

It should not be argued that the *smṛti* concerning the excellence of *brahmacarya* contradicts the *śruti* that prescribes the duties of a householder, such as the *agnihotra*, because their subject matters are distinct. For the *śruti* regarding the *agnihotra* and so forth applies to one who has entered into marriage out of passion for women; whereas the *smṛti* on *brahmacarya* applies to a person who, due to dispassion or defects such as blindness, is ineligible for marriage. It is for this very reason that Manu speaks of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhikatva*) as being optional: "A disciple seeking the highest goal should not dwell permanently with a non-Brāhmaṇa teacher, nor even with a Brāhmaṇa who is not learned in the Vedas."

Nor should one allege a contradiction with the Vedic injunctions prescribing the duties of a householder, such as the *agnihotra*, for the *brahmacarya-smṛti* (the rule of celibacy), because their respective scopes are different. For the Vedic texts concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth apply to one who has married under the influence of passion for women; whereas the *brahmacarya-smṛti* applies to a person who, due to dispassion or defects such as blindness, is ineligible for marriage. For this very reason, Manu speaks of lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhikatva*) as being optional: "But if he should prefer to dwell permanently with his teacher's family, he should serve him with devotion until the liberation of the body."
And likewise Viṣṇu says:

"For those who are humpbacked, dwarfs, born blind, eunuchs, lame, afflicted, or diseased, there shall be the performance of vows for as long as they live, but without a share [of the inheritance]. [73]

Furthermore, Dakṣa states that even for those who have performed marriage and other rites, who are not yet in a formal stage of life (*anāśramin*), and who are devoted to the recitation of mantras and austerity, staying [without an āśrama] is not appropriate:
"A twice-born man should not remain without an āśrama for even a single year;
for he who remains without an āśrama becomes liable to perform penance."
One who is always devoted to recitation, fire-offerings, charity, and self-study,
yet has fallen away from his stage of life (āśrama), does not obtain the fruit even while performing these acts.
He himself has stated that, by proceeding from one stage of life (āśrama) to another, one should not accept what was previously rejected:
"There may be a forward progression through the three [lower stages], but no retrogression; there is no greater sinner than he who goes against the natural order. (1.50)

Thus ends the section on the student (the *brahmacārikāṇḍa*) in the legal compendium (*nibandha*) on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, who himself arose from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas. Now begins [the section] in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.

The section on studentship (*brahmacāri-prakaraṇa*) has been stated as being common to all; now, the duties of the householder (*gṛhastha-dharma*), which have reached their proper occasion, are being described. And these are as follows: "O King, a man who is without a wife does not become fit for [sacred] rites."
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, O King.
"A wife is the foremost cause for men to attain dharma, artha, and kāma" (74).
From such observations as these, [these goals] do not exist without a wife. And since she [the wife] appears after the time of the ritual bath, he says:
"But having given a gift to the teacher, or with his permission, one should bathe."
Having brought either the Veda or the vows, or indeed both, to completion.

Having brought both the Veda and the vows to completion according to the previously stated method, he should perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). The arrangement among these various options depends upon one's capacity, the time available, and other such factors. If, due to illness, he is unable to go on alms-rounds and so forth, or if he is incapable of resisting royal or divine calamities, then he may bathe after completing only the Veda or only the vows. For this very reason, a threefold classification is recorded in the Smṛtis: the *vidyā-snātaka* (one who has bathed after learning), the *vrata-snātaka* (one who has bathed after the vows), and the *vidyā-vrata-snātaka* (one who has bathed after both learning and the vows). Therefore, for such a person, the completion of study or the knowledge of its meaning occurs at a time subsequent to the bath and marriage. For this same reason, the author will state later:
Having introduced the subject with the words, "A householder should perform the rites prescribed by the Smṛti every day in the nuptial fire," it continues:
"He should master the meanings of the Vedas and various other scriptures."
Furthermore, the knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas must necessarily be acquired. Thus Vyāsa says:
"A twice-born man should not allow himself to be satisfied with the mere recitation of the Veda;
for one who rests content with recitation alone sinks like a cow in the mud."
Just as a beast of burden does not obtain the fruit of its labor,
so too a twice-born man who lacks understanding of the meaning does not enjoy the fruit of the Vedas.
All study of the Veda and likewise all study of the Dharmaśāstra,
if done by one who does not understand their meaning, is like the threshing of husks.
He who, having studied the Veda according to the prescribed rules, does not reflect upon the meaning of the Veda,
is equal to a Śūdra along with his lineage and does not attain the status of a worthy recipient.
Having studied even a little, one who is devoted to comprehending the meaning of the Vedas and knows how to perform religious duties attains the heavenly world.
That which one studies devoid of sacred learning (śruta) will be of no benefit either in this world or the next;
however, even sacred learning alone is sufficient for one's complete deliverance.
Even a small amount of learning that has been properly accumulated and mastered is superior to the mere recitation of the Vedas by one of the three twice-born classes.
Just as knowledge and action combined are said to lead to liberation, so too, when joined with the sacred learning one has studied, they are supreme; not by themselves alone.
A wise person should not honor, even with mere words, those twice-born who are constantly afflicted by their studies alone and deprived of wealth, treating them as if they were mere cattle.
Even after studying a single quarter-verse of the Rigveda at the outset, one who knows its meaning according to the proper method excels;
for sacred learning is the weightiest means for accomplishing dharma.
And there is a scriptural passage:
"This man is like a pillar, a mere carrier of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning.
But he who knows the meaning attains all that is auspicious; his sins shaken off by knowledge, he goes to the heavenly realm."

They say that a withered tree is a mere stump. Just as it becomes burdened by the load of grass and other things placed upon it, yet does not obtain any consciousness of bearing the weight or the experience of the load—whereas a living being alone, by virtue of being the support for the load, becomes the bearer of the load—so too is this person: one whose self is distressed by the study of the Veda ending in its memorization, yet who does not understand what is expressed therein—the division of injunctions, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), mantras, and names—nor even now exerts himself toward the knowledge thereof. However, he who has now attained the understanding of the meaning is, because of his qualification and the fulfillment of ritual action, as well as through vigilance regarding expiations for lapses and proficiency in his own duties, seen to enjoy in its entirety the auspicious fruit of merit. And by means of the secondary merit produced from the knowledge of the meaning—which destroys defects such as the obstruction of all paths, both seen and unseen—he reaches the "No-High" (*nāka*) up to the world of truth (*satyaloka*), having dispelled the accumulated sins (*dūrita*). Thus it is said: [The verse follows: *śuṣkavṛkṣaṃ sthāṇum āhuḥ...* [etc. Thus it is.
One man, though seeing, has not perceived Speech; another, though hearing, does not hear her.
But to yet another she has revealed her body, as a longing wife, beautifully robed, reveals herself to her husband.

The meaning of this is: indeed, one person, though seeing, does not see; indeed, another, though hearing, does not hear—this speech of great significance, being ignorant of it. But to him [who knows], Speech reveals her own body; she discloses her form like a lovingly-desiring, well-dressed wife to her husband. Just as a wife, desiring her husband, reveals her own self while beautifully attired, even so does Speech reveal her own self to the knower of Speech. And Manu says: "That which is studied but not understood is merely recited as a chant;
like dry fuel in a fireless place, it never blazes forth."

And so forth. Furthermore, since the requirement for one following the *smārta* (tradition-based) path is merely a thorough knowledge of the *Gṛhya-sūtras* and similar texts, and that thorough knowledge does not arise from listening to other treatises and the like—because such a person requires only an understanding of the sequence of rituals and so on—if one were ineligible for everything without listening to other treatises, then a religious student (*brahmacārin*) would likewise be ineligible for the fire-rituals (*agnikārya*) and other such duties. Therefore, whatever one performs, one does so having known it, but not by knowing everything simultaneously. Thus, this injunction—"having known, one should perform"—is also accepted. As for how he should bathe, he says: "To the guru," as previously mentioned, "the desired boon" (*vara*), as stated by Kātyāyana and others: "A cow is the boon for a Brāhmaṇa, a village for a Kṣatriya, a horse for a Vaiśya," and so on; this refers to the capacity to provide for the guru's needs and the like, whether that be something other than those or otherwise.
One should bring grain, garments, and vegetables to please the teacher;

having given such things as specified by Manu and others, or even without giving them if permitted by him, [one may perform the bath]. For this very reason, Gautama says: "At the end of his studies, the teacher is to be invited with a gift, or for one who has received permission, there is the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). The mastery of the Veda is indeed a combination of the study of the Veda together with the knowledge of its meaning. Therefore, it is recorded in the Smṛti: "Having studied the Veda and understood the meanings pertaining to the meters, one should bathe. Manu also [says the same].

"By means of various specific austerities and vows prescribed by rule, the entire Veda, together with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born"—thus [the text] shows that it must be mastered both in terms of the words and their meaning. And "by means of vows" refers to those previously mentioned, such as those set forth in the passage beginning, "One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, and garlands. Consequently, this is what was stated by Bhaṭṭa:
Therefore, it is understood that one staying in the teacher's household and avoiding honey, meat, and the like,
practices dharma because such inquiry is not in contradiction [with dharma].
Thus, this [statement] contradicts that [previous one], because those [duties] are specifically prescribed for the period following the return home (*samāvartana*). For this very reason, it is said:

"A twice-born person who has undergone initiation (*upanayana*) shall perform the kindling of the sacred fires, the practice of begging for alms, sleeping on the ground, and what is beneficial for the teacher, until his return home."
Thus it is restricted. Furthermore, one who has not returned from the teacher's house is certainly not called a *snātaka*;
therefore, one should not entertain the misconception that the *snāna* rite is identical to the *samāvartana*.
Having been permitted by his teacher and having performed the ceremonial bath according to the rules,
the twice-born man, upon returning home, shall marry a wife of the same caste who possesses auspicious marks.

Thus, because of the recollection of this distinction, the *snātaka* has been demonstrated by Manu and others: "One should first honor with a cow that son who is recognized for his own duty (*svadharma*), who inherits the father's Veda-wealth (*brahmadāya*), and who is seated upon the couch wearing a garland. [77]

That *snātaka*—known for being intent on taking a wife and entitled to inherit his father’s *brahmadāya* (the Veda); by this, his fitness for study is indicated; *dāya* means inheritance, by which his eligibility is expressed. Otherwise, even a son of a woman from all castes (*sarvarṇā*), if he has acted improperly, does not receive it; thus, in the absence of such [legitimacy], there would be no [inheritance]. If the father lacks wealth, he should perform the marriage ceremony even after acquiring it through gifts and other means, and he should attend to the *gṛhya* rites beginning with the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). Otherwise, the *pākayajña* and other rites would remain unaccomplished, since they are rooted in material wealth. For this very reason, Gautama says: "The acquisition of wealth is for the sake of accomplishing marriage. The mention of the garland (*sraj*) is for the purpose of obtaining ornaments. *Talpa* means a bed. One should honor—that is, worship—the one situated there first with a cow. By the word "cow," the *madhuparka* is indicated, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "Having chosen the officiating priests, one should bring the *madhuparka* for the *snātaka* who has arrived, and for the king. That [offering] becomes twofold: either intending to cause [the cow] to be given, saying "give [her]," or intending to release her, saying "let her loose.
