One should know these nine types of *snātaka* Brāhmaṇas who beg for alms for the sake of dharma: one who maintains his lineage, one who intends to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who possesses all his Vedic knowledge, one seeking funds for his teacher, one seeking funds for his father or mother, one seeking funds for Vedic study, and one who is afflicted by illness. (1.51)
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

Having remained chaste in his student life, he should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks—one who has not belonged to another before, who is beautiful, who is not a sapinda relative, and who is younger than himself. (1.52)

He whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has not been violated at all—*vipluti* meaning a lapse—is not subject to penance (*prāyaścitta*), nor is he ineligible for marriage; however, there is this distinction: if he has violated it prior to the ceremonial bath (*snāna*), then the penance of an *avakīrṇin* applies, according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): "An *avakīrṇin* is that celibate student who, having gone to a woman, has spilled his seed. But if it occurs after the bath, then the general penance applies.
If she drinks liquor, is untruthful in her conduct, is hostile,
or is afflicted by disease, she may be superseded.
Likewise,
having offered the sacred fires to a wife who has died before him during the funeral rites,
he may again perform the act of taking a wife.

Because of the observation of such traditional injunctions (*smaraṇa*), there is a danger that a marriage already contracted might become nullified due to the resulting impairment of one's celibacy (*brahmacarya*). To prevent this contingency, the phrase "one whose celibacy is unimpaired" (*aviplutabrahmacarya*) must be understood as a qualification of the person performing the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) mentioned previously. "She should be endowed with auspicious marks" (*lakṣaṇairyuktām*). These marks are both external and internal. The external ones pertain to the body, voice, and so forth. As Manu says:
"One who has no deficient limbs, bears an agreeable name, walks like a swan or an elephant, has fine hair on her body and head, soft limbs, and speaks sweetly. (MDh 3.10)

The phrase "of ten [types] of ten" means this. A girl who possesses auspicious characteristics (*lakṣaṇyā*) should be chosen, but one who is the opposite of these should be rejected, as it is said: "One should not marry a tawny (*kapilā*) girl, nor one with extra limbs, nor one who is diseased;
nor one without body hair, nor one with excessive hair, nor one who is talkative, nor one who is reddish-brown (*piṅgalā*)."
Likewise, she should be avoided even by name, as it is said:
"One should avoid for the sake of a wife a woman named after a deity, a river, a mountain, or a gandharva; one should avoid her whose name is that of a bear, a tree, or a river."

For example: [One should not marry] a girl whose name is that of a constellation, a tree, or a river; nor one named after an outcaste or a mountain; nor one named after a bird, a snake, or a flower; nor one named Vibhīṣaṇā.

When, however, the internal [signs] are subtle, then the examination prescribed by Āśvalāyana should be performed. In that regard, having stated, "She who is endowed with the characteristics of intelligence," he himself raises an objection: "The characteristics are difficult to discern. The answer to this is: "Having made eight lumps [of earth], one should consecrate the lumps with the mantra: 'In the beginning, *ṛta* was born first; upon *ṛta*, *satya* is established. If this maiden is of noble birth, let her here choose that which is *satya*; let that which is *satya* be seen. Then he should say to the maiden, 'Take one of these. If she takes from a field, one should know that her offspring will be possessed of both kinds of *satya*. From a cow-pen, she will be rich in cattle. From the soil of a sacrificial altar (*vedipurīṣa*), she will be radiant with Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcas*). From an inexhaustible pool, she will be endowed with everything. From a gambling ground, she will be a gambler. From a crossroads, she will be prone to wandering. From barren soil, she will be unfortunate. From a cemetery, she will be a killer of her husband. [Regarding the phrase] "one who has not belonged to another before" (*ananyapūrvikā*), meaning one who has not previously been given to another—this should be understood as referring to a girl betrothed by word (*vāgdattā*), and not to one who has already undergone the sacramental rites (*saṃskṛtā*), because the latter is considered a remarried woman (*punarbhū*). As Manu says: [Manu 9.69–70].
If the husband of a maiden should die after the verbal betrothal has been made true,
her own brother-in-law shall marry her according to this procedure.
Nor should it be suspected that the giving of the bride-price (dāna) is thereby nullified in that case.
If the groom should die first after the bride has been given with water and speech,
but she has not yet been led away by the mantras, she remains the daughter of her father alone.

Thus, according to the Smṛti of Vasiṣṭha. The same should be understood even in the case of one who has been abducted by force: "A girl who has been abducted by force is not consecrated even by mantras; she is to be given to another according to the prescribed rule, just like a maiden."

Because this has been stated by that very [author]. And this should be understood as occurring after the performance of the penance (*prāyaścitta*). A "beloved" (*kāntā*) is so called because she is desirable, providing delight to the mind and the eyes. And this is prescribed by way of excluding those who are inauspicious and the like, based on the injunction: "One should marry her upon whom one's mind is fixed. He will later explain *sāpiṇḍya* for those who are not *sapiṇḍas*. Some say she should be younger both in terms of birth and in stature. Vasiṣṭha says: "A householder, having subdued anger and joy, being permitted by his teacher, having bathed, should take a wife who is of a different *ārṣeya*, who has not had sexual intercourse, who is younger in age, and of equal status. The term "householder" (*gṛhastha*) here is a metaphorical designation of what is to be (the future) as if it were already accomplished, for the purpose of attaining those duties. By this, even one who has not yet married, provided he intends to enter the householder stage and has turned away from other stages of life (*āśrama*), is qualified for the duties of a householder. Nor is it restricted by the rule: "Having been a student (*brahmacārī*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, a forest-dweller (*vanī*); having been a forest-dweller, a renunciant (*pravrajita*)," because we see the adoption of other stages of life without such a restriction. Thus says the Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa.
"Having given the teacher his fee, he should dwell with whomever he wishes; once he has become dispassionate, the wise man should renounce. Thus says the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Having acquired knowledge and then offered the teacher’s fee to the guru,
O protector of the earth, one who desires the householder’s life should take a wife.
Or he may pass away while practicing celibacy according to his resolve;
or else, he should perform service to his guru, or even to the guru’s son or other [disciples].
"Or he may become a forest-dweller (vaikhānasa), or alternatively, a wandering mendicant (parivrāj) according to his desire. Thus [ends verse 1.52].
He states further qualifications:
[One should marry] a woman who is free from disease, has brothers, and is not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*;
likewise, she must be beyond the fifth degree on the mother’s side and the seventh degree on the father’s side. (1.53)
She should be healthy and not afflicted by a chronic disease; she must have brothers, out of fear that she might be designated as an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). As Manu has said:
[80] "A wise man should not marry a girl who has no brother, or whose father is unknown, for fear that she might be an appointed daughter according to the law."
By this means, even a girl who has been kept secret becomes [one's own]; not only one who is given after being formally designated with the words:
"The son who is born of her shall be my son."

Thus, a wife whose fruit is pleasure and sons suffers a deficiency of one limb if the son belongs to another. He will speak of the *putrikā* (appointed daughter) later. It should be understood that the phrase "not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra*" (*asamānārṣagotrajām*) means "not born of the same *ṛṣi*" and "not born of the same *gotra*. Consequently, the prohibition regarding a woman of the same *gotra* is based solely on her being of the same *gotra*, not with regard to having the same *ṛṣi*. Likewise, even a woman with the same *ṛṣi* does not depend on having the same *gotra*. For this very reason, Gautama says: "Marriage is with those who do not have the same *pravara*. And "sameness" occurs through the combination of both name and number; it does not occur when there is a discrepancy between them. Even where there is equality of number, if there is a difference of one or two, there too there is simply "non-sameness. Furthermore, where the *ṛṣis* are optional—such as *Āṅgirasa-Ambarīṣa-Yauvanāśva* versus *Māndhātṛ-Ambarīṣa-Yauvanāśva*—there too she is to be avoided, because the state of sameness is only partial (*pākṣika*). Moreover, the mention of "not having the same *ṛṣi*" is not a qualification of the *gotra*, because of the traditional teaching of their distinction: "Marriage is with those who do not have the same *pravara*."
But having married a woman of the same lineage (sagotrā) or likewise one with the same ancestral invocation (samānapravarā),
a twice-born man should abandon her and then perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

This is also because there are separate penances [for each]. Furthermore, there is the abandonment of the *upabhoga* (enjoyment/sexual union), but not of her [the woman herself]. Thus Sumantu says: "Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, the daughter of a paternal aunt, or one of the same *ārṣa* lineage or *gotra*, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance; having abandoned her, he should maintain her. This should be understood as applying when it was done unintentionally (*amatipūrva*). Baudhāyana states: "If one approaches a woman of the same *gotra* unintentionally, he should maintain her like a sister; if she has given birth, he should perform a quarter of a year-long *Kṛcchra* penance. If it was intentional (*matipūrva*), the penance is more severe. As Gautama says: "Those related by the womb of the mother or father, an atheist, one who performs censured acts, an outcast (*patita*), one who abandons those who should not be abandoned, and one who abandons an outcast—these are outcasts. Manu also [says the same].

"They are not to be approached as kinswomen; for by approaching them, one falls downward. From this, it follows that one born of a fallen woman is indeed fallen. Now, an objection may be raised: since the prohibition of *sapiṇḍa* women is already established by the exclusion of those of the same *gotra*, why is it stated separately in the subsequent verse, "one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* and is younger"? The answer is: no; this is for the purpose of excluding those born in her lineage. Otherwise, a girl born in the lineage of a woman who is not born of the same *ṛṣi* or *gotra* might become eligible for marriage. And this status of being a non-*sapiṇḍa* should be understood to apply to the mother's side as well, as Manu says:
She who is not a sapinda of the mother and not of the same gotra as the father is recommended for the twice-born in the matter of marriage and sexual union.

"She who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother"—the word "and" (*ca*) implies [not being a *sapiṇḍa*] of the father as well. If only this much were said, namely "she who is not of the same lineage (*asagotrā*"), the reason he specifically mentions the father is with reference to the son of a woman belonging to another (a *kṣetrika* son). Otherwise, those [sons] would belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to the other.

Thus, there would be the marriageability of one who belongs to the same *gotra*. She is recommended for what? For the act of taking a wife (*dārakarma*), that which cannot be accomplished without a wife. And lest that [marriage] occur merely by [general] statement, he says: "In sexual union" (*maithune*), that which is to be accomplished through the couple (*mithuna*) and not by either one individually, such as the *pākayajña* and other rites. Therefore Āpastamba says: "For from the grasping of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*), there is jointness in ritual acts. The mention of "jointly" (*saha*) is for the purpose of showing that they have equal entitlement (*samānādhikāra*), like two oxen yoked together. Consequently, she is to be supported by the husband with the thought, "I shall perform the giving and so forth; you too must make the resolve"; and she too must act in the same way, otherwise there is a fault—thus there is joint entitlement. And from this follows the sharing of the enjoyment of a single fruit and the sublation of the arising of separate fruits. By the rule, "And she who is not a *sapinda* of the mother," the prohibition against marrying the daughter of a maternal uncle and others is established, because she is a *sapinda* of the mother.
Beyond the fifth and the seventh [generation] on the mother's side, and likewise on the father's side.

Thus, the meaning is that marriage should be performed—that is, it ought to be done—after passing over five generations on the mother’s side, beginning with the maternal grandfather. Likewise, seven on the father’s side. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says under the heading "one should not take a wife": "On the mother’s side up to the fifth person, and on the father’s side up to the seventh. Now, one might ask: since it has already been stated "not a *sapiṇḍa*," for what purpose is it stated again "up to the seventh on the father’s side"? True; however, it is for the sake of a restrictive rule (*niyama*) that even in the case of the progenitor (*baijina*), [the limit is] the seventh. As Gautama says: "But beyond the seventh from the paternal kinsmen and beyond the fifth from the maternal kinsmen of the progenitor. Nārada also [says the same].

One should not marry a girl who is within seven generations on the father’s side or five generations on the mother’s side from one’s paternal or maternal relatives; likewise, she must not belong to the same *gotra* or have the same *pravara*.

And Paiṭhīnasi says: "One should choose a maiden who does not share the same *ṛṣi* lineage (*asamānārṣeyī*). One should avoid five generations on the mother’s side and seven on the father’s side; or three on the mother’s side and five on the father’s side. In this regard, the settled option is that one avoids five generations if they are of the same caste (*samānajātīya*), and three if they are of a different caste (*asamānajātīya*). Furthermore, she is not to be married in the seventh or fifth generation, according to the verse: "Those for whom the marriage rite takes place in the seventh or even the fifth [generation], and their descendants as well, are outcasts who have fallen into the state of *Śūdras*."

Thus says Viṣṇu. Furthermore, if the marriage with the daughter of one’s maternal uncle is permissible because they belong to different *gotras*, then the marriage with the daughter of one’s mother’s sister would also be permissible, by virtue of the same logic. This would hold true if the authority belonged solely to the *smṛtis*. However, the authority of the *śiṣṭas* (the learned and virtuous) is also recognized. As Manu has said: "The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the *smṛti* and the conduct (*śīla*) of those who know it, as well as the practice (*ācāra*) of the virtuous and the tradition of those who know the Veda."

By means of this exclusion (*vyatireka*), he demonstrates the conduct of the virtuous (*sādhu*) so that their authority may be established even when there is a contradiction with the scriptures. Otherwise, there would be no separate mention of "character" (*śīla*), "conduct" (*ceṣṭita*), and "behavior" (*ācāra*) of the virtuous as distinct categories. Furthermore, the virtuous have been defined: "Those by whom the Veda, along with its supplements (*paribṛṃhaṇa*), has been mastered according to the proper method—those Brahmins are to be known as the *śiṣṭas*, who are the direct witnesses (*pratyakṣa-hetu*) of the Śruti."

It is not that those learned in the Vedas do not exist there, nor that this practice has not been followed by them; for Baudhāyana has clearly demonstrated the authority of such conduct: "There are five kinds of conflicting practices: to the south, eating with one who is uninitiated, eating with one's wife, eating stale food, eating the leavings of others, and marrying the daughter of a paternal aunt or a maternal uncle. Likewise, there are five to the north: selling wool, drinking *śīdhu* liquor, trading with people of both classes (using coins struck on both sides), being a professional soldier, and sea-voyaging. One commits no fault by performing these in the other region, because they are authoritative in that region; thus, the authority of custom is established through its very force. If Gautama had not stated immediately after this, "But Gautama says this is false," then one might think both should be respected. However, he says, "But one should disregard both of these, because they conflict with the *smṛti* of the learned (*śiṣṭa*). And the conflict with *smṛti* is shown: "Beyond the fifth degree from maternal relatives... and because of the *smṛti* of Vasiṣṭha: "The learned (*śiṣṭa*), moreover, is one whose soul is free from desire. The learned do not act in violation of the scriptures out of mere whim. [83] The mention of Gautama is for the purpose of presenting a single view, as it is not a total rejection. Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Local and family customs are authoritative provided they are not in conflict with the *āmnāya*. *Āmnāya* means the Veda. If it is argued that there is no conflict with it, we say no; for since even sexual intercourse with a sister and so forth would appear to be non-conflicting, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the authority of a practice established through logic does not arise from a blind tradition. As for what was also said...
Come, O Indra, with these thy companions who are worthy of praise; enjoy this sacrifice of ours in the struggle for booty.
They have left thee satisfied, as one leaves the daughter of his maternal uncle; thy fortune has flowed away like the flood of waters, as if to a paternal aunt's daughter.

Thus, although these mantras are not injunctive, they indicate the rejection of marriage. How so? A certain person is being entreated: "O Indra, come to our sacrifice along with those other lords of Soma who have been invoked and are worthy of praise. Having arrived, at the winning of booty—that is, on the occasion of partaking the food consisting of Soma—be pleased. The word "Soma" is connected [to the verb]. Having thus entreated him, the text provides a restatement of his nature for the purpose of praising Indra: "Those lords of Soma who came as your companions, having become satiated by drinking Soma once, abandoned it—they renounced it. Just as one abandons a paternal aunt (the daughter of one's father's sister), who is utterly undesirable as a wife because she is unfit to be related to one's own maternal uncle, so too did they abandon the Soma intended for you, being free from further desire. But this portion of Soma belongs to you alone, like a flood of water, until the completion of the rite. And thus, by this, a prohibition is shown. As for that which is heard in the Śruti: "We go to the third person"—that too is for another purpose, namely, the arrangement of the *snus* (daughter-in-law). Furthermore, because of scriptural passages such as "Prajāpati meditated upon his own daughter and shed seed upon her," it would lead to an over-extension [of the rule]. Moreover, [the practice is forbidden] because of the observation of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
"Having approached a paternal aunt, a sister, a daughter of one's own sister, a mother’s [sister], or a maternal uncle’s wife, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
The mention of "sister" is for the purpose of removing any doubt; nor should it be suspected that this refers only to those who have not been married, since he states immediately thereafter:

"A wise man should not take these three as wives; they are not to be approached because of kinship, for by marrying them he falls low. Likewise, there is a restriction for the giver of the girl as well, as Āpastamba says: "One should not give a daughter to those of the same *gotra*, nor to those related to the mother through birth, nor to those related to the father within seven degrees," and because of the traditional rules regarding penance [for violating this].

"Having married the daughter of a maternal uncle, or likewise one belonging to the mother's *gotra*, or even one having the same *pravara*, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. [84] The mention of "mother's *gotra*" is for the purpose of excluding her just as one excludes the father's *gotra*, because the relationship of progenitor and progeny is indistinguishable in both cases. Śātātapa also says:

"Having married a woman of the same lineage (*gotra*) as well as one of the same *pravara*, and likewise having married the daughter of one's maternal uncle, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
When this is the case, no confusion of mind should arise from any [apparent] explanation, nor should doubt be entertained regarding the activity [of the text], because the scripture is clear. (1.53)
From a great family of Vedic scholars renowned for ten generations,
though prosperous, yet free from the defect of hereditary diseases.

It is prescribed that a girl should be taken from a family renowned for ten generations on the mother’s side and five on the father’s side. As Āśvalāyana says: “One should first examine the family, both on the mother’s and the father’s side. Furthermore, this refers to one from a great family of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*). According to the rule *śrotriyaś chando ’dhīte* (Pāṇini 5.2.84), one becomes a *śrotriya* through the Vedic study mentioned there; thus, it characterizes one who is learned in the sacred revelation. And “from a great family” means from one prosperous with sons, grandsons, cattle, female slaves, villages, and so forth. Since such [qualifications] might otherwise apply to all [families], he states an exception: she should not be taken even from a flourishing family if it is afflicted by contagious diseases. Contagious diseases are those transmitted through semen and blood, such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*), hemorrhoids (*arśas*), and the like; as well as by defects such as impotence and so forth. For this very reason, Manu says:
"Even if they are great and prosperous in terms of cattle, goats, sheep, and grain—one should avoid these ten types of families in forming a marriage alliance. [Thus it is said:
"One whose religious rites are neglected, one who has no male heirs, one devoid of Vedic study, one with excessive body hair, and one afflicted with hemorrhoids..."
"Those suffering from consumption, disease, epilepsy, leucoderma, and those born into families afflicted by leprosy. Thus it is said.

*Hīnakriyam* means devoid of the prescribed rites such as *garbhādhāna* (conception ceremony) and others. *Niṣpuruṣam* means one where there is an abundance of births of daughters and the like. *Niśchandam* means devoid of the study of the Vedas. *Lomaśam* means excessively hairy. *Arśasam* means afflicted with the disease of hemorrhoids (*arśas*). Hārīta also says: "Those families that are afflicted by leucoderma, leprosy, abdominal dropsy, consumption, diseases, short lifespan, or hemorrhoids; those lacking *ārṣeya* (Vedic lineage); and those with a common *ārṣeya*—these families, even if they have not fallen from their status, are to be avoided. Offspring conform to the nature of the family; thus, the first six [types] are excluded. Because they are unfit for sacrifice, they lack *ārṣeya*. Because they are devoid of divinity, they lack *brahma*. Because they belong to a single lineage, they have a common *ārṣeya*. [85] Therefore, having examined seven generations on the father's side and five on the mother's side, one should take as a wife a maiden who is excellent, has brothers, and is endowed with knowledge of her family and *nakṣatra* (birth star). One should choose her accordingly. *Āmayāvin* here refers to one suffering from other contagious diseases. Here, the six beginning with leucoderma are to be avoided. The reason for this is: "Offspring conform to the nature of the family. *Anārṣeyam* means one whose *gotra* and *pravara* (ancestral lineages) are not remembered. Its exclusion is due to its being unfit for sacrifice (*ayajñiya*). It is unfit for sacrifice because one whose *gotra* and *pravara* are not remembered has no entitlement to sacrifices. *Abrahma* means the absence of Vedic study. The reason for its exclusion is "because of the lack of divinity," meaning it is devoid of divine rites. "A *nagnikā* is ten years old," according to the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*. Yama also says the same.

One should declare these fourteen families to be ineligible for marriage; among Brāhmaṇas, one should avoid those who lack a lineage of ancestral seers (anārṣeya) as well as those who serve as officiating priests.
One should avoid those who are excessively tall, excessively short, or of an improper complexion;
as well as those with missing limbs, those with redundant limbs, and those born of diseased families.
One should avoid families of those with vitiligo, leprosy, and the like;
one should always avoid families of those driven by lust and those who are excessively hairy; as well as families of those suffering from epilepsy and those who suffer from jaundice.
In this context, *ṛtvijas* refers to censurable priests. *Kāmakula* means a family in which lust predominates. *Ativarṇa* means excessively dark or excessively fair. || 1.54 ||

Furthermore: A bridegroom of the same caste who possesses these very qualities, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), carefully examined for virility, young, wise, and beloved by the people, is the best. (1.55)

A bridegroom who is endowed with these aforementioned qualities and free from defects is excellent, provided he is of the same caste or of a higher caste and is a *śrotriya* (learned in the Vedas). He must be carefully examined for virility, because that is the root of the purpose of manhood. And the examination is as stated by Nārada:
"A man should be examined for virility by his own bodily characteristics;
if he is found to be fully virile, he is worthy to receive a maiden."
His collarbones, knees, and bones are well-knit; his shoulders and hair are firm;
his temples are large; his skin is thin; and his gait and voice are unhindered.
If his semen floats upon the water, and his urine is clear and frothy, he shall be a male by these characteristics; one who possesses the opposite traits is a eunuch.
[86] Sixteen types of impotence have been observed by the wise in the treatise;
the method for their treatment, both curable and incurable, has been explained in due order.
One who is naturally impotent, one who is castrated, and likewise one whose testicles have been removed;
as well as one who has become so through a teacher’s curse, through disease, or likewise through the wrath of the gods.
The jealous man, the eunuch, he whose semen flows through the urethra, he whose vulva is in his mouth,
the one whose seed is ejected involuntarily, the one whose seed flows like a torrent, the modest man, and likewise the husband of another woman.
In that regard, one should perform the first two remedies for the duration of a month known as a *pakṣa*;
the time for this triad is traditionally held to be a year.
The other four [defects] that have been proclaimed— envy, ignorance, and so forth—
must be abandoned by a woman who has lost her virginity, just as one would abandon a fallen man.
If a husband has been superseded by the force of a flood or by the seed [of another], even though he has performed his marital duties,
the woman must wait for half a year before taking another husband.
Even for a man of noble birth, the penis falls away through union with a wanton woman;
having cast that man of inferior character aside for a year, the woman resorts to another.
If a man who belongs to another should become unfaithful toward his own wife, she may obtain another husband; this is the ordinance of Prajāpati.
Women were created for the sake of offspring; women are the field and men are the seed-bearers.
The field should be given to one who possesses seed; one without seed does not deserve the field.

*Subaddha* means well-knit; *jatru* is the joint between the neck and the shoulders; *ghāṭā* is the back part of the neck. A *nisargapaṇḍa* is one who is born entirely devoid of sexual organs and testicles. A *vadhra* is one whose testicles have been removed. A *pakṣapaṇḍa* is one whose sexual power is intermittent. [These conditions arise] solely from a teacher’s curse, or from divine wrath—that is, from anger generated by reviling the gods. An *īrṣyāpaṇḍa* is one whose semen is paralyzed by jealousy regarding his own wife. A *sevya* is one who, when served in various ways by a woman, develops a desire for intercourse. A *vātaretas* is one for whom, at the end of intercourse, only wind is emitted through the penis. A *mukhebhaga* is one who performs the function of the vulva (*bhaga*) only in the mouth of another. An *ākṣiptaretas* is one whose semen flows backward at the time of emission. A *moghabīja* is one whose semen is incapable of conceiving an embryo. A *śālīna* is one whose penis falls away upon contact with an audacious woman. An *anyāpati* is one whose virility is directed toward a woman other than his own wife. He should wait for a month; that is, he should observe her for the duration of a month. [87] [To these men, if their condition was known beforehand, a maiden should not be given. (If, however, she is given out of ignorance, she should be kept until a cure has been attempted among those for whom treatment exists. If they are incurable, after giving her away, she should be taken back and given to another. He should be young, not old. He should be wise, with an undeluded mind, because the mind is the root of everything. For this very reason it is said: "One should marry a girl into a wise family. He should be beloved by the people, not someone disliked by them, because both the seen and the unseen results depend on that. Gautama also says: "One should give [a girl] to one endowed with learning, conduct, kinship, and character. (1.55)
Furthermore:
As for what is said—that the acceptance of a Śūdra woman as a wife by those of the twice-born classes—is not my opinion, because in that case, one's own self is born [from her]. (1.56)

As for what is said—that a Brahmin may have four wives, a Kṣatriya three, and a Vaiśya two—it is the inclusion of a Śūdra woman [among them]. That is certainly not my view. Why? Because he himself is born from her; therefore she is called *jāyā* (wife), according to the Vedic revelation: "That which is born again from her. Manu also says:
"The twice-born who, out of delusion, marry women of lower caste, quickly lead their families, along with their descendants, to the status of Śūdras."
Likewise: "By taking a Śūdra woman onto his bed, a Brāhmaṇa goes to a low state;
by procreating a son upon her, he is indeed fallen from Brāhmaṇahood. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, it has been stated:
"Even in times of distress, for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya who remains steadfast, a Śūdra woman is never prescribed as a wife in any traditional account."
Thus, that [statement] is for the purpose of an absolute prohibition regarding those two, not for the purpose of permitting the Vaiśya and others. 1.56.
He states the sequence of secondary options:

"Three wives in the order of the castes, two likewise, and one respectively, are the wives for the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; she who is born of the Śūdra caste [is the wife] of the Śūdra. (1.57)

Furthermore, when there is no wife of the same caste (savarṇā) possessing the characteristics of a remarried woman (punarbhū), and the previous wife has passed away, and when one is not required to remain without an āśrama nor is eligible for another āśrama—provided he possesses sufficient means and has young children—then in that state, three, two, or one wife may be taken by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas respectively according to the order of castes; for a Śūdra, his own wife of the same caste remains the fourth and primary one. As Manu says:
"A Śūdra woman is declared to be the wife of a Śūdra, and she as well as his own [caste-woman] are prescribed for a Vaiśya."
They would belong to the king himself, and they would also belong to the one of noble birth.

"But for those who proceed out of desire, these [wives] shall be inferior in the following order. This means that for those who proceed out of desire and not out of religious duty (*dharma*), they are therefore considered base. They are taken "in order" and not out of sequence; for Manu has shown the fault in deviating from the sequence: "The one who marries a Śūdra woman falls [from his caste], according to Atri and the son of Utathya."

"By the birth of a son for Śaunaka, [he becomes] the offspring of Bhṛgu through that child. Regarding this, the opinion of Atri and Gautama is that one who marries a Śūdra woman falls by the mere act of marrying her; according to Śaunaka, it is by the birth of a son; and according to Bhṛgu, it is by being her offspring. And this should be understood as applying when the order is inverted. Otherwise, it is said: "The sons of a Brāhmaṇa, according to the castes [of their mothers], receive four, three, two, or one shares."
Thus, there would be no distinction between the portions; nor should that [guest] be made the primary recipient in the giving of *śrāddha* and other offerings, for it is said:
"He whose offerings to the gods, ancestors, and guests have him as their primary recipient—his ancestors do not eat, and he does not go to heaven."
Because of this statement [1.57].
He describes the forms of marriage: "In the Brāhma marriage, having invited [the groom], a girl adorned according to one's means is given;
the son born of that union purifies twenty-one persons on both sides. (1.58)

The marriage known as *brāhma* is appropriate for Brahmins. In that rite, having invited a groom who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics, the bride should be given once his desire is known; she is bestowed after being adorned according to one's means. Manu also says:
"Having clothed and honored him, and having invited him himself, the giving of a daughter to one possessed of learning and good character is proclaimed as the *brāhma* dharma."
Devala also says:
"Then, having adorned a well-bred, auspicious girl who is endowed with noble lineage and youth, one should give her to a worthy man; this is called the Brāhma marriage."
And Yama says:
"They know that maiden who is given away with water as a *brahmadāya*."

The designation *brahmadāya* (the gift of a Brāhmaṇa) is used in the context of the *śrāddha* rite for the purpose of denoting the status of being a "purifier of the assembly. One born of such a union purifies twenty-one generations on both sides—the maternal and paternal lineages—provided he acts according to the prescribed rules. Thus says Gautama: "The virtuous purify their ancestors. On this point, Manu states: "A son born of a Brāhmaṇa wife who performs meritorious deeds liberates ten ancestors and ten descendants, as well as himself—the twenty-first—from sin. [89]

Good conduct (*sukṛtam*) is said to consist of performing what is enjoined and avoiding what is prohibited. Āśvalāyana states: "One born under that [constellation] purifies twelve descendants and twelve ancestors on both sides. (1.58)

The phrase "the Daiva marriage" is understood to follow from the context; so too the phrases "is given" and "adorned according to one's means. When a maiden, having been adorned according to one's ability, is given as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) who is performing a sacrifice, that indeed is the Daiva marriage.
The Ārṣa [form of marriage], however, involves taking two cows;

having accepted a pair of cattle from the groom, the daughter is given to him after being adorned according to one's ability—this is the Ārṣa marriage. Śaunaka says: "Having given a pair of cattle, one should marry her; that is the Ārṣa.
He states the fruit of these two [forms]:
One born first purifies fourteen generations, and one born later purifies six.

One born of the first marriage, produced by the Daiva rite, purifies seven ancestors and seven descendants. The latter, the Ārṣa marriage; one born of that purifies three ancestors and three descendants—thus, six persons in all. (1.59)
Having said, "May both of you practice dharma together," she is given to the suitor;

that form of marriage, in which the girl— having been adorned according to one's ability— is given to the seeker of a bride after saying to both the bride and the groom, "May both of you practice dharma together," is the Prājāpatya marriage.
He states its fruit: "Born from that [rite], he shall purify six generations of his lineage along with himself. (1.60)
One born of such a marriage purifies six ancestors, six descendants, and oneself as the thirteenth. On this point, Devala says:
"These four forms of marriage are righteous and centered on the offering of water;
being without bride-price and worthy of Brahmins, they deliver both families."
"Sons born of a woman given in marriage to these four types of men purify the lineage of both the giver and the receiver up to the seventh generation. (1.60)
The Āsura [form of marriage] results from the taking of wealth;

when the father and others, having received wealth from the suitor, bestow the daughter for his sake and for her own sake, that is the Āsura marriage. [90] The Gāndharva [marriage] is by mutual agreement.

The Gāndharva marriage is that acceptance of a maiden which arises from a mutual agreement between the bride and the groom—of the nature "you are my wife" and "you are my husband"—and is independent of any gift.
The Rākṣasa marriage is from abduction by force; that acceptance of a maiden, the taking of a maiden after having conquered the girl's kinsmen in battle, is the Rākṣasa marriage.
The Paiśāca [form of marriage] is when one takes a maiden by fraud. || 1.61 ||

When one abducts a maiden by deceit and takes her for himself, that is the *paiśāca* marriage. Some read "by means of the maiden’s deception" (*kanyakāchalāt*); its meaning is: the taking of her through the maiden’s own deception is the *paiśāca* marriage. These are the eight forms of marriage. Although the word *vivāha* (marriage) is primarily applied to the bride’s circumambulation of the fire seven times (*saptapadī*), it nevertheless refers—on account of its ritual context—to the entire collection of rites prescribed in the various *Gṛhya-sūtras* and other scriptures that establishes the status of wifehood. That collection receives the designations of *brāhma*, *ārya*, and so forth, according to its specific qualifying characteristics (*upādhi*). It is precisely because of these qualifications that the words *dāna* (giving) and *vivāha* (marriage) can be used in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). For example: "Having adorned the maiden, he should give her with water; this is the *brāhma* marriage. This, however, is not the sole meaning of the word *vivāha*. If it were, then after stating, "The tonsure (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), the cutting of the beard (*godāna*), and marriage (*vivāha*) should take place during the northern course of the sun, in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious constellation," the subsequent statement, "Before those [rites], he should offer four oblations of clarified butter," would be inconsistent. For these oblations do not precede the giving of the maiden. Therefore, since there is a distinction between *dāna* and *vivāha*, the apposition of the two terms must be explained only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*). Precisely because giving is not itself the marriage, Śaunaka describes the acceptance of the maiden—which constitutes the marriage—even without a formal gift, in the case of marriages such as the *gāndharva*: "Having made a mutual agreement, he should take her; that is the *gāndharva*. The meaning is: having reached a mutual understanding between the girl and the groom—such as "I am yours" and "You are my husband"—he should approach and accept the maiden. Thus, while no formal gift exists here, the marriage (*vivāha*) does occur. The distinguishing characteristic of this from the other marriages is the mutual agreement between the girl and the groom. In the same way, the status of marriage in the *rākṣasa* and *paiśāca* forms should also be understood as being devoid of the formal gift of the maiden. Battle and deception are their respective distinguishing characteristics. As Manu says regarding the *rākṣasa*: "Having slain and split open [the heads] of those weeping and of the [bride's kin] who are weeping, [one takes] the weeping [maiden]; that is the *rākṣasa* [marriage]. And Manu likewise speaks of the *paiśāca*.
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged,
that is declared to be the eighth and most sinful of marriages, the Paiśāca.

Thus, just like the words *upayamana* and *pāṇigrahaṇa*, the term *pariṇayana* is also used in the treatises to denote the entire collection of rites according to the maxim of the "man with the staff" (*daṇḍin*). Among these forms of marriage, Manu states: "Of these marriages, this one is lawful for this caste, and this one is unlawful; one should know that for a Brāhmaṇa there are six in the direct order, for a Kṣatriya four excluding the last [two], and for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra those same ones, provided they exclude the Rākṣasa form."

One should know that the six forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma and ending with the Gāndharva are not contrary to the dharma for a Brāhmaṇa. One should know—that is, understand—that the four inferior forms of marriage mentioned later, beginning with the Āsura and ending with the Paiśāca, belong to the Kṣatriya; and for the Vaiśya and Śūdra as well, one should know those same [four] excluding the Rākṣasa. Among these also, he states which are commendable:
"The wise know the first four to be commendable for a Brāhmaṇa;
the Rākṣasa alone for a Kṣatriya; and the Āsura for the Vaiśya and Śūdra."

The four forms of marriage—the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, and Prājāpatya—are commended for the Brāhmaṇa. The Āsura and Gāndharva, however, are neither commended nor censured. For the Kṣatriya, moreover, the Rākṣasa alone is commended; the Āsura and Gāndharva are as before. For the Vaiśya and Śūdra, however, the Āsura alone is commended; the Gāndharva is as before. The Paiśāca, on the other hand, is indeed censured for all castes, for it is said:
"The eighth form of marriage, the Paiśāca, is declared to be the most sinful among marriages," according to this general Smṛti rule. As for that which was stated by Manu himself:
"Regarding the four inferior forms for a Kṣatriya, one should know that those same [forms], excluding the Paiśāca, are lawful for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra in times of extreme distress.

(92) This [statement] is intended as a concession for castes other than Brāhmaṇas during extreme adversity. Therefore, it is established that there is no concession for a Brāhmaṇa to the Paiśāca form even in times of distress. 1.61.
A living being should be taken [as the fee] for brides of equal caste; for a Kṣatriya bride, he should take an arrow;
for a Vaiśya bride, he should take a goad; but for the marriage of one born of the highest caste (a Brāhmaṇa), [the fee is as prescribed]. 1.62.

When a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*) is being wedded by a groom, her hand should be taken. A Kṣatriya woman being wedded by a Brāhmaṇa should take hold of an arrow; likewise, the groom should take that arrow as if it were her hand. But a Vaiśya woman being married by a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should take hold of a goad, the instrument for driving oxen. The term "first-born" (*agryajanman*) refers merely to a man of a higher caste. Manu says: "In a marriage with a man of a higher caste, the hem of the garment should be taken by a Śūdra woman. (MDh 1.62)
He states the authority for giving away the daughter and the sequence thereof:

"The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman (sakulya), or a maternal uncle (janajī)—in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent person is the giver of the daughter, provided they are present. (1.63)

Among the father and others enumerated in their proper order, in the absence of each preceding one, the succeeding one who is in his natural state (*prakṛtistha*) becomes the giver of the girl. One whose intellect is undisturbed is "in his natural state. A gift of a girl made even by a father who is not in his natural state is as good as not made at all. As Nārada says:
"Even if he is independent, whatever act a person performs while having fallen from his natural state, that too shall be as if unperformed, because of the loss of his independence."

Even one who is independent (*svatantra*)—and thus worthy of independence by virtue of being a father or the like—if he becomes dependent (*paratantra*) due to not abiding in his natural state (*aprakṛtistha*), then the act performed by him, such as the giving away of a daughter in marriage (*vāgdattādi-karman*), should be understood as unperformed. Likewise: "The father himself may give the daughter, or the brother with the father's consent;
likewise the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, a kinsman (*sakulya*), or a relative (*bāndhava*)."
But if, in the absence of a [suitable] match, all [the suitors] abide in their natural state,
then when she is not abiding in her natural state, members of their own caste may give her [in marriage].

Viṣṇu states: "The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman (sakulya), the maternal grandfather, and the mother—these are the givers of a maiden; in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is the giver, provided he is of sound mind. (1.63)
[93] By not giving her in marriage during each fertile season (*ṛtu*), one incurs the sin of killing an embryo (*bhrūṇahatyā*).
The giver of a maiden is the one who has the authority; by not giving her, he instead incurs the sin of killing a fetus, indeed he incurs it in its entirety. As for the teaching of Manu:
A maiden, even if she has reached puberty, may remain in her father's house until death if she so desires;
however, he must never give her in marriage to one who is devoid of good qualities.

Thus, this statement intends to mean that when a qualified bridegroom is available, [the girl] must not be given to one devoid of qualities; it does not mean that seeing the girl's menses is not a defect. For if that were the case, there would be a contradiction with other scriptural statements. And so says Kāśyapa: "If a maiden, while still belonging to her father's lineage, sees her menses before being consecrated [in marriage], she incurs the sin of foeticide for her father; such a maiden is declared to be a *vṛṣalī*."
A *vṛṣalī* is ineligible for religious duties.
However, that Brahmin who, being weak in knowledge, should choose her as his bride—
one should know him to be the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, unworthy of invitations to *śrāddha* rites and excluded from the row of diners.
Nārada says: "A maiden must announce to her kinsmen that she has reached puberty.
"A maiden should not neglect her menses; she should inform her kinsmen.
If they do not give her to a husband, they shall be equal to slayers of Brahmins. Thus he spoke.
On this point, Saṃvarta says:
"The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother—
these three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses."
But in the absence of givers, a maiden may choose a husband for herself from among eligible suitors.

In the absence of givers such as her father and others, the maiden herself shall choose as her husband a suitor who is fit for union—meaning one of equal or superior caste, free from defects such as loss of caste (*pātitya*), and so forth. And this must be done before the appearance of her menses. Once that has appeared, even if her father and others are present, the maiden may choose a suitor by herself; she need not await the command of her father or others. As Baudhāyana says:
"A woman who has reached puberty should wait for the command of her father for three years;
then, in the fourth year, she may take a suitable husband."
One should go even to one who is non-existent, similar, or devoid of virtues.

[She should choose] one who is similar [to herself] and virtuous. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu—"Having passed three menstrual periods, a maiden may choose a husband for herself"—that should be understood to apply when a virtuous suitor is available. But if such a suitor is not found, she should wait for three years. On this point, Manu says: [94] * *manuḥ*: "If a maiden has reached the age of puberty and has not been given away [in marriage], she shall wait for three years; after that, she may choose a husband of equal status from her own family. * *yājñavalkyaḥ*: "A maiden who has reached the age of puberty may, with her father's permission, take a husband for herself from a family of equal status. * *nāradaḥ*: "If a maiden has not been given away within three years after reaching puberty, she may abandon her father and take a husband for herself. * *parāśaraḥ*: "If a maiden remains unmarried after three menstrual periods have passed, she may choose a husband for herself; she incurs no blame, and he whom she chooses is not at fault. * *vyāsaḥ*: "If a maiden does not obtain a husband of equal status after three years, she may take him for herself; she incurs no sin, nor does he whom she takes. * *śātātapaḥ*: "If a maiden remains unmarried after three menstrual periods have passed, she may choose a husband for herself; she incurs no blame, and he whom she chooses is not at fault. * *bṛhaspatiḥ*: "If a maiden remains unmarried after three menstrual periods have passed, she may choose a husband for herself; she incurs no blame, and he whom she chooses is not at fault. * *kātyāyanaḥ*: "If a maiden remains unmarried after three menstrual periods have passed, she may choose a husband for herself;
