A maiden choosing her own husband shall not take for herself any ornament belonging to her father, her mother, or given by her brother; if she should take it, it would constitute theft.
Regarding even the bride-price, he himself has said:
"But one who takes away a maiden who has reached puberty must pay a bride-price to her father;
for by obstructing her seasons, he would overstep his authority as master."
*Śulka* means price. 1.64.
A maiden is given only once; he who abducts her shall be subject to the punishment for theft.
Even if she has been given away, one may take her back from the previous husband if a more excellent suitor arrives.

A daughter must be given by her father or other guardian only once; having given her away, one who takes her back incurs the punishment for the theft of a maiden, which will be described later. If another suitor who is more distinguished or superior is obtained after she has been promised to one by word, then she should be given to that [new suitor] and not to the former. Regarding this, Gautama says: "Having made a promise, one should not give [the girl] to one who is unrighteous. Nārada states:
"In the relationship between a woman and a man, the formal choosing (*varaṇa*) is prescribed first;
the grasping of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) follows the choosing; this relationship has three stages."
The relationship [between husband and wife] is threefold: betrothal, taking of the hand, and sexual enjoyment.
Of these two, the former is said to be indefinite because defects may be discovered after the betrothal;
however, the mantras recited at the time of taking the hand constitute the definitive characteristic of a wife.
Their completion, however, should be understood by the learned as occurring at the seventh step.

The meaning of this is as follows: *aniyata* means the absence of restriction (*aniyama*) regarding those two—the bride and the groom. It refers to a situation where, even though she has been chosen, she is not married, or even though she has been betrothed by word, she is not given away. To state the time and cause of such a situation, it is said: "because of the choice, due to the perception of defects. After the choice (*varaṇa*), the lack of restriction arises from the mutual perception of defects between the bride and the groom. The term "from the choice" (*varaṇāt*) is an exclusive statement; the meaning is that [the lack of restriction occurs] only after the choice, and not after the marriage itself. The reason for this is: "the mantras of the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇika*). It is not proper to abandon a woman who has acquired the status of a wife through the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) produced by those mantras. And likewise:
But if a groom, having accepted a maiden, should depart for another country, she may,
after three menstrual seasons have passed, choose another groom.
Kātyāyana says: When a man who has been chosen as a suitor should perish, after three menstrual periods have passed, the maiden may choose another suitor. [95]

These two statements refer to the case of a girl who has been verbally betrothed (*vāgdattā*). "The arrival of passion" (*raktāgama*) means the appearance of menstruation. "He who, having given the bride-price (*śulka*) as well as the woman’s property (*strīdhana*), should depart—she must be kept for one year and then given to another according to the rule."

This also should be understood as applying prior to the marriage ceremony. Vasiṣṭha says: "If the bridegroom should die first after she has been given by water and word, but before she has been led away by the mantras, the maiden belongs to her father alone."

The meaning is that one who has been brought [to the altar] by means of a mantra—that is, brought during the marriage rite by one possessing the mantra—does not become consecrated [if she is subsequently married again]. Kātyāyana states:
"But when a maiden previously given to one man should be married by another, she ought to be given again to the one to whom she was originally promised, even though she has already been consecrated."
The phrase "if he is more virtuous" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 1.65 ||
One who gives [a maiden] without disclosing a defect shall be punished with the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*).

If the giver of a maiden, knowing the defect of the maiden himself, gives her to the groom without informing him—provided that the defect is not perceptible to the groom—then he shall be fined eighty thousand *paṇas*. Regarding the defects of a maiden, Nārada says:
"One afflicted by long-standing or loathsome diseases, one who is deformed, or one who has already had sexual intercourse."
And a maiden who has developed an inclination for another man is proclaimed to have the defects of a maiden.

Sumantu states: "If a maiden who has been married is found to be of low birth, engaged in censurable acts, or afflicted by disease, she should be abandoned provided her virginity remains intact; however, if her virginity is destroyed, she must be maintained and supported. As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"If a man gives away a defective maiden without disclosing her faults, the king shall impose upon him the punishment prescribed for the first degree of violence (pūrvasāhasa)."

Thus, this refers to cases other than those involving defects that constitute grounds for renunciation. Two hundred and seventy *paṇas* constitute the first *sāhasa* fine. Regarding this, Manu says: "Even after having formally accepted an irreproachable maiden, one may abandon her if she is diseased, severely defiled, or was presented through deception."
Nārada has stated the defects that serve as grounds for rejecting a groom, which are various and exceedingly corrupt:

"One who is insane, one who is outcasted, one who is impotent, one who is unfortunate, one whose kinsmen have been abandoned, and the two previously mentioned defects of the maiden—this is the group of defects in a groom. [96]
Long illness, loathsome disease, and physical deformity are the prior defects.

One who abandons a girl who is not defective is liable to punishment; specifically, a suitor abandoning a girl who is free from the defect of being defective shall be punished with the highest amercement. On this point, Nārada says:
But a man who, having accepted an unblemished maiden, should abandon her—
even if he has fallen in love with another— must be punished and shall have to marry that very same maiden again.
One who is to be disciplined is to be punished; however, one who falsely defames [another] shall pay a fine of one hundred [paṇas]. 1.66.

One who speaks falsely, saying "this girl is not marriageable," shall be fined one hundred *paṇas*. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu—"one who says a girl is defective when she is not defective shall be punished with the highest amercement"—that refers to cases involving the declaration of defects that render her unfit for marriage. (1.66)
He states the definition of a *punarbhū*:
"A *punarbhū* is one who, whether previously unviolated or violated, has been consecrated again.

She who, having already been married—whether her virginity was lost or not—is wedded again according to the prescribed rule by her former husband or by another husband, she is a *punarbhū*. As Manu says:
If she is still a virgin, or even if she has returned after having left,
she deserves to undergo the marriage rite again with her new husband.

The meaning of this is as follows: when a man has married a woman who is impotent, fallen from caste, insane, or similar, and while such husbands still live—or when her husband dies without fault—she takes another husband; that husband is a *paunarbhava*. She, having been consecrated again by the marriage rite through him, is a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman). Alternatively, she who abandons her original husband—who is free from defects such as impotence and capable of providing maintenance—and after engaging in sexual intercourse with others, returns to that very same first husband, is one who has gone away and returned (*gatapratyāgatā*) and is one whose virginity is destroyed (*kṣatayoni*). That husband is a *paunarbhava*. Regarding the nature of these two types of *punarbhū*, Vasiṣṭha says: "A *punarbhū* is she who, having abandoned her husband from childhood and lived with others, re-enters his household; or she who, having abandoned a husband who is impotent, fallen, or insane, takes another husband; or she [who does so] when he is dead—she becomes a *punarbhū*. Therefore, the defining characteristic of a *punarbhū* is the state of being consecrated again.
A woman who, having abandoned her husband of equal caste, resorts to another out of desire is a *svairiṇī*.

She who, having abandoned her husband of the same caste, resorts out of passion to another man for sexual enjoyment even without a marriage ceremony, is a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman). The mention of the *svairiṇī* is for the purpose of distinguishing her from the *punarbhū* (a remarried woman); and that distinction is made known for the sake of identifying the son of a *punarbhū* and his legal status as a husband. (1.67)

To avoid the contingency of remarriage, he states the rule for the procreation of a son by a brother-in-law: "A brother-in-law, or a sapinda, or one of the same gotra, being authorized by the husband's elder and desiring a son, shall approach his wife during her season, anointed with clarified butter. (1.68)
He may approach her until conception occurs; otherwise, he would become an outcast.
Born according to this rule, he shall be a son known as a *kṣetraja*.

Whether the husband is dead or living, if he is incapable of procreation, a woman who is childless and desirous of offspring—provided she is fit for conception—may, with the permission of her elders for the sake of producing progeny, be approached by her husband’s elder or younger brother, or in their absence by a *sapiṇḍa* or a *sagotra*, after his entire body has been anointed with oil, during her fertile period (*ṛtukāla*). Once conception has occurred, he must desist. By approaching her in a manner contrary to what has been prescribed, he becomes an outcast (*patita*). A son born in this manner is known as a *kṣetraja*. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
Having stated the rule, Manu himself has indeed prohibited it;
because of the decline of the age, this cannot be performed by anyone according to the prescribed injunctions.
In the Kṛta and Tretā Yugas, men were endowed with austerity and knowledge;
however, in the Dvāpara and Kali Yugas, a decline in the power of men has been ordained.
The sons who were produced in many ways by the ancient seers cannot be produced now by men, due to their lack of power.
Manu says:
"The wise declare that these eleven sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, as previously described, are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the failure of religious rites."
These sons who have been mentioned incidentally as born from the seed of others belong to him from whose seed they were born, and not to anyone else.
Now, from the Brahmapurāṇa:
A woman who, upon the death of her husband, has abandoned him of her own accord, may bear a child to a man of the same caste; such a son born to her husband is called *paunarbhava*.
If that young widow has been abandoned by her husband while still a child, or if she has been taken up by anyone at all, then she must be consecrated for the sake of her husband.
If she has left for her husband's house without fault,
she should again be restored by her brother through the performance of penances and other rites in due order.
Furthermore, the remarriage of women, the succession of sons through a brother-in-law,
and the independence of women must never be practiced in the Kali Yuga.
"For there are men in this world who are sinners during the Kali age. (1.68–69)
Regarding the action to be taken toward an unfaithful wife, he says:
"One should cause the unfaithful wife to dwell deprived of her authority, soiled, subsisting on mere alms, humiliated, and sleeping on the ground. (1.70)

Having deprived her of wealth and religious merit, and having reduced her to a state where she possesses only a soiled body and clothing, subsists on mere food sufficient for the maintenance of life, and sleeps upon the ground, the husband shall cause the unchaste wife to dwell in a single part of the house. Regarding this, Manu says:
"The husband shall confine a woman who has committed adultery in a single room;
he shall compel her to perform that same penance which is prescribed for a man regarding the wives of others."
Nārada: In the case of infidelity by a woman, there shall be shaving of the head and sleeping on the ground;
however, once she has performed the penance, she becomes fit for social intercourse.
"And one should never despise those who have performed purification," according to the statement of Manu (1.70).
He speaks in praise of women:
"Soma bestowed purity upon women, and Gandharva gave them a melodious voice;
Pāvaka granted them complete sanctity; therefore, women are indeed pure. (1.71)

The god Soma bestowed purity upon women; Gandharva, an auspicious voice; and Pāvaka, fitness for all sacrifices. Therefore, these women are pure and worthy of sacrifice. The word *hi* indicates what is well known. 1.71.

Purification is prescribed for sexual intercourse during the fertile period; abandonment is ordained in the case of pregnancy, as well as in the killing of the husband or in the commission of a great sin.

When there has been infidelity, purification occurs upon the appearance of her menses; and this applies to mental infidelity. As Manu says: "A woman defiled in mind [is purified] by her menses. Consequently, prior to the appearance of the menses, she is unfit for social intercourse (*asaṃvyavahāryā*). For the sake of resuming social intercourse, she must be made to perform penance (*prāyaścitta*). As Vasiṣṭha says: "In the case of mental infidelity toward her husband, she should eat barley gruel or rice with milk for three nights and sleep on the ground. After the three nights, submerged in water, she should offer oblations with the *Gāyatrī* mantra recited one hundred and eight times for each head [of the mantra]. It is known that she thus becomes pure. [99] The rule regarding "abandonment when a fetus is conceived" refers to the case of a Śūdra fetus. As Vasiṣṭha says:

"The women of the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya castes who have had sexual intercourse with a Śūdra are purified by penance if they have not conceived; others are not. In the event of the abortion of her own fetus or the death of her husband, she must be abandoned by her husband and her kinsmen. The word "and" (ca) is intended to include other grounds for abandonment mentioned in other scriptures. On this point, Manu says:
If a woman who has bathed after her menses does not approach her husband,
she shall be proclaimed throughout the village as a destroyer of the embryo and banished.
Vasiṣṭha says: But four [wives] are to be abandoned: one who has gone to a pupil, one who has gone to a teacher, one who especially kills her husband, and one who has approached a degraded man.
In this context, "pupil" refers to the husband's pupil; "teacher" means father; and "outcaste" (juṅgita) means one who has fallen from his caste or one born of an inverse (pratiloma) union.
Those who know the Dharma recognize three crimes for a woman in this world:
the murder of her husband, the destruction of an embryo, and the causing of an abortion of her own fetus.

Regarding her, in the case of the *mahāpātakas* (great sins) which are common to both women and men among the causes for abandonment, as well as in the case of the specific causes for abandoning a woman such as approaching a disciple (*śiṣyagamana*) and so forth, there must be abandonment with one's whole being. Alternatively, this is the meaning: when adultery has occurred, if there is no certainty of conception due to the onset of the fertile period (*ṛtu*) characterized by the appearance of menses, then purification—the performance of expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*)—must be carried out as the cause of purity. But if the conception itself was caused by adultery, there is only abandonment of the adulterous woman and no expiation. Not only in that [specific] conception, but also upon the killing of one's own husband or of a conception acquired in any manner whatsoever, there is abandonment and not expiation. However, regarding the *mahāpātakas*, abandonment is stated as a special rule. When *mahāpātakas* common to both women and men exist, abandonment should consist of ceasing sexual intercourse, physical contact, conversation, and joint religious duties; it does not, however, take the form of banishment from the house. As Manu says:
One should apply this very same rule even to women who have fallen [from their status]; however, clothing and food should be given to them, and they should dwell near the house. (1.72)

The wife who may be superseded is declared [as follows]: she who drinks liquor, she who is diseased, she who is deceitful, she who is barren, she who destroys wealth, she who speaks unpleasantly, she who bears only daughters, and likewise she who hates her husband. (1.73)

[Drunkards and others are grounds for supersession (*adhivedanīya*). This means that when wives are of such a nature, another wife may be taken. [100] Thus far. A drunkard (*surāpī*) is one who drinks intoxicants (*madya*). Here, by the word *surā*, intoxicant is intended, not specifically the liquor *surā*. For drinking that [specific *surā*] would be a cause for abandonment alone due to its being a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), and not merely a ground for supersession. Therefore, Manu says: "A woman who drinks intoxicants, is untruthful in conduct, is hostile, is diseased, is violent, or is wasteful of wealth—she may always be superseded."

A woman who is diseased is one suffering from a chronic illness; a rogue is a deceiver; a barren woman is childless; a destroyer of wealth is one who causes the loss of property; and one who speaks unpleasantly is harsh-tongued. Such a wife may be superseded (*adhivettavyā*). The meaning is that even while these women are present, another wife may be married. On this point, Manu says:

"A barren woman may be superseded in the eighth year, one whose children have died in the tenth, one who gives birth only to daughters in the eleventh, but one who speaks unpleasantly may be superseded immediately."
Likewise:
"But she who is diseased, yet beneficial and endowed with virtuous conduct—she should be informed and taken as a second wife; she must never be treated with contempt."
The mention of "the diseased woman" implies both a woman who bears no offspring and one whose offspring are female; for this very reason, another Smṛti states:

"One may abandon from the sacred water (tīrtha) a wife who is diseased, who bears only daughters, who is barren, insane, or devoid of menses, provided she is not otherwise at fault—but not so from the perspective of dharma."

The *tīrtha* is the source (*yoni*). This refers to cases where there is no desire for another wife. As for what Āpastamba stated: "While one's wife is endowed with both virtue and progeny, one should not take others. One may take another upon the failure of either. For before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), she is connected to the ritual acts only when the fire has been established," in this context, the phrase "before the establishment of the fires" is not an injunction, but rather a restatement of what is already established by propriety. Therefore, Baudhāyana says: "One should perform this very sacrifice in the event of transgression regarding a wife and in the event of transgression regarding a priest. Transgression regarding a wife (*dāravyatikrama*) is taking a second wife without the scriptural cause for supersession (*adhivedana*), namely the *pavitreṣṭi*. One should sacrifice on account of that very cause; and this is not possible before the establishment of the fires, because those rites are accomplished through the three fires (*tretā*). Thus it is established that there is supersession for one who has established the fires. Before the establishment of the fires, even a second wife is connected to the ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* by virtue of her eligibility. As Āpastamba said: "For when the fire is established, she is connected to the ritual acts. As for the statement of Viṣṇu:
In sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, one should not perform them with a second wife;
otherwise, even with hundreds of well-performed rituals, his merit will be fruitless.

Thus, while that elder wife remains faultless, this [text] refers either to the case where she is the sole second wife with whom one has the right to perform rituals, or to the case of a second wife of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), or to the case of a second wife married by one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). This also applies to the following:
"The first wife shall be the partner for religious duty (*dharma*), the second is for increasing pleasure (*rati*);
in that case, only the visible fruit is produced, not the invisible."

As for the injunction regarding the re-establishment of the sacred fires (*punarādheya*) upon taking a second wife, that should be understood to apply when the first wife has become unrighteous or has died, and not merely upon the marriage of a second wife. Manu says:
"But a woman who has been superseded (*adhivinnā*), if she should leave the house in anger, must be immediately restrained or abandoned in the presence of the family."
The meaning is: "in the presence of the family of the father and others. || 1.73 ||
But she who has been given away must be maintained; otherwise, a great sin would ensue—provided she is living either in her own home or in her father's home, as is understood from the context.
Where there is harmony between husband and wife, there the three aims of life flourish.

Dharma, artha, and kāma constitute the threefold set (trivarga). This thrives when husband and wife act in harmony and accord; therefore, one should strive for that end—this is the intended meaning. It is stated as "the threefold set" with the intention that liberation (mokṣa) belongs only to the householder who performs the sacrifice to Brahman, not to everyone. 1.74.
Whether her husband is dead or alive, she who does not approach another man attains fame in this world and rejoices with Umā in the next. (1.75)

The word *vā* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The rest is not obscure. This is stated as an incidental result even for the husband’s non-transgression [of fidelity]. Manu has said that the husband, too, should not be unfaithful to his wife: "Mutual non-transgression should last until death; this should be known as the supreme duty of husband and wife in brief. (MDh 9.101)
The rule regarding the non-deviation from both [the husband and the wife] is eternal, because there is a traditional teaching of penance for its transgression. 1.75.

[102] Abandoning a wife who is obedient, skillful, the mother of heroes, and sweet-spoken, he shall be made to pay a third part of his estate; if he is without property, he must provide maintenance for her. 1.76.

If a man abandons a wife who is endowed with qualities such as obedience to his commands, he must be made to give her a third part of his wealth; this is understood from the context to be by the king. However, if he possesses only enough wealth for her maintenance, he must provide that maintenance alone. The word "striyāḥ" (of the woman) is used in the genitive case with the sense of the dative. (1.76)

"The word of the husband must be carried out by women; this is the supreme duty of a woman. By "wives," it means the word of the husband must be fulfilled by them. Performing that establishes its utility for a visible purpose, and it is itself a dharma. Furthermore, this is not equal to other duties of women, such that one might choose between them as alternatives. Rather, it is superior to them, and therefore other duties are to be performed only in accordance with it. For this very reason, Manu prohibits those duties that conflict with it: "For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, and no fasting."

"By serving her husband, she is exalted in heaven. Thus, religious observances (*vrata*) and the like, provided they do not conflict with service to the husband, should be performed with his permission. As Śaṅkha says: "At the husband's permission, one may undertake vows, fasts, and so forth. This refers to the case of a woman whose husband has not gone abroad; for regarding a woman whose husband is away, it is stated in the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"When the husband has thus departed on a journey, the auspicious wife should be left [by him]."
A woman should perform the propitiation of Hari through fasting and other such observances.
Thus it is seen in the Śrutis and other sources: her conduct is auspicious and unerring.
For one who has been defiled by a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) must be awaited until purification.

If the husband is guilty of a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), then she must wait until his completion of the penance; the meaning is that one who is joined with a mortal sin is not to be served. And this should be understood to apply when the husband becomes fallen after the time of marriage. Prior to marriage, even if she has been wedded by one who is fallen, she is not [truly] a wife, because of the absence of the scripturally ordained wedding ceremony. (1.77)
Because one attains the infinity of worlds and heaven through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, therefore women should be enjoyed and must be well protected. 1.78.

"Lokāś cānantyaṃ ca dyauś ca" is a *dvandva* compound in the sense of a collective whole (*samāhāra*). From that, the genitive singular case ending is applied. And those—namely, the attainment of worlds, the attainment of infinity, and the attainment of heaven—occur respectively through sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons. Since this is so, women, who are the causes for sons and the rest, should be enjoyed and must be protected during their fertile periods (*ṛtukāla*). Because of the injunction to protect them in order to avoid misconduct (*vyabhicāra*), it implies that this fruit is not produced by offspring born of misconduct. And thus says the Śruti:
"Be vigilant; guard this thread, lest others sow seeds in your field.
In the life hereafter, one becomes the son of the progenitor; the owner makes this thread in vain.
And here, the word *dyu* refers to the world of the sun (*sūryaloka*). Thus says Manu:
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the sun.

*Bradhna* is the Sun. Just as the fruit of a *śrāddha* rite performed for one's father accrues to that father's own father and grandfather, so too does the satisfaction of the ancestors—father and the rest—result from the procreation of a son by a woman married to her father. 1.78.

Having thus stated that [the birth of] a son is conducive to welfare, he describes the means for producing him: "The women's *ṛtu* consists of sixteen nights; during those, one should approach them on the even nights. The *ṛtu* of women—the period for conception—consists of sixteen days and nights starting from the appearance of the menses. Having restated this well-known period, he prescribes: "During those, one should approach them on the even nights. One should approach them in order to produce a son, because of the completion of the sentence: "One should procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks. And so says Manu: *Ṛtuḥ svābhāvikaḥ strīṇāṃ rātrayaḥ ṣoḍaśa smṛtāḥ | caturbhiritaraiḥ sārdham ahobhiḥ sadvigarhitaiḥ ||* "The natural *ṛtu* of women is traditionally said to consist of sixteen nights, together with four other days which are censured by the virtuous. *Ṣoḍaśartuniśāḥ strīṇāṃ tasmin yugmāsu saṃviśet | evam putro bhavaty eva nāputro bhavati kvacit ||* "One should approach women during their sixteen *ṛtu*-nights on the even nights. In this way, a son is born; one never remains without a son. *Yugmāsv eva prajāyante kumāryaś cāparās tathā | ayugmāsv api jāyante striyaḥ puṃsavanāni ca ||* "On even nights, both daughters and others are born; likewise, on odd nights, females and *puṃsavana* (masculine offspring) are produced. *Yugmāsu putrā jāyante kanyā ayugmāsu rātriṣu | tasmād yugmāsu gantavyaṃ putrakāmena vai nareṇa ||* "Sons are born on even nights and daughters on odd nights; therefore, a man desiring a son should certainly approach his wife on the even nights. *Gacched vāpy ṛtau striyaṃ na vā gacchet |* "He may approach his wife during her season, or he may not. *Ṛtau tu gacchan naraḥ patnīṃ śreṣṭho dharmavid bhavet |* "But a man who approaches his wife during her season becomes an excellent knower of dharma. *Paryāyeṇa tu gacchantaḥ santānayanti mānavāḥ |* "Men who approach her in turn perpetuate their lineage. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Sa gacchen nirayaṃ ghoraṃ brahmahā caiva jāyate ||* "...he goes to a terrible hell and is born as a slayer of a Brahmin. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and is present... *Vināśaṃ tasya tāḥ śukraṃ prajā caiva vināśayet ||* "...his semen and his progeny shall surely perish. *Ṛtusnātāṃ tu yo bhāryāṃ sannidhau nopagacchati |* "But he who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her period and

"Sons are born on even nights, and daughters on uneven nights; therefore, one who desires a son should approach his wife during her season on even nights. Thus it is said: "He should remain celibate, however, and avoid the four nights beginning with the day of the new moon. (1.79)

He should remain a celibate student (*brahmacārin*)—that is, indeed averse to sexual intercourse—on the *parvan* days, namely the two fifteenth days [of the lunar month]. Since the possibility arises that one might approach a woman based on the injunctions, "He should approach her during the fertile period (*ṛtu*)" or "Or he may act according to his desire," this is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) regarding the *parvan* days for approaching a woman. By stating "he should remain a celibate student on the *parvan* days," the mention of *parvan* includes those other lunar days that are excluded by other scriptures. Regarding this, Manu says: "A twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies (*snātaka*) should always remain a celibate student on the new moon day, the eighth, the full moon, and the fourteenth, even during the fertile period."

Here, due to the association with the word *amāvāsyā* (new moon), the words *caturdaśī* (fourteenth) and *aṣṭamī* (eighth) refer to the fourteenth and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights, but not to those occurring during the menstrual period (*ṛtu*). By the force of the word "also" (*api*), these lunar days are to be avoided even outside the menstrual period. Likewise, one should avoid the first four nights of the menstrual period. And so says Manu:
"Of those [nights], the first four are censured, as is the eleventh; likewise the thirteenth. The remaining ten nights are auspicious."

The eleventh and thirteenth days of the lunar fortnight belong to the season (*ṛtu*) and not to the fortnight itself. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day; those born by day are impotent, of little vigor, short-lived, and few in number. Therefore, one should avoid this. This [prohibition] applies even outside the fertile season (*anṛtu*). As Āpastamba says: "The vow of the householder is: no sleeping during the day. One should not approach a woman on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth days of the lunar month. Nor after eating at a *śrāddha*, nor after giving [food], nor when invited to a *śrāddha*. Nor while observing a vow, nor when initiated for a sacrifice. One should not approach her in a temple, a cemetery, an empty dwelling, or at the roots of trees. Not by day, nor during the two twilights. Not one who is unclean, nor he himself being unclean. Not one who is anointed with oil, nor one afflicted by disease, nor he himself being afflicted by disease. One desiring to live a long life should not approach a woman who is deficient in limb, nor likewise one who is older than himself, nor a pregnant woman. Here, "vow" (*vrata*) refers to an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*). There is no fault if she is a pregnant woman who desires it. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Moreover, it is known from the *Kāṭhaka* tradition: 'May those of us who are about to be born tomorrow lie down with their husbands'—this is the boon granted to women by Indra. Baudhāyana [says]:
"But for him who engages in sexual intercourse with his mouth when she has taken his hand in marriage, there is no atonement in this world; thus spoke Prajāpati."

Hārīta, however, desires that conception (*garbhādhāna*) take place on the fourth day: "On the fourth day, when she has bathed, or during even-numbered nights, he should approach her as in the rite of conception and bestow the Brahman-germ. Consequently, because it is both prescribed and prohibited, approaching a woman on the fourth day is optional. This is a restricted option (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*): the rule applies on the fourth day once menstruation has ceased; there is a prohibition if it has not ceased. Thus says Manu: "When her menses have ceased, a woman who was menstruating becomes pure through bathing."

"Virtuous" (sādhvī) means one who is fit for the prescribed rites beginning with the ceremony of conception (garbhādhāna). Devala says: "When there are multiple sacred sites [to visit] simultaneously, one should proceed according to the order of castes, starting with the Brahmins; or for the sake of protection, one may follow the order of marriage, even if she is childless."

The meaning is that, regarding the purpose indicated by the word *yoni*, among several wives, he should approach a wife either simultaneously, or according to the order of castes, or according to the order of marriage; or, if she is childless, he should approach her first. [105] Āpastamba says: "Having united with her, he should not sleep with her during the night. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:

"Because of the suspicion of conception during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse; however, having approached a woman outside the fertile period, bathing is required as if after voiding urine or feces."
These two, husband and wife, would both be impure when they have gone to bed;
once the woman has risen from the bed, she becomes pure, while the man remains impure.
The ellipsis is to be supplied as "they bring about the purification of their husband. Gautama says: "Having engaged in sexual union, she should not delay regarding purification. (1.79)
Proceeding in this manner, a man should avoid a woman who is emaciated, in her menses, or pregnant;
thus, on an auspicious day when the moon is in conjunction with a favorable asterism, a man shall procreate a son endowed with excellent marks.

Having made the woman emaciated by means of light food and other such methods, and having avoided the asterisms of Maghā and Mūla, when the moon is well-placed in another asterism, a man approaching his wife once during her fertile period (*ṛtu*) in the manner described shall procreate a son endowed with auspicious marks. Furthermore, through the favorable position of the moon, the configuration of the planets at that time—which, according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*), bestows the birth of a son—is indicated.

In this context, the observances for a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*) are stated as a corollary. Regarding this, Paiṭhīnasi says: "She shall wear soiled clothes for three nights. She must not bathe, nor anoint herself, nor clip her nails, nor spin rope, nor brush her teeth, nor wear a garland, nor use perfumes, nor consume aphrodisiacs (*vṛṣyāṇi*), nor drink from a broken vessel. Aphrodisiacs are substances that increase virility; a "broken vessel" (*kharva*) refers to the left hand. Vasiṣṭha states: "For three nights, a woman in her menses remains impure. She must not apply collyrium, nor anoint herself, nor bathe in water, nor sleep on the ground, nor sleep during the day. She must not touch fire, nor spin rope, nor eat meat, nor look at the planets, nor laugh, nor perform any [other] action, nor drink from a broken vessel or with cupped hands (*añjali*). [This is] optional, for there is a Vedic text stating, 'Or she may drink from cupped hands,' or 'from a copper vessel' (*lohitāyasa*). Copper is *lohitāyasa*. This collection of observances is to be understood as applying when the onset of menstruation causes impurity for three nights, not merely upon the appearance of blood. Regarding the specific night that constitutes the cause for the three-night impurity, Atri says:
If a woman who has become menstruating bathes and then becomes menstruating again within eighteen days, no state of impurity is found.
[106] For less than nineteen days it shall be one day; thereafter, for two days;
from thirty days onwards, among those who follow, one shall be impure for three nights.

And this count of days begins with the day of the ritual bath (*snāna*), because of the statement, "of her who has bathed. As for the other *smṛti* text which says, "Impurity does not exist prior to the fourteenth day," one should resolve the apparent contradiction by relying on a regulation based on the nature of the onset of the menses. A man must also perform the strengthening of his own power. As Bṛhaspati said:
If the woman’s semen (śukra) is in excess, a female will be born; if the man’s is in excess, a male will be born.
Therefore, for the sake of increasing the semen, one should consume aphrodisiacs (vṛṣya) and unctuous foods.
One should make the woman eat light food; in this way, she shall produce a son. || 1.80 ||
Now he states the occasion for approaching one's wife during her season:
"Or he may act according to his desire, remembering the boon granted to women;
yet he should remain devoted to his own wife alone, since women are declared to be protected. (1.81)

Not transgressing the desire or wish of his wives, he may approach them even outside the fertile period (*ṛtu*), because a boon was granted to women by Indra. Regarding Indra and women, it is stated in the *Taittirīyaka*: "They said, 'Let us choose a boon: let him come to us during the season; let us obtain offspring; let us unite according to our desire until the birth. Therefore, women obtain offspring when he comes during the season, and they unite according to their desire until the birth, for that was their chosen boon. He should remain faithful to his own wife. For it is traditionally taught (*smṛta*) that women must be protected from infidelity. And that protection is achieved by the husband through his own faithfulness and by acting according to the women's desires. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates that approaching them outside the season is optional. Consequently, one who is capable of protecting his women even if he does not approach them [during the season] should approach them only during the season. Regarding the superior fruit for such a man, Vasiṣṭha says: "A Brāhmaṇa who approaches his wife during the season and offers oblations according to the rule does not fall from the world of Brahman. But the other [type of man] may act according to his desire. (1.81)
Women should be honored by their husbands, brothers, fathers, kinsmen, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, brothers-in-law, and other relatives with ornaments, clothing, and food. (1.82)
[107] Women are to be honored by their husbands and others with gifts of ornaments, clothing, and food; this is an absolute necessity. Manu states that there is sin in failing to do so:
"Where women are well-honored, there the gods rejoice."
Where these are not honored, there all ritual actions are fruitless.

"Those houses which female relatives curse when they have not been honored perish on all sides, as if struck by a magical spell (kṛtyā). Here, "female relatives" (jāmayaḥ) refers to sisters; this term is also indicative of daughters-in-law, daughters, and others. As Bṛhaspati says:
A wife should be honored by her husband with garments, ornaments, and decorations,
as well as during festivals by her father and mother, and by her mother-in-law, father-in-law, and kinsmen.
The combination of ornaments and so forth pertains to the husband; however, with respect to others, there is either optionality or combination according to one's capacity. 1.82.
He states the duties of women:
Restrained in her household utensils, skillful, cheerful, and averse to wasteful expenditure, she should worship the feet of her parents-in-law, being entirely devoted to her husband. (1.83)

*Upaskara* refers to household utensils, such as ladles, stools, and the like. She whose *upaskara* is well-restrained (*saṃyata*) is called *saṃyatopaskarā*. She should be skillful (*dakṣā*), meaning quick in her actions; joyful (*hṛṣṭā*), meaning satisfied with whatever materials are at hand; and averse to wasteful expenditure. She should perform the salutation of the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law every day. She should be devoted to her husband and have her husband as her primary concern. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "Now, the duties of a woman: sharing the same vows and conduct as her husband; honoring her mother-in-law, father-in-law, elders, deities, and guests; keeping household utensils well-restrained; being open-handed (not stingy); keeping vessels well-secured; lack of interest in root-magic (*mūlakriyā*); and devotion to auspicious customs. *Mūlakriyā* refers to the practice of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*). Likewise, there is the speech of Lakṣmī addressed to the Earth.
Among women who are always well-adorned, devoted to their husbands, sweet-spoken, open-handed, blessed with sons, careful in guarding household goods, and fond of making offerings;

I am ever established as the creator of the worlds among those women who are well-adorned in dress, who have conquered their senses, who are free from vice, who are not greedy, who regard righteousness, and who are endowed with compassion. [108]

Śaṅkha says: "She should not go out without being addressed [by her husband]. She should not go without an upper garment. She should not walk hurriedly. She should not speak with a stranger, except for merchants, renunciants, elders, and physicians. She should not expose her navel. She should wear her clothing down to the ankles. She should not reveal her breasts. She should not laugh uncovered. She should not harbor hatred toward her husband or his relatives. She should not stay in one place with courtesans, rogues, unchaste women, female renunciants, fortune-tellers, sorceresses, witches, those of ill-repute, and the like; for they declare that through such association, one's character becomes corrupted. Thus says Vyāsa.
Constantly sitting at the doorway, likewise peering out of the window,
idle chatter, and laughter— these are the vices of women of good family.
Manu says:

Drinking [intoxicants], association with wicked people, separation from her husband, wandering about, sleeping [at night], and residing in another's house—these are the six things that corrupt women. (1.83)
Furthermore:
A woman whose husband is away from home should avoid sporting with her body, adorning herself, attending social gatherings or festivals, laughing, and visiting the houses of others. (1.84)

"Amusement" refers to activities such as gambling; "bodily adornment" refers to bathing, anointing with unguents, and so forth; "social gathering" is a meeting of people; and "festival" refers to the Kaumudī festival and others. She should avoid witnessing these, as well as laughter and traveling to another's house, while her husband is away on a journey. Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "For women of good family whose husbands are away on a journey and who lack independence, there shall be no engagement in swinging, dancing, amusements, viewing spectacles, applying cosmetics, visiting gardens, riding in vehicles, sitting in open seats, excessive drinking and eating, playing with balls, or the use of perfumes, garlands, ornaments, tooth-sticks, collyrium, mirrors, or personal decoration."
"When her husband has gone abroad, she should live established in her observances after having provided for her maintenance;
but if he has gone abroad without having so provided, she should live by means of blameless crafts.

The meaning is: when the husband has gone abroad after having arranged for her livelihood, his wife should live by that livelihood, adhering to a rule of eating only a small amount of food. If he has gone abroad without having made such arrangements, she should live by means of "blameless crafts"—that is, she should live only by those crafts through which no reproach arises. (1.84)
The father shall protect the maiden; once married, the husband; and in old age, the son. In their absence, her kinsmen shall protect her; a woman never possesses independence. 1.85.

[109] A father should protect and guard a maiden who is unmarried; her husband, once she is married; and in old age, her son. In the absence of these—the father and the others—it is the kinsmen and relatives who should protect her. Although this dependence has been stated, the prohibition of independence therein is intended to establish the king's authority over women when no relatives exist. And so says another Smṛti:
"But at the end of both families, the king is the woman’s protector and lord."
He should provide for her maintenance and restrain her if she deviates from the path. Thus (ends verse 1.85).
She should not be deprived of her father, mother, son, brother, mother-in-law, father-in-law, or maternal uncles; otherwise, she would be blameworthy in the absence of her husband. 1.86.

Living without her husband, she must not be separated from any one of her father or other [relatives]. If she were so, she would become censurable by the learned. By the preceding verse, it was stated that the protection of women must be performed by the father and others; by this [verse], it is ordained that in the absence of her husband, a woman must not be without her father or other [relatives]. (1.86)
He states the fruit of the aforementioned duties of women:
"Devoted to her husband’s pleasure and welfare, well-conducted, and with senses restrained, she attains fame in this world and the unsurpassed state after death. (1.87)

"Priya" means pleasant; "hita" means beneficial. She who practices the duty of a wife as taught—being diligent in what is both pleasant and beneficial to her husband—and who has her senses restrained, becomes famous in this world and, after death, attains the most excellent state in the hereafter. An action that grants happiness immediately is "pleasant" (*priya*); one that grants happiness in its ultimate result is "beneficial" (*hita*). Regarding this, Manu says: "She who remains devoted to her husband from the time of giving [her hand] until the end of her life attains the world of her husband, just like Arundhatī."
Bṛhaspati says:
She who is distressed when he is distressed, joyful when he is joyful, dejected and emaciated when he is away on a journey,
and who would die when her husband dies— she is to be known as a devoted wife (*pativratā*).

When [the husband] has died, death for her occurs through that very act of entering the great fire. As Aṅgiras said: "For all women indeed, when the husband has died, no other duty is ever to be known except for falling into the fire."
As long as a devoted wife does not burn her body in the fire upon the death of her husband,
she is by no means released from her female body.
For those women who have taken refuge in the state of virtuous conduct and whose husbands have departed— distraught by the wound of separation—
once that power has faded away, what path other than entering the fire remains for them?
[110] When the lord, the husband, has set, having gone to heaven— that is, being deceased— Hārīta says:
Listen now to the fruit that belongs to that woman who, being virtuous and firm in her vows, follows her husband when he has died.
As many as there are hairs on a human being— three and a half crores—
for that many thousands of years one is honored in the heavenly world.
Just as one who has mastered a mantra forcibly extracts a snake from its hole,
so too does she take her deceased husband and depart by the power of her asceticism.
She who follows her husband purifies three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and the family into which she is given as a bride.
Vyāsa says:
A woman who dies first shall take the fire; one who ascends the funeral pyre after her husband shall take his sin;
and in the absence [of other heirs], she shall take the husband's wealth even while living, provided there are no surviving kinsmen.
Whatever evil deed has been committed against a slayer of a Brahmin, a betrayer of a favor, or a slayer of a friend,
that wife purifies her husband by dying after taking him with her.

The meaning is "having taken [him] and embraced him. For this very reason, the author of the Kalpasūtra states that she should lie down together with the body of her husband: "They cause the wife to lie down together on the north side. Now, learn of the power of that devoted wife who, having heard news of her beloved's death while he was in a foreign land, ascends the blazing fire.
"Vṛtta" means dead.
Even if he has entered hell, bound by most cruel nooses,
having reached the place of torment, and been seized by the servants of Yama;
Helpless and miserable, he remains writhing, bound by his own past actions;
just as a snake-catcher seizes a serpent from its hole unexpectedly.
In the same way, taking her husband with her, she goes to heaven by the power of asceticism;
there, devoted supremely to her husband, she is praised by hosts of apsarases.
She rejoices together with her husband for as long as fourteen Indras endure.

Based on the statement, "She rejoices together with her husband," the enjoyment of heaven along with the husband is a fruit that accrues solely to the wife; thus, the contradiction—that the husband, though not the agent, experiences the fruit of the wife's act of entering the fire—is easily resolved. As for the attainment of happiness by the husband, that arises from the merit residing in the husband himself. The merit performed by the wife removes the sin that acts as an obstacle to that [attainment]. Furthermore, the remover of an obstacle is not itself the primary cause of the effect. As for the scriptural teaching that the destruction of the husband’s sins is the fruit of the merit performed by the wife, even there the meaning is not primary but secondary; "destruction" (kṣaya) here is like a mere cessation, consisting in the prevention of the immediate yielding of results for the husband’s sin through the wife’s merit. — Bṛhaspati.
A wife is considered half of one's body, sharing equally in the fruits of merit and demerit;
when she follows her husband in death, that virtuous woman acts for his ultimate benefit.

Furthermore, following the husband in death (*anvārohaṇa*) is non-obligatory because it is performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*). For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "When the husband has died, [the wife may observe] celibacy (*brahmacarya*) or follow him in death. Nor should it be argued that the Smṛti texts concerning *anvārohaṇa* contradict the Śruti text, "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the full span of life," because their subject matters (*viṣaya*) are different. The Śruti prohibits death by one's own will in a general sense, whereas the Smṛti prescribes the specific act of entering the fire upon the husband's death. Thus, there is no contradiction due to the difference in subject matter. There is likewise no contradiction with Śruti texts of general scope, such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice" or "One should offer the Agnihotra as long as one lives. And so says the Brahma Purāṇa:
When her husband has died, there is no other refuge for virtuous women;
there is nothing else that can alleviate the burning pain of separation from their husband.
Having placed her purified hand upon his chest, she may enter the fire;
according to the teaching of the Rigveda, a virtuous wife does not become a suicide.
When purification has been completed after three days, one obtains the eternal Śrāddha.

Vedic scriptural passages such as "These women, not widows... [exist]. Therefore, these Smṛtis are authoritative. Nor can the act of ascending the funeral pyre (*anvārohaṇa*) be prohibited by the general rule "One shall not kill," for by this [rule], the killing of one who is to be killed—other than the agent—is prohibited, but not self-slaughter. That [self-slaughter], however, is prohibited by the passage "Therefore, indeed, not before the end of one's lifespan. And it has been stated that this [general Vedic rule], being of a general scope, is restricted by the Smṛti concerning the specific case of ascending the pyre, which functions to prohibit self-slaughter other than that [specific instance]. Nor should it be said that a Smṛti contradicted by a Vedic text of general scope lacks authority; for there is no contradiction here due to the difference in scope between the general and the specific. For contradiction exists only when the scope is identical, not when there is a difference in the scope of the specific. Consequently, by means of the Smṛti concerning the specific case, a Vedic text that serves as its own source is inferred to be of a specific scope itself. And that [inferred text], being more powerful than the Vedic text of general scope, becomes the cause of its restriction. Now, they record a prohibition of ascending the pyre for a Brāhmaṇa woman, as for instance Paiṭhīnasi [does]: [The text continues with the citation from Paiṭhīnasi.]
Following the husband in death does not exist for a Brāhmaṇa woman, according to the injunction of Brahmā;
however, for the other castes, this is recorded as the supreme duty of women.
A Brahmin woman, while living in her state of grief, brings greater benefit to her husband than she does when dead.
Virāṭ said: One should follow a living husband, but one must not go [with him] when he is dead;
while living, a brother-in-law (bharu) may act for her benefit, but by dying [with him], she becomes a self-destroyer.
Aṅgiras:
A woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who follows her deceased husband [to death] does not, by that self-slaughter, lead either herself or her husband to heaven.
Vyāghrapāda said:
A Brāhmaṇa woman, deluded by grief, should not die together with her husband;
by killing herself, she incurs the fate of one who has committed suicide.

Renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is the abandonment of the enjoyment of sexual intercourse and other such pleasures. It is true that they remember this; however, it is through another [textual] tradition that their domain is established. As Uśanas said: "A Brahmin woman ought not to go [to another man] after mounting a separate funeral pyre; this is remembered as the supreme duty of women toward other women."

Consequently, the prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa woman following [her husband] refers specifically to the case of ascending the funeral pyre separately. For this very reason, in the Rāmāyaṇa and other texts, it is narrated that Brāhmaṇa women and others cremate their own bodies after first embracing the body of their husbands. For this same reason, the author of the Kalpasūtra prescribes the wife’s reclining to the north of the deceased as a mandatory rule without distinction. However, they say that her being raised up by a brother-in-law or another [kinsman] occurs only when there is a desire for a son on her part, or a desire for the world of the living. Furthermore, the prohibition against following [the husband] is not based on the cause of her being a Brāhmaṇa; rather, it is caused by grief. As for those verses of Vairāja and Āṅgirasa which appear to prohibit the mere act of a Brāhmaṇa woman following [her husband], they are subsumed under the specific prohibitions [already mentioned]. Therefore, no fault exists for a Brāhmaṇa woman who follows [her husband] according to the injunction; however, for one who acts out of grief and the like, there certainly is. (1.87)
When another wife of the same caste exists, one should not have her perform religious duties.

[113] The meaning is that when a wife of the same caste is present, one should not have another wife of a different caste perform religious duties; that is, one should not practice dharma with her. It follows by implication that even in the absence of a wife of the same caste, one may practice with the other. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha states a prohibition against performing religious rites with a Śūdra woman alone: "Women of dark complexion are for pleasure only, not for dharma. Here, "dark-complexioned" refers to a Śūdra woman.
In the performance of religious duties with wives of the same caste, he must not do so with another wife except the eldest.

If [the wives] are of the same caste (*savarṇā*), however, and the eldest is not defective, he should not perform religious duty (*dharma*) with another wife in her absence; rather, even the younger wives should be made to perform their duty together with the eldest. Thus says Āpastamba: "While his wife is endowed with both virtue and offspring, he should not take others; but upon the failure of either, he may do so. For before the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), she who is already present at the *ādhāna* becomes connected with the ritual acts. Baudhāyana says: "The binding together of the wives is simultaneous"—thus indeed said Baudhāyana—"one should bind each one individually, cause each one to look toward the *gārhapatya* fire, and cause each one to gaze at the clarified butter (*ājya*)," and so forth. Kātyāyana [says]:
The twice-born should know that the rite of establishing the sacred fires is not accomplished even by one wife alone;
for it is considered unperformed if all [the wives] do not participate in the ritual grasping of the hand (anvārambhaṇa).

Therefore, the interpretation that "only the eldest wife is the partner in dharma (sahadharmacāriṇī) and not the others" is to be disregarded, as it contradicts the Kalpasūtras and the Dharmaśāstras. As for the statement of Viṣṇu: "In sacrifices such as the Agnihotra, one should not perform [the rite] with a second wife;
otherwise, his sacrifice becomes fruitless even if hundreds of other rites are well-performed."

This refers to a case where the second wife is of a different caste (*asavarṇa*), or it refers to one who was married while the sacred fires were still present. Since she has the authority to perform the re-establishment of the fires (*punarādhāna*) once the fires have been lost, she has joint authority with her husband in the *agnihotra* and other rites. Kātyāyana states: "A man with many wives should have the service of maintaining the sacred fires and so forth performed by his wife of equal caste;
however, if there are many such wives, the eldest one shall be the one authorized for the sacrifice."
Or she who has borne heroic sons, who carries out his commands,
who is skillful, sweet-spoken, and pure— one such as this he should employ here.
Or they may perform the work according to the sequence of days, or according to seniority if they lack the capacity;
or they may divide it and do it together, according to their knowledge and without deceit.

Dakṣa said: "She is declared to be the lawful wife provided she remains faultless; if a fault exists, there is no fault [in replacing her], for another woman endowed with virtues should be taken. (1.88)
[114] Having cremated his virtuous wife with the *agnihotra* fire, the husband shall, without delay, take another wife and the sacred fires according to the prescribed rule. 1.89.

When she with whom he performed the *agnyādheya* has died after having fulfilled her duties, the husband, having cremated her according to the rules with the Vaitāna fires, shall—if she was a wife of a different caste—obtain her [share] through gifts according to the rule, without delay, from the fires. In that case, if a wife of the same caste is not available, the performance of the *agnyādheya* and other rites may be carried out even with a wife of a different caste, excluding a Śūdra woman. As Viṣṇu says:
"Even when his wife has died, he must not abandon the Vedic fire;
even by means of a substitute, he should complete those rites for as long as he lives."

The meaning of this is as follows: after performing the funeral rites for his deceased wife, a Vedic practitioner should not abandon those [fires]; rather, he should re-establish them. In the event that a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) cannot be obtained, he should complete the ritual acts for the rest of his life even with a wife of a different caste, though under certain conditions. However, this does not mean that even when the wife has died, the Vedic fire must not be abandoned, nor that one should burn her with it. For if that were the case, it would be difficult to avoid contradicting the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhya* scripture which states: "These fires become like those for the dead who are maintained when the wife has died. Likewise, the phrase "even by means of a substitute (*upādhi*) that ritual act" does not mean that the completion of the rite should be performed with a wife made of *kuśa* grass or gold; for a wife is not something that can be replaced. As Satyāṣāḍha says: "There is no substitute for the master, the wife, the son, the place, the time, the fire, the deity, the ritual act, or the word. Although the wife’s role as a performer of the ritual acts for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*) might theoretically be replaceable, a mere effigy made of *kuśa* grass or the like cannot serve as a substitute because it lacks the capacity to perform that specific function. Indeed, the wife’s duty is not merely to be present nearby; rather, her duties consist of actions such as husking the grain and gazing at the clarified butter (*ājya*), while her presence nearby is merely implied by those functions. Therefore, the previously stated interpretation alone is logical. Furthermore, regarding what was said... [text continues].
Others, being householders, having fashioned a wife out of kuśa grass,
perform the agnihotra sacrifice tirelessly throughout their lives.
This statement is solely for the purpose of praising the Agnihotra and does not enjoin its own meaning, for the reason already stated. [115]

But is it not the case that for wives who have been taken again (*punarāhṛta*), the entitlement to perform the *agnihotra* and other rites is untenable, because they lack the purificatory consecrations (*saṃskāra*) produced by the *anvārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice and the *hotṛ-homa*? Nor can the wife perform the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and other rites independently for the sake of her own consecration, because she is restricted to joint entitlement (*sahādhikāra*). Nor can the husband perform them, since he is already consecrated; his consecration results from the performance of the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and other rites which are auxiliary members (*kratvaṅga*) of the sacrifice. Indeed, one who has already undergone the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and other consecrations is not enjoined by scripture to perform the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and so forth again. Therefore, the *agnihotra* must be performed by one who is without a wife. Thus says the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*: "Therefore, one without a wife should take up the sacred fires. This is incorrect. For all the *Śrutis* enjoin the *agnihotra* and other rites for one who is with a wife. The *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* passage is also consistent when understood as being intended for praise (*stuti*). Furthermore, this statement—"one without a wife should take up the fires"—refers to a case where the wife is either menstruating or in childbirth, not to a case where a wife simply does not exist. This being so, there is no contradiction with other *Śrutis*. This sentence is not an injunction (*vidhi*). Therefore, in the absence of any conflict with *Śruti*, the Smṛti statement, "He should take a wife according to rule," is indeed authoritative. Consequently, by the force of this statement, one must accept that the husband’s entitlement to the *anvārambhaṇīyā* and other rites exists through the assumption of a restoration of his previous consecrations. For this very reason, Baudhāyana speaks regarding the matter of taking a wife again: "Regarding one who has sacrificed and is re-establishing the fires, should he offer the *Sāṃnāyya* or not? Some say he should offer it; others say he should not. [The sacrifice then becomes untouched by impurity. When he sacrifices again, then he should offer it]. The meaning of this is as follows: having raised the doubt whether the Adhvaryu priest should offer the *Sāṃnāyya* or not for one who has sacrificed (performed a Soma sacrifice) and is re-establishing the fires after his wife has died—even though another has been taken—the proponent states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*): "Some say he should offer it. Their intention is this: although the wife lacks the consecration produced by the Soma sacrifice—which is the cause for her entitlement to the *Sāṃnāyya*—because she did not perform the Soma sacrifice together with him, nevertheless, because she stands in a subordinate relation (*guṇabhāva*) to the sacrificer and the sacrificer possesses the necessary consecration, he should indeed offer the *Sāṃnāyya*.

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "Now some say, 'One should not bring it,' for the sacrifice is indeed in contact with the body. By the word "body," the embodied self (*ātman*) is indicated. Indeed, through the sacrifice, a refinement (*saṃskāra*) conducive to the performance of the *sāṃnāyya* offering is imparted to the self. And the refinement belonging to the Soma sacrifice, which resides in the sacrificer and his wife, is not useful for the *sāṃnāyya* sacrifice; nor is a newly married wife possessed of that refinement. Therefore, one should certainly not bring it. Rather, "only when one is to sacrifice again with Soma should one then bring it."

Furthermore, because they impart a refinement (*saṃskāra*) characterized by fitness for performing subsequent rites, the *Hotṛ-homa* and the *Anvārambhaṇīyā* are equal to the *Soma* sacrifice; therefore, this same interpretation is appropriate for them. Consequently, it is established that a wife who has died after the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*) is to be consecrated with those very Vaitānika fires. If one’s wife is incapable of performing the religious duties, he should bring another wife capable of such duties and perform the *ādhāna*; otherwise, however, he should simply perform the *ādhāna* [for himself]. As for the statement: "He who would burn a second wife with the Vaitānika fires... [the rest follows].
If the first [period] remains unexpired, however, that indeed is equal to drinking liquor.

This statement of Devala refers to the case of one who has not performed the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) on the second day [of impurity]. Otherwise, it would be invalid as it would contradict the Vedic injunction: "They cremate the one who has established the fires with his fires. Nor should it be argued that the term *āhitāgni* occurring in the Śruti becomes restricted to a specific meaning by virtue of the Smṛti; for, as the provider of the intended object already grasped in the text, it has no requirement toward a specific qualification, just like the word "cup" (*graha*) in the injunction "he cleanses the cup" (*grahaṃ saṃmārṣṭi*). (1.89)

Thus ends the section on Marriage [and the Section on the Distinction of Castes and Classes] in the *Yājñavalkīyadharmaśāstranibandha* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the glorious Vidyādharas.

This section is commenced for the purpose of understanding the designations useful in common practice regarding those born of the aforementioned marriages to wives of the same caste as well as those of a different caste, and likewise those born of women who are wanton or born in the inverse order of castes:
"From men of the same caste, sons of the same caste are indeed born to wives of the same caste; through blameless marriages, these sons increase the lineage. (1.90)

Sons begotten by a husband and wife of equal caste (savarṇā) become of the same caste as those two. The mention of "sons" (putra) here refers generally to offspring. Sons born of a woman married through blameless forms of marriage become the cause of the increase of qualities such as spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) for the lineage. On this point, Manu says:
"In the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma form, in their respective order, sons endowed with spiritual luster and esteemed by the learned are born."
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and excellence, wealthy and renowned,
possessing abundant enjoyments and most righteous, they live for a hundred years.
And among the other remaining types of improper marriages, cruel and untruthful sons are born who are haters of the Veda and of dharma.

This refers to the domain of Brahmins: through blameless marriages with women, one's offspring become blameless; through blameworthy ones, they become blameworthy among men. Therefore, one should avoid those who are blameworthy. (1.90)
He speaks of those born in the direct order (anuloma):
"From a Brahmin, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born of a Kṣatriya woman; an Ambaṣṭha from a Vaiśya woman; and a Niṣāda, or alternatively a Pāraśava, from a Śūdra woman. (1.91)

From a Brāhmaṇa father and Kṣatriya or other wives, sons known as Mūrdhāvasikta, Ambaṣṭha, and Niṣāda are born. Furthermore, the term *pāraśava* is another name for the Niṣāda. Gautama states: "Those born from wives who are immediate, one-removed, two-removed, or three-removed [in caste] are called Savarṇa, Ambaṣṭha, Ugra, Niṣāda, Dauṣmanta, and Pāraśava; these are the *anuloma* (direct-order) offspring born of wives of different castes. For a Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya wife is immediate; the son born of her by him is a Savarṇa. From a Kṣatriya, on an immediate Vaiśya wife, an Ambaṣṭha is born. From a Vaiśya, on the immediately following Śūdra wife, an Ugra is born. From a Brāhmaṇa, on a Vaiśya wife one degree removed, a Niṣāda is born. From a Kṣatriya, on a Śūdra wife one degree removed, a Dauṣmanta is born. From a Brāhmaṇa, on a Śūdra wife two degrees removed, a Pāraśava is born. There should be no contradiction regarding this variation in nomenclature. Viṣṇu says: "Sons born of wives of the same caste are of that same caste; however, those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) have the caste of their mother. (1.91)

From a Kṣatriya father and Vaiśya or Śūdra mothers, the sons Māhiṣya and Ugra are recorded; from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra wife, the son is Karaṇa. This is the rule prescribed for wives who have been duly wedded. (1.92)

From a Kṣatriya father and a Vaiśya mother is born a Māhiṣya; from a Śūdra mother, an Ugra. From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother is born a Karaṇa. [118] The rule stated by the phrase "from those of the same caste (savarṇa) upon women of the same caste," etc., is recorded by the sages as referring to wives who have been wedded (*vinnāsu*). However, since even sons such as the *kṣetraja* and others, though born of unwedded women (*avinnāsu*), are admitted to belong to a caste, the term "wedded" (*vinnāsu*) is intended as an illustration of the method for the procreation of sons prescribed by the scriptures. Precisely because they possess Brahminhood, Baudhāyana—after stating "Brahmins are the officiating priests"—declares an exclusion for those born of another's field (*parakṣetra*), saying: "having excluded those of the *śabaleya*, *bāhaleya*, son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), son of another's field (*parakṣetra*), *sahoḍha*, *kānīna*, *anujāvara*, and those with two ancestral lineages (*dvipravara*). As for that which was stated by Devala:
But he who is begotten by the second [class] upon a wife of equal caste is known as an Avarīṭa; by birth, he follows the dharma of a Śūdra.
Likewise,

those sons who are born of women of the same caste but are deprived of their vows and lack the purificatory rites are excluded from the community; though begotten by a man of the same caste, they are considered outcasts because they have failed in their religious observances.

Thus, this refers to sons born of *niyoga* (authorized union) or through adultery, excluding those recognized by the scriptures as *kṣetraja*, *kānīna*, *sahoḍha*, *gūḍhotpanna*, and *paunarbhava*. Furthermore, these individuals such as the *mūrdhāvasikta* and others are not distinct from the *kṣatriyas* and other castes; rather, they receive the specific names of *mūrdhāvasikta* and so forth due to the distinctions of the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of their respective fathers, such as Brāhmaṇas and others. As Śaṅkha says: "One born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya wife is indeed a Kṣatriya; one born to a Kṣatriya from a Vaiśya wife is indeed a Vaiśya; one born to a Vaiśya from a Śūdra wife is indeed a Śūdra. (1.92)
He states the names of those born in the inverse order:
"From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka;
but from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla is born, who is excluded from all religious duties. (1.93)
A Vaiśya woman from Māgadha and a Śūdra woman both gave birth to a Kṣattṛ;
furthermore, a Vaiśya woman begot a son, the Āyogava, from a Śūdra.

From a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra, respectively, upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, there arise the Sūta, the Vaideha, and the Caṇḍāla. Among these, the Caṇḍāla is excluded from all *dharma*. The meaning is that he is ineligible for those duties which constitute the *dharma* of all the castes (*varṇas*), but not for all duties whatsoever. As Devala says: "Purification of one's own caste, bowing to all, forbearance, purity in conduct, not insulting others, supporting one's own dependents, performing one's own specific duty (*svakarma*), and avoiding the principal duties (*pradhānakarma*)—these are the duties of a Caṇḍāla. [119] Consequently, *varṇadharma* refers to the principal duty, while *svakarma* refers to one's own livelihood. A Kṣatriya woman begets a Māgadha from a Vaiśya and a Kṣattṛ from a Śūdra. A Vaiśya woman begets an Āyogava from a Śūdra. These designations are used for conventional usage in other treatises. Regarding this, Manu says:
The training of horses and charioteering for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas;
work related to women for the Vaidehakas; and the way of trade for the Māgadhas.
The killing of fish is the characteristic mark of the Niṣādas and of those who subsist on the flesh of dogs;
likewise,
the abandonment of one's body for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow is [the mark] of those who do not adorn themselves [for worldly ends].
And the protection of women and children is the cause of success for outsiders.
*Upaskāra* means taking the root; *abhyavapatti* means favoring. 1.93–94.
From a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother, a Rathakāra is born.

The Māhiṣya has already been described. A Karaṇī is one born from a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother. From her, one born of a Māhiṣya father becomes a Rathakāra. Because he is entitled to perform Vedic rites, he is mentioned separately among those of mixed origin. Thus says Śaṅkha: "The Rathakāra is born from the immediate (anantara) union of a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya woman; for him there are the rites of sacrifice, giving, and the initiatory ceremony (upanayana), as well as the study of the science of horses, chariots, and weaving, and his livelihood."
But those born in the inverse and direct orders are to be known as non-existent and existent [respectively]. || 1.95 ||

Those born from a man of lower caste by a woman of higher caste are *pratilomaja* (born in the inverse order). Those born from a man of higher caste by a married woman of lower caste are *anulomaja* (born in the direct order). Among these, the *pratilomaja* are non-existent [in the true sense] and wicked; the meaning is that they are excluded from the [caste] classes. The *anulomaja*, however, are existent and virtuous; because they share the same caste as their mother, they become entitled to the duties of the Kṣatriyas and other [higher castes]. || 1.95 ||
An elevation of caste is to be known as occurring in the seventh or even the fifth generation.
