The term *yugyam* refers to the pair consisting of husband and wife. In that context, it should be understood that the status of belonging to the same caste as the father occurs either in the seventh or even the fifth generation. This applies specifically to women born in the direct order (*anuloma*), because it is only in their case that the status of being a wife is possible; it does not apply to those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), since they are excluded from the caste system and thus do not possess the status of a wife (*ajāyā*). The alternative mentioned depends on specific qualities. When a woman of a lower caste is procreated by a man of a higher caste through an unprohibited path, she gives birth to a daughter who likewise gives birth to another, and so on; thus, the offspring born in the seventh generation from such a male-female pair becomes equal in caste to the father.
Regarding the equality [of status] resulting from the transposition of occupations:

when there is a transposition or violation of those occupations that constitute the livelihoods of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others—such as when the sons, grandsons, and so forth born to a Brāhmaṇa who subsists on the occupation of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya themselves subsist on that very same occupation—then the offspring born in the seventh or fifth generation becomes of the nature of the caste of the person whose livelihood they are subsisting upon.
And as before, the upper [vowel] is placed after the lower one. 1.96.

As with the mixing of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), the mixing of occupations (*vṛttisaṃkara*) should also be understood as being higher or lower, as before. This designation emphasizes the state (*bhāva*); therefore, the meaning is that one should understand [the status] as either higher or lower. In the case of the mixing of occupations according to the natural order (*ānulomya*), there is a higher status. As Vasiṣṭha says: "Those who subsist by their own duty may adopt the next lower occupation, even if it is more sinful. In the case of the mixing of occupations against the natural order (*prātilomya*), there is a lower status—as when a Vaiśya lives by the occupation of a Kṣatriya, or a Kṣatriya lives by the occupation of a Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, following the rule "they may adopt an occupation," Vasiṣṭha adds: "but never a higher one. (1.96)

Thus ends the third chapter, on the Distinction of Classes and Castes, in this legal digest on the Institutes of Yājñavalkya, composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of the glorious Jīmūtavāhana, the king of the Śilāhāras and descendant of the noble Vidyādhara dynasty.
Now, in the section on the duties of the householder (Chapter 4) within the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary:

having explained the taking of a wife along with its related matters— on the grounds that a householder possesses the authority to perform religious duties only when accompanied by a wife— the author now declares the duties of the householder.

[121] A householder should perform the *smārta* rites every day in the marriage fire (*vivāhāgni*), or in the fire obtained at the time of inheritance; however, he should perform the *śrauta* rites in the *vaitānika* fires. 1.97.

The householder (*gṛhī*)—meaning one who possesses a wife—should perform daily the *smārta* rites prescribed in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* in the *vaivāhika* fire, that is, the fire consecrated by the marriage ceremony. This word *gṛha* denotes the wife, not the house. By using the term "in the *vaivāhika* fire," [the author] indicates that through the marriage rite, a certain excellence conducive to the *gṛhya* rituals arises within the fire. For otherwise, the successful performance of the rites would not occur in the *vaivāhika* fire, because fire perishes moment by moment. Due to the permanence of the marriage consecration (*saṃskāra*), the *vaivāhika* fire characterized by it becomes permanent. Consequently, it is indicated that although the fire may have been extinguished, it is regenerated through the marriage rite. Regarding this, Kātyāyana states the causes for the marriage consecration: [The text continues with the citation from Kātyāyana.]
If one who has taken a wife crosses the boundary while the marriage fire is still maintained,
it is prescribed that he must perform the re-establishment of the fire (punarādheya) once the time for the daily oblation has passed.

When the two fires have been extinguished, destroyed, or consumed by fire, one should carefully preserve the fire; when it has become completely quenched, a re-establishment of the sacred fires is prescribed.
Marīci:
When a sudden disappearance of smoke occurs even though the fire is at a distance, a re-consecration (punarādheya) must be performed; no other expiation is prescribed.

This concerns the case when the sacrificer is away on a journey and the fires have been consigned into the kindling woods (*samāropa*). Baudhāyana states: "If the fires are deposited in an impure place, one should consign them [into the woods], churn out the fire, and perform the *pavamāneṣṭi*. This refers to the fires used for the sacrificial rites (*vaitānāgni*). "If it is the marriage fire (*vivāhāgni*) and the sacrificer possesses the two kindling woods (*araṇi*), then, having churned the fire as before, he should perform the *pavamāneṣṭi* and offer oblations of cooked rice (*caru*) to the deities, or perform full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*). If he does not possess the kindling woods, he should bring a common (*laukika*) fire and proceed with the offering of cooked rice—whether by means of cooking that was not specifically prescribed for the rite or by performing the ritual extraction (*uddharaṇa*).
That fire should be understood as a common fire; it requires re-establishment (*punarādheya*)."

"And one should perform the domestic (*gṛhya*) rites in the fire brought at the time of the partition of inheritance. *Dāya* means paternal wealth; *āhṛta* means brought or established. One should perform the Śrauta rites, such as the Agnihotra, in the Vaitānika fires, namely the Gārhapatya and others. This is merely restated as it is already established by the Kalpasūtras and Gṛhyaśāstras, for the purpose of precluding the connection with the Śrauta fire of marriage for those rites—such as the planetary sacrifice (*grahayajña*)—prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras and Purāṇas. [122] Kātyāyana says: "Having deposited the fire in his own wife and likewise having appointed a priest..."
A Brahmin who has business should travel abroad; he should never remain away for long without a valid reason.
"Even while traveling, one should perform the daily obligatory rites with the mind, remaining untiring;
having sat down and purified oneself, one should perform them all at the proper time. Thus it is said.

Hārīta says: "One should not travel during the two fire-periods (*agnivelā*) or on the *parvan* days. The meaning of "the two fire-periods" is the two times for the *agnihotra* sacrifice. Regarding those who are prone to travel (*prāyāyuka*), Laugākṣi states: "Having offered the evening oblation, one should offer the morning oblation at that very same time. The *Maitrāyaṇīyapariśiṣṭa* states: "The sages were indeed prone to travel; they became distressed by their *agnihotra* [due to being away from home] and saw the possibility of performing all the offerings at once. Thus, for a two-night period, a three-night period, a six-night period, an eight-night period, or even half a month, they performed the *agnihotra*. Therefore, a traveler, one who is ill, or one who is distressed should perform the *agnihotra* for half a month. At the beginning of the fortnight and at the end of the *parvan*, both in the evening and in the morning, there are fourteen portions of four ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*), a single pouring of water, a single fuel-stick, a single offering, and a single wiping of the hands—this is the rule for the morning. The meaning of this is as follows: The sages, being prone to travel and habitually away from home, became distressed because the *agnihotra* was not being performed at its proper time, and thus they looked toward a rule for times of distress (*āpad-dharma*). They perceived that all the offerings could be performed simultaneously. Among these, the offerings belonging to the end of the fortnight, the two-night period, the three-night period, the six-night period, the fortnight, or the half-month period—they performed them all at once. Therefore, anyone else who is traveling or afflicted by illness should likewise perform the half-monthly *agnihotra*. The procedure for this is as follows: On the day of the sacrifice at the beginning of the fortnight, in the evening, he pours out fourteen portions of four ladlings all at once. This is mentioned as an illustration; the point is that one should complete the count of four-ladling portions so that the morning of the *aupavasathya* day (the day before the full moon or new moon) is covered by the final evening offering of the preceding fortnight. In this way, the number of four-ladling portions required to cover the morning of the *aupavasathya* day must be prepared at the time of the morning offering. Generally, this amounts to fourteen; however, the mention of that number is merely illustrative, as the count may sometimes be thirteen or fifteen.
Regarding one engaged in a long journey, the Śruti states: "As many oblations as he intends to offer, so many fourfold-drawn portions of ghee should he take up all at once. (1.97)
[123] Having attended to the needs of the body and performed the rites of purification, the twice-born man should perform the morning twilight devotion, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth. 1.98.

Having concluded his reflection on the body—that is, reflection concerning the health or illness of the body—the twice-born householder, having performed the rites of purification, should perform the morning *saṃdhyā* preceded by the cleaning of the teeth. That which has the cleaning (scouring) of the teeth as its prerequisite is called "preceded by the cleaning of the teeth. Here, the *saṃdhyā* prescribed for the religious student (*brahmacārin*) is extended to the householder as well; its being preceded by the cleaning of the teeth is what is enjoined by this [text]. Śaṅkha says: "Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, one should perform the voiding of urine and feces. [This is stated] in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
Having gone quickly from the shelter toward the southwest for a distance of about one arrow-shot, he should void his excrement while covering his head;
however, he must never touch his head with his hand.
Aṅgiras says:
Having placed the sacred thread behind his neck, hanging down his back,
a householder may void excrement or urine, or he may do so with it held over his ear, being composed in mind.
Having risen during the last watch of the night and sipped water,
he should cover the ground with grass and clothe himself with his garment for the following day.
Restraining his speech with effort, avoiding spitting and exhaling,
he should void urine and feces in a clean place, being fully composed.
Dakṣa says: When the time of dawn has arrived, one should perform purification according to the rules;
thereafter, one should perform the ritual bath preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
Vṛddhaparāśara says:
"If the mouth remains stale, a man is perpetually impure;
therefore, with every effort, he should consume a tooth-stick."
Kātyāyana says: Having risen, washed his eyes, become pure, and composed himself,
he should rinse his teeth with a mantra after reciting it.
"O Lord of the Forest, grant me long life, strength, fame, luster, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence. Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya.
One should first rinse [the teeth] and then eat; having rinsed them, one should likewise discard [the twig].
Facing either north or east, one should use a twig that is astringent, bitter, or thorny.
Having eaten in the morning and remaining silent, one should consume a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) that is twelve finger-breadths long, as thick as the tip of the little finger, and well-rounded. —
Garga.
For Brahmins it should be ten finger-breadths, for Kṣatriyas nine finger-breadths,
for Vaiśyas eight finger-breadths, and for Śūdras it is measured at seven.
For women, however, it is exactly four finger-breadths; of this there is no doubt.
For one facing eastward, there is stability, happiness, and indeed bodily health.
In the south there is leprosy; in the west, defeat;
in the north, the loss of cattle, women, and attendants.

Viṣṇu states: "One should not use a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*, nor one produced from *śreṣmātaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *vibhītaka*, *dhava*, or *dhanvana*; nor one produced from *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, *pippala*, *iṅguda*, or *guggulu*; nor one produced from *bandhūka*, *nirguṇṭhī*, *śigru*, *bilvaka*, or *tinduka*; nor one produced from *pāribhadra*, *vālmīka*, *mocakya*, *śalmalī*, or *śaṇa*. It should not be sweet, nor sour, nor dried at the top; it should not have hollows, nor a foul odor, nor be slimy. *Mocakya* means produced from the *daka-lī* tree. Vyāsa says:
"On the first day (*pratipad*), the new moon (*darśa*), the sixth, and the ninth days, [one should avoid] brushing the teeth."
One should use leaves, or else wood, or even blades of grass, for the scraping of the tongue.
Made from a thorny milky tree, measuring twelve finger-breadths in length,
as thick as the tip of the little finger, and with a brush-like tuft made from half a joint.
The tooth-stick and likewise the tongue-scraper have been prescribed;
for the sake of purification, one should rise in the morning and consume the tooth-stick.
A woman whose husband is away from home must not eat during a funeral rite (śrāddha) or a sacrifice (yajña), even if she is observing her religious observances (niyama).
This prohibition applies to the performer of the *śrāddha*, not to the eater.
In the absence of tooth-sticks, or on a forbidden lunar day,
one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with twelve mouthfuls of water.
According to the Purāṇas: On the first day of the lunar fortnight, the new moon, the sixth, the fourteenth, the eighth, the ninth,
and on Sundays, one should avoid using a tooth-stick.
Yama says: On the fourteenth day, the eighth day, the new moon, the full moon, and on the sun’s transit (saṃkrānti),
one should avoid shaving, women, oil, meat, and the tooth-stick.

Uśanas says: "One should not split the tooth-stick, nor should one clean the teeth with the fingers. Another Smṛti states: "One should never use a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa*, *kākubha*, or *dārbha* wood. If one should use them, I shall declare the expiation for that: one should gaze upon a cow. [125]

Kātyāyana says: Just as during the day, so too should one bathe every morning without sloth; having cleansed one's teeth in a river or similar place, or at home, that [latter act] is indeed without mantras.

The phrase "like a non-mantra" is intended to prohibit the extensive recitation of mantras; for this very [author] has said: "Because the time for the oblation is brief and the ritual of bathing is extensive, one should perform a concise bath in the morning; the omission of the oblation is censured."
The body is utterly impure and endowed with nine apertures; it exudes [impurities) day and night. Morning bathing is the means of purification.
They praise the morning bath, for it indeed brings about both visible and invisible benefits.
Viṣṇu:
He who desires to enjoy pure pleasures comparable to the moon and the sun should always bathe in the morning for two months, Māgha and Phālguna.
Yama says: One who constantly bathes at dawn during the two months of Māgha and Phālguna,
having duly worshipped the gods and the ancestors, is liberated from all sins.
Having offered oblations into the fires, one should recite the mantras dedicated to the deity Sūrya with a concentrated mind.

Having performed the fire-sacrifices according to the Śrauta and Smārta rites in accordance with one's own scripture, one should—concentrated, that is, with a one-pointed mind—recite the mantras dedicated to the deity Sūrya as studied in one's own Vedic branch. As stated in the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
"Beginning with the morning twilight while the stars are still visible, one should proceed according to the prescribed rule."
One should practice the Sāvitrī mantra until the sun becomes visible.
Then, having reached his dwelling, the wise man should always perform the fire-oblation;
indeed, the performance of the oblation by himself is prescribed at the conclusion of the twilight rites.
Whatever fruit may arise from one’s own burnt offering cannot be obtained by another;
[this applies to] the officiating priest, a son, a teacher, a brother, a sister’s son, or a husband.
Whatever is offered by these very [means], that indeed is an offering made by oneself.

The husband or the son-in-law [is the sacrificer]. However, in the case of the Śrauta rites, one among the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or a student (*antevāsin*) should offer the oblation. To this effect Āśvalāyana says: "One should offer the oblation oneself on the festival days (*parvan*); at other times, one of the officiating priests or a student may do so. Manu says:

"Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is uninitiated (*asaṃskṛta*), shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the Agnihotra."

As for the statement of Śaunaka: "[126] 'From the taking of the hand onwards, one should perform the *gṛhya* rites oneself, or the wife, or the son, or the daughter, or the resident pupil (*antevāsī*)'; this does not contradict the *Mānava* rule concerning the *vaitāna* (śrauta) rites, because that [statement of Śaunaka] pertains specifically to the *gṛhya* domain. Thus, those rites for which no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is prescribed must be performed by the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) alone. Regarding those for which no fee is prescribed, Kātyāyana says: "In cases of distress, one may perform them oneself; otherwise, they should be done by the priest. Furthermore: "The oblation must be offered in the presence of both husband and wife; it should not be offered by the priest or others in their absence. For an oblation offered in their absence would be fruitless."
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "O twice-born one, that pure man who, with devotion, worships the sun as it emerges at dawn with three handfuls of curd and unbroken grains."
Whatever impurity has been accumulated by one whose mind is thus purified,
that is instantly incinerated and reduced to ashes for him.
Dakṣa says:
Having first performed the rites for the deity and beheld the maṇḍala of the Guru,
the forenoon is prescribed for all ritual acts dedicated to the deity.
From the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: Thereafter, a man should perform his proper daily observances, such as grooming his hair,
looking into a mirror, applying collyrium, and touching auspicious objects like dūrvā grass.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "If one desires long life, one should see one's own self reflected in clarified butter. Kātyāyana says:
He who, having risen in the morning, sees one who is most wicked, unfortunate, intoxicated, naked, or with a cut-off nose— that is a characteristic sign of the Kali age.
He who, having risen early in the morning, beholds a Vedic scholar, a fortunate person, a cow, and likewise a fire-altar built with bricks, is liberated from all calamities.
And he should master the meanings of the Vedas as well as various treatises. || 1.99 ||

"One should master the meaning of the Vedas"—this is the statement of the goal (*sādhya*). "Various sciences" (*śāstrāṇi vividhāni*)—this is the statement of the means (*sādhana*). Thus, the meaning of the sentence is: "One should master the sciences in order to master the meaning of the Vedas. Consequently, there is an inclusion of only those sciences that serve as the means for mastering the meaning of the Vedas—namely, etymology (*nirukta*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), hermeneutics (*mīmāṃsā*), and so forth—and not of Buddhist treatises and the like. For this very reason, he will later declare the study of those [heterodox works] to be a minor offense (*upapātaka*). The meaning of the *Smṛti* is already included by the term "meaning of the Vedas," because the mastery of that [meaning] consists in the performance of the meaning of the Vedas; therefore, the retention of the Vedas and so forth is established by implication. For this same reason, he will state in the list of minor offenses: "the destruction of what has been studied. — Dakṣa.
The acquisition of the Veda first, then its reflection, its practice, its recitation,
and its impartation to disciples— thus the study of the Veda is fivefold.
For this very reason, Manu says:
One should constantly study the scriptures that increase the intellect, as well as the Vedic Nigamas, for they are quickly conducive to prosperity and welfare.
Having reached the further shore of the Veda, one should practice it again and again;
one should purify the scripture and, having studied it, should never abandon it again.
The restrictive rules (niyamas) are the means for determining the meaning of words, such as the Nighaṇṭus and similar works. || 1.99 ||

One should approach a lord (*īśvara*) for the sake of accomplishing one’s *yoga* and *kṣema*. *Yoga* is the acquisition of what is desired; *kṣema* is its preservation. One should approach—that is, go to—a lord who is capable of accomplishing that purpose and worthy of effecting the success of one’s *yoga* and *kṣema*. Gautama says: “For the sake of *yoga* and *kṣema*, one should resort to a lord, and not to anyone else, except for deities, teachers, and righteous persons. Manu says: “One should, however, resort to deities and the most excellent of the twice-born who are righteous.”
And on the festival days, one should likewise protect the Lord and the gurus.
Having bathed, he should likewise gratify and worship both the gods and the ancestors.

Having bathed at midday according to the prescribed rule, one should satisfy the gods and the ancestors according to the prescribed rule; by the use of the word "and," [the sages and] humans are also included. Likewise, one should worship—that is, honor—the gods and the others. Śaṅkha says: "The daily, the occasional, the optional, that which is an auxiliary to a ritual act, the removal of impurities, and likewise the sixth, the ritual bath—thus the bath is proclaimed to be sixfold."
A man who has not bathed is unfit for the recitation of prayers, the offering into the sacred fire, and other such rites;
therefore, the morning bath is proclaimed as the obligatory daily bath (nityasnāna) for that purpose.

Having touched a Caṇḍāla, a corpse, a sacrificial post, and so forth, or having touched a menstruating woman who has not yet bathed, one who is otherwise fit for bathing must bathe; for that is indeed an occasional (naimittika) bath.
Whatever bathing with flowers and so forth is enjoined by the rules of the astrologers, that is indeed designated as optional (kāmya); one should not perform it without a specific desire.
He who, desiring to recite purificatory mantras, or wishing to worship the deities and ancestors,
performs a ritual bath, that is proclaimed as being an ancillary part of the rite (kriyāṅga).
The bath called *malāpakarṣaṇa* (removal of impurities) is preceded by anointing with oil;
its purpose is indeed the removal of impurities, and not otherwise.
In lakes, in natural pools, at sacred fords, and in rivers, the ritual bath is prescribed;
therein, the bath is considered to be the ritual act itself.

This is the bath; the meaning is that the ritual action is prescribed as something to be performed. In that regard: "The optional [bath] should be performed exactly as enjoined by the injunctions, as well as the obligatory and the occasional, which are auxiliary to the ritual acts and serve to remove impurities."
In the absence of a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), however, one should perform the rite with warm water or with other water;
likewise for one who has bathed, it may be done with water heated by fire or even with the water of others.
The purification of the body is to be understood as such, yet one does not obtain the full fruit of bathing;
the limbs are cleansed by water, but the fruit arises from bathing at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
Since bathing alone is the rite to be performed in lakes, natural reservoirs, sacred fords, and rivers,
bathing is remembered as the most meritorious act.
Dakṣa says: Furthermore, in the fourth part [of the day], one should fetch earth for the purpose of bathing,
as well as sesame, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth, or perform the bath in artificial water.
One should not take seven kinds of earth: from an anthill, from a place where there are rats, from within water, from a cremation ground, from the root of a tree, or from a temple.
And water remaining after another person has bathed should always be avoided by wise people who desire their own welfare.
The meaning is that one should perform the fetching of the clay during the fourth part of the day divided into eight parts. Śātātapa says:
"In a pure place, clay free from pebbles, stones, and the like should be collected;
clay is traditionally held to be of three kinds: red, yellowish-white, and white."
Yogayājñavalkya says: Listen, for I shall describe the bath that destroys all sins;
[one should take] earth, cow dung, darbha grass, and fragrant flowers.
Being restrained and pure, he should fetch as much water as required for bathing;
having gone to the water's edge, he should duly set it down separately upon the ground.
Having divided that clay and the cow dung into three parts, the wise one should perform the washing of the lower, superior, and middle limbs with them.
One should perform the washing with separate portions for each, avoiding any mixing of the earth.
Dakṣa says:
The removal of impurities by means of mantras is prescribed for the water at one's side;
however, the twilight bath (saṃdhyā-snāna) is performed with water on both sides [of the body]. These are proclaimed to be the locations for bathing.
"On the side" means on the bank. Śaunaka says:
"On the riverbank, in a pure place, one should fetch earth and *kuśa* grass;
being self-restrained, one should take earth, *dūrvā* grass, *apāmārga*, and cow dung."
Then, one should perform a bath with clay in a particular place thereafter.
Vasiṣṭha says: The head should be washed with one application of clay; likewise, the area above the navel with two;
the body below that with three; and the feet with six.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice according to the rule, one should wash the entire body.

Śaunaka says: "With the verses beginning *gāyatryādityā ava hi khyāta* and *ato devā*, one should consecrate the clay. The *ṛṣi* and other details for the *gāyatrī* verse are well known. For the verse *ādityā ava hi khyāta*, Trita is the *ṛṣi*; the Ādityas are the deity; the *jagatī* is the meter. *ādityā ava hi khyātādhi kulād iva spaśaḥ | sutīrtham arvato yathānu no neṣathā sugam | anehaso va ūtayaḥ suūtayo va ūtayaḥ ||* For the verse *ato devā*, Medhātithi is the *ṛṣi*; Viṣṇu is the deity; the *gāyatrī* is the meter. *ato devā avantu no yato viṣṇur vicakrame | pṛthivyāḥ sapta dhāmabhiḥ ||* Then, with the verses *yata indra*, *svastidā viśaspatiḥ*, *vi rakṣo vi mṛdhaḥ*, and *idaṃ su me janitah*, one should throw the clay toward each direction in order, starting from the east. For the verse *yata indra*, Bharga is the *ṛṣi*; Indra is the deity; the *bṛhatī* is the meter.
O Indra, from whatever we fear, grant us freedom from that fear. O Maghavan, be able to help us with your protections; strike down our enemies and our adversaries.
Bestower of well-being upon the people; the seer is Bhāradvāja; Indra is the deity; Anuṣṭubh is the meter.
May Indra, the bestower of well-being, lord of the people, slayer of Vṛtra, dispeller of foes, the controller, the bull, the drinker of Soma, and the granter of fearlessness, go before us.
Drive away the Rakṣas, strike down the adversaries; break apart the jaws of Vṛtra.
O Indra, slayer of Vṛtra, destroy the fury of the enemy who assails us.

This indeed is my [hymn]; Vimada is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Indra is the deity (*devatā*). Triṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*). "O singer (*jaritar*), take heed of this well from me: the rivers carry away the curse as their remedy.
The fox has devoured the lion who was facing him; the jackal has devoured the boar from the thicket."
Vasiṣṭha says: Then one should perform the cleansing with earth first, accompanied by the mantra:
"O Earth, trodden by horses, trodden by chariots, and trodden by Viṣṇu!"
You were lifted up by the boar, by Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms;
O Earth, I take you along with progeny and wealth.
O Earth, you were bestowed by Brahmā and consecrated by Kāśyapa;
O Earth, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me.
O Earth, grant me nourishment; everything is established in you.
For the verses beginning with "aśvakrānta," Yajñavalkya is the seer (*ṛṣi*); clay is the deity; the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter.
And again, with cow dung, saying thus:
"The foremost, the foremost of the herbs that move in every forest."
O cow dung, which is the purifier and cleanser of the bodies of those wives of the bull,
drive away my diseases, my sorrows, and my sins.
"Agram agram" (The tip, the tip): Viśvāmitra is the seer; cow dung is the deity; Anuṣṭubh is the meter.
With the two verses beginning "Kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt" (From joint to joint), one should touch limb by limb—with *dūrvā* grass, it is understood.
Growing from joint to joint, from knot to knot,
even so, O *dūrvā* grass, extend for us by a thousandfold and a hundredfold.
"O divine brick, you who spread with a hundred and grow forth with a thousand—to you we shall offer worship with an oblation. Thus [it is said].
Agni is the seer (*ṛṣi*). Dūrvā grass is the deity (*devatā*). Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandas*). Likewise.
Wash away our sin, wash away our misdeed, wash away [all] evil;
O Apāmārga, drive away from us the evil dream.

Thus, with the *anuṣṭubh* verse seen by Sindhudvīpa, the deity of the *apāmārga*, one should touch limb by limb according to the prescribed path. Śaunaka says: "Then, having approached the waters with the verse beginning 'The waters within the gods' (*hiraṇyaśṛṅgā yā apo devīr*), and having touched the waters with 'May they be friendly to us' (*sumitrā naḥ*), one should cast them outside with 'May they be unfriendly' (*durmitrāḥ*). Regarding the verse "The waters within... (*apsv antar*): Dīrghatamas is the seer (*ṛṣi*); Indra is the deity; the *triṣṭubh* is the meter. Regarding "O divine waters, I invoke you" (*āpo devīr upahvaye*): Medhātithi is the seer; the waters are the deity; the *gāyatrī* is the meter. Regarding "Within the waters... (*apsv antar*) and "May they be friendly to us" (*sumitrā naḥ*) as well as "May they be unfriendly" (*durmitrāḥ*): Śunaḥśepa and Vāmadeva are the seers respectively; the waters are the deity; the *yajus* is the meter. Then:
Having entered the waters that are pure like Indra and so forth, one should mutter [the mantra] mentally;
right there one should sing the Sāmans, or else mutter the Vyāhṛtis.
Having recited "May Śiva protect me," one should plunge into the water with the mantra "These waters... [131].

The phrase *āpo asmān* (Waters, us... is the remainder [of the verse]. One should conclude with *yā sūrya...* (Those which, O Sūrya...). With the two hymns *tarat sa mandī* and *samudrajyeṣṭhā*, and with the purifying [hymn] *yat kiṃ cedam* and *imaṃ me gaṅga*, [one should sprinkle] with *kuśa* grass—the word *kuśaiḥ* being understood as the remainder. Therein: the Ṛc *eto nv indram* has Tiraścīnāṅgiras as the seer, Indra as the deity, and Anuṣṭubh as the meter; *śivena mā cakṣuṣā* has Agni as the deity; *āpo hi ṣṭhā* has the Waters as the deity and Jagatī as the meter; *idam āpaḥ* has Ambarīṣa Sindudvīpa as the seer, the Waters as the deity, and Anuṣṭubh as the meter; *āpo asmān* has Vāmadeva as the seer, the Waters as the deity, and Triṣṭubh as the meter; *yā sūrya raśmibhiḥ* has Vasiṣṭha as the seer, the Waters as the deity, and Triṣṭubh as the meter; *tarat sa mandī* is in Gāyatrī; the four-verse hymn *samudrajyeṣṭhā* has Vasiṣṭha as the seer, the Waters as the deity, and Triṣṭubh as the meter; *yat kiṃcedam* has Vasiṣṭha as the seer, Varuṇa as the deity, and Triṣṭubh as the meter; *imaṃ me gaṅga* has Sindhukṣit Praiyamedha as the seer, the Rivers as the deity, and Jagatī as the meter. Then:

Having bathed and sipped water, one should recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times in the midst of the water. The Aghamarṣaṇa consists of the triplet beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca. For this [hymn], Aghamarṣaṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Bhāvavṛtta is the meter, and Anuṣṭubh is the meter; according to the Caturviṃśatimata.
Immediately after bathing, one should then offer libations to the ancestors and the deities.
Having crossed over, one should wring out the garment; thereafter, the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā-karma) follows.
From the Purāṇa:
"Bathing is said to be of three kinds—daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and for the sake of a desired object (kāmya).
Libation (tarpaṇa), however, is proclaimed as being an ancillary part (aṅga) of that."

Kārṣṇājini says: "Standing in water reaching up to the navel, one should meditate with a mind focused on the [deity]; and one should offer libations"—this is the ellipsis. [This is from] the Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa.
Then, one should satiate with water the hosts of ancestors and sages, as well as the gods and so forth;
likewise the deities and the hosts of deities, and the sages and the hosts of sages.
Then he should constantly satisfy the ancestors and the hosts of ancestors;
thereafter, he should offer water to all the planets and to the sages.
Immediately after that, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder, he should offer it to the ancestors with the word "svadhā."
From the Purāṇa:
Having performed the libation for the deities while facing east and being pure,
one shall always thereafter be entitled to perform the libation for the ancestors.
Yogayājñavalkya states:
"Otherwise, the wise man, having placed the sesame seeds with his left hand,
should pour water according to the prescribed rule using the *pitṛ-tīrtha* on the right hand."
Therefore, this refers to libation performed while standing on dry land; otherwise, it means libation performed while standing in water. And so says another Smṛti:
"Having filled his arm with sesame seeds, one should offer libations to the ancestors while standing in water.
One who desires the satisfaction of the ancestors must not perform it while standing on dry land."
One should give with an open hand; one should not display a seal (mudrā) there.
The *mudrā* is the joining of the tips of the forefinger and the thumb. [This is] the tiger. Now, he who offers water with both hands—that fool shall go headfirst to the Kālasūtra hell.
Yama, however, says:
"Having joined the two hands together, one should fill them with a handful of water;
having drawn up water to the depth of a cow's horn, one should pour it into the midst of the water."
Regarding this, Kārṣṇājini states the settled rule:
"At a śrāddha and at the time of a marriage, [the gift] is given with one hand;
but at libations (tarpaṇa), it is indeed with both hands—this is the ancient injunction."

Alternatively, the followers of Āśvalāyana should perform [the rite] with the right hand alone; for, by the force of the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) stating that "in the absence of a specific instruction, one should follow the right," [this is established]. Gobhila says: "A twice-born man should always satisfy the gods with white sesame seeds, humans with variegated sesame seeds, and the ancestors with black sesame seeds."
If one should perform the libation for the deities and ancestors with sesame seeds grown on the limbs [of an animal], that water becomes blood; the giver shall become a sinner.
If one were to make sesame seeds into the shape of body hair and thereby offer libations to the ancestors,
the ancestors would be satiated by that blood and filth.

Furthermore, if one's limbs are hairless, making an offering with sesame seeds does not constitute a fault; this refers specifically to the case of making offerings on dry land. Marīci states: "In the absence even of sesame seeds, [one should offer] accompanied by gold and silver;
in their absence, however, one should sprinkle water with *darbha* grass or again with a mantra."
On the seventh lunar day, on Sundays, and likewise on one's birthday,
a householder who desires servants, sons, and a wife should not perform the libation with sesame seeds.
One who desires learning, sons, or a wife should avoid sesame seeds on the seventh lunar day of either fortnight, at night, during the two twilights, and on the five [specified] occasions.
On the seventh lunar day, one should not consume neem, apply oil as an eye-salve, offer sesame seeds in libations, or eat from a copper vessel. (From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*).

One should not offer libations to the ancestors or the gods while on the backs of elephants, horses, or chariots, nor on a boat, nor on a place paved with bricks; nor should one do so while standing on dry land in any instance where one is not actually on solid ground.
Hārīta says: One wearing wet clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation in the water;
one wearing dry clothes should perform libations, sipping of water, and recitation on land.
Viṣṇu:
If a man, standing on dry land, offers water into the water, that water does not reach the ancestors; it is useless for them.
Just as one might do on an impure spot, one may satisfy the deities and ancestors with water;
indeed, according to one's desire, for everything is established in water.
Kārṣṇājini says:
One should offer handfuls of water for the deities and the ancestors in the water;
however, for those who have died without having received the sacraments, one should again offer water on dry land.
Furthermore, it should be understood that one standing on dry land must offer a handful of water to those who have not been consecrated with the funeral rites.
Then, having wrung out the bathing garment, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again.
"And those born in our family who died childless, or as cattle, or as goats..."
May they accept this water from the wringing out of my garment, given by me.
Thus ends the mantra for wringing out the garment. Hārīta says:
"That lowest of men who, while still wearing clothes wet with water, performs the ritual sipping (ācamana) while standing on dry ground—the *pretas* indeed drink the water dripping from his garment."
Dakṣa says:
When a Brahmin has bathed and sips water (ācamana) after placing his feet both in water and on dry land,
he becomes pure in both respects and thus fit for performing his duties.
A tiger [having emerged] from a body of water should go away swiftly while reciting the verse "āpo asmān".
Then, having taken two clean garments, he should sip water twice.
Jābāli says:
Having bathed and put on his garment, the ascetic (yati) should cleanse his shins with earth and water;
yet, having performed his bath while still wearing wet clothes, he voids excrement and urine.
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one becomes pure again through bathing.
A cowherd who has bathed should not wipe his limbs, nor with his hand wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apassavya),
nor should he shake out his hair; furthermore, he should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while standing.
Vyāsa says: One should not apply ointments without having bathed, nor should one wring out one's garment;
rather, after bathing, a man should wear his clothes while they are still damp.
If one wipes the face with the bathing cloth, or chews a tooth-stick after having bathed,
or applies ointment with the back of the hand facing another, Lakṣmī departs once these acts have been committed.
Satyavrata said:
He upon whose forehead a bright vertical mark made with clay is seen—even if he be a Caṇḍāla—he is a pure soul and is certainly worthy of worship; of this there is no doubt.
Vyāsa says:
He who, having taken with supreme devotion the clay produced on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
anoints his limbs with it, shall possess great merit.
Having bathed, Uśanas says that one should not shake one's head, nor should one wring water from one's limbs;
nor should one touch a garment worn previously, nor oil, nor fat.
Yogayājñavalkya states: "In the absence of a washed garment, one may use those made of hemp, linen, or wool;
or a kutapa blanket or a yoga-band, by means of which one becomes 'doubly clothed'."
*Kutapa* refers to a woolen blanket; this concerns the upper garment (*uttarīya*). Likewise:
"If one is unable to perform that supreme procedure for bathing which has been explained in detail, then this [following] procedure is prescribed."
Bathing within the water, as well as sprinkling and sipping water,
the consecration of the water, and the visualization of the sacred site (tīrtha).
This practice of performing the ritual bath by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa Sūkta three times daily has been taught by the great-souled ones.
Likewise:

"Because the body lacks the capacity [to perform the ritual] independently, some wise teachers maintain that there are seven types of ablution starting from this one, depending on the power of time and other factors."

The seven ablutions, in their proper order, are: that performed with mantras, that on the ground, as well as that pertaining to fire, that pertaining to wind, the celestial, that pertaining to water, and the mental.

The ritual bath with mantras is performed with the hymns beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; the earthly bath consists of clinging to clay; the fire-bath is known to be with ashes; and the wind-bath is traditionally said to be with the dust raised by cows.
That which occurs under a shower of rain is called the divine bath;
immersion in water is the Vāruṇa bath; and the contemplation of Viṣṇu is the mental bath.
The ritual bath with [ordinary] water is prescribed as being equal in result to the mantra-bath in due order;
however, it is traditionally held that all are equal in fruit when considered in terms of time, place, or incapacity.
[135] Some wise men maintain that mental bathing is the most excellent;
for this was recited by Vyāsa in the praise of the sacred ford of the self (ātmatīrtha).
Likewise:
"May the waters be auspicious for us," "From the pillar," "O Waters, you are most beneficent," and "The Expiation of Sin"—
the ritual bath with mantras is declared to consist of these four Vedic hymns.
When a state of impurity has arisen, one should indeed perform a bath;
however, with the previously mentioned mantras, otherwise there shall be a ritual sprinkling (mārjana).
Jābāla says:
When one is unable to perform a full bath, a partial bath (without the head) may be performed at will;
or they know that wiping the body with a wet garment also constitutes a bodily purification.
Kātyāyana says:
For two months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, all rivers are in their menstrual period;
one should not bathe in them, except for those that flow into the ocean.
Those whose course does not extend for eight thousand bow-lengths,
and which do not flow with the sound of "nadī" (river), are proclaimed by you as mere pits.
At the Upākarma and the Utsarga ceremonies, as well as at the ritual bath for the deceased,
and during lunar or solar eclipses, no impurity due to menstrual flow is found.
On the surface of the earth, all waters—even those situated in wells—become equal to the waters of the celestial river during an eclipse of the moon or sun; of this there is no doubt.
The celestial river is the Gaṅgā. Devala says:

"During an eclipse, at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), at marriages, on occasions of calamity or prosperity, and during optional vows, one should perform bathing, giving gifts, and other rites even at night."
A wise person should always avoid bathing in a river at sunset;
having bathed in one river, a knower of dharma should not praise another river.
Manu says: One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight,
nor repeatedly with one's clothes on, nor in an unknown body of water.
Nārāyaṇa: Having approached according to the tradition, wearing the sacred thread and with his topknot tied,
and holding the purifier (kuśa grass) in his hand, he should mentally recollect the syllable Om, the Lord of Sacrifice.

Having remembered the meter, the seer, and the deity according to the ritual for the morning twilight, and having restrained his breath and sipped water while holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*).

One should perform the sprinkling with water while reciting the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and then properly cast a handful of water into the air while reciting "ud u tyaṃ citram" as well as "tac cakṣur deva" and "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad."
Thus, with arms raised and concentrated in mind, he should mutter [the mantra] while looking at the sun;
having thus performed the worship of the Sun-god with the Gāyatrī according to his ability.
"A wise person should not perform recitation loudly, especially that of the Sāvitrī," so says Bṛhaspati.
"Concentration of the mind, purity, silence, and reflection on the meaning of the mantra [are required]."
Undistractedness and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of the recitation. || 1.100 ||
He describes the sacrifice to Brahman:
"One should recite the Vedas, the Atharva, the Purāṇas, along with the Itihāsas, according to one's ability;
and for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), one should recite the knowledge concerning the supreme self. (1.101)

One should recite according to one's ability—that is, to the best of one's capacity—the Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, as well as the *Atharvaveda*, the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas such as the *Mahābhārata*, and the science of the self (*vidyā*), meaning the Upaniṣadic texts. This is for the purpose of accomplishing the sacrifice of recitation (*japa-yajña*), that is, for the accomplishment of the *brahmayajña*. The separate mention of the "science of the self" is for the sake of emphasizing its importance. When "Vedas" is already stated, the inclusion of the *Atharva* is for the purpose of completing the meter; furthermore, it serves as an indicator for the *Aṅgirasas*, because it is heard in the Śruti: "The streams of fat [flowed] from the *Atharvāṅgirases*. — Manu.
Restrained and established in the daily rite near water,
he should go to the forest and, with a concentrated mind, recite the Sāvitrī.
That which one studies daily according to one's ability, beginning from the start of the Veda and proceeding step by step from top to bottom after bathing, is known as *svādhyāya*.

Śaunaka says: "Having gone out from the village either before sunrise or at dawn, having stepped into the water, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), dressed in unwashed clothes, and having spread out a large quantity of *darbha* grass with its points facing east, he should sit upon it facing east. Having performed the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) and joined his right and left hands together, with the *pavitra* blades in his hand, looking at the junction of heaven and earth, or closing his eyes, or in whatever way he deems himself composed—he being thus composed—should recite his *svādhyāya*. He recites the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *Oṃ*, followed by the *Sāvitrī*: first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse, and finally the whole verse; this is the third [method]. "Composed" means concentrated. Likewise: "Having recited as much as he thinks fit, he concludes with this [verse]: 'Homage to Brahman'. By the word "conclusion" (*paridhāna*), there is no repetition [of the verse]. [137] Bṛhaspati.

That [offering] should be performed either before the libation (tarpaṇa), or after it, or in the morning before the oblation (āhuti), or at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva; it does not depend on any other occasion.
That is the meaning: it is the *brahmayajña*. Manu says:
"In the daily obligatory rite, there is no suspension of study, for that is remembered as the *brahmamantra*;
it is meritorious, offered with the oblation of the Veda, and consecrated by the *vaṣaṭ* of non-suspension."
Likewise:
"In the case of the auxiliary sciences of the Veda, in private Vedic study, and in the daily obligatory rites,
as well as in the mantras for the fire-oblation, there is no restriction regarding days unfit for study."

The *vedopakaraṇa* refers to the auxiliary sciences of the Veda (*vedāṅga*). Āpastamba states: "Now, if the wind should blow, or there should be thunder, lightning, or a clap of thunder, one should recite a single *ṛc*, a single *yajus*, or a single *sāman*. [One should say: 'Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ! Truth, austerity—I offer this into faith. By this, indeed, on that day, his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) becomes as if performed with austerity. In this context, the mention of "the wind blowing," etc., is an illustration for occasions when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*). Following the *brahmayajña*, the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods and others must be performed. Thus says Bṛhaspati:
For the sake of accomplishing the *brahmayajña*, one should mutter sacred knowledge pertaining to the self (*adhyātmika-vidyā*),
or otherwise, having muttered the *praṇava*, one should then begin the libation (*tarpaṇa*).
Having put on a white garment on a wide-spreading sacrificial grass (barhis) on dry ground, one who performs the ritual sacrifice should perform the libation (tarpaṇa); never, however, in a vessel.
Having taken the root from the vessel, one should place it in another auspicious vessel, or on the ground, or in a pit filled with water; but not on dry land where there is no sacrificial grass.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states: "If one should spill [water] that has been drawn up, one should mix sesame seeds into the water;
otherwise, if it is in the left hand, one should then perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*)."
Likewise,
with his left hand held in contact [with the disciple], having invoked [the deity] as before with mantras by name and lineage, and having spread auspicious kuśa grass;

Facing south, having bent his left knee, he should worship the gods— the Suras— on blades of grass with their tips pointing east, and the ancestors— the Pitṛs— on blades with their tips pointing south,

using both hands and the same mantras as before, namely those stated in the *Śrāddha-prakaraṇa* of the *Yājñavalkya-saṃhitā*, beginning with "O Viśvedevas, come hither" (*viśve devāsa āgata*) and "Desiring you" (*uśantas tvā*).
O All-Gods, come hither; hear this my invocation;
sit down upon this sacred grass.
"Desiring you, we invoke you; desiring you, we kindle you.
Desiring them, bring the Pitṛs who desire [you], so that they may eat the oblation. Thus says Kātyāyana.
One should satisfy the gods with water containing unbroken grains (akṣata) using the *devatīrtha*.
Vyāsa says:
"The gods [receive] one handful each; Sanaka and the others, however, receive two each."
The ancestors deserve three handfuls each, but women, only one handful each.

The *Likhita* states: "Facing east, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), one should perform the libation to the deities with the *devatīrtha* using *kuśa* grass blades pointing eastward, while covering both hands with the thumbs tucked inside. The *Yogayājñavalkya* says:
"One should first offer libations to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Prajāpati;
then to the gods, the meters, the Vedas, and the sages rich in asceticism."
He likewise [conquered] the Ācāryas and the Gandharvas, as well as the sons of the Ācāryas,
the year with its constituent parts, and the goddesses and Apsarases.
Likewise, he [beheld] the gods, the trees, the nāgas, the oceans, and the mountains;
as well as the rivers, humans, yakṣas, and indeed the rākṣasas.
And the Piśācas, the Suparṇas, the Bhūtas, as well as the animals,
the trees, the medicinal herbs, and the fourfold collection of living beings.
Following the inclusion of Viṣṇu,
then, having placed the sacrificial thread over the shoulder (nivīta) with alertness,
one should separately satisfy the humans with the *prājāpatya* tīrtha.
Kārṣṇājini says: Sanaka, Sananda, and the third, Sanātana;
as well as Kapila, Āsuri, Voḍha, and Pañcaśikha.
These seven humans are proclaimed to be the sons of Brahmā.
From the Padma Purāṇa:
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Pracetas, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Nārada.

Baudhāyana says: "Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), [he offers] to the south: 'I satiate the fathers with *svadhā* and homage; I satiate the grandfathers with *svadhā* and homage; I satiate the great-grandfathers with *svadhā* and homage; I satiate the mothers with *svadhā* and homage,' and so forth. Likewise: 'He pours water along the path of the rite, saying: "Carrying strength, nectar, clarified butter, honey, milk, ambrosia, and flowing libation—you are *svadhā*; satiate [them]; be satiated; be satiated," and so forth. Furthermore, from the Purāṇa, there is the mantra for the final añjali-offering."
For those in my family for whom the funeral rice-balls have been interrupted, and who are bereft of sons and wives—
may this offering of sesame-water be inexhaustible for them.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "The gods, asuras, yakṣas, nāgas, gandharvas,
rākṣasas, piśācas, guhyakas, siddhas, kūṣmāṇḍas, trees, and birds."
May all creatures— those that dwell in water, those that live on land, and those that depend on the air—
quickly attain satisfaction through this water given by me.
And for those who abide in all the hells and in the various torments,
this water is offered by me for their nourishment.
May those who are not kinsmen, as well as those who were kinsmen in another birth,
and whoever desires [offerings] from us, all attain complete satisfaction.
Yogayājñavalkya states: Kavyavāḍ, Anala, Soma, Yama, and likewise Aryaman;
the Agniṣvāttas, the Somapas, and also the Barhiṣads.
If one whose father is still living should know these [ancestors],
then he should cause the offerings to be given to those ancestors to whom his own father gives them, or else to those [to whom his grandfather gives].
A twice-born man whose father has died should offer salutations and the *svadhā* invocation to the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas,
as well as to these very ancestors who have passed away.

The word "should satisfy" (*tarpeyet*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The formula for the practice is: "I satisfy the fire that carries the offerings to the ancestors" (*kavyavāhanam analaṃ tarpayāmi*). Regarding the abbreviated libation for one who is incapable [of the full rite], the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
"Uttering the words, 'May the world from Brahmā down to a blade of grass be satisfied,' one should offer three handfuls of water while performing the abbreviated libation."
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
Having wrung out the bathing cloth and washed it, being self-restrained and pure,
one should perform the worship of the gods, beginning with Brahmā, free from envy.
Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra, as well as the god Viṣṇu and the Sun—
therefore, I consider none other to be more worthy of worship than Janārdana.
He who offers flowers or even water with the Puruṣasūkta...
By him, this entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, would be honored.
This [is prescribed] for one who is unable to perform the worship. In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*, following the *brahmayajña*:
"Then one should offer the *arghya* to Manu, accompanied by sesame seeds, flowers, and water;
having raised it up to the head with the mantra *haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*."
Having paid homage to the God in the water and then returned home,
one should worship Viṣṇu there with the ritual of the Puruṣasūkta.
The seer is Vāmadeva; the metre is Jagatī; the deity is Sūrya. Likewise:
"In the waters, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial mound, and in images—in these six places, the sages have prescribed the proper worship of Hari."
For those who perform rituals, Hari is the god in the fire; for the wise, he is the god in heaven; for those of limited intellect, he is in images; and for yogis, he is in the heart.
The sphere of water is his; therefore Hari is always present within those waters, and because he is omnipresent, he is likewise present upon the sacrificial ground for one whose self is purified.
The deity of this hymn, composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter and concluding with a Triṣṭubh verse, is Puruṣa, who is the seed of the universe; Nārāyaṇa is remembered as its seer (ṛṣi).
One should place the first [syllable] on the left hand and the second on the right hand;
one should place the third on the left foot and the fourth on the right.
One should place the fifth on the left knee and the sixth on the right;
one should place the seventh on the left side of the abdomen and the eighth on the right.
The ninth [digit] is in the center of the navel, the tenth likewise in the heart;
the eleventh is in the region of the throat, and the twelfth on the left arm.
One should place the thirteenth [digit] on the right side, the fourteenth in the region of the mouth,
the fifteenth on the two eyes, and the sixteenth on the head.
Having thus performed the ritual of placement (nyāsa), one should thereafter practice meditation;
with the first verse, however, one should invoke the deity Puruṣottama.
One should offer a seat with the second [verse], and water for the feet with the third;
the guest-offering (arghya) should be given with the fourth, and water for sipping (ācamanīya) with the fifth.
On the sixth day, the bath should be offered; on the seventh, the garment;
on the eighth, the sacred thread; and on the ninth, the ointment.
On the tenth day, flowers should be offered; on the eleventh, incense;
on the twelfth, one should give a lamp; and on the thirteenth, the food offering (naivedya).
On the fourteenth day, one should perform prostration; on the fifteenth, circumambulation;
having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one should perform the ritual dismissal on the sixteenth.
One should offer water for rinsing the mouth after bathing, clothing, and the food offering;
by worshipping in this very manner, one attains perfection within six months.
Nārāyaṇa, who dwells in the center of the solar disc, seated upon a lotus throne, adorned with armlets, golden earrings, and a crown— He should be meditated upon at all times.
"Golden-hued, wearing a necklace, and holding the conch and discus"—thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya on Yoga:
"Having thus worshipped the Lord of Gods and meditated for a moment upon Him who is stainless."
Then he should look at the sun with the verse: "The swan dwelling in purity."
Having bathed and been gazed upon by Brahmā, he goes to the abode of Brahmā and does not fall back to a lower state.

In the Narasiṃha Purāṇa: "A person should always worship the Lord of Gods, Narasiṃha himself— the Imperishable (Acyuta)— with the eight-syllabled mantra, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings."
This mantra is the bestower of all goals, the supreme remover of all sins;
it is remembered as the glorious dispeller of all suffering and the performer of all pacification.
For this eight-syllable mantra, Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi);
the goddess Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the deity (devatā).
One should offer all things, such as perfumes and flowers, by means of this very [mantra];
Viṣṇu, worshipped through the image, becomes pleased at that very moment.
What need has he for many mantras, what need has he for many sacrifices?
The mantra "Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya" accomplishes all goals.
From the Purāṇa:
"One who worships Śiva, Bhāskara, Agni, Keśava, Kauśikī, and Tāyin does not go to a lower state from the world of the gods. [142]
Kauśikī is Durgā; Tāyin is the Buddha. || 1.101 ||

Having described the *brahmayajña*, he speaks of the great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*): "The offering of bali, the svadhā-offering, the burnt oblation (*homa*), the private recitation (*svādhyāya*), and the hospitable reception of guests—these are the great sacrifices for beings, ancestors, gods, Brahman, and men. (1.102)

The *balikarma* is the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*). The *svadhā* is the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*); the giving of food and other offerings to the ancestors is indicated by the word *svadhā*. The fire-sacrifice (*homa*) performed here in the common fire or the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) in the evening and morning is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*). A specific form of Vedic study is the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The honoring of guests is the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*). Manu states the etymological derivation of these very terms: "The *ahuta*, the *huta*, the *prahuta*, the *brāhmahuta*, and the *prāśita*—these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices."

Recitation is the *ahuta* offering; the fire-oblation is the *huta*; the offering to the spirits is the *prahuta*; the oblation to the elemental beings is the *bhautika bali*; the worship of the foremost of the twice-born is the *brāhmaṃ huta*; and the libation to the ancestors is the *prāśita*.
One should offer the *bhūtabali* from the remains of the food offered to the gods.
From the food offered as an oblation (*havya*) to the gods, one should take the remainder of that cooked food and offer it as a *bali* to the spirits (*bhūta*). Likewise:
"One should always cook food on the domestic fire (*śālāgni*) or even on the common worldly fire."
In the very same fire upon which one cooks the food, the oblation is prescribed to be offered.

Whether in a worldly or a Vedic rite, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice must be performed upon the water, the fire, the offerings, the discarded food, and the earth, for the removal of the five slaughtering-places.

Āśvalāyana says: "Then, in the evening and in the morning, one should offer oblations of prepared sacrificial food (haviṣya). Kātyāyana says: "Among sacrificial foods, barley is considered the primary; rice is prescribed as secondary.
One should avoid mung beans, kodrava, gaura rice, and so forth, even when all other options are unavailable."

Āpastamba states: "There is no offering of alkaline or salty substances. One may offer sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) that has been mixed with the food of others. Having swept away the ashes toward the north, one should offer therein; that which is thus offered becomes as if unoffered in the fire. The meaning of this is: an offering in the fire must not be performed with sacrificial food mixed with alkaline or salty substances or with the food of others. "The preparers of the food should be Āryas. One should avoid facing food while laughing, breathing heavily, or sneezing. Having touched one's hair, limbs, or clothing, one should touch water. Or, Śūdras supervised by Āryas may be the preparers. Likewise: "Food prepared out of sight should be placed over the fire and sprinkled with water; they declare that very act to be purifying. Dakṣa says:
And in the fifth portion, a distribution is prescribed according to what is appropriate for the ancestors, the gods, human beings, and even insects.
Vyāsa says: Thereafter, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (śākhā),
using consecrated food consisting of sacrificial oblations (havis) accompanied by sacrificial side-dishes (vyañjana).

With those very same foods, one should offer the bali-oblation; having sprinkled the remainder with water and placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), one should carry everything toward the south with the utterance "svadhā."
Āpastamba says: "Regarding the bali offerings, the purification of their place consists of wiping it with the hand, sprinkling water, placing the offering down, and finally pouring water around it."
One should cast food upon the ground for dogs, outcasts, and crows.
One should place food for dogs and the like upon the ground. The term *caṇḍāla* is intended to include those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*) and others. Thus says Manu:
"For dogs, for the fallen, for dog-cookers, for those afflicted with foul diseases, for crows, and for worms, one should gently place food upon the earth."

In this context, the mention of "those who accept the fallen" (patitagrahaṇa) is intended to include those who carry a skull in their hand and others of similar description. Thus, the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"Formerly, the Daityas were conquered by the gods and defeated in battle;
some then went forth with skulls in their hands, while others adopted the vow of nakedness."
Some were shaven-headed with eyes anointed and wearing saffron robes;
yet they were gentle in speech while being ill-behaved, excluded from the practice of purity.
Some Dānavas were disguised as those covered in human bones and hair;
others appeared as those who do not belong to any stage of life (anāśramin), those observing vows, those with matted locks, or those with shaven heads, all in vain.
That man who would teach expiatory rites and the like for a fee,
being pitiless, a breaker of moral bounds, an atheist, and a reviler of the Vedas;
He who reviles those who are sick, those observing vows, or those performing sacrificial sessions;
he who reviles the seers or the gods, reviles his very self.
That Brahmin who proclaims [his own learning], yet does not teach out of pride;
the gambler, the drunkard, and the one who buys and sells sacrifices—[these are excluded].
A merchant, a usurer, a village messenger, a slanderer,
as well as a house-burner, a poisoner, one who eats from a sacrificial vessel (kuṇḍāśin), and a seller of Soma.
One who deals in salt, one who deals in perforated goods, an oil-presser, a forger, one who falsely insists on a teacher's instruction, and a rogue who deceives his teacher; |||
One who has abandoned the Vedas because of intoxication, a killer, one who violates the teacher’s bed,
one who causes the intermixture of castes, one devoted to women, and likewise a libertine toward women;
One who misappropriates deposits, a deceitful person, as well as one who treats the body [for profit],
who disparages a commodity while buying it and praises it while selling it;
One who kills women, children, or Brahmins; a cow-killer; one who is deceitful;
one who causes the intermixture of castes; an artisan; and one who performs forbidden acts.
He who abandons the duties of his own caste, who delights in the work of others,
and who drinks the semen of men— that man is a corrupt "vaginal-mouth" (mukhebhaga).
These Daityas have been fully described; however, they were not created by the Self-born One himself, who merely kept in mind that a portion for the Rākṣasas must be given in sacrifices.
One should offer an oblation from the house to those powerful obstructing spirits;
for the Brāhmaṇa, that is the Kṛta Age, and there the ancestors are the deities.
The Tretā Yuga and the Kṣatriya are present there, and the deities are to be worshipped;
the Dvāpara [Yuga] and the Vaiśya are to be known as being there, and the Buddha is worshipped therein.
"The Śūdra is the Kali Yuga; therein, the heretical castes are to be honored.
This is the mantra for the offering of the *bhūtabali*:
"Those spirits who roam by day and by night, seeking the offering, the servants of Vituda."
"Desiring nourishment, I offer this oblation to them; may the Lord of Nourishment bestow nourishment upon me.
Thus says Vyāsa:
"Those belonging to Indra, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yama, and likewise those belonging to Nirṛti..."
May the crows accept this ball of rice offered by me.
"Having given two dogs—one black and one brindled—born of the lineage of Vaivasvata, according to this procedure, one should afterwards perform the ritual sipping of water (upaspṛśet).
The rite called Vaiśvadeva, beginning with the fire-oblation (anna-homa) and ending with the scattering of food for the dogs and others, must be performed every morning and evening. As Manu says:
In the evening, when food has been prepared, the wife should offer the *bali* oblation without reciting mantras;
for this is called the *vaiśvadeva*, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.

In the absence of male performers, the wife shall perform the Vaiśvadeva rite without the mantras. The mention of the "offering of bali" (baligrahaṇa) is intended as an illustration for the Vaiśvadeva. Thus says Gautama:
"The Vaiśvadeva and the bali-offering must be performed morning and evening;
even by one who does not eat, they must be done constantly, otherwise one becomes guilty of sin."

Its commencement is in the morning and its conclusion is in the evening. As Laugākṣi says: "With the words 'To the beings that roam by day,' [he offers] by day; with the words 'To the beings that roam by night,' [he offers] by night. (1.103)
Food and even water should be given daily to the ancestors and to men.

Food should be given every day—that is, every single day—to the ancestors and others. However, the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) should offer it to his three maternal ancestors, while those who belong to both lineages (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) should offer it to both sets. Regarding this, Vyāghra says:
"The son of an appointed daughter must, by rule, perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather."
Then, because of the connection between both, he should perform [the rite] for both as well.

When there is an agreement with the giver of the girl, namely, "May the offspring born of her become the provider of *svadhā* for you and me," the son of one who has performed the marriage is connected to both [families]. To men and guests, it should be given daily—that is, every day. The word "daily" (*anvaham*) is connected to each [recipient] individually. In the absence of food, water [is to be given]. Here, "daily" is enjoined (*vidhīyate*), while the other [details] are restated (*anūdyate*). Manu says:
"One should perform the *śrāddha* day after day with food and drink, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing satisfaction to the ancestors."
Laghuhārīta:
"The daily śrāddha (nityaśrāddha) should be without an invocation to the gods (adaiva), and it should be devoid of the water-offering (arghya), the funeral cake (piṇḍa), and so forth.
[In] the Matsyapurāṇa:

I shall first describe the daily rite (nitya), which is devoid of the offering of water (arghya) and the invocation (āvāhana); one should know that as the non-ancestral (adaiva). The ancestral rite (pārvaṇa) is prescribed for the sacred festival days (parvan).
Kātyāyana says: Even if one should feed a single Brahmin for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña),
it is not without a deity if there is no other eater or even no food to be offered.
Having set aside some food according to his ability and in accordance with the rules,
the twice-born man should give it day after day to the ancestors and to human beings.

Having said, "This for the ancestors," he should cause the utterance of *svadhā* to be made. [146] "Without the gods" (*adaivam*) and so forth is one sentence; "if there is no other" (*nāsti ced anyaḥ*) is another. Devala says:
"A Brahmin who feeds [guests] without ghee in his own home while clarified butter is available..."
In the next world, the householder falls into a terrible hell.
Having himself eaten sweet food,
if a Brahmin subsequently feeds another Brahmin light and poor-quality food, he shall dwell in hell for a long time.
Śātātapa says: The sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña), the ancestral rite (śrāddha), the daily gratification of guests,
and the study of one’s own Vedic recitation (svādhyāya) should always be performed in this sequence.
"Perpetually" (*nityam*) is an adjective qualifying the *śrāddha*. Pracetās states:
"There is no offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), no invocation (*āvāhana*), no funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), and no dismissal (*visarjana*);
there is following [the guests], a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and the treatment of guests for three [ancestors]."
The status of a guest should be assigned to a learned Brahmin who has arrived even when there are more than three [other guests]. *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
One should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day after day with food or even with water;
for the sake of the ancestors, one should feed Brahmins, or indeed a single Brahmin.
Nārāyaṇa says:
Having appointed one or several Vedic scholars facing the east, [the performer], wearing the sacred thread around his neck (nivītī),
with his mind fixed on them, composed and meditating upon the sages, [should proceed].
Then, having provided a seat and the offering of water (arghya), one should recite for those who have eaten;
then, having set aside food according to one's ability, one should offer it with the words "Hanta."
One should perform one's daily private recitation every day, and one should not cook food for oneself alone.

*Svādhyāya* (the study of one's own Veda) refers to the study of one’s own *śākhā*, and not to the *śākhā* alone, because the latter is not something that can be performed as an action. Therefore, one should perform the study of one’s own *śākhā* every day (*anvaham*), day after day. This repetition of the term for the *brahmayajña* is for the purpose of prescribing this specific quality (*guṇavidhi*) of "daily. Likewise, one should not cook food for oneself alone. Here, "self" (*ātman*) is intended in its exclusive sense. Consequently, cooking for the sake of the gods and others, as well as for oneself, does not constitute a fault. As Manu says: "For those who [cook] for the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and themselves..."
He who does not offer oblations to these five is not truly living, even though he breathes.

And thus, there is no contradiction with his own statement: "He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin. For this very reason, the Śruti says: "One who eats alone becomes the consumer of only sin. (1.104)
Having first fed the children, the daughters living in the household, the elderly, pregnant women, the sick, young girls, guests, and servants, the husband and wife may eat what remains. (1.105)

[147] Having fed the children and other guests, the husband and wife should eat what remains from the meal. These include: the child due to incapacity; likewise the aged; the married daughter residing in her father’s house (the *svavāsinī*); the pregnant woman for the sake of nourishing the fetus; the sick person due to physical weakness; the guest by virtue of scriptural injunction; and the servants because they carry out the household duties. Manu says: "The women of the household, maidens, the sick, and likewise the pregnant."
One should feed them first to the guests, without hesitation.
But that unwise man who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
The meaning is that he does not perceive himself being devoured by dogs and vultures; and consequently, eating together with children and others does not constitute a transgression. || 1.105 ||
A twice-born man eating his food should always perform the *apośāna* rite both before and after; he must ensure that the food is neither "naked" nor "immortal. (1.106)

The one who brings water sends the young student with the *apośāna* [formula]. By that sending, its purpose is indicated here by the term *apośānena*. Consequently, food must be made "not naked" (*anagna*) and "immortal" (*amṛta*) by the twice-born through the *apośāna* performed both before and after the meal. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says: "The *apośāna* is the undergarment; the subsequent sipping is the upper garment. Thus, the food becomes truly not naked and likewise immortal."
Baudhāyana says: On a smeared, level, pure, and smooth site,
[one should prepare] a square, a triangle, a circle, or a semicircle.
The mandala should be constructed in due order among the Brahmins and the other castes.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: Having seen the food, one should first bow down; then, with palms joined in reverence (*prāñjali*), one should say, "May this be ours forever," and then pay homage with devotion.

Baudhāyana says: "At all times when one has urgent business, having washed his hands and feet and sipped water (ācamya), sitting facing the east in a clean, enclosed place, he should pay homage to the food being brought forth with the words, *bhūr bhuvaḥ svar om*, and restrain his speech. Once the food is set down, he should sprinkle water around it clockwise with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛtis*). Without releasing the food from his left hand, he first drinks water with the formula, *amṛtopastaraṇam asi* ("Thou art the under-layer of immortality"), and then offers the five oblations of breath (*prāṇāhutis*) with the food: *'In faith, seated in the out-breath (*prāṇa*), I offer immortality; may thou enter me auspiciously for the sake of non-burning; svāhā to the out-breath! The same formula is to be applied according to the respective marks for the in-breath (*apāna*), the diffused breath (*vyāna*), the upward breath (*udāna*), and the equalizing breath (*samāna*). In this manner, he should consume more food silently. He should meditate on Prajāpati in his mind. Furthermore, they quote:"

Seated and facing the east, he should eat his food with speech controlled and without making any noise; without spilling any and with full attention, having finished eating, he should touch fire and perform the ritual sipping of water.

With hands raised, he should perform the consecration of the oblation (*hutānumantraṇa*), reciting: "Having entered into faith, may the immortal oblation enter me; O Śiva, enter me as auspiciousness; swell my vital breath with food. The phrase "having entered into faith" is to be applied accordingly to each term—apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—as required by the context. With the syllable "Om," [he should think]: "May my self be united with Brahman for the sake of immortality. In all cases, the self-sacrificer (*ātmayājī*) is superior to those who sacrifice with ritual offerings (*kratuyājin*). He said this very thing: "One should offer oblations thus in secret, both morning and evening, or at least in the evening with water. Thus it is said.
Whether he be a student or a householder, if one practices austerity while fasting,
he becomes an outcast through the neglect of the fire-sacrifice of the vital breaths (prāṇāgnihotra).

"Except for the penance; regarding the penance, the rule is the same. The phrase "regarding the penance, the rule is the same" means that the same procedure applies when a penance is to be performed. Furthermore, they cite this example: "He who never eats between his morning meal and his evening meal is always fasting."

Āpastamba: "Having sipped water, one should hold the hands raised until they become wet; then one should touch fire. *Prodakau* refers to those two hands from which water has flowed away toward the south. Hārīta: "One should not eat from a vessel made of black iron or earthenware. Viṣṇu: [149] "One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
