One should not eat when there is trouble with the king. A maintainer of the *agnihotra* fire should eat only when he considers the *agnihotra* sacrifice to have been performed. He should also eat when he considers the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice to have been performed on a festival day (*parvan*), provided he considers it to have been performed on that festival day. One should not eat while suffering from indigestion, nor at midnight, nor at midday, nor during the two twilights. One should not eat while wearing wet clothes, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor naked, nor while seated on a broken seat, nor while lying down, nor from a broken vessel. One should not eat food from which the oil has been extracted, nor roasted grain (*dhānā*) by day, nor curd mixed with sesame by night, nor groats (*saktu*), nor the leaf-vegetables of the *kovidāra*, *vaṭa*, *pippala*, or hemp (*śaṇa*). One should not take clarified butter (*ghṛta*) without having first eaten, offered oblations, or washed one's feet and hands; nor should one do so while still impure from a previous meal. One should not gaze at the moon, the sun, or the stars, nor touch one's head. While wearing a garland or being anointed with unguents, one should not consume anything entirely without leaving a remainder, except for curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, groats, meat-paste (*palala*), and water."
One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor while standing;
many should not look on at one person, nor should many eat together at one place.
In an empty house, in a firehouse, or in a temple, under any circumstances whatsoever.
"There is no fault in [classifying] copper, silver, gold, conch, crystal, and stone as either distinct or non-distinct. Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O great sage, one should eat five morsels from a vessel that has been set aside;
the remainder should be set apart before eating—the reason for this shall now be heard."
Contact with droplets and the dust from the feet or clothing below does not defile; even if a Brahmin eats with his mouth when performing a rite for the ancestors, he is not tainted.
Regarding the meal for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), the meaning is that the vessel should not be placed directly on the ground, nor should it be smeared with anything. In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"One should eat with the mind focused on that [deity], beginning first with sweet flavors;
likewise, salty and sour [flavors] in the middle, and those that are pungent, bitter, and so forth at the end."
One should eat liquid food first, not hard food in the middle, and liquid food again at the end;
thus, one does not lose strength and health.
Śātātapa says:
If a Brāhmaṇa, weak through ignorance, drinks water with his mouth while his hand is available, he will become a dog; it cannot be otherwise.
The twice-born who drinks water lifted up with his left hand commits an act equal to the drinking of liquor; so said Manu, the Lord of Creatures.
The foolish man who, having washed his hands, drinks the rinsing water (gaṇḍūṣa) causes the gods,
the ancestors, and even himself to perish.
A mouthful (*gaṇḍūṣa*) is a handful of food from a meal. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"That which one eats with the palm of the hand, that which is eaten with a hissing sound (*phūtkāra*), and that which is eaten with fingers spread apart—each of these is like eating beef."
One should not eat while suffering from indigestion, nor if one is not very hungry;
one should not eat while standing upon an elephant, a horse, a chariot, a camel, or a palace.
Whether staying within a cremation ground, or having gone to a temple, or even while lying down, one should not eat; nor should one eat food held in the hand, nor food placed upon a seat.
Neither with wet clothes, nor with a wet head, nor without the sacred thread;
neither with legs outstretched, nor with one foot placed upon the other.
Nor while remaining in a state of attachment, nor while seated on a couch;
nor with his head wrapped, nor with his bowl placed in his lap.
One should not study wearing only a single garment, nor in the midst of wicked people, nor while wearing sandals or shoes,
nor while seated upon leather, nor with one's sides wrapped in leather.
One should not eat the remnants of a mouthful, nor drink the remnants of what has been drunk;
one should chew vegetables, roots, fruits, and sugarcane with the teeth.
One should not sprinkle food with more food that is scattered and contained within the bowl;
nor should one eat in haste while in the midst of many who are eating.
One should not scatter food in vain, nor should one go anywhere while still impure from eating.
Śaṅkha says: "One who has not been invited should not go to the seat of honor; one seated at the seat of honor should not eat first; one should neither give more nor accept more. Bṛhaspati says:
"While eating, one should never touch food with the left hand;
one should not touch one's foot, head, or bladder, nor should one touch the vessel with the foot."
Āpastamba says: "One should eat sparingly; likewise, one should eat on ground that has been smeared with cow-dung. Devala says:

"Having taken a small portion of the remnants of the meal from everything, one should sip water. One should pour those remnants, along with water, onto the ground for those whose portion is the leavings."
The mantra for this is:
"May [this offering] remain inexhaustible for those living beings who existed previously and now dwell in the Raurava hell—the abode of demerit—and in the Padma and Arbuda hells. Thus it is said.
Having eaten, one should sip water according to the prescribed rule with a concentrated mind;
then one should cleanse the mouth and hands with earth and rubbing agents.
Vyāsa says:
Having touched the vital organs with water and the navel with the palm of the hand,
one should depart after eating, but not while the hand is still wet.
Even after sipping water, one remains impure as long as the vessel has not been removed;
even when it has been removed, one remains impure as long as the ground is not wiped clean.
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A man, established in himself with a tranquil mind and having assumed his seat,
should perform the remembrance of his chosen deities."
May Agni, impelled by the wind, nourish the earthly element;
may he digest [my food] within the space of my teeth through the ether; may my mouth be thus perfected.
May this food serve for the strength of my body, the earth, the waters, fire, and wind;
and may the merit resulting from its transformation bring about ordained happiness for me.
May food be nourishing for the prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna breaths; may happiness ordained for me be attained.
May Agasti, Agni, and the submarine fire digest all the food I have eaten;
may they grant me the well-being resulting from its proper measure, and may I be free from disease within my body.
Just as the Lord Viṣṇu is the sole primordial essence of all distinctions between the senses and the body,
by that Truth may all food within me undergo transformation for the sake of bestowing health upon me.
Viṣṇu is the eater, and food is likewise his transformation;
by that truth, may this food which I have eaten be digested.
Having recited this and rubbed his belly with his own hand,
he should perform his duties without weariness and with diligence, ensuring they cause him no exhaustion.
One should not eat before a solar eclipse during the day, nor after a lunar eclipse in the evening;
one should not eat during the time of the eclipse, but may eat after bathing once both have been released.
Likewise, on the following day, having bathed and seen [the sun or moon], one may eat even if they were eclipsed at the moment of setting.
Another Smṛti states:
"If water is applied to the eyes after rubbing the surface of the fingers,
that water will very quickly dispel cataracts."
Likewise: "If one constantly remembers Śaryāti, Sukanyā, Cyavana, Śakra, and the two Aśvins at the end of a meal, one shall never be afflicted by eye diseases. (1.106)
[152] But when guests of the various social classes arrive, one should give according to one's ability, in the proper order.

When guests from the various classes (*varṇa*), such as Brāhmaṇas and others, are present, they should be fed according to the order starting with the Brāhmaṇas, provided one is able to do so. For one who is unable, the feeding of a Brāhmaṇa guest is mandatory. As Baudhāyana says: "Now, therefore, the five great sacrifices (*mahāyajña*); these indeed are the great sessions (*mahāsatra*): the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to the ancestors, the sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to beings, and the sacrifice to men. Day after day, one should offer *svāhā* to the gods until water is reached; thus he completes the sacrifice to the ancestors. Day after day, one should study one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) starting from the syllable *Oṃ*; thus he completes the sacrifice to Brahman. Day after day, one should offer the ritual oblation (*bali*) to beings until flowers [are offered]; thus he completes the sacrifice to beings. Day after day, one should give food to Brāhmaṇas until roots, fruits, and vegetables [are given]; thus he completes the sacrifice to men. Therefore, the censure regarding the failure to honor a guest refers specifically to the failure to honor a Brāhmaṇa guest. As Viṣṇu says:
If a guest departs from a householder with his hopes frustrated, he takes away that householder’s merit and bestows his own demerit upon him.
For this very reason, Manu states that the hospitality of Kṣatriyas and others should be performed according to their own wish:
"But if a Kṣatriya should come to the house in the manner of a guest,
one may feed him as one pleases once the Brahmins have finished eating."
"Even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, if they have arrived at the household as guests,
he should feed them along with his servants, practicing kindness (*ānṛśaṃsya*). Here, "kindness" means the absence of harshness.
A guest must not be turned away in the evening, even if one can offer nothing more than words, grass, and water. 1.107.
A guest who arrives in the evening is not to be sent away nor rejected; the meaning is that he must be entertained. As Manu says:

"A guest brought by the setting sun in the evening is not to be sent away by the householder, whether he has arrived at the [proper] time or at an improper time; the householder should not go to bed without having fed him."

But in the absence of food, he should not be turned away even by speech, grass, or water; the meaning is that one should offer hospitality even with these. And so says Āpastamba: "At the proper time, O Master, the two [host and guest] should not refuse one who comes seeking food; in the absence of food, there are these: ground, water, grass, or kind words. (1.107)
O monks, alms should be given with respect to one who observes vows.

[153] Alms should be given after having honored and worshipped the monk, the ascetic, the one who observes vows, and the celibate practitioner. Alms consist of food measured by a mouthful. In the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*:
And one should give alms to a monk, a wandering mendicant, or a celibate student,
having set aside from the unprepared food a portion provided with all kinds of condiments.
If a mendicant arrives at the house for alms while the Vaiśvadeva offering has not yet been performed,
one should set aside a portion for the Vaiśvadeva, give him alms, and then dismiss him.

Gautama says: "The giving of alms after pronouncing a blessing is 'appūrva'"; *appūrva* means preceded by water (*udakapūrva*). This refers to the case of an ascetic (*yati*) according to the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Alms should be the size of a mouthful; four mouthfuls constitute an *agra*;
the wise know that four times an *agra* is a *hantakāra*."
Whether it be a full meal, a morsel of food, or even a mere alms-gift,
one should not eat without first giving something according to one's own means.

This is a distinct ritual act from the daily *śrāddha* and the reception of guests. Viṣṇu states: "In the absence of mendicants, one should give the first portion to cows or cast it into the fire; even when food is already being eaten, one should not turn away a mendicant. The meaning is that this applies even when the householder is already eating, provided that food remains. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), the giving of mouthfuls to cows and so forth is included. As Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "One should always, day after day, provide a mouthful for the cows. (From the Mahābhārata).
He who always gives a handful of grass with food to another’s cow,
even without having taken his own meal, goes to the heavenly world.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "O daughters of Surabhi, benefactors of heaven, pure ones who are heaps of merit,
O cows, mothers of the three worlds, may you accept my morsel of food."
One should always give a mouthful of grass to cows with this mantra,
or provide them with scratching, fodder, a morsel, or even a daily meal.
By giving that, men would acquire merit equal to the gift of a cow.
The gift of alms is an illustration for the gift of food offerings and the like; as stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Furthermore, that which has been offered to Brahmā should be given to the Brahmins;
that which belongs to Viṣṇu to the Vaiṣṇavas (Sātvatas); and that which belongs to Śiva to those whose limbs are smeared with ashes."
Whatever is offered to the Sauras, to the Śāktas, to the Goddesses, to women,
and to the Mothers— whatever is offered at all— that should be given.
Whatever [is intended] for the spirits, ghosts, and demons, that one should cause to be buried in the ground.
And one should feed friends, relatives, and kinsmen who have arrived at the proper time. || 1.108 ||

A *sakhi* is a friend; *sambandhins* are those related by marriage, such as fathers-in-law and sons-in-law; *bāndhavas* are kinsmen on the mother’s side. One should feed these when they arrive at the time of a meal. Regarding others who have arrived at the house after the householder has already eaten, Manu says:
"Other friends and relatives as well, who have come to the house out of affection, he should feed with his wife according to his ability, using the food that is ready."
And from this statement it is understood that the wife should eat after her husband has eaten. || 1.108 ||
One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a learned Brahmin (śrotriya),
along with hospitable treatment, a seat, delicious food, and pleasant, truthful speech.

One should provide—that is, cook and prepare—a large bull or a steer for a learned *śrotriya* worthy of the *madhuparka* who has come to one's house; in the absence of that, a goat. Thus says the Śruti: "He who comes as the purchased Soma is indeed a guest; therefore, just as one would cook a large bull or a large goat for a king or a Brahmin, so too is this [the offering] for him; for that is human. Likewise, the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa* states: "All those who follow the King [Soma] are treated with hospitality; when King Soma has arrived, they churn the fire. Just as when a human king arrives, or another worthy person, they slaughter a bull or a cow for him, even so do they slaughter for him when they churn the fire; for Agni is the sacrificial animal of the gods. Consequently, the claim made by some that one should merely provide for the *śrotriya* through speech and not cause injury is contrary to the Śruti. The prohibition "one must not harm any living beings" does not apply to the killing that is an integral part of the *madhuparka*, just as it does not apply to the killing of the animal for Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*). For this very reason, Manu says: [and so forth].
Manu declared: "In the honey-mixture (madhuparka), in the Soma sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or deities—only in these instances may animals be slain, and nowhere else."

And so says Śaunaka, the author of the Gṛhyasūtra: "When the water has been sipped, they announce the cow; having muttered, 'My evil has been struck down, my evil is struck down,' [the guest] should say, 'Om, do it,' if he intends to have it performed. Having muttered, 'She is the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus,' [he should say], 'Om, release her,' if he intends to release her. There is no madhuparka without meat. [155] Here, the madhuparka is prescribed by way of providing a large bull or a large cow. Likewise, *satkriyā* is hospitality, *pūjā* is worship, and *anvāsana* is seating him when he has sat down. *Svādubhojana* is food with clarified butter. And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Now they also cite: 'For a Kṣatriya who has arrived as a guest, one cooks food with clarified butter. Pleasant speech and auspicious words—these are what must be performed. 1.109.

However, every year the following are worthy of the guest-offering (arghya): the accomplished student (snātaka), the teacher, the king, a dear friend, one for whom one’s daughter is being wed, and likewise the officiating priests at a sacrifice. (1.110)

Every year, those such as the *snātaka* are worthy of the *arghya* offering and should be honored with the *madhuparka*. A *snātaka* is one who has returned [from his teacher’s house]. An *ācārya* is defined by the characteristics already mentioned. A *pārthiva* is a member of the royal class (*rājanya*). A *priya* is one who is pleasing or agreeable. A *vivāhya* is the father of a daughter-in-law or a son-in-law. *Ṛtvij*s are defined by the characteristics already mentioned. They, having been honored with the annual *madhuparka*, are again worthy of the *arghya* at each sacrifice. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include the father-in-law and others. Thus says Śaunaka: "Having chosen the *ṛtvij*s, one should bring the *madhuparka*; for a *snātaka* who has arrived, for a king, and for an *ācārya*, a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, and a maternal uncle. Here, because of the inclusion of the term "who has arrived," it is understood that the *snātaka* and others are to be honored only when they have come to the house. For the *snātaka*, the *pārthiva*, and others, the honoring is performed provided they are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*); otherwise, it is not.
"One should provide a large bull or a large goat to a Śrotriya"—thus there would be a contradiction. 1.110.
It has been explained how one should behave toward a guest and a learned man (*śrotriya*). Now, he states their definitions:
"A traveler is to be known as a guest; a *śrotriya* is one who has mastered the Vedas.
And so says Manu:
A Brahmin staying for even a single night is considered a guest;
because he stays only temporarily, he is therefore called an *atithi*.

One who has reached the completion of Vedic study according to the prescribed rule is a *śrotriya*. Here, by the word "Veda," one's own *śākhā* (branch) is intended. Thus Āpastamba states: "By studying each [of the Vedas] in accordance with the law (*dharma*), one becomes a *śrotriya*. The repetition of the word "each" (*ekaikam*) is justified by the distinction between the students of the different Vedas. For this very reason, Baudhāyana says: "Having studied one *śākhā*, one becomes a *śrotriya*."
These two are to be honored by a householder who desires the world of Brahmā.

[156] These two—the guest and the *śrotriya*—are to be honored and worshiped by the householder who desires the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). From the force of the statement, it is understood that this is also an incidental fruit of the obligatory [rite]. It should be noted that while the honoring of the *śrotriya*—specifically one distinguished as a *snātaka*, a king, or the like—has been described as consisting of the *madhuparka* offering, the present rule ordains honor for one distinguished merely by being a *śrotriya* or merely by being a guest, for the sake of the aforementioned fruit. (1.111)
Furthermore:
one should not have a taste for another's cooking unless invited by one who is blameless.

One should not desire the food of another, having set aside the host who is beyond reproach. Kātyāyana states: "When invited by one who is blameless, one should not decline; nor, once invited, should one accept other food [from elsewhere]."
One should avoid fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, as well as overeating. || 1.112 ||

One should avoid the fickleness and lack of restraint of speech and the other senses. On this point, Gautama says: "One should not engage in the restlessness of the genitals, the stomach, the hands, the feet, the eyes, or speech; and one should avoid overeating," because it is the cause of ill health and other such evils. Likewise, Manu states: "Excessive eating leads to ill health, shortens life, prevents attainment of heaven, is unmeritorious, and is loathed by the world; therefore, one should completely avoid it."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "One should take food ending with milk, but one should not drink curd afterwards;
one should fill half the stomach with solid foods and one part with water."
One should leave a fourth part remaining for the purpose of the movement of the vital air.

One should follow a learned guest (*śrotriya*) who has been satisfied as far as the boundary. One should follow a learned guest who has become satisfied until reaching the boundary. There are three kinds of boundaries: the boundary of the dwelling (*vāstu-sīmā*), the boundary of the village (*grāma-sīmā*), and the boundary of the field (*kṣetra-sīmā*). And that [distance] is to be determined in consideration of the qualities of the person to be followed. As Manu says: "A seat, a lodging, a bed, following [the guest], and respectful attendance..."

"One should act with the highest toward the highest, with the lowest toward the lowest, and with equality toward equals. Thus, it has been stated that one should follow [the teacher] when he departs. If, for some reason, he remains [there], then Śaṅkha states what must be done: "[157] One should sit together [with him] at dusk; having obtained permission, one should go to sleep; one should wake up first; one should follow him when he sets out; and, having received full permission, one should return."
One should spend the remainder of the day with learned and beloved kinsmen. || 1.113 ||

One should spend the remainder of the day—the portion of the day still remaining—in the company of learned, virtuous, beloved, and dear kinsmen and relatives. In this regard, Dakṣa says: "Having eaten, one should sit comfortably and digest that food; one should pass the sixth and seventh parts of the day with the study of Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
"In the eighth [month], however, there is worldly activity; after that, the external twilight. Thus it is said.
The journey of the world is the stability of the world. 1.113.
Having performed the evening twilight devotions, having offered oblations into those fires and attended to them,
and having eaten with his dependents without excessive greed, he should then retire to rest.

Having performed the evening twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) in the afternoon according to the rules, having paid homage to the sacrificial fires (*vaitāna*) or the domestic fire (*aupāsana*), and having duly offered oblations and worshipped them, he should attend to their respective deities through the silent recitation of mantras (*japa*) and other rites. Surrounded and attended by his servants, sons, and others, he should eat until moderately satisfied, perform any other necessary duties, and then retire. For the purpose of sleep, he should lay down his body upon his bed. Dakṣa says: "Having performed the fire-oblation, the time for eating, and whatever other household duties there may be, one should thereafter practice a little Vedic study (*svādhyāya*)."
One should spend the first and last watches of the night in the study of the Vedas;
by sleeping during the middle two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman.

Āpastamba states: "One should always adorn oneself for the sake of one's wife during the night. By the word *dāra* (wife) here, the senior lawful wife (*jyeṣṭhā sadbhāryā*) is meant. The meaning is that one should adorn oneself specifically for her, and not for another woman. Viṣṇu states: "One should not sleep with wet feet; nor with the head toward the north or west; nor naked; nor along the ridge of a house; nor in the open air; nor on a bed made of *pālāśa* wood, nor on one made of five kinds of wood, nor on one made of elephant-bone, nor on one that is broken, nor on one scorched by fire, nor on one made from a tree watered by a jar, nor in cremation grounds, empty dwellings, or temples; nor among fickle people, nor among women; nor above grain, cows, teachers, or fire; nor while impure from food; nor by day; nor at twilight; nor on ground covered with ashes, nor on moist ground, nor on a mountain peak. Uśanas states: "One should not sleep with oil smeared on the head; nor, unless initiated, on a black skin. Here, "black" refers to the spotted deer (*hariṇa*). (1.114)

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate what is beneficial for oneself. The final watch of the night is the *brāhma-muhūrta*; having risen at that time and abandoned sleep, one should contemplate—that is, reflect upon—what is beneficial for oneself. This includes the "good" (*śreyas*), which consists of the three aims of life (*trivarga*). As Manu said: "Dharma and Artha are called the good; Kāma and Artha, and Dharma alone [are also called the good]."
In this world, wealth alone is indeed superior; such is the established doctrine regarding the three aims of life.
Dharma, artha, and kāma constitute the threefold set (trivarga). Likewise, one should reflect upon and contemplate: "This is the highest good; thus must it be accomplished by me.
One should wake during the Brāhma-muhūrta and reflect upon dharma and artha, as well as physical austerities rooted therein and the true meaning of the Vedas.
Vyāsa says:
"Having reflected thus—'What would happen to me by doing this? What would happen to me by not doing it?'—a wise man should either perform his duties or refrain from them."
Again and again one must awaken to this: "What good deed have I done today?
Have I given a gift, or caused another to give, or have I spoken words of truth?"
Rising again and again, one must remain vigilant, for a great danger has arrived:
which of these—death, disease, or sorrow—will fall upon me today?
When a night has passed during which one has performed not even the slightest virtuous deed,
the wise man should know that very day to have been barren.
One should not neglect dharma, artha, and kāma at their proper times, according to one's ability. || 1.115 ||

One should practice Dharma at the time that constitutes a constituent part of Dharma; one should not pursue Artha and Kāma at the expense of that [Dharma]. Likewise, at a time for Artha that is not in conflict with Dharma, one should pursue Artha alone. Similarly, at a time not occupied by either of those two, one should pursue Kāma. In this way, according to one's capacity, Dharma, Artha, and Kāma are not neglected. And so says Gautama: "One should not let the forenoon or the midday pass fruitlessly; one should devote them to Dharma, Artha, and Kāma according to one's ability, but among these, Dharma should be paramount. Manu says: "One should abandon Artha and Kāma if they are devoid of Dharma."
And even that dharma which results in unhappiness and is indeed censured by the world. || 1.115 ||
He states the grounds for respect along with their proper sequence:
"One is to be respected according to the order of knowledge, ritual action, age, kinship, and wealth;
even a Śūdra, if he possesses these in abundance, deserves respect on account of old age. (1.116)

Those possessing [these qualities]—learning and the rest—are to be honored according to the specific actions prescribed for them: by virtue of their learning, age, kinship, and wealth. One who possesses learning is to be honored by those possessing age, kinship, and wealth; one who possesses action (karma) is honored by those possessing kinship and wealth; one who possesses age is honored by those possessing kinship and wealth; and likewise, one who possesses kinship is honored by one who possesses wealth, but not otherwise. Learning (*vidyā*) is that which was mentioned here as the *Purāṇas*, *Nyāya*, and so forth. Action (*karman*) is the performance of prescribed rites. Age (*vayas*) is that which is greater than the age of the person honoring him. Kinship (*bandhu*) refers to relatives. Wealth (*vitta*) is property. Those twice-born (*dvija*) endowed with these are to be honored. When those possessing learning and the other qualities are assembled, honor should be accorded according to their sequence, without transgressing the order; the meaning is that each preceding one is more venerable than each succeeding one. A Śūdra who is endowed with each of these qualities—action and the others—in abundance, or who has reached old age, deserves honor from others except for the formal salutation (*namaskāra*). Here, "old age" refers to being over eighty. As Gautama says: "Even a Śūdra is superior if he is over eighty. Likewise, he states that caste (*jāti*) is also a cause for being honored: "Wealth, kinship, action, caste, learning, and age are to be honored, but each subsequent one is stronger than the preceding. However, sacred learning (*śruta*) is the most venerable of all, because Dharma is rooted in it. Thus, caste is a cause for being honored; however, even one of low caste who is endowed with superior qualities and learning becomes more venerable than one of high caste. As Manu says:
Wealth, kinship, age, action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding.
Among the three [higher] castes, he who possesses many and excellent qualities is worthy of honor, even if he is a Śūdra who has reached his tenth decade of life.

The tenth part of a hundred years is the *daśamī* (the tenth stage). It is reckoned as being more numerous and, in its excellence, more virtuous. Therefore, disregarding birth, one who possesses much learning must be honored by one with little learning; and one of superior learning by one with inferior learning. The same applies to ritual actions (*karman*) and so forth. 1.116.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed the ritual ablution, women, the sick, ascetics, and holders of the discus; among these, O King, the one who has performed the ablution is to be honored even by a monarch.

An *vṛddha* is one who has reached the tenth stage of life; according to the *Smṛti*, "the way must be yielded to one who carries a wheel and is in his tenth stage. The tenth stage refers to the final period of life. A *bhārī* is one who carries a burden. A *nṛpa* is a member of the royal caste (*rājanya*). A *snāta* is a *snātaka* (one who has performed the ceremonial bath after Vedic studies). A woman and a sick person are well known. A *vara* is one who has set out to marry a maiden. A *cakrī* is a cart-driver. To these, the way must be yielded; when they meet on the road, one should step aside from the path. Among them when assembled on the road, the king is to be honored. And among kings, the *snātaka* is to be honored if he is a Brāhmaṇa. As Āpastamba says: "When meeting a Brāhmaṇa, the king must yield the way; the way belongs to the Brāhmaṇa, as well as to one carrying a load, one who is ill, and a woman. The way must be yielded by all to those superior in caste by the other castes. For the sake of their own welfare, the way must be yielded by all even to those who are uncultured, outcastes, intoxicated, or insane. Furthermore, the "woman" here should be understood as one who is pregnant, as Baudhāyana says.
The way must be yielded to a Brahmin, to a cow, to a king, to one who is sightless,
to an elderly person, to one afflicted by heat, to a pregnant woman, and to one who is weak.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The way must be yielded to children, renunciants, and those distinguished by learning, craft, or virtue. (1.117)

Sacrificing, studying, and giving are for the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya; for the Brāhmaṇa, however, there is additionally the acceptance of gifts, as well as officiating at sacrifices and teaching. 1.118.

Sacrificial rites (*ijyā*) and so forth are for the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya; by the use of the word "and" (*ca*), they are also the means for accomplishing dharma for the Brāhmaṇa. However, receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) and the like are the means for subsistence (*vṛtti*) for the Brāhmaṇa alone. The term "exclusivity" (*adhikatva*) refers to the unique status of receiving gifts and so forth; the meaning is that receiving gifts and the like belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone. For this very reason, the word "Brāhmaṇa" (*vipra*) is used in the locative sense of "domain" (*viṣaya-saptamī*). And "domain" (*viṣaya*) implies existence nowhere else. Therefore, the threefold means of subsistence—receiving gifts and so forth—belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone. As for the statement: "In times of distress, study [of the Veda] from one who is not a Brāhmaṇa is ordained," that merely permits a non-Brāhmaṇa to act as a teacher (*adhyāpana*), but does not grant him the status of a means of subsistence. For this very reason, Manu says immediately thereafter:
"Following after and serving the teacher for as long as the study lasts. [161]

The meaning is that service consists precisely in following [the teacher]. A non-Brāhmaṇa is the teacher of a Brāhmaṇa only for as long as the study lasts; afterwards, once he has been taught, the Brāhmaṇa alone is the teacher. As Gautama says: "In times of distress, the acquisition of knowledge from a non-Brāhmaṇa by a Brāhmaṇa involves following him and serving him; when the study is completed, the Brāhmaṇa becomes the teacher. And thus, Vasiṣṭha’s statement—"Those who cannot subsist by their own duty may adopt the next lower occupation, but never a higher one"—is not inconsistent. In the phrase "sacrifice, study," the mention of sacrifice (*ijyā*) indicates, by synecdoche, those duties of the twice-born other than giving and studying. (1.118)
The primary duty of a Kṣatriya is the protection of the subjects;

that is, the protection of the subjects is the foremost and principal task for a Kṣatriya. Furthermore, this duty known as the protection of the subjects is primary because it is the cause of dharma. For the author will state later—beginning with "he takes a sixth part of their merit"—that, in the course of discussion, there is the mention of both the sixth part of merit and the sixth part of wealth.
Agriculture, trade, and animal husbandry are recorded as the duties of the Vaiśya, involving diligent effort.

Usury is living off the interest on gold and other assets; agriculture is well known; trade is the business of a merchant—and by that, trade is meant taking grain and other goods at a low price and giving them back at a high price; cattle-rearing is the protection of livestock. All of this is the primary occupation for a Vaiśya. (1.119)

The duty of a Śūdra is service to the twice-born; if he cannot subsist by that, he may become a merchant, or he may live by various crafts while performing what is beneficial for the twice-born. (1.120)

For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is the primary means of livelihood; however, service to Brāhmaṇas is also his duty. As Manu says: "Service to the Brāhmaṇas alone is declared to be the distinguished occupation of a Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs, that shall be fruitless for him."

"Excellent" means superior, because it is the cause for the practice of *dharma*. "Fruitless" means devoid of *dharma*; thus, service to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya by a Śūdra is solely for the sake of livelihood. As he (Manu) himself says: "But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, should serve a Kṣatriya;
and a Śūdra wishing to live [by service] should also serve a wealthy Vaiśya."
[162] One should not cause offense to a Brahmin, whether for the sake of heaven or for the sake of both worlds;
for that which is called the "Brahmin" is indeed his state of having accomplished all that is to be done.
And he [Manu] himself states that the twice-born should provide for his livelihood according to their ability:
"They should provide him with a livelihood from their own family and so forth, as is appropriate,
having considered his capacity, his skill, and the number of dependents he maintains."
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments,
the dregs of grain, and old household utensils.

"Pulāka" refers to grains with undeveloped kernels. "Paricchada" means household utensils. If he cannot subsist by that service to the twice-born, then he should become a merchant; the meaning is that he should live by trade. Or he may live by various crafts, such as painting and the like. However, if a Śūdra is unable to perform service for the twice-born and finds himself in a situation where his wife and children face deprivation, he may live by the work of artisans.

And from another Smṛti passage: "Those actions by which, while being performed, one does not become unworthy of serving the twice-born (dvijāti) should be practiced; those arts and crafts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served—these are the crafts and manual labors. Even in that case, what is beneficial to the twice-born must be performed. And so Devala says: "The duty of a Śūdra consists of service to the twice-born, avoidance of sin, maintaining his wife and family, agriculture, cattle-rearing, carrying loads, trade in merchandise, painting, dancing, singing, and playing the flute, lute, drum, mṛdaṅga, and other instruments. This is stated in the Narasiṃha Purāṇa under the section on the Śūdra.
One should be a giver even when unasked, one should resort to agriculture for the sake of livelihood,
and one should listen to the Purāṇas and perform the worship of Narasiṃha.
In the Mahābhārata:
A Brāhmaṇa blazing like fire is to be served from a distance by a Śūdra;
however, he may be served upon being touched by a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya.
Regarding the rules for listening to the Purāṇas, it is stated in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"Vaiśyas listen with one-pointed attention standing before Śūdras; likewise, Kṣatriyas before Vaiśyas; and Brahmins before Kṣatriyas. (1.120)
Having described the occupations of a Śūdra, he states his duty:
[163] "Delighting in his wife, pure, supporting his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites (śrāddha)."
One should not neglect the five sacrifices by performing them with the mantra of salutation (namaskāra). || 1.121 ||

He whose delight is in his wife alone is as described. By this, the avoidance of infidelity toward his wife is enjoined upon him as a matter of duty (*dharma*). He should be pure, performing the purifications prescribed by the scriptures. He should be a supporter of his dependents—namely, his sons, wife, and others. He should be devoted to the performance of *śrāddha* rites. He should perform the five sacrifices mentioned above with the mantra consisting of a salutation (*namaskāra*), and he should not omit or abandon them on the grounds that he has not studied the Vedic mantras. Here, the word "mantra" refers to the employment of a salutation in place of all mantra functions; otherwise, because they serve the same purpose, it would apply only to the functions of *svāhākāra* and *svadhākāra*. Now, one might object: since a Śūdra is without sacred fire (*anagni*), how can he have the right to perform rituals accomplished through fire? Nor should it be said that he possesses a marriage fire, for there is no *vivāha-homa* (marriage-consecration oblation) for a Śūdra. Indeed, there is no oblation without a mantra, and a Śūdra does not possess mantras. Furthermore, the use of a salutation as a mantra is prescribed specifically for the five sacrifices, not even for the marriage ceremony. Therefore, the reason for his eligibility regarding rites accomplished through fire must be stated. It is replied: Even for a Śūdra who lacks the sacred fire, the *vaiśvadeva* and other such rites are to be performed in a common (*laukika*) fire, because they are prescribed for him here [in this text]. This is just as in the case of the sacrifice of the *niṣādasthapati*. Moreover, even for the twice-born, the *vaiśvadeva* rite is not restricted solely to the marriage fire; how much more so for a Śūdra? As for what Gautama stated concerning the Śūdra—"Some say he should sacrifice himself with *pākayajñas*"—that refers to the common fire. (1.121)
Now he states the dharma common to all social classes:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, charity, self-control, compassion, and patience are the means of dharma for everyone. (1.122)

The avoidance of killing as enjoined by non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). Truthfulness is speech that accords with reality; moreover, it must be applied only in a way that is beneficial to living beings, according to the words of Vyāsa: "Truth is declared to be that which is beneficial to living beings. Even truth should be spoken only if it is pleasant:
"One should speak what is true and pleasant; one should not speak what is true but unpleasant;
nor should one speak what is pleasant but false—this is the eternal law (*sanātana-dharma*)."

This is according to the statement of Manu. Non-stealing (*asteya*) is the non-appropriation of what is not given. Purity (*śauca*) consists of the avoidance of forbidden food and so forth. Likewise: "Purity is said to be of two kinds: external and internal;
that which is performed with earth and water is known as external, while purity of disposition is the internal."

Control of the senses (*indriyanigraha*) is the restraining of the senses from prohibited objects. Generosity (*dāna*) is the giving away of one’s own wealth to a worthy recipient without expectation of a return favor. Self-restraint (*dama*) is the cessation of prohibited mental activities. Compassion (*dayā*) is the desire for the welfare of living beings. Forbearance (*kṣānti*) is patience, the avoidance of anger; another traditional text (*smṛti*) states, “Forbearance is the endurance of dualities. However, in the reading *damaḥ kṣamārjavam dānam*, *ārjava* means straightforwardness or equanimity of mind, according to the alternative statement, “Straightforwardness is equanimity of mind. Non-violence and the other virtues are each a means of accomplishing *dharma* for all social classes (*varṇa*), because they alone are the subject under discussion here. In this context, *dharma* is intended as having the nature of a transcendental merit (*apūrva*). On this point, Vyāsa says:
Compassion, non-violence, serenity, sharing with others, performing ancestral rites, hospitality toward guests, truthfulness, and freedom from anger.
Contentment with one's own wife, purity, constant freedom from malice, self-knowledge, and forbearance— O King, these are the common duties for all.
Likewise: truthfulness, self-restraint, austerity, contentment, modesty, forgiveness,
uprightness, knowledge, tranquility, compassion, and meditation— this is the eternal dharma.
Truth is said to be that which is beneficial to living beings; self-restraint is the taming of the mind;
austerity is the non-abandonment of one's own duty; and purity is the avoidance of intermixture.
Contentment, renunciation of sense-objects, modesty, desisting from what ought not to be done,
forbearance, endurance of the pairs of opposites, straightforwardness, and equanimity of mind.
Knowledge is the awakening to the meaning of reality; tranquility is the peace of the mind;
compassion is the desire for the welfare of living beings—this is the eternal Dharma.
Bṛhaspati says:
Compassion, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, lack of miserliness, and lack of greed are common to all [virtues].
Whether toward others, one's circle of kinsmen, a friend, or an enemy, one must always protect them when they are in distress; this is proclaimed as compassion.
Whether toward a Brahmin or toward oneself, or even when suffering has arisen somewhere, one does not become angry nor does one strike back; that is proclaimed as patience (kṣamā).
One who does not destroy the virtues of the virtuous, praises even those of meager merit,
and does not delight in the faults of others is proclaimed to be free from envy (anasūyā).
Avoidance of forbidden food, association with blameless persons,
and steadfastness in one's own duty— this is proclaimed as purity.
Whatever action causes the body to suffer, even if that action is very beautiful, it must not be performed; that is called "effortlessness."
Constantly practicing what is praiseworthy and never engaging in what is blameworthy—
this indeed has been declared as auspiciousness by the seers who perceive reality.
One should give even a small amount with an undepressed inner self;
whatever is given day after day, however little it may be, that is called non-miserliness.
One should indeed practice contentment with whatever has arisen, like food;
not considering the wealth of another, that is proclaimed as being free from desire.
The meaning is that one should not do that by which the body is excessively afflicted. || 1.122 ||

One should likewise practice a conduct that is appropriate to one's age, intelligence, wealth, speech, dress, learning, birth, and actions—a conduct that is straightforward and free from deceit. (1.123)

*Vayaḥ* (age) refers to the stages of the body, such as childhood, youth, and so forth. *Buddhi* is intelligence. *Artha* is wealth. *Vāk* is speech. *Veśa* is the arrangement of clothing, hair, and the like. *Śruta* is the acquisition of knowledge from a teacher, such as the *Purāṇas* and other sciences. *Abhijana* is lineage. *Karma* is [activity] such as *yoga*. One should practice their *vṛtti*—their mode of being—in a manner that is similar, mutually appropriate, free from envy, straightforward, not crooked, and not deceitful. This is what is meant: one should act with dress, speech, intelligence, and conduct that are respectively suited to one's age, occupation, wealth, learning, and lineage. And so says Bṛhaspati:
"According to one's learning, according to one's action, according to one's wealth, and according to one's age,
a person should behave in such a way that they are not arrogant because of their residence or other such factors.
(1.123) Having thus spoken by way of digression, he addressed the twice-born man regarding the subject at hand:

A twice-born man who possesses more than three years' worth of food may indeed drink Soma; that is, he whose store of grain sufficient for the maintenance of his dependents exceeds the duration of three years, that twice-born man may drink Soma—the meaning being that he should perform the Soma sacrifice. However, there is a specific qualification in the *Manu-smṛti*: "He whose food for three years is sufficient for the satisfaction of his dependents..."
Or even if there should be more, he desires to drink that Soma.
Therefore, if a twice-born man drinks Soma when the substance is very small, even though he has previously drunk Soma, he does not obtain its fruit.

This refers specifically to the subject of the *nitya-somayāga* (the obligatory Soma sacrifice). For Viṣṇu says: "One who possesses food sufficient for three years should sacrifice with the Soma every year; in its absence, [one should perform] the Vaiśvānarī [offering]. Now, one might object: since the injunction "for twelve nights, being initiated, he should collect the sacrificial fee (*bhṛti*)" implies by its very force that the priests' fee must be provided through begging alone, the commencement of the statement regarding one who has more than three years' worth of food is redundant. Not so. Precisely from the force of commencing this sentence, it is understood that if, while begging, one finds nothing or receives too little, the prescribed giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be performed even with previously accumulated wealth—neither failing to give it nor giving less than the prescribed fee. As for the statements in the Kalpasūtras and the Śruti, such as "the sacrificial fee must indeed be given at a sacrifice, even if it be small," these should be understood to apply to a case where a sacrifice has been commenced by one possessing more than three years' worth of food, but the previously accumulated wealth is lost and what was begged for is insufficient. Alternatively, the giving to the *sadasya*, *aprasarpaka*, *ātreyī*, and others, as well as the feeding of Brāhmaṇas, should be performed with previously accumulated wealth and not with what is begged for, because there is a specific rule restricting the latter to the giving of the *dakṣiṇā* alone. Thus, the commencement of the sentence is meaningful for the purpose of establishing this restriction.
One whose food supply lasts for a year may perform the rites pertaining to the Soma sacrifice before [the Agnyādheya].

Those rites such as the Agnihotra and others which are to be performed prior to the execution of the Soma sacrifice must be performed when there is rice sufficient for the annual maintenance of dependents; and this refers to optional (kāmya) cases, not to obligatory (nitya) ones, because that would entail a contradiction with the revealed scripture (śruti). 1.124.
Every year the Soma sacrifice is to be performed, as well as the animal sacrifice at each solstice;
likewise, the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must indeed be observed.
In the absence of these, the twice-born should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.

A Soma sacrifice (*somayāga*) should be performed every year; a Paśu sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) at each solstice (*ayana*); and likewise, one should perform the Āgrayaṇeṣṭi with new rice, *śyāmāka* millet, and barley. Regarding the rule, "At the end of the grain harvest, [one should sacrifice] with the New Grain Sacrifice" (*navasasyeṣṭyā*), the word "grain" (*sasya*) here indicates the autumn and spring seasons. For generally, the end of the old [harvest] occurs during those two seasons, autumn and spring. Therefore, Āśvalāyana says: "When one is satiated by the rains, then one should sacrifice with the Āgrayaṇa. And this refers specifically to the rice-Āgrayaṇa. The barley-Āgrayaṇa, however, takes place only in spring, for it is only then that they are "new. The *śyāmāka*-Āgrayaṇa is performed in either autumn or the rainy season, as they are new in both. Likewise, the Cāturmāsya sacrifices must be performed at their proper time. Laugākṣi states: "Now, the Cāturmāsyas [are performed] on the full moon of Caitra or Phālguna. By this much, having restated the Soma sacrifice and other rites, [the text] prescribes that in the event of their impossibility due to lack of wealth, one should perform the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice—dedicated to the deity Vaiśvānara—in lieu of them. The use of the term "sacrifice" (*iṣṭi*) even for the Vaiśvānarī rite being performed in place of the Soma sacrifice is intended to ensure the acquisition of the entire set of auxiliary elements (*aṅgavarga*) belonging to the Vedic (*śrauta*) Vaiśvānara sacrifice. Otherwise, by the maxim "through the assumption of its function, there is the acquisition of its properties," the properties of the Soma sacrifice would apply; or, because it is a Smārta rite, the Smārta procedure (*itikartavyatā*) would apply. As for the verse of Manu:
At the end of each year, one should regularly perform the Vaiśvānara iṣṭi for the purpose of expiating the failure to perform the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices when they cannot be performed.

Thus, that [text] also prescribes the *iṣṭi* sacrifice specifically for the purpose of the Soma and other rites; it does not, however, prescribe it as a subsequent expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Rather, through the word "expiation" (*niṣkṛti*) found in the scripture, it declares the necessity of performing the *iṣṭi* because an expiation is possible. For this very reason, it says immediately thereafter: "The twice-born who performs a duty according to the rules for times of distress when there is no distress does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter; so it has been determined."
"By all the gods, the Sādhyas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the great ṛṣis, fearing death in times of distress, a substitute for the Creator was appointed. Thus it is said.

Therefore, it is understood that the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is a substitute (pratinidhi) and not a penance (prāyaścitta). Furthermore, in this context, the phrase "of these" refers to the sacrifices beginning with Soma and ending with the Cāturmāsya, and not to the animal and Soma sacrifices alone, because there is no distinction in their context. As for what was stated by Manu—"of the prescribed animal and Soma sacrifices"—that is for the sake of illustration, otherwise the use of the plural number would be untenable. The sacrifice is to be performed for each of the Soma sacrifices and others according to its specific contingency; due to the absence of the original substance, the Vaiśvānara sacrifice is to be employed when the subsequent [substitute] becomes available, and not from any other cause. Thus says Śaṅkha.
"A twice-born man who possesses more than a three-year supply of grain may drink Soma without weariness;
likewise, a twice-born man of meager wealth should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice. (1.125)
One should not perform a deficient rite when the necessary materials are available, for it will fail to yield its fruit.

With respect to the qualified performer (*adhikārin*), there are two types of injunctions regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*): one that requires the inclusion of all constituent parts (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhārī*) and one that allows for the inclusion of only those parts that are possible (*śakyāṅgopasaṃhārī*). Among these, the ritual action that falls within the scope of the injunction allowing for possible parts is called *dhīnakalpa*. In that case, a desirable (*kāmya*) rite intended to yield its specific fruit should not be performed in a deficient form (*hīnakalpa*). The reason for this is stated as: "When the substance (*dravya*) is present, it yields the fruit. This is because it becomes a yielder of fruit only when the substance is present. The word "substance" (*dravya*) is intended to indicate all the constituent parts (*sarvāṅga*). Since the rite becomes a yielder of fruit only when the substance is present—that is, when all constituent parts are performed—here the term "yielder of fruit" (*phalaprada*), though mentioned only once, is connected to both the reason and the consequence according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). A rite that yields its fruit should not be performed in a deficient form; yet, when the substance is present, it becomes a yielder of that fruit. (And so Manu says: [Manu 4.20]: "One should always perform the rites according to one's ability, even if only with water, with faith, and according to the rule. [Manu 4.22]: "But one who, possessing wealth, does not perform the rites according to the rule, is born as a beast for as many times as he was capable of performing them. [Manu 11.30]: "A man who, being wealthy, does not give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor perform sacrifices, lives in vain, like a beast, for this world and the next. [Manu 11.39]: "One who, having the means, does not give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor perform sacrifices, is a thief of his own self, O best of the twice-born.
