[Manu 11.71]: "One who, possessing wealth, does not give gifts, nor offer oblations, nor perform sacrifices, is
"He who does not abide by the secondary rule when the primary rule is available—that fool has no fruit pertaining to the hereafter.
And here, the phrase "when the substance exists" is intended as an indicator of the capacity for the primary rule. 1.126.
One becomes a Caṇḍāla by performing a sacrifice with wealth begged from a Śūdra;
if one does not give what was obtained for the sake of a sacrifice, one may become a vulture or even a crow. (1.127)
He who begs from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice becomes a Caṇḍāla after death. And so Manu says:
"A Brahmin who knows the Dharma should not beg wealth from a Śūdra for the sake of a sacrifice;
for a sacrificer who has begged [thus] is born as a Caṇḍāla after death."
Those who, having approached Śūdras for the sake of wealth, officiate as priests at their Agnihotra sacrifices,
are indeed censured among those who discourse on Brahman.
Treading with his foot upon the heads of those who constantly perform sacrifices while serving outcastes, the donor shall cross over all difficulties.

These two statements refer to one who establishes the sacred fires after having acquired wealth from a Śūdra. Thus, he who does not employ the entire wealth obtained for the sake of sacrifice in that sacrifice shall become either a Bhāsa or a crow; a Bhāsa is a particular kind of bird. Regarding this, Manu says: "Having begged wealth for the sake of a sacrifice, if a Brahmin does not employ it all [for that purpose], he goes to the state of a Bhāsa or a crow for a hundred years. (1.127)

Whether one possesses grain in a granary or a jar, or gathers enough for three days, or even for tomorrow, or lives by gleaning ears and picking up grains— among these, each succeeding way of life is superior to the preceding.

One who possesses grain measured by a *kusūla*—a granary—is a *kusūladhānya*. A householder may also be one whose grain-receptacle is a *kumbhī* (a jar), which is a measure smaller than a *kusūla*, or one who possesses grain of that quantity. One who has grain sufficient for three days’ subsistence is a *tryāhika*; he may be such. One who possesses grain sufficient for subsistence until tomorrow is an *aśvastana*; he may be such. *Śila* is the gathering of grains and the like by hand. *Uñcha* is the gathering of individual fallen grains. *Śiloñcha* is both *śila* and *uñcha*; he may live by that. Among these aforementioned modes of livelihood, each subsequent one is superior to each preceding one; it is more highly praised because it possesses a greater degree of merit (*dharma*) and is a cause for conquering worlds such as heaven. Regarding this, Manu says:
He may possess grain sufficient for a granary, or grain sufficient for a single jar;
or he may have enough for three days, or he may not even provide for tomorrow.
Among these four types of twice-born householders,
each subsequent one is to be known as superior in terms of dharma and as the greatest conqueror of worlds.
Among them, one performs six duties; another proceeds with three;
one with two; but the fourth lives by the sacrifice to Brahman.

By the term "six duties" (*ṣaṭkarman*), he indicates the duties of a Brāhmaṇa, such as sacrificing for oneself and officiating at sacrifices for others, for the purpose of prescribing the three modes of livelihood included therein, beginning with receiving gifts (*pratigraha*). The statement "another proceeds by means of three" prescribes three modes of livelihood even for one who possesses grain in a jar (*kumbhīdhānya*). The phrase "one [proceeds] by means of two" permits officiating at sacrifices and teaching for one who has enough for three days (*tryahaihika*). Since receiving gifts might also come from a contemptible person, that is prohibited. The fourth is the "one for whom there is no provision for tomorrow" (*aśvastana*); he should live by teaching, which is a perpetual sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmasattra*). Thus, these characteristics, such as possessing a granary of grain (*kusūladhānyatva*) and so forth, belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone; for it is not possible for another [caste] to have a livelihood consisting of receiving gifts and the like. (1.128)

Thus ends the section on the duties of the householder in the *Yājñavalkyadharmaśāstra-nibandha* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of the Vidyādharas, [and] descended from the illustrious Śilāhāra king Jīmūtavāhana.
Now begins the section on the observances of a Snātaka in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary:
He should not strive for wealth that conflicts with Vedic study, nor from any random source whatsoever.
And one should never be satisfied by resorting to contradictory consequences. || 1.129 ||

One should not desire wealth that obstructs the acquisition of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Nor should one seek even wealth that does not so obstruct it from any source whatsoever—meaning from a donor from whom it is forbidden. Furthermore, one should not seek it through prohibited activities such as gambling or through addiction to things like singing; "addiction" (*prasaṅga*) means attachment, and singing and the like are called addictions because they cause such attachment. Alternatively, addiction refers to the occurrence of undesirable consequences (*aniṣṭāpatti*), taking the form of generating fear, such as: "If I do not give this to him, he will do this undesirable thing to me. And one should be content with whatever has arisen. On this point, Manu says:
Relying upon supreme contentment for the sake of happiness, one should remain self-restrained;
for happiness has contentment as its root, while the opposite is the root of suffering.

In this context, for every statement, by way of demonstrating that "this is to be done" and "this is to be avoided," there is enjoined a mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—consisting of the activity of the mind in the form "I shall do this; I shall not do that"—which is denoted by the word *vrata*. This is because they are prescribed in the Śruti, beginning with the words "His vow (*tasya vratam*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha, starting with "Now, therefore, the vows of the *snātaka*," has laid down these [rules]. And these resolves are to be performed immediately after the *samāvartana* ceremony, since they are prescribed for the *snātaka*. (1.129)
Since wealth must be sought for this purpose, he says:
"One who is suffering from hunger should seek wealth from a king, a pupil, or a patron;

one who is sinking due to hunger should desire wealth from any one of these, such as a king, and should strive to obtain it through acceptance of gifts and other means. The mention of the "king" is intended to indicate any pure donor.
And one should avoid those who are hypocritical, rationalizers, heretics, and those who act like herons. || 1.130 ||

One who practices dharma for the sake of winning over the world is a hypocrite (*dambhī*). A *haituka* is one who, by resorting to logic (*hetu*), subverts the dharma declared in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, and creates doubt everywhere through the power of reasoning. A *pāṣaṇḍī* is one who performs what is prescribed in scriptures outside the Veda. One whose livelihood consists solely of the conduct of a *baka* (heron)—that is, a life distinct from the stated stages of life (*āśrama*)—is a *bakavṛtti*. One should avoid these; the meaning is that one should not have social dealings with them. Manu says:

"One should avoid, even by mere word, heretics (*pāṣaṇḍinaḥ*), those engaged in improper acts (*vikarmasthān*), those who act like cats (*baiḍālavratikān*), the deceitful (*śaṭhān*), logicians (*haitukān*), and those who live like herons (*bakavṛttīn*)."
He himself has described those who perform forbidden acts and those established in improper conduct, such as those who follow the "vow of a cat":
"One who displays the banner of dharma while being ever covetous, deceitful, and a hypocrite toward the world;
who is violent and intent on deceiving everyone—such a person is to be known as one who follows the 'vow of a cat'."
He whose banner of righteousness is always held aloft like the banner of the gods,
yet whose sins remain concealed— that is the vow known as "the cat's."
One who looks downward, is deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends,
crafty, and falsely humble, is described as one who behaves like a heron (bakavṛtti).

[He is] deceitful and stubborn. [171] In this regard, within the *Viṣṇudharmas*, Pulastya spoke to Dālbhya—who had developed a desire for knowledge through the penance resulting from seeing and conversing with heretics—concerning the characteristics of those who inquire about heresy:

"Those who, having transgressed the dharma proclaimed by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* which arises from the divisions of caste and stage of life, proceed according to their own whims by means of fallacious arguments..."
Those fools who delight in improper actions, who are intoxicated by the arrogance of their sophistry,
who are heretics, ill-behaved, and the lowest of men— they deserve hell.
One should never disregard those wicked heretics, men who persist in improper actions, and those who observe the "vow of the cat."
Having conversed with these [deities], the wise man should meditate upon the Imperishable One who dwells in purity.
May the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu bring to rest all injuries to my body and speech through their afflictions; may there be peace for me here, now that the Infinite One has entered my heart.
May he who is my inner and outer purity, the stainless and imperishable one, perform that internal purification; in him, who is pure, may I always remain pure.
May the Lord Viṣṇu, who is free from external injury, wise, unborn, and infinite in nature, being established in the mind, lead it to purity.
Having conversed thus, this should be recited by the lowest heretics here:
"Homage to the one who dwells in purity," and having said this, one should look at the sun with steady gazes.
Likewise:
heretics, those of evil conduct, those who praise the qualities of forbidden food, those who eat unconsecrated food, and the *vrātyas* who are devoid of purificatory rites.
Heretics of evil deeds, hypocrites with deceitful intellects,
creators of the intermixture of castes, they live by the pretext of dharma.
Lacking purity, crooked in their ways, and asserting that nothing else exists—
such as these are those who have been cast outside the true path proclaimed by the Vedas.
Censuring the entire range of ritual actions characterized by the Ṛg and Yajur Vedas,
they cause both themselves and others to dwell in hell.
The sight, conversation, and touch of these should always be avoided by men; for it has been declared that [the same applies] when they are seen, and likewise when conversed with.
Having bathed after contact with them, the wise man, desiring purity, should remember the one who dwells in the pure (the Sun);
he should always avoid conversation and physical touch with these lowest of men.
But even an ordinary person who observes the conduct of the virtuous is superior,
because those of unrefined intellect revile your Vedic ritual.
All heretics feel no affection for the Vedic ritual;
for they are said to be destined for the lower realms, having resorted to a demonic nature.
Likewise:
For those deluded by that, discernment quickly comes to an end;
with their wisdom destroyed, men perform improper actions day after day.
Having abandoned the dharma consisting of their own specific caste,
those deluded by ignorance, thinking it to be dharma, commit sin.
From that very [attainment], they develop an arrogance of knowledge;
even when restrained by their friends and by compassionate scholars, they do not desist.
The fools provide an answer accompanied by fraudulent reasoning;
thereby they themselves [deceive] another man of dull intellect.
By engaging them in improper actions, they cause them to fall away from their own duty.
From the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"If the abandonment of religious rites occurs in anyone's house for even one month,
a wise man should look at the sun after beholding that person."
How much more so, then, for that twice-born man who has completely abandoned the three Vedas,
and who associates with heretics and sinful yogis who oppose the teachings of the Vedas?
One should not honor, even with a mere word, heretics, those who persist in improper acts, those who act like cats, the deceitful, sophists, and those who behave like herons.
Therefore, one should avoid those who engage in conversation, social contact, and laughter with the wise, as well as those who are extremely wicked, heretics, and those of evil conduct.
These are known as "naked ones" (nagna); having seen them, they destroy the merit of a Śrāddha. By conversing with them, one's merit perishes for a single day.
One should never speak with these sinful heretics;
by conversing with them, the merit produced on that day is destroyed.
In the Skanda Purāṇa:
"O Goddess, having seen a thankless man who is despised even among those in hell,
one should look upon the Moon, Fire, and Sun for the sake of purification."
There is an option regarding the Soma and the others, according to what is possible. || 1.130 ||

Wearing white garments, with hair, beard, and nails kept short, he should be pure. He should wear white clothes and likewise have his hair, beard, and nails cut short—meaning one whose hair, beard, and nails are low (shortened) is so described. Furthermore, he should always remain pure and self-restrained. Gautama states: "He should not wear a garment that is dyed red, ostentatious, or worn by another; however, having washed it, he may wear it at will. The meaning is that he may wear a garment previously worn by another after washing it. In the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra], there is another specific rule: "And he should not wear worn-out or dirty clothing, provided he has the means to do otherwise."
Likewise:
One should not wear sandals, clothing,
a sacred thread, ornaments, an umbrella, or even gold that have been worn by others.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: A self-restrained man should wear clothing that is always unblemished, as well as auspicious medicinal herbs and gems belonging to Garuḍa.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"One should not wear red garments, nor those that are variegated or black;
nor should one wear two garments in reverse order, nor speak while so dressed."
One should avoid clothing that has been bitten by insects and that which is excessively defiled.
In the Mahābhārata:
"The garment for the bed should be one thing indeed, but another for the streets;
and for the worship of the gods, it must certainly be yet another."
One should not eat while a burden is being carried, nor while wearing only a single garment, nor while standing. || 1.131 ||
One should not eat while looking at one's wife, nor while being looked at by her, nor while standing dressed in only a single garment. 1.131.
One should not fall into doubt, nor should one speak unpleasantly without cause;
one should neither speak what is harmful nor what is untrue; one should not be a thief, nor should one be a usurer. 1.132

One should not fall into doubt—that is, doubt regarding one's life—or otherwise, one should not entertain uncertainty or excessive apprehension regarding a settled matter. One should not speak what is unpleasant, harmful, or untrue, except when there is a scriptural justification. One should neither be a thief nor a usurer. Manu says:
"One should not travel with untrained draft animals, nor with those afflicted by eye disease, nor with those whose horns, eyes, or hooves are broken, nor with those whose tails are deformed."
One should not go out too early, nor too late, nor at midday;
one should not associate with an unknown person, nor alone, nor with low-caste people (vṛṣala).
And riding upon the back of cows is always to be condemned. [174]

Viṣṇu: "One should not stay at the foot of a tree at night; nor at a slaughterhouse or a prison; nor should one cross a river in vain. Without having offered water to the deities and the ancestors, one should not stand upon a riverbank. One should not look down into a well, nor leap over it. One should not set out on a journey alone, nor with unrighteous persons, nor with enemies. One should not travel during the two twilights, nor where water is not available, nor too hurriedly, nor in a continuous [uninterrupted] manner. Baudhāyana: "One should not travel the road with an outcaste or with a woman. (From the Viṣṇupurāṇa).
One who desires protection for the body should always go with an umbrella in rain or heat, with a staff at night or in forests, and wearing sandals.
A wise man, wandering about, should not look upward, nor sideways, nor into the distance;
he should walk while looking at the surface of the earth for only the distance of a yoke.
Likewise:
One should not mount a defective vehicle, nor should one rely on the shade of a riverbank.
One should not go alone into a deserted forest, nor should one dwell in an empty house.
In the Devīpurāṇa: One should not travel at night without a companion, nor on a wrong path, nor at a crossroads.

Āpastamba states: "One should not pass by a forest or a woman without first speaking to a *śrotriya* (one learned in the Vedas). Paiṭhīnasi says: "One should not walk between a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, or a sacred fire; or, having obtained permission, one may pass. Yama declares:
"That twice-born man who walks between two persons who are nearby and engaged in study becomes a sinner who does not enter the womb of dogs or donkeys."

It has been stated that "one should not speak unpleasantly without cause"; following from that context, something else is also said. In this regard, Devala says—where the term "faults" (*doṣāḥ*) is understood to carry over—"In that context, harsh speech, defamation, calumny, falsehood, idle chatter, and cruelty constitute the six types of verbal faults. To state the actual defects of others regarding their country, family, caste, learning, craft, appearance, conduct, means of livelihood, retinue, body, or occupation—that is [defamation].
Furthermore, whatever other censurable speech produces anger or terror, that too should be known as harsh, as well as anything else of that same kind."
To call one who has lost his sight "one with eyes," or to call a Caṇḍāla a "Brāhmaṇa"—
such praise or blame arising from hatred is more severe than harsh speech.
If one calls a *vṛṣala* a "vṛṣala," or a fallen man a "fallen man," there is fault even by speaking the truth; if one speaks falsely, the fault becomes twofold.

The proclamation, illustration, or defamation of those very same harsh words is slander (*paiśunya*). Slander is the reporting of faults in the presence of teachers, kings, kinsmen, husbands, friends, or associates for the purpose of harming their interests. Falsehood (*anṛta*) is of two kinds: untruth (*asatya*) and non-fulfillment (*visaṃvāda*). Among these, speaking otherwise than what has been seen, heard, or inferred is untruth; the failure to carry out what was previously promised is non-fulfillment. Falsehood arises in a person from passion, hatred, fear, greed, courtesy, apprehension, shame, deceit, or even negligence.
Falsehood is more serious than the harming of another's life or the seizing of another's property; it is not so in cases such as idle chatter.
Therefore, one should never produce those causes of falsehood within oneself;
or, if they have arisen, one should pacify them by means of factors that counteract them.
Idle chatter should be recognized as arising from talk about the king or the country, from imagining the welfare of others, and from the occasion of joking laughter.
They consider harsh speech regarding secret parts, limbs, or names, as well as any other base utterance concerning the sexual union of men and women, to be [sexual misconduct].
Thus, by speaking such faulty speech consisting of six types of alternatives,
one abandons both this world and the next and encounters manifold misfortunes.
The welfare and harm of human beings reside solely in speech;
therefore, one should employ speech with vigilance and after careful examination.
For a word ill-spoken is indeed most difficult to remedy later;
moreover, speech joined with fault will swiftly lead to one's downfall.
Regarding this, Yama says:
"Whether one sees a fallen person directly or indirectly, one must not offer a rebuke; one should protect oneself by means of oneself."

One should not deny what has been known by any means of proof or fallen [upon oneself]; the meaning is that one should not speak of it. One should protect oneself from association with such things. "The tears that fall from the weeping of those falsely accused—those destroy the children and livestock of the false accusers immediately."
Dakṣa says:
Falsehood, adultery, as well as the eating of forbidden food,
approaching those who should not be approached, violence, and likewise theft.

The practice of non-Vedic dharma, and being excluded from the dharma of friendship—these nine prohibited actions one should avoid. [176] *Maitra* means friendship; *bahiṣkaraṇa* means abandonment. Devala says:
One should never listen to the secrets of others in their home,
nor should one proclaim the faults of others in public assemblies.
Yama said: One should never, under any circumstances, speak nor listen to wicked speech,
especially that of Brahmins, regardless of who the speaker may be.
One should never speak harsh words to Brahmins under any circumstances;
one should remain silent during their censure and should not utter any reply.
One should neither utter slander against brahmins nor cause it to be uttered;
whatever is wholesome toward brahmins, that alone one should quickly practice.
Wherever censure or reproach of Brahmins takes place,
one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place to another.
Furthermore:

"Wearing a Dākṣāyaṇī [girdle], a sacred thread (brahmasūtra), carrying a bamboo staff, and possessing a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). Here, *dākṣāyaṇa* refers to gold; *brahmasūtra* is the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*); and *veṇu* is a bamboo cane. He should possess these, together with a water-pot. — Manu.
He should carry a bamboo staff, a water-pot containing water,
a sacred thread, a Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.

The *veda* is a handful of *darbha* grass. Regarding the two golden [objects], they are made of gold. Laugākṣi says: "One should wear gold that is unalloyed (*anupasṛṣṭa*). Unalloyed means free from black spots. Baudhāyana says: "A *snātaka* should wear an inner garment and an upper garment, carry a bamboo staff, and a water-pot containing water; he should also have two sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), a turban, an antelope skin, sandals for the feet, and an umbrella.
Moreover: "One should circumambulate clockwise deities, clay, cows, Brahmins, and trees. (1.133)

One should perform circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*) of deities and the like; the meaning is that one should proceed while keeping them to one's right hand. Manu says: "One should perform circumambulation of clay, a cow, a deity, a Brahmin, clarified butter, honey, a crossroads, and well-known trees."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should pay homage to earth that has been dug up, to crossroads, and to well-known trees;
and one should circumambulate all auspicious objects encountered on the road.
"A wise person should perform inauspicious and left-handed rites," so it is said.
Medicines are prescribed, as well as black grain,
cotton, dry grass, and dried cow dung.
Where there is fuel and charcoal, as well as two inauspicious serpents,
so too is a man who is smeared with filth, pale, and naked.
One with disheveled hair, one afflicted by disease, one wearing dyed garments, a madman, a eunuch, a wretched person, and a neuter— these are [excluded].
Likewise iron, mud, leather, and hair-ties;
and similarly, oil-cakes and other such things from which the essence has been extracted.
Cāṇḍālas, Śvapacas, and other such men who are prison guards,
executioners, or performers of evil deeds, as well as a pregnant woman and one who is ill.
Husked grain, ashes, potsherds, bones, and whatever vessels are broken;
empty vessels, and likewise a corpse accompanied by lamentation.
And other such things are inauspicious when seen;
likewise, the sound of musical instruments is inauspicious if it is broken, terrifying, or discordant.

O knower of dharma, the command "Come" is praised when spoken from the front, but not from behind; however, the command "Go" is censured when spoken from the front, though it is acceptable from behind.
"Where are you going? Stay! Do not go! What will you gain by going there?
and other such words that are undesirable are considered to be portents of misfortune.
Likewise, the presence of carnivorous animals at the banners and other such objects is censured,
as is the stumbling of mounts and the falling of heaps of garments.
And as one is departing, there may be a blow to the head at the gate or similar places;
the falling of umbrellas, banners, and other cloths would also be inauspicious.
O twice-born one, a wind that is harsh and dry, rising from all directions,
contrary to the grain, and low-lying, should be known as a bringer of fear.
Favorable winds are gentle, smooth, pleasant to the touch, and bring about auspiciousness;
whereas those that are harsh, rough-sounding, violent, carnivorous, and contemptible are inauspicious.
Likewise, when an inauspicious halo or rain is observed,
and the first sign is seen, there is the destruction of misfortune.
The wise man should offer praise to Śaṅkara and likewise to Madhusūdana;
then, upon seeing the second [image], he should enter his house against the current.
One born without sexual organs is a *napuṃsaka*. A male who has lost his virility due to some other cause is a *ṣaṇḍa*.
Now, O sinless one, I shall describe the desired auspicious objects:
white flowers are excellent, as are full water-pots.
O Bhārgava, aquatic flowers, meat, fish, cows, horses,
and elephants are [the sacrificial fees], while the goat is the single bound animal.
The thirty gods, friends, Brahmins, the blazing sacrificial fire,
courtesans, O highly fortunate one, dūrvā grass, and fresh cow dung.
Gold, silver, and likewise copper, as well as all kinds of gems,
O knower of dharma, and also medicinal herbs such as vacā and siddhārthaka.
The Nṛvardhamāna vehicle and likewise the Bhadrapīṭha,
as well as the sword, the discus, the banner, the earth, and the weapon itself.
All the royal insignia, the corpse devoid of weeping,
ghee, curd, milk, and various kinds of fruits.
The svastika, the vardhamāna, the river-curl with the kaustubha gem,
rivers arranged in variegated patterns, and other supreme auspicious signs.
Unbroken grains, as well as the principal items, a mirror, collyrium,
yellow pigment (rocanā), a golden pitcher, and honey.
There were conch shells, sugarcane, and various edible foods, as well as auspicious words;
there was the pleasant sound of musical instruments, deep and captivating.
The notes Gāndhāra, Ṣaḍja, and Ṛṣabha, as well as other sounds and tones that are intelligent, auspicious, pleasant, and resonant like the trumpeting of elephants, are praised.
Favorable winds are praised, as are lightning and the rainbow;
favorable planets are praised, but the lords of the directions are especially so.
O knower of dharma, faith, trustworthiness, and the honoring of those worthy of honor— these are weapons, as is whatever is auspicious in the mind.
In this matter, the satisfaction of the mind alone is the supreme cause for proceeding;
on one side are all the external signs, and on the other side is the satisfaction of the mind.
Lack of eagerness for vehicles, joy of mind, obtaining auspicious dreams, reports of victory,
and a mind inclined toward the accomplishment of auspicious goals— these should always be known as bringing about victory.

A vehicle with a man mounted on it, a man who is increasing in stature, a seat for the bathing of a deity, and a *bhadrapīṭha* (an auspicious throne). The *nandyāvarta* and other such configurations, made of gold, wood, and so forth, are well-known from the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) and the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*). Viṣṇu says: "Upon seeing a person with a missing limb, one should turn back; likewise, those who are disaffected, those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, dwarfs, and ascetics; as well as salt, a rope, and fetters. However, at the time of departure, one should welcome a lute, sandalwood, fresh vegetables, a turban, ornaments, and a young maiden. (1.133)
One should not urinate on a river, in the shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes.

One should not perform the act of urination—or the voiding of feces—in rivers and the like. [This refers to] a river that is without water; for if it contains water, the prohibition is already established by the specific mention of "water. Nor should one do so in the "shade," meaning a shade that provides sustenance to the public. Thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not urinate in a river, nor on a path, nor on ashes; nor on cow-dung, nor in a ploughed field, nor in a sown field, nor in the shade of grassy areas that provide sustenance. A "cow-pen" (goṣṭha) is a place where cattle graze. Likewise, Manu says: "One should not void urine on a path, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen."
Neither on ploughed ground, nor in water, nor on a funeral pyre, nor on a mountain.
One should never [discharge urine] in a dilapidated temple, nor on an anthill;
nor in pits containing living creatures, nor while walking, nor while standing on a path.
Neither having reached a riverbank nor on the peak of a mountain.

Even though mountains are included [among forbidden places], the specific mention of "mountain peaks" is for the purpose of showing favor toward locations other than the peak in times of extreme distress. As for Yama: "Dust, charcoal, potsherds, temples, royal roads, cremation grounds, fields, and threshing floors..."

Devala says: "One should not void urine or excrement at a crossroads or near a gate; nor on ploughed land, nor where crops are growing, nor on a sacrificial ground, nor beneath trees sacred to sacrifice. Viṣṇu says: "Nor on saline soil, nor in a place defiled by others; nor near a garden or water; one should not void urine or excrement in the open air. Śaṅkha and Likhita say: "One should not discharge urine or excrement in an uncovered place; nor while wearing only an inner garment, nor while naked. [And one should avoid facing] fire, the sun, cows, the moon, the twilight, water, women, or the twice-born. (1.134)

One should not urinate facing toward fire and other such objects while looking at them; likewise, Gautama states: "One should not cast away urine, feces, or impure substances while facing the wind, fire, Brahmins, water, deities, or cows; nor should one stretch out one's feet toward these deities. Yama says:
"One should not urinate facing the sun, nor should one look at it even once.
Having looked at the sun, one should gaze instead at a cow, fire, or a Brahmin."
Facing the sun, facing the wind, facing a cow, and facing a twice-born man;
facing the moon, facing water, and constantly facing the two twilights.
It destroys the wisdom and the very path of one who urinates;
those who urinate while facing these [directions] become short-lived.
Āpastamba: "One should not void urine or feces while wearing shoes. (1.134)

Furthermore: One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at one engaged in sexual intercourse; nor should one look at urine or feces, nor, while impure, at the eclipsed moon or stars. (1.135)
One should not look at the sun, nor at a naked woman, nor at a woman engaged in sexual intercourse, nor at urine or feces. Nor should one look at the impure, or at Rāhu, or at the stars. Manu says:
"One should never look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun;
nor at it when eclipsed, nor when reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky."

Viṣṇu: "One should not look at the sun when it is obscured by a cloth, nor when it has entered [the reflection] in a mirror, water, or similar surfaces. Hārīta: "One should not look at a naked woman or man, nor at the moon or sun at their rising or setting. Gautama: "One should not look at another's wife while she is naked. Āśvalāyana: "One should not look at a naked woman except during sexual intercourse"—this refers specifically to one's own wife. Manu: "One should not eat together with one's wife, nor look at her while she is eating, sneezing, yawning, or sitting at her ease."
A twice-born man desiring splendor should not look upon a woman who is applying collyrium to her own eyes, nor one who is anointed, nor one who is uncovered, nor one who is giving birth.

Viṣṇu: "One should not look at the face of an angry guru; nor one's own reflection in oil or water; nor in a mirror that is soiled; nor at one's wife while she is eating; nor at any naked woman; nor at one who is urinating; nor at an elephant that has broken loose from its tethering post; nor at a fight involving bulls or other animals when they are in a precarious position; nor at one who is insane; nor at one who is intoxicated. Devala:
"One should not look at outcasts, the deformed, Caṇḍālas, or those who have eaten the leavings of others.
It is better for men not to converse with such persons even if they happen to come within one's line of sight. (1.135)
Uttering every mantra while saying, "This is my vajra," one may go about unsheltered during rain; nor should one sleep with the head facing west.
When it rains, he should go about with his head uncovered, reciting the mantra: "May this thunderbolt of mine drive away evil. He should also avoid sleeping with his head toward the west. 1.136.
Moreover: One should not throw spittle, blood, excrement, urine, or poison into water;
one should not warm one's feet over a fire, nor should one step over it. (1.137)

Spittle refers to saliva and such things discharged from the mouth; blood is *asṛj*; feces is *śakṛt*; urine and poison are well known. If the reading is *retāṃsi*, semen is also included as a well-known substance. One should not cast these into water. Regarding warming one's feet or stepping over them, one should not do so toward the fire. Yama says:
"One should not cut down a sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), nor should one discharge phlegm into water;
nor should one discharge semen, poison, urine, feces, or blood [into water]."
Neither bones, ashes, nor skulls, nor hair, nor thorns [should be present].
A *caitya* is a tree situated on a funeral pyre; *citi* means a cremation ground. Manu says: "One should not blow upon a fire with one's mouth, nor look at a naked woman;
one should not throw impure things into the fire, nor warm one's feet over it."
One should not place it underneath anything, nor should one step over it;
one should not place it beneath one's feet, nor should one cause it to suffer the oppression of breath.

Kātyāyana says: Whether intending to offer or having already offered, one should not blow on the fire with the hand, a bellows, a wooden splinter, or a piece of wood, nor should one do so with a fan or similar objects.
[182] One should blow upon the fire with the mouth alone, for it was born from the mouth;
as for the worldly practice of saying "one does not blow upon the fire with the mouth," that is merely a conventional application.
Viṣṇu: "One should not throw blood or poison into fire. Devala:
"One should not cast fire into fire, nor should one extinguish it with water."

Āpastamba: "One who is not pure shall not sit near the fire at a distance of more than an arrow's length, according to some; nor should he place it upon a bed. Gautama: "One should not hold fire and water simultaneously. 1.137.

Moreover: One should not drink water from one's cupped hands; one should not wake a sleeping person; one should not play with dice, which destroy righteousness; and one should not lie down to sleep with those who are diseased. (1.138)

The hands joined together, with the left and right [hands] properly aligned, constitute the *añjali* gesture. One should not drink water with that [gesture]. One should not wake a person who is lying down and asleep. One should not play with dice. One should not lie down together with persons who destroy dharma, those who are outcastes (*patita*), and those who are diseased. In this context, "lying down together" is intended as an illustration for social intermixture (*saṃkara*). For this very reason, Manu says: "One should not lie down with outcastes, nor with Caṇḍālas, nor with Pukkasas;
nor with fools, nor with the arrogant, nor with those of the lowest castes, nor with those who dwell among the lowest."
One should avoid sitting on the same seat or eating together with outcasts,
as well as with others who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) and those performing censurable acts.
The mention of "play" (*krīḍā*) is intended to indicate addiction in general. Thus Manu says:
"He should not dance, nor should he sing, nor should he play musical instruments;
he should not clap his hands, nor should he shout, nor should he dye his clothes."
"Red" means attached; one should not cause detachment regarding that which is not forbidden. The meaning is that one should not act with a mind possessed by aversion. Likewise:
"One should not engage in futile exertion, nor drink from cupped hands;
one should not eat food while holding it on one's lap, nor should one ever be a seeker of idle curiosity."
The suffix [is used] in the sense of constant connection or excellence. 1.138.
Furthermore:
One should avoid contrary actions, crossing a river by means of a corpse's smoke, and standing upon hair, ashes, charcoal, water, or a skull. (1.139)
[183] One should avoid actions contrary to longevity, such as [entering] smoke from a corpse and crossing a river, as well as remaining among hair and the like. Manu says:
"The morning sun, smoke from a corpse, and likewise a broken seat are to be avoided."
One should not cut one's nails or body hair, nor should one tear at one's nails with the teeth.
One should not crush a clod of earth, nor should one tear grass with the fingernails;
one should not perform fruitless action, nor any that results in future suffering.
The man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites his nails, is a slanderer,
and is impure— he quickly goes to destruction.

The future is the transformation [of action]. Here, by the word "karma," intention (*saṃkalpa*) is meant. One should not perform that which is fruitless or false, consisting of the execution of what has been intended. One should avoid the habit of crushing clods of earth and so forth. Likewise:
"One should not scratch one's own head with both hands joined together;
nor should one touch it while impure from food remnants, nor bathe without [first washing] it."
"Then," means with the head bowed.
One should avoid seizing the hair and striking the head;
furthermore, having bathed one's head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil.

The syntactical connection is as follows: having bathed the head with oil, one should not touch any other part of the body with that same oil; or rather, on that day, one should not touch the body with any oil whatsoever. Viṣṇu states: "One should not scratch the head or the belly with both hands joined together. Furthermore, one should avoid crossing a river by means of one's arms or by a precarious raft. And so Manu says: "One should not cross a river by means of both arms. Vasiṣṭha says: "And one should not board a precarious boat. Manu [also says]: "One should not step upon hair, ashes, bones, or potsherds."
One who desires to live a long life should not [use] cotton seeds nor chaff.
Likewise:
one should not intentionally step upon fragrant unguents, water used for bathing, food, feces, urine, phlegm, spittle, or vomit.

Viṣṇu: "One should not stand upon a crossroads, nor at the foot of a tree at night, nor in an empty dwelling, nor in a slaughterhouse or a prison. Gautama: "One should not stand upon impure things. Śaṅkha and Likhita: "One should not stand upon the footprint of a snake; one should not stand upon heaps of grass or pebbles. *Pada* means a place or spot. Āpastamba: "One should not stand upon the hand of a Brāhmaṇa that has been smeared with food and not sprinkled with water. The meaning is that one should not stand upon a spot smeared by a Brāhmaṇa's hand if it has not been consecrated by sprinkling. 1.139.
Furthermore:
One should not point out a cow suckling her calf, nor should one ever enter through any opening other than the door;
nor should one accept gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures. (1.140)

One should not mention to another a cow that is suckling or giving milk to her calf. One should not enter a village by a way other than the gate. One should not accept wealth from a king who is greedy, who does not spend his riches, who acts contrary to the scriptures, and who has transgressed the sacred law. Baudhāyana says: "One should not speak of a cow suckling [her calf] to another. Manu says:
"One should not pass through a village or an enclosed house by a way other than the gate."

Gautama: "One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or those who are unrighteous. Having conversed with them, one should meditate upon those who perform meritorious deeds. Or one may converse with a Brāhmaṇa. One should call a non-cow 'a cow'; one should call what is inauspicious 'auspicious'; [one should call] a skull 'the auspicious vessel' (bhagāla); [one should call] Indra’s bow 'a jewel-bow' (maṇidhanus). One should not point out a cow suckling another's calf to anyone else, nor should one drive her away. Viṣṇu: "One should not point out a cow grazing in another's field, nor should one display an omen. Manu: "One may wander from house to house for the sake of secret matters, but not without a specific purpose. (*Kula* means a house. Vasiṣṭha: "One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited; if one does go, one should circumambulate it and return again. Gautama: "One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited, but one may go at will to see it. Manu: "One may go at will to pay homage, or if desirous of seeing the sacrificial rites. (1.140)
In receiving gifts, the butcher, the oil-presser, the gambler, the prostitute, and the king are wicked;
each subsequent one among these is ten times more wicked than the preceding one. (1.141)

Regarding the matter of accepting gifts, whoever is subsequent among those beginning with the butcher (*sūnin*) incurs a fault ten times greater than the one preceding him. Therefore, accepting a gift from such a person incurs a tenfold fault; hence, one should avoid accepting gifts from them. A *sūnā* is a place for slaughtering living beings; one who possesses such a place is a *sūnin*, a slaughterer of animals. A *cakrin* is an oil-presser. A *dhvajin* is a seller of liquor. A *veśyā* is so called because she renders the hearts of others helpless, or alternatively, because she lives by her appearance (*veśa*); *veśa* here means erotic adornment. A *narādhipa* is a king; he too is indeed corrupt according to the previously mentioned qualifications, since accepting a gift from him is forbidden. And so says Manu: [185] "One becomes purified by giving away all one's possessions to those who perform sacrifices, or by renouncing life in the forest; but one is purified even more quickly by giving to a knower of the Brahman. (MDh 11.24) "From a *sūnin*, an oil-presser, a liquor-seller, a public woman, and a king—one should avoid accepting gifts, as they are ten times worse in succession. (MDh 4.213) "And from these five, a king is the worst; for the world is supported by the king, and the king is supported by the world. (MDh 4.84) And likewise: "One who accepts gifts from kings, or from those who live by weapons, or from those who live by women, goes to hell. (MDh 4.84) And: "A king is always impure; his food is always unfit to be eaten. Yet, when he bestows a gift upon a worthy recipient, that gift becomes pure. (MDh 4.91) And: "But the acceptance of gifts from a king is declared to be the most censurable among all forms of accepting gifts. (MDh 4.87) And: "Accepting a gift from a king is like swallowing poison; yet, O Brāhmaṇas, it is better to swallow poison than to accept a gift from a king. (MDh 4.89) And: "A king is said to be the soul of all castes; therefore, one should not accept anything from him, lest he consume the sacrificer. (MDh 4.90) And: "If a king accepts a gift from a Śūdra, he falls into hell; and the giver also sinks along with him, like one who has swallowed poison. (MDh 4.88) And: "By accepting a gift from a king, a Brāhmaṇa is immediately defiled, even if he is otherwise pure; he is purified only after performing a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (MDh 4.92) And: "From a *sūnin*, an oil-presser, a liquor-seller, a public woman, and a king—one should avoid accepting gifts, as they are ten times worse in succession. (MDh 4.213) And: "One should avoid the food of a king, as well as the food of those who live by weapons, the food of a woman, and the food of a king. (MDh 4.216) And: "The food of a king is always impure; it is always unfit to be eaten. Yet, when he bestows a gift upon a worthy recipient, that gift becomes pure. (MDh 4.91) And: "But the acceptance of gifts from a king is declared to be the most censurable among all forms of accepting gifts. (MDh 4.87) And: "A king is said to be the soul of all castes; therefore, one should not accept anything from him, lest he consume the sacrificer. (MDh 4.90) And: "If a king accepts a gift from a Śūdra, he falls into hell; and the giver also sinks along with him, like one who has swallowed poison. (MDh 4.88) And: "By accepting a gift from a king, a Brāhmaṇa is immediately defiled, even if he is otherwise pure; he is purified only after performing a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (MDh 4.92) And: "One should avoid the food of a king, as well as the food of those who live by weapons, the food of a woman, and the food of a king. (MDh 4.216) And: "The food of a king is always impure; it is always unfit to be eaten. Yet, when he bestows a gift upon a worthy recipient, that gift becomes pure. (MDh 4.90) And: "If a king accepts a gift from a Śūdra, he falls into hell; and the giver also sinks along with him, like one who has swallowed poison. (MDh 4.88) And: "By accepting a gift from a king, a Brāhmaṇa is immediately defiled, even if he is otherwise pure; he is purified only after performing a *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (MDh 4.216) And: "The food of a king is always impure; it is always unfit to be eaten. Yet, when he bestows a gift upon a worthy recipient, that gift becomes pure. (MDh 4.91) And: "But the acceptance of gifts from a king is declared to be the most censurable among all forms of accepting gifts. (MDh 4.87) And: "A king is said to be the soul of all castes; therefore, one should not accept anything from him, lest he consume the sacrific
A king is considered equal to a butcher who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses; therefore, the acceptance of gifts from him is terrible.
He who accepts gifts from a greedy king who acts contrary to the scriptures shall,
in due course, go to these twenty-one hells.
Tāmisra, Andhatāmisra, Mahāraurava, Raurava, the hell Kālasūtra, and likewise Mahānaraka.
Saṃjīvana, Mahāvīci, Tāpana, Saṃpratāpana, Saṃghāta, Kākola, Kuḍmala, and Pūtimṛttika.
The iron stake and the boiling cauldron, the path and the Śālmalī river,
the forest of sword-leaves, and the iron prison as well.
Knowing this, learned Brahmins who discourse on the Veda and desire the highest good after death do not accept gifts from a king. 1.141
He states the auxiliary elements of the rule for Vedic study:

"The commencement of the [Vedic] chapters (upākarma) takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, or under the asterism Śravaṇa; or under the asterism Hasta when the medicinal herbs have appeared; or on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. (1.142)

The *adhyāyas* are those which have been studied; they are the *svādhyāyas*. The rite called *upākarma*, which is a purificatory (*saṃskāra*) rite for them, should be performed on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. That [lunar day] in which the asterism Śravaṇā is conjoined with the moon is the *śrāvaṇī*. Alternatively, the suffix *enap* is added to the word *śravaṇa* in the sense of the locative case (saptamī), meaning "in the asterism Śravaṇā. Or else, the *upākarma* should be performed on the fifth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Hasta, provided that the plants have come into being. "The coming into being" (*bhāva*) of the plants—such as rice and so forth—means their appearance, that is to say, the sprouting of shoots. This qualification should also be understood to apply to the *śrāvaṇī* full moon and the asterism Śravaṇā. When there is no appearance [of the plants] on the *śrāvaṇī* full moon, then it should be performed under the Śravaṇā [asterism] of Bhādrapada. On this point, Manu says:
Having performed the ritual commencement (*upākarma*) according to the rules on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada,
a Brahmin, being disciplined, should study the Vedas for four and a half months.

Having performed the *upākaraṇa* (the commencement of Vedic study), he should study those same [Vedas] for five months. Those for whom the fifth month is half-full are so described; the meaning is that from the *upākarma* onwards, he should study his own recitation (*svādhyāya*) continuously for four and a half months during both the bright and dark fortnights. According to the *Purāṇa*: "At the *upākarma* and at the *utsarga*, having assembled at the proper time and having fashioned the sages out of *darbha* grass, one should worship them and then offer libations."
Likewise, having fashioned seven sages beginning with Gautama out of darbha grass, the twice-born man,
having worshipped them according to his ability, should offer libations and recite the Ṛgveda verse.

In order to indicate that even a householder has the qualification for receiving and studying [the Veda], the rule for study is placed in that same section. For this very reason, Śaunaka says: "One who has completed his studies [may live] according to the rule of a student; others [say he may live] according to the rule, provided he does not approach his wife," so say some. (1.142)
He states the rule for the ritual of suspension (utsarjana):

"At the full moon of Pauṣa, under the asterism Rohiṇī, or likewise on the Aṣṭakā day, one should perform the suspension of the Vedic meters according to the rules outside [the village], at the edge of the water. (1.143)

The full moon conjoined with the asterism Puṣya is the Pauṣī; the month in which that occurs is Pauṣa. On the Rohiṇī day of that same month—meaning on its Aṣṭakā, i.e., the eighth day of the dark fortnight—one should perform the *utsarga* (suspension) of the *chandāṃsi*, meaning the Vedas, at the edge of water, that is, in the vicinity of water, outside the village. Here, by the word *chandobhiḥ* (by the meters), the study of them is indicated. One should now abandon that manner of Vedic study which was performed from the time of the *upākarma* onwards during the bright and dark fortnights, but not entirely. For this very reason, Manu says:
From this point forward, however, one who is self-restrained should recite the Vedic meters during the bright fortnights;
he should recite the Vedāṅgas and the secret Upaniṣads during the dark fortnights.

Thus, immediately after the *utsarga*, he has stated another method regarding the study of the ritual texts (*karmādhyayana*). And the *utsarga* must be performed according to the rules and according to the *Gṛhya-śāstra*. On this point, Manu says: "A twice-born man should perform the *utsarjana* of the Vedic meters outside [the village] under the asterism Puṣya, or on the first day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, in the forenoon."

If the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) takes place on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, then the concluding ceremony (*utsarjana*) occurs on the first day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa in the forenoon; if, however, it takes place on the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, then [the conclusion] occurs in Māgha.

[187] Regarding the Upākarma and Utsarga ceremonies, he states the exclusion of specific days as a supplementary rule for the period of Vedic study: "There is no study for three days upon the death of a pupil, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a relative."
Likewise, at the Upākarma and Utsarga ceremonies, as well as when a learned scholar of one's own Vedic branch is present.

For three days—that is, for three full days and nights—one must observe *anadhyāya*, which means the avoidance of study. The cause for this is stated as: "when the pupil, the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*guru*), or a relative has died. Here, the "teacher" (*guru*) should be understood as the *ācārya*. Thus says Manu: "They declare that there is impurity (*āśauca*) for three nights when the *ācārya* has passed away. In this context, "relatives" (*bandhu*) refers to those who are not *sapiṇḍas*, because for *sapiṇḍas*, rules such as ten days of impurity have already been prescribed. The phrase "there is a three-night suspension of study" is to be supplied [to the rule] regarding the *upākarma* and *utsarga* ceremonies. However, Manu states that for the *utsarga*, one may optionally observe a suspension of study for a "two-day period" (*pakṣiṇī*), for one day, or for three nights.

"Having thus performed the ritual dismissal outside according to the scriptures and in accordance with the rules, one should cease for the night of two days (a *pakṣiṇī* rātri) or for one day and night. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that there is likewise a three-day suspension of study when one who has studied the *śrotriya* (a Vedic scholar) of one’s own *śākhā* dies. Āpastamba says: "Having performed the *upākarma* on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one should not study during the first month at nightfall. Likewise, while engaged in teaching, one should avoid sexual intercourse during the rains and autumn. The same applies from the *upākaraṇa* until the *utsarjana*. The teacher must observe these restrictions: he should avoid greed, meat, funeral feasts (*śrāddha*), and sexual intercourse; he may approach his wife only during her season. This refers to the subject of one who has returned home (*samāvṛtta*). Therefore, Śaunaka states: "One who has returned home should study according to the rule for a student (*brahmacārin*); others say he may approach his wife according to the rule, but some say that is [only] the *prājāpatya* [form]. The meaning is that approaching one's wife in that manner is the *prājāpatya* form [of marriage]. 1.144.
Furthermore:
during twilight, thunder, a hurricane, an earthquake, or the falling of meteors;
Having completed the Veda and having studied the Āraṇyaka day and night, || 1.145 ||

In the evening and morning twilights, during the sound of thunder—even when not in the twilight periods—during a hurricane, an earthquake, or the fall of a meteor, one must suspend Vedic study for a full day and night (*ahorātra*) after completing the recitation and having studied the *Āraṇyaka* portion of the Veda. Hārīta states: "If there is thunder at the evening twilight, they should not study for the night; if there is thunder at the morning twilight, [they should not study] for a day and a night. Āpastamba says: "During the twilight, if there is thunder, [one should not study] for the night. If there is lightning until the time of sleep—that is, until the point of rising from improper rest—and if lightning flashes near dawn, such that a black or red cow standing within the range of a *śamyā*-throw can be perceived, then during that time while it is flashing, there is a suspension of study for the day including the preceding evening. If there is thunder in the small remaining part of the night, some say the suspension lasts from that point until midday. The meaning of this is: "During the twilight" refers to the time characterized by the junction of day and night; if there is thunder (*stanite*) or the sound of clouds (*meghadhvanau*), one should not study for the intervening night. "Until the time of sleep" means until the cessation of sleep, that is, until the time of rising. "Near dawn" means when lightning flashes before the break of day; or alternatively, when a cow—whether black or red—is recognized within a space measured by the throw of a *śamyā*. When lightning flashes in the latter part of the night, there is a suspension of study for the day including the evening. If there is thunder in the small remainder of the night, there is a suspension for the day including the evening due to that cause. Alternatively, if thunder occurs after midnight, there is a suspension for the day including the evening. Manu, however, prescribes a suspension of study lasting until the same time the next day (*ākālika*) in the case of hurricanes and similar phenomena.
In the event of a thunderclap, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries,
one should know these to be occasions for the suspension of study (anadhyāya) lasting until the same time the following day, even during the proper season.
"Even during the proper season" means even during the rainy season. "Until the same time tomorrow" (ākālika) means lasting until the time of the occasion [has passed]. And likewise:
"In a village overwhelmed by thieves, in a panic caused by fire, and in all extraordinary portents, one should know that there is no study until the same time [tomorrow]. Thus it is said.
Consequently, there is an option regarding whether the period is one day and night or not; the same applies to other types of cosmic cycles (*kalpa*). Yama states:
"In the event of the raising of Indra’s banner, likewise upon the falling of meteors, and similarly during an earthquake, there shall be a suspension of study for three nights. [189]

Vasiṣṭha: "When there is a conjunction of a meteor and lightning, [the suspension of study lasts] for three nights; when there is a meteor or lightning together with light, even outside the [rainy] season, it is until the same time the next day. When a meteor is seen in spring or lightning is seen in the rainy season, there is no study as long as the light remains; that is, during the day. Outside the aforementioned season, when lightning or a meteor flashes, the suspension of study must be observed for the remainder of the day and until the same time on the second day; such is the meaning. (1.145)
Moreover:
on the fifteenth, the fourteenth, or the eighth day; during an eclipse of Rāhu; at the junctions of the seasons; or having eaten, or having accepted a gift related to a Śrāddha ceremony— || 1.146 ||

On the fifteenth, fourteenth, and eighth days of both the bright and dark fortnights; likewise during *rāhusūtaka* (an eclipse), when the moon or sun is eclipsed; and at the junctions of the seasons (*ṛtusaṃdhi*)—that is, at the transitions between the seasons beginning with spring—one must observe a fast for a day and night after eating or receiving food related to a *śrāddha*. *Rāhusūtaka* refers to the sight of an eclipse. *Śrāddhika* means that which is connected to a *śrāddha*. Having eaten cooked food from such a *śrāddha*, or having received raw food, one should not study for a day and night. This is according to the *Nṛsiṃhapurāṇa*: "Indeed, on the Mahānavamī, the Dvādaśī, and also on the Bharaṇī [nakṣatra]..."
Likewise, on the Akshata-tritiya day, a twice-born man should not teach his disciples.
On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, known as Rathasaptamī,
the best of the twice-born should avoid seeing a corpse being carried away, whether it is still on the ground or otherwise.

*Mahānavamī* is the ninth day of the bright fortnight of *Aśvayuja*. *Mahādvādaśī* is the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of *Kārttika*. *Bharaṇī* is the day immediately following the full moon of *Proṣṭhapadā*. *Akṣatatṛtīyā* is the third day of the bright fortnight of *Vaiśākha*. *Rathasaptamī* is the seventh day of the bright fortnight of *Māgha*. Regarding the rule "one should not study," Gautama states: "The three full moons of *Kārttika*, *Phālguna*, and *Āṣāḍha*, and the three *Aṣṭakās*—some say for three nights, others say not for the last one. The meaning is that for three nights starting from the aforementioned full moons. By the word *Aṣṭakā*, the three-night period beginning with the seventh day—which constitutes a limb of the *Aṣṭakā* ritual—is indicated. The final *Aṣṭakā* is that of *Māgha*; some declare that alone to be the cause for the suspension of study. Pāraskara says: "The three *Aṣṭakās* occurring in the dark fortnights starting from *Pauṣa*; some say those starting from *Mārgaśīrṣa*. Śaunaka, however, says: "There are *Aṣṭakās* on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. Śātātapa says:
On the fifteenth day, the fourteenth day, on the *aṣṭakā* days, during great festivals, at twilight, on the thirteenth, the eighth,
and also on the first day; one who desires intelligence should always [study] on the thirteenth and the fourteenth.
And on the seventh lunar day, during the evening twilights, one should neither remember nor recite [the name].
Manu says:

Having accepted an invitation to an Ekoddiṣṭa śrāddha, a twice-born man shall not recite the Veda for three days; nor [shall he do so] during the impurity resulting from the birth of a king or from an eclipse of Rāhu.
As long as the fragrance and the smear of a single funeral meal remain on the body of a learned Brahmin, so long one should not recite the Veda.

*Ketana* means an invitation. *Ekānudiṣṭa* means a rite for a single deceased person. And thus, there is an option between one day and three nights regarding the impurity caused by Rāhu (*rāhusūtaka*). *Rāhusūtaka* refers to the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse). For this very reason, Hārīta states: "Upon the death of a teacher, a king, or a learned *śrotriya*; upon the death of a fellow student; upon the sighting of Rāhu during an eclipse of the moon or sun; upon the falling of Indra’s banner; and upon the death of an *ācārya*, [the impurity lasts] for three nights. (1.146)
Furthermore:
"If an interval is created by a beast, a frog, a mongoose, a dog, a snake, a cat, or a mouse, it is a day and night; likewise when there is the falling or the rising of Śakra. (1.147)

*Antaram* means passing between a student and a teacher. When this occurs due to animals, frogs, and the like, there is a suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) for a day and a night; that is to say, from the moment of their passage until sunrise. Likewise, *śakrapāte* refers to the time characterized by the rising of Indra’s banner. *Śakrapāta* occurs under the asterism *Bharaṇī* immediately following the month of *Proṣṭhapada*. The raising of Indra’s banner (*śakrocchrāya*) occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of that same *Proṣṭhapada*. Regarding this, Garga says:
"When the sun has entered Leo and the moon reaches the first quarter of the asterism Aśvinī during the beautiful bright fortnight..."
"He rises, worthy of worship by the multitude of various temples, and then sits down in the southern direction, O wielder of the thunderbolt.
And here, by the word *hari*, the asterism Śravaṇā, whose presiding deity is Hari, is indicated; and that too is for the sake of illustration, since he himself has said:
"On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Proṣṭhapada..."
"The king should cause Śakra to rise up in Viśvaśravaṇa and Vāsava. Thus [it is said].

By the word *viśva*, the *vaiśvadeva* lunar mansion *uttarāṣāḍhā* is indicated; by the word *vāsava*, the *vasu*-deity lunar mansion *dhaniṣṭhā*. Therefore, the raising of the banner for Indra (*śakra*) occurs specifically on the twelfth day. Gautama [191]: "If someone passes between [the teacher and the pupil], the *upasadana* must be performed again. In the case of a dog, a mongoose, a frog, or a cat passing between, there is fasting and staying away from home for three days. For others, there is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). The same applies to studying in a cremation ground. When anyone passes between them, the *upasadana* must be performed. *Upasadana* is that very rite which is prescribed daily, beginning with "having grasped the hand with the hand," and so forth; that alone must be done again. Regarding the passage of a dog or other such animals, there is fasting for three nights. And "he shall stay away for three days" (*tryahaṃ ca vivaset*). As for what Vasiṣṭha says—"In the case of those studying, if someone passes between them, there is fasting for a day and night. There is no ritual bathing and they must stay apart for three nights; but for dogs, cats, mongooses, and fast-moving creatures, it is a day and night"—that refers to the case of one who is unable to fast for three nights. "For others, there is breath control and the consumption of clarified butter" means this applies when someone other than a dog or similar animal passes between them. (1.147)
Furthermore:
[One should not study] when there is the sound of dogs, jackals, donkeys, owls, the *sāman* chants, arrows, or those afflicted by pain;
nor in the vicinity of impure substances, corpses, *śūdras*, outcastes, cemeteries, or those who have fallen from their status.
In an impure place, or when one is oneself impure; during a downpour of lightning and thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; while in the midst of water; at midnight; or during an excessive windstorm. (1.149)

During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mist, while running, when there is a foul odor, and when a learned man has arrived at one's house. || 1.150 ||

When there is the sound of donkeys, camels, vehicles, elephants, horses, or boats, or when trees are being cut down on a barren field—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study. 1.151.

When the sounds of dogs and the like—where "kroṣṭṛ" means a jackal, "ulūka" an inauspicious bird, "bāṇa" a particular kind of lute, "ārta" one who is suffering, and "śva" etc. are well known—are heard, there is a suspension of study for that time. Likewise when in the vicinity of impure things and the like; "antya" refers to those lower than Śūdras. Likewise during the impurity of the place or oneself, as well as during a flash of lightning—"saṃplava" meaning its repeated occurrence. Likewise after eating, as long as the hands are still wet; likewise in the midst of water, at midnight (the two middle watches of the night), as well as when there is a violent wind blowing excessively. Likewise during a dust storm, a specific portent, or the burning of the quarters; likewise during the two twilights, as well as in mist or smoke, and when there is fear caused by thieves and the like. Likewise for one who is running, there is no study. Likewise when there is a foul odor, when a learned person (*śiṣṭa*) possessing the aforementioned characteristics has arrived at the house, or when mounting a donkey and the like—"yāna" meaning a chariot and so forth, and "iriṇa" meaning barren salt-earth. The sages know these thirty-seven causes, beginning with the sounds of dogs and jackals, to be temporary suspensions of study to be observed at the moment the cause occurs. Herein is a specific detail; likewise Manu says:
[192] One should never recite the Ṛgveda or the Yajurveda while the sound of a lute is being heard.

Regarding the continuation of the suspension of study (*anadhyāya*), Baudhāyana states: "In the presence of sounds of dancing, singing, instrumental music, or weeping, as well as during times of distress, [there is no study] for that duration. Āpastamba says: "At a cremation ground, [there is no study] within the range of a *śamyā*-throw on all sides. Some say that a *śūdra* and an outcast (*patita*) are like a cremation ground if they are in the same house. However, in the case of a *śūdra* woman, there is no study while looking at her or being looked at by her. One who intends to study the Veda, if he desires to speak with a menstruating woman, should first speak with a Brāhmaṇa and then speak with her; but having spoken with her, he must speak again with a Brāhmaṇa before he may study. Yama [says]:
One should never study under the shade of the Śleṣmāntaka, the Śālmali, or the Madhuka trees,
nor under the Kovidāra or the Kapittha;
likewise:
Not during battle, nor in an army, nor likewise in a dispute or a quarrel.
Hārīta says: "Upon the arrival of Brāhmaṇas, having offered the *arghya* and other honors and having obtained their permission, they may study. Likewise:
Not while standing under a tree, not while standing at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), nor in water, nor in assemblies.
And one should not study at all in a place that is very crowded.
One should not study while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor while sitting with the knees bound by a cloth; nor after eating meat, nor food provided at a birth-impurity (sūtaka).
Likewise:
A twice-born man should not recite while a row of dogs, donkeys, or camels is barking;
nor should he study at the edge of a cremation ground, at the edge of a village, or even in a cow-pen.
Likewise:
when blood has flowed from the body due to being wounded by a weapon.

Gautama states: "After eating at a festival, there is a suspension of study for one who has already begun his lessons for four *muhūrtas* during the night; some say this applies to a city festival. After eating following the initiation (*upanayana*), there is a suspension of study for a day and a night for one who has begun his lessons. For one who has already begun his lessons, after eating even when it is not a festival, there is a suspension as previously described. Regarding "four *muhūrtas* during the night," this refers to the thirteenth lunar day. Thus Uśanas says: "On the thirteenth [lunar day], one should not study during the first four *muhūrtas*. Following the rule that this constitutes a suspension of study, Vasiṣṭha adds: "And on a bed separated from its coverlet, or with a garment separated from its lining that has not been washed. All these occasions of suspended study must be avoided by one desiring perfection in dharma and perfection in knowledge, since the resulting transgression is no different. Likewise, Yama says:
[193] The wise declare that the offerings made by the twice-born are their vulnerabilities;
through these vulnerabilities, the sacred knowledge (brahman) acquired by a Brahmin flows away.
I cut short his life, progeny, cattle, wisdom, and whatever merit he has earned,
who studies or recites the Veda during periods when study is forbidden.
As for the statement of Manu:
"A twice-born man should always diligently avoid two occasions of non-study:
an impure place for Vedic recitation and an impure self."

This refers to the study for the *brahmayajña* (sacrifice to Brahman), because it is based on a statement studied within that specific context. For, with reference to the *brahmayajña*, the followers of the Taittirīya school recite: "Now, there are two occasions of non-study for this very sacrifice: when one is personally impure, and when the place is [impure]. (1.148–151)
Having thus stated the occasions when study is forbidden, he speaks of the subject at hand:

"One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a sacrificial priest, a graduate, a teacher, or a king, nor on that of another’s wife, nor on blood, excrement, urine, spittle, or the remains of unguents. (1.152)

One should not step upon or stand upon the shadow of deities and the like, nor upon blood and such substances. Since the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) and the teacher (*ācārya*) are already included by the mention of the *snātaka*, their separate mention indicates that the word *snātaka* here refers to one who has recently returned from his studies. Alternatively, it should be understood that one must not step on the shadow of any *snātaka* other than the officiating priest and the teacher. "Deities" refers to images of gods. "Spittle" refers to saliva and similar secretions discharged from the mouth. "Udvartana" refers to substances used for rubbing the limbs during massage. On this point, Manu says: "Of deities, of a guru, of a king, and likewise of a *snātaka* and a teacher..."
One should not intentionally step on the shadow of a tawny person or of one who is consecrated for a sacrifice.
Yama [prescribes] brown and tawny [animals], such as cows and the like.
One should not step upon the shadow of gods, twice-born men, gurus, the wise, snātakas, teachers, or ministers; nor should one step upon the shadow of a tawny person or even that of one's own guru.
One should never step upon one's own shadow when it belongs to a eunuch,
an outcast, a Caṇḍāla, an enemy, or someone afflicted with disease.

Viṣṇu: "One should not step over the shadow of a Brāhmaṇa, a deity, a teacher, a kinsman, or one who has been initiated. In this connection, something else is also stated; regarding that, Manu says: "At midday and at night, after eating a Śrāddha meal or food containing meat, and during both twilights, one should not frequent a crossroads. [194]
Likewise:
One should not serve an enemy, nor the companions of an enemy,
nor one who is unrighteous, nor a thief, nor the wife of another.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not stand together with those who are arrogant or deceitful. (1.152)
Furthermore:
Brahmins, snakes, Kṣatriyas, and one’s own self must never be treated with contempt.
A Brahmin, a snake, a Kṣatriya, and one’s own self are not to be despised. On this point, Manu says:
One who desires prosperity should never, under any circumstances, despise a Kṣatriya, a serpent, or a learned Brāhmaṇa, even if they appear weak.
For these three, when treated with contempt, utterly consume men;
therefore, a wise person should never hold these three in contempt.
One should not despise oneself on account of former failures;
one should not curse oneself out of anger, nor should one sleep during the day.
One should not scratch the ground at night, nor should one touch cows during the night.
Likewise: One should not revile or despise Brahmins, kings, the elderly, one's own kin, or even children who are peaceful; rather, one should honor them as if they were deities.
Furthermore:
Until death one should desire prosperity; one should not touch anything that strikes at one's vital points. 1.153

One should seek fortune for as long as one lives; therefore, realizing that it is difficult to attain, one must not be negligent in practicing the means to achieve it—this is the intended meaning. Likewise, one should not strike at the vital point (marman) of any enemy or even a neutral person; the sense is that one should avoid exposing the faults of others. And so says Manu:

"One should not revile those who are deficient in limbs, those with redundant limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those lacking in beauty or wealth, nor those of low birth. (1.153)
Moreover:
One should discard remains of food, feces, urine, and water from the feet at a distance;
one should cast away such things as food remnants far from the house.
Furthermore: One should always practice the conduct properly prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (1.154)

Conduct (*ācāra*) is defined as an injunction—either positive or prohibitive—that relies upon worldly actions for the sake of assisting human well-being (*puruṣaniḥśreyasa*). Among these, conduct prescribed by the *Śruti* includes characteristics such as the branding of the cow, for example: "One should perform the ear-cutting on the right ear," and so forth. However, the scriptural statements (*smṛti-vākya*) concerning the subject matter of conduct are now presented. Regarding this, Vyāsa says: "A man desiring prosperity should always bathe with *āmalaka* fruits;
however, he should avoid doing so on the seventh and fifth lunar days, as well as on festival times."
The new moon day is a festival day. As that same author says:
"One should especially avoid *dhātrī* fruits with great care on the new moon day, the ninth day, and the seventh day."
Dhātrī means *āmalakī*. Likewise:
On the seventh lunar day, one should not touch oil, nor wear blue clothing;
a man should not bathe with *dhātrī* and *āmalaka* fruits, nor should he engage in quarreling.
Since it destroys these three— vigor, progeny, and fame— one should therefore avoid a wet-nurse.
Likewise: "The sixth, eighth, fifth, and fourteenth days of both fortnights;
on these occasions, sin is present in oil, meat, the razor, and the female organ."
Oil on the sixth day shortens one's lifespan; likewise, meat on the eighth day [is forbidden];
sensual enjoyment on the fourteenth day [is avoided]; and shaving on the new moon day [is prohibited].

The fifteenth day is [forbidden] for eating meat, the fourteenth for anointing with oil, and the eighth for sexual intercourse with a village woman; these [days] may cause even one who is blazing to fall.

Village-dharma is sexual intercourse. One should not touch raw oil, nor should one cut trees and the like on the first day of the lunar fortnight, on Sundays, on the sixth lunar day, or likewise on a day when one has undergone purgation.
On the tenth day, an unwise man should not bathe without first asking about oil;
for him, four things perish: life-span, progeny, fame, and wealth.
If one is anointed with oil on the sixth lunar day, the new moon (kuhū), or likewise on the Raktā tithi, out of delusion,
one is deprived of [one's lifespan] by four years for each such instance.
The man who uses oil on the fifth, the tenth, the full moon, the thirteenth, and the third [lunar days]—
"From anointing with it, or from touching it, and likewise from eating it, there shall be an increase for those four: wealth, progeny, strength, and longevity.
— Vṛddha-Manu.
One should avoid food, sexual intercourse, and sleep during the twilight hours, as well as ritual action, Vedic study, giving gifts, and receiving them.
From eating, one incurs disease; from sexual intercourse, one becomes fierce;
from sleeping, one becomes unlucky; and in this state, even ritual action is fruitless.
The student goes to hell and does not obtain the fruit of the gift;
the recipient becomes a sinner. Therefore, one should avoid [studying] during the twilight periods.
Śātātapa says: A new moon day (Amāvāsyā) coinciding with a Monday, a seventh lunar day with a Sunday,
or a fourth lunar day with a Tuesday yields fruit equal to that of the equinoxes (Viṣuvat).
If the new moon day (amāvāsyā) should indeed fall on a Tuesday,
by merely bathing in the Ganges, one obtains the merit of giving a thousand cows.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
Upon the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), there is birth-impurity for all castes;
one must bathe with one's clothes on and avoid the food of those who are impure due to birth.
"Sūtaka-anna" refers to food [given during] the impurity of Rāhu. Likewise:
"The gods are satisfied at the time of contact, the ancestors likewise;
humans at the middle period, and the Rākṣasas at the time of release."

The meaning is that one should perform the rites dedicated to the gods and ancestors at the very moment of contact. Likewise: "Secret gifts, selfless knowledge, and well-guarded austerities—these have infinite fruit."
