Likewise:
"A single cow given to one who is healthy and at ease, a hundred to one who is ill,
a thousand to one who is dying, and those [gifts] are equal to that [gift to one who has died]."
Likewise: gold, a horse, sesame seeds, an elephant, a female slave, a house, land, a chariot, a maiden, and a tawny cow— these are indeed the ten great gifts (mahādāna).
He who, having given, later regrets the gift, and he who, having received, begs for it—
both that giver and that beggar go to hell.
Remembrance means remorse. Likewise:
"In every case, a gift endowed with merit is established even when given to outcastes and the like;
it is especially so when given at the proper place and time, according to the prescribed rule, and to a worthy recipient."
He who, having acquired wealth even from those who possess nothing, bestows it upon the virtuous,
delivers himself— the master of that wealth— from the difficult-to-cross [ocean of existence].
Likewise:
"Only two should be cast into the water with a great stone tied around their necks:
the wealthy man who does not give, and the poor man who does not practice austerity."
Likewise: "The dwelling together with virtuous qualities by one who has turned away from sins is to be understood as 'upavāsa' (fasting/abstinence), which is devoid of all enjoyments."
Flowers, ornaments, garments, perfumes, garlands,
and ointments do not constitute a fault during a fast, with the sole exception of cleaning the teeth.
Likewise, during a fast or a śrāddha ceremony, one should not use a wooden tooth-stick for cleaning the teeth;
indeed, the contact of wood with the teeth destroys seven generations of one's lineage.

Therefore, when fasting with leaves and such, one should perform the cleaning of the teeth; however, at a *śrāddha*, the eater must not do so with a wooden stick. Devala says: "Celibacy, purity, truthfulness, and the avoidance of meat—these four are determined to be the most excellent among religious observances (*vrata*)."
But for women, celibacy flows away through looking at them, touching them, or even conversing with them; it does not flow away when approaching one's own wife during her fertile season.

The meaning here is as follows: from looking at women or the wives of others with one's own natural mind—this is the meaning—the *brahmacarya* (celibacy) intended for the purpose of fasting on the tenth day and other such occasions flows away or perishes; this is the meaning. "Not [by looking] at one's own wife during the fertile period" means that through looking at, touching, conversing with, or engaging in the proliferation of talk regarding domestic affairs with one's own wife, that *brahmacarya* is not destroyed; likewise, it is not destroyed by "transgressing during the fertile period. Transgression (*saṃkrama*) refers to sexual union for the sake of producing offspring; even when practiced during the fertile period for such purposes, the *brahmacarya* does not flow away or perish. The absence of the "flowing away" of *brahmacarya* despite looking at one's own wife and so forth is because, in the context of fasts, it is undertaken under the specific vow known as the "sword-edge vow" (*asidhārāvrata*).
The fast is indeed impaired by drinking water repeatedly, by chewing betel,
by sleeping during the day, and by sexual intercourse.

And in this context, sexual intercourse refers to occasions other than the fertile period. One who observes the religious fast should engage in intercourse at night—at the beginning and end of the day, that is, in the evening and morning—and during the middle [watch]; he must certainly not do so during the four watches of the day.
The inclusion of the word "dharma" is for the purpose of excluding [the performance of] expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*).
On the tenth day, having taken a single meal while abstaining from meat and sexual intercourse,
one should fast on the eleventh day of both fortnights.
Holding an udumbara vessel filled with water and facing north,
the wise man should either undertake the fast or make his formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
The deities are pleased with him, and his desire is fulfilled;
otherwise, mortals of small intellect suffer in vain.
*Audumbara* means copper. Alternatively, the meaning is that one should resolve upon a vow other than fasting:
"Having remained without food on the eleventh day, O Lotus-eyed One, I shall eat on the following day; O Acyuta, may You be my refuge."
From the Purāṇa: Keśava should be [worshipped] in Mārgaśīrṣa; Nārāyaṇa is prescribed for Pauṣa;
Mādhava in the month of Māgha, and likewise Govinda in Phālguna.
In the month of Caitra he is Viṣṇu; in Vaiśākha, Madhusūdana;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, Trivikrama; and in Āṣāḍha, he becomes Vāmana.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, he is to be known as Śrīdhara; after that, as Kṛṣīkeśa;
in Āśvayuja, as Padmanābha; and thereafter, he is considered to be Dāsodara.
In all months indeed, even in the intercalary month (malimluca), there are the enemy of Naraka,
Śrī, Vāgīśvarīkānta, Kriyāśakti, and Vibhūti.
Desire (icchā), joy (prīti), delight (rati), as well as illusion (māyā), intellect (dhī), and greatness (mahimā)—
by means of these powers, she dwells together with the Śuklavāsas goddesses in due order.
Vāsudeva is to be worshipped during the twelve [days] by those who have observed the fast;
likewise, during the dark fortnight, he is worshipped by the twice-born as Śaktiyukta.
Kṛṣṇa, Ananta, Acyuta, Cakrī, Vaikuṇṭha, Janārdana, Upendra,
Yajñapuruṣa, Vāsudeva, and likewise Hari.
The twelfth is Yogīśvara, and Puṇḍarīkākṣa as well;
Rukmiṇī is the beloved, and Prīti is the fifth Śakti and Siddhi.
Likewise, Śrī, Mahimā, Lakṣmī, and Kānti are considered the ninth;
Prāpti and that named Prākāmya, as well as Laghimā, are recorded as the twelfth.
Likewise, standing before the deity at the conclusion of the vow, one should recite:
"O Keśava, by means of this vow, may [the darkness] of the blindness caused by the gloom of ignorance [be dispelled] for me."

Becoming inclined toward grace, be the bestower of the eye of wisdom. O Acyuta, you who are well-pleased with my vow, destroy that threefold sin—committed by me, ignorant as I am, from birth until the dissolution of the body through body, mind, and speech—with my intellect scorched by afflictions; do this thrice with the three steps.
Whatever fragmentary vow has been performed by me, blinded by ignorance,
O Blessed One, may it become complete for me here through your grace.
"O Puruṣottama, just as the entire world is but You alone, so too, O Keśava, may my vow be both fragmented and unfragmented. Thus it is said.
And likewise:
One should not drink water from a conch shell, nor should one eat tortoises or pigs;
on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of both fortnights, one should not eat at all.
This refers to householders who have sons; for it is stated in another Smṛti:
"But on the day of a solar transit (saṃkrānti) during the dark fortnight, or during an eclipse, one who has a son should not observe a fast, due to the loss of sons, relatives, and wealth."
From the Matsya Purāṇa:
On the occasion of the end of a lunar day, at the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), and during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
one who is endowed with sons and grandsons should not observe a fast.
From the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
On the day of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), on Sundays or Fridays,
and on the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*), one should not observe a fast along with its subsequent breaking (*sapāraṇa*).
And so forth. As for the statement:
"He who, out of delusion, discriminates between the two Ekādaśīs—the bright and the dark—becomes a killer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief of gold, and a violator of the Guru’s bed."
Thus says the Purāṇa; and furthermore, in the Viṣṇudharmottara:
"The foolish-souled person who, out of delusion, transgresses the Ekādaśī, whether white or dark, during its fast, does not behold the world of Viṣṇu."
Thus, as for the Matsya Purāṇa: "He who, fasting on the eleventh day, eats on the twelfth—
whether in the bright or the dark fortnight— that is indeed the great Vaiṣṇava vow."

Thus, that [rule] refers to subjects other than householders who have sons. Just as a householder with sons has no entitlement [to certain rites] on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) and so forth, the same applies to the *dinakṣaya* (the loss of a day). This is stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:

"When two lunar-day endings (*tithyanta*) fall on a single weekday, that is a *dinakṣaya*. On that day, there may be bathing, recitation (*japa*), and fire-offerings (*homa*), but not fasting (*upavāsa*) for one in the householder stage."
Regarding the inability to perform the undertaken Ekādaśī vow, the Varāha Purāṇa states:
"When physical incapacity arises while a vow is at hand,
one should have one's lawful wife or a son observe the restrictive rules."

The Ekādaśī vow must not be abandoned even during periods of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (mṛtaka). As it is stated in that very same source: "Even when one has fallen into the greatest calamity, or when joy has arrived, or indeed during birth-impurity and death-impurity, the Dvādaśī vow must not be abandoned."
Likewise:
even during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), a man, having bathed and bowed mentally to Hari, should not eat on the eleventh day; thus his vow is not violated.
Likewise, having eaten on the twelfth day at the end of the period of impurity, and having worshipped Janārdana according to the prescribed rite, one should feed the most excellent of the twice-born.
A man should never eat on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), even if a death has occurred;
however, he may eat on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) after bathing and bowing to Viṣṇu.
Regarding what must be done if the Ekādaśī vow is somehow transgressed, it is stated in the Varāha Purāṇa itself:
"If the Ekādaśī is violated and the Dvādaśī remains thereafter,
one should fast on that Dvādaśī if one desires the supreme state."
"Disturbed" means that the fast has been missed for some reason; it is stated in that very same source that the Ekādaśī vow is obligatory:
"One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
however, one who eats on the eleventh day does not behold the world of Viṣṇu."

He states the fault incurred even by failing to complete a desired vow: "That man who, having properly undertaken the vow of fasting on the eleventh day, does not bring it to completion, goes to hell."
He also says regarding another vow:
"The man who, having undertaken a vow such as that of Ekādaśī out of delusion,
does not bring it to completion, his destination shall be most wretched."
When the Ekādaśī vow has commenced for one who has no son, and a son is subsequently born, it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa what should be done regarding those days on which fasting is prohibited:
"In the event of a prohibition against fasting, one should partake of some food;
one does not incur fault by this, and the fruit of the fast is still attained."
Regarding "the preparation of food," it is also stated in that very same place:
"At night, sacrificial food (haviṣya), or rice-free grain, or fruit, sesame seeds, milk, or water, or clarified butter;
or the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), or even air—each subsequent one among these is more highly praised."
And the night rite must be performed at a fixed time,
when the shadow facing west becomes twice the length of a man;
then one should know it to be night, but otherwise it would not be night.
This is because of the observation of another Smṛti text: "Furthermore, as stated in another Smṛti:
'One should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight;
this is the duty of forest-dwellers and ascetics, while a householder should always [fast] only on the bright fortnight.'"

Thus, even there, the word *gṛhin* (householder) refers to one who has a son, in accordance with the previously cited statement. The term *vanastha* (forest-dweller) and so forth is for the sake of illustration; by this, it includes even a householder who is childless. He states the rule for *nakta* (eating at night) regarding a specific type of day-end (*dinakṣaya*): "When the eleventh [tithi] remains as a mere fraction and the twelfth has reached its end, that twelfth is to be known as 'exhausted' (*kṣīṇā*); in that case, *nakta* is prescribed."
This rule applies specifically to householders who have sons; however, one who is sonless must certainly fast. As it is stated in the Purāṇa:

"When the eleventh and twelfth lunar days extend to the end of the night and the thirteenth day follows, there is the merit of a hundred sacrifices; yet, the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should be performed on the thirteenth day."
If the eleventh day is pierced by the tenth and the twelfth day has come to an end, one should perform the nakta meal there; fasting is not prescribed.

The meaning is this: if on the day of Ekādaśī there is Daśamī, but on the day of Dvādaśī there is no Ekādaśī, and on the day of Trayodaśī there is no Dvādaśī, then one should perform *nakta* (eating at night) and not the fast (*upavāsa*). Thus, it should be considered that these two verses refer to one and the same subject, stated with reference to the distinction between householders who have sons and those who do not. Furthermore, when a full Ekādaśī occurs and continues into the second day, and Dvādaśī occurs on the third day, then one should abandon the first Ekādaśī and fast on the second; as it is said in another Smṛti:

[204] "If even a *kalā* or a *kāṣṭhā* of the twelfth day remains on the following day, twelve twelfth days are lost if the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) is performed on the previous one. Regarding this very subject, if the twelfth day is not seen on the third day, then for a householder the fast is on the previous eleventh day, while for an ascetic it is on the subsequent one. As it is said in the *Purāṇa*:
Where the eleventh day is complete and that same [eleventh] reappears at dawn,
the ascetic should observe the vow on the latter day, while the householder should fast on the former.
Regarding this very subject, he [the Lord] remembers the favor of breaking the fast for an ascetic:

"Where the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) is complete and the same [eleventh day] recurs at dawn, there the merit is equal to a hundred sacrifices, yet the breaking of the fast is on the thirteenth day. Thus it is said.
And so it is stated in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"Where even a single Kalā of Ekādaśī is followed by Dvādaśī, that day is to be honored even at the loss of a full day; it is the most excellent lunar day for ascetics."
Furthermore, that which was stated by Baudhāyana:
"Where the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) lasts for even a fraction of a moment and the twelfth day (dvādaśī) follows thereafter,
there the merit is equal to a hundred sacrifices, provided the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) occurs on the thirteenth day."
Having fasted on the eleventh day when it is joined with even a single digit [of the moon],
and then eating on the thirteenth day while the twelfth day remains, a person attains union with Viṣṇu.

Thus, that [statement] also refers specifically to ascetics (*yati*), because it is heard that the fruit is union with Viṣṇu (*viṣṇusāyujya*). However, the injunction regarding the merit of a hundred sacrifices is intended as praise and is not an injunction for its own sake. Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"On the end of a lunar day, at the sun's passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), and during eclipses of the moon and sun, fasting must be observed; one attains union with Viṣṇu."

Thus, even that [text] refers to a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who is distinct from a householder with sons. Furthermore, it should be understood that within this very same verse, these lines indicating the prohibition of breaking the fast on the thirteenth day refer to a householder who has sons. This is the distinction between the householder and the ascetic (*yati*) in this context. Moreover, as for what is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Where the Ekādaśī is touched by two [days], Hari is present there; one who is devoted to Viṣṇu, whether having desires or being desireless, should observe the fast on that very day."

Thus, that too has the same scope as the preceding [text]. However, it should be understood that for those householders who have sons, the rule regarding this *nakta* (eating at night) applies. That which touches both the tenth and the twelfth is called "double-touched" (*dvispṛk*). As for what was stated by Nārada: "By fasting on the twelfth day when it is joined with the remainder of the tenth, a man here is indeed released from the religious merit accumulated over a year."
Thus it is said: "Where the eleventh lunar day (Ekādaśī) is followed by the tenth,
there shall be the destruction of one's offspring, and after death, one shall go to hell."

Thus, this should be understood to apply when the eleventh day (ekādaśī) occurs on the second day [of the lunar fortnight]. However, in its absence, for householders who have sons, it is said that there is a fast on the eleventh day pierced by the tenth (daśamī-viddhā), while for others, there is no fast. For this very reason, the Mahābhārata states:
"Gāndhārī fasted on [an Ekādaśī] joined with the remainder of the tenth;
her hundred sons were lost. Therefore, one should avoid that [pierced Ekādaśī]."
But when the extraction of the arrow is complete, the fruit is unimpaired;
where there is the Viśalyā Dvādaśī, Hari is present there.
Indeed, by fasting for even that single day, one does not see rebirth in a womb.
For it is so remembered there. As for the prohibition against breaking the fast on the thirteenth day, as stated in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*:
"Having fasted on the eleventh day, the breaking of the fast is prescribed on the twelfth;
one should not do it on the thirteenth, because of the loss of twelve twelfth days."
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "But for him who, having fasted on the eleventh day, performs the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day,
twelve twelfth days are lost."

This and other such [passages] concern the householder (*gṛhin*). Their meaning is: "A householder should not fast on that [Ekādaśī] where the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) on the thirteenth day would occur if the [fast were observed] on the Ekādaśī. For this very reason it has been said:
"The ascetic (*yati*) should observe the later [Ekādaśī], but the householder should fast on the earlier.
As for the rule regarding the breaking of the fast on the thirteenth day, as found, for instance, in the Baudhāyana [text]:
Where even a single *kalā* of the eleventh day exists, provided that the twelfth day follows thereafter.

The passage beginning with "ityādi" refers to the subject of the *brahmacārin* (celibate student) and the forest-dweller (*vanastha*). Its purport is that when there is a conflict between two *ekādaśīs*, the second *ekādaśī* should be observed by the *vrātya* and others. Furthermore, the prohibition against breaking the fast on the thirteenth day (*trayodaśī*) is to be understood as applying when the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) does not extend through the sunrise; it is not intended to forbid breaking the fast at the time of the *trayodaśī* even if that *dvādaśī* exists. If it were otherwise, it would serve no visible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). On the contrary, when there is a conflict between two *ekādaśīs*, the rule prescribing that the householder (*gṛhin*) should fast on one of them serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*), as it provides for the required practice. Thus says Mārkaṇḍeya:
By eating once a day, by eating only at night, likewise by eating only what is unasked for, by fasting, and by giving gifts— one should not fail to observe the twelfth day.

In this context, the injunction for eating a single meal (*ekabhakta*) and so forth should be understood as intended for one who is incapable of fasting or for whom fasting is prohibited. Even for a householder with sons, on that *ekādaśī* day when fasting is forbidden due to the conjunction of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*), a solar eclipse, or a lunar day deficiency (*dinakṣaya*) during the dark fortnight, the performance of penances such as the *kṛcchra* is not prohibited, even if such penances would otherwise be applicable. As Jaimini stated in the *Smṛtimīmāṃsā*:
"On a Sunday, at the sun’s transit, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a householder who has sons must not observe a fast."
"This prohibition of fasting on account of that [occasion] has been presented;
it should not be understood as applying to incidental circumstances, for an ascetic must always observe fasts."

In the phrase "of the fast on account of that" (*tannimittopavāsasya*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the *ekādaśī* because it is the subject under discussion, not to [the days] such as Sunday (*āditya*) and so forth. This is because Sunday and the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*) are mentioned here merely as conditions (*nimitta*) for the prohibition of fasting on the *ekādaśī*, and thus they are not the primary subject. As for the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), since it is impossible for it to occur on the *ekādaśī*, it is a cause for the prohibition of fasting independently. Therefore, the prohibition to be understood here is not one concerning the fasts resulting from the performance of *kṛcchra* penances and the like; for for a wandering ascetic (*parivrājaka*), fasting is eternally unprohibited.
Others, however, read and explain it differently: "On the day of the sun, at the transit of the sun, or during an eclipse of the moon or sun,
a householder who has sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast."

The prohibition concerns fasting on the occasion of [an ordinary] Sunday, not fasting on the occasion of Ekādaśī when it happens to coincide with an unavoidable Sunday and so forth; for it is said that "one must always fast on Ekādaśī. Herein it is explained: the statement beginning with "on the day of the Sun" (*āditye ahani*), which is recited within the context of Ekādaśī fasting, should be interpreted by overriding its immediate context (*prakaraṇa*) since there is no contradiction. Furthermore, the reason—that fasting is obligatory—is not consistent, because even for obligatory acts such as the taking of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup, a prohibition is observed. Moreover, this negative particle (*nañ*) does not function as a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), but rather as an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). This being the case, it forms a single syntactical unit with the injunction to fast; whereas in the case of a simple negation, there would be a split in the sentence structure. Therefore, an exclusion is that which takes up a similar object. Furthermore—

Where the positive injunction is primary and the negation is secondary, that should be understood as *paryudāsa* (exclusion), wherein the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the subsequent word; for example:
"Bring a non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇam ānaya*).
Where the injunction is subordinate and the negation is primary,
this is a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation), wherein the negative particle (*nañ*) is connected with the verb.

Just as in the case of one who eats at a *śrāddha*, this should be explained by means of an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). That is, on an eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) conjoined with Sunday and so forth, one who is not a householder with sons should fast. Alternatively, a householder who has sons should perform that other vow instead of fasting. Thus, since there is no injunction for fasting on that eleventh day when it is conjoined with Sunday and so forth, it is established by the statement "a householder with sons should not [fast]" that [fasting] is prohibited. This is not like the case where it is said, "The initiated one does not give gifts, he does not sacrifice," whereby something already enjoined is subsequently prohibited. Therefore, the former explanation alone is superior. As for what was stated by Hārīta:
When there is not even two *ghaṭikās* of the twelfth lunar day on the thirteenth,
that very eleventh lunar day which is mixed with the tenth must always be observed as the fast-day.
Thus, as it was also said by Ṛṣyaśṛṅga: "If on the day of the fast-breaking (pāraṇā), even a single moment (kalā) of the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) cannot be obtained,
then the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) should be observed for fasting, even if it is pierced by the tenth lunar day (daśamī)."
Thus, as for the Matsya Purāṇa: "The Ekādaśī that is pierced by the tenth day (Daśamī) does not increase on the following day;
that lunar day alone is always to be observed as a fast by both householders and ascetics."

Thus, all that collection of statements prescribing the fast for householders who are childless should be understood in this way; however, for those with children, the rule for eating only at night (*naktabhojana*) has already been shown in this regard. The *Kūrmapurāṇa* states:
"One intending to fast should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils, chickpeas, *koradūṣaka* grain, vegetables, honey, and food belonging to others."
"Upāvatsyan" means "while observing the fast. "Kāṃsya" refers to eating from a vessel made of bell-metal. Consequently, this vow [is observed] on the tenth day. From the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
Bell-metal, meat, wine, honey, oil, false speech, physical exercise, travel abroad, sleeping during the day, and the application of collyrium.
Sesame paste and lentils—these twelve indeed belong to a Vaiṣṇava.
The word "should abandon" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By avoiding bell-metal, meat, food belonging to others, alkaline substances, oil, honey, liquor,
and sexual intercourse on the twelfth lunar days (dvādaśīs), a man merges into the body of the Slayer of Kaṃsa.

Viṣṇu says: "Having fasted on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Vāsudeva on the twelfth day (dvādaśī) with flowers, incense, ointments, lamps, and food offerings, as well as by satisfying the fire and the Brāhmaṇas. Having completed this vow for a full year, one becomes purified from sins. By performing it throughout one's life, one attains Śvetadvīpa. By doing so on both the twelfth days of the fortnights for a year, one attains the heavenly world; by doing so throughout one's life, one attains the world of Viṣṇu. Likewise: "The fifteenth, the full moon, and the two fifth and twelfth days..."
For one year, he remained constantly abstaining from food, with his senses fully conquered.
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the heavenly world.
From the Purāṇa:
"The twelfth days of the bright fortnights occurring in the months of Caitra, Āṣāḍha, Āśvayuja, and Pauṣa—
these are remembered as particularly distinguished by the name 'twelve-day' (dvādaśī) festivals."
Likewise: "The twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is the supreme tithi;
it is the Bhīmasena-dvādaśī, and it is distinguished above all other twelfth days."
Yama said: During the solstices, the equinoxes, and likewise during lunar and solar eclipses,
those who have observed a fast and offer water are liberated from all sins.
Those who, having observed a fast, offer water along with food and other offerings on the days marking the beginning of the Yugas, shall attain worlds of great prosperity.
That day in the year upon which the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky is declared by the experts of the calendar to be the Great Full Moon (Mahāpūrṇimā).
On that day, acts such as giving gifts and observing fasts are proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
likewise so is the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) of the bright fortnight when it is conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa.
The *sāṃvatsara* is one who knows the luminaries (astronomy). In another Smṛti:
"When the moon and Jupiter are in the lunar mansion named after the month, and the sun is fifteen [tithis] from that, and it is the full moon day on a Thursday—that lunar day is called 'Mahāśabdā'."
At Harikṣetra, at the Gaṅgā, at the ocean, and likewise at Naimiṣa,
bathing, giving gifts, and performing śrāddha on Mahāśabda-tithi yield infinite merit.
Now follows the determination of the auspicious Śravaṇadvādaśī:
When the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight,
then that twelfth day is remembered as the highly meritorious Vijayā-dvādaśī.
[209] When the Śravaṇa asterism occurs on another auspicious lunar day as well,
a fire-oblation and fasting performed then bestow the fruit of a thousand horses.
Visits during the Śravaṇa asterism are considered meritorious, equal to Kurukṣetra;
they are especially so when conjoined with Mercury, and particularly on the third lunar day.
If the third lunar day is found conjoined with the asterisms of Budha (Mṛgaśirā) and Śravaṇa,
then acts such as giving gifts and observing fasts on that day are proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
In some places, the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is obtained there by the mere hearing [of the name];
having fasted on the eleventh day (ekādaśī), one should worship Hari there on the twelfth day.
Whichever lunar days (tithis) are declared meritorious due to their conjunction with an asterism (nakṣatra),
one should perform that vow on those very days, with the exception of Śravaṇa-dvādaśī.
The meaning is that what is prescribed for the Śravaṇa-dvādaśī should be performed on the Ekādaśī. And so says the Matsya Purāṇa:
"If, during the bright fortnight on the twelfth day (dvādaśī), the asterism Śravaṇa occurs, one should fast on the eleventh day (ekādaśī) and worship Hari on that twelfth day."

And this should be understood to apply when the twelfth day (dvādaśī) is joined with the asterism Śravaṇa while being untainted by the eleventh day (ekādaśī). However, if it is tainted by that [eleventh day], then the twelfth day alone should be observed as the fast. As it is said in that very same source: "If the twelfth day, touched by Śravaṇa, should touch the eleventh day, that indeed is the Vaiṣṇava yoga known as Viṣṇu-śṛṅkhala."
Having fasted there according to the prescribed rules, a man whose impurities are completely destroyed attains unsurpassed perfection, from which return to worldly existence is difficult to find.

"Untouched by Śravaṇā" means conjoined with Śravaṇā. The word *śravaṇā* is also feminine. By stating "untouched by Śravaṇā," he implies that even when the conjunction with Śravaṇā is slight, it is suitable for the fast on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) and so forth. Thus says the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"A twelfth day touched by Śravaṇā is remembered as entirely most meritorious;
but it is not praised merely to the extent that it is conjoined with it."
Even if it is devoid of Ekādaśī, the Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī should be observed as a fast. As Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"If a Dvādaśī joined with the Śravaṇa asterism is obtained, that Dvādaśī should be fasted upon, and the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) should take place on the Trayodaśī. [210]

This is the procedure for the Ekādaśī vow when it has not been previously undertaken. However, if one begins it, the fast is observed on the Ekādaśī itself, while on the Dvādaśī there is only the injunction for worship. As it is said:
"While the previous vow is not yet completed, one must certainly not undertake another vow.
For one who is unable to perform two fasts, the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa prescribes as follows:
Having observed the meritorious twelfth day (dvādaśī) conjoined with the Viṣṇu asterism (Śravaṇā),
a person undoubtedly attains the merit arising from the eleventh day (ekādaśī).
Thus, having observed the Ekādaśī, one should fast on the Dvādaśī;
a person undoubtedly attains the merit of the preceding fast.
Indeed, there is no fault arising from fasting on the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*) due to the impossibility of breaking the fast (*pāraṇā*),

for one should break the fast only after having fasted on the eleventh (*ekādaśī*) and then fully observed the twelfth. There is no violation of the injunction here, for Hari is the deity of both days.
Thus, according to the Viṣṇuśṛṅkhala view, the performance of the Śravaṇadvādaśī vow is accomplished by means of a single fast alone, as it follows incidentally. From the Viṣṇurahasya:
"On this occasion, the fast is on the twelfth day, while the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) is on the thirteenth;
even though [the latter] is prohibited, it must be performed—this is the command of the Supreme Lord."
Likewise:
"The twelfth day (dvādaśī) in the month of Bhādrapada which is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism is indeed highly meritorious; it is known by the name Vijayā."

One who bathes there according to the prescribed rite shall obtain the fruit of all holy fords (tīrthas). By worshipping Acyuta with devotion, one obtains the merit of ten years. Thus concludes the consideration of the auspicious Janmāṣṭamī.

If the eighth lunar day in the month of Nabhas should coincide with the constellation Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), even if it lasts for only a single Muhūrta, it should be observed as a fast; it yields great fruit.

The asterism of Prajāpati is Rohiṇī. In the month of Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa), one should observe the fast on that most meritorious eighth lunar day which is joined with the asterism Rohiṇī even for a single muhūrta during the day or night.

In this context, the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) is the primary element, while Rohiṇī is its qualification. Furthermore, a continuous conjunction with the asterism is not required here, because of the scriptural statement: "even for a single moment. Nor should this day be rejected even if it is pierced by the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*). As it is said in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"The eighth day conjoined with Rohiṇī should be observed even if pierced by the seventh;
one should perform the fast on that day, and the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) at the end of the lunar day."

The meaning of this is as follows: if on the seventh lunar day (*saptamī*) there is [the asterism] Rohiṇī for only a single *muhūrta*, and the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*) overlaps with Rohiṇī for a short duration on the following day, but on that second day the *aṣṭamī* and Rohiṇī do not exist for even a moment, then the *aṣṭamī* overlapping with the *saptamī* should be observed. However, the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) should take place on the ninth day once the asterism has passed. But when, on the second day, the *aṣṭamī* exists for even a short time, then the *aṣṭamī* overlapping with the *saptamī* must be avoided. Thus it is said in the *Padma Purāṇa*: "An *aṣṭamī* joined with the *saptamī* should be carefully avoided."
When Kṛṣṇā had not yet been pierced, that son of Devakī was born.
Just as the Nandā [tithi] joined with Śravaṇa is avoided when overlapped by the previous day,
so too the eighth [lunar day], even if accompanied by its proper asterism, is avoided when overlapped by the previous day.
If the eighth day is joined with the previous [seventh] at sunrise on the first day,
even for a single muhūrta, that eighth day shall be considered complete.
O best of the twice-born, if on the eighth day conjoined with the seventh lunar tithi there occurs the Rohiṇī asterism,
and it should persist for even a single muhūrta on the following day;
"Then the vow was proclaimed on the second day by Vyāsa and others.

Regarding the phrase "the eighth day joined with the previous [tithi]": if the eighth day were joined with the seventh by even a mere moment (truṭi) at sunrise, that eighth day should not be accepted as the [valid] eighth day. Even if it lasts for only two ghaṭikās on the ninth day, that very [eighth day] becomes a complete eighth day; this is the meaning. The *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* states:
"One should never perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) on the eighth day or under the Rohiṇī asterism."
It would destroy the entire fruit previously acquired through fasting.
The lunar day (tithi) destroys eightfold [the merit], and the asterism (nakṣatra) fourfold;
therefore, one should diligently perform the breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) at the end of the lunar day.
The Nakṣatrānta is radiant. Likewise:
"In Jayantī, a fast should be observed, which destroys even the greatest sins;
it must be performed with great devotion, and Keśava should be worshipped."
The eighth day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, when conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism, is Jayantī.
Thus concludes the determination of the auspicious Janmāṣṭamī.
Mārkaṇḍeya says: When Siṃhāditya is in the fourth lunar day of either the dark or bright fortnight, the moon becomes visible;
this causes a false accusation. Therefore, one should not look at it then.
From the Purāṇa:
"Whoever offers water to Bhīṣma on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Māgha is instantly released from the sins committed throughout the year."
To him of the Vaiyāghrapadya gotra and the Sāṅkṛtya pravara,
who is childless, I offer this water for Bhīṣmavarman.
Having performed the lustration ceremony according to his capacity for the increase of strength,
the king should observe an auspicious wagtail near water, a cow-pen, or similar locations.
The king should not see a red wagtail, nor one that is yellow or black;
rather, he should see one of the full, svastika, or bhadra varieties.
From the Padma Purāṇa:
One should always bathe at dawn during the months of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries;
celibacy and the consumption of sacrificial food (haviṣya) destroy even the greatest sins.
Likewise: he who, at the arrival of the evening twilight on the full moon day, should offer an eight-limbed lamp with sesame oil for one month without interruption.
He who with devotion [worships] the Lord of Śrī correctly is never separated from Śrī;
[he who worships] Dāmodara in the sky during the month of Tulā together with Lohayā.
I offer this lamp; homage to Ananta, the Creator!
Thus ends the mantra for the offering of a lamp. *Nabhasi* means in the sky. Likewise:
"The ninth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Kārttika is for the festival of the ancestors;
on that day, bathing, burnt offerings, and gifts yield infinite fruit."
From the Liṅga Purāṇa:
He who, firm in his vows and desiring liberation, constantly worships Śiva on the eighth and fourteenth lunar days, shall obtain his desired fruit.
Viṣṇu says: The seventh day of the bright fortnight of Māgha is equal to a solar eclipse;
bathing on that day at the time of dawn yields great fruit. [213]
Likewise: On the seventh day of the month of Māgha, at the very moment the sun rises,
bathing there according to the prescribed rite destroys even the most heinous sins.
Likewise: On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Punarvasu,
one who bathes according to the prescribed rules in flowing waters shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
One should worship the fierce one with *aśoka* flowers and drink the buds of the *aśoka*.
Ugra is Śiva.
Those who drink the eight buds of the Aśoka tree on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra under the asterism Punarvasu shall never experience sorrow.
I drink you, O Aśoka, who are desired by auspicious women and produced in the month of Madhu; you who are free from sorrow, make me too free from sorrow.
Thus is the mantra for drinking. Likewise:
"When the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight of Caitra coincides with a Tuesday, one should bathe in the Gaṅgā and fast, so that the state of being a piśāca may never recur."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight coincides with the asterism Punarvasu, it is known by the name Vijayā; it is the most excellent of all lunar days.
O best of beings, if the Puṣya asterism occurs on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight,
or on the twelfth day, then that pair [of days] brings about the destruction of all sins.
Vyāsa said: O Bhārata, having bathed on the third or the fourth day of the bright fortnight,
or on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, why should one grieve?
Whether in the bright fortnight or the dark fortnight, the fourth or the fourteenth day joined with a Tuesday is as meritorious as the new moon day (kuhū) joined with a Monday.
Likewise: "The new moon on a Monday, the seventh on a Sunday,
and the fourth on a Tuesday yield fruit equal to that of the equinox."
If either the Sinīvālī or the Kuhū tithi should fall on a Monday,
a bath performed in silence bestows the fruit of donating a thousand cows.
The eighth day of the bright fortnight, when conjoined with the Moon in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, is complete;
those who observe the religious vows on that day shall never have their prosperity impaired.

The son of the lord of the twice-born is the son of Soma—that is, Budha. Likewise: "Having performed the worship of the deity according to the rules on the second day of the bright fortnight of Jyeṣṭha, one should eat at night; thus one shall obtain the desired land."

*Vidhi* is Brahmā, and his worship should be performed with the *Gāyatrī*. Now, as an incidental discussion, some statements concerning the subject of *khaṇḍatithi* (defective lunar days) are recorded. In that regard, when there is a doubt—since the lunar days such as the first (*pratipad*) are twofold—as to whether the rites that must necessarily be performed on them should be done during those [days] that extend over sunrise or rather those that extend over sunset, certain supporting statements are seen for both positions. As Devala says:
"The lunar day upon reaching which the sun sets..."
That lunar day (tithi) is to be known as complete for the purposes of bathing, giving gifts, recitation of mantras, and so forth.
Whichever lunar day the sun reaches at its rising,
that lunar day should be known as complete for the performance of rites such as giving gifts and Vedic study.
One should not join the remainder of a lunar day after having omitted the day that has arrived;
for one does not offer oblations into ashes after setting aside a blazing fire.
To resolve this contradiction, the *Śivagītā* in the *Viṣṇudharmottara* states:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, second, fourteenth,
thirteenth, and new moon days should be observed as fasts when they are conjoined with the following [tithi]."
In this context, the thirteenth and fourteenth days of the dark fortnight alone are to be taken. Thus says the Nigama:

"The sixth, the eighth, the new moon, and the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight—these are to be honored when joined with the following [day], and likewise the following days when joined with the preceding."
The subsequent ones are higher than those. Consequently, for the sixth and the others, the subsequent [tithis]—namely the seventh, ninth, fourteenth, and first—occur respectively. Likewise:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, and fourteenth of the bright fortnight are to be honored when joined with the supreme [deity]."
The meaning is "by the subsequent lunar day. Likewise:
"Of the pairs [1–2], fire [3], pairs [4–5], elements [5–6], six [6], sages [7], Vasus [8], and apertures [9]—the twelfth is joined with the eleventh, and the full moon with the fourteenth."
[215] Even among the *pratipad* days, the pair of lunar days consisting of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) yields great fruit.
This same pair, when reversed, is a great defect that destroys previously accumulated merit.

In this context, because of the expression "a pair of lunar days" (*tithyor yugmam*), the terms *yugma*, *agni*, and so forth are understood to indicate specific lunar days such as the second and third, and so on. Consequently, the designation of lunar-day pairs should be seen as follows: the pair consisting of the second and third (associated with *yugma* and *agni*), and the pair consisting of the fourth and fifth, which form a *yugma*. This being the case, the pairs of preceding and succeeding lunar days for the tenth, the bright fortnight’s thirteenth, and the bright fortnight’s first must be avoided. Furthermore, the statement of Devala beginning with "the lunar day having reached which... refers to those lunar days—the second and others—that were previously declared acceptable when pierced by the subsequent lunar day; that is the scope in which it should be understood. And as for what was stated by that same author:

Regarding the statement, "The lunar day (tithi) upon reaching which the sun sets," that also refers to those lunar days which are to be accepted when they are pierced by the preceding lunar day. And as for what was stated by Baudhāyana:
"That is the lunar day, and that is the day-and-night (ahorātra), during which the sun has risen."
Even when the waxing fortnight declines toward its setting.

Having restated that the second and subsequent lunar days (*tithi*) are to be adopted when they extend into the [following] sunrise because they are "pierced by another" (*paraviddha*), [the text] then prescribes their adoption even when they do not extend into the sunrise due to being subject to waning (*kṣayagāmin*), provided they are "pierced by the preceding" (*pūrvaviddha*). Furthermore, when it is required what should be done if the rite prescribed for the second day and so forth cannot be performed on the second day etc. as extending into the sunrise in its entirety, but can be performed on the contrary [day], the *Bhaviṣyapurāṇa* states:
"In the case of vows, fasts, ritual bathing, and the like, when there is even a single *ghaṭikā* [of the tithi remaining at sunrise]..."
"That lunar day (tithi) is to be accepted at sunrise, even if it is otherwise [in the case] of rites for the ancestors.
As for that which was stated by Mārkaṇḍeya: "In the bright fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun rises is to be accepted."
In the dark fortnight, the lunar day on which the sun sets is to be taken.

Thus, in this context, the term "bright fortnight" (*śuklapakṣa*) indicates rites for the gods (*devakārya*), because those are generally prescribed for the bright fortnight; and by the term "dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*) are indicated. Regarding rites for the gods, whatever is prescribed for a lunar day (*tithi*) that extends across sunrise should be accepted provided it does not violate the prohibitions concerning the overlapping of lunar days. However, for rites for the ancestors, one should accept the day that extends through the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), regardless of the rules regarding overlapping. As it is said in another Smṛti: "Whether a lunar day extends through midday or not, one should perform the rituals upon it; its increase or decrease is no cause [for alteration]."

And this refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, because that is prescribed for midday. From the statement, "In the case of the *śrāddha* and other rites, [the time] belongs to the afternoon," it is understood that in rites pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*), the overlapping of lunar days (*tithivedha*) is not a fault. For this very reason, Gārgya states the specific overlapping of lunar days that makes them suitable for fasting:
"The eleventh, eighth, sixth, full moon, fourteenth, new moon, and third—these are to be observed as fasts when joined with the subsequent day."

By the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that the other [dates] must be taken as *pūrvaviddhā* (preceded by the previous day) for the purpose of fasting (*upavāsa*). As for the statement from the *Nigama*: "The even-numbered days, those joined with fire (the third), and those joined with the yoke (the sixth)," which prescribes the acceptance of the full moon and the third day when they are *pūrvaviddhā*, that should be understood as referring to rites other than fasting, in order to avoid contradiction with the statement of Gārgya: "The eleventh, the eighth," and so forth. Furthermore, regarding the fourteenth day, only the bright fortnight (*śukla*) day that is *paraviddhā* (overlapping with the next day) is to be honored. As Baudhāyana says: "The eleventh, the eighth, the sixth, and the fourteenth of the bright fortnight..."
"Those [days] joined with the later [tithi] are to be honored; those joined with the earlier [tithi] are superior.

However, the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇacaturdaśī) must be rejected if it is overlapped by the following day, for it is said: "This [overlap] destroys the merit performed on the previous day, which is fraught with great fault."

This is due to the force of the statement. When there is an overlap (*vedha*) with the preceding lunar day (*tithi*) for the second and subsequent days, the sixth and subsequent lunar days necessarily emerge on the following day; therefore, in such a case, the overlap with the *nāga* (the fifth lunar day) and others must be avoided. However, when even a sixth and subsequent lunar day that is overlapped by a very small portion of the fifth and other preceding lunar days is to be accepted—even if optional rites have already begun, they remain mandatory—then, this being the case, words such as "twelfth" or "eighteenth" are intended to indicate the possibility of the sixth and other days being overlapped by the preceding ones, rather than intending their own literal meaning; thus it should be understood. Regarding the phrase "likewise with ten and fifteen," here "ten" (*dig*) means the tenth lunar day (*daśamī*). As for the doubt whether, when a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) is to be observed for fasting, it should be taken as extending until sunset or otherwise, the *Śaṅkaragītā* [provides the answer].
"The lunar mansion on which the sun sets should be observed for the fast, or that with which it is joined at midnight, O Nārada. Thus [it is said].

And this should be understood to apply when the *nakṣatra* (lunar mansion) alone is to be observed as the fast-day, without regard for its conjunction with a specific lunar day (*tithi*). However, where a lunar day conjoined with a *nakṣatra*, or a *nakṣatra* conjoined with a lunar day, is prescribed as an integral part of a ritual act, there their conjunction must be expected to exist continuously from sunrise onwards, with the exception of Rohiṇī, the eighth lunar day (*aṣṭamī*), and Śravaṇa-Dvādaśī. From this, the following meaning is established: a lunar day available at the time of a mandatory rite such as a vow (*vrata*) is to be rejected if it is afflicted by a prohibited conjunction (*vedha*); however, if it is afflicted by an acceptable conjunction, it should be accepted even if it does not extend throughout the entire time of the rite. Both obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites are necessarily mandatory once they have been commenced; indeed, they are always mandatory. But when such a rite is about to be commenced, it should be undertaken only when the lunar day prescribed for the time of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) extends through that period, because the resolve itself constitutes the vow. And that resolve should be made in the morning, due to propriety. Manu says: [Manu 4.95] "One should perform the daily rites in the morning, and those connected with the moon and the stars at their proper times. [Manu 4.96] "The daily rites, the occasional rites, and the rites already commenced are always mandatory; but one who has not yet commenced them may perform them on a day when the moon is full. [Manu 4.97] "One should undertake a vow (*vrata*) on a day when the moon is full, or on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*), or on the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), or on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). [Manu 4.98] "One should avoid the two junctions (*sandhyā*) and the two twilights (*upāntyau*), as well as the day of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) and the day of the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). [Manu 4.99] "One should not eat meat, nor drink liquor, nor engage in sexual intercourse; one should sleep on the ground and remain chaste. [Manu 4.100] "One should not look at the rising sun, nor at the setting sun, nor at the sun when it is eclipsed, nor at the sun when it is reflected in water. [Manu 4.101] "One should not step over a rope to which a calf is tied, nor cross over the shadow of a deity, a Brahmin, or a teacher. [Manu 4.102] "One should not void urine or excrement facing the sun, nor look at one's own reflection in water while impure. [Manu 4.103] "One should not eat food placed in one's lap, nor food placed on a chair, nor food that is stale, unless it is clarified butter or honey. [Manu 4.104] "One should not eat food with only one hand, nor food without using both hands, nor food that is not offered, nor food that is mixed with impurities. [Manu 4.105] "One should not eat food that is sour, nor food that is bitter, nor food that is pungent, nor food that is salty, nor food that is very hot. [Manu 4.106] "One should not eat food that is cold, nor food that is burnt, nor food that is raw, nor food that is cooked by another, nor food that is not consecrated. [Manu 4.107] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of iron, nor food that is served in a vessel made of wood, nor food that is served in a vessel made of stone. [Manu 4.108] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of clay, nor food that is served in a vessel made of lead, nor food that is served in a vessel made of tin. [Manu 4.109] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of brass, nor food that is served in a vessel made of copper, nor food that is served in a vessel made of silver. [Manu 4.110] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of gold, nor food that is served in a vessel made of pearl, nor food that is served in a vessel made of coral. [Manu 4.111] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of glass, nor food that is served in a vessel made of crystal, nor food that is served in a vessel made of mother-of-pearl. [Manu 4.112] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of ivory, nor food that is served in a vessel made of horn, nor food that is served in a vessel made of bone. [Manu 4.113] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of leather, nor food that is served in a vessel made of silk, nor food that is served in a vessel made of wool. [Manu 4.114] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of cotton, nor food that is served in a vessel made of hemp, nor food that is served in a vessel made of jute. [Manu 4.115] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of bamboo, nor food that is served in a vessel made of reed, nor food that is served in a vessel made of cane. [Manu 4.116] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of grass, nor food that is served in a vessel made of straw, nor food that is served in a vessel made of leaves. [Manu 4.117] "One should not eat food that is served in a vessel made of mud, nor food that is served in a vessel made of sand, nor food that is served in a vessel made of ash. One should constantly perform one's own duty as revealed by the Veda without sloth;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.

"Constantly" means without desire for results. "The supreme goal" is liberation (*mukti*). Furthermore, it should be explained that action performed together with the knowledge of the Supreme Self conduces to liberation, in accordance with other scriptural statements. Likewise:
"One should not become attached to any objects of the senses out of desire;
one should withdraw the mind from excessive attachment to these."
Likewise: "One should always perform the Agnihotra at the beginning and end of day and night;
and indeed, with the Darśa sacrifice at the end of the half-month, and with the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice as well."
At the end of the grain harvest, a twice-born man should perform the sacrifice for new grain; likewise, at the end of each season, he should perform the ritual sacrifices;

every four months, he should perform the Cāturmāsya and other offerings; at the end of the sun’s course (the solstice), he should offer an animal sacrifice; and at the end of the year, he should perform the Soma sacrifices.

Since the beginning and end of the day and night are prescribed as the times for the performance of the *agnihotra*, they are deemed suitable; thus, by means of these two, the preceding and succeeding times related to them are indicated and enjoined here. For this very reason, the commencement of the evening oblation (*sāyaṃhoma*) takes place in the afternoon, while its conclusion occurs at the onset of night (*pradoṣa*). For those who offer after sunrise, however, it is when the sun has risen. Similarly, because the end of the half-month is extremely subtle, it serves to indicate the time capable of supporting the performance of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices. It is for this reason that the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* [state]:
"The ends of the fortnights are to be observed as fasts; the beginnings of the fortnights are to be sacrificed to."

The end of the fortnight (*pakṣānta*) is the fifteenth day (*pañcadaśī*); the beginning of the fortnight (*pakṣādi*) is the first day (*pratipat*). In this context, "fasting" (*upavāsa*) refers to the collection of ritual acts such as bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*), the kindling of the fires (*agnyanvādhāna*), and so forth; "worship" (*abhījyā*) refers to the practice of touching the hands and other such rites. This is to be understood as occurring when both the fifteenth and the first days of the fortnight extend across the sunrise and sunset, and likewise when the first day of the dark and bright fortnights possess the non-appearance and full rising of the moon respectively. However, when the full moon rises on one and the same day and is not seen, then the sacrifice (*yāga*) takes place on that very day. As Āpastamba says: "On the day when the moon rises full before [the new moon], one should fast on that *Pūrṇamāsī* day, or [on the day] when it will be full tomorrow. Likewise: "On the day when [the moon] is not seen, that is the *Amāvāsyā*, or [on the day] when it will not be seen tomorrow. Even though fasting is prescribed for the day characterized by the non-appearance of the moon or its full rising by such statements as "having recognized the moon as incomplete or having recognized it as complete, one should kindle the fires," nevertheless, because the sacrifice is the primary element, the time for the fast must be taken in such a way that it is not sublated by the visibility [of the moon] and so forth at the time of the sacrifice, according to the principle: "In case of a conflict between a subordinate part (*aṅga*) and a quality (*guṇa*), the former prevails because it exists for the sake of the latter. Therefore, when the lunar days (*tithis*) are diminished, the fast for the *Amāvāsyā* occurs on the day-night when the moon is not seen or has fully risen. But when the non-appearance of the moon or its full rising extends over two days, or in that same case if the junction (*saṃdhi*) of the fifteenth and the first day occurs during the day, then one should fast on the previous day and sacrifice on the day containing the junction, and not on the following day even if it contains the junction and is joined with the sight of the moon. For by sacrificing on the day containing the junction, the proximity to the junction is favored; whereas if the sacrifice were performed on the following day joined with the non-appearance of the moon, it would be remote. And a sacrificial time closer to the actual junction is superior to one that is remote. The Śruti states: "One should sacrifice with the oblation on the *Pūrṇamāsī* when the junction is during the day; one should sacrifice on the *Amāvāsyā* when the junction is during the day. Indeed, the words *Pūrṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* are well-known to refer to the fifteenth days, not to the first days (*pratipat*). For this very reason, there is another Śruti: "One should sacrifice around the junction (*abhitaḥ saṃdhim*)," meaning on both sides of it. In that regard, if the junction is during the day, the sacrifice is on the day prior to the junction; if the junction is at night, it is on the subsequent day in the forenoon. In all these cases, however, the sacrifice is only in the morning, based on such statements as "Then, in the morning, after the Agnihotra has been offered. Therefore Baudhāyana says: "Regarding this they cite: 'After midnight on the *Pūrṇamāsī*, the moon becomes full. It remains full through the remainder of that night and throughout the entire day until midnight of the following night; this is called the nocturnal junction (*rātrisaṃdhi*). Now regarding the *Amāvāsyā*: on the day preceding the sacrifice day, after midday, the sun begins to take over from the moon—the *Amāvāsyā* begins. It continues through the remainder of that afternoon, through the entire following night, and until midday of the next day; this is the junction. One should sacrifice around this junction. The meaning of this is: the phrase 'regarding this they cite' implies 'they cite the Śruti. 'On the *Pūrṇamāsī*' is the specification of the subject. 'After midnight the moon is filled' means that the *Pūrṇamāsī* period commences. It continues through the remainder of that night and the subsequent entire day until midnight of the following night; this is stated to be the nocturnal junction. Now regarding the *Amāvāsyā*: on the day preceding the sacrifice day, after midday, the sun begins to take over from the moon—the *Amāvāsyā* begins. It continues through the remainder of that afternoon, through the entire following night, and until midday of the next day; then the first day (*pratipat*) begins. This is the junction during the day. Having encompassed this nocturnal junction, one should kindle the fires on the day prior to the junction and sacrifice on the following day. Thus, aiming at this junction during the day, one sacrifices on that morning. Having thus cited the Śruti, he speaks in order to explain the words "midnight" and "midday" found therein: "For the night is to be joined [with the junction] on the *Pūrṇamāsī*, and the day on the *Amāvāsyā*. By this, it is established that the words "midnight" and "midday" in the Śruti are indicators (*upalakṣaka*) of the nocturnal and daytime junctions, and are not intended to be taken literally. To state that these two Śruti passages concerning the *Pūrṇamāsī* and *Amāvāsyā* are for the purpose of illustration, the subsequent Sūtra says: "There are two *Pūrṇamāsīs* and two *Amāvāsyās*; [one should know] each preceding *Pūrṇamāsī* and each succeeding *Amāvāsyā*. The meaning is this: there are two *Pūrṇamāsīs* characterized by the nocturnal and daytime junctions. Among them, the daytime junction is the preceding *Amāvāsyā* or *Pūrṇamāsī*, while the nocturnal junction is the succeeding one. Therein, the preceding *Amāvāsyā* was mentioned, but not the *Pūrṇamāsī*; he expresses that [latter] by way of analogy: "each preceding *Pūrṇamāsī*. The meaning is: one should understand the preceding *Pūrṇamāsī* to be like the preceding *Amāvāsyā*. Consequently, it is established that on this *Pūrṇamāsī* where the junction is during the day, the sacrifice is on the following day and the fast is on the preceding day. Similarly, the succeeding *Pūrṇamāsī* was mentioned, but not the *Amāvāsyā*; defining that *Pūrṇamāsī*, he says: "each succeeding *Amāvāsyā*. One should understand the succeeding *Amāvāsyā* to be like the succeeding *Pūrṇamāsī*. Consequently, the meaning is that one should place the nocturnal junction of the *Amāvāsyā* and the *pratipat* between the fast and the sacrifice. Thus, the view of Baudhāyana is that the proximity to the junction alone is to be favored, and not the timing of the fast as the non-appearance or full rising of the moon.

Some authors of *Kalpasūtras*, however, state that the fast (*upavāsa*) should be observed on the day when the junction (*sandhi*) occurs during the daytime, and the sacrifice (*yāga*) should be performed on the following day; they say this provided that on that [first] day there is no sight of the moon or if its rising is full. In that case, both interpretations of the scriptural injunction (*śāstrārtha*) are equally valid without distinction. Nevertheless, for those who practice according to the authority of a specific *sūtra*, the scriptural meaning for them is exactly as stated in that [particular] *sūtra*, just like the scriptural meanings regarding whether the fire is kindled before or after sunrise (*uditānuditahoma*). Regarding the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, however, a doubt arises when the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) does not fall in the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) of the very day of the fast (*aupavasathya*), but rather on the day of the sacrifice (*yajanīya*): should it be performed on the fast-day itself, or on the day of the sacrifice? On this point, some say: "Therefore, on the previous day [the new moon], the offering is made to the ancestors, and on the following day they sacrifice to the gods; having ransomed this sacrifice from the ancestors, the sacrificer proceeds [with the main ritual]. By the force of such Vedic statements (*śrutivākya*), and by the statement of the *Kalpasūtra* authors concerning the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādhāna*)—"Now, in the afternoon, they perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*"—it follows that it must be performed on the fast-day itself. As for the statement, "[On] the new moon, in the afternoon, they perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*," there the word "new moon" (*amāvāsyā*) is intended as an indirect indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the fast-day; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statements.

That is incorrect. For in the passage, "In the afternoon on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*)," the word *amāvāsyā* does not indicate the day of preparation (*aupavasathya*). Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence for this; for here the meaning of the word *amāvāsyā* is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), and figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not appropriate within an injunction. Therefore, in the statement, "On the previous day, [the rite] is performed for the ancestors," the word "previous day" (*pūrvedyuḥ*) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). It is not a fault to resort to figurative indication for a restatement, insofar as it follows what has already been established by other means. Thus, the word "previous day" indicates the new moon day, since the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is prescribed for that very day. And although the new moon day is complete [in duration], it is understood by the term "previous day" in relation to the day of sacrifice (*yajanīya-dina*). As for the statement, "Then, in the afternoon, they perform the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*," that should be understood as referring to the new moon day when it extends into the afternoon of the day of preparation. The rule, "The offering to the ancestors (*kavya*) is performed on the following day (*bhūte*)," refers to that same subject and does not concern the day of fasting on the pure fourteenth day (*śuddha-caturdaśī*), because that would contradict the direct scriptural hearing (*śruti*) enjoining the new moon day. Therefore, according to the view that fasting occurs on the pure fourteenth day, the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* must be performed on the very day of sacrifice, having carried forth the southern fire (*dakṣiṇāgni*) in the afternoon of the new moon day. However, its sequence with the "placing of fuel on the fires" (*agnyanvādhāna*) is not fixed; even though it is a subordinate element, a sequence is only postulated among those ritual acts that have already been established as qualified by time and other factors. For this very reason, regarding the rule, "On the new moon day, he prepares the altar (*vedi*) on the previous day," there is no retroactive displacement (*apratikarṣa*) of the acts preceding it when the altar is displaced forward. — Manu: [Manu 3.279–281] "The *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is always to be performed after the *Darśa* sacrifice, or before the *Paurṇamāsa* sacrifice, or even independently. One should not give counsel to a Śūdra, nor his leavings, nor what has been prepared for sacrifice;
one should not teach him the Dharmas, nor prescribe a vow for him.
For he who teaches him the Dharma and he who likewise instructs him in the vow—
both go together with that very person into the darkness called "the unrestrained."
A *vrata* is an expiatory rite (*prāyaścitta*). Yama says:
"Both he who teaches a *vṛṣala* and he who is taught by a *vṛṣala* shall dwell for a hundred autumns in a terrible hell."

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not give to Śūdras kṛsara, pāyasa, apūpa, meat, curds, honey, ghee, or a black antelope skin; nor should one give anything prepared, except for what is raw. Āpastamba says: "One should not give the remains of food (ucchiṣṭa) to a non-Brāhmaṇa. Having scraped off the morsels with his teeth, he should place that which adheres to the teeth into the remnant and then give it. The meaning is that having scraped it with the teeth—that is, having scraped off the food stuck to the teeth—he should place that which was on the teeth into the remnant and give it. Likewise, one should avoid anger and other defects that burn living beings. He himself states them: "We shall enumerate the defects that burn living beings: anger, joy, wrath, greed, delusion, hypocrisy, malice, falsehood, overeating, slander, envy, lust, resentment, lack of self-control, and lack of application. In this context, *krodha* is anger toward those who should not be corrected, such as one's father and others. *Harṣa* is pride. *Ropa* is anger toward those who should be corrected. *Lobha* is turning away from the expenditure of wealth prescribed by law, as well as unjust acquisition. *Moha* is lack of discrimination. *Atyāśa* is overeating. *Manu* refers to grief. *Anātmya* is the notion of non-self (*nairātmyabuddhi*). *Ayoga* is lack of concentration regarding what is prescribed. Hārīta says: "One should properly restrain the fires born of the stomach, semen, desire, anger, and wealth. From the fire of the stomach arise all defects of the mind and the organs of action through the pursuit of desires; when touched by these, the purity of being (*sattva*) is lost—so say the teachers. Now, from the male fire arises semen; its emission outside the fertile period is a defect, whereas its emission during the fertile period is explained by the rules of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). That very [fire] is the first of the world because it originates from primordial volition; from the latent disposition (*āśaya*) desire (*kāma*) arises. The fire of affection binds; that desire, characterized by longing, is of many kinds. Overcome by it, one remains unsatisfied amidst worldly desires and sinks into the whirlpool of desire within the cycle of many births. That single fire is desire. For the scripture says, 'Desire is indeed the Lord Vaiśvānara. Its restraint is its regulation; that has been explained. And there are two verses here regarding the song of desire:"
Whether in engagement or in withdrawal, I am the guarantor in all respects;
in all matters, I am according to reality—apart from me, nothing exists.
"He who perceives me as I truly am in all things and in all beings reaches the further shore of the journey; others, who speak according to their desires, do not. Thus it is said.

Overpowered by the fire of anger, one is held in low esteem even by one's own kin, becomes unapproachable and untrustworthy. One does not deliberate upon what ought or ought not to be done, nor what should or should not be said. Possessed by this state, one transgresses against teachers who speak for his welfare and sends himself to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Having experienced there a terrible torment resembling that of the hells, he is born among the animal wombs of cruel carnivores. There, he becomes an object of reproach for all living beings. Eventually attaining human status, he comes to be hated by all people. For anger is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*); its restraint is forbearance (*kṣamā*). This has been explained. Overwhelmed by the fire of greed, one considers oneself superior to those who employ wealth for meritorious purposes. One desires the acquisition of even improper riches. Through attachment to such wealth, he too is born among the animal wombs. For greed is of the nature of darkness; its restraint is contentment (*saṃtoṣa*). This also has been explained. Thus it is said:
The fire of the stomach, the fire of semen, the fire born of desire, the fire born of anger, and the fire born of wealth—
he by whom these are truly conquered is known as one who practices the fivefold heat (pañcatapas).

"He who restrains these impulses— the impulse of speech, the impulse of the mind, the impulse of anger, the impulse of the tongue, and the impulses of the belly and the genitals— that Brahmin they shall indeed call the most devoted to Brahman or a sage."

From *pauṃsna*, meaning from human activity; from *sāhasa*, meaning arising from force. "Of that man" (*tasya puṃsaḥ*). "That [occurs] outside the proper season" (*tad-anṛtau*); "that" refers to that very thing, namely, through such celibacy (*brahmacaryeṇa*). "That very same" (*tad eva*): the first is the act of approaching one's own wife, which is common to both the proper and improper seasons; the second is that same act characterized by the avoidance of the proper seasons. Thus, the third consists of the rule of approaching only during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), and the fourth is the state of having the semen drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretastva*). "Intention" (*saṃkalpa*) is the cognition of the beauty of an object; "desire" (*kāma*) is the longing for an object; "inclination" (*āśaya*) is repeated cultivation [of that thought]. "Destroyed" (*naṣṭa*) means destruction. "Utilizes" (*upayuṅkte*) means he longs for. Viṣṇu.
In this world, there are three gates to hell that lead to the ruin of the self:
desire, anger, and greed; therefore, one should renounce these three.

Āpastamba says: "By renouncing the various outflows (*āsrava*)—the activities of the mind, speech, nose, eyes, ears, skin, genitals, and stomach—one becomes fit for immortality. By renouncing—that is, completely abandoning—the activities of the mind and so forth, which are the outflows that cause attachment, a person becomes fit for, or capable of, immortality, which is liberation. Devala says: "Now, therefore, we shall explain the faults of sin born of mind, speech, and body. Among these, delusion, passion, hatred, pride, greed, intoxication, grief, the sense of 'mine,' egoism, fear, joy, and restless thought—these twelve are mental."
And for them, there arises a threefold delusion, which is the source of all evils:
the triad consisting of ignorance, doubtful knowledge, and false knowledge.
Vijñāna is the independent discernment of all branches of knowledge and their meanings;
it is the non-perception of defects. Knowledge is otherwise than this; it is ignorance.
Wandering between the unwholesome and the wholesome is doubt;
they call it false knowledge, which perceives what is harmful as beneficial.
From unrighteousness arises ignorance, which is nescience (avidyā), and that is doubt;
from both of these, a most wicked form of erroneous knowledge is produced.
From ignorance comes the attainment of suffering; through doubt, one is bound again;
and from false knowledge, the deluded man thus falls into the wombs of darkness.
Manu:
One should not harm one's teacher, a lecturer, a father, a mother, a preceptor, a Brāhmaṇa, cows, or any ascetics whatsoever.
A twice-born man who merely threatens a Brahmin with the intent to kill him revolves in the Tāmisra hell for a hundred years.
Having intentionally struck [another] even with a blade of grass out of anger,
one is born for twenty-one lifetimes in the wombs of the wicked.
If blood flows from the body of a Brahmin who is not fighting,
that man, due to his lack of wisdom, undergoes very great suffering after death.
For as many particles of dust as the blood gathers from the surface of the earth,
for that many thousands of years shall the one who caused it remain in hell.
Therefore, a learned man should never even threaten a twice-born person;
he should not strike him even with a blade of grass, nor should he cause blood to flow from his body.
But by threatening a Brahmin for a hundred years, or by striking him for a thousand, one falls into hell through the intent to kill.
Devala says:
One should not plunge into water naked, nor should one step upon fire with the feet;
one should not smear the body with oil remaining after it has been used to anoint the head.

Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not gather fruits with bricks; nor should one exchange fruit for fruit. One should not be a hypocrite or a deceiver. *Kalka* means hypocrisy (*dambha*), and *kuhaka* refers to such things as the practice of enchantment (*vaśīkāra*); the meaning is that one should not possess such qualities. "One should not learn the language of the Mlecchas. Devala says: "One who is impure should not look into a well, nor should one rub one foot with the other."
Likewise: One should not personally inform others of the death of a friend or their suffering;
one should never cause friends pain through excessive indulgence or out of foolishness.
For out of courtesy, even a poor man endures the suffering caused by a friend. Manu says:
One should diligently avoid whatever action depends upon others.
Whatever is under one's own control, that indeed one should cultivate with effort.
Everything dependent on another is suffering; everything dependent on oneself is happiness.
One should know this, in brief, to be the defining characteristic of happiness and suffering.
Whatever action brings satisfaction to one's inner self while performing it, that one should perform with diligence; but one should avoid the opposite.
That action which is dharma—this is the meaning. Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Even in the midst of dire calamities, one should not desire the property of others;
one should not eat anything that is forbidden to eat, nor should one practice what was done in the past."
One should not recite the names of one's own sages, tutelary deities, or ancestors; this is the meaning.
One should not plunge into water deeper than the knees. One should not look at a naked woman, nor at a man, except...

"By nature" means unintentionally. "He shall not wash one foot with the other. He shall not wipe [himself] with *darbha* grass. He shall not act in opposition to the great multitude. He shall not associate with social circles. He shall not enter into gatherings of groups or kinsmen. He shall not officiate at the sacrifice of one for whom he should not sacrifice. He shall not offer instruction in response to a challenge."
*Anuyoga* is the instruction for study, such as "Recite this section (*anuvāka*) for the sake of receiving wealth.
[The scriptures state: "One should not desire the sale of the *brahman*; one should not say 'Drive the cow' while it is being driven; nor should one speak arbitrarily in the midst of an assembly.
Speaking arbitrarily (*svairavāktva*) means speaking in accordance with the whims of the assembly.
"One who is not appointed should not go to the seat of honor; one should neither give nor accept anything extra.
The word "food" (*bhojya*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "One should not perform the consecration (*saṃskāra*) for those who are insane or mute."
The meaning is that he should not initiate [a pupil]. "He should not enter into association with killing or binding":
