he should not enter into an association, that is, a meeting, for the purpose of killing or binding.
"Not a forest fire"—a forest fire (*dāva*) is a wild conflagration.
"Not the difference between husband and wife; not the source of sages, nor of rivers, nor of great-souled ones."

*Prabhava* means the source of origin. [225] "One should not give liquor; one should not accept it; one should not proclaim what is righteous (*dharma*); one should not conceal what is unrighteous (*adharma*); one should not wear garments in a counter-clockwise direction; one should not scratch the ground; one should not strike with the foot; one should not play musical instruments with the limbs or mouth; one should not look into wells or pits; one should not perform actions loathed by the world; one should avoid everything that is contrary. Hārīta says: "One should not be repelled by the urine or dung of a cow; one should not let loose one's topknot on the road."
Śikhā refers to the hair.

He should avoid rubbing grain, trampling grass, pounding clods of earth, scratching with sandalwood, and playing the lute with his fingernails or teeth. He should avoid self-praise and insults, as well as intoxicants and fermented acids. He should not wear a garland that is red or scentless, except for one made of golden lotuses or water-lilies. He should not kindle the fire with wood that is impure, damp, or rotten. He should not travel during the two times of the fire (at dawn and at dusk). On festival days or in times of distress, if he must travel abroad, he should remain silent during those two times of the fire and mentally contemplate them in their respective directions. Having learned that the oblation has been offered according to the ritual formulas, he should perform the worship with the verse "prati va enā" and then address [the fire].
With this homage I approach you; with this hymn I beg for the favor of the gods.
O Maruts, being pleased, grant us what is known; cast away our malice and unyoke your horses.

One should not tend the fire with blades of *arbha* grass; one should not offer oblations with things unfit for sacrifice. One should give the remains of the offering to a Brāhmaṇa. On the day of the vow (*vratyāha*), one should avoid black gram, lentils, honey, meat, cooked food belonging to others, and sexual intercourse.
The day of the vow is the day on which the fire is formally established (*agnyanvādhāna*).

One should not speak loudly at night; one should not exchange one's upper garment for one's lower garment; one should not engage in slander against the gods, gurus, or Brahmins; nor should one prevent anything being given to them. For thieves who have died are born again as benefactors to their former owners. Therefore, one should neither commit theft nor cause it to be committed; one should not show contempt.
They say that censure is the path of death and deceit is the path of darkness;
integrity, arising from the realization that one is the self of all beings, is the path of Brahman.
Because of sin, or from calamities, or due to the possibility of the transmission of disease, and because success is not seen [thereby], those who maintain separate purity are superior.
One should use a seat, a bed, or a vehicle after placing a barrier between oneself and it;
moreover, Brahmins say that even with one's own kin, eating together in a single group is not recommended.
Vyāsa says: Those men who protect their own bodies from lice, bedbugs, gadflies, and the like that bite them, as if they were their own children, go to heaven. [226]
In the Kālikā Purāṇa: "That man who enters a temple while wearing shoes goes to the terrible hell named Tāmisra."
Bṛhaspati:
Those who sit in a single row and do not touch one another,
having established a boundary with ashes— among them there shall be no commingling.
"By fire, by ashes, and especially by water;
by a door, and by the path around a pillar—by these six, a row is divided. Thus says Hārīta.
The gods protect the pure, and the ancestors protect the pure;
the *rakṣasas* and others who are evil-doers fear the pure.
Seeing a man who has fallen away from purity, the Rākṣasas,
Yakṣas, Piśācas, Bhūtas, and others such as these, assail him in this world.
Knowledge, charity, austerity, renunciation, the performance of mantra-rites and rituals,
auspicious customs, and religious observances— all these are fruitless for one who has fallen away from purity.

For two months one should let the calf suckle; in the third month, one should milk it from two teats; in the fourth month, from three teats; for the remainder of the time, according to the rule and according to its strength.
For children, the practice of fasting, self-restraint, and the bearing of heavy burdens is not recommended;
nor is it for the elderly or the weak, according to the word of Prajāpati.
Nastaḥ is the piercing of the nose. Likewise:
"One should never speak excessively to the elderly, nor even command them;
one should not remain seated while they are standing, for in this way one casts away one's lifespan."
Likewise: Pigeons are auspicious in the home, as are parrots and mynas;
these are praised in the house, as indeed are oil-drinking insects.
When vultures, hawks, pigeons, and bees dwell there as scavengers, one should practice tranquility alone.
These are inauspicious: reviling great-souled beings and never speaking of the secrets of great-souled beings.
One who desires prosperity should not perform the ritual of drinking water at night;
after eating, one should avoid adornment, and roasted barley flour (saktu) should be avoided at night.
A man should always have his beard trimmed while facing either the east or the north, O Indra among kings; in this way, he obtains a long life. Likewise:
One should avoid sharing a bed with a woman who has recently given birth, as well as eating together with her.
One should also avoid food, sexual intercourse, and sleep during the twilight hours.
One should perform ritual acts and Vedic study, as well as giving and receiving gifts;
one should not ride upon cows, donkeys, or camels, nor should one approach a woman during the daytime.
One should not perform bathing, walking for exercise, sleeping, or being naked.

Viṣṇu: "One should not play with any weapons; one should avoid censuring gods, Brahmins, scriptures, or great-souled persons. On the sacred festival days (parvan), one should not cut even a blade of grass. (Viṣṇupurāṇa) A wise man should never enter into conflict with those who are superior or with those who are inferior.
According to the king, both dispute and marriage are appropriate only with those of equal status.
Another Smṛti states:
"One should not engage in the sale, brewing, giving, or taking [of liquor]. Uśanas says:
"One should not mention the lunar day of the fortnight, nor should one point out the constellations.
Āpastamba says:
"The Brahmin who performs his bath, recitation, and [other rites] at a sacred ford (tīrtha) obtains the fruit thereof."
One who achieves success is bound by faults; for him, that very success becomes its own fruit.
Paiṭhīnasi says: "Water is indeed always unfit for drinking during the two middle watches of the night;
likewise, neither bathing nor the ritual of sipping water (ācamana) should be performed."
One should not engage in conversation with those who are intoxicated, careless, insane, or fallen.
"Careless" means one whose nature is characterized by negligence.
One should not climb a tree that has not flowered. Likewise, one should not speak out against someone else when they are being given something.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: One should not go to the place of Bali’s sacrifice, nor to a bathing ground, nor to a cemetery, nor to a prison, nor to a condemned execution ground.
One should not stand for long with knees raised in the inner apartments, a treasury, a gambling house, or likewise a brothel; nor should one step over a calf’s tethering rope.
One should not perform a bath while wearing garlands, nor should one go about with only two garments without a specific reason;
"without a reason" means without a cause.
One should not adopt the dress of a barbarian, nor likewise their language.
One should not yawn or stretch with the mouth uncovered;
one should conceal one's birth star, the essence of one's wealth, and the impurities within the house.
[228] One should not suppress one's impulses, except for the impulse of anger;
nor should a disease be neglected, O Bhārgava, for even a slight one may become death.
One should not perform the *huṃ* [mantra] first; one should not carry a corpse, nor fire or water.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not hold water and fire together. "Together" means in one [hand], namely, both the hand and the foot. Mārkaṇḍeya says: "One who has just eaten should not exert himself; he should avoid serving low-born persons;
he should not step with one foot upon the other, nor scratch himself, nor clean his teeth."
One should avoid reviling the Vedas, the scriptures, kings, fire, and the gods;
likewise, one should not do so while seated on nothing, nor while sleeping, nor while standing.
Likewise, one should always avoid shaving when one has eaten, when one has bathed, when one is angry,
or even when one is eager for a journey or battle.
One should carefully avoid flowers that have blossomed out of season, as well as fruits likewise,
and anything else that appears abnormal.
A portentous phenomenon is like a transformation.
Likewise, the shadow of a wood-apple tree during the day, curd at night, a *śamī* tree,
and a cotton tooth-stick— these take away one's fortune even from Indra himself.
One should likewise avoid anointing the head on the eighth, sixth, ninth, and fourteenth lunar days, as well as on the junctions of the lunar phases (parvan).
In the same way, one should avoid bathing with *āmalaka* fruits on the seventh lunar days;
however, except for the obligatory daily bath, one should not bathe on the tenth lunar days either.
On all new moon days, one should not wear new clothing;
likewise, one should especially avoid [touching] the tails of cows, elephants, horses, goats, and donkeys.
One should cast away from a distance any water that has been touched by a winnowing basket,
wind, the tips of fingernails, or water used for bathing, as well as water from a cloth or a jar.
The dust, hair, and water from a broom destroy previously accumulated merit;
one should not offer the remnants of garlands or ointments to anyone.
Except for deities, Brahmins, and teachers, O descendant of Bhṛgu,
one should not approach a woman who is pregnant, impure, or has white hair.

One should not eat with a woman who is menstruating, nor with one who has already eaten, nor in a place other than the vagina; furthermore, one should not sleep in those places where [such acts have occurred].
A man who has been initiated, having performed the *śrāddha*, should avoid [forbidden acts] with effort.
"Initiated" means one whose initiation has not yet been released; as stated in the *Purāṇa*:
"That atheist who, out of delusion, performs a ritual here without having sipped water (*ācamana*)."
For all his actions indeed become futile; of this there is no doubt.
Śātātapa says:
Through contact with the dust of goats, sheep, dogs, crows, camels, donkeys, owls, pigs, and domestic birds, both longevity and fortune are diminished.
Baijavāpa says:
The dust raised by chariots, horses, elephants, grain, and cows is auspicious; however, that from a broom, goats, sheep, donkeys, and clothing is inauspicious.
The *samūhinī* is a broom. According to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Having washed his hands, a man should take hold of the medicinal herbs and the *amalaka* fruit;
having performed the shaving of the beard, he should wash that [area] again."
Manu says: One should be endowed with auspicious conduct, self-restrained, and have conquered the senses;
one should mutter prayers and offer oblations, for then no misfortune occurs.
One should constantly and untiringly study the Veda at the proper times;
for they declare that to be his supreme duty, while any other is called a secondary duty.
Through constant study of the Vedas, through purity, through austerity,
and by non-injury toward living beings, one remembers one's former birth.
Transmigrating through his former births, he practices Brahman once again;
and through the practice of Brahman, he enjoys the infinite and eternal fruit.
One should constantly perform the Sāvitra and Jāti oblations on the festival days (parvan).

*Jāti* means birth. The meaning is that one should always perform *ājya-homa* (oblations of clarified butter) dedicated to the deity Savitṛ for the purpose of pacifying misfortune on the fifteenth days of both the dark and light fortnights. Regarding the phrase "one should always worship the ancestors on the *aṣṭakās* and the *anvaṣṭakās*," the ellipsis to be supplied is "according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *Gṛhya-sūtra*. *Nityam* means at all times.
Having saluted his elders, he should offer them his own seat;
he should attend upon them with palms joined in reverence and follow behind them as they depart.
One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities; one should also avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, anger, and harshness. [230]

One whose conviction is that "there is no destiny" (daiva) is a nihilist (*nāstika*); his state of being is nihilism (*nāstikya*). Censure is the determination that the Veda lacks authority. Reviling is the disparagement of the deities, such as Brahmā and others; for example: "Brahmā went to his own daughter," or "The Lord cut off the head of Brahmā. Stiffness is the failure to bow due to egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). Pride is egoism. Anger is intolerance. Harshness is verbal cruelty.
"For that man who is unrighteous, whose wealth is false, and who always delights in violence—he does not prosper in happiness in this world."
Even when suffering on account of righteousness, one should not turn the mind toward unrighteousness,
seeing that the wicked who act contrary to dharma quickly meet with their downfall.
Unrighteousness practiced in the world does not bear fruit immediately like a cow;
but returning slowly, it cuts away the very roots of the doer.
If [the fruit] is not for oneself, nor for one's sons, nor for one's grandsons or great-grandsons,
then indeed the dharma thus performed does not become fruitless for the doer.
One should not perform a vow after committing a sin under the pretext of dharma;
by concealing one's sin with a vow, one merely practices deception toward women and Śūdras.
The meaning is that one should not perform a penance under the pretext of practicing the Dharma.

He who, though not possessing the [proper] marks, subsists by making a living through the dress and appearance of those who possess them, takes upon himself the sin of those who possess the marks and is born among the animal species.

Those who belong to the stages of life (*āśrama*) are those who bear the marks (*liṅgin*), such as the staff and so forth. He who, though himself not bearing such marks, subsists by means of their marks—such as the practice of receiving alms and the like—partakes of the sin of those belonging to the stages of life and enters the womb of an animal.
A wise man should constantly practice the *yamas*, but not necessarily the *niyamas* at all times;
for by failing to perform the *yamas* while devoting himself solely to the *niyamas*, he falls.
Purity, sacrifice, austerity, charity, study of the Vedas, restraint of the generative organ,
observance of vows, fasting, silence, and bathing— these are the ten niyamas.
Compassion, forbearance, truthfulness, non-violence, self-restraint, straightforwardness, meditation, serenity, gentleness, and kindness— these are the ten *yamas*.
One should not be proud of one's asceticism, nor should one speak untruth with one's gaze;
even when distressed, one should not revile Brahmins, nor should one boast of gifts received.

"Sacrifice perishes through falsehood; austerity perishes through pride; life-span perishes by insulting Brahmins; and a gift perishes by boasting. (231) "Pride" (*vismaya*) here means self-praise (*ślāghā*). From such passages of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, one should understand the proper conduct (*ācāra*). And all of this must necessarily be performed by a *snātaka*. Thus says Manu:
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
For a man of evil conduct is censured in the world;
he constantly partakes of suffering, being diseased and short-lived indeed.
Even if he lacks all auspicious marks, a man who always observes proper conduct, possesses faith, and is free from envy, lives for a hundred years. (1.154)
Furthermore:

One should not touch cows, Brahmins, fire, or food while impure from eating; nor should one touch cows and the others with one's foot. Here, "impure" (ucchiṣṭa) refers to being physically unclean. Manu says:
Having touched these [impure objects], one who is pure should always touch the vital breaths with water,
as well as all the limbs and the navel with the palm of the hand.

Here, by the word *prāṇa*, the apertures located there—the ears and so forth—are indicated; and by the word *gātra*, the chest, head, and shoulders are meant, since their touch is seen to be a cause of purification in the section concerning sipping water (*ācamana*). And this touching of the *prāṇas* and so forth is prescribed for the purpose of purification.
Furthermore: one should not engage in reviling or striking others; that is, one should neither revile nor strike another.
Regarding this, he states an exception: "One may strike one's son and one's pupil. (1.155)
The striking or favoring of these two is for the sake of instruction, and not otherwise. Thus Manu said:
"One should not raise a staff against another, nor should one strike him down in anger;
however, one may strike both a son and a pupil for the sake of instruction."

A disciple is one who is to be disciplined. The separate mention of the son follows the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*). For this very reason, Viṣṇu employed the word *śāsya* itself, stating: "One should discipline the one to be disciplined; one should strike him. Here, he states the specific rule:
on the lower part of the body, not on the head nor on the chest.
Otherwise, a man striking in a manner contrary to this would become possessed of sin. [232]

One should strike him on the lower part of the body, below the navel; one must not strike him on the upper parts—the head or the chest. Since the exclusion of the head and chest is already established by the restriction to the lower part of the body, their separate prohibition implies that the striking may be performed elsewhere on the upper body for the purpose of correction. For this very reason, Viṣṇu states: "One should punish the offender by striking him only on the back with a split bamboo cane or a rope. Otherwise, even a teacher who inflicts such punishment would become a sinner. (1.155)
One should diligently practice Dharma through action, mind, and speech.

In this context, "with effort" (*yatnāt*) is that which is enjoined; the other [terms] are restated (*anūdyate*). This being so, the word *karmaṇā* (by action), because it functions as a restatement and due to its association with the words *vāk* (speech) and *manas* (mind), refers to the body through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇayā*). Consequently, the meaning is as follows: whatever duty (*dharma*) one should perform with the body—such as the practice of austerity (*tapas*) and so forth; whatever one performs with the mind—such as sacrifice (*yajña*) and giving (*dāna*) and so forth; and whatever one performs with speech—such as the study of the Vedas (*vedādhyayana*) and so forth—one should perform that with effort and reverence, meaning one should not be negligent. For dharma is the cause of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*). Therefore, Manu says:
One should gradually accumulate dharma, just as ants build up an anthill;
neither son, nor wife, nor kinsman remains when dharma alone stands firm.
A living being is born alone, and alone indeed it perishes;
alone one experiences the fruit of good deeds, and alone likewise that of evil deeds.
Having abandoned the dead body on the ground like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, the relatives depart with averted faces; dharma alone follows him.
Therefore, one should always gradually accumulate merit for the sake of having it as a companion.
Regarding this, he states an exception:
"One should not practice even that which is consistent with dharma if it does not lead to heaven or is loathed by the world. (1.156)

One should not perform such acts as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), even if they are prescribed by the scriptures and constitute a duty (*dharmya*), if they do not lead to heaven, do not bear fruit in the hereafter, yield results only in this world, and are despised and censured by the worldly. For while malevolent magic is indeed prescribed by Baudhāyana in certain instances—as in the statement, "One falls [from his caste] if he does not practice malevolent magic against the six [offenses]"—Manu also says:
"A Kṣatriya should overcome his own misfortune through the strength of his arms;
a Vaiśya and a Śūdra through wealth; but the best of the twice-born through recitation and fire-offerings."
"By one's own effort and by the effort of a king, one's own effort is more powerful;
therefore, a twice-born man should subdue his enemies through his own effort alone.

[233] Therefore, practices such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), the slaughter of cows for the *madhuparka* offering and similar rites, the forced labor of widows, and marriage with Śūdra women—though prescribed, these should not be performed because they do not lead to heaven and are loathed by the world, especially in the Kali age. For this very reason, the traditional authorities (*smṛti*) declare:
In the Kali Yuga, one should not perform the Gopashu sacrifice, nor the Satrayaga, nor the Kamandalu rite, nor the Suraprayoga, nor the initiation of a mendicant.
The monk is the Paramahaṃsa. Likewise:

"In the Kali age, one should avoid these five: the unblemished [sacrifice], the human sacrifice, the cow-sacrifice, the water-pot [asceticism], and the procreation of sons through the husband's brother."
For this very reason, there is a traditional injunction regarding a secondary option (*anukalpa*) for the *madhuparka* offering. As Mārkaṇḍeya states:
"Then, for the sake of the animal intended for the *madhuparka*, one should offer a substitute consisting of a vessel of seeds together with gold and indeed along with wealth."
The Lord Bhṛgu has said that in the Kali age, animal sacrifice must not be performed.

In this context, the animal for the *madhuparka* offering is indeed a cow. This is because of the traditional recollection (*smaraṇa*) of the injunction regarding the act of killing a cow in passages such as, "To him, [the guest] with sword in hand said, 'The cow... and because the prohibition against killing a cow is established in the Kali age. || 1.156 ||

[One should not eat] together with mother, father, guests, brothers, paternal kinsmen, maternal relatives, maternal uncles, children, the elderly, the sick, teachers, physicians, dependents, and kinsmen. || 1.157 ||
Having avoided disputes with officiating priests, family chaplains, ministers, wives, slaves, and kinsmen, the householder shall conquer all the worlds.

Having avoided disputes and quarrels with his mother and others, he conquers and enjoys all the worlds, beginning with the earth (*bhūr*). "Female relatives" (*jāmayaḥ*) refers to sisters and those living in one's own household; "relatives by marriage" (*saṃbandhinaḥ*) refers to those connected through matrimony; a "physician" (*vaidyaḥ*) is either a medical practitioner or one learned in Vedic knowledge; a "dependant" (*saṃśritaḥ*) is one who has taken refuge, namely a disciple; "blood relations" (*sanābhayaḥ*) are those of the same *sapinda* lineage; the others are well known. Manu, however, states that for one who avoids the aforementioned disputes, there is the destruction of all sins, and for one conquered by teachers and others, there is the fruit of conquering the world of Brahmā and the rest:
"With children, the elderly, physicians, kinsmen, relatives by marriage, and blood relations..."
By one's mother and father, by sisters, by a brother, by a son, and by a wife.
One should not engage in a dispute with one's daughter or with the group of servants.
Abandoning these and disputes, one is liberated from all sins;
and by conquering these, a householder conquers all these worlds.
And here, the phrase "by these" refers to the intention of the teachers who will be mentioned later:
"The teacher is the lord of the world of Brahmā; the father is the master in the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is the lord of the world of Indra; and the officiating priests are the lords of the world of the gods."

Sisters-in-law are the kinsmen of the world of the Apsarases; paternal relatives are the kinsmen of the world of the Viśvedevas; and one's mother and maternal uncle are the kinsmen of the worlds of the Waters and the Earth.
The young, the old, the emaciated, and the afflicted should be known as lords of space (ākāśa).
An elder brother is equal to a father; a wife and son are one’s own body.
One's own shadow is one's own group of servants, but a daughter is the ultimate object of pity; therefore, when reviled by these, one should always endure it without distress.
An object of compassion; free from fever, free from burning. 1.157.
Moreover:

"One should not bathe in the waters of others without having removed five lumps [of earth]. Without removing—that is, without casting outside—five lumps from the waters belonging to another, one should not perform a bath therein. By this, it is implicitly prescribed that even when bathing in the waters of others, one must first remove the lumps of earth in the event that the water required for the primary constituent parts of the bath (to be described later) is unavailable. However, from those waters which have been released by their owner for the benefit of others in accordance with the scriptures, lumps of earth are not to be removed, because they do not belong to another. On this point, Manu says:
One should never bathe in water-reservoirs belonging to others;
for by bathing there, one becomes tainted with a portion of the evil deeds of the reservoir’s builder.
Baudhāyana says: A wise man should never bathe in a body of water dug by another,
nor in a well without having first removed five or seven lumps of earth.
Now he states the primary waters suitable for the constituent parts of the bath:
"One should bathe in rivers, in natural ponds dug by the gods, in lakes, and in pools. (1.159)

One should bathe in rivers and the like. A "river" (*nadī*) is a flowing stream. That which is remembered as having been "dug by the gods" (*devakhāta*) is a reservoir. "River water" refers to a body of water with an uninterrupted flow; a "lake" (*hrada*) is stationary, natural water. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), pools, springs, and so forth are also included. Thus says Manu: "One should always perform one's bath in rivers, in reservoirs dug by the gods, in lakes, in ponds, in springs, and so forth."
Kātyāyana describes the nature of a *garta* (pit): "Those whose course does not extend for eight thousand bows, and which do not carry the designation 'river,' are proclaimed to be *gartas*. [235]

The meaning is that those waters do not flow with the sound of a river. A small flow of water from a mountain or similar source is a *prasravaṇa*. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya states the sequence according to their excellence: "Water situated on the ground is more meritorious than [water] drawn up; after that, spring water; even more meritorious than that is lake water; and better than that is said to be river water."
Therefore, the water of a sacred ford is meritorious, but the body is meritorious in every respect.
Yogayājñavalkya states:
When abundant and very pleasing water is available,
a twice-born man should not bathe in a small amount of water, nor should he abandon a river to bathe in an artificial pool.
Rivers that do not flow to the ocean yield the fruit of a three-night fast;
those that flow to the ocean yield the fruit of a fortnight; and the lord of rivers (the ocean) yields the fruit of a month.

"Yielding the fruit of three nights" means yielding the fruit of a three-night fast. The same applies to a fortnight and a month as well. Incidentally, something regarding the subject of bathing in the ocean and so forth is stated here. Regarding this, another Smṛti says:
"The Aśvattha tree and the ocean should never be touched;
one may touch the Aśvattha on Saturdays and the ocean on festival days."
Manda is Saturn. Parvan refers to the new moon and the full moon. Likewise:
"One should not touch the lord of rivers (the ocean) on any occasion other than a parvan, except at the Bridge of Sindhū, the Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, or Puruṣottama."
Likewise, having begun the ritual actions such as bathing and the *śrāddha* ceremony according to the rules,
one should consecrate the skin with mantras and here cast seven stones upon it.
O you who were born from Pippalāda and who cause terror to the world,
this stone has been given by me to you as a provision for food.
Vyāsa said: "Agni is your source and the earth is your body; Viṣṇu is the placer of your seed and the navel is immortality.
Speaking this truthful word, O Pāṇḍava, one should then plunge into the lord of rivers."
Whatever sin one has committed anywhere throughout hundreds of thousands of births,
one is liberated from all those sins simply by bathing thus in the salt waters.
Otherwise, O best of the Kurus, the great ocean— the lord of waters and of divine origin— must not be touched even by the tip of a blade of kusha grass, O son of Kunti.
Another Smṛti states:
"One should perform both shaving and fasting at all sacred fords. Marīci says:
Between the months of Nabhas and Nabhasya, all rivers are in their menstrual flow;
one should not perform bathing, nor the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors, in them.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
The Gaṅgā, daughter of the Sun, the Sarasvatī born from the Plakṣa tree,
and those others known as rivers, are not overcome by passion.
The Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra is born from the Plakṣa tree; this is according to another Smṛti:
"The Kālindī, the Gomatī, and the Gaṅgā were created by the gods as purifiers;
because of their commonality and their possession of [purifying] qualities, dust does not overcome them."
The city:
The Gaṅgā, the Dharmadrava, the meritorious Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī—
all are free from the contact of dust within and are pure at all times.
Gārgya says:
When the water has receded, bathing in a river must be avoided by the twice-born; likewise, one should avoid the washerman’s landing-place and the area within ten cubits above it.
A marketplace, a flow against the current, the mixing of dust with water, and the settling of river-water on a road—
these do not defile the Ganges, for it is itself a stream of dharma.
One should not bathe in those small streams on earth that dry up in the summer, nor until the appearance of clouds in the rainy season.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"However, the first surges of water from a river are not to be taken, nor are waters that have been agitated by someone, or those emerging from a bathing place on the bank."
The foremost [impurities] are those of new [substances]. And so it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Goats, cows, buffaloes, and Brāhmaṇa women who have recently given birth, as well as rainwater that has reached the ground, become pure after ten nights."

A *tīrtha* is a path for descending into water. Vyāsa says: One should avoid water that has flowed away from a river, water that has been bypassed by a river, and water that has returned after having gone away.
A man should always avoid bathing in a river after sunset;
one who knows the Dharma, having bathed in a river, should not praise another river.
One should not bathe after having hidden oneself, nor at a sacred bathing place within the water;
one should not urinate in a wooden trough, nor should one cross a river while intending to bathe.

The meaning of this is as follows: that which has fallen from a river—having emerged from it and then become separated from it—and proceeds toward a confluence with that same river, yet fails to join it; that which is thus abandoned by it, moving in a whirlpool, coming and going; or that which is hidden by means of a cloth or similar object; and one should not bathe at one sacred ford (*tīrtha*) with water from another sacred ford. 1.159.
Furthermore: one should avoid the beds, seats, gardens, houses,
and vehicles of others that have not been given.

One should avoid the beds, seats, and other such things belonging to another that have not been given by them; the meaning is that one should avoid making a livelihood from them. "Garden" (*udyāna*) means a grove (*upavana*). The rest is well known. Regarding this, Manu says: "He who uses his carriage, bed, seat, well, garden, or house without them being given shall incur a fourth part of the sin."

Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the observances of the *snātaka*, in this legal compendium (*nibandha*) on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara race.
Now begins the sixth chapter on edible and non-edible food, as well as what is fit and unfit to be consumed, in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary.
Now he begins the section concerning what may and may not be eaten, and what may and may not be consumed. In that regard, he states those things which must not be eaten:
"One should not eat the food of one who maintains no sacred fire, except in times of distress. (1.160)

Even though one possesses the qualification [to perform rites], one should not eat the food of one who has not maintained the Śrauta and Smārta fires, nor of one who has abandoned the sacred fires, except in times of distress. (1.160)
[The food] of misers, bound thieves, eunuchs, actors, flute-players, those accused of crimes, usurers, courtesans, and those initiated into a guild; 1.161.
One should not accept food from physicians, the sick, the angry, unchaste women, the intoxicated, or enemies;
nor from the cruel, the fierce, the outcaste, the apostate, the hypocritical, or those who eat the leavings of others. (1.162)

[The food] of those whose wives have no husbands, of goldsmiths, of those who have conquered their villages by means of their wives, of those who sacrifice for the village, of those who sell weapons, of blacksmiths, weavers, and those who subsist by keeping dogs; 1.163.
[Gifts] from a cruel man, a king, a dyer, an ungrateful person, one who lives by slaughter, a washerman, a vintner, and those who live in the house of a paramour; 1.164.
One must not eat the food of these, nor likewise that of a seller of *soma*.

[238] One must not eat the food of misers and others, nor that of a seller of *soma*. A miser (*kadarya*) is one who, out of greed, neither consumes his own existing wealth nor gives it away. As it has been said:
He who, out of greed, causes suffering to himself, his religious duties, his children,
his wife, his parents, and his servants, is known as a miser (kadarya).

"Baddha" means one who is bound in fetters. "Caurya" is a thief. "Klība" is a eunuch. "Raṅgāvatārī" refers to actors and the like. "Vaiṇa" is one who lives by playing the lute (*vīṇā*) or one who lives by cutting bamboo. "Abhiśasta" is one accused of having committed a sinful act. "Vārdhuṣya" is living on prohibited interest; by this term, one who possesses that [profession] is indicated. Alternatively, a usurer (*vārdhuṣika*) is one who practices self-praise and disparagement of others. Thus says Viṣṇu: "He who reviles another's livelihood and praises his own qualities is indeed called a usurer, and is censured among those who discourse upon the Veda."

A *gaṇikā* is a prostitute (*veśyā*). A *gaṇa* is a group (*saṅgha*). Their food is not to be eaten by another. A *dīkṣī* is one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*); his food is not to be eaten prior to the offering of the omentum (*vapā*) of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*). Thus says the Śruti: "One should eat only when the omentum has been offered. Āpastamba, however, states: "Even before the offering of the omentum, that which remains after the substance intended for the sacrifice has been set aside must be eaten even by the initiated. An initiated person is one for whom the purchase of the King (Soma) has been performed. It is only upon the completion of the Agni-Soma sacrifice, when the omentum has been offered, that the food of the initiated may be eaten. The Brāhmaṇa text states: "When the substance has been designated for the sake of the sacrifice, they may eat from the remainder. A physician (*cikitsaka*) is one whose livelihood is medical practice; this includes both a proper physician and others who are not. An afflicted person (*ātura*) is one suffering from disease. An angry person (*kruddha*) is one who is provoked. An unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*) is an adulteress. One intoxicated (*matta*) is so by wealth and the like, or by liquor, if he is other than a Brāhmaṇa. An enemy (*vidviṣ*) is a foe. A cruel person (*krūra*) is one whose anger is persistent. A fierce person (*ugra*) is one skilled at inflicting pain on others, or one born of a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother. An outcast (*patita*) is one who has committed a mortal sin such as killing a Brāhmaṇa; he is distinct from a thief, as the latter is included under the term "thief" (*caura*). Alternatively, the term "thief" refers to someone other than an outcast. A *vrātya* is one who has fallen away from the *Sāvitrī* initiation. A hypocrite (*dāmbhika*) is one who performs religious duties for the purpose of fame, gain, and the like. One who eats the leavings of others (*ucchiṣṭabhojī*) is habituated to eating the remnants of others' meals. A woman without a hero (*avīrā*) is one devoid of husband and sons. A goldsmith (*svarṇakāra*) is well known. One conquered by a woman (*strījita*) is one dependent on a woman. A village priest (*grāmayājaka*) is one who officiates for many. A seller of weapons (*śastravikrayī*) is one who lives by selling swords and the like. A blacksmith (*karmāra*) is an ironworker. A weaver (*tantuvāya*) is a maker of woven cloth or one who mends torn garments. One who lives like a dog (*śvavṛttavān*) is a servant. Or, "one whose conduct is like that of dogs" (*śvavṛtī*) means one who behaves like a dog, namely a hunter; Gautama says: "A hunter is one who hunts with arrows. Viṣṇu, however, says that the food of a hunter who hunts with arrows is not to be avoided: "The food of a hunter who hunts with arrows is not to be rejected. A pitiless person (*nṛśaṃsa*) is a killer. A king (*rājā*) is a sovereign, not necessarily a Kṣatriya. A washerman (*rajaka*) is one who dyes clothes and the like. An ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*) is one who destroys a favor received. One who lives by slaughter (*vadhajīvī*) is one who lives by killing living beings. A laundryman (*celadhāva*) is a washer of clothes. One who lives by liquor (*surājīva*) is one whose livelihood is liquor. One whose house contains a paramour (*sahopapativeśmā*) is one whose home is shared with the wife of another. A seller of Soma (*somavikrayī*) is a seller of the Soma plant.
In this context, something else is also stated from the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The food of a Brāhmaṇa invited by a Śūdra is unfit to be eaten; likewise, the food of a Śūdra invited by a Brāhmaṇa is unfit to be eaten."

Paiṭhīnasi states: "The food of an astrologer (*sāṃvatsara*), a bell-ringer (*ghāṇṭika*), and a village headman (*grāmakūṭa*) is poison. Likewise, the blood of a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivitti*), an elder brother whose younger brother marries first (*parividdha*), one whose offspring has been pierced [by a weapon], the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, the husband of a *didhiṣū*, and the son of a remarried woman (*punarbhū*) is blood. An astrologer is one who lives by the stars. A bell-ringer is one whose craft is the bell. As it is said: "Bell-ringers (*ghāṇṭikāḥ*) are those craftsmen of bells at the time of awakening kings. A village headman is well known. The definitions of the *parivitti* and others are to be observed in the section on *śrāddha*. One whose offspring has been pierced is one whose male organ has been pierced. Yama says:
One who lives by the wheels [of a cart], a musician, gamblers, thieves,
a liquor-seller, one who lives off his wife, and those who teach or perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
A potter, a painter, a usurer, and a seller of leather.
The *cakropajīvī* is a cartwright; the *gāndharva* is a singer; the *dhvajī* is a seller of liquor. Likewise:

just as water that was undrinkable when flowing out [of a source] becomes drinkable once it has entered a river, so too food and drink that have come according to rule do not become defiled when passed through the vessels of the twice-born.
The exits are the channels for the flow of water from the streets.

One may always eat at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, but at that of a Kṣatriya only on the festival days (parvan), and at that of a Vaiśya only during the [agricultural] seasons; never, however, at the house of a Śūdra.
And likewise during customary festivals;
as well as the food of one supported by a king, the food of a thief, and likewise food during the periods of birth-impurity or death-impurity— such food causes even one who stands in heaven to fall.
He who eats the food of one who is arrogant, foolish, of wicked conduct, evil-minded,
or lacking in faith, is indeed a killer of an embryo (bhrūṇahā).
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "One should regard Viṣṇu as a son-in-law and should not provoke his anger;
however, one should certainly not eat in the house of a man whose daughter remains childless."
A Kṣatriya may indeed engage in coming and going with a woman through the Gāndharva rite.
But one should never eat after giving away a daughter who was to be given as a Brāhma gift;
for he who eats out of delusion shall dwell in hell, feeding on pus.
A woman wedded according to the four types of marriage beginning with the Brāhma is one given by the Brāhma rite (brāhmadeyā). Vasiṣṭha says:
"One may eat the food of a person who is full of faith, especially even that of a thief;
but never the food of one who performs many sacrifices for others, nor of one who initiates many [into the Veda]."

In the context of what is unfit to be eaten (*abhojya*), Āpastamba states: "He who avoids all [such food] and he who eats all kinds of food. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should avoid the food of those who are frightened, censured, weeping, wailing, reviled, sneezing, eating, astonished, insane, or expelled, as well as the food of a king and a domestic priest. Regarding the consumption of the food of a miser and others, Manu prescribes an expiation:
"Having unintentionally eaten the food of any one of these, one should fast for three days;
having eaten it intentionally, or having consumed semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the *Kṛcchra* penance."

The word *kṛcchra* (hardship) is used here in the sense of *atikṛcchra* (extreme hardship), according to the statement of Śaṅkha: "Among these, [the rule applies] to the eating of food" (*atikṛcchraḥ*). (1.161–164)
That which has been smelled by a cow, that which is the leavings of a bird, and that which has been intentionally touched with the foot—|| 1.165 ||

Nor [should one eat] the food of backbiters, liars, and likewise of usurers and bards; nor meat that has not been honored, nor meat prepared in vain, nor that which is infested with hair or insects. (1.166)

One should avoid food that is fermented, stale, or leftover; food touched by a dog, looked upon by an outcast, touched by a woman in her courses, or food whose preparation has been announced; and likewise, food obtained through barter.

One should avoid food smelled by a cow and the like, as well as meat not prepared for a ritual purpose (*vṛthāmāṃsa*). A *śakuna* is a bird. A *piśuna* is a slanderer who points out faults. An *anṛtī* is a liar. A *cākrika* is an oil-presser; according to the traditional distinction found in the phrase "the accused, the outcaste, the oil-presser, and the cartwright," he may also be a cartwright (*śākaṭika*). A *vandī* is a panegyrist. *Anarcita* refers to that which is given with contempt. *Vṛthāmāṃsa* is meat not intended for occasions such as a *śrāddha*. *Śukta* is food that has turned sour over time. *Paryuṣita* is food prepared on the previous day. *Ucchiṣṭa* is what remains after someone has eaten. *Saṃghuṣṭa* is food announced by crying out, "Who will eat? *Paryāyānna* is food taken in rotation, such as, "On this day one must eat at his house, and on that day at his. If the reading is *paryācānta*, it means food where the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) has been bypassed or neglected. The mention of the dog is illustrative of crows and other such animals. The mention of the outcaste (*patita*) includes *caṇḍālas* and others. (From the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*).
That which is defiled by its origin, defiled by its preparation, corrupted by the time [of its offering],
defiled by association, and that which is naturally loathsome by its very nature.
He states the examples of those things that are defiled by their very nature and so forth:
"One should avoid garlic, leeks, onions, mushrooms, eggplants, bamboo shoots, and bottle gourds— these are defiled by their nature."
One should not eat that which is defiled by action— that which has been seen separately by those who have fallen from their caste—
and that which is known to be defiled by time, namely, that which is stale or has remained for a long duration.
Among the various preparations, curd is permitted as food, with the exception of honey;
likewise, that which has been touched by liquor or garlic, or that which is mixed with colostrum and the like, is not desired.
For this is defiled by association; one should treat it like the leavings of a Śūdra.
Indeed, the nature of the Śūdra's leavings should be understood as previously demonstrated regarding Śūdras.
But when doubt arises regarding the food in the heart,
it should be known as *sahṛllekha*, while its natural state is *purīṣa*.
For it is shown by the example that "that which is corrupted in taste is so because of a defect in the flavor," as in the case of milk-rice,
milk-cakes, and the like, [if consumed] on that very same day.

Regarding the *alābu* here, one is the long gourd (*dīrghālābu*) and the other is its opposite. This is because the long variety is fit for the *śrāddha*, whereas the short variety—being naturally defective and thus as censurable as the onion—is unfit to be offered at a *śrāddha*. For this very reason, it is said: "The long gourd, the *grīvaka*, the small *karkarī*, and likewise the *trapusī* [are fit]. Thus, the long gourd is fit for the *śrāddha*. As for the other, Hārīta states that it is unfit for the *śrāddha*: "One should avoid pippalī, *samuka*, *mṛṣa*, *bhūstṛṇa*, *asurī*, mustard, *surasa*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *alābu*, *vārtāka*, *pālakyā*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, safflower, *piṇḍamūlaka*, and buffalo milk. Thus, it is not to be offered at a *śrāddha*. (Hārīta)
One should never eat onions, garlic, fermented liquids, exudations from trees, kudhūndu, white eggplant, or kumbhāṇḍa.
A *kumbhāṇḍa* is a particular fruit resembling a pomegranate. Devala says:
"A wise man should not consume seeds except in the event of illness;
for by eating them, he would destroy the infinite fruits that come from those seeds. [242]

Vasiṣṭha: "The leavings of one who is not one's teacher (*aguru*) are not to be eaten; likewise, one's own leavings and food defiled by leavings. Āpastamba: "Food defiled by one who is impure (*aprayata*) becomes impure, but it is not necessarily unfit for consumption. In the case of food in which there is hair, or something else unclean (*amedhya*), or which has been touched by unclean things, or where there is an insect that frequents unclean places; or where there is a piece of mouse-dung, or it has been stepped on by a foot, or touched by a garment, or seen by a dog, or touched by the hem of a garment, or brought at night by a female slave, or where one eats while a Śūdra touches him, or among those eating in the same row who are unworthy, or where one gives his leavings without rising or sips water, or where they give food after having reviled [the recipient], or where food is smelled by humans or other unclean things—[these are cases of impurity]. The meaning of this is: food touched by an impure person becomes impure, but it is not, however, unfit for consumption. Making an impure food item rest upon fire, or sprinkling it with water, or touching it with gold or the mouth of a goat, renders it pure again. But food touched by an impure Śūdra is indeed unfit for consumption. "Mouse-dung" (*mūṣakalā*) means mouse-excrement. "Mūṣa" means a mouse; food in which there is its limb, such as a tail, is unfit for consumption—this completes the sense of the sentence. "Touched by the hem of a garment" (*sicā*) means touched by the edge of a cloth; "brought at night by a female slave" (*dasyā*) means brought by a male slave (*dāsena*). Devala: [follows].
One should not consume food that has been licked by a dog, a cat, a crow, a cock, or a mouse, for it is entirely impure in every respect.
One should also avoid food that, though pure, has been defiled by flies, worms, or small insects,
or even by hair, body hair, or nails.
From the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If a server is touched by a Śūdra who is impure from eating remnants,
he shall not consume anything whatsoever that he might offer while holding it in his hand."
Likewise:
"One should not eat what remains from the meal of a Śūdra, even if it is situated in a vessel."—
Vasiṣṭha.
Whether it be ghee or oil, a Brahmin must not consume that which has flowed from his nails;
Yama has declared that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow's flesh.
Likewise: "Fats, salt, and condiments that have been given with the hand do not reach the giver; rather, the eater consumes the sin."
Therefore, one should give with something intervening, such as a blade of grass or even a piece of wood;
one should never give directly with the hand, nor ever with an iron vessel.
In the Brahmapurāṇa: One should not eat food given by a Śūdra with only one hand,
nor ghee, oil, salt, water, or milk-rice (pāyasa).
And almsfood, even if placed directly into one's hand, should not be accepted from just anyone anywhere.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not eat food that has been sold, nor what has been cooked twice, nor what is stale, except for meat preparations (rāga), sacrificial porridge (caru), side-dishes (ṣāḍava), curd-mixture (dadhi), molasses, curds, and products made from wheat or barley flour. Śaṅkha says:
"Cakes, roasted flour, parched grains, buttermilk, curds, ghee, and honey—these may be eaten when purchased, provided they have not been used as a coating for the vessel."
Āpastamba says:
Only two types of ascetics are to be fed—the student and the householder.
The food of a wandering mendicant (muni) is not to be eaten, as is the case with all those who bear sectarian marks (liṅgin).
He who eats during a birth-impurity or a death-impurity, when an eclipse of the moon or sun has occurred,
or while sitting in the shadow of an elephant, shall not become a man again.
He speaks for the purpose of prohibiting the consumption of food from specific types of Śūdras:
"Among Śūdras, the slave, the cowherd, the family friend, and the artisan are those whose food may be eaten, as well as the barber and he who offers himself [as a servant]. (1.168)

The locative case in "among Śūdras" (*śūdreṣu*) is used for specification (*nirdhāraṇa*). Therefore, among Śūdras, those such as slaves (*dāsa*) and others are whose food may be eaten, but not other Śūdras. A slave (*dāsa*) is one who has been purchased and so forth; a cowherd (*gopāla*) is the protector of cows; a farmer (*kula*) is one who cultivates his own field. And thus says Devala:
"A slave, a barber, a cowherd, a potter, and a cultivator—these five born of the Śūdra womb are whose food may be eaten even by Brāhmaṇas."

Alternatively, a *kulamitra* is a friend of one’s family; "family" (*kula*) means lineage, and "friend" (*mitra*) is well known. An *avasūrī* is a fellow cultivator who works together through mutual enterprise. A barber (*nāpita*) is well known. And that Śūdra who, even though not purchased, offers himself—through actions of speech, mind, and body—to a twice-born man and gives himself [to him as a servant]; the food of those whose servants and so forth he is may be eaten by him alone. Hārīta says:
"A family friend, a son of the family, one who gives alms, a pupil, a close friend—he whose gain brings joy and who becomes a protector in times of fear."
These are the Śūdras whose food may be eaten when their minds are found to be pure.

A family is a cultivator; his son is a *kulaputra* (son of noble family). A friend is a companion. It is perceived that he becomes gracious. Regarding the case of a Śūdra other than those previously mentioned, Manu said:

"A learned twice-born man who does not perform *śrāddha* rites should not eat the cooked food of a Śūdra. In the absence of other means of subsistence, he may accept from him raw grain sufficient for one night."
"One who lacks faith" (*aśrāddhī*) means one unworthy of receiving ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*), that is to say, an *asac-chūdra*. Certain cooked foods may be eaten by others; as Sumantu says:
"One may eat milk products, barley meal (*saktu*), oil, oil-cake (*piṇyāka*), cakes (*apūpa*), and whatever else is prepared with milk from a Śūdra."
Likewise,
Manu has declared that these may be eaten by those who do not consume the food of a Śūdra: pungent food, cooked food, food cooked in fat, milk-rice, curd, and barley-meal.
For a twice-born man who does not eat the food of a Śūdra, [Aṅgiras says]:
Milk that is placed in its own vessel is always pure;
milk from a Śūdra that has come to one's own house may be accepted even if it has been transferred to another vessel.
If a Brahmin, having turned away from a Śūdra’s house, should consume milk or even curd,
that too is recorded in the Smṛti as "Śūdra-food" (śūdrānna).
"By one who has desisted" means by one who has desisted from eating the food of a Śūdra. In the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"A wise man, having sprinkled it with water, may accept Śūdra food that has come to his house. Śaṅkha says:
Yama has declared that even a Śrotriya may eat the food of a Śūdra for the sake of his house, horses, chariots, or land, and especially for the sake of cattle.
Dakṣa says:
One whose limbs are nourished by the essence of a Śūdra’s food does not attain the desired goal, even if he constantly studies, performs fire-sacrifices, or recites prayers.
Vasiṣṭha says:
He who engages in sexual intercourse while the food of a Śūdra remains in his stomach—
his sons belong to the one whose food it was, for from that food his seed is produced.
Hārīta says:
He who dies with the food of a Śūdra still remaining in his stomach indeed attains the state of a donkey, the state of a camel, or the state of a Śūdra.
Aṅgiras:
That twice-born man who for six months eats the censurable food of a Śūdra shall become a Śūdra while alive and, after death, is reborn as a dog.
And this being the case, it should be understood that the favor of eating the food of a Śūdra is permissible only in times of distress. 1.168.
He states an exception to the rule that "one must not eat food that has been kept overnight":
"Food that has been kept overnight may be eaten if it is mixed with oil or fat, even if it has been stored for a long time;
likewise, preparations of wheat, barley, and cow's milk may be eaten even if they are not mixed with oil. (1.169)

Food that has been smeared with ghee or other fats may be eaten even if it has stood for a long time and is stale (*paryuṣita*). Likewise, preparations made from wheat and similar grains may be eaten even if they are stale, provided they are not mixed with fats. Yama says:
"A twice-born man should never eat foods that have turned sour."
When they have been washed, they are faultless, provided that it be a time of distress.
That which is mixed with lentils or black gram, as well as that which has become stale,
one should eat after washing it and sprinkling water over it.
Likewise: cakes, parched grain flour, fried grains, stuffed cakes,
barley meal, vegetables, meat, broth, soup, and rice-and-sesame porridge.

Barley gruel, barley meal, and whatever else is mixed with oil or fat—all of this may be eaten even if it has stood overnight, provided it has not turned sour; however, one should avoid that which has become sour.
Curd mixed with substances such as molasses that has become stale is to be avoided;
likewise, beverages and other items prepared with honey or clarified butter [are forbidden when stale].
"Rājamāṣa beans, large mung beans, as well as vṛṣa, yava, and śaka; masūra lentils, śatapuṣpā, safflower, and śrīniketana—these grains are inedible and must not be given to anyone. Thus it is said.

In the *Brahma Purāṇa*, even the lentil (*masūra*) is specified as being unfit for consumption. Consequently, at a *śrāddha* ceremony, there is no option to eat lentils as one might with peas (*kalāya*). Devala states:
"One should not eat milk-rice (*pāyasa*) at night; if it has been eaten, one should not sleep during the night.
One should not discard milk when it is obtained, for milk is remembered as a sacred substance."

Likewise: curd is fit to be eaten even when it has turned sour, as is anything else produced from curd; and likewise, that which is a sour fermented liquor made from recommended bulbs, roots, fruits, or flowers.
That which remains unaltered is pure; that which causes alteration is unfit for consumption.

This refers to [liquids made] with bulbs, roots, fruits, flowers, and so forth. The meaning is this: if a fermented drink (*satpāna*) made from bulbs and the like does not cause such alterations as delusion (*moha*), then it may be consumed. Another Smṛti states:
"In whose house the *saphalā* and *kumbhikā* plants are always present..."
Therefore, vinegar should be taken from that [source] alone, and never from any other.
Likewise:
one should not eat the stalks of the lotus, unless they are devoid of fruit and root. (1.169)
Furthermore:
[246] One should avoid the milk of a cow that is in heat, one whose calf has not yet passed ten days, or one that is nursing.
The milk of camels, of one-hoofed animals, of females, of wild animals, and likewise of sheep—[these are forbidden]. || 1.170 ||

A *saṃdhinī* is a cow that has recently returned from being with a bull. An *anirdaśā* is one for whom ten days have not yet passed since birth. An *avatsā* is one whose calf is dead. One should avoid the milk of each of these cows individually. [One should avoid] the milk of a camel (*auṣṭram*), that of a female camel (*uṣṭrikā*); that of a single-hoofed animal (* aikaśapham*), such as a mare; that of a woman (*striṇam*); that of wild animals (*āraṇyakam*) such as the *eṇī* deer and others; and that of a sheep (*āvikam*). The phrase "one should avoid the milk" is to be connected with each of these. Vasiṣṭha says: "The milk of cows, buffaloes, and goats within ten days [of calving]. The word "to be avoided" is understood. Manu says:

The milk of all wild animals, with the exception of the female buffalo, is to be avoided—this is the remainder [of the sense]. The mention of "female" (*straiṇam*) is intended as an illustration for females other than goats that have two teats. Thus says Śaṅkha: "The milk of all [animals] with two teats is unfit to be eaten, with the exception of the goat. When milk is prohibited, its derivatives should also be understood as prohibited. For Śaṅkha says:
"A wise man, upon eating the derivatives of those milks which are unfit to be eaten..."
One should diligently observe this vow for seven nights with a concentrated mind.

The vow consists of subsisting on cow's urine and barley gruel (*yāvaka*). Hārīta states: "One should not drink the milk of a *syandinī* (a cow that flows milk spontaneously) or a *vṛṣasyantī* (a cow in heat), for she becomes *ṛtumat* (fertile). Gautama says: "[One should not drink the milk] of a *syandinī*, a cow that has recently calved (*yamasū*), and a *saṃdhinī* (a cow in heat). The ellipsis is "one should not drink the milk. A *syandinī* is one whose milk flows of its own accord; a *yamasū* is one whose calf is stillborn or has died. Baudhāyana states: "Milk is unfit for drinking [from a cow] that has no calf or from one whose calf is another's. From the *Brahmapurāṇa*:

"The scum of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), the cream of clarified butter, the milk of a cow within seven days of calving (*peyūṣa*), and likewise the milk of a cow while still wet with blood, as well as curd mixed with jaggery, sprinkled with black pepper, or curd that has stood overnight."
If, through negligence, one begs for curd that is curdled, undrinkable, tasteless, and frothy,
one should observe the "wing-vow" (pakṣavrata) in the forest.

*Peyūṣa* is the milk of one who has recently given birth; and that lasts as long as moisture persists. Moisture is the state of being accompanied by *rajas*. "Decayed" means split open. Āpastamba says:
"Whether he be a Kṣatriya established in his duty, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra—whoever drinks the milk of a tawny cow (*kāpila*), there is no greater evildoer than he. [247]
From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"The Śūdra who drinks the [milk] of Kapila is cooked in hell;
a Brāhmaṇa should drink the remnant of the oblation, for otherwise he becomes a beast."
From the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Even at the time of the primary ritual, one should not consume curd at night, except when desiring to offer the *madhuparka*. (1.170)
Moreover:
sacrificial offerings intended for the gods, excrement, blood, wood-cutting tools, meat that has not been consecrated, things born of filth, and mushrooms; 1.171.

The *naivedya* for the deity consists of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), such as cooked rice (*caru*) and sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), intended for the deity prior to the *homa*, or that which has been taken up for the purpose of offering it. *Śigru* is the *saubhāñjanaka* (the drumstick tree). "Red" refers to red-colored exudations from trees. "From felling" (*vraścana*) refers to exudations produced from the cutting of trees, even those that are not red; thus says Manu: "Red exudations from trees, as well as those produced from felling."

Meat that has not been consecrated refers to the flesh of animals such as cattle that have not been consecrated—that is, not specifically intended—for the sake of the gods and other [deities]. *Viḍjā* refers to plants such as *taṇḍulīyaka* that grow from excrement. *Kavakas* are fungi resembling mushrooms. One should avoid each of these individually. Baudhāyana states:
"The flowers and fruits of trees grown in impure ground, even if they bear blossoms and fruit, are not at all defiled."
And by this, it is established by implication that one should avoid those [roots] that have grown in impure ground, distinct from trees. || 1.171 ||
Furthermore:
carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, parrots, peckers, ṭiṭṭibhas, cranes, single-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds [must not be eaten]. 1.172.
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, baka, and viṣkira birds;

Those birds that eat raw flesh are the carnivorous birds, such as vultures and the like; *kravya* means raw meat. The *dātyūha* is the *cātaka*. Those that feed by pecking are the *pratuda*s, such as hawks and the like. The single-hoofed animals are horses and the like. The village-dwellers are pigeons and the like. The *koyaṣṭi* is the *kovaka*. A *plava* is one whose livelihood is solely by floating, such as the water-fowl (*pāriplava*) and others. Those that feed by scattering [food] are the *viṣkira*s. All specific types of birds, with the exception of the single-hoofed ones, such as the *dātyūha* and others, are included here. One should avoid eating the single-hoofed ones, such as horses and the like. In this context, there are seven domestic animals, such as horses and so forth. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "The cow, sheep, goat, horse, mule, donkey, and human—these are the seven domestic animals. Here too, the sheep (*avi*) is to be eaten. Thus says Hārīta: "One may eat of domestic and wild animals: sheep, goats, rams, buffaloes, antelopes (*hariṇa*), rhinoceroses (*khaḍga*), *ruru* deer, bulls, *ṛśya* deer, *nyaṅku* deer, and wild boars; likewise, one may eat rabbits (*śaśaka*), porcupines (*śalyaka*), *medha*, iguanas (*godhā*), tortoises, partridges (*tittiri*), peacocks, *vārdhrīṇasa* cranes, quails (*lāvaka*), *kukkara*, *kapiñjala* partridges, and scaled fish, provided they are available. The *ṛśya* is a deer with many branches on its horns, well-known as the *eṇa* (the spotted antelope) which has soft horns. The *nyaṅku* resembles a *saṃbara* but is hornless. (1.172)
Moreover:
"Kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī are in vain. (1.173)

One should avoid *kṛsara* and similar foods when they are prepared without being intended for the ancestors (*pitṛ*) or the gods (*deva*). *Kṛsara* is rice mixed with sesame and mung beans. *Saṃyāva* consists of wheat flour balls cooked in ghee and milk. *Śaṣkulī* refers to preparations of wheat fried in oil or ghee; the rest is well known. Since the avoidance of *kṛsara* and such foods is already established by the general prohibition against cooking solely for one's own sake, their specific mention here is for the purpose of prescribing a particular expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for consuming them. (1.173)
Furthermore: the *kalaviṅka*, the *kākola*, the *kurara*, the *rajjudālaka*, web-footed birds, the *khañjarīṭa*, and wild animals or birds that are unknown [should not be eaten]. (1.174)
Blue jays, red-footed birds, meat from a slaughterhouse, dried meat, and fish.

The *kalaviṅka* is said to be the domestic sparrow; since it is forbidden for those living in villages, it is mentioned again here because it frequents both environments. The *kākola* is the *droṇakāka* (the raven), according to the *Nigama*: "the *droṇakokila*. The *rajjudālaka* is the woodpecker, so called because it splits ropes and the like. *Jālapāda* refers to unknown species of beasts and birds other than swans and the like. Here too, the *kalaviṅka* and others are specific types of birds distinct from known beasts. *Sauna* is meat obtained from a slaughterhouse; *vallūra* is dried meat. Both *sauna* and *vallūra* are to be avoided even among edible beasts and the like. Fish are well known; one should avoid them. (1.174)
He states the penance for consuming those things declared to be forbidden:
"Having eaten intentionally, one should dwell for three days observing a fast. (1.175)

Having intentionally eaten any one among the substances beginning with the milk of a cow in heat (*saṃdhinī*) and ending with fish, one should fast for three nights; however, if done unintentionally, one should fast for one day, according to the traditional teaching of Manu: "In the case of the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day. (MDh 11.157) [1.175]
Furthermore:
Having eaten onions, a village pig, a mushroom, a village cock, garlic, or leeks, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (1.176)

*Palāṇḍu* is a specific type of bulbous root. *Viḍvarāha* is a village pig. *Chatrāka* resembles a mushroom. *Grāmakukkuṭa* (village cock) and *laśuna* (garlic) are well known. *Gṛñjana* is a specific type of bulbous root; it is commonly known as *gartanaka* in the north. Having intentionally consumed these even once, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. However, Manu states that through the habitual intentional consumption of these, there is loss of caste (*pātitya*): "Having knowingly eaten mushrooms, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, onions, and *gṛñjana*, a twice-born man falls [from his caste]."
Consequently, the penance for drinking liquor is incurred. However, regarding repeated consumption when it was unintentional, that same author says:
"Having unintentionally eaten these six, one should perform the Kṛcchra Sāntapana;
for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should also perform the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa, or fast for a day. Thus it is said.

Regarding eating these once unintentionally, Śaṅkha says: "Upon eating garlic, onion, leek, village-pig, village-cock, or *kumbhīka*, one should drink milk for twelve nights. Regarding eating them once, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Garlic, leek, onion, and *parārikā*;
and another *parārikā* with long leaves—that is what is called [the latter]."
And those who were satisfied with what they had obtained gave it the name "great herb" (mahauṣadha); they praised that gṛñjana, which is favored by the Yavanas and grows in the forests of Śaśapura.
Sṛsaka, sanāśāka, tumbura, gareṭaka,
then that which is called pūyanaka, lavatarkā, and dāruṇā.
These thirteen types of mushrooms are also highly censured;
they resemble a lump of dough, are broken into pieces, are like a fungus, or resemble a funeral monument (caitya).
The *chatrāka* is like an umbrella; there are three kinds that grow from the earth, as well as various types of trees from which that *chatrāka* also arises.
When trees are cut by weapons, whatever sap, blood, or sprouts arise anywhere within them, even at the very limit of their bark;
Even if these items, beginning with onions, have been consumed through negligence,
a Brahmin should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, as well as the Kṛcchra and Sāntapana penances.
Or, being well-composed, he may observe for one month the vow of dwelling in the forest.

The category of "unfit" (asamartha) and so forth refers to the following alternative list from another Smṛti: "Haraṇḍu, palāṇḍu, lavatarka, parārikā, gṛñjana, and yavaneṣṭa—these are the ten species of onion (palāṇḍu). (1.176)
Among five-toed animals, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the pangolin, and the hare may be eaten; and among fish, the siṃhatuṇḍaka and the rohita may likewise be eaten. (1.177)
Likewise, the pāṭhīna, rājīva, and saśalka fish may be eaten by the twice-born.

The *sedha* and others ending with the *śaśa*, as well as among fish the *siṃhatuṇḍaka* and other specific types of fish, are to be eaten by the twice-born (*dvijāti*). The meaning is that this general prohibition against eating five-toed animals and this prohibition against eating fish do not apply to them. The fact that the *sedha* and others possess five claws is merely restated (as a known fact) for the purpose of making it known that the meat of other five-toed animals is not to be eaten. The *sedha* is the porcupine (*śvāvit*), which is a specific type of carnivorous tiger-like animal; alternatively, the *sedha* is a specific creature resembling a creeping vine. The rabbit (*śaśa*) and the tortoise (*kūrma*) are well-known. The *śallaka* is the hedgehog (*śalalī*). The mention of the "twice-born" is intended as an inclusive indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). Thus says Devala:
Thus it has been stated in its entirety what is edible and what is inedible for all castes, including those born in the natural order (anuloma), and especially for women as well.

Vasiṣṭha states: "The porcupine, the hedgehog, the hare, the tortoise, and the iguana are among the five-toed animals that may be eaten. Among domestic animals, those with teeth only on one side [of the mouth] may be eaten, as well as fish—excluding the *ceṭa*, the *gavaya*, the porpoise, the crocodile, and the crab—and those of deformed shape, those with webbed heads, and likewise the *gau*, the *gavaya*, the *śarabha*, and the *āja*. Furthermore, the cow and the ox are edible when they have lost their teeth. Up to the term "those who have lost their teeth," each preceding word should be connected to the verb "having forbidden" (*abhikṣya*). Regarding the cow and the ox, they are known by the followers of the Vājasaneyaka to be both edible and pure. However, regarding the rhinoceros and the wild boar, there is disagreement; thus, there is an option concerning whether they are edible or inedible. And that option is restricted: the rhinoceros is edible at a *śrāddha* rite, but not otherwise. The "wild boar" is the forest pig. (1.177)
Therefore, listen to the rule regarding meat, concerning both its consumption and its avoidance. [1.178]
In a life-threatening emergency, at a śrāddha ceremony, when food has been consecrated by sprinkling, or at the desire of a twice-born man.
Having worshipped the gods and the ancestors, one who eats meat incurs no fault. (1.179)

The eating and the avoidance of meats have been explained; hereafter, listen to the rules and causes that will be described. Among these, the cause for eating meat—such as when life is at stake—is explicit in the scriptures; however, in the case of avoidance, the absence of such a cause is implied by the sense. "Life at stake" refers to being caused by disease or by the lack of food. Thus says Manu: "But that man who, having been duly appointed [for a sacrifice], does not eat meat, goes to the state of an animal for twenty-one births after death."
One who is appointed or invited to a rite for the gods (*daiva*) or a funeral rite (*śrāddha*). And so says Yama:
"But he who, having been invited to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods, should reject meat, goes to hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body."

By the word *prokṣita* (sprinkled with water), meat from an animal sacrifice (*paśuyāga*) is indicated. Consequently, the meat in the form of the *iḍā* portion must indeed be consumed by the officiating priests and the patron at the animal sacrifice. "At the desire of a twice-born" means according to the wish of a twice-born; the meaning is that he who is desired by the twice-born, saying "meat should be eaten by you," may eat it. One should eat the remainder, even if it is not left over, of the meat offered to the gods and the ancestors. When eating meat on these specific occasions, one does not incur sin. (1.178–179)
He states the rule for avoidance:
"That man of evil conduct who kills animals contrary to the prescribed rule shall dwell in a terrible hell for as many days as there are hairs on the bodies of those animals. (1.180)

Except for those occasions prescribed by rule, he who, being of evil conduct, kills an animal to eat its flesh, shall dwell in hell for as many days as there are hairs on that animal. By this, the fact that the killing of animals—which is otherwise prohibited—is a cause for dwelling in hell is made known. This is just as, in the passage "He who threatens a Brāhmaṇa shall be punished with a hundred [strokes]," a relationship between the means and the end is established between the threatening of a Brāhmaṇa and the resulting torment. Therefore, this is not merely a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*), but a declaration whose literal meaning is intended to be conveyed. On this point, Manu says:
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller,
the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it— these are all slayers. — Yama.
But he who eats the flesh of living beings who desire life—
whether they have been killed by him or have died naturally— is exactly like the killer himself.
Likewise: "Whether by means of wealth, by enjoyment, or even by killing and binding—this threefold slaughter is to be known; yet in that regard, the enjoyer is the one who exceeds [the others]."
Now, in the Mahābhārata: "The man who does not eat meat during the four months of the rainy season attains four blessings: renown, long life, glory, and strength."
Likewise: "O lord of men, one should especially avoid honey and meat during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika; for dharma is prescribed here [in this regard]."
Yama says: One may eat meat consecrated by a Yajus mantra according to the prescribed rule;
one should not eat meat killed for no purpose, and one should avoid the flesh of the back.
"Back-meat" refers to the meat from the joints of the back. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"A twice-born man should not cause himself to take the meat of an animal being slaughtered, nor the meat from the back, nor the contents of the womb, nor even dried meat."

In the context of the rule that [certain animals] are always unfit to be eaten, Gautama states: "Animals with teeth in both jaws, those without hair, those with long hair, those with solid hooves, and the sparrow, the *plava*, the *cakravāka*, and the swan. The *keśin* is the yak (*camarī*). 1.180.

Now he states the fruit of abstaining from the consumption of meat other than that which is prescribed: "By refraining from meat, a Brahmin becomes a sage even while dwelling at home; he attains all desires as well as the fruit of the horse sacrifice. (1.181)

Even while being a householder, by abstaining from meat one becomes equal to a sage; the meaning is that one becomes an ascetic (*tāpasa*). One attains all desires and the fruit of the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*). The present tense ending in the word "avāpnoti" (he attains) should be interpreted as an injunctive mood, as in the case of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice. 1.181.

Thus ends the sixth chapter, on edible and non-edible foods, in the legal digest (*nibandha*) on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the family of the venerable Vidyādharas.
Now begins the seventh chapter, on the Purification of Substances, in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary.

Now he begins the section on the rules for the means of purifying substances (*dravya*). Purification (*śuddhi*) is the removal of defects from a substance. For a substance from which defects have departed is said to be "pure. And in the scripture (*śāstra*), it is stated that a substance contaminated by crows and the like becomes pure through washing. Therefore, even in that case, what is denoted by the word "purification" is precisely the removal of the defect produced by contact with crows and so forth. Since a defect is not perceivable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), one infers—on the basis of the fact that the injunction for purification would otherwise be inexplicable—that some kind of defect arises in the substance due to its contact with crows and the like. Various means for removing that defect, such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) and washing (*prakṣālana*), are prescribed by the scripture. It is inferred solely from the force of the injunction for purification that a person should not engage in worldly transactions (*saṃvyavahāra*) with an impure substance, but only with one that has been purified. Furthermore, if a transaction can be accomplished even with a fragment of a substance such as a rag or a potsherd, then that too must be purified according to the rules.
