But having touched these [objects] belonging to oneself, one becomes pure by washing them and sipping water (ācamana).
Having emerged from the water, one should sip water; likewise, after descending into it.
Hārīta says: "One who desires to sleep should sip water.
A washerman, a leather-worker, a hunter, one who lives by killing birds, a cleaner, a butcher, an actor, and likewise a fowler—"
One who possesses a discus, one who possesses a banner, an executioner, and village cocks and pigs.
If any part of the body of twice-born persons— excluding the head— should be touched by these,
they are considered pure once they have washed that part with water and sipped water (ācamana).

A *rajaka* is one who dyes clothes and the like; a *nirṇejaka* is a washerman; a *naṭa* is a specific caste of actor; and an *anaṭa* is a stage-manager (*śailūṣa*) who lives by appearing on the stage. According to the *Padma Purāṇa*:

"After completing recitations, burnt offerings, gifts, the funeral rice-balls for ancestors, water libations, and the consumption of all kinds of food, a Brahmin should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)."
[280] By coming into contact with those of the three [lower] castes, one should sip water and become purified;
however, upon contact with those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the abandonment of ritual action is prescribed.
Upon contact with artisans, a twice-born man should perform the rite of sipping water (ācamana);
however, upon contact with those of the inverse castes (pratiloma), there should be an additional breath-control (prāṇāyāma).

This applies to the time of preparatory ritual action (*karmaprayoga*). If a Brahmin is somehow touched by another Brahmin who is impure from food remnants (*ucchiṣṭa*), he shall become pure simply by sipping water; so said the sage Āpastamba.
Another Smṛti states:
"Upon touching [such a person], a twice-born man should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) for the sin incurred thereby;
indeed, among all castes, they are the supreme purifiers."
Prajāpati says:
Even though one is already purified at the commencement of a specific rite,
having performed the ancestral rites (pitṛkarma), one becomes pure by sipping water once.
This is specifically prescribed by Śātātapa:
"If one person touches an impure object, he alone becomes defiled; another who has merely passed it does not become defiled. This rule applies to all types of objects."
Parāśara says: Upon sneezing, spitting, being defiled by food remnants from the teeth, speaking untruth,
or conversing with outcasts, one should touch the right ear.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa states:
After performing the act of spitting during the practice of breath-control (vātakarman), after cleaning the teeth, after sneezing,
and upon conversing with an outcaste, one should touch the right ear.
This applies at times other than those prescribed for the performance of rituals, according to the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Even after eating sugarcane, water, fruit, roots, betel, milk, or medicine, one must perform the rites of bathing, giving gifts, and water-libations."
Another Smṛti states:
"Having eaten fruits such as grapes, sugarcane, milk, roots, ghee, curd, betel leaf, medicine, leaves, or sacrificial oblation, one need not rinse the mouth. (1.196)
The muddy waters of a street, even when touched by outcasts, dogs, or crows,
are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks.

Mud on the streets, as well as water, and houses and the like constructed with baked bricks, even when touched by outcastes and others, are purified by wind alone. "Rathyā" means a road; "kardama" means mud; "antya" refers to the *caṇḍāla* and so forth; the rest is well known. Vyāsa says:
"Roads, mud, water, boats, paths, and grass..."
And those constructed with baked bricks are purified by air alone.
Śaṅkha says:
"If a man is touched above the navel by the mud or water of a street, or by spittle and the like, he is purified immediately by bathing."
Yama states: Having entered a village thoroughfare that is muddy during the rainy season,
it is prescribed that there should be three applications of clay on the shins and twice as many on the feet.
And these two statements refer to that mud in which no impurity is perceived, either by its form or by its smell. (1.197)

Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the Purification of Substances, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara race.
Now, in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary, the section on gifts (8).

Immediately following this is the rule for the section on gifts. He will prescribe that cows and other such things are to be given to a worthy recipient (*pātra*). For that purpose, in order to praise the recipient—and since Brāhmaṇas alone possess the status of a worthy recipient—he speaks this praise of them.
Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the preservation of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the ancestors and the gods, and for the protection of dharma. (1.198)

Having performed austerities, Brahmā created the Brāhmaṇas for the preservation of the Vedas, for the satisfaction of the gods and the ancestors, and for the protection of Dharma. Therefore, they are praiseworthy because they originate from a distinguished cause and because they possess purposes such as the protection of the Vedas that cannot be accomplished by anyone else. Austerity (*tapas*) is the conquest of all the senses. (1.198)
Furthermore: "The Brahmins, devoted to sacred learning and study, are the source of all.
This means that the Brahmins, who are devoted to sacred learning and study, are the source—that is, the masters—of every object existing upon the earth. And so says Manu:
Indeed, upon being born on earth, a Brāhmaṇa is born as the lord of all beings for the protection of the treasury of Dharma.
[282] “Everything that exists in this world belongs to the Brāhmaṇa;

by virtue of his preeminent lineage, the Brāhmaṇa indeed deserves all this. Thus it is said. *Śruta* is the comprehension of the meaning of the words of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, along with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), as received from a teacher. *Adhyayana* is the recitation of the *Śruti* and other texts. Those whose nature is such that they cultivate—that is, properly practice—*śruta* and *adhyayana* are called *śrutādhyayanaśīlinaḥ*. In the reading *śālinaḥ*, it means those who take pride in those two.
Those devoted to ritual action are superior to them, but those who possess the highest knowledge of the inner self are superior even to them. (1.199)

From those whose activity is exhausted merely by hearing and studying [the Vedas], there are those devoted to action (*kriyāparāḥ*), for whom the performance of dharma is primary. Here, the word "action" (*kriyā*) also includes the avoidance of unrighteousness (*adharma*). This is because their success in hearing and studying follows as a matter of course; for those devoid of that [learning] do not become devoted to action. Compared to those who are merely practitioners of dharma (*dharmiṇaḥ*), the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavidaḥ*) are most praiseworthy. (1.199)
Having thus praised the Brahmins, he describes the characteristics of a worthy recipient:

"One does not become a worthy recipient by learning alone, nor even by austerity; where conduct and these two [learning and austerity] both exist—that indeed is proclaimed to be a worthy recipient. (1.200)

*Vidyā* is knowledge concerning one’s own duty (*svadharma*) and *Brahman*. Neither by that alone—without austerity (*tapas*)—nor by austerity alone—which consists in the performance of one’s own duty but lacks knowledge—is one a worthy recipient (*pātra*). For, that Brāhmaṇa in whom conduct characterized by right behavior exists, and in whom both knowledge and austerity reside, is proclaimed as a worthy recipient by the great sages. He is called a *pātra* because he rescues (*tārayati*) the giver from sin. Therefore, Manu says:
"One should always practice the duty of giving, consisting of sacrifices and rites for prosperity, with a well-pleased disposition, having found a worthy recipient according to one's ability."
Whatever may be asked for, it should be given by one who is free from malice;
for a worthy recipient will surely arise who shall deliver one from all [suffering].

Vasiṣṭha said: They declare such a person to be a worthy recipient— one who is rich in Vedic study, of noble birth, tranquil, established in the sacrificial rites, fearful of sin, possessed of great knowledge, patient toward women, righteous, a protector of cows, and exhausted by the observance of vows.
One who possesses a [pure] lineage and noble birth;

those who are patient and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses, and who have desisted from killing living beings; householders who are restrained in accepting gifts—such Brāhmaṇas are capable of delivering one across [the ocean of existence].
Vyāsa says regarding giving: That which is given to one's mother and father, to brothers, sisters, and daughters,
and that which is given to one's wife and sons, is irreproachable and leads to heaven.

"A gift to a father is said to be a hundredfold, a thousandfold to a mother, an infinite gift to a daughter, and what is given to a uterine brother is inexhaustible. [283] By virtue of the authority of such statements, one must necessarily give what is about to be described—cows, land, and so forth—even to those lacking in learning, beginning with one's mother. And so says Manu:
One who is capable of giving to strangers while his own people live in misery—this is a mere semblance of dharma; it is like the taste of honey that turns into the flavor of poison.
He who performs funeral rites for the deceased by oppressing his dependents brings about a result that is unpleasant both while he is alive and after he has died.

A *aurdhvadaihika* is an action whose fruit is realized in the world hereafter; *udarka* means the end or conclusion. *Dakṣa* means skillful. That gift which is given out of compassion (*dayā*) even to those who are unworthy recipients (*apātra*), as well as to the wretched, the blind, and the miserable, conduces to infinite results.
Śātātapa says: "The twice-born man who bypasses a nearby person while he is studying,
whether at a meal or during a gift-giving, destroys his family unto the seventh generation."
From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
But that fool who, bypassing a Brahmin who is nearby— provided he is not an outcast—
should feed one who is far away though rich in virtues, shall go to hell.
Therefore, a wise man should not neglect his neighboring Brahmins,
nor any of his relatives, nor his daughter's son, nor his brother-in-law.
O lord of the house, O protector of the earth, a man should especially not neglect his sister’s son, nor his other kinsmen,
even if they are fools.
Having passed beyond it, one would go to the most terrible Raurava hell.
A neighbor is one who dwells in a house nearby. A *viṭpati* is a son-in-law. In the *Mahābhārata*:
"O King, those who are devoted to him, whose wealth is his, whose home is his, and who depend upon him—when these seekers are in need, a gift given to them yields great fruit."

"Arthī" means one who desires wealth. Those who have been robbed of all their possessions by powerful men, though they are innocent, long for those who are well-protected; gifts given to them yield great fruit.

The meaning is that they have had all their property confiscated by powerful and mighty men. When Brahmins whose wealth and wives have been seized during a calamity in the country approach for the sake of money, what is given to them yields great fruit.
For ascetics who are constant in austerity, as well as for those who are the best of mendicants—
whatever is given to such seekers yields great fruit.
The capable man begs for the sake of averting calamity and for the sake of his family;
having thus investigated, one should give— this is the rule for all acts of giving.
Moral conduct is to be known through living together; purity through social interaction;
and wisdom through conversation. By these three, a worthy recipient is examined.
Saṃvarta says:
That gift which is given to one who is learned in the Vedas, who is poor, and especially to one who asks—
that gift brings about auspicious results.
Devala says:
First is the *mātra*, then the *brāhmaṇa*, and after that the *śrotriya*;
likewise the *anūcāna*, the *bhrūṇa*, the *ṛṣikalpa*, the *ṛṣi*, and the *muni*.
Thus, these eight types of Brāhmaṇas have been first declared in the Śruti.
Among them, each succeeding one is superior, especially by virtue of learning and conduct;
however, even one born merely by birth in a family of Brahmins is superior.
One who has not fallen away from his duties but is devoid of ritual action is called a *mātra*;
he is upright, having transcended the single aim [of worldly life] and being a receiver of the Veda.
He is called a Brāhmaṇa who is modest, truthful, and compassionate,
having studied one Vedic branch along with its ritual manuals and the six auxiliary sciences.
A Brahmin devoted to the six duties is called a Śrotriya, one who knows the Dharma;
he is a knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, pure in soul, and free from sin.
Having acquired the remainder like a *śrotriya*, he is traditionally known as an *anūcāna*.

The remaining characteristics are devotion to the six duties, just like that of a *śrotriya*. One who has attained this is called *anūcāna*; the meaning is that he is one endowed with the qualities of an *anūcāna*.
One who is restrained by sacrifices, study, and teaching, who eats only the remnants, and whose senses are conquered, is called a *bhrūṇa* by the wise.
"Leaving aside what has been eaten by servants and others;
having acquired all knowledge, both worldly and Vedic,
he who remains constantly self-controlled while established in his stage of life (āśrama) is remembered as being equal to a seer (ṛṣikalpa)."
With vital energy drawn upward, fierce in asceticism, restrained in diet, and free from doubt,
the seer shall be capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, remaining true to his word.
Withdrawn from worldly life, knowing all principles, and free from desire and anger,
the sage remains established in meditation, actionless, self-controlled, and regards a clod of earth and gold as equal.
[285] Thus,
those eminent Brahmins known as the "Triśuklas," who are exalted by their lineage, learning, and conduct, are honored at the Soma sacrifices and other rites.

Those whose three [acts]—ancestry and so forth—are white and pure are called *triśukla*. *Savana* refers to the Soma sacrifice. Vasiṣṭha says: "He whom no one knows as either existent or non-existent, as unlearned or widely learned, as of good conduct or bad conduct—he is a Brāhmaṇa."
Yoga, austerity, compassion, charity, truthfulness, purity, sacred learning, modesty, knowledge, realization, and faith— this is the defining characteristic of a Brāhmaṇa.
Likewise: "One vessel consists of the Veda, and another vessel consists of austerity; but the most excellent of all vessels is he in whose stomach no food of a Śūdra has ever entered. (1.200)

Now he describes the specific rules for giving to a worthy recipient (*pātra*) by means of a gift-object, as well as the prohibition against giving to an unworthy recipient (*apātra*): "Objects such as cows, land, sesame seeds, and gold should be given, duly honored, to a worthy recipient;
nothing at all should be given to an unworthy recipient by a wise man who desires his own welfare. (1.201)

Each substance, beginning with cows, should be offered to a worthy recipient after being honored by one who desires his own welfare and the attainment of heaven and other such goals. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes food and other gifts mentioned in other treatises. Since a wise person knows that sin arises from giving to an unworthy recipient (*apātra*), he should not give even the slightest thing to such a person. Although the prohibition against giving to the unworthy is already established by the force of the injunction that "it must be given to a worthy recipient," the author begins a separate prohibition to indicate that in the absence of a primary worthy recipient, any recipient other than those specifically forbidden is acceptable. Here, the term *apātra* does not mean something other than a *pātra*, but rather the opposite of a *pātra*. That which is prohibited from being a *pātra* is what is opposed to it. Manu describes those to whom gifts should not be given: [Manu 4.93–95] "One should not give to a Brahmin who sells the Vedas, nor to one who is officiating at a sacrifice for a multitude, nor to one who subsists by the profession of arms, nor to one who is a physician. "One should not give to one who tends cattle, nor to a trader, nor to one who has a wife and yet goes to another's wife, nor to one who is a servant of the king. "One should not give to one who is a gambler, nor to one who is a slanderer, nor to one who is a thief, nor to one who is a drunkard, nor to one who is a heretic. (Note: The specific verses from Manu are provided here as they are the source for the list of those excluded from being *pātras*.)
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born man who acts like a cat,
nor to one who acts like a heron, nor to a sinner, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas.
For wealth, even if acquired according to the rules, when given to these three types of persons,
leads to misfortune for the donor and likewise for the recipient in the next world.
Misfortune is transgression. When one pursues the practice of a vow while having a selfish motive as the primary cause,
concealing his sin under the guise of that vow, that is called the "cat-vow" (*baiḍāla-vrata*).

The meaning is that *kāraṇa* refers to the Dharma. *Vrata* refers to penance (*prāyaścitta*). But he who, having accepted a stage of life (*āśrama*) and remaining there, does not abide by its rules—that vow is called "cat-like" (*baiḍāla*) due to the violation of the stage of life.
[286] There is no fault in accepting gifts from those who lack vows, who lack mantras, and who subsist merely by birth; for a stone cannot save one with a stone.
Wealth must never be given to one who has abandoned the Agnihotra sacrifice, who acts against the wishes of his teacher, or who is constantly a doer of evil.
Twice-born men who teach the Śūdra do not deserve to receive gifts;
by teaching a Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa falls—of this there is no doubt.
Vasiṣṭha said: Seeing the hands of a Brahmin who is devoid of Vedic learning and lacks ritual practice, the cow, the horse, gold, and the earth cry out to the donor.
Dakṣa says: What is given to a rogue, a hypocrite, a wrestler, one of base learning, a gambler, a cheat, a flatterer,
a wandering minstrel, or a thief, becomes fruitless.
Vyāsa says: A seed sown in salt-waste, that which is offered as an oblation into ashes,
and that which is given to those devoid of ritual action— none of that bears fruit either in the next world or in this one.
Vṛddha-Manu:
Even if he is a worthy recipient, that Brahmin who, having accepted a gift,
employs it for unworthy purposes, to him nothing at all should be given.
One who accumulates wealth by accepting gifts from all sides,
yet does not employ it for the sake of the Dharma— that thief one should not honor.
Yama says:
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar have been lost for three generations is indeed called a "wicked Brāhmaṇa," as is he who is the husband of a Śūdra woman.
Vasiṣṭha says: Those who cohabit with a woman in her courses, those who maintain no sacred fires,
and those whose family lacks Vedic learning— all these follow the dharma of Śūdras.
Manu says: A gift given to a non-Brahmin yields an equal reward; to one who calls himself a Brahmin, it is twofold;
to a teacher, it is a thousandfold; and to one who has mastered the Vedas, it is infinite.
The meaning is that the fruit [of the gift] is equal to the extent of the wealth given. Śātātapa says:
"A gift given to a temple-attendant (devalaka) is not desired; a gift to a usurer is unstable;
and a gift given to a washerman is ordained to be fruitless."
And he who bestows upon those without marks the livelihood appropriate for those with marks is cooked in the terrible sin of killing a Brahmin; of this there is no doubt.
And six types of non-Brāhmaṇas have been declared; the sage Śātātapa said:
"The first among them is one who depends on a king, and the second is a buyer and seller."
The third is one who performs sacrifices for many; the fourth is a priest for a village;
the fifth, however, is one who is hired for those [sacrifices] of a village or a city.
But that twice-born man who does not attend upon the morning twilight before the sun has risen, nor the evening twilight while the sun is still present, is considered the sixth type of non-Brahmin.
Vyāsa says: One born from the seed of a Brāhmaṇa, yet devoid of the purificatory rites of mantra and subsisting merely on his birth-status, is indeed not a Brāhmaṇa.
One who has undergone the rites beginning with conception and likewise the initiation ceremony,
yet neither performs ritual acts nor studies the Veda, is called a "pseudo-Brāhmaṇa" (brāhmaṇabruva).
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"A gift to a Śūdra is considered equal [in merit]; to a Vaiśya, it is remembered as twice that;
a gift to a Kṣatriya is threefold, and to a Brāhmaṇa, it is remembered as sixfold."

Thus, this refers to the subject of the gift of food, based on the statement of Gautama: "The others [receive] prepared food. Prepared food means cooked food; the others are the Kṣatriyas and so forth. Manu says: "If one gives to the undeserving and does not give to the deserving, one is deprived of both wealth and merit through the failure to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy."

In this context, a distinguished form of giving has been prescribed by means of a gift such as a cow and so forth to a worthy recipient (*pātra*). Regarding that, Devala states the meaning of the word "giving" (*dāna*) and its intermediate subdivisions: "The bestowal of wealth upon a worthy recipient with faith is designated as 'giving' (*dāna*); its detailed explanation shall now be set forth."
"Objects" refers to the things to be given; their "bestowal" is the act of relinquishment extending to the point of establishing a relationship of master and servant with respect to the recipient.
Giving is said to have two causes, six bases, six limbs, and six results of maturation; it is fourfold, threefold, and characterized by three types of destruction.
In that regard, he speaks of the state of having two causes:
"Neither smallness nor greatness in a gift brings about prosperity;
faith and capacity—these six are declared to be the causes of gifts."
These two are indeed causes of increase and decrease for those to whom gifts are constantly given in the alms-bowl.

The first *vā* has the sense of "as if," while the second is used for conjunction. Just as meagerness is not the cause of the prosperity resulting from a gift, neither is abundance; rather, it is faith and capacity. Capacity consists of generosity and the absence of regret. He states that there are six bases:
"Dharma, wealth, and pleasure, as well as modesty, joy, and fear—these six are declared to be the bases of gifts. [288]
That which is given to worthy recipients without regard for any motive,
but solely with the intention of renunciation, is called the gift of Dharma.

That which is given incidentally, without regard for any specific purpose, is called "gift for the sake of wealth" (arthadāna) by those following the Vedic tradition; it is motivated by the desire for rewards.
That which is given out of attachment to women, drinking, hunting, and gambling, or to unworthy recipients out of passion, is called "the gift of desire."
When a person, having heard in an assembly what was requested by supplicants, gives that object out of shame,
such a gift is known as a "gift out of shame."
When something is given with joy after seeing or hearing pleasant things,
those who contemplate Dharma call that gift "joy-giving" (harṣadāna).
That which is given out of fear for the sake of countering verbal abuse and physical injury from those who cause suffering is called the gift of fear.
He states that there are six constituent parts:
"The giver and the recipient, faith, the deity, righteousness,
as well as place and time— these they know to be the six limbs of gifts."
Free from disease, righteous in soul, desirous of giving, free from vices, pure,
and possessing irreproachable livelihood and actions— the giver who possesses these six qualities is praised.
One who is pure in three respects, of simple livelihood, compassionate, with all senses intact, and free from the defects of birth— such a Brāhmaṇa is called a worthy recipient.
The threefold toll has been explained.
Constant goodwill toward supplicants upon seeing them,
as well as hospitality and freedom from envy— that is proclaimed as faith (*śraddhā*).
Whatever wealth has been acquired by oneself without harming others or causing distress—
whether it be small or large— is said to be "givable."
If a substance is difficult to obtain here, or if it is at a time when it is likewise rare,
then those [specific] place and time for giving and so forth would be excellent, and not otherwise.
"Depending on the excellence or deficiency of the state, place, time, and the qualities of both the recipient and the donor,
even an inferior gift may become superior, or a superior gift may otherwise become inferior.
[289] Thus he explains the sixfold ripening.
Bad fruit, fruitless, inferior, equal, vast, and inexhaustible—
these six types of maturation are taught as the sixfold pair of results according to their ripening.
For that reason, what is given to an atheist, to one who harms others, to an outcaste, to a slanderer, or to a killer of an embryo, shall yield evil fruit.
An inferior person, such as a kṣatriya or others,
may give even a great gift that is fruitless if it is devoid of faith;
a gift that causes harm to others, even if vast, shall reach a state of deficiency.
Even that which has been given as previously described, if it is with a defiled mind,
that gift will have an equal result due to the fault of its intention.
Through all six [perfections] as previously described, giving becomes of vast fruition; "fruition" here refers to the result.
A gift given out of compassion attains inexhaustibility.
Compassion is *anuśrośa*. That which is given is *dāna*, such as cows and other gifts. He describes the fourfold [types] beginning with *dhruva*:
*dhruva*, *ājasrika*, *kāmya*, and *naimittika* in order.
This Vedic path of giving is thus described by the twice-born as being of four kinds.
Water-stations, groves, ponds, and so forth, which certainly yield all desired fruits—
that is called "perpetual" when it is given day after day.
Whatever is desired for the sake of offspring, victory, sovereignty, women, or children—
that gift which is established upon desire is designated as "kāmya" (optional).

It is traditionally taught that the occasional rite (naimittika) is threefold— dependent on time, dependent on action, and dependent on purpose— and is described as being both with oblations and without oblations.
He states the threefold nature:
"Nine are superior, four are middling by way of their arrangement;
the remaining are inferior. They know this to be the threefold nature.
Food, curd, honey, protection, cattle, land, gold, horses, and elephants—
these are the supreme gifts, owing to the excellence of the substances given.
Knowledge, clothing, shelter, enjoyments, and medicines—
these are the intermediate gifts, so called because they consist of intermediate substances.
Shoes, swings, vehicles, umbrellas, vessels, and seats;
lamps, cooked food, fruits, and so forth—these last items may be kept for many years.
Because the categories of meaning are numerous, they are not intended in the case of the remaining numbers;
therefore, the wise know that the remaining ones are all "inferior" (adhamāni) among the pronominal stems (sarvanāman).
He speaks of perishability:
"What is desired, given, or studied perishes through boasting;
and through praise and regret, one's vital energy is broken and wasted."
Therefore, one should not vainly proclaim the merit performed by oneself. They say that such a person who speaks thus has truly realized his debt.
Thus, a gift endowed with all virtues and free from the aforementioned defects yields its desired fruit, like a wish-fulfilling cow.
In this world, one gains fame known as "the giver," and in heaven, vast enjoyments;
and in a third birth, within an excellent lineage, one produces faith in giving.
Even if one gives away the entire earth acquired through unjust means to an unworthy recipient,
provided it is devoid of faith, one shall not attain any prosperity whatsoever.
By giving even a handful of vegetables, offered with faith and devotion to a great and worthy recipient, one shall attain all prosperity.
Manu says: One should always perform sacrifices and works of public utility with diligence and faith;
for when performed with faith and with wealth acquired by righteous means, those two become inexhaustible.
The Mahābhārata:
The ritual of the single fire, that which is offered in the three fires,
and the gift given within the sacrificial altar— these are so designated.
Reservoirs, wells, ponds, temples,
the gift of food, and groves— this is designated as *pūrta* (meritorious works of public utility).
Nārada said: Hospitality and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice are designated as *iṣṭa*;
likewise, lotus ponds, oblong ponds, and temples for the deities [are so designated].
The gift of food, a grove, and a reservoir are designated as *pūrta*;
likewise, whatever gift is given on the twelfth lunar day is designated as *pūrta*.
And by this word "etcetera," other forms of giving—such as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth—are included.

Sacrifice (*iṣṭa*) and works of public utility (*pūrta*) are said to be the common duty (*dharma*) of the twice-born. A Śūdra may be entitled to the duty of *pūrta*, but not to the Vedic [sacrificial] duty.
Manu: He who accepts what has been honored and he who gives what has indeed been honored—both of them go to heaven; in the opposite case, they go to hell. [291]
Yama said:
"Indeed, he who gives a gift out of great respect to those possessed of virtue,
having obtained wealth after death, enjoys it together with his sons and grandsons."
Great respect means reverence.
Furthermore, by giving a gift here that does not harm others, the wise man indeed obtains wealth after death that results in happiness and has a happy conclusion.
Āpastamba: "All gifts are preceded by water. (1.20.1)
It is not only that one should not give to an unworthy recipient, but rather, such a person should not accept gifts either; thus he says:
"One who is deficient in learning and austerity must never accept a gift;
by accepting it, he leads both the donor and himself downward. (1.202)

By one who is devoid of learning and austerity, and lacking the characteristics of a worthy recipient (*pātra*), [a gift] is accepted; thus it is called "acceptance" (*pratigraha*). That should not be accepted. For one who lacks learning and the like, by accepting [gifts], leads both the donor and himself to hell. (1.202)
One should give daily to a worthy recipient, especially on auspicious occasions;
even when asked, one should give with faith and according to one's ability. (1.203)

Every day, one should give to a worthy recipient before sunrise. On special occasions such as the *saṃkrānti* and others, however, it should be given with particular care and respect. It should be given whether requested or—noted by the word "api"—even unrequested; among these, giving unrequested is most highly praised. Thus says Śātātapa:
"The end of the ocean may indeed be seen, but no end at all is seen for that gift which is given after approaching [the recipient] and that gift which is given unrequested."
Likewise:
"The gift that is given after having gone [to the recipient] is said to yield infinite fruit;
that given when [the recipient] has been summoned yields a hundredfold merit; but when [the recipient] has asked for it, it yields half of that."

The phrase "in a worthy recipient, purified by faith, according to one's ability" is to be connected with each subsequent clause. Regarding the time for the purpose of giving, Devala has stated: "dependent on time, dependent on action," and so forth. In that context, the time is prescribed as "every day" and so on, referring to the mere period of the day; by this, the night is excluded. By the phrase "on specific occasions," particular times such as the solstices (*ayana*) and others are indicated. Thus says Śātātapa: "At the solstices and other such times, whatever desirable wealth is in the house should always be given;
likewise at the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* [the beginning of the six signs] and when the moon and sun turn back."

The meaning is that this applies to two who are currently engaged in liberation, but not to those who are already liberated, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: "But during an eclipse, at that very time. Vyāsa says:
Whatever offerings to the gods (havya) and ancestors (kavya) are given by donors at the time of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti),
the Sun-god bestows them back perpetually in birth after birth.
A gift at the waning of the moon yields a hundredfold; at the end of the day, a thousandfold;
at the equinox, a hundred-thousandfold; but at the vyatīpāta conjunction, it is infinite.
Saṃvarta says: Whatever is given during the solstices, during the six aśītimukhas,
or during an eclipse of the moon or sun, that gift becomes inexhaustible.
On the new moon day at the end of the lunar fortnight,
when three lunar days (tithis) occur within a single solar day (sāvana),
that is declared to be a "day-destruction" (dinakṣaya); the fruit [of a rite] performed then is a thousandfold.
Vasiṣṭha says: The two transits [of the sun] into Capricorn (Mṛga) and Cancer are the northern and southern solstices respectively;
"Mṛga" refers to Capricorn.
At the equinoxes of Libra and Aries, and in the intervals between them, as well as when the sun is in Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo— these are the other [auspicious times].
This is called Viṣṇupada; its fruit is greater than that of the equinox.
The sun’s transit occurs in Virgo, Gemini, Pisces, and Sagittarius as well.
The sixty-eighth [day] is declared to be the "mouth" (ṣaḍaśītimukhī), possessing the qualities of the sixty-eight through its fruits.
There are two meritorious periods: the past and the future, namely the northern and southern solstices;
however, during an eclipse, that specific time is meritorious, as is the past northern solstice.
The auspicious time (*parvakāla*) occurs before and after all transits (*saṃkrānti*). For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha himself has stated the established rule:
"In the case of Cancer, thirty *nāḍīs* are prescribed; in Capricorn, twenty;
but when the transit occurs in Libra or Aries, there are ten *nāḍīs* on both sides."

Here, the term "occurring" (*vartamāna*) and "on both sides" (*ubhayataḥ*) are connected with all [the signs] beginning with Cancer, because there is no difference in their requiring a complement. Furthermore, regarding that specific [connection], the proximity of the reading for one [sign] is not a restrictive factor for the syntactic connection, as it is otherwise established by its being unavoidable.

However, when sixty *nāḍikās* are said to have passed after the *ṣaḍaśīti*, this is intended to indicate an abundance of fruit. For this very reason, he states that even at the mouth of the *ṣaḍaśīti*, the time of the lunar node (*parva-kāla*) occurs earlier.
When the sun enters the signs of Capricorn, Pisces, Aries, and Virgo in Viṣṇupadī,
and when the transit occurs at night while moving from the east to the north;
The transition occurs during the portions of the night that have passed and those yet to come;
however, the wise have declared that five *nāḍīs* in the forenoon are meritorious.
"But in the afternoon, there are five [periods] for both Śrauta and Smārta rites.

By this, it is stated that when the Saṃkrānti occurs during the night of the Ṣaḍaśīti, the rite for the Saṃkrānti should be performed in the afternoon. "Nṛyu" refers to the zodiac sign of Gemini (Mithuna). And the period called Puṇya at the Viṣṇupadī Saṃkrānti lasts sixteen [nāḍīs] both before and after [the moment of transition].
On the day of the sun's transit, the entire day is proclaimed to be meritorious.
When a transit occurs at night, it is taught that half a day is prescribed for bathing and giving gifts;
if it occurs before midnight, the ritual action takes place after midday.
In the case of an upward transit, it lasts for two *praharas* after sunrise;
however, if the Sun transits at the completion of midnight, [the duration is different].
They say that two days are meritorious, with the exception of the signs of Capricorn and Cancer.

In this regard, the established rule is as follows: if the transit occurs during the first watch of the night, bathing and other rites should be performed in the latter half of the preceding day; however, if the transit occurs at another time, they should be performed in the forenoon of the following day. As for the statement: "One should perform bathing, giving, and so forth during an eclipse, a solar transit, a wedding, a calamity, or a festive increase (vṛddhi), as well as during optional vows—even at night."

Thus, this refers to the transits of Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*), because of the statement: "except for Capricorn and Cancer. By this statement, bathing and other rites during the night are permitted specifically during the two solstices (*ayanadvaya*). The prohibition—"one should not perform bathing at night"—applies only to other transits. As for the verse: "In Cancer, the merit is thirtyfold; likewise in Capricorn it is twentyfold;
in the future southern transit (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and in the past northern transit (*uttarāyaṇa*), [the merit is likewise]."
Thus [it is said], for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of that merit; it is not, however, for the purpose of a restrictive rule. For this very reason, it is said:

"A gift given at the equinox in the middle, at Viṣṇupada, at the beginning of the southern solstice, when the six-aśīti-mukha has passed, and likewise during the northern solstice, yields abundant fruit."
Thus they remember. For this very reason, it was stated by him without qualification:
"The moment of the transit is subtle and difficult to discern even for those with measured vision;
yet, through its conjunction, thirty nāḍīs below and above are purified."
When the sun's transit occurs at midday, the merit of bathing and giving gifts lasts for half a day;
when it occurs at night, it lasts for a day, as does the merit on the days of the equinoxes and solstices.
Whichever channels are situated nearby, those are remembered as the most meritorious.

Thus, this meaning is established: disregarding whether the transit (*saṃkrānti*) has already passed or is yet to come, one should perform bathing, giving, and other rites at that half-day during which the past or future transit is imminent. Now, the subject at hand is stated: even an action such as violence becomes a cause for giving in the form of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). As it was said by Manu: "One should bestow upon a Veda-knowing Brāhmaṇa wealth sufficient for his livelihood, or a house together with its furniture, or even one's entire property."
Such is the case in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*). Wealth also serves as a cause for giving, as stated in the *Mahābhārata*:
"One who possesses ten cows should give one cow; one who possesses a hundred cows should give ten;
one who possesses a thousand cows should give a hundred. All these are recorded as yielding equal fruit."

It has been stated that one must give even when requested; regarding this, Manu specifies those to whom one must certainly give: "One who seeks offspring, one who intends to perform a sacrifice, a traveler, one who has given away all his possessions, one seeking wealth for the sake of a teacher, one seeking wealth for the sake of his father or mother, one seeking wealth for the sake of Vedic study, and one who is afflicted by illness."
One should indeed not consider those Brahmins who subsist on the alms of dharma as mere *snātakas*;
gifts should be given to them according to their specific knowledge.
"For food, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), should be given to these foremost of the twice-born;
for others, cooked food is given on the ground outside the sacrificial altar."

One who seeks a marriage alliance is one who desires to marry a girl for the sake of continuing his lineage (*sāṃtānika*). One who intends to sacrifice is one who is about to perform a *Soma* sacrifice (*yakṣyamāṇa*). A traveler is one who has set out for the sake of religious duty (*dharma*). One who possesses all his wealth is one who has performed the *Viśvajit* sacrifice. One who seeks the teacher's purpose is one who seeks to provide for his teacher; likewise, those seeking the purpose of their father, mother, or Vedic study, as well as the afflicted and the sick. All these are *snātakas* because they have returned from their studies. They are "mendicants for the sake of dharma" because they practice the prescribed form of begging. By the word "Brāhmaṇa," Kṣatriyas and others are excluded. By the word "dakṣiṇā" (sacrificial fee), only material goods such as cows are meant here, and not the payment for officiating priests, because that is impossible in this context. Others refers to Kṣatriyas and so forth. "Outside the sacrificial altar" means elsewhere than at a sacrifice. The phrase "within the sacrificial altar" is connected with the statement that food should be given along with a fee; for Gautama states: "To those begging outside the sacrificial altar. "Prepared food" means cooked food. (1.203)
[295] [1.204] He states the procedure for the gift of a cow.
A milch cow of good disposition, with golden horns and silver hooves, accompanied by a garment, a bronze vessel, and a monetary gift, should be given away.

That cow whose horns are joined with gold is *hemaśṛṅgī*. She is distinguished by hooves made of silver; she is well-behaved and virtuous; she is provided with clothing, meaning she is covered with cloth; she is accompanied by a bell-metal vessel (*kāṃsyapātra*); she is yielding milk, meaning she has abundant milk; and she is accompanied by a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), specifically gold—such a cow should be given as a gift. As stated in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"The man who gives a cow along with her calf, together with a bell-metal milking vessel, having golden horns, silver hooves, and scented with fine silk and linen..."
Having honored a Brāhmaṇa with perfumes and garlands, [he should give] a bed provided with coverlets and endowed with many flowers and fruits.
One should bind that [seat], which is occupied by all the gods, with both hands using a soft, smooth cord on the inside.
O you of excellent vows, he should then offer kusha grass, golden seeds, sesame seeds, and white mustard seeds with water, using this mantra:
The cow, who consists of all the gods, who milks forth [all desires], who likewise consists of all the worlds,
who is the cause of all the worlds, and who is saluted by all the gods.

"I bestow this great being for the sake of inexhaustible merit. *Oṃ hrīṃ! Homage, O Blessed One! Mother of Brahmā, Sister of Viṣṇu, Deity of Rudra, Deliverer from all sins! Remember your true form! O Iḍā, at the end of Iḍā; O Havyā, O Cāndrī, O Ghṛtimatī, O Sarasvatī, O Suśrutā! Come, come! Huṃ! Do, do! O you who consist of all the worlds! Come, arrive, arrive! Svāhā!* This is the mantra for the "Cow's Ear" (dhenukarṇa) recitation. Both the recipient and the giver go to heaven.
"If it is remembered by Karṇa previously, O best of the twice-born," so it is said in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Having thus given that cow, wherever one may be born..."
Wheresoever she may go, she forcibly delivers living beings;
having gone to the heavenly world, a man rejoices like an immortal.
Born as a human by her, he becomes possessed of a thousand cows, endowed with great strength,
handsome, wealthy, and blessed with many sons.

*Dukūla* is silk (*patrorṇa*). *Kṣauma* is cloth made from the bark of the flax plant (*atasī*). "Perfumed and covered" refers to her praise, beginning with the words "occupied by the gods. The meaning is that one should bind [her] with both hands; "with a rope" means with a cord. In the *Mahābhārata*:
"Having honored the twice-born and having saluted them on the following morning, one who is firm in his vows should present the *rohiṇī* cow for the purpose of giving."
And one should employ the invocation: "O Samaṅgā Bahulā! and so forth.
In the Brahmapurāṇa:
One should give a cow to a householder Brahmin who is well-versed in the Vedas—
a cow whose horns are adorned with gold and which is decorated with cloth and bells.
O King, by giving a cow with a bronze milking vessel along with a sacrificial fee, one delivers seven generations from hell and shall attain heaven.

In the Mahābhārata: When one’s livelihood is failing or when one is suffering excessively—for the sake of agriculture, for the purpose of a fire-sacrifice, upon childbirth, for the sake of a teacher, or for the increase of the lineage—one should indeed give a cow; such is the distinguished time.
Aṅgiras said:
A cow should be given to one who is learned in the Vedas, especially so;
she indeed delivers all those [ancestors], seven times seven and seven more.
In the Nandipurāṇa: "That cow, when given to an unworthy recipient, leads the donor to hell and causes the recipient,
along with twenty-one generations of his lineage, to fall."
In the case of vessels, those who maintain the sacred fire are foremost among the internal [recipients] and are pure;
likewise, the deities are foremost in the gift of a cow—for this is indeed the highest [form of giving].
In the Mahābhārata:
"O lord of the earth, there is nothing superior to the gift of a cow. For a cow acquired by righteous means, when given away, indeed delivers one's entire lineage."
O Lord, those who give a cow cross over whatever difficult passages there may be, as well as the evil deeds they have committed and their very sins.

Having fasted for three nights, one should then give cows, satisfied and accompanied by their calves, to those who have been gratified; having given them along with the customary offerings, one should subsist on cow's milk products for three days while observing the excellent vows.
Jābāla says: He who gives a cow, unasked for, to the Agnīdhra priest for the purpose of the oblation, has undoubtedly given the earth filled with all wealth three times over. (1.204)
Now he states the fruit [of this gift]:
"The giver of this attains heaven for years equal in number to its hairs.
One who gives this cow, described according to the aforementioned method, attains—that is, obtains—heaven for as many years as there are hairs upon it.
He states the excellence of the fruit resulting from the quality [of the cow]:
"If she is a Kapila cow, she delivers even the seventh generation of her lineage. (1.205)

If a cow of the kind described above is given as a *kapilā*, she delivers the giver from hell for seven generations of ancestors. By the use of the word "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*), she also endows the giver with the previously mentioned fruit. Saṃvarta says:
"A single *kapilā* is considered equal to the gift of ten cows."

Bṛhaspati says: By giving away a tawny cow with golden horns, silver hooves, accompanied by a cloth, a bronze vessel, and clarified butter, along with her calf, one rescues seven generations of one's lineage.
In the Ādipurāṇa: "Those who bestow a tawny cow (kapilā), covered with cloth and well-adorned,
with horns plated in gold, hooves of silver, and beautified by a bell around her neck and a tail-ring;..."
O observer of noble vows, he who gives a thousand cows, or even a single tawny cow (kapilā), covered with white cloth and accompanied by the sound of ringing bells, [attains great merit].
Long ago, Brahmā, the best among the knowers of Brahman,
declared that there are as many hairs on the body of Kapila as there are pores of the skin.
He who gives a black cow, covered with cloth and well-adorned, rejoices in heaven for as many thousands of millions of years.
And by giving according to the prescribed rule to the twice-born, one does not see the world of Yama;
as a giver of longevity, health, and sovereignty, one shall obtain all desires.
Adorned with golden horns and ornaments, beautiful with silver hooves,
covered with cloth, and auspicious— such a cow should be given to an excellent yogin.
And hear now the fruit of the merit for one who gives a white cow:
whatever sin has been committed since birth, whether on the mother's side or the father's side;
Just as water drawn up by the hand vanishes at that very moment,
so too one is purified in every way merely by the words, "I give land here. (Mahābhārata 298)
Having given away a tawny milch-cow that has a calf of the same color,
which is well-behaved and provided with clothing, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
One with a calf of the same age and similar appearance, well-behaved and of good character— by giving such a milch cow, a Rohiṇī, whose calf is of equal age,
covered with cloth and endowed with excellent qualities, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having given a white, milch cow with a calf of the same color,
well-behaved and covered with cloth, one is glorified in the world of Indra.
Having given away a brindled, milk-yielding cow that has a calf of the same color,
one who is firm in her vows and covered with cloth is glorified in the world of Soma.
Having given away a cow, the color of wind-blown dust, accompanied by her calf, fulfilling all desires,
and provided with clothing, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu.
Having grasped the tail of the cow with his very pure hand,
the householder or the Brahmin learned in the Vedas should cause that acceptance [of the gift] to be recited.
The white cow bestows enjoyment and liberation; the one born [as such] destroys sin.
The black cow should be known as the bestower of heaven, and the tawny cow increases one's lineage.
The red [form] should be known as the bestower of beauty; the yellow, the destroyer of poverty;
the dark-brown, the bestower of sons; and the blue, the increaser of dharma.
"A tawny cow destroys all sins, and one of various colors bestows liberation.
Thus ends the gift of a cow. 1.205.
He states that the gift of a cow with her calf (*ubhayamukhī*) is the means for attaining specific results along with the prescribed ritual procedure:
"A donor who gives a cow with her calf according to the previously mentioned rite obtains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on her body. (1.206)

One with its calf is "savatsā"; its hairs are "savatsā-romāṇi. A cow that has given birth half-way (ardhaprasūtā), called "ubhayatomukhī," when given away along with those [hairs]—that is, equal to them in number—saves both families up to the seventh generation. By giving—that is, bestowing—them according to the previously mentioned procedure, one attains heaven for as many *yugas* as there are hairs. A *yuga* consists of four thousand years by divine reckoning. || 1.206 ||
[299] As long as the two feet and the face of the calf are visible within the womb, for that long the cow is to be known as the earth, so long as she does not release the fetus. 1.207.

As long as the two feet and the mouth of the calf, while it is being born, are visible in the birth canal, for that duration the cow is to be known as the Earth, until the joy of the womb has ceased. Consequently, by the gift of such a cow, the donor obtains the fruit of a gift of the Earth. Following the rule that "one should give [the cow] with both heads," Cyavana states:

The time for its gift is the time of birth; it does not wait for any other time. All auspicious times—including the *vyatīpāta*, the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the solstices (*ayana*), the *ṣaḍaśītimukha*, the *viṣṇupada*, and others ending with eclipses—are suitable. At that very moment, having approached a distinguished Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, character, truthfulness, purity, conduct, and the qualities of noble birth, and who has been known for a long time, the donor should prostrate and say: "I am exceedingly distressed and afraid of this bottomless and shoreless ocean of *saṃsāra*. O Master, having found you, a worthy recipient of gifts, please accept this out of a desire to favor me, and not out of a desire for wealth—thereby delivering ten ancestors before me, ten descendants after me, and myself. The donor should then address him with the mantra: "Thou art the great earth, the bearer of all, the cow of plenty... (*tvaṃ mahīm avaniṃ viśvadhenām*, RV 3.6.16). When he has departed, the donor should kindle the fire and satisfy the gods, the ancestors, the rivers, the mountains, the trees, the oceans, the *nāgas*, and the plants with their respective mantras. These are the words of those mantras: [Mantras follow... ...these are the words of those mantras. One should give according to one's ability, as much as one can afford. Having given, one should perform the *svastyayana* rite. Then, having fed the Brāhmaṇas, one should dismiss them with the words, "May you be satisfied. [Thus for the gods:

Desiring, bring the desiring ancestors here to eat the oblation."
Thus for the ancestors.
O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Paruṣṇī, Asiknī, Marudvṛdhā, Vitastā, Ārjīkīyā, and Suṣomā: accept this hymn of praise and listen!
[Thus regarding the rivers:
Pressed by the stones and prepared for us by our prayers, the pure one illuminates the two worlds, his parents;
he flows through the sheep’s wool as if through a strainer, a stream of honey swelling day after day. [300]

"O Lord of the Forest, grow with a hundred shoots; may we grow with a thousand shoots."
You, whom this sharpened axe has led forth for great good fortune.
[Thus for the trees.
Those whose chief is the ocean, purifying themselves from the midst of the flood, they go forth without resting;
those which Indra, the bull, the wielder of the thunderbolt, dug out—may those divine waters protect me here.
[RV 5.4.16] Thus for the oceans: Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the strike of the bowstring;
the hand-guard, knowing all the ways, as a man, may it protect the man from every side.

"Honey the winds blow for the one who follows the cosmic order; honey the rivers flow;
may the plants be sweet for us."
[RV 1.6.18] Thus for the plants. These are the mantras for the deities and others ending with the plants. Following that, one should satisfy the earth with mantras addressed to the earthly realm:
"I praise Heaven and Earth for primordial consciousness; Agni, the radiant heat, for the journey and for the sacrifice."
With those aids by which you quicken Kāra for his share in the battle, come hither with them, O Aśvins.

The ruddy one has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, four-footed,
eight-footed, nine-footed, possessing a thousand syllables in the highest heaven.

He has made the gods absorbed in the divine by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the sacred by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the holy by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the sublime by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the transcendent by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the ineffable by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the immeasurable by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in the boundless by the offering. He has made the gods absorbed in

One should cause these and other such benedictions (*svastyayana*) to be recited. Now they cite its efficacy: "Even for one who has consumed forbidden food, drunk what should not be drunk, or for a slayer of a Brahmin, a slayer of a mother, or a slayer of a father, this [rite] purifies immediately—even for one who has gone to his teacher’s wife, his own daughter, his master’s wife, his mother, his mother’s sister, his father’s sister, his maternal uncle’s wife, his sister, his sister’s daughter, his pupil’s wife, or any other woman who should not be approached—he should give to a Brāhmaṇa the 'double-headed' [cow] along with her appurtenances (*parikara*). The appurtenances should consist of gold, silver, gems, fields, grain, garments, liquids, salt and other salts, sandalwood and other perfumes; or half of that, or a quarter, or even his entire property together with her, he should give to the Brāhmaṇa for the sake of liberation from the great sins (*mahāpātaka*)."
In the Matsya Purāṇa,
the Fish [Incarnation] said:
"One adorned with golden horns, silver hooves, and a tail decorated with pearls..."
O King, [he gave] a cow with a bronze milking vessel and her calf to an eminent brahmin.
By giving a cow while she is in the process of calving, one obtains a great fruit of merit for as long as the calf remains within the womb and has not yet emerged from it.
To that extent, the earth—including its mountains, forests, and groves—is to be understood as the "cow";
the earth bounded by the four oceans becomes given, of this there is no doubt.
O lord of men, for as many hairs as there are on the cow and her calf,
for that many series of yugas he is honored in the world of the gods.
He who gives abundant sacrificial fees will undoubtedly deliver his fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers from hell.
Flowing with ghee and milk, auspicious, and having curd and milk-rice for their mud,
these rivers grant all desired objects wherever he may go.
For him, O King, Goloka and Brahmaloka are easily attained.
And women with faces like the moon, with complexions equal to refined gold,
with large hips, breasts, and slender waists, and with eyes like lotuses, serve him incessantly.
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
Having fashioned a cow with golden horns and silver hooves,
and having placed gold or even silver into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa...
Then, one should place the tail of a tawny cow in the hand of the Brahmin;
having placed water in his hand, he, endowed with purity, should cause him to recite the formula.
By him, the earth—including its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves, and filled with jewels—would have been given; of this there is no doubt.
By this gift, which is equal to the gift of the earth, a human being goes,
together with his ancestors who have been delivered, to that supreme state called Viṣṇu.
One who steals the property of a Brahmin, a killer of cows, a destroyer of the embryo, one who divulges secrets, one joined with great sins (mahāpātaka), a deceiver, and a defiler of Brahmins;
Even one who reviles Brahmins and defames their sacred rites—
though thus possessed of such a sin— is purified by the gift of cows.
And whoever should give a cow with two faces covered in abundant gold,
on that day he should pass the time subsisting on milk-rice or on milk alone.
O beautiful woman, [I shall give] a thousand pieces of gold, or even half of that;
or half of that again, or a hundred, or fifty, or even half of that.
One should give according to one's ability, free from stinginess regarding wealth;
please accept this cow with two faces, and may you truly be my protector.
"May my lineage be pure; be ever a bringer of well-being.
Having recited "Irāvatī dhenumatī," one should then recite the *devy-ūna*.
I accept this cow specifically for the sake of my family;
may there be constant well-being for you, and may there be auspiciousness at the end—salutations, salutations!
"O Earth, I entrust this to you; I receive it from you. 'Who has given this to whom?'—thus one should release the Brāhmaṇa and lead the cow and the wealth to his home."
Thus ends the gift of the "two-faced" cow.
Having given a cow in any manner whatsoever—whether it be a milch cow or even one that is not milch—the donor is honored in heaven, provided the animal is healthy and free from affliction. (1.208)

In whatever manner—namely, by giving a cow, whether it be a milch-cow (*dhenu*) or not a milch-cow (*adhenu*), provided it is free from disease and not emaciated—one is honored and glorified in heaven. A *dhenu* is one that has recently calved; an *adhenu* is one that has not recently calved. "Not emaciated" means not thin.
On this point, the *Mahābhārata* states:
"One should not give a cow that is emaciated, or one without a calf, or one that is barren, or likewise one afflicted by disease."
One should certainly not give a cow that is crippled or exhausted to a Brāhmaṇa.
Likewise:
[one should not give] a cow that has already drunk water, eaten grass, been milked dry, or whose senses are impaired;
nor one that is frantic, maimed in limb, whose calf has died, or that eats excessively.
One who has hair on her clothes, whose excrement or bones are found [on them], who is a flesh-eater, who suffers from a running sore,
who is bald, who is a *punarnavā* (reborn), who gives birth to twins, or whose breasts constantly leak.
And one should not give a bull that has defects to the Brāhmaṇas.

The state of being grown is indicated by such factors as having drunk water and having eaten grass. "Khalāḥ" means those of bad character. Regarding a single act such as the gift of a cow, some scriptures describe the fruit as great while others describe it as small; this must be determined based on the abundance or scarcity of the virtues of the giver, the recipient, the place, and the time. As Manu says:
"Depending especially upon the excellence of the recipient and also upon the presence of faith, one obtains the fruit of a gift—whether small or large—after death."

In connection with the procedure for the gift of a cow, the rules for the "molasses-cow" (guḍadhenu) and others are now illustrated. Regarding this, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states: "I shall now proclaim the form and the fruit of the rite of the molasses-cow, which destroys all sins."
One should place a black antelope skin, four cubits in length with its neck pointing eastward,
upon the ground that has been smeared with cow dung, after carefully spreading darbha grass over it.
A cubit is the length of an *aratni*.
One should likewise prepare a small antelope skin for the calf;
one should position the cow facing east with her feet toward the north, together with her calf.
[The donor] should face the east and have his head toward the east; the calf should likewise be positioned. An excellent jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu) should always consist of four bhāras [of sugar];
one should make the calf from one bhāra, while the middling [cow] is recorded as being two bhāras.
A calf may be given for half a load;
however, it is said that a calf may also be given for a full load, or as a fourth part, according to the extent of one's household wealth.
A hundred *pala*s make a *tulā*, and twenty *tulā*s make a *bhāra*. Thus it has been said:
"A *tulā* is a hundred *pala*s in the feminine gender; a *bhāra* would be twenty *tulā*s.
The cow and calf, with their mouths full of ghee, are clothed in white thread and garments."
They had ears like oyster shells and feet like sugarcane; their eyes were like pearls from oyster shells; they possessed veins like white threads and were clad in white woolen blankets.
Their backs were like copper balls, their hair was white as yak-tail whisks,
they possessed a pair of eyebrows like coral, and were endowed with breasts of fresh butter.
Their tails were covered in linen, their udders were made of bell-metal, and their pupils were of sapphire;
the "pupils" (tārake) refer to the central parts of the eyes.
Their horns were adorned with gold and their hooves were joined with silver.
The two teeth, joined with various fruits, are the nostrils and the casket of fragrance;
having fashioned them thus, one should worship them with incense and lamps.
May that Goddess, who is the prosperity of all beings and who dwells among the gods,
dispel my sin in the form of this cow.
May she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu, and Svāhā in the fire,
and the power of the Moon, Sun, and Indra— may she, in the form of a cow, be for our prosperity.
May that cow who possesses the splendor of the four-faced Brahmā, the splendor of Kubera the giver of wealth,
and the splendor of the world-protectors, grant me my desires.
She who is the *svadhā* of the foremost ancestors and the *svāhā* of the sacrificial eaters—
the cow that removes all sins— therefore, grant me peace.
Having thus addressed that cow, one should present it to the Brāhmaṇa;
this is the procedure for all cows that is taught here.
O lord of men, I shall describe the nature and the names of those ten cows which, when recited, destroy all evil.
The first is the jaggery-cow; likewise, the second is the sesame-cow;
the third is the ghee-cow; and the fourth is the water-cow.
The milk-cow is renowned, and likewise the honey-cow;
the seventh is the sugar-cow, and the eighth is the curd-cow.
The ninth [cow] is the cow of flavor, and the tenth should be according to its actual form;
for the liquid cows there should be jars, but for the others, there should be heaps [of grain].
A *kumbha* contains five hundred and twelve *palas*. As it has been said:
[305] "Two *palas* are considered a *prasṛta*; double that is a *kuḍava*.
Four *kuḍavas* make a *prastha*, and four *prasthas* make an *āḍhaka*."
Four of those *āḍhakas* are declared by the wise to be one *droṇa*. A *kumbha* is two *droṇas*, a *śūrpa* is [the same], and a *khārī* is sixteen *droṇas*.
In this regard, some men desire even a golden cow;
others, as well as great sages, [desire one] made of fresh butter and jewels.
This very same procedure should be followed, and these are recorded as the necessary implements;
accompanied by the mantras and the invocation, all of these are to be used at every festival.
These [gifts], which bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation, should be given according to one's faith;
all of them have been described by me to you in the context of the jaggery-cow (guḍadhenu).
All [these] bestow the fruits of sacrifices without exception, remove all sins, and are auspicious;
especially so during the solstices, the equinoxes, or on the meritorious occasion of Vyatīpāta.
Gifts such as the "jaggery-cow" (guḍadhenu) and others should be bestowed on festival days such as solar and lunar eclipses.
Thus concludes the Cow of Virtues (*guṇadhenu*). Now follows the Cow of Sesame (*tiladhenu*). Vasiṣṭha, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*, says:
"I shall describe the Cow of Sesame, which is for the propitiation of Keśava."
O Lord of Men, she becomes truly given when the supreme rite for her is performed.

Having given this, even one who has killed a Brahmin, a cow, or his father; one who has violated the teacher’s bed; one who has set fire to a house; one who has administered poison; or even one devoted to every kind of sin [is purified].
Whether one is tainted by a great sin (mahāpātaka) or tainted by secondary sins (upapātaka),
one is liberated from all evils and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
On a surface of the earth smeared with unguents and covered with cloth and skins,
one should fashion a cow made of sesame seeds, adorned with all kinds of jewels.
One should provide a beautiful cow with golden horns, silver hooves, and a sense of smell for fragrances;
she should have a tongue that relishes sweet food, possess excellent qualities, and be provided with a rope and a blanket.
One should fashion [the image] with feet like sugarcane, a copper-colored back, eyes of pearl,
ears adorned with excellent leaves, and auspicious teeth resembling fruit.
One should fashion a cow with a garland as its tail, provided with breasts made of fresh butter,
adorned with charming fruits and edibles, and furnished with jewels and pearls.
One should prepare it with one *droṇa* of sesame seeds and one *āḍhaka* for the calf;
it should be covered with a pair of auspicious cloths and provided with a beautiful parasol.
Having fashioned [the image] endowed with such a configuration, one possessed of faith should give it away with a bronze milking vessel, saying: "May Keśava be pleased."
Having correctly recited it according to the prescribed rite and having offered it with this, O lord of men,
one is completely liberated from all sins, [delivering] one's father along with one's grandfather.
Likewise, one should worship the great-grandfather and the four preceding ancestors;
as well as oneself, one’s son, grandson, great-grandson, and the three below him.
O protector of the earth, the man who gives a sesame-cow is delivered [from saṃsāra];
and he who receives it according to the prescribed rite likewise obtains such a fruit.
Likewise, there are fourteen [kalpas] for those men who give, who rejoice in the giving,
and who behold the sesame-cow being given away.
Those wise ones as well, being free from all demerit, go to the supreme goal— [to one who is] peaceful, of excellent conduct, and likewise free from envy.
A man should give a sesame-cow to a righteous person who is complete in the Vedas;
he who subsists on sesame for three nights and then bestows that sesame-cow [obtains great merit].
Having stayed there for one night, O lord of men, that man eats sesame seeds;
for him, whose sins have been purified by that gift, O King, there is great merit.

"Even more meritorious than the Cāndrāyaṇa vow is that consumption of sesame seeds. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the specific measurement of the *tiladhenu* (sesame-cow), the *Padmapurāṇa* states: "The cow should consist of sixteen *āḍhaka*s of sesame, and the calf should consist of four."
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*: Vinītāśva said:
"O lord of men, listen now to the ritual procedure for cows."
I shall explain their ritual procedure as well as whatever specific characteristics they possess.
On the surface of the earth, which has been smeared [with cow dung] and covered with a black antelope skin and kuśa grass,
having prepared a bedding of cloth, one should place a cow there.
Having placed the cow facing north together with her calf, the wise man should fashion the cow from sixteen *prasthas* and the calf from four.
Its feet are said to consist of sugarcane stalks, its teeth of fruit;
its tongue is made of flour, and its nose is said to consist of fragrance.
Having made the face with jaggery and the two eyes with pearls,
with ears made of excellent leaves, the back is traditionally said to be made of copper.
Its tail should be made of hemp, its hair of small pearls,
and one should fashion its blanket with white woolen cloths, O King.
One should fashion necklaces of various forms from fruits,
and the breasts with fresh butter, adorning her with all ornaments.
Having covered [the cow] with gold-tipped horns, silver hooves, and endowed with the five jewels,
one should then cover her with *darbha* grass and cloths.
Having covered it, O Indra among kings, and sprinkled it with sandalwood,
one should worship it with merits and honor it with the scents of incense.
Having thus prepared such [an offering] for that most excellent of the twice-born, who is a worthy recipient,
who observes good vows, possesses virtuous conduct, and especially maintains the sacred fires;
O King, such a sesame-cow should be given to one who is wise, of virtuous conduct, and learned in the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O Indra among kings, she is to be worshipped and praised in every way with this mantra:
"Oṃ! She who is the Lakṣmī of all beings, and she who resides among the gods."
May that Goddess, in the form of a cow, dispel my sin— she who is Rudrāṇī, ever dear to Śaṅkara, and who dwells within the body.
In that form, may that goddess grant me peace—
she who is Lakṣmī upon the chest of Viṣṇu, and Svāhā of the Fire-god.
May that power of the Moon, the Sun, and Indra, which takes the form of a cow, be for our prosperity;
may that Lakṣmī who belongs to the Four-faced One, and that Lakṣmī who belongs to the Giver of Wealth, [be for our prosperity].
May that Lakṣmī who belongs to the world-protectors be a cow granting boons to me;
may she who is Svadhā for the foremost of the ancestors, and Svāhā even for the enjoyers of the sacrifice.
The cow removes all sins; therefore, grant me peace.
May food be produced for me instantly, as well as drink and all flavors.
"O sesame-cow offered to a twice-born, fulfill our desires!"—
this is the mantra for the gift.
Having thus addressed that cow, one should present it to the Brāhmaṇa.
Having recited this, one should indeed give him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
[308] Having had the gold recited first, one should cause it to be given according to one's ability;
one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth when one possesses the means.
Now follows the mantra for the recipient:
"O Goddess, I accept you especially for the sake of my family;
nourish me with all my desires, O sesame-cow; obeisance be to you."
Thus ends the section on the sesame-cow. Now follows the gift of the ghee-cow. Vasiṣṭha, in the Viṣṇudharma, says:
"In the absence of sesame seeds, one who is restrained in his vows should likewise give a ghee-cow."
O King, listen now with a single-minded focus to the procedure by which that [is accomplished].
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, the Lord of the World, as before with flowers, perfumes, incense, and other offerings, the man [should perform] the consecration with ghee and milk.
Having fasted for a day and night, one should consecrate the deity named Ghṛtārcis with a jar of cow’s clarified butter, adorned with flowers and garlands.
It should be joined with a bronze vessel and a pair of white cloths,
together with the Hiraṇyagarbha [image], and adorned with gems, coral, and pearls.

The *garbha* means the middle; the meaning is that the jar is accompanied by gold situated in the middle, as well as by gems and other such items. One should make the two feet out of sugarcane, the hooves likewise out of silver, the two eyes out of gold, and the two horns out of *aguru* wood.

On the side made of the seven precious substances, one should fashion a cloth covering and a new woolen blanket; one should make the fragrance with aloe-wood and camphor, and the breasts out of fruit.
Likewise, one should smear the tongue with sugar, the mouth with jaggery and milk,
the tail with linen thread, and the body hairs with white mustard seeds.
Endowed with faith, one should fashion a back made of copper;
O lord of men, having thus conceived the form of the ghee-cow.
In the same way, through conceptual construction, one should conceive of the ghee and the calf as belonging to the cow.
The calf should be made with one-fourth the size of the cow, for it is observed to be so elsewhere;
having mentally fashioned that cow as a highly fortunate Brahmin whose radiance is like ghee,
one should then, being self-restrained, present it to him.
O best of the twice-born, accept this for my benefit;
may the Lord of Gods, the Supreme Person whose flame is ghee, be pleased with me.
Having recited this, O lord of men, one should give a cow to a Brahmin,
fashioned according to the proper proportions with ghee, jewels, and gold.
Having given [this] and stayed for one night while subsisting on ghee, O lord of men, one is liberated from all sins; now hear the fruit of that gift.
In all those most meritorious worlds, rivers flowing with ghee and milk arise, where the mud consists of milk-rice (pāyasa). Therein one is reborn.
After his father’s passing, he leads seven generations of his ancestors and those who come after them; O King, freed from all stain, he leads them to those celestial worlds.
O best of kings, this prosperity has been described for those with desires;
men who give a cow of ghee without desire go to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the section on the ghee-cow.
Now, the water-cow. Vasiṣṭha, in the Viṣṇudharma, says:
"I shall describe the water-cow, by the gift of which Viṣṇu is pleased."
The god of gods, Hṛṣīkeśa, the giver of all, the creator of all beings.
O tiger among men, [he should offer] a water-pot filled with gold and silver,
containing gems within, and provided with all varieties of grain grown in the village.
Covered with a pair of white garments and adorned with sprouts of dūrvā grass,
it is joined with kuṣṭha, māṃsī, puru, uśīra, vālaka, and kāka.
He was accompanied by a vessel of *priyaṅgu* seeds, wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*),
provided with sandals and an umbrella, and seated upon a mat of *darbha* grass.
O King, it was prepared with four sesame vessels in the four directions,
covered at the opening with a vessel of curd mixed with ghee and honey.
Having fasted and honored Vāsudeva, the Lord of Waters,
with flowers, incense, and offerings according to his means, he should do so with due respect.
Having mentally conceived the water-cow and worshipped that jar,
one should likewise worship the calf made of water that has been prepared.
Having thus worshipped Govinda along with the water-cow and her calf,
he— wearing white garments, tranquil, free from passion, and devoid of envy— should proceed.
O Indra among kings, one should give [this] to a twice-born for the sake of pleasing Keśava, who reclines upon the waters;
may Keśava, the source of the universe, who reclines upon the waters, be pleased with me.
O Lord of the Earth, whoever should offer [this] to a Brahmin after having recited it,
he must thereafter subsist on uncooked food for one day and night.
O lord of men, by giving a water-cow according to this rite,
one obtains all delights, both those that are divine and those that are human.
When a water-cow is given, there is no doubt that men will enjoy bodily health and the perpetual pacification of all ailments.
Thus ends the ritual procedure for the water-cow. Now follows the ritual procedure for the salt-cow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O Kṛṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who are proficient in all the scriptures!
Tell me here that which is proclaimed as the most excellent among gifts.
By giving this gift, all other gifts indeed become perfected;
there shall be the fulfillment of all desires and the destruction of all evil.
O you of noble vows, tell me that expiation and purification.
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen, O King, I shall describe the most excellent of all gifts,
known as the salt-cow (lavaṇadhenu), which grants all desires to men.
Having given this, even one who has killed a Brahmin, a cow, or his father; one who has violated the teacher’s bed;
a betrayer of trust; one of cruel soul; or even one devoted to every kind of sin [is purified].
He is liberated, of this there is no doubt, and he goes to the world of Śiva;
endowed with auspicious cattle and wealth, long-lived, and unconquered.
A man is born in this world endowed with all his desires;
O Indra among kings, I shall now describe the ritual procedure for the preparation of salt.
Having smeared the ground with cow dung and spread a layer of *darbha* grass,
one should lay out a sheepskin facing the eastern direction and remain seated thereon.
