Having covered it with cloth, a wise man should fashion a cow;
one who possesses great wealth may do so with a full āḍhaka measure, while one of limited means may use less.
She should be made with horns of gold, hooves of silver, feet of sugarcane, and breasts of fruit;
her tongue should be made of sugar, and she should likewise possess a nose for smelling fragrances.
One should fashion her two ears from oyster shells born within the belly of the ocean;
one should provide two horns from sandalwood wood and place barley grains in her mouth.
One should place sesame seeds on the heels and wheat as well, according to one's ability;
in this manner, one should provide the seven grains as they may be available.
He should place a woolen blanket around his neck with a silk thread, likewise a small umbrella on his back, a copper vessel on his buttocks, and a lump of molasses at his anus.
One should place a cloth on the tail, threads at the region of the udders,
honey at the region of the vulva, and one endowed with fruit on all sides.
Having thus properly established the state consisting of the essence and the crop,
a person should also place the *vatsaka* in a measure of one-fourth part.
Having thus worshipped the cow with garlands, garments, and ornaments,
and having bathed, performed the worship of the deity, and honored the Brahmins;
Having given a cow along with a sacrificial fee to a well-behaved Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtuous conduct, accompanied by his son and wife, O King.
Good fortune, supreme intelligence, health, and all forms of prosperity come to men by giving a cow made of mercury; of this there is no doubt.
And his residence in heaven is certain for as long as the dissolution of all beings.
Having fashioned this "flavor-cow" with a load of woolen cloth and blankets for its neck,

a measure of salt for its udder, and a deerskin upon its back, and having given it to a brahmin according to the prescribed rite, one shall dwell in this world endowed with all the happiness found among cows.
Thus ends the procedure for the salt-cow according to the *Bhaviṣyottara*. Now follows the procedure for the sugar-cow.
Vinītāśva said:
O King, listen now to the account of the sugar-cow exactly as it is:
on a surface of the earth smeared with unguents, upon which a black antelope skin and kuśa grass have been spread.
O King, a cow made of sugar weighing four bhāras is always declared by the virtuous to be the best, with the calf being one-fourth of that weight.
Half of that is said to be the middle [size], and the smallest is by a fourth part;
likewise, O child, a person should fashion the calf by a fourth part.
Then, one should fashion a calf with one-fourth of eight hundred [palas];
one should have the cow made according to one's own capacity, so that it does not cause distress to oneself.
Having placed all the seeds on every side in the four directions,
[the cows] had golden faces and horns and eyes of pearl.
The face should be made with jaggery, and likewise the tongue from flour;
it should be provided with a blanket of silk thread and equipped with bells and ornaments.
Her feet are made of sugarcane, her hooves of silver, and her udders of fresh butter;
she has ears adorned with excellent leaves and is decorated with white chowries.
Equipped with the five jewels, provided with darbha grass and wool,
accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and properly adorned with perfumes and flowers.
Adorned with such ornaments and covered above with garments,
and having decorated it with perfumes and flowers, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
To one who is learned in the Vedas, poor, of virtuous conduct, and wise;
especially to one who knows the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences and maintains the sacred fire.
It should be given to one who is free from envy, and certainly not to one possessed by malice;
likewise during the solstices, the equinoxes, the Vyatīpāta yoga, and the Ṣaṇmukha yoga.
During these meritorious times, one should cause [the gift] to be given even by chance.
"Six-faced" means having sixty-eight faces. "Yadṛcchayā" means according to whatever desire one has; the lengthening of the vowel is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
Having seen a worthy recipient, a twice-born man who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), one should welcome him at home and offer [the gift] to such a person, presenting it by the tail-end.
The donor should stand facing either the east or the north;
having positioned the cow facing the east, he should place the calf to her north.
At the time of giving, however, one should recite those mantras and present [the gift],
having clothed the brahmin deity with rings, earrings, and head-ornaments.
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one’s own ability, avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth;
and one should place the fee, along with sandalwood, flowers, and fragrance, into the hand.
One should offer a cow and must not look at its face;
one should subsist on sugar for one day, and the Brāhmaṇas should dwell there for three days.
The cow removes all sins and bestows all desires;
one whose every wish is fulfilled is born [thereby], of this there is no doubt.
They too, beholding it being given, go to the supreme goal;
so also the person who hears this with devotion or even reads it.
He is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a sugar-cow (*śarkarādhenu*) among the duties of giving in the *Bhaviṣyottara*.
Now, regarding the great gifts (*mahādāna*),
[the following is] from the *Matsyapurāṇa*.
The sages said: "Acquisition of wealth by righteous means, its increase, and its protection,
as well as its bestowal upon worthy recipients, is taught in all the scriptures."
"By what means, O dear one, does a wise and wealthy man of noble mind become one who has accomplished his purpose?
Tell me in detail regarding the giving of great gifts."
Sūta said:
I shall fully proclaim that unsurpassed great gift which was declared by the powerful Viṣṇu among the duties of giving.
It causes the destruction of all sins for human beings and destroys bad dreams—
that which was proclaimed on earth by Vāsudeva in sixteen ways.
It is meritorious, purifying, life-prolonging, auspicious, and the destroyer of all sins;
it is honored by the deities, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Hara, and others.
[314] But the foremost among all gifts is that known as the Tulāpuruṣa;
next is the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha, and after that, the Brahmāṇḍa.
The gift of the wish-fulfilling tree, the fifth being the gift of a thousand cows;
likewise the gift of the golden cow of plenty and the gift of the golden horse.
Likewise, the gift of a chariot with golden horses, as well as a chariot with golden elephants;
similarly, the gift of five ploughs, and likewise the gift of land.
The twelfth is the Viṣṇucakra, followed by the Kalpalatā;
then the gift of the seven oceans and likewise the Ratnadhenu.
In the same way, the jar of the great elements (mahābhūtaghaṭa) is proclaimed as the sixteenth;
the slayer of Śambara fashioned all of these in ancient times.
Then the Blessed Vāsudeva, Ambarīṣa, Bhārgava,
Kārtavīryārjuna, Rāma, Prahrāda, and Pṛthu as well.
Other rulers of the earth, such as Bharata and others, might perform some [great deeds],
because great gifts on this earth are accompanied by thousands of obstacles.
Any one of these tasks, by the grace of Vāsudeva,
cannot be accomplished otherwise on this earth, even by Śakra himself.
Therefore, having propitiated Govinda, Umāpati, and Vināyaka,
one should perform the principal act of the great gift, being approved by the Brahmins.
Janārdana, being thoroughly pleased with Manu, spoke this very thing;
I shall relate how it was said here, so listen, O best of sages.
Manu said:
"O Acyuta, tell me of those great gifts which are purifying and auspicious in this world, and which, being secret, ought to be bestowed."
Matsya said:
I shall duly describe to you, in their proper sequence, those sixteen divine great gifts which have not yet been mentioned.
This ritual of the Tulāpuruṣa is first prescribed for those [who perform it] during the auspicious solstices, equinoxes, Vyatīpāta yoga, or at the end of a day (the conjunction of planets).
At the beginnings of the Yugas, during eclipses, likewise at the beginnings of Manvantaras,
at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), on the day of Vaidhṛti, and on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days;
On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, on the twelfth days of the lunar fortnights, on the Aṣṭakā days, during sacrifices,
festivals, and weddings, and upon seeing a bad dream or a portentous marvel;
Or, when a worthy Brahmin is available, or wherever faith arises—
whether at a sacred ford (tīrtha), a temple, a cow-pen, or by a well, a grove, or a river.
Whether at home or in the forest, by a pond or a spring,
great gifts should be bestowed by one who fears the terrors of saṃsāra.
Since life is impermanent and wealth is exceedingly fickle,
one should practice the Dharma as if seized by the hair by Death.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
[one should prepare] a pit measuring sixteen aratnis, or ten or twelve cubits.
The wise and learned man should cause a mandala to be made with four auspicious faces;
the altar in the center should be seven cubits long, or otherwise five cubits.
In the middle of that, the wise man should construct an archway made of solid wood.
This archway is for the purpose of supporting the balance.
A wise man should construct four pillars in the four directions,
provided with excellent girdles and bases, and at the entrance, complete sacrificial pits equipped with ritual seats.
The offerings of sesame, clarified butter, incense, and flowers were exceedingly beautiful, each measuring the size of a hand.
Then, to the northeast, there should be an altar measuring one cubit for the worship of the lords of the gods, beginning with the planets;
there, the worship of Brahmā, Śiva, Acyuta, and Sūrya should be performed with fruits, garlands, and garments.

Banners of the colors of Lokeśvara should be placed all around, and in the center there should be a flagstaff equipped with small bells. At the gates, four archways (toraṇas) made from milky trees should also be constructed.
At the doors, two jars should be placed here, provided with fragrant incense, garments, and jewels;
they should be made from śāka, iṅgudī, sandalwood, devadāru, śrīparṇa, bilva, priyaka, or gold.
Having dug two pillars with a span of four cubits and made them firm, five cubits in height, the distance between them should be four cubits;
and the upper beam should be of the same dimension as those [pillars].
Its limb is of the same species as the pillar-tree;
and a balance of the same species, suspended by a golden beam in the middle and joined with a counterweight,
is four cubits in length, while its width is ten finger-breadths.
The balance should be made of gold, adorned with two iron rings and chains,
joined with gold and a jeweled garland, and enriched with flower garlands and ointments.
One should draw a wheel joined with the interior of a lotus on the ground, strewn with various powders and flowers;
and above it, one should place a five-colored canopy adorned with flowers and fruits.
Now, the twice-born who are knowers of the Vedas should be appointed—those endowed with handsome appearance, noble lineage, and good character;
those skilled in ritual procedures, eloquent, and well-disposed; and those preeminent among the twice-born who are born in the land of the Āryas.
And the teacher should be one who knows the meaning of the Vedas, born in a noble land, endowed with good character, noble lineage, and handsome appearance;
he should be devoted to the Purāṇas, exceedingly skillful, and possess a clear, profound, and sweet eloquence.
Clad in white garments, beautiful with earrings, golden threads, armlets, and neck-ornaments;
two experts in the Ṛgveda should be stationed to the east, and two experts in the Yajurveda should be appointed to the south.
Two twice-born men learned in the Sāma-veda should be stationed behind, and two learned in the Atharva-veda should be placed to the north;
[these are for the worship] of Vināyaka and the others, the planets, the world-protectors, the Vasus, Aṣṭakas, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts.
There should be four oblations for Brahmā, Acyuta, Īśa, and Arka-vanaspati, each with its own mantra;
likewise, their respective hymns (sūktas) should be recited in their proper sequence according to their nature.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the preceptor, accompanied by the sound of trumpets and taking the offerings of food, flowers, and incense,
shall invoke the lords of the worlds in their proper order with these mantras, joined by the patron of the rite.
Oṃ! Come, come! Vajradhara, Lord of the Gods, praised by all the immortals, Siddhas, and Sādhyas, fanned by a host of Apsarases—protect our sacrifice; homage be to you!
Oṃ, homage to Indra!
Oṃ, come, come, O carrier of oblations, lord of all the immortals, who are served on every side by the foremost of sages;
together with the host of the world of Tejovatī, protect my sacrifice, O Sage; homage be to you!
Oṃ, obeisance to Agni.
Oṃ, come, come, Vaivasvata, Dharmarāja, you whose divine form is worshipped by all the immortals!
Lord of the auspicious, inauspicious, joy, and the beautiful left [path], protect us for our welfare; we bow to you, our friend.
Oṃ, homage to Yama!
Oṃ, come, come, you who are the leader of the hosts of *rakṣasa*s, together with the multitudes of *vetāla*s and *piśāca*s!
Protect my sacrifice, O auspicious lord; you are the Lord of the World, O Blessed One—homage to you!

[317] Oṃ, obeisance to Nirṛti. Oṃ, come, come, O Parjanya, together with the hosts of water-deities, the oceans, and the great Apsarases; being praised by the lords of the Vidyādharas and the immortals, protect us, O Blessed One; homage to you!
Oṃ, salutation to Varuṇa.
Oṃ, come, come for the protection of my sacrifice, mounted upon a deer together with the hosts of Siddhas;
Lord of the vital breaths, ally of Kālakavi, accept this worship, O Blessed One, homage to you!
Oṃ, obeisance to Vāyu.
Oṃ, come, come, O Lord of Sacrifice! Perform the protection of the sacrifice together with the host of constellations.
Together with all medicinal herbs and the ancestors, accept this worship, O Blessed One; obeisance to you.
Oṃ, obeisance to Soma.
Oṃ, come, come, O Lord of the Universe, wielder of the trident, together with your excellent skull-topped staff and ascetic’s wand;
O Lord of the World, Lord of Beings, for the success of the sacrifice, accept this worship, O Blessed One, salutations to you!
Oṃ, homage to Īśāna!
Oṃ, come, come, O Lord of the Maruts, sustainer of the underworld, being sung of by Naga maidens and Kinnaras;
together with the host of Rākṣasas and the world of the immortals, protect our sacrifice, O Ananta!
Oṃ, homage to Ananta.
Oṃ, come, come, O Lord of the Universe, O Chief of Sages, together with the world, the ancestors, and the deities!
For our constant welfare, protect this sacrifice; you are the Grandsire, O Blessed One—homage to you!
Oṃ, salutation to Brahmā.
Whatever beings there are in the three worlds, both stationary and moving,
may they, together with Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the gods, grant me protection.
Gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas;
sages, Manus, cows, deities, and mothers as well.
"May all of you, filled with joy, perform protection at my sacrifice.
Having thus invoked the gods, he should give golden ornaments to the officiating priests.
And golden earrings, threads, bracelets,
as well as finger-rings, sacred threads, garments, and beds.
One should give double the amount of ornaments, clothing, and so forth to the preceptor;
meanwhile, the reciters should chant the Śāntika chapter in every direction.
The chapter on pacification is the hymn beginning with “śaṃ na indrāgnī.
Having fasted, they all performed the consecration in this manner.
One should have the Brahmins recite benedictions at the beginning, the end, and in the middle.
Then, having been bathed with auspicious sounds by the foremost of Veda-knowers,
he circumambulated [the image] three times and took handfuls of flowers in his joined palms.
Wearing white garlands and garments, he should consecrate that scale with the mantra:
"Homage to you, O power of all the gods; you are established in truth."
The Sustainer of the World, created by the Source of the Universe, has been made the witness;
on one side are all truths, and likewise hundreds of falsehoods.
O Tula, you have been established among those who perform righteous and unrighteous deeds for the welfare of the world;
you are proclaimed here as the standard of measure for all beings.
Lifting me up from saṃsāra, deliver me; homage be to you!
That god who is the lord there, the twenty-fifth principle (puruṣa).
O Goddess, he is established within you; therefore, salutation after salutation!
Oṃ, salutations, salutations to you, Govinda, known as Tulāpuruṣa!
"O Hari, having reached this auspicious time and performed this consecration, do you deliver us from this mire of saṃsāra."
Having again performed a circumambulation, the wise man, equipped with sword, shield, and armor, and adorned with all his ornaments, should mount that scale.
Then, having placed Dharmarāja together with the Soma-thread,
he sat gazing at the face of Hari with his two hands held in fists.
Then, other eminent brahmins should place upon the other side of the scale pure gold, equal to or exceeding [the weight of] the [other] items.
O Lord of Men, one who desires prosperity should perform [the rite] while standing upon the ground;
having remained there for a mere moment, he should then speak as follows.
Oṃ, salutations to you, the eternal witness of all beings;
O Goddess, you were created by the Grandfather, the Supreme Lord.
By you the entire great world—both moving and unmoving—is sustained;
you abide within the self of all beings. Salutations to you, the upholder of the universe!
[319] Then, having descended, one should first offer half to the preceptor;
thereafter, one should give the other half to the officiating priests, preceded by the offering of water.
One should present village-jewels to the preceptor and to the officiating priests;
having obtained their permission, one should likewise cause them to be given to others as well.
One should honor the poor, the helpless, and those distinguished by their virtues along with the Brahmins.
A wise man should not keep consecrated gold in his house for long.
Since it brings fear while persisting and causes sorrow and disease for men,
one attains abundant welfare by quickly taking possession of another's property.
Whoever performs the Tulāpuruṣa rite according to this procedure shall dwell in the station of a world-protector for the duration of each Manvantara.
Being honored by apsarases, he shall then go to the city of Viṣṇu by means of a celestial chariot, sun-bright and garlanded with networks of tinkling bells.
For as many as a hundred billion eons, he is honored in that world.
Through the exhaustion of his karma, he is once again born here on earth with his footstool anointed by the crest-jewels of the sovereign kings of monarchs;
endowed with faith, he becomes a performer of a thousand sacrifices, his majesty as a lamp surpassing that of all the world of earthly rulers.
He who, endowed with devotion, sees this being given away, or remembers it in another world, or recites it here in this world;
or he who hears it, reads it, or possesses that which is like the moon in form—he attains the abode cherished by the god Purandara.
Thus concludes the gift of the person on the scale (*tulāpuruṣadāna*). Regarding this, there are specific details from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*:
"In the center of that [area], one should have a beautiful altar constructed, one cubit in height."
Water-pots with sprouts at their openings should be placed at the four gates.
Endowed with the five jewels and placed upon seven kinds of grain; the five jewels are:
gold, diamond, sapphire, ruby, and pearl. Thus.
There are seven types of grain: those of the village, those of the forest, and those both of the village and the forest.
Rice, barley, wheat, sesame, and mustard—both varieties—as well as sugarcane and millet, are known as the village plants.
Veṇu, śyāmāka, nīvāra, jartila,
gavedhuka, āraṇyajā, and markaṭikā— these seven are the best kinds of grain for eating.
[320] "Aṇus, rājamāṣas, māṣas, mudgas, kodravas, kuhīnakas, and sahīnas—these seven are known as the intermediate pairs. Thus it is said. Furthermore:
On this very point, some sages maintain that there are sixteen officiating priests;
having first offered the two libations (āghāra) and the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga), the best of the twice-born [should proceed].
The oblation is said to be performed with one's own name preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *svāhā*.
Likewise,
according to this very same procedure, some desire it to be made of silver,
while others, the best among Brahmins, desire it to be made of camphor.
Likewise, on the third day of the bright fortnight, women proud of their beauty offer [the deity] with saffron, salt, and molasses.
In that case, one should cause the mantras or the fire-oblations to be offered in this very manner.

Thus ends the specific procedure for the gift of the balance (*tulādāna*). Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme great gift known by the name Hiraṇyagarbha, which destroys even the greatest sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day, as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift,
[he should provide] the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
Having fasted, the wise one should likewise perform the invocation of Lokeśa;
having performed the recitation for the auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*), he should likewise perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*).
Let the brahmins bring a beautiful golden vessel,
seventy-two finger-breadths in height, with a golden lotus in its interior.
The sickle and the needle are likewise praised when their width is reduced by one-third, they are shaped like a drum (muraja), and their ten edges are set with jewels.
A golden lotus stalk with its sheath, joined externally with the sun;
likewise, a golden covering for the navel and a sacred thread.
In the same way, one should place a golden staff and a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) at its side;
the lid should be shaped like a lotus and exceed [the base] by one finger-breadth all around.
Adorned with a string of pearls and provided with petals of ruby, it should be placed upon a drona measure of sesame seeds in the center of the altar; then one should worship it.
Then, with auspicious sounds and the resonance of Vedic chanting,
those who had mastered the Vedas bathed the site where all medicinal herbs and water were kept.
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with all ornaments,
and holding a handful of flowers, one should recite this mantra:
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha and to Hiraṇyakavaca;
homage again and again to the lord of the gods of the seven worlds, the sustainer of the universe.
The worlds, headed by Bhūrloka, are situated within your womb;
likewise are the gods beginning with Brahmā. Homage to you, the sustainer of the universe!
Salutations to you, the support of the worlds; salutations to you, the refuge of the worlds.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, within whose womb resides the Grandfather (Brahmā).
For you alone are the self of all beings, established within every single being.
"Therefore, deliver me from this entire ocean of suffering and saṃsāra.
Having thus addressed him, he entered into the midst of that [assembly] and sat facing north.
Having grasped both Dharmarāja and Caturmukha with his two fists.
Placing his head between his knees, he should remain for five breaths;
[this constitutes] the rites of conception (garbhādhāna), the male-making rite (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana).
Then those bulls among the twice-born should offer prayers for Hiraṇyagarbha with auspicious chanting; thereafter, the preceptor should cause him to rise.
They should perform the sixteen rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (jātakarman), as well as the others;
and having given the needle and other items to the guru, one should recite this mantra:
Oṃ, homage to Hiraṇyagarbha; indeed, homage to the womb of the universe.
Homage indeed to him who has become the abode of the world of moving and unmoving beings.
O best of immortals, I was previously born of a mortal mother;
O Lord, now that I have been conceived in your womb, I shall possess a divine body.
Then, with four pitchers, those bulls among the twice-born,
their limbs refreshed and adorned with all ornaments, should perform the ceremonial bath.
"By means of the mantra 'Devasya tvā,' as you stand upon the golden throne,
today we shall gaze upon the limbs of you who have been born."
"Live long and be happy with this divine body!
Then the wise man should present that Hiraṇyagarbha to them.
They should be honored with one's entire being, or many [others] may do so by his command;
there, one should offer all the ritual implements to the guru.
Wooden sandals, leather shoes, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a seat, a vessel, a village, or even a district— whatever else may be dear to him.
Whoever offers this gift of Hiraṇyagarbha on an auspicious day according to this rite is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
In the pure realms of the world-protectors, he shall dwell for the duration of a manvantara;
for as long as a hundred crores of kalpas, he is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Freed from the impurities of the Kali age, honored by hosts of Siddhas, and fanned by Apsarases with pure whisks,
even a single such person shall deliver his hundred ancestors, as well as his kinsmen— sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons— even if they are submerged in hell.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of Hiraṇyagarbha according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish [incarnation] said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme rite known as the Brahmāṇḍa."
That which is the best among all gifts, and the destroyer of great sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day, as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift,
[he should provide] the sacrificial priests, the assembly, the ritual materials, ornaments, and garments.
In the same way, one should perform the invocation of Lokeśa and likewise the consecration;
this should be done with [an image] weighing more than twenty palas and up to a thousand, according to one's capacity.
The wise one [should offer] a golden cosmic egg joined with two halves,
accompanied by the eight elephants of the quarters and endowed with the six Vedāṅgas.
Endowed with the eight world-protectors, with the four-faced one situated in the center,
possessing the peaks of Śiva, Acyuta, and Arka, and accompanied by Umā and Lakṣmī.
Containing the essence of the Vasus, Ādityas, and Maruts, and endowed with great jewels,
its length and breadth extend from one span up to a hundred finger-breadths.
One should place [the image], covered with silken cloth, upon a drona-measure of sesame seeds;
likewise, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around it:
śyāmāka, grain, barley, mung beans, sesame, rice, black gram, wheat, kodrava, horse gram, satīna, and peas.
And they say that the eighteenth [type] consists of chickpeas, peas, large beans, kidney beans, and millet, together with lentils.
To the east, one should place Ananta; Pradyumna to the southeast;
Prakṛti in the southern region; and after that, Saṃkarṣaṇa.
To the west, the four Vedas; beyond that, Aniruddha;
to the north, Agni; and beyond that, Hema-Vāsudeva.
A wise man should worship ten golden figures of Guda seated upon pedestals on all sides;
he should also place ten full water-jars wrapped in cloth.
Ten cows indeed should be given, along with gold, and milking vessels;
together with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and a mirror.

Having been bathed by eminent Veda-knowers at the conclusion of the fire-oblation and the consecration ceremony with various kinds of food, both hard and soft, as well as with rice, lamps, sugarcane, fruits, garlands, and unguents;
Oṃ, homage be to you, O Lord of the Universe, abode of the universe, progenitor of the world; O Blessed One, homage to you!
O Lord of the worlds of the seven ṛṣis, the gods, and the spirits of the earth, grant protection along with [your] womb.
May those who suffer become happy; may the sins of all beings, both moving and stationary, come to an end.
O Brahmāṇḍa, may the defects of the universe reach their dissolution for those whose transgressions have been struck down by the weapon of your gift.
Having prostrated before the God who contains the universe of immortals, one should distribute [the gift] among the twice-born, dividing it tenfold;
having assigned two portions therein to the preceptor, one should then share the remainder equally in due order.
In the case of very small-scale rites, the Guru alone should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the method of the single-fire ritual;
he alone is most worthy of worship by those of limited means with the prescribed garments, ornaments, and other offerings.
Thus, the person who, having performed this entire gift of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa-dāna), attains a great celestial chariot,
reaches with his body purified by shaken-off impurities the state that brings joy to Murāri, accompanied by great celestial nymphs.
He shall ferry across his father, grandfather, sons, grandsons, kinsmen, dear ones, guests, and eight hundred wives;
and having shattered the mass of his sins with the gift of the Cosmic Egg (brahmāṇḍa), he shall bring joy to his entire maternal lineage as well.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa according to the *Mātsya-purāṇa*. Herein follow the specific details from the *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa*:
"Having fashioned a golden Brahmāṇḍa endowed with all auspicious characteristics..."
By gods, asuras, and humans, and by gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas.
It is joined by rivers, oceans, and likewise by mountains;
it is adorned with hundreds of millions of celestial palaces and by lakes.
Likewise: "O King, one should conceive the fourteen worlds within its limbs.
And likewise:
Joined with two parts of a *kalaśa* (or *śakala*), well-compacted in the shape of a jar; likewise,
having fashioned a pavilion of flowers, the wise one should install it there.
It was situated atop a drona-measure of sesame seeds and smeared with powdered saffron.
Having covered it with a pair of garments and perfumed it with incense, fragrance, and other scents,
one should then bring eighteen measures of grain, each weighing one *droṇa*.
The wise man should install it either in a house or in a pavilion; likewise,
he should offer sesame seeds into the fire in the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O King, one should perform ten thousand oblations with the five great mystical utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis).
The recitation of the Rudra-mantra should be performed by the wise immediately after that;
then, on the occasion of a festival, one who has bathed, wearing white garments and being pure, [should proceed].
One should worship Brahmā with devotion, with hands joined in a gentle *añjali*, saying:
"Salutations to the foundation of the world; salutations be to you, the abode of the universe."
Be a bringer of auspiciousness within the Brahmāṇḍa for those submerged within the realm of speech;
whatever beings exist within the interior of the Brahmāṇḍa, [grant them well-being].
May all of them—
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, the guardians of the world, and likewise the planets— grant me incomparable nourishment.
May the constellations, as well as the Nāgas, the Ṛṣis, and the Maruts—
all of them— be pleased with me for seven future births.
Having recited this, one should then present the Brahmāṇḍa, which grants all desires;
having performed that along with the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), one should worship the twice-born (brāhmaṇas) stationed in the various directions.
Thus concludes the specific procedure for the gift of the Brahmāṇḍa according to the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Matsya said:
Hereafter follows the unsurpassed [account] known as the gift of the Kalpapādapa (Wish-fulfilling Tree).
I shall proclaim the great gift that destroys all sins.
[325] Then, having reached an auspicious day, as in the case of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa,
one should perform the recitation for the declaration of the auspicious day (puṇyāhavācana) and likewise the invocation of Lokeśa.
One should have a golden tree fashioned, complete with various fruits, as well as the officiating priests, the consecration of the pavilion, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
One should have various kinds of garments and ornaments made;
according to one's means, one should have them made from more than three palas up to a thousand palas.
Then, one should have a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) fashioned out of refined gold;
it should be placed upon a prastha measure of jaggery and covered with a pair of white cloths.
One should worship Kāmadeva together with his wife, accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, possessing five branches and accompanied by the Sun, situated below.
One should likewise arrange the lineage from the front, with a fourth part;
on the right side is Mandāra, together with Śrī, upon clarified butter.
In the west, however, one should offer the *pāribhadra* tree along with *savitri*, cumin, and likewise *surabhi*; and in the case of sesame seeds, one should offer *haricandana*.
One should fashion [the images] with a third part [of the material], joined with sesame seeds and fruits,
provided with silken garments, and endowed with garlands of sugarcane.
Likewise, [he should offer] eight full water-pots, sandals, a seat, and a vessel,
together with a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, and a throne.
Likewise, there should be a canopy above provided with fruits and garlands;
similarly, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around.
Oṃ, homage to you, the wish-fulfilling tree who grants desired objects;
homage to you, the divine sustainer of the universe, whose form is the universe itself.
Since you alone are the soul of the universe, Brahmā, Sthāṇu, and Divākara;
you are the embodied and the unembodied, the supreme seed—therefore, protect me, O Eternal One.
You alone are the entirety of the nectar of immortality, the infinite and imperishable Puruṣa; being endowed with [auspicious] lineages and other such qualities, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Having thus addressed him, one should give the wish-fulfilling tree to the preceptor,
and one should likewise provide the means for progeny and other blessings to the four officiating priests.
In minor matters, one should act as if toward a single fire; the teacher alone is to be honored. One should not practice stinginess regarding wealth, nor should one be full of pride.
Whoever offers a great gift according to this rite,
being liberated from all sins, shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Surrounded by Apsarases, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Kiṃnaras,
he shall deliver as many beings— past and future humans— as there are hairs on his body.
Being praised upon the back of heaven, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, accompanied by his sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons.
Such a man shall remain in heaven for a hundred kalpas, become a king of kings,
endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa, and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
One who is devoted to the stories of Nārāyaṇa shall go to the supreme state of Nārāyaṇa.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Kalpavṛkṣa according to the Mātsya Purāṇa.
There is a specific detail regarding this in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Soul of the Mountain, whatever man or woman is childless must give a golden Kalpa-tree endowed with all virtues.
One may also adopt an artificial son, such as a tree or a stationary object;
or else, one may designate a son born of another as one's own son.
By that [act], one who possesses sons shall go to heaven in this world, there is no doubt;
furthermore, a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) made of pure gold should be fashioned.
He has many branches and beautiful wings, endowed with manifold blossoms;
he possesses great trunks, is handsome in form, and his body is adorned with jewels.
One should fashion divine fruits for it made of gold,
and one should likewise construct an excellent pedestal made of silver all around.
One should fashion four golden trees at the four corners, entwined with coral sprouts and draped with strings of pearls.
[327] O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall now describe the measurement of gold:
it may be one thousand, half of that, or even half of that again.
One should have a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) constructed for the fulfillment of all desires,
especially during an eclipse of the moon or sun, or upon seeing a bad dream or a portentous marvel.
On one's birth star, on the equinoxes, or again on the anniversaries of the Yugas,
whether on the bank of a river, in a house, or even in a temple,
one should have a pavilion constructed there in a place sloping toward the east or the north.
O King, one should cause a single, very beautiful sacrificial pit to be made in the southeast, measuring ten cubits in size and adorned with three girdles.
And there, Brahmins who recite the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas should be employed;
and the instructor there should be either the second or the fifth [of those].
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with copper vessels,
one should place a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpapādapa) upon a prastha measure of jaggery.
One should fashion a five-branch tree accompanied by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, together with the Sun; and below it, one should represent Kāmadeva along with his wife.
To the east, upon the salt [ocean], he should place the Saṃtāna tree together with Gāyatrī;
likewise, on the southern side, upon the clarified butter, the Mandāra tree together with Śrī.
In the west, there is the Pārijāta tree together with Umā;
likewise, Jīraka with Surabhi, and Haricandana among the sesame seeds.
One should arrange eight eastern pitchers all around, provided with silken cloths and accompanied by garlands of sugarcane.
Having performed the ritual transfer of the fire into the hearth and having consecrated the tree,
the Brahmins, with perfectly purified inner selves, should perform the fire-oblation (homa).

Having first offered the two āghāra oblations and the two ājyabhāga portions, the wise practitioner should then nourish the deities installed with their respective mantras by means of the homa sacrifice.
Thereafter, they should perform the fire-oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis;
O lady of excellent complexion, through ten thousand [recitations], the success of the sacrifice shall be attained.
Then, having risen at dawn and bathed, being pure and clad in white garments,
one should circumambulate three times and utter this mantra:
Homage to you, the wish-fulfilling tree, who bestows desired objects;
homage to you, the God who grants prosperity, whose form is the universe.
Since you alone are the soul of the universe, Brahmā, Sthāṇu, and Divākara; since you are the supreme seed, both manifest and unmanifest, therefore protect me, O Eternal One.
Having addressed him thus, he should give the wish-fulfilling tree to the preceptor;
then, he should assign the lineage and other items to the four officiating priests.
O Goddess, listen as I describe the fruit of the merit for one who bestows this gift according to this procedure.
Whether it be a woman or even a man, such a person is rare indeed upon this earth;
for twenty-one generations of ancestors, both on the mother’s side and the father’s side.
He shall deliver others and become one who has fulfilled his purpose in birth after birth;
[he destroys] whatever sin was acquired during the ten stages of life throughout the three states of existence.
It washes away that [sin] without doubt, and one goes to the world of Brahmā;
having stayed there for a day of Brahmā, one then goes to the abode of Śiva.
Having spent a very long time even there in the world of merit,
and having dwelt in such places as these, one is born again as a human being.
Healthy, powerful, heroic, handsome, and likewise fortunate,
he exercises sovereignty for ten births with all thorns removed.
Indeed, whether a man or a woman, having given this gift, shall obtain this very fruit;
this was proclaimed by Bhava, the destroyer of worldly existence, concerning Gaurī.
And I have told you all this, O scion of the Pāṇḍu lineage.
He who, having mentally envisioned a golden wish-fulfilling tree endowed with the four celestial trees,
bestows it upon a Brahmin learned in the Vedas on an auspicious day while remaining self-restrained, attains his desired goal in no small measure and without fail.
Thus ends the specific procedure for the gift of the Kalpavṛkṣa (Wish-fulfilling Tree) in the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
The Fish [Incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Great Gift (mahādāna).
Known as the Gift of a Thousand Cows, it is supreme and removes all sins.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, such as the beginning of a Yuga or a Manvantara,
one should observe a three-night vow of consuming only milk, or even for a single night.
One should perform the invocation of Lokeśa as in the ritual of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa;
likewise, one should perform the recitation for an auspicious day and the rite of fire-offering (homa).

One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the bull— endowed with auspicious marks, along with the assembly of officiating priests, the sacrificial requisites, ornaments, and coverings— in the center of the altar.
Having extracted ten cows from a thousand cows,
one should set aside that thousand cows adorned with garments, garlands, and ornaments.
Having brought inside ten [cows] adorned with golden horns and silver hooves, one should worship them with garments and garlands.
Equipped with golden bells, adorned with bands of gold,
wrapped in silken cloth, and provided with perfumes and garlands.
It was adorned with peaks made of gold and gems, and embellished with chowries;
it was equipped with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, vessels, and seats.
In the midst of ten cows should be Nandikeśvara, made of gold,
clothed in silken garments, and adorned with perfumes and garlands.
On the peak of a heap of salt, combined with jasmine, sugarcane, and fruit,
one should perform all this without doubt using more than a hundred palas.
According to one's capacity, one should perform all of this, starting from as little as three thousand *palas* up to a hundred cows, using even a tenth part of that amount.
Having secured an auspicious time, he was bathed by eminent Veda-knowers with the sounds of auspicious songs and with baths using water infused with all medicinal herbs.
Holding a handful of flowers, one should recite this mantra:
"Oṃ, homage to those who are the embodiments of the universe and to those who are the mothers of the universe."
Salutations again and again to the Rohiṇīs who dwell in all things;
within the limbs of cows reside the twenty-one worlds.
May Brahmā and the other gods, as well as the Rohiṇī mothers, protect me;
may cows be before me, and indeed cows behind me as well.
The cows are ever in my head; I dwell in the midst of the cows, because you are indeed the eternal Dharma in the form of a bull.
"O eternal abode of the Eightfold Form (Aṣṭamūrti), protect me from this!
Having thus addressed him, one should then offer Nandikeśvara to the Guru.
The wise man should present to the ten officiating priests a pair of oxen equipped with all necessary implements, and he should offer one cow to each of them.
One may give ten or five to others with their permission;
however, one should not give a single [consecration] to many, as it would cause harm.
And many [cows] should be given by the illustrious one for the increase of health;
furthermore, the giver of a thousand cows should observe the milk-vow for one day.
One who desires abundant prosperity should either cause others to hear or listen themselves to the glorification of the great gifts; on that day, they should observe celibacy.
Whoever, by this rite, becomes a giver of a thousand cows,
shall be liberated from all sins and attended by the Siddhas and Cāraṇas.
In a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun, garlanded with networks of tiny bells,
he is honored by the immortals in the world of all the world-protectors.
He shall remain for the duration of each Manvantara, accompanied by his sons and grandsons;
having transcended the seven worlds, he shall thereafter proceed to the city of Śiva.
In that same way, the wise man, together with his sons and grandsons, shall deliver one hundred and one ancestors,
as well as his maternal grandfathers.
He may remain for as long as a hundred kalpas and become a king of kings once more;
devoted to the meditation on Śiva, he shall perform a hundred horse-sacrifices.
Having attained the world of Viṣṇu, one is then released from bondage;
and the ancestors rejoice in the auspicious giver of a thousand cows.
Perhaps there may be among us a son or even a grandson who,
having become a giver of a thousand cows, shall deliver us from hell.
He may even be a laborer for him, or likewise one who merely beholds him—
whosoever shall ferry us across this ocean of saṃsāra.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a thousand cows according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish [Purāṇa] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme procedure for the Kāmadhenu (the wish-fulfilling cow).
It bestows all desires upon men and destroys even the greatest of sins.
In the same manner, the invocation of Lokeśa and the fire-offering (homa) should be performed by the wise;
one should construct the sacrificial pit, the pavilion, and the altar-platform just as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
In the case of very small [offenses], the preceptor alone, being composed, should perform [the rite] like the single-fire ritual;
he should have a cow and a calf fashioned from exceedingly pure gold.
The best [image] is one thousand palas; the middling is half of that;
the smallest is half of that again—thus is the Kāmadhenu proclaimed.
According to one's capacity, even if unable, one should have [the rite] performed with more than three palas;
having placed a black antelope skin upon the altar together with a prastha of molasses.
One should place that cow upon a raised platform, adorned with great jewels,
accompanied by eight jars and fruits, and provided with various kinds of fruit.
In the same way, one should arrange eighteen kinds of grain all around;
likewise, one should provide eight stalks of sugarcane together with various fruits.
Likewise, there was a vessel, a fly-whisk, and a copper milking-pail;
she was adorned with a pair of silken garments, beautiful with lamps, parasols, and ornaments;
she possessed a fly-whisk, earrings, a bell, a neck-ornament, and sandals with silver soles.
A *galartikā* is an ornament for the neck;
it is surrounded on all sides by all the flavors, with turmeric, many flowers and fruits,
cumin, *kustumburu*, and sugar, and has a five-colored canopy above.

Then, having bathed amidst the auspicious sounds of Vedic chanting and having circumambulated [the image] with flowers in hand, he should invoke her with the mantras prescribed by the preceptor; then, with *darbha* grass in his hand, he should present it to the twice-born.

You are the abode of the assembly of all the gods; you belong to the Lord of the Universe, the triple-pathed river Gaṅgā, and the mountains. Having had the multitude of my sins shattered by the weapon of your gift, I have attained supreme bliss; I bow down to you.
Having obtained you, who bestows upon the world the fruits desired by each, what mortal would ever undergo the suffering of existence?
Grant freely for the sake of quelling the suffering of *saṃsāra*; the hosts of gods declare that you are the wish-fulfilling cow.
He who, having invited a Brahmin endowed with beauty, noble lineage, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities, shall bestow this golden cow,
attains the abode cherished by the god Purandara and reaches the station of the Moon-crested Lord, surrounded by throngs of celestial maidens.
Thus concludes the procedure for the gift of the Kāmadhenu according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish (Matsya) said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the auspicious procedure for the gift of the golden horse.
By the giving of which one enjoys infinite fruit in this world.
[332] Having reached an auspicious lunar day, one should perform the recitation by Brahmins;
likewise, the invocation of the World-Protectors (Lokeśas) is to be done as in the case of the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.

A wise man should perform the sacrifice of the golden horse (Hemavājimakha) with a single fire for minor rites, including the officiating priests, the pavilion, the materials, the ornaments, and the coverings.
One should place it in the middle of the altar upon a black antelope skin and sesame seeds;
one should have a golden horse fashioned and draped with silk cloth.
According to his capacity, a wise man [should give] from three palas up to a thousand palas,
along with sandals, shoes, an umbrella, chowries, a seat, and vessels.
Provided with eight full water-pots, accompanied by garlands, sugarcane, and fruits,
one should likewise offer a bed with its furnishings, together with a golden image of the Sun.
Then, having been bathed with a bath of all medicinal herbs by the preeminent Veda-knowers,
he should, holding a handful of flowers, recite this mantra:
Salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods, you who were eager to retrieve the Vedas;
in the form of a horse, protect me from this ocean of saṃsāra.
Since you yourself, having become sevenfold in the form of the meters, cause the worlds to revolve around the sun,
therefore protect us, O Eternal One.
Having recited this, one should present that horse to the Guru;
by giving it, through the destruction of sins, one attains the eternal world of the Sun.
One should honor all the officiating priests with gifts of cattle according to one's means,
and one should present all kinds of grain and ritual implements to the preceptor.
Having given away everything, including his bed and other possessions, he should eat only sesame seeds;
likewise, he should cause the recitation of the Purāṇas and perform the eating of food and other rites.
He who performs this rite of the golden horse, being honored in heaven by the lords of the gods,
becomes liberated from sin and, being fully worshipped, attains the city of Murāri along with the Siddhas.
Thus ends the gift of the golden horse in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift.
This meritorious [work] called Aśvaratha is the destroyer of great sins.
Then, having reached an auspicious day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
one should perform the invocation of the World-Lords (Lokeśas) as in the ritual for the gift of the Tulāpuruṣa.

Having placed sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, one should cause a chariot to be fashioned out of gold, along with the sacrificial priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
It had seven horses or four horses, four wheels, and beautiful poles,
and was joined with a sapphire jar in the form of a banner.
It is endowed with the eight world-protectors and possessed of petals of ruby;
there are four full jars and eighteen kinds of grain.
It was provided with silken garments and a canopy above;
it was adorned with garlands, sugarcane, and fruit, and accompanied by a man.
Whatever a person is devoted to, he should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) under that name;
[this includes] the parasol, the chowrie, silk garments, sandals, and wooden shoes.
A wise man should give a bed and a seat together with cows according to his means; from three *palas* up to a *bhāra*, he should have it made according to his capacity.
One should give [the gift] joined with eight, or four,
or even two horses, together with a golden lion-banner.
Likewise, both wheel-protectors were mounted on horses like the two Aśvins;
then, having reached an auspicious time, he was bathed by the twice-born as before.
Having circumambulated three times clockwise, holding a handful of flowers and wearing white garlands and garments, he should offer [the gift] and utter this mantra:
Oṃ, salutations again and again to the destroyer of sins, the soul of the Vedas, the steed of the Vedas;
to the sovereign lord of all abodes, who is both existence and non-existence—O forest fire to the thickets of the masses of sin, grant me peace!
You alone are the creator and the supreme treasure-house of the Vasus, Aṣṭakas, Ādityas, and the hosts of Maruts;
therefore, may my heart, through the destruction of the flood of sins, attain single-minded devotion to Dharma.
Thus, he who performs this gift of horses and chariots, which destroys the fear of worldly existence,
shall have his body liberated from the layers of impurity and attain the supreme state of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
With a body of radiant splendor that has surpassed the power [of the sun], he occupies the unbroken orb of the mild-rayed moon;
there he dwells for a long time with the Lotus-born Brahmā, while the lotus-like faces of the Siddha maidens drink him in like bees.
Whoever thus recites or hears of this gift of a golden horse-chariot shall never go to the city of hell; rather, he shall go again to the abode of the Enemy of Hell (Śiva).
[334] Thus ends the gift of the golden horse-chariot in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the auspicious golden elephant-chariot,
by the gift of which a human being goes to the abode of Hari.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, as in the case of the Tulāpuruṣa gift,
the wise man should perform the recitation by Brahmins and the invocation of the Lords of the World (Lokeśas).
The assembly of officiating priests, the requisites, ornaments, clothing,
and so forth— here too, having fasted likewise, there is a meal together with the Brahmins.
One should fashion a golden chariot in the shape of a flower-cart, adorned with jewels,
featuring variegated gables and equipped with four wheels.
Endowed with the eight world-protectors (lokapālas), joined with Brahmā, the Sun, and Śiva;
in the center, it is accompanied by Nārāyaṇa and attended by Lakṣmī and Puṣṭi.
Having placed a drona-measure of sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, one should establish the chariot;
likewise, the eighteen types of grain, along with vessels, seats, and sandalwood.
One should place a lamp, shoes, an umbrella, and a mirror, along with sandals;
on the banner, one should depict Garuḍa, and at the front of the pole, Vināyaka.
Above it was a canopy adorned with various fruits,
made of five-colored silk and decorated with unfading flowers.
It was accompanied by four water-jars and eight cows,
adorned with four golden elephants and decorated with strings of pearls.
Having fashioned [the image] according to its true form and yoked with two elephants, one should present it;
one should make it from five palas upwards, even up to a bhāra, according to one's capacity.
Then, bathed with auspicious sounds by the foremost of Veda-knowers,
he circumambulated [the deity] three times and took handfuls of *kusuma* flowers in his joined palms.
One should recite this mantra and announce it to the Brāhmaṇas:
"Homage, homage to you, who are served by Śaṅkara, Padmaja, Arka, the Lords of the Worlds, the Vidyādharas, and Vāsudeva; O you whose chariot consists of splendor, protect me from that [danger]."

That supreme state, most secret, the cause of Murāri’s bliss, which is inwardly devoid of qualities and forms— O Lord, you who are mounted upon the chariot are that very state which sages, whose minds are focused solely on yoga, perceive in meditative absorption.
Since you alone are the vessel for churning the jar of bliss for those submerged in the ocean of existence,
therefore, by quelling the flood of sins, show favor by granting the golden chariot of Mādhava.
Having thus prostrated, he who causes the gift of a golden elephant and chariot to be made— his body liberated from all sins—
attains that super-sensory state of the Moon-crested Lord, which is frequented by hosts of Vidyādharas, gods, and the foremost of sages.

One who has bestowed gifts of elephants and chariots leads his kinsmen— even those who have committed a multitude of sins and who suffer the terror of being consumed by the mass of blazing flames— to the eternal abode of Viṣṇu, including all his fathers and grandsons, even from the Raurava hell.
Thus ends the gift of the elephant-chariot in the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Matsya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift (mahādāna).
This is called the Pañcalāṅgalaka, which destroys great sins.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, such as the beginning of a Yuga or an eclipse,
a man should give a gift of land endowed with five furrows.
He may also give a market town (kharvaṭa), a hamlet (kheṭaka), or a village rich in crops;
or even a hundred nivartanas of land, or half of that, according to his capacity.
The wise one, having fashioned five plows out of *suradāru* wood,
likewise made those five out of gold, equipped with all necessary implements.
And ten excellent bulls, endowed with the characteristics of a bull,
adorned with golden horns, and beautified by pearl-ornaments on their tails.

One should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the hall for those [images] which have silver feet and forehead-marks, are adorned with red silk garments, and are provided with garlands of flowers and sandalwood paste.
The preceptor should offer oblations of cooked rice with milk to Parjanya, Āditya, and the Rudras;
he should present these in that very same vessel to the disciple for whom he performs the rite.
Likewise, the wise man should perform the invocation of the world-protectors (lokeśa) using palāśa fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and black sesame seeds, in the same manner as the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
Then, amidst auspicious sounds, he— clad in white garlands and garments—
having summoned a brahmin couple, honored them with golden necklaces and finger-rings.
One should honor [the preceptor] with silk garments, bracelets, and jewels;
likewise, one should offer a bed complete with its furnishings and a single milch cow.
Likewise, one should cause the eighteen gifts to be offered on all sides;
then, having performed a circumambulation and holding a handful of flowers, one should proceed.
One should recite this mantra and then offer the formal announcement:
"Since all the hosts of gods, as well as all things mobile and immobile..."
Therefore, may my devotion be auspicious toward Śiva, who abides within the body of the bearer of the world's burden;
for [all other gifts] do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of a gift of land.
Other gifts may be mine, but let my devotion to Dharma alone be firm.
Thirty daṇḍas, each seven cubits long, constitute a nivartana.
Prajāpati has declared that the measure of a *gocarma* is reduced by one-third;
a wise man who gives a hundred *nivartanas* according to this measurement [attains great merit].
By this rite, his accumulation of sins is quickly destroyed;
or else, he should give half of that, or even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide.

Merely by staying in such a dwelling, even he is liberated from sins. As many furrows as there are on the surface of the earth, so many hairs grow on the body of the daughter of the Earth (Pṛthivī); for that many years shall a man who makes a gift of land remain in the city of Śaṅkara.

Approaching a great celestial chariot with its fly-whisks being waved by hosts of Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Suras, Asuras, and Siddhas, he is honored together with his fathers, grandfathers, and kinsmen; becoming a leader of the immortals, he proceeds to the city of Śambhu.
Even the status of Indra does not escape decay when the gift of cows, land, and the yoke-bearing plough is bestowed;
therefore, one should perform the gift of land, which destroys the mass of accumulated sins and leads to supreme prosperity and liberation from the cycle of existence.
Thus ends the gift of the five-ploughed field according to the *Mātsya Purāṇa*.
The Fish [incarnation] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed gift of the earth.
It brings about the destruction of the evils of men and the eradication of inauspiciousness.
One should have fashioned a golden earth resembling Jambudvīpa,
consisting of the boundary mountains and provided with Mount Meru in its center.
Endowed with the eight world-protectors, comprising the nine continents,
possessed of hundreds of rivers and streams, and encircled by the seven oceans.
It is strewn with great jewels and joined with the [images of] Vasu, Rudra, and Arka,
made from a thousand palas of gold, or half of that, or according to one's ability.
One may perform it with three hundred [palas], or with two hundred, or even with one hundred;
a wise person, even if incapable, should perform it with at least five palas.
As in the case of the *tulāpuruṣa* rite, the wise man should perform the invocation of Lokeśvara,
as well as the preparation of the sacrificial circle, the officiating priests, the ornaments, the garments, and so forth.
Having spread a black antelope skin upon the altar, one should place sesame seeds on top;
likewise, the eighteen kinds of grain and the flavors, such as salt and the rest.
Likewise, one should arrange eight full water-pots all around,
as well as a silk canopy and various kinds of fruits.
Having thus prepared beautiful garments and pieces of sandalwood for her, preceded by the rite of consecration (adhivāsana), he performed the ceremony.
Wearing white garlands and garments, adorned with white ornaments,
he then performed a circumambulation while holding a handful of flowers.
Then, having reached an auspicious time, one should recite these mantras:
"Oṃ, homage to you, for you alone are the abode of all the gods."
And since you are the nurse of all beings, protect us, O Vasundharā;
for because you sustain the treasures (vasus), you are called Vasudhā, the stainless one.
From that, Vasundharā was born; therefore, protect us sufficiently from fear, O Mountain, so that even the Four-faced One may not reach your end.
Salutations to Anantā; therefore, protect me from the mire of saṃsāra.
You alone are Lakṣmī in Govinda, and you abide as Gaurī in Śiva.
Gāyatrī resides at the side of Brahmā; Jyotsnā is in the moon and Prabhā in the sun;
Buddhi is renowned in Bṛhaspati, and Medhā is established among the sages.
Because she stands pervading the entire universe, she is therefore considered Viśvaṃbharā (the Sustainer of the World).

O Goddess, protect us from the ocean of saṃsāra through these forms: Sthiti (Stability), Dhṛti (Fortitude), Kṣamā (Forgiveness), Kṣoṇī (the Earth), Pṛthvī (the Broad One), Vasumatī (Possessing Wealth), and Rasā (the Tasting Ground).
Having thus addressed that goddess, one should present her to the Brahmins;
or else, one should bestow half of the land, or a fourth part, upon the preceptor.
And having bowed down to the officiating priests, he should dismiss them;
the wise man who gives a golden earth according to this rite—
But when the auspicious time has arrived, he indeed attains the station of Viṣṇu by means of a sun-colored celestial chariot garlanded with networks of tinkling bells.
Having gone to Nārāyaṇapura, one shall dwell there for three kalpas;
furthermore, one shall deliver twenty-one generations, including one's father, sons, and grandsons.
Whoever recites this thus, or even hears it incidentally, though their body be entirely covered by a multitude of impurities,
goes to heaven, being escorted by celestial damsels to that station frequented by thousands of gods who bear the moon upon their crests.
Thus ends the gift of the golden earth according to the *Mātsya Purāṇa*.
The Fish [Purāṇa] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift (*mahādāna*).
It is renowned as the Viśvacakra, the destroyer of great sins.
One should have a universal wheel (viśvacakra) fashioned from pure refined gold;
the best is made with a thousand palas, while the middling is made with half of that.
The smallest universal wheel (viśvacakra) is declared to be half of that;
even one who is unable may offer another [wheel] weighing more than twenty palas.
Then there is the sixteen-spoked wheel, adorned and surrounded by eight ornaments;
within it stands Viṣṇu upon a lotus-navel, established in yoga, with four arms.
With Śaṅkha and Padma at his sides, surrounded by the eight goddesses;
likewise, in the second enclosure, one should place the one reclining on the waters in the east.
Atri, Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Brahmā, and Kaśyapa;
the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, Narasiṃha, and Vāmana.
Rāma, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, Buddha, and Kalki appear in succession;
in the third enclosure is Gaurī, surrounded by the Mothers and the Vasus.
In the fourth [layer] are the twelve Ādityas and the four Vedas;
in the fifth are the five elements and the eleven Rudras.
In the sixth [enclosure], one should cause the eight world-protectors and likewise the elephants of the directions to be fashioned;
in the seventh, all weapons and auspicious objects should be made.
One should place the deities at intervals within the eighth [section] once again;
one should arrange everything all around in the same manner as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
Then, one should fashion the Viśvacakra— the equipment consisting of the assembly of officiating priests, ornaments, garments, and so forth— upon a black antelope skin spread over sesame seeds.
Likewise, there were eighteen kinds of grain, flavors such as salt and the like,
eight full jars, and various garments.
One should arrange garlands, sugarcane, fruits, jewels, and a canopy;
then, having bathed and wearing white garments, the householder [should proceed] amidst auspicious sounds.
At the conclusion of the fire offering and the preliminary consecration, having taken a handful of flowers,
one should recite this mantra three times while performing a circumambulation from left to right.
Salutations to Viśvamāyāya; salutations to the one whose self is the universal wheel (Viśvacakra). You, who are the embodiment of supreme bliss, protect us from the mire of sin.
Since yogis always behold this as consisting of light,
I bow to this wheel of the universe, which transcends the three qualities (guṇas).
The discus is situated in Vāsudeva, and Mādhava is within the center of the discus;
I bow to these two as they abide here in the form of mutual support.
The discus, which consists of the universe and removes all sins, is both the weapon and the garment of Hari; therefore, deliver me from this [bondage].
Having thus addressed [the recipient], he who, free from envy, should give the Viśvacakra,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
Having reached the realm of Vaikuṇṭha, he becomes the eternal four-armed one;
served by throngs of apsarases, he shall dwell there for three hundred kalpas.
Or, having personally fashioned a universal wheel (viśvacakra) every day, one should bow down to it;
his lifespan will increase constantly, and his prosperity shall become vast.
Thus, he who bestows the golden sixteen-spoked abode of Hari— the dwelling place of the gods of the entire world—
approaches that temple and, having been long approached by the perfected ones (siddhas), is honored by them with their bowed heads.
He becomes unbearable to his enemies and incomparable in beauty to amorous women;
he is worthy of the Lord Keśava of Sudarśana, having burnt away all sins through the gift of a golden Sudarśana.
The excellent form of Murāri, which completely destroys the sixteen spokes of the enemy that is heavy,
committed sin— having shattered worldly existence on all sides— furthermore overcomes the fears arising from *bhava* within one's home.
Thus ends the gift of the Fish and the Universal Wheel.
The Fish said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Great Gift.
It is called the Great Kalpa-creeper, which destroys the series of transgressions.

[340] Having reached an auspicious lunar day (tithi) and performed the recitation by Brahmins, one should provide for the circle of officiating priests (ṛtvij), including their sustenance, ornaments, clothing, and so forth.
One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation of Lokeśvara, as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite;
one should fashion ten auspicious wish-fulfilling creepers (kalpalatā) out of gold.
Endowed with various flowers and fruits, adorned with various silken garments,
and graced by pairs of Vidyādhara-s and Suvarṇas.
The Siddhas, desiring to take away the necklaces, and the birds, desiring the fruits, [must be warded off];
the deities who resemble the world-protectors must be installed upon those [images].
One should place that Brahmī of infinite power upon the salt,
beneath it, between the two creepers, in the auspicious one who holds a lotus and a conch in her hands.
Seated upon an elephant in the east, she holds a thunderbolt as her weapon;
situated on a goat in the southeast, she has a sacrificial ladle (sruva) in her hand at the fire-altar.
Upon which two [seats] she is mounted as Mahiṣārūḍhā, holding a staff atop rice;
Nairṛtī, accompanied by a sword, should be installed with ghee in the southwest.
Vāruṇī is on a water-vessel in the west; Nāgapāśinī is on salt in milk;
Patākinī is on a banner in the northwest; and [the goddess] is on a deer atop sugar in the north.
Saumyā should be established upon sesame seeds; Śaṅkhinī is situated within a treasure;
Māheśvarī is mounted upon a bull; and Triśūlinī is in fresh butter.
Likewise, the Mālinīs, who grant boons, should be fashioned together with their children;
according to one's capacity, they should be prepared from five palas up to a thousand.
And above all of them is a five-colored canopy;
there are also ten cows, water-pots, and pairs of garments.
He should offer two cows to the preceptor and likewise others to the officiating priests;
then, having bathed to the sound of auspicious music, the wise man, clad in white garments, [proceeds].
Having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should recite these mantras:
"Homage, homage to the quarters, who destroy all evil, who protect the lords of the worlds within the cosmic egg,
who bestow fruits exceeding even those hoped for, and who are like young brides upon the wish-fulfilling creepers."
Thus, he who makes the gift of all the women of every quarter— which brings about the destruction of existence within cyclic rebirth—
dwells in the world of the Nāgas for twenty years, like Pitāmaha, bestowing his desired fruits.
One whose body is purified by the destruction of a multitude of heavy sins shall ferry even a hundred ancestors across the ocean of existence,
[to that state] surrounded by throngs of thousands of the finest celestial women and celebrated by the Lotus-born Brahmā.
Thus,

whoever here recites, remembers, and likewise contemplates this ritual for the offering of a golden wish-fulfilling creeper to the celestial damsels of the quarters, shall attain the station served by Indra.
Thus ends the gift of the Kalpalatā according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish [Purāṇa] said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe that which destroys great sins.
The [rite] named Saptasāgaraka destroys all sins.
Having reached an auspicious day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
the wise man should perform the invocation of the Lords of the World (Lokeśas) just as in the Tulāpuruṣa rite.
The wise practitioner should cause seven golden sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be made, along with the assembly of officiating priests, ornaments, clothing, and other requisites.
Furthermore, one should make them the size of a span or even the size of an elbow; they should weigh more than seven palas and up to a thousand palas, according to one's capacity.
All [the vessels] should be placed full of sesame seeds;
first, the wise man should fill the sacrificial pit with salt.
The second [offering] is likewise with milk, the third again with clarified butter,
the fourth with molasses, and the fifth indeed with curd.
In the same manner, one should bathe the auspicious golden Brahmā with sugar for the sixth bath and with water from sacred fords for the seventh, within the salt.
One should worship Keśava in the midst of milk, Maheśvara in the midst of clarified butter,
Bhāskara in the midst of molasses, and the Lord of the Immortals (Indra) in the midst of curd.
One should place Lakṣmī upon sugar, Pārvatī in the midst of water,
all kinds of gems everywhere, and grains on all sides.
One should determine the remainder here as well according to the procedure for the Tulāpuruṣa rite;
then, at the conclusion of the Vāruṇa oblation, he is bathed by the preeminent among those who know the Vedas.
Having circumambulated three times clockwise, one should recite these mantras:
"Salutations to you, the eternal foundations of all rivers."
Salutations again and again to those who dwell in the various abodes of living beings and in the oceans!

Since you gladden the multitudes of living beings in the three worlds with the nectar of milk, water, clarified butter, curd, honey, salt, sugarcane juice, and wealth, may you therefore grant me the complete destruction of my sins.
Since you alone among all the worlds bear the expansion of holy fords, gods, asuras, fragrances,
jewels, penance, sacrifices, ointments, and ornaments for the sake of the world’s destruction of sin, may prosperity likewise be mine.

Thus, filled with long-standing wonder, he gives away oceans here containing both liquids and dry land, along with heaps of stainless gold and jewels; he attains the station of Hari, which is worshipped by the immortals.
Adorned by the destruction of all his sins, he is fully capable of instantly leading three hundred generations— fathers, grandfathers, and sons—
even if they are crowded within the realms of hell, to the abode of Śiva.
Thus ends the gift of the seven oceans according to the Matsya Purāṇa.
The Fish said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed great gift (mahādāna).
It is known as the Jewel-Cow, which bestows the fruit of Goloka upon men.
Having reached an auspicious lunar day, and having performed the invocation of the World-Lords (Lokeśas) as in the Tulāpuruṣa gift, one should prepare the Jewel-Cow (Ratnadhenu).
Having spread a black antelope skin upon the ground and provided a drona-measure of salt,
one should fashion a cow made of jewels according to the prescribed rite of formal resolve (saṃkalpa).
A wise person should place eighty-one rubies in the mouth,
and likewise, one should arrange one hundred topazes in the nose.
A golden tilaka on the forehead, a hundred pearls for the eyes,
a hundred corals for the pair of eyebrows, and two shells are prescribed for the two ears.
Its peaks were made of gold, its head consisted of hundreds of diamonds,
and upon its neck was a jeweled eye-socket composed of hundreds of *gomeda* gems.
On its back it has a hundred sapphire [stones], on its two sides a hundred lapis lazuli,
on its belly likewise crystal, and on its waist a hundred saugandhika [stones].
The hooves should be made of gold, and the tail of strings of pearls;
in its vital breath, there should be sun-crystals, moon-crystals, camphor, and sandalwood.
One should fashion the body hairs from saffron, the navel from silver,
and likewise arrange a hundred emeralds at the anus.
Then one should place other jewels at all the joints;
one should fashion the tongue from sugar and the cow-dung from molasses.
One should offer cow urine with clarified butter, as well as curd and milk in their natural state; one should place a yak-tail fan at the tip of the tail, and a copper milking vessel nearby.
One should likewise have golden earrings and ornaments made according to one's means;
and in this same manner, one should provide a calf with a fourth part [of that amount].
Likewise, all kinds of grain, auspicious pillars made of sugarcane,
all varieties of fruits, and a canopy of five colors.
Having performed the arrangement in this manner, one should likewise perform the supreme fire-oblation and other rites;
then, having given the sacrificial fee to the officiating priests, one should address the cow.
Having invoked [the cow] as in the case of the "Jaggery-Cow" (guḍadhenu), one should then recite this:

"Since they declare you to be the abode of all the hosts of gods— Rudra, Indra, Soma, Brahmā, and Vāsudeva— therefore, O Goddess, who are joined by all the deities of the three worlds, protect me, who am being tormented by the ocean of worldly existence."
Having thus addressed him and turned toward him with devotion, one should offer that [image] to the brahmin preceptor preceded by water;
he who, having observed a fast on this meritorious day, offers it, goes to the abode of Murāri with his body liberated from sins.
Thus, the knower of all rites, having bestowed the gift of the jewel-cow, attains a brilliantly shining celestial chariot;
freed from every impurity, he goes to the abode of Śambhu together with his kinsmen, sons, and grandsons, possessing a form as beautiful as that of Madana.
Thus ends the ritual for the Jewel-Cow in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*.
The Fish [Incarnation] said:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed Great Gift (*mahādāna*)."
It is called the "Jar of the Great Elements," which destroys the great transgressions.
Then, having reached an auspicious lunar day and performed the recitation by Brahmins,
[he should provide] the officiating priests, the pavilion, the ritual materials, ornaments, coverings, and so forth.
One should perform the rites beginning with the invocation of Lokeśvara as prescribed for the Tulāpuruṣa rite;
one should have a beautiful golden pitcher fashioned, set with great jewels.
One should construct it according to measure, from one span up to a hundred finger-breadths;
it should be filled with milk and ghee and adorned with a wish-fulfilling tree.
Likewise, one should depict Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara seated in the lotus posture;
and similarly, one should represent the earth, together with its mountains, being lifted up by the Boar.
And Varuṇa seated upon a golden crocodile,
Hutāśana (Agni) seated upon a ram, and Vāyu with a deer-made seat.
Likewise, one should fashion Vināyaka as the lord of space, seated upon a mouse;
these [deities], joined with the five Vedas, should be placed within the center of the jar.
The *Ṛgveda* shall have an *akṣasūtra* (rosary), the *Yajurveda* a lotus, and the *Sāmaveda* a lute; one should place a cow to the right.
Furthermore, in the hand of the Atharvaveda are the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and a lotus;
the Purāṇaveda is the bestower of boons, holding a rosary and a water-pot.
All kinds of grains, a chowrie, a seat, a mirror, sandals, shoes, an umbrella, lamps, and ornaments [should be placed] all around.
