Then, having bathed at the conclusion of the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should utter this mantra while [pointing to] the bed, the water-pitcher, and the five-colored canopy:
Homage to you, the supports of all the gods, in the moving and the unmoving;
to the great elements and the primordial deities: may there be peace, may there be auspiciousness for me!
Since there is nothing whatsoever within the cosmic egg that exists apart from the great elements,
may my prosperity be inexhaustible.
Having uttered this, whoever offers the jar of the great elements,
being liberated from all sins, goes to the supreme goal.
Accompanied by his paternal kinsmen and being praised by excellent women, he proceeds to the realm of Viṣṇu in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
The man who performs these sixteen great gifts shall not be reborn again in this world.
Whoever thus recites this, or hears it correctly here in the presence of Vāsudeva, together with his sons, father, and wife,
shall indeed rejoice for an eon in the abode of the Enemy of Tripura, within the palace of the Sun and Lakṣmī, like the celestial damsels of Amarāvatī.
Thus ends the gift of the jar of the great elements according to the Matsya Purāṇa. Now follow the gifts of mountains,
as described in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Umāpati said:
O best of sages, I shall describe the gift of Mount Meru in its tenfold form,
by the giving of which a person attains worlds honored by the gods.
Since one attains [the fruits] through these Purāṇas and Vedas that have been composed,
I shall therefore describe the ritual procedure for the mountains in their proper sequence.
The first is the mountain of grain; the second is the mountain of salt;
the third is the mountain of molasses; and the fourth is the mountain of gold.
The fifth should be a mountain of sesame seeds, the sixth a mountain of cotton;
the seventh should be a mountain of ghee, and likewise the eighth a mountain of jewels.
[345] Likewise, there is the tenth, the Śarkarācala (sugar-mountain), which is for the sake of the King;
I shall describe the ritual procedure for these in due order and according to the rules.
During the solstices, at the equinoxes, on auspicious occasions, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the end of a day (the new moon),
on the third day of the dark fortnight, during an eclipse, or at the waning of the moon.
During marriage festivals or sacrifices, or again on the twelfth day,
or on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight, or under an auspicious constellation, according to the prescribed rule.
Mountains of grain and other such gifts should be given according to the ritual injunctions of the scriptures,
whether at a sacred ford, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or at a confluence of rivers.
One should devoutly construct a square mandala facing north,
or likewise sloping toward the northeast, or facing east, according to the prescribed rule.
Having spread kuśa grass upon ground smeared with cow dung,
one should fashion a mountain in its center, accompanied by mountains as its foothills.
In this world, the best mountain would consist of one thousand *droṇas* of grain;
the middling, five hundred; and the smallest would be three hundred.
In the center, however, there should be Mount Meru, made of great rice and joined with three golden trees.
In the east, it is joined with pearls and diamonds; in the south, with gomedaka and puṣparāga gems.

And in the western quarter, there should be a surface of mother-of-pearl slabs, adorned on all sides with emeralds and sapphire gems, with gentle lapis lazuli lotus stalks, pieces of sandalwood, and creepers of coral.
Brahmā, the Lord Viṣṇu, the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), and the Sun-god should also be made of gold here;
likewise, the placement upon the head should be performed with gold by the hosts of the twice-born without envy.
Its four peaks are made of silver, and its slopes are likewise silver;
likewise, its caves are covered with sugarcane and bamboo, and it has streams of ghee-water flowing in all directions.
There shall be a row of clouds with white garments in the east, and yellow ones in the south;
then in the west, variegated garments, and in the north, a line of clouds with red garments.
Having established the eight world-protectors, headed by Mahendra, in their proper sequence upon silver [pedestals],
there should be rows of various fruits all around, as well as delightful garlands and ointments.
And above it, a canopy of five colors, adorned with unfading flowers and white in hue;
having thus offered that foremost mountain of the gods, which shines exceedingly with gold.

Then, one should establish the supporting mountains (viṣkambhagiri) in the four directions, respectively, as a fourth part [of the central mountain], adorned with flowers and ointments, beautiful, and covered with various garments.
One should have that [image] made, adorned with barley and marked with young camels and *kadamba* trees, shining with a golden Kāma,
and richly endowed with flowers, garments, and ointments, as well as with a lake of milk-red water and a forest.
Shining with silver fashioned in the form of a conch shell, Mount Gandhamādana should be placed here on the southern side,
consisting of a heap of wheat or made of gold, together with the Lord of Yakṣas, Mānasa, made of gold.

It should be joined with garments and a silver forest; thereafter, one should fashion Mount Maināka and Mount Tila, their forms appearing adorned with fragrant incense, ointments, and heaps of flowers.
One should have it fashioned with golden pippala trees made of hiraṇya, and likewise with a grove of silver flowers;
having placed that vast mountain in front, covered with cloth and with lakes of curd and white water, one should then place it to the north.
One should fashion that mountain, consisting of minerals even on its own flanks, well-clothed with a great form and arrangement adorned by ornaments,
topped with golden banyan trees like flowers, and resplendent with a golden cow.
Then, having abandoned that [image] which was joined with a radiant silver covering and adorned with a beautiful golden garment,
he performed the fire-oblation with four venerable lords of the twice-born, who were knowers of the Vedas and Purāṇas and possessed irreproachable conduct and appearance.
Having prepared a sacrificial pit to the east, shaped like an elephant's head, one should perform the rite with sesame seeds, barley, ghee, fuel-sticks, and *kuśa* grass;
and at night, keeping a vigil with gentle songs and musical instruments, I shall describe the invocation of the mountain deities.
O abode and treasury of all the hosts of gods, O celestial mountain, quickly destroy whatever is adverse within our homes!
You alone are the Blessed Lord, the Ruler, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun;
you are the supreme seed, both manifest and unmanifest; therefore, protect us, O Eternal One!
Since you are the abode of the world-protectors, of the Universal Form,
and of the Rudras, Ādityas, and Vasus, therefore grant me peace.
Since your head is not empty of immortals and women,
therefore deliver me from the ocean of saṃsāra with its entirety of suffering.
Having thus worshipped Meru, one should also honor Mandara,
because you [are adorned] by Caitraratha and by Bhadrāśvavariṣa.
O Mandara, you shine forth; therefore, quickly become a source of satisfaction, for you, O Gandhamādana, are the crest-jewel of Jambudvīpa.
[347] May my fame be firm because of this splendor of the Gandharva forest,
since you have been honored by both the Ketumāla and the Vaibhrāja forests.
Since it possesses golden peaks, may there be certain prosperity for me;
since it is surrounded by the Northern Kurus and the Sāvitra forest.
"O Supārśva, you shine eternally; therefore, may there be inexhaustible prosperity for me.
Having thus addressed them all, at the clear dawn once more—
Having bathed, one should then give the middlemost of the excellent mountains to the preceptor,
and afterwards, O Sage, the subsidiary mountains to the officiating priests in due order.
O Nārada, one should give twenty-four cows, or ten, or seven or eight according to one's capacity; or, if lacking the means, one may give five.
Or one may give a single tawny cow that yields milk to the preceptor;
this indeed is recorded as the rule for all mountains without exception.
Those very same ones are remembered as the Brahmins for the worship, and those very same ones are considered the ritual implements;
they always constitute the representation of the world-protectors and of Brahmā and the other deities.
In all the mountains, it is taught that the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with one's own mantra;
one should always observe a fast, though if unable, eating only at night is prescribed.
O Nārada, listen now in due order to the procedure for all mountains,
as well as the mantras to be used at the time of the gift and the fruit obtained from these mountains.
Food is declared to be Brahman, for food is proclaimed to be the vital breaths;
from food all beings arise, and by food the world subsists.
Since food alone is Lakṣmī and food alone is Janārdana,
therefore protect us, O best of mountains, in the form of a mountain of grain.
Whoever gives a mountain made of grain according to this rite is honored in the world of the gods for more than a hundred manvantaras.
Attended by sages, he ascends to the heights of heaven in a radiant celestial chariot crowded with hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas.
Upon the exhaustion of karma, one attains the sovereignty of kings in this world; of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of grain.
The Fish said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of salt (lavaṇācala),
by the gift of which a person attains the worlds approved by Śiva.
The best salt-mountain should be made with sixteen droṇas;
the middling one should be half of that, and the lowest is recorded as being made with four droṇas.
One who lacks wealth should nevertheless have [the structure] built beyond the measure of Droṇa according to his capacity;
he should separately construct the supporting mountains (viṣkambha-parvata) with a quarter of that size.
One should always perform the ritual procedure for Brahmā and the others as before;
likewise, one should install all the world-protectors made of gold.
One should likewise place lakes, Kāmadeva, and others here;
one should also perform a vigil at this rite—now learn from me the mantras for the giving of gifts.
Since this mountain of salt was produced from the essence of good fortune,
protect me from sins by being of that very nature, O best of mountains!
Since all food essences are not palatable without salt,
and since it is eternally dear to Śiva and Śivā, therefore grant me peace.
Since that which has arisen from the body of Viṣṇu increases health,
therefore, in the form of a mountain, protect me from the ocean of saṃsāra.
Whoever should give a mountain of salt according to this rite shall dwell in the world of Umā for a kalpa, and thereafter attain the supreme goal.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of salt.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of jaggery,
by the giving of which a man becomes illustrious and, being honored, attains heaven.
The best [type of vessel] is considered to hold ten bhāras, the middling five,
the inferior three bhāras, and one with little wealth [should have] half of that.
In the same way, there is the invocation, worship, the golden tree, and the honoring of the gods.
In the same manner, one should fashion the supporting mountains as the abodes of the world-protectors,
just like the mountain of grain, and should recite this mantra:
Just as this Janārdana is the supreme Soul of all among the gods,
so too is the Sāmaveda among the Vedas and Mahādeva among the yogis.
Just as the *praṇava* is among all mantras and Pārvatī is among women,
so too is sugarcane juice always considered the most excellent among liquids.
Therefore, O Mountain of Molasses, grant me supreme fortune,
surpassing that of all the gods, asuras, nāgas, yakṣas, ṛkṣas, and birds.
Moreover, it is the dwelling place of Pārvatī; therefore, protect me always.
He who gives a mountain made of molasses according to this rite,
being honored by the Gandharvas, is glorified in the world of Gaurī.
Furthermore, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents,
endowed with long life and health, and unconquered by enemies.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of jaggery.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme mountain of gold,
by the giving of which a human being goes to the abode of Brahmā.
The best [stūpa] consists of one thousand palas, the middling of five hundred;
the inferior is half of that, and likewise even one of small means [should build] according to his ability.
One should give more than one *pala*, according to one's capacity and free from envy;
O bull among sages, one should prescribe everything just as in the case of the mountain of grain.
Having likewise fashioned the supporting mountains, one should utter this mantra:
"Homage to you, the seed of Brahmā; homage indeed to the womb of Brahmā."
Since you bestow infinite fruit, therefore protect me, O mountain;
since you are the offspring of Agni, and since you are the womb of the Lord of the World.
Therefore, protect [us] in the form of the Golden Mountain; salutations, salutations! Whoever should give a mountain of gold according to this rite—
He goes to the supreme abode of Brahmā, which produces bliss;
there he shall remain for a hundred kalpas, and from there he goes to the highest goal.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of gold.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the mountain of sesame seeds according to the prescribed rite,
by the offering of which a person goes to the unsurpassed world of Viṣṇu.
O best of brahmins, a mountain of sesame seeds made with ten *droṇas* is considered the highest, one with five is the middling,
and one with three is proclaimed as the lowest.
[350] And as before, all else—the supporting mountains and so forth—is the same.
O bull among sages, I shall now proclaim the mantra for the offering exactly as it is.
Since sesame, mung beans, and black gram were produced from the sweat of Viṣṇu’s body at the slaying of Madhu, may they be auspicious to us here.
Since protection in offerings to gods and ancestors is achieved through sesame seeds alone, deliver us from worldly existence, O Lord of Mountains; O Sesame Mountain, salutations be unto you!
Having thus addressed [the deity], whoever should give this unsurpassed mountain of sesame seeds attains the station of Viṣṇu, from which return is difficult to obtain.
A person attains long life both in this world and the next;
honored by the ancestors, gods, and gandharvas, he shall go to heaven.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of sesame.
Likewise, a mountain of cotton is considered excellent here with twenty loads;
ten are declared to be middling, and five are regarded as inferior.
O best of sages, one who possesses little wealth should give according to his burden, avoiding any stinginess regarding his riches, as if he were approaching a mountain of wealth.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should offer this and utter the following:
"Since you alone are always the protection for the worlds here."
Therefore, O Karpāsācala, may you be the destroyer of the flood of my sins;
thus, whoever should give this lord of mountains made of cotton on the occasion of a festival [attains great merit].
He shall dwell in the world of Rudra for a kalpa, and thereafter he shall become a king here on earth.
Thus concludes the gift of the mountain of cotton.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of ghee—
divine, consisting of radiant nectar, and the destroyer of great sins.
A supreme mountain of ghee should consist of twenty jars of ghee;
one of ten is declared to be middling, while one of five is remembered as the lowest.
Even one who possesses little wealth should construct the supporting mountains here according to the prescribed rule with two [parts]; likewise, he should fashion them with a fourth part.
One should place vessels of polished rice upon jars;
they should be made closely joined, high, and arranged according to the prescribed ritual for aesthetic beauty.
One should wrap it with white cloths and with sugarcane stalks, fruits, and so forth;
the remaining ritual procedure here is recited as being the same as that for the Mountain of Grain.
Preceded by the formal acceptance (adhivāsana), one should likewise perform the fire sacrifice and worship of the deities;
then, when the night has turned into dawn, one should present [the offerings] to the Guru.
In the same manner, with a tranquil mind, he gave the supporting mountains to the officiating priests;
for from the union of clarified butter and the luster of nectar, they were produced.
Therefore, may Śaṅkara, the soul of the universe whose radiance is ghee, be pleased with me;
for Brahman consists of light, and that is established within ghee.
Therefore, O Supporter of the Earth, protect us in the form of the mountain of ghee;
by this rite, one should offer the excellent mountain of ghee.
Even one joined with great sins comes to the world of Śaṅkara,
traveling upon a vehicle yoked with swans and cranes and adorned with garlands of tinkling bells.
Surrounded by celestial chariots, apsarases, siddhas, and vidyādharas,
he shall sport together with his ancestors until the dissolution of the earth.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of clarified butter.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of jewels;
with a thousand pearls, the mountain becomes unsurpassed.
The middle [mountain] is five hundred [yojanas high], and the lowest is recorded as two hundred;
the peripheral mountains (viṣkambha-parvatas) should be on all sides one-fourth [the height] of these.
To the east with *vajra* and *gomedaka*, and to the south with *indranīla* gems combined with *puṣparāga*,
the wise should fashion Mount Gandhamādana.
To the west, one should place the Vipula mountain mixed with lapis lazuli and coral;
and to the north, one should arrange it with rubies and gold.
One should imagine everything everywhere to be like a mountain of grain;
likewise, having performed the invocation, one should visualize the trees and the Vedas as being made of gold.
One should worship with flowers and water; at dawn, there should be the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
As before, one should address these mantras to the preceptor and the officiating priests.
Just as all the hosts of gods abide within all jewels, you are indeed eternally composed of jewels; therefore, protect us, O Great Mountain!
Since Hari bestows satisfaction through the gift of jewels by means of his ever-blissful grace, therefore protect us, O Supporter of the Earth!
He who gives this great mountain of jewels according to this rite goes to the world of Viṣṇu, honored by the lord of the immortals.
Having dwelt here for more than a full hundred kalpas, that lord of men,
endowed with beauty, health, and virtuous qualities, shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brahmin, has been committed here or in the hereafter,
all of that goes to destruction like a mountain struck by a thunderbolt.
Thus ends the gift of the mountain of jewels.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the unsurpassed mountain of silver,
by the giving of which, O lord of men, a person goes to the world of Soma.
The best silver mountain is made of ten thousand palas;
the middling is said to consist of five thousand, and the inferior is recorded as being half of that.
If one is unable [to build it larger], one should always have it constructed beyond twenty cubits according to one's capacity;
likewise, one should have the supporting mountains (viṣkambhaparvata) constructed with a quarter of that measure.
As before, one should fashion Mount Mandara and the other peaks according to the ritual rules out of silver; likewise, the wise practitioner should worship the World-Protectors made of gold.
In this case, the pedestal should be made of gold and fashioned with the images of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the Sun;
whereas for all others, that which would otherwise be silver should here be made entirely of gold.
One should perform the remaining rites as before, such as the fire-oblation and the ritual vigil;
likewise, at dawn, one should present a mountain of silver to the preceptor.
Holding darbha grass in his hand and free from envy, he should give the supporting mountains— adorned with abundant garments and ornaments— to the officiating priests while reciting this mantra.
Since silver is beloved by the ancestors, by the lords of monkeys, and by Śiva,
therefore protect us from this ocean of worldly existence filled with sorrow.
Having made this declaration, the man who gives an excellent silver mountain obtains the fruit of ten million cows.
Honored by hosts of Gandharvas, Kinnaras, and Apsarases, that wise man shall dwell in the world of the gods until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus ends the gift of the silver mountain.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the excellent mountain of sugar,
by the giving of which Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra are always pleased.
A great mountain (mahācala) should be made with eight loads of sugar for the best [type];
four loads are declared for the middling, and two loads are considered for the inferior.
A man of meager wealth who is unable to provide the full weight or even half the weight [of gold] should construct the supporting mountains (viṣkambhaparvata) with one-fourth of that amount.
Having prepared everything like a mountain of grain and combined it with nectar,
one should likewise place three golden trees upon Mount Meru.
The Mandāra, the Pārijāta, and the third, the Kalpapādapa—
these three trees one should place upon the heads of all.
A pair of *haricandana* trees should be planted on the eastern and western sides on all mountains, and especially so on the mountain of sugar (*śarkarācala*).
On Mandara, Kāmadeva shall always face west;
and on the peak of Gandhamādana, Dhanada shall face north.
Facing east, Haṃsa should be the embodiment of the Veda, vast and immovable;
Supārśva and Surabhī, made of gold, should face south.
Having performed all the rites, such as the invocation and the sacrifice, like those for the mountain of grain,
one should then give the middlemost of the excellent mountains to the preceptor.
To the officiating priests, he should recite these four verses regarding these mountains:
"This supreme mountain of sugar, the essence of the nectar of good fortune."
Therefore, O Lord of Mountains, may you always be a source of joy;
for those drops that fell to the earth while they were drinking the nectar have become [the source of your delight].
May this Śarkarācala, arisen from that [mountain], protect us—
since the sugar was produced from the center of the bow of the Mind-born [God of Love].
O Great Mountain, you who are composed of that [essence], protect [the donor] from the ocean of saṃsāra;
for he who gives a mountain of sugar according to this rite [attains such merit].
Completely liberated from all sins, he ascends [a vehicle] resembling the moon, the sun, and fire, and goes to the abode of Śiva accompanied by his attendants.
He shall ascend to heaven on the very same vehicle as Viṣṇu;
thereafter, at the end of a hundred kalpas, he shall become the sovereign of the seven continents.
Endowed with long life and good health, for as long as three arbudas of births,
one should eat according to one's capacity, free from envy toward all mountains.
At all times, he should eat alkaline and salty food with his permission;
he should cause all the mountain-provisions to be brought to the residence of the Brāhmaṇas.
One who possesses the wealth of honor should behold these [images] with devotion; one should touch those being offered here by men with devotion;
and one who hears of them with devotion and bestows his mind upon them becomes free from stain and goes to heaven.
Thus ends the gift of the sugar-mountain. Now the gift of the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina) is considered. Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

Then, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having prepared a black antelope skin complete with its hooves, with golden horns and silver hooves, adorned with a pearl on its tail, one should spread it out upon a woolen cloth (*āvika-vastra*). There, one should cover it with sesame seeds. One should make a golden navel and cover it with a pair of unwashed garments (*ahata-vāsas*). One should decorate it with all kinds of jewels and perfumes. Having placed four metallic vessels filled with milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter in the four directions, one should give it to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), who is adorned and covered with a pair of garments. Now, there are these verses:
But he who should give a black antelope skin, complete with its hooves and horns,
covered with sesame seeds and cloths, and adorned with all kinds of jewels;
By him the earth, together with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves, extending to its four boundaries, would have been given; of this there is no doubt.
"He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a Brahmin crosses over his evil deeds.
Thus it is said in the *Yamagāthās*.
He who gives even a single path provided with cattle, land, and gold,
having abandoned his evil deeds, shall attain union with Brahman.
Yoked with four oxen and likewise provided with land,
it should be given to a learned celibate student who is capable of receiving such a gift.
In the Matsya Purāṇa,
the Fish [Incarnation] said: "The full moon day of Vaiśākha and the eclipses of the moon and the sun..."
Likewise, the full moon days of Māgha, Āṣāḍha, and Kārttika.
The Turāyaṇa vow begins on the twelfth day; a gift given on that day yields great fruit.
O King, to whom should this be given by a twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires?
[355] Listen as I describe the manner and the procedure by which it is performed, O Lord of Men: on a pure spot smeared with cow dung.
First, having spread out a beautiful woolen cloth,
he then placed upon it a black antelope, complete with its horns and hooves.
Its horns should be made of silver, and likewise its teeth;
its tail should be of coral, and similarly, pearls for the two eyes.
Having made it equal in size to himself with sesame seeds, the wise man should cover it with a cloth;
he should make its center golden and especially adorn it.
One should place perfumes and foods according to one's ability in the directions of that [mandala],
and one should offer four vessels of mineral pigments in the directions in due order.
Having offered ghee, milk, curd, and honey into golden vessels according to the rule, proceeding in order from the east;
Likewise, having placed a branch of the campaka tree, an unblemished jar,
and musical instruments, one who possesses auspicious wealth should establish them.
One should wipe all his limbs with a worn-out yellow cloth;
one should cause vessels made of metal to be placed at his feet.
Whatever sinful deeds I have committed out of desire in this world,
may they be swiftly destroyed for me by the gift of a vessel of iron.
Having filled it with sesame seeds, one should place it under the left foot;
whatever sins have been committed unintentionally or those arising from desire.
"By the gift of a bronze vessel, may those [sins] always perish for me;
having filled it with honey, one should indeed place it at the right foot."
May the sin arising from my slandering others, from backbiting, and from eating the flesh on the back— may that sin be purified by the praise of this copper vessel.
May my falsehood regarding a maiden, my theft of cattle,
and my abduction of another's wife go quickly to destruction through the gift of a silver vessel.
These two [feet], made of copper and silver, should be placed with the feet upwards;
[this shall purify] whatever sin has been committed by the evil-minded one throughout thousands of births.
O Janārdana, by the gift of a golden vessel, quickly destroy [all obstacles]:
gold, pearls, coral, pomegranate, and citron.
In a praiseworthy vessel, one should place ears of grain, hoof-shaped pieces, and rhizomes;
having prepared these as prescribed, along with all varieties of vegetables and fruits.
O Lord of the Earth, the learned best of the twice-born who maintains the sacred fires,
having bathed, clothed in a pair of garments, and adorned according to his means,
is declared to be the recipient of the gift at the tail-end of the bull.
One should give a golden-navelled [image], saying, "May the bull-bannered Lord be pleased.
Having given it according to this rite, one should seek a black antelope skin as desired.
O King, that twice-born man is not to be touched, for he is like a funeral pyre or a sacrificial post;
one should avoid him from afar, even when he is intent on giving and possesses faith.
Having sent that brahmin to his own home,
O king of kings, one should perform a ritual bath within a mandala using a full water-pot and beneath a branch of the chickpea plant (*caṇaka*).
Having placed the preceptor’s water-pot upon his head with this mantra, [the disciple should say]:
"May the ocean satisfy you"; then the sixteen *ṛc* verses are to be recited.
Having put on two unwashed garments and sipped water, one attains purity;
likewise, having carried a well-sealed jar and set it down at a crossroads.
O best of kings, the prosperity that results from this cannot be described even by hundreds of sacrifices;
nevertheless, listen to it in brief.
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of a gift of the entire earth;
as a bird moving at will, one conquers all the worlds.
Until the dissolution of all beings, he undoubtedly attains heaven;
he knows no death of a son nor separation from his wife.
And one shall never, in this world, suffer the loss of wealth or country.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the black antelope skin (kṛṣṇājina). Now follows the gift of the Kālapuruṣa (the Time-Man).
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
Then, O son of Pāṇḍu, having reached an auspicious day on level and beautiful ground, on the fourteenth or the fourth lunar day, or under the Viṣṭi yoga.
The male figure should be fashioned from black sesame seeds, with silver teeth and golden eyes;
he should be tall, holding a raised sword in his hand, and adorned with hibiscus flowers.
Wearing red garments and adorned with garlands, he is decorated with a conch-shell necklace;
his waist is bound by a sharp dagger.
Although he was equipped with a pair of sandals, a black woolen blanket lay by his side,
and he held a ball of rice for alms in the palm of his left hand.
Having performed it in this manner and holding a handful of flowers,
the sacrificer, with a tranquil mind, should utter this mantra:
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers and having offered the sacrificial oblation, you are called "Kāla" because you bring everything to an end; by that very name, you are impelled.
O observer of noble vows, you are unattainable even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others;
yet you have been worshipped by me with devotion and entreated by me for happiness.
"O Lord, do whatever is appropriate for you; salutations, salutations!
Having thus worshipped him, one should present [the image] to a Brāhmaṇa.
The Brahmin should first be honored with garments and ornaments;
having given a sacrificial fee according to one's ability and having prostrated, one should bid him farewell.
Whoever bestows this gift according to this rite,
for him there shall be no fear of death, nor shall there be anything caused by disease.
He becomes one who possesses unspoken sovereignty, free from all afflictions;
at the end of the body, having pierced the abode of the Sun, he goes to the supreme goal.
Having returned here from the exhaustion of his merit, he becomes a righteous king,
a performer of sacrifices, endowed with prosperity, and accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Having worshipped the Kālapuruṣa according to the rules and having given him to a brahmin— the cause for the arising of both auspicious and inauspicious fruits—
one who possesses a body is not overcome by delusion through diseases consisting of all manner of ailments, by virtue of that [gift's] power.

Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Kālapuruṣa (the Person of Time) according to the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. Now follow the gifts associated with lunar days (tithis). Regarding this, Viṣṇu says:

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon is in conjunction with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should present a *prastha* measure of powdered salt with a golden center to a Brāhmaṇa. By this rite, beauty and good fortune (*saubhāgya*) arise. If the full moon of Pauṣa should fall under the asterism Puṣya, on that day, having rubbed the body with a paste of white mustard seeds, having been sprinkled with a jar of cow’s ghee, and having bathed with all medicinal herbs, all perfumes, and all seeds, and having bathed the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva with ghee, and having worshipped him with flowers, incense, lamps, perfumes, food offerings, and so forth, and having offered oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava hymns and Bārhaspatya mantras, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to pronounce a blessing (*svasti*) with excellent ghee. One should give a pair of garments to the performer of the rite. By this rite, one prospers. If the full moon of Māgha should fall under the asterism Maghā, by performing a *śrāddha* with sesame seeds on that day, one becomes purified. If the full moon of Phālguna should fall under the asterism Phalgunī, by offering a well-prepared bed with a fine mattress to a Brāhmaṇa on that day, one obtains a beloved wife who is charming, virtuous, beautiful, and wealthy; even a woman obtains such a husband. If the full moon of Caitra should fall under the asterism Citrā, by giving a variegated garment to a Brāhmaṇa on that day, one obtains good fortune. On the full moon of Vaiśākha, having gratified seven Brāhmaṇas with sesame seeds mixed with honey and having pleased Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from sins. If the full moon of Jyaiṣṭha should fall under the asterism Jyeṣṭhā, by the gift of an umbrella and sandals on that day, one obtains lordship over a city. On the full moon of Āṣāḍha, when it is joined with the asterism Āṣāḍhā, by the gift of food and drink, one obtains that very same reward in an inexhaustible form. On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, when it is joined with the asterism Śravaṇā, by giving a water-cow (*jaladhenu*) accompanied by food and covered with a pair of garments, one attains the heavenly world (*svargaloka*). On the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, when it is joined with that asterism, by the gift of a cow, one becomes completely liberated from all sins. On the full moon of Āśvayuja, when the moon has entered the asterism Aśvinī, by giving a vessel filled with ghee along with gold to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a light like a lamp-fire. If the full moon of Kārttika should fall under the asterism Kṛttikā, on that day at the rising of the moon, one should give a white bull or one of another color, provided with all kinds of grain, jewels, and perfumes, in the midst of lamps to a Brāhmaṇa. One does not see the fear of the wilderness. On the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, having fasted and worshipped Vāsudeva with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), having offered them as oblations and given them away, whatever one bestows on that day becomes inexhaustible. When the full moon of Pauṣa has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, having fasted and bathed with sesame seeds, having offered sesame-water, having worshipped Vāsudeva with sesame seeds, having offered oblations of them, and having eaten them, one becomes purified from all sins. When the full moon of Māgha has passed, having reached the twelfth day of the dark fortnight conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇā, one should offer two lamps with two large wicks before Vāsudeva. On the right side, having given a balance of ghee weighing eight [units] more, with a complete garment dyed with safflower (*mahārajana*), and on the left side, having given a balance of sesame oil weighing eight [units] more, with a complete white garment—having performed this, in whatever kingdom, in whatever region, and in whatever family one is born, one becomes radiant there.
Yama says: On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should honor seven or five Brahmins with black sesame seeds mixed with honey, or else with other [white] sesame seeds.
"May the King of Dharma be pleased"—whatever dwells in one's mind [should be uttered];
whatever sin has been committed throughout one's life perishes at that very moment.

Likewise: On the full moon day of Vaiśākha alone, having fasted for three nights and bathed, one who is self-restrained and pure should feed ten Brahmins according to the rule, offering them *kṛsara*.
Having given white or black sesame seeds mixed with honey to ten Brahmins, one should have them pronounce a blessing over those very gifts.
One should satisfy the ancestors and the gods with the thought, "May the King of Dharma be pleased";
whatever sin has been committed throughout one's life, one is released from it at that very moment.
He shall dwell in the heavenly world for ten million times ten million years, without a doubt;
he shall not behold me alone, yet he is not defiled by sin.
Jābāla says:
By offering cooked food and a water-pot, especially on the full moon day of Vaiśākha,
and dedicating it to Dharmarāja, one obtains the fruit of gifting a cow.
By satisfying seven or five Brahmins with water-pots containing gold and sesame seeds, one removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
In the Mahābhārata: On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should give sesame seeds to the twice-born;
sesame seeds should also be eaten, and one should always perform anointing with them.
Those who desire their own welfare and wish to constantly accomplish their tasks should do so with their whole being while at home.
Regarding expiations that have not been specifically prescribed, Saṃvarta says:
"When the month of Māgha has arrived, one should fast on the full moon day."
By giving sesame seeds to Brahmins, one is liberated from all sins.

In this context, the giving of gifts is prescribed for the full moon day because it is the primary act; consequently, by implication, the fast is observed on the fourteenth day. Having been devoted to fasting on the full moon day of Kārtika, one who gives gold, food, and clothing overcomes evil deeds.
Yama said: On the ninth lunar day of the dark fortnight of Kārttika, under the asterism Maghā,
having fasted for a full day and night, one should feed [the Brahmins] for the sake of Dharmarāja.
By honoring Brahmins with devotion according to the prescribed rules, one is glorified in the heavenly world;
likewise, by placing sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin.
Having quickly given everything to a Brahmin, one overcomes all evil deeds;
by giving a cow with both udders flowing, one obtains the fruit of the gift of land.
Having offered oblations of sesame seeds into the fire on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha,
and having given sesame seeds to the twice-born, one is liberated from all sins.
Yama is indeed pleased with him who always gives a cake along with gold to a Brahmin on a Sunday.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: He who, with a pure mind and composed, having reached the new moon day of the dark fortnight, should give vessels of sesame seeds to the Brahmins.
Having gratified the ancestors, that bull among men attains the world of the ancestors inexhaustibly and prospers in happiness for a long time.
Now, regarding gifts associated with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatradāna*). On this point, Viṣṇu states:
"Every month, when the moon is in the constellation Revatī, one becomes possessed of beauty by feeding Brāhmaṇas with *paramānna* (rice-pudding) mixed with honey and clarified butter."
And by feeding Brāhmaṇas with milk-rice along with sacrificial fees every month under the asterism Revatī, one is born endowed with beauty.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said: "O Bhārata, whatever is to be given during the conjunction of a specific lunar mansion (nakṣatra)..."
I shall fully declare that to you, which destroys all sins.
O highly fortunate one, by satisfying virtuous Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with ghee under the asterism Kṛttikā, one attains imperishable worlds.
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, on the day of Rohiṇī,
for the sake of discharging one's debt, one should give gifts of meat, food, clarified butter, milk, and grain to a twice-born man.
Having given a milch cow together with her calf under the lunar mansion presided over by Soma, one,
seated upon a divine celestial chariot, attains unsurpassed heaven.
O best of men, by offering krisara prepared with oil with a concentrated mind under the asterism Ārdrā, a man overcomes all difficulties whatsoever.
By giving well-cooked cakes filled with sesame seeds under the constellation Punarvasu,
one is born into a family that is illustrious, endowed with beauty, and possesses abundant food.
Having given gold, whether fashioned or unformed, as a meritorious gift,
he shines like the moon in worlds devoid of light.
Likewise, he who gives a beautiful silver image under the asterism Aśleṣā becomes liberated from all fear and is born learned in the scriptures.
By giving vessels filled with sesame seeds during the month of Māgha,
a man is born endowed with cattle and sons.
O best of the twice-born, by giving a mare at the time of the Phalgunī festival,
one attains the worlds of the meritorious that are frequented by the gods.
Having given a golden lotus during the conjunction with Uttarāphalgunī,
one attains the world of the Sun, freed from all afflictions.
Having given a golden elephant to a guest according to one's ability,
one proceeds to the abode of Śakra, seated upon the back of a choice elephant.
O Bhārata, having given a bull and sacred perfumes under the Citrā constellation,
one wanders in the world of the Apsarases and rejoices in the Nandana grove.
Furthermore, by giving wealth here during the Svāti asterism— whatever is desired by oneself—
one attains most auspicious worlds and great fame in this world.
O Great King, under the asterism Viśākhā,
one should give a cart adorned with draft-oxen, equipped with a side-saddle, and filled with grain, clothing, and other such goods.
Having given [these], he gratifies his ancestors and enjoys infinity after death;
that man does not encounter difficult states such as Raurava and the like.
Having given as much as he desires to the Brahmins, he attains his desired goal;
likewise, by giving woolen blankets and upper garments under the constellation Anurādhā.
Having given black pot-herbs, along with their roots, to brahmins, a mortal dwells in heaven for more than a hundred years, surrounded by hosts of gods.
By giving during the Jyeṣṭhā constellation, one attains preeminence and finds the desired goal;
by giving roots and fruits to Brahmins with a concentrated mind during the Mūla constellation, one obtains the same.
He gratifies all the ancestors and attains the unsurpassed goal;
furthermore, if a man offers vessels of curd under the Pūrva-āṣāḍhās, he gains great merit.
Having given [a daughter] in marriage to a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with noble lineage and conduct and has mastered the Vedas,
one is born after death into a family possessing abundant wealth of cattle.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, possessing cattle and wealth,
he [should offer] *udamantha* mixed with clarified butter and abundant honey and molasses.
Having given [a gift] under the Uttarāṣāḍhās, one shall obtain all desires; but having given milk mixed with ghee and honey under the conjunction of Abhijit, one shall obtain all desires.
The meritorious person who gives an excellent book here for the purpose of listening dwells in heaven among wise men who know the Dharma.
By giving a pair of oxen to a Brahmin under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, a person travels at will by vehicle through all the unobstructed worlds.
Wherever one is born in this world, one obtains all flavors;
likewise, by giving agallochum and sandalwood during the conjunction with Śatabhiṣā.
After death, one attains the worlds of the Apsarases and beautiful fragrances;
during the conjunction of Pūrvabhādrapadā, one should cause rājamāṣa beans to be given as a gift.
Provided with all kinds of edible fruits, he indeed becomes happy after death,
who gives a sheep along with clothing under the constellation Uttarā-phalgunī.
He who gives a cow with a bronze milking vessel under the asterism Revatī gratifies all the ancestors and enjoys infinity after death.
Having departed this life, she approaches the donor, bringing with her his desires;
by giving a chariot yoked with horses under the asterism Aśvinī, one becomes the best among men.
Having given a sesame-cow to the twice-born under the asterism Bharanī, one is born into a radiant family, endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots.
A man obtains well-prolific cows and likewise fame after death;
thus has this region of the Dakṣiṇā been declared according to its conjunction with the lunar mansions.
This [account], which pacifies all sins and destroys all calamities, has been told here to you by Devakī, by Nārada, and by me.
And here there is no restriction of time, nor likewise any sequence of lunar mansions;
O Indra among kings, wealth and faith are said to be the cause in this matter.
If, having examined the Vedas, the Blessed One declared here that giving is the duty of the son of Kamalāsana,
then what has not been accomplished in this world by him who, possessing wealth, gives to one of virtuous conduct, O Pārtha?
[363] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of constellations (*nakṣatradāna*) according to the *Bhaviṣyottara-purāṇa*. Now follow the gifts according to the months (*māsadāna*).

Viṣṇu states: By giving ghee daily to Brāhmaṇas throughout the entire month of Āśvina and thereby pleasing the two Aśvins, one becomes possessed of beauty. In this very month, by feeding Brāhmaṇas daily with products of the cow, one becomes possessed of good health. In the month of Māgha, by offering oblations of sesame seeds into the fire daily and feeding Brāhmaṇas with boiled grain mixed with ghee, one attains a blazing digestive fire.
Likewise:
One should always give ghee to a twice-born man in the month of Āśvayuja;
having gratified the two gods, the Aśvins, one is born endowed with beauty.
A man who gives sesame seeds indeed obtains his desired offspring,
especially during the month of Māgha, and particularly on the dark lunar fortnight.
Yama says: Having fed brahmins with kṛsara according to one's ability during the winter season,
one attains a blazing digestive fire and goes to the heavenly world.
And by feeding Brahmins with ghee and milk-rice along with ritual fees every month under the asterism Revatī, one is born endowed with beauty.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "By giving sesame seeds in the month of Jyeṣṭha, especially on the full moon day, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice; of this there is no doubt."
In the Devīpurāṇa:
"He who gives a cow made of sesame seeds on the full moon day of Māgha during the northern transit of the sun,
and that best of the twice-born who gives variegated garments in Caitra,"
In Vaiśākha, barley and wheat should be given; in Jyeṣṭha, jars filled with water;
and in Āṣāḍha, sandalwood mixed with camphor should be given, which yields great fruit.
Fresh butter is considered appropriate in the month of Nabhas, an umbrella in Proṣṭhapada,
and sweetmeat balls (laḍḍukas) rich in the color of jaggery and sugar in Āśvina, O Sage.
He who offers the gift of a lamp in the month of Kārttika gains great merit and attains all desires, as described in sequence in the Mārga and other scriptures.
One should give a cow made of ghee in the month of Pauṣa, one made of sesame seeds in Māgha, and likewise one made of water in Jyeṣṭha; with a cow of ghee as its calf, this yields great fruit.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should give a beautiful cow that yields great fruit;
its horns are said to be made entirely of gold, and its hooves of silver.
O Sage, the calves should be given according to the prescribed rite, accompanied by bronze vessels with bells, beautifully adorned with small tinkling bells, along with yokes and garlands.
[364] Having worshipped, according to the prescribed rite, either the Goddess, Brahmā, and Sūrya, or Viṣṇu, in an excellent twice-born who is endowed with natural conduct and character;
An adorned cow should be given to one who is free from desire and anger, who does not beg,
who is of good conduct, humble, and endowed with discipline.
From the gift of a cow, one obtains all desires that are delightful in their respective worlds.
Likewise: "In the month of Āṣāḍha, there should be a water-cow; in Bhādrapada, a [milk-]cow is always [to be given]."
In the month of Māgha, there should be a sesame-cow; by giving it, one obtains benefit.
He who gives sesame seeds to Brahmins in the month of Māgha does not behold the hell crowded with all manner of beings.
Yama said: I shall declare the purification for the accumulation of great sins, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally, as well as that which is the very means for attaining heaven.
A heap of white and black sesame seeds, thirty-two finger-breadths high and as wide as a man, should be prepared on a level spot.
If one has the means, one should have a golden image eight finger-breadths high cast;
one should fill the jars with honey, milk, curd, and clarified butter.
According to the extent of one's means, one should give to a learned Brahmin who is a petitioner during the month of Māgha, or in Vaiśākha, at the equinoxes, and during the sun’s northern course.
"Whatever sin has been committed throughout one's entire life perishes at that very moment.
In the *Vāmana Purāṇa*:
"O giver of gifts, in the month of Māgha, sesame seeds and a cow made of sesame should be given."
And likewise, sacrificial fuel such as wood and other offerings are indeed for the purpose of pleasing Mādhava.
O bull among men, in the month of Phālguna, rice, cows, and clothing together with a black antelope skin should be given for the sake of pleasing Govinda.
In the month of Caitra, for the sake of pleasing Viṣṇu, these— variegated garments, beds, and seats— should then be given to Brahmins.
In the month of Vaiśākha, fragrant perfumes and garlands should be given to the foremost of the twice-born for the gratification of Madhusūdana.
A water-pot, a water-cow, a palm-leaf fan, and sandalwood paste should always be given by virtuous people for the pleasure of Trivikrama.
A pair of sandals, an umbrella, and *lavana* and *āmalaka* fruits should be offered with devotion in the month of Āṣāḍha for the pleasure of Vāmana.
Clarified butter, jars of milk, and likewise a cow made of ghee should be given to a wise man in the month of Śrāvaṇa for the pleasure of Śrīdhara.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa), honey, and ghee,
as well as salt and rice with excellent jaggery, for the propitiation of Hṛṣīkeśa.
In the month of Āśvayuja, sesame seeds, horses, bulls, curd, copper, liquids, and so forth should be given by men for the sake of pleasing Padmanābha.
In the month of Kārttika, a person should offer silver, gold, lamps, jewels, pearls, and so forth, for the pleasure of Dāmodara.
Donkeys, camels, mules, elephants, carts, oxen, goats,
and sheep should be given by men month after month in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa for the pleasure of Keśava.
Palaces, cities, and the like, as well as houses and garments,
should be diligently offered in the month of Pauṣa for the sake of pleasing Nārāyaṇa.
In the month of Pauṣa, for the sake of pleasing Puruṣottama, one should diligently offer female and male servants along with their ornaments and food endowed with the six flavors.
Alternatively, the fourth quarter [of the offering] is that which is to be given for the fulfillment of all desires:
whatever is most cherished, and whatever auspicious thing there is in the house.
"For that very thing should be given for the sake of pleasing the God of gods, the Wielder of the Discus. (1.208)
In connection with the gift of a cow, various acts of giving have been mentioned; now the subject at hand is being stated:
Massaging one who is weary, attending to the sick, worshiping the gods, washing the feet of the twice-born, and clearing away their remnants are equal to the gift of a cow. (1.209)

Massaging those who are weary and so forth, each is equal in its fruit to the gift of a cow. "Weary" means exhausted; "massaging" refers to the removal of that fatigue. "Attending to the sick" includes medical treatment and the like. The rest is well known. Regarding the washing of the feet and the clearing away of the remnants of a twice-born man's meal, this applies to both equals and superiors. Yama says: "Removing the garlands from an image of a deity, sweeping the temple of a deity, and bathing all the deities are considered equal to the gift of a cow."
In the *Nandipurāṇa*: "Since health is the means for attaining dharma, artha, and kāma,
therefore, by the gift of health, a man becomes a giver of everything."
One who establishes a medical hall equipped with excellent medicinal supplies,
attended by skilled physicians, and provided with ghee, food, and honey;
The physician, however, should be learned in the scriptures, wise, experienced in the successive transmission of medicinal herbs,
knowledgeable regarding the roots and leaves of plants, and aware of the proper time for their extraction.
The wise one who knows the tastes, potencies, and post-digestive effects of rice, meat, and groups of medicinal herbs,
and who understands their application, enters the bodies of embodied beings with his intellect.

One who knows the elements, what is wholesome, and diseases; one who is untiring in knowing the etiology; one who knows the premonitory signs of diseases, and one who knows the subsequent treatment for them.
One who knows the place, time, and procedure, as well as the medical conventions;
one who is a knower of the eight-limbed Ayurveda and a knower of the application of medicinal formulations.
Wherever such a virtuous physician is employed,
he who relies upon the Dharma should likewise establish a hall of health.
That man is righteous in the world, he has accomplished his purpose, and he is pure,
just as one is restored to health in a proper infirmary by means of medicines that soften and digest the humors.
Even by curing a single sick person of their ailment, one endowed with compassion goes to the abode of Brahmā, accompanied by seven generations of their lineage.
The wealthy man, according to his means, and the poor man shall both partake of the fruit; for the poor man, where is there a house, and likewise, where is there a physician for his health?
Furthermore, if a mortal is restored to health by someone using roots, sandalwood, or other such remedies, he shall attain the aforementioned imperishable world.
He who liberates those afflicted by disease through his own skillful means— those whose conditions vary according to the accumulation or diminution of wind, bile, phlegm, and other humors.
He too goes to auspicious worlds that are attainable by those who perform sacrifices.

Surgery (śalya), surgery of the head and neck (śālākya), internal medicine (kāyacikitsā), demonology (bhūtavidyā), pediatrics and related fields (kaumārabhṛtya), the treatise on horses (aśvatantra), the treatise on elixirs (rasāyanatantra), and the treatise on aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇatantra)—these are the eight branches of Āyurveda as stated by Suśruta. Thus ends the gift of health. 1.209.
Furthermore: land, lamps, food, horses, clothing, water, sesame, ghee, and shelter— [one should give these].
Having given draft animals, gold, and oxen, one is honored in heaven.

The meaning of the statement is that one attains heaven by the gift of land, lamps, and so forth. Land should be given as fertile or fruit-bearing; its greatness [as a gift] is established precisely through that means. "Having given excellent, fertile land, one is glorified in heaven"—thus says Saṃvarta. It also serves for the destruction of sins, as Bṛhaspati has said:
Whatever sin a human being commits from birth onwards,
he is purified by the gift of land even as small as a cow-hide.
Thirty *daṇḍas* measured by a staff of seven cubits constitute one *nivartana*;
by giving ten of those as a *gocarma*, one is glorified in heaven.

Even by the gift of a cow consisting of mere leather, one attains heaven. As for the statement, "The giver of land attains heaven for a hundred divine years, and likewise for two hundred and fifty years," that is due to the gradation resulting from doubling and so forth. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Manu, "The giver of land attains land," that refers either to the intention of [attaining] land after falling from heaven, or to the intention of giving a smaller portion of the self; for such a gift possesses manifold forms. For this very reason: gold, silver, copper, gems, pearls, and riches...
"All this would be given by one who bestows the earth.

This is not said with the intention of referring to the entire earth, because that is impossible. Likewise, in the case of giving lamps and so forth, the attainment of heaven occurs due to the excellence of the recipient or through repetition.
For it is especially by the excellence of the recipient and also by one's faithfulness [that the result is attained].
Whether small or great, one obtains that fruit of giving after passing away.
Because of this statement; otherwise [it would contradict]:
"The giver of water attains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, supreme vision."
"One who gives clothing attains the same world as Candra; one who gives a horse attains the same world as Sūrya.

Thus, from the specific nature of the gift—such as clothing and so forth—the specific fruit is determined, as well as by the number, such as two or three. "May you stay in this house," said to one whose mental fluctuations have ceased and who has arrived, is *pratiśraya* (shelter). *Naiveśika* refers to the giving of a maiden for the purpose of establishing a household. Precisely for this reason:
"But one who is destitute of mother and father [is supported] by means of sacraments, marriage, and so forth."
"For one who establishes [this], no measure of merit can be found here. And:
"Neither by the Agnihotra sacrifice, nor by the Aśvamedha, nor by any other means is that supreme good attained after death which is attained by a Brahmin who has established [this]."

"By means of what has been established" means by means of a gift such as a dwelling that has been consecrated (*pratiṣṭhāpita*). "Skilled" (*dakṣa*). [The text says: "Gold indeed is *svarṇa*; moreover, there is a distinction in the fruit according to the place, time, recipient, the gold itself, and its quantity. Likewise: "In the high heaven stand those who give sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); those who give horses are with the Sun. Those who give gold partake of immortality; O Soma, those who give clothing prolong their life."

Thus, immortality and liberation have been shown. Likewise: "Having given golden draft-oxen, one is honored in heaven. Garga says: "The giver of land obtains land; the giver of gold, long life; the giver of a house, excellent dwellings; the giver of silver, supreme beauty."

And this should also be understood to apply to the gift of gold; however, there is a specific distinction of fruit regarding ornaments: "One who is adorned, having given an ornament, is honored in heaven.
One who is fit for the burden is called *dhurya*.
"The ox [yields] prosperity and nourishment; the giver of a cow [attains] the summit of the sun.

In this case as well, there is a distinction in the fruit based on the particularity of the vessel, place, time, and so forth, as well as the particularity of giving two, three, or more. In the *Viṣṇudharma*, the Blessed One said:
By the gift of an umbrella one obtains an excellent house; likewise, by the gift of a chariot and sandals, and by the gift of draft-oxen, one attains the worlds of Purandara.
He himself has also declared that the gift of gold is most excellent, as is the gift of refined gold;
so too for the man who bestows upon a twice-born a house for a wedding, endowed with every excellence.
Even for one endowed with the virtues of Vedic study and good conduct, the worlds are most excellent;
yet, he who bestows a daughter in marriage as a *brahmadeyā* and makes a gift of land to a Brahmin attains even higher realms.
The gift of clothing and food is likewise distinguished; such a person attains the world of Śakra, which is difficult to reach.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to the gift of land.
Thus have those who know the Dharma declared; listen as I recite it to you.
The giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years;
the one who seizes it, and the one who consents to its seizure, shall dwell in hell for exactly that many years.
Among all gifts, the gift of land is said here to be the most excellent;
for land is immovable and inexhaustible, and it bestows all desires.
The giver of land, having ascended to heaven, prospers for eternal years;
and upon attaining rebirth, he will certainly become a lord of the earth once more.
Just as the Earth-goddess always makes her giver her husband,
so too does a cow, when given with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), make her giver a lord of men.
Even if he has committed a sin, one should accept [the gift] from a donor of land;
for by giving land, one becomes pure, since the earth is indeed meritorious.
"Indeed, 'Priyadattā' is her secret, eternal name;
it should always be recited by the giver for her constant delight."
Whatever sin a man afflicted by the lack of livelihood may commit,
he is purified even by the gift of land the size of a cow-hide.
O one of great wisdom, he who gives the earth bestows all these things: gold, silver, copper, gems, pearls, and wealth.
Having given land that has been ploughed by the furrow, provided with water and endowed with fruit,
or even a shelter provided with water, one attains the supreme state.
He who gives land strewn with jewels to a twice-born man,
being liberated from all sins, is glorified in the heavenly world.
Those who bestow upon Brahmins land together with sugarcane, barley, wheat, and rice, do not approach Yama.
He who gives to a preeminent twice-born man land that milks all desires and is endowed with every kind of crop goes to the world of Brahmā.
A man who makes a gift of land is liberated from all fear;
O King, indeed, no other gift excels the gift of land.
For that bull among men who gives land that is auspicious and rich in all flavors,
the worlds of that high-souled giver of land are never exhausted.
By giving land that provides a livelihood to one who is emaciated, whose servants are emaciated, whose means of subsistence are exhausted, and who is perishing,
a person becomes a performer of a perpetual sacrifice (satrin).
The ancestors clap their hands; the grandfathers leap for joy:
"A giver of land has been born in our lineage; he shall deliver us."
In the Ādityapurāṇa: "He who, as a lord of the earth, should give this sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), shall,
upon taking birth again, become a lord of the earth once more."
"The certainty regarding all phenomena is that as is the gift, so is the enjoyment;
one should either cast off the body in battle or bestow this earth as a gift."
Thus they declare this to be the supreme blessing for those of the warrior class;
even from kings who have committed evil deeds, the virtuous accept gifts.
They desire no purifier other than the earth, for this is the supreme one;
"Priyadattā" is the eternal, secret name of this queen.
Whether it be charity or knowledge, the name of this [goddess] is most dear;
indeed, he who bestows even a piece of land the size of a cow-hide [is rewarded].
Liberated from all sins, he goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
the giver of land dwells in heaven for sixty thousand years.
Both the one who seizes it and the one who consents to its seizure shall dwell in hell;
so too he who takes away land, whether given by himself or given by another.
Having become a worm in a dog's excrement, he sinks down together with his ancestors.
In the Matsya Purāṇa: Whatever sin a man oppressed by the need for a livelihood may commit,
he is purified even by the gift of land measuring only a *gocarma*.
Whatever fruit one may obtain by giving a thousand pieces of gold,
that same fruit is ordained for the gift of land the size of a cow-hide.
In the Mahābhārata:
One should never, under any circumstances, give land that is saline, scorched,
surrounded by a cremation ground, or occupied by outcasts.
Thus ends the gift of land.
Regarding the gift of lamps, Saṃvarta says:
Having given a lamp at a temple, or among the twice-born, or at a crossroads.
He shall always be intelligent, endowed with wisdom, and possessed of vision.
In the *Viṣṇudharma*:
"The man who offers a lamp high up in the sky during the month of Kārttika, having delivered his entire lineage, shall attain the world of Viṣṇu. [371]
The determination regarding Kārttika is to be understood from the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*, as follows: "Those who, never ceasing, daily kindle a thousand lamps in the temple of Viṣṇu, day and night."
"The month of Āśvayuja is Tāmisra, while the bright fortnight of Kārtika is Śuklapakṣa.
Thus [it is said]. The mantra for the offering of lamps is:
"To Dāmodara, in the sky of the month of Nabhas, under the sign of Libra, together with Lolā..."
"I give you this lamp; homage to the infinite Creator.
Likewise: "Whenever, O best of men, a time of merit arrives..."
At the time of a solar transit, during a solar eclipse, at the full moon, and during the Vaidhṛti yoga.
When the northern course has arrived, as well as the southern course,
on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight, on the fourteenth day, and at the end of the day;
Then, having bathed on either the seventh or the sixth lunar day, a man devoted to his vows,
being self-restrained, should offer [the gift] to the assembly of the Bhavats and the Earth-Gods.
And a lamp burning with a cloth wick inside a pot of ghee.
The meaning is that [the word] occurs in the sense of a group or collection. Likewise:
"One should cause a full wick made of red cloth and ghee to be offered to Sūrya, blazing with four *prastha* measures, while reciting this mantra."
One should always offer the wick with the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ";
for Kṛṣṇa, with a yellow cloth, and for the Trident-bearer, with a white cloth.
One should cause a lamp to be offered for Gaurī with a wick made of cloth dyed with safflower and ghee;
for Durgā, one should kindle a full wick dyed with lac.
Having worshipped with a silk cloth, honey, and ghee in the Madhukūpaka well, and having offered white flowers, one should awaken Lalitā.
O Indra among kings, having heard those Vedic verses with this mantra, [one should recite]:
"May your mind, O child, be drawn hither even from the highest dwelling place,
O Agni, by my song that yearns for you."
We implore the eternal Dharma, the observer of cosmic order, Vaiśvānara, the lord of the light of Truth.
Agni Vaiśvānara, shining upon the back of heaven,
dispels the darkness with his light.
"Kāma, the sole sovereign, shines over all that has been and that is to be"— thus ends the mantra. In this manner, those who offer a lamp according to this rite,
having placed a jar of ghee in a wide and spacious vessel, [attain the highest goal].
They go to the abode of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun;
they remain there, shining brightly, until the dissolution of the world.
O King, a lamp should be offered with ghee or even with oil;
however, a lamp should never be given with fat, marrow, or similar substances.
A wise person should not perform any ritual with lamp oil;
indeed, extinguishing a lamp or causing it harm is censured.
He who performs such actions shall have eyes like blossoming flowers;
one who steals a lamp becomes blind, and one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed.
By giving a lamp with a wick made from lotus fibers and scented oil,
a person becomes free from disease and fortunate.
Having kindled a lamp with camphor for the God of gods,
one obtains the merit of a horse sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage.
Thus ends the offering of lamps. Now, the gift of horses, as stated in the Devīpurāṇa:
Whether it be a horse, or a draft animal, or even beautiful sandals—
he who, being well-restrained, gives such a gift to Brahmins;
For him, there are divine vehicles equipped with chariots, banners, and flags; moreover, no path here ever becomes difficult for him at any time.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: "O Goddess, he who gives as a gift a horse adorned with gold, possessing auspicious marks,
attains the world of the Gandharvas by that deed."
Regarding the gift of food, Saṃvarta says:
"The giver of food is happy, prosperous, and well-satisfied in all his undertakings. (Mahābhārata, 373)
Nārada said:
O lord of men, there is no gift superior to the gift of food;
by food this entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is sustained.
"Food is indeed the life-breath of living beings," so said Prajāpati;
therefore, O King, the giver of food is called by the wise the giver of life.
In this world, the giver of food becomes possessed of cattle, wealth, and beauty;
and after death, he is born long-lived, strong, and happy.
He who, with a concentrated mind, constantly gives food to guests, goes to the same world as Brahmā; thus said Parāśara.
A gift equal to food has never existed, nor will it ever exist;
therefore, the virtuous desire especially to give food.
Even after having committed a very great sin, he who subsequently becomes a giver of food is liberated from all evils and goes to the heavenly world.
In this world, the ancestors hope, just as farmers long for good rain:
"A son or a grandson will provide us with food here."
Whoever should give unblemished food to one traveling on a road,
who is weary and has never been seen before, shall attain a meritorious destination.
One should not inquire about [the guest's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or learning;
when requested by a Brahmin, one should simply give food without hesitation.
Whether he is of bad conduct or virtuous conduct, whether a fool or a scholar—
whosoever arrives at the conclusion of the Vaiśvadeva offering is a guest who serves as a bridge to heaven.
One should always feed a Brāhmaṇa who is peaceful and endowed with virtuous conduct, whether he has been seen before or not, and whether he is a friend or an enemy.
He whose food a hundred virtuous Brahmins eat,
given with a joyful mind, shall not be reborn in the state of an animal.
O King, having fed a thousand men who are knowers of the Vedas—
those who understand logic, those who know the Dharma, and likewise those who know the Smṛtis and the Bhāṣyas— [one attains great merit].
He does not go to a terrible hell, nor does he undergo the cycle of rebirth;
O Bhārata, he has effectively fed ten thousand Brāhmaṇas.
A man shall be liberated from unrighteousness even if he is always devoted to sinful acts. Bṛhaspati says:
The gift of food is remembered as productive of merit and superior to all other gifts.
From food, the procreation of life for human beings is always produced.
But he who provides even a mere means of sustaining life to a Brahmin,
especially during a famine, shall attain the imperishable heaven.
A man endowed with gold, jewels, and fine garments may die while not eating;
yet even one wearing only tattered clothes lives on, provided he eats.
Therefore, one should give well-prepared food along with a sacrificial fee to the Brahmins;
by that, one attains fame in this world as well as infinite heaven.
In the Āditya Purāṇa: "There is no gift superior to the gift of food; neither has there been, nor will there ever be.
[It bestows] sons, progeny, cattle, intelligence, women, and all desires in every respect."
One obtains everything through the gift of food; there is no doubt in this matter—provided that the food is offered with respect and devotion.
That [nectar] delights the limbs, yet it is not nectar when devoid of human [hospitality]. A donor who gives with joy is rare to find, and one who enjoys with joy is likewise rare.

Both the giver who gives with joy and the enjoyer who does not disdain the food go to heaven; so too do he who gives food even when it is unpleasant and he who does not take pleasure in the food [offered].
Both of them shall dwell submerged in hell for a hundred autumns.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The gift of clothing is proclaimed to be the most excellent of all gifts."
For clothing belongs to all the deities; one attains union with all of them.
A giver of clothing shall be well-attired and endowed with beauty and wealth;
however, one should not give to a Brāhmaṇa clothing that is dyed with indigo, nor that which is tattered.
One desiring great merit should not give what is damaged;
by giving a garment of cotton, one is honored in the heavenly world.
Having given even that [cloth] with its fringes, one shall obtain ten times that merit;
by giving a garment made of sheep’s wool, one attains the world of the Bhṛgus.
By giving a goat to Aṅgiras and linen cloth to Bṛhaspati, one attains the world of the Vasus; likewise by giving garments of Kuśa grass and silk.
Likewise, by giving [a seat] made of *kṛmi* grass, one is glorified in the world of Soma;
and by giving one made of deer-hair (*mṛgalomika*), one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By giving clothing made of bark, one attains the world of the Vasus;
by the gift of cloth, one becomes radiant and pleasing to behold for all.
He shall possess the enjoyment of pleasures and be truly captivating to women.
Thus concludes the gift of clothing.
Now follows the gift of water. Saṃvarta says:
The giver of water attains incomparable satisfaction and becomes free from thirst for all things.
In the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa,
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said:
When the month of Phālguna had passed and the great festival of Caitra had arrived,
on an auspicious day declared by the Brahmins, endowed with the strength of the planets and the moon.
A wise person should have a pond constructed that provides shade for wealth and is delightful,
either in the center of a city or in a wilderness devoid of water.
Whether in a temple of the deities or at the foot of a variegated tree,
it should be most cool, delightful, and provided with various seats.
One should have a divine mandala constructed, firm and capable of withstanding cold and heat;
in its center, one should place auspicious gems and beautiful jars.
A Brahmin endowed with virtuous conduct, having paid the appropriate wage, [should gather] mushrooms that have not grown out of season and whose tops are covered with cloth.
One should establish a water-station attendant who has many sons and followers,
and who tirelessly causes men to drink water.
Having thus constructed such a water-shed on an auspicious day according to the prescribed rites,
the best of men should, at the commencement, feed the twice-born according to his capacity.
Then the wise man should release it with this mantra:
"This drinking-water, common to all, is offered to all beings."
"By the offering of this, may the fathers and grandfathers be satisfied;
thereafter, four handfuls of water should be given, which cannot be withheld."
Or, O Great King, the supreme sustenance for living beings lasts for three fortnights:
[food] rich in fragrance, flavorful, and cool, placed in a beautiful vessel.
One who possesses faith, looking upon it with an unobstructed mind, should bestow it;
he should cause a twice-born man to receive food for him every day according to his ability.
Listen to the fruit of merit for him who, according to this rite, gives excellent water that destroys dehydration during the summer.
He who is honored by all the gods obtains that same fruit of merit which results from the gift of a hundred tawny cows properly bestowed.
Having ascended a celestial chariot resembling the full moon,
he indeed goes to the abode of the Lord of the Gods, being honored by hosts of apsarases.
Having been served by yakṣas and gandharvas for thirty million years,
he returns here upon the exhaustion of his merit and becomes a twice-born brahmin learned in the four Vedas.
Beyond that, this [attainment] is difficult to reach again;
it is especially hard for one who desires merit but is unable to provide even a water-station.
Every day, a water-pot filled with cool, pure, and clean water, its mouth wrapped in a rag, should be placed at the house of a Brahmin.
O lord of men, its concluding rite (udyāpana) should be performed month after month with cakes,
savory pastries, and cooked foods that fulfill all desires.
Having sprinkled water with this mantra while dedicating it to Śaṅkara, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and likewise Vāsava, the man [should proceed].
This vessel of Dharma, embodying Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, has been given;
by its grace (through this gift), may all my desires be fulfilled.
The mantra for the gift of the Dharma-jar:
Whoever bestows the Dharma-jar according to this rite obtains here the fruit of establishing a water station; of this there is no doubt.
Even a man who may be incapable of making the gift of a Dharma-vessel should,
with self-restraint, constantly attend upon the root of an Aśvattha tree.
"May the Blessed One Janārdana, who takes the form of the Aśvattha tree, be pleased with me.
Having uttered this and having offered salutation daily, [this] destroys all evil.
Whoever performs the watering at the root of a tree for four months also obtains that fruit; this is the eternal Vedic revelation.

[377] That man indeed lives for the sake of dharma in this world of living beings, whose water-station— filled with pleasantly cool water that dispels fatigue— is available for the enjoyment of all people when they have reached the road of another on their journey.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of water-sheds (*prapā*) according to the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.
In the *Mahābhārata*:
"Sesame seeds should always be given by the twice-born according to their ability."
Furthermore, through constant giving, sesame seeds indeed fulfill all desires.
Likewise, by the gift of clarified butter, one obtains a long life;
and by giving shelter in this world, as well as by granting fearlessness.
Having given land in such a manner, a Brahmin is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Regarding the gift of a house, the Kālikā Purāṇa states:
"Likewise, having performed the marriage for those born in families of Vedic scholars..."
Then, among the eleven twice-born men who were learned in the Vedas and possessed of virtuous conduct—
Then one should construct eleven beautiful houses;
having had them made, one should worship them with various kinds of grain.
Female slaves, cows, and buffaloes; beds, seats, and sandals;
and various vessels made of copper and clay.
Bowls for the purpose of eating, all kinds of utensils,
as well as iron and gold, and especially garments;
