Having thus gathered these excellent provisions, he should employ them in those households;
and for the sake of their livelihood, he should provide for each one according to his ability, even by the hundreds.
Even hundreds of ploughings, each one separately,
may be granted as a domain, a market town, a hamlet, or even a village for the sake of a settlement.
One should indeed unite the form of Soma with those brahmins, while meditating upon them;
there, those eleven [brahmins] are of the nature of images of the couple.
Having reflected with supreme devotion, he should establish them in those houses;
having entered, he should cause the best of the twice-born to undertake the maintenance of the *agnihotra* fires.
A man should act according to the rule and as is proper for his own welfare;
this is the ancient rule regarding those born of an unblemished lineage.
One should always cause the twice-born, who are distinguished by their devotion to Śiva and Śakti, to perform [the rites];
for that fool who employs his own servants for the offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).

There would be no fruit for him; the Vedic revelation regarding divine matters is certain, as is the case with sacrifices, gifts, vows, and so forth, as well as pilgrimages to sacred sites and the like.
But whatever being causes this to be done in such a manner, by him everything has been performed;
he goes to a celestial chariot that shines like the sun and is adorned with garlands of jewels.
Having ascended that meritorious station, adorned by celestial women and surrounded by thousands of other divine beings, he dwelt there.
Having enjoyed all the pleasures available in the world, he attains that [state] upon realizing,
through the power of his own wealth, that he should marry at least one twice-born man.
By that [means], a man who is a devotee of Śiva certainly attains that station;
through that [station], the attainment of the station occurs according to the rule.
Dakṣa says:
For one who establishes a person deprived of parents through sacraments, marriage, and so forth,
there is no limit to the measure of merit in this world.

In the Āditya Purāṇa: "O chief of sages, that twice-born man who reinstates a protector of the earth fallen from his kingdom shall dwell here on the back of the celestial vault (nākapṛṣṭha); of this there is no doubt."

Regarding the gift of gold, these are the words of Viśiṣṭha addressed to Bhārgava Rāma: "O best of Brahmins, having extracted all other jewels, gold has arisen as a mass of splendor; it is the supreme and most excellent jewel among them."
For this reason, the gods, gandharvas, uragas, rākṣasas,
humans, and piśācas, being self-restrained, uphold it.
O best of the Bhrigus, with crowns, armlets, and various kinds of ornaments, it shines brilliantly there when the gold is held aloft.
Therefore, it is remembered as the supreme purifier among all purifiers;
even after giving land, a cow, or anything else here in this world.
O Lord, the gift of gold is distinguished as supreme;
it is said that gold is indeed inexhaustible and purifying.
Bestow this most excellent purifier upon the foremost of the twice-born;
for gold alone is prescribed everywhere as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Those who bestow gold indeed become servants of the gods;
for Agni is all the deities, and gold has that very nature.
Therefore, for one who gives gold, all the deities are effectively given.
In the Nandipurāṇa: Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen *māṣas* are traditionally held to constitute one *suvarṇa*; by giving that [weight of gold], a donor shall attain heaven.
Likewise:
"Therefore, one should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a worthy recipient with all one's heart;
for gold given to an unworthy recipient causes the giver to fall into the ocean of hell."
Thus concludes the gift of gold.
Now follows the gift of a bull from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa.
Kṛṣṇa said:
Listen as I describe to you the meritorious fruit of the gift of a bull;
it is purifying, sanctifying, and indeed the most excellent of all gifts.
A single draft-ox capable of bearing the yoke is equal to ten milch-cows;
indeed, that one alone excels the gift of ten cows.
O son of Pāṇḍu, he who carries [the burden], moves about with well-nourished limbs, is free from disease,
young, auspicious, of good character, and devoid of all faults.
He becomes a savior in saṃsāra; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having adorned a peaceful bull, when an auspicious day has arrived—
O King of kings, one should present [the gift] joined with a silver plough to a Brāhmaṇa;
listen to that mantra, for I shall speak it to you.
You are Dharma in the form of a bull, the bringer of joy to the world; you are the foundation of the eightfold form. Therefore, protect us, O Eternal One!
Having given this along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and having prostrated, one should dismiss [the recipient];
thereby, the sin committed over seven lifetimes through the actions of speech, mind, and body is destroyed.
All that indeed goes to dissolution by the performance of the gift of a cow;
likewise, the gift of a bull, radiant and beautifully adorned.
Having ascended that divine chariot which travels at will, he rises to the heavenly world;
O lord of the earth, as many hairs as there are on that bull, so many years shall he dwell there.
For that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of cows;
having descended from Goloka, he becomes a twice-born man in this world.
O Great King, that performer of sacrifices, possessed of great splendor and honored by all Brahmins,
to whomsoever you give this excellent bull as prescribed, [he shall attain his goal].
I shall also tell you about that vessel which bestows life upon men.

Those who are patient and self-controlled, whose ears are filled with sacred learning, who have conquered their senses and desisted from killing living beings, and who are restrained in accepting gifts— those householders are true Brahmins, capable of delivering others across the ocean of existence.
Those who bestow a bull that is radiant, capable of bearing burdens, firm-necked, and endowed with every excellence,
truly become partakers of the fruit of the merit that arises from giving ten cows upon this earth.
Thus ends the gift of a bull from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. 1.210.
Furthermore:
By giving a house, grain, fearlessness, sandals, an umbrella, a garland, ointment, a vehicle, a tree, a beloved object, or a bed, one shall become supremely happy. (1.211)
The giver of a house and such shall become exceedingly and pre-eminently happy. Regarding the gift of a house in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, the Fish [Incarnation] said:
"Having constructed one built of baked bricks, or even one made of stone or wood..."
Or it may even be made of clay, endowed with auspicious characteristics.
Abounding with abundant offerings and flowers, accompanied by a cow,
and provided with *arjuna* trees, *sarala* trees, vegetables, and other charming things.
With *tiniśa*, *sarja* trees, *kadamba*, and *vañjula* trees growing in auspicious locations, it is endowed with the characteristics of a suitable site (*vāstu*).
One should perform the ritual placement according to the rule, as well as the beautiful decoration of the ground;
the sweeping and the sprinkling should be carried out with the third [mantra] of the Teacher.
With the hymn *sa na indrāgnī* from the *Śāntātīya*,
as well as auspicious offerings prescribed in the science of architecture (*vāstuvidyā*),
one should perform the rite for the five deities there, accompanied by forty [verses].
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rule, the householder should then give a gift;
this should be done during the solstices, the equinoxes, on auspicious occasions, during the Vyatīpāta yoga, or at the end of a day (the new moon).
At the beginnings of the Yugas, during eclipses, as well as at the beginnings of the Manvantaras,
at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), on the day of Vaidhṛti, and on the full moon and eighth lunar days;
During sacrifices, festivals, and weddings; upon seeing bad dreams;
when there is an abundance of materials and Brahmins; or wherever faith arises.
[381] Therefore, one who fears the terrors of saṃsāra should give the gift of a house,
because life is impermanent and fortune is exceedingly fickle.
Having understood this, one should construct in the northeast a square pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit,
level and adorned with a girdle (mekhalā) and a womb (yoni).
To the northeast, there should be an altar measuring one cubit for the worship of the lords of the gods, beginning with the planets;
there, the worship of Brahmā, Śiva, Acyuta, and Sūrya should be performed with fruits, flowers, and perfumes.
At the gates, archways should be constructed even with the leaves of milk-exuding trees;
and in the center, one should place a full water-jar adorned with garlands, perfumes, incense, garments, and jewels.
Then, having offered oblations into the mouth of the fire according to the procedure prescribed in the Gṛhya-sūtras,
one should cook a divine *sthālīpāka* sacrificial porridge with cow’s milk.
Then he should indeed offer that sacrificial porridge (caru) to the household deities situated in the center;
and, according to the correct application of the ritual rules, he should duly present the bali offering and pour a stream of milk all around.
One should first initiate the Brahmin and, once he is fully satisfied, ask for his forgiveness.
To the south, one should prepare a bed provided with a pillow and a lamp.

The householder donor, having taken hold of the hand of his wife— who is covered in white garments and accompanied by Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa— and who is herself dressed in white, adorned with golden earrings, and made beautiful by armlets and neck-ornaments, should recite this mantra:
Come, come, O Nārāyaṇa of divine form, whose lotus feet are worshipped by all the immortals!
O Lord of the worlds, both auspicious and inauspicious, accompanied by Lakṣmī, please accept this home.
Salutations to the Lord of the Kaustubha gem and to Him whose armor is gold;
salutations again and again to the Sustainer of the World who sleeps upon the Ocean of Milk.
Homage to Hiraṇyagarbha, homage indeed to the womb of the universe;
homage to him who has become the abode of the world of the moving and the unmoving.
The worlds, headed by the earth-world, are situated within your body;
they rejoice until the end of the kalpa, just as a householder rejoices in this dwelling.
O Lord of Gods, by your grace, this twice-born man, joined with his sons and grandsons and engaged in the performance of the five great sacrifices, shall dwell as long as the moon and stars exist.
Having spoken thus to the Lord of Gods together with his consort, he seated that best of the twice-born upon a bed placed atop a prastha of sesame seeds.
Then he should speak these words: "O best of the twice-born, accept this house, filled with all kinds of grain and provided with every household utensil."
There, one should present all the household requisites for the couple,
including sandals, shoes, an umbrella, ornaments, a seat, and vessels.
May all household utensils and ornaments, whether complete or incomplete,
become entirely perfect through your grace, O Janārdana.
Whoever offers cooked food according to this rite is honored in the world of Brahmā for as long as a hundred billion kalpas.
Whoever offers [an image] made of stone or even wood according to the prescribed rites shall dwell in the delightful Ocean of Milk in the presence of Nārāyaṇa.
And he who gives a house made of clay, furnished with all its appurtenances,
shall dwell in the worlds of the world-protectors after death for the duration of an *amantantara*.
Freed from the impurities of the Kali age, honored by hosts of Siddhas, and fanned by Apsarases with garlands of celestial whisks,
even a single such person may deliver his hundred ancestors, as well as his kinsmen— sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons— even if they are submerged in hell.
Having enjoyed divine pleasures there, he shall then become a king of kings on earth,
endowed with the strength of Nārāyaṇa and devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
"One devoted to the stories of Nārāyaṇa shall live happily for a hundred years;
therein [is contained] the group of five deities together with forty.
Regarding this, the following is the procedure:
Having fashioned eighty-one squares with dust and gold,
one should subsequently smear and anoint them, having stirred everything together with a cord on all sides.
Ten lines extending eastward and ten extending northward should be understood as forming nine groups of nine in all divisions of the site-plan.
Having divided the site into eighty-one squares, the expert in sacred sites should worship the deities occupying those squares— thirty-five in total— within all types of sites.
Thirty-two are to be worshipped externally, and thirteen subtle ones internally;
I shall declare them by name, so listen to their locations as well.
One should worship the nine deities of the squares, beginning from the northeast corner:
Śikhin, Parjanya, Jayanta, and Kuliśāyudha (Indra).
Śūnya, Satya, and Bhṛśa, as well as Vāyu in Ākāśa;
then Pūṣan and Vitatha, and both Gṛhakṣata and Yama.
Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, Mṛga, and likewise Pitṛgaṇa;
then Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadanta, and Jalādhipa.
Asura, Śeṣa, Pāpa, Roga, Ahi,
Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, Sūrya, Aditi, and likewise Diti.
These thirty-two are on the outside; now hear of the four within.
A wise person should worship those situated in the four corners starting from Īśāna.
Āpa, Sāvitra, Jaya, and likewise Rudra;
in the center on the nine squares is Brahmā, and eight [deities] are situated near him.
One should know all those who are separated by one [from the previous]; hear their names starting from the east:
Aryaman, Svitra, Vivasvat, and Vibudhādhipa.
Mitra, then Rājayakṣman, and likewise Pṛthvīdhara in sequence;
the eighth is Āpavatsa—these are recorded as being situated around Brahmā.
Āpa, Epa, Vatsa, Parjanya, Agni, and Diti—
this is the group of the Pādikas, thus [arranged] completely in the corners.
In the midst of that, however, there are always two doors facing outward;
they are Aryaman, Vivasvat, Mitra, and Pṛthvidhara.
Around Brahmā, in all directions, there are those triple-footed [regions] on every side.

In this regard, the procedure is as follows: having prepared a level, square area in the middle of the house, one should lay down ten threads there at equal intervals, and likewise ten extending from north to south. In this way, eighty-one squares are produced. Therein, Śikhī (the Fire-god) is to be worshipped in the square located in the northeast corner (*īśānakoṇa*). To his immediate right is Parjanya; to the right of that, in the square made contiguous with the one to its west, is Jayanta. Likewise, Indra is to the south of him; to his south is Śūnya; likewise to his south is Satya; likewise to his south is Bhṛśa. Then, in the single square to the south of that is Ākāśa. To its south, in the single square of the southeast corner (*āgneyakoṇa*), is Vāyu. Then, to the west is Pūṣan; to the west of that is Vitatha. Likewise, to the west is Gṛhakṣata; to the west of that is Gandharva; likewise to the west of that is Bhṛṅgarāja. Then, in the single square to the west is Mṛga. In the southwest corner (*nairṛtakoṇa*) is Pitṛgaṇa. To the north of that, in a single square, is Dauvārika; to the north of that is Sugrīva. To the north of Viyad is Varuṇa. Likewise, to the north of him is Puṣpadanta; likewise to the north of him is Varuṇa; likewise to the north of him is Asura; likewise to the north of him is Śeṣa. To the north of him, in a single square, is Pāpa. In the northwest corner (*vāyavyakoṇa*) is Roga. To the east of that is Ahi; to the east of that is Mukhya; likewise to the east of that is Bhallāṭa; likewise to the east of that is Soma; likewise to the east of that is Sūrya; likewise to the east of that is Aditi. In a single square is Diti. In the center, the nine squares being combined, is Brahmā. To his east, combining the squares to the south and north, is Aryaman. To his south, in a single square, is Savitṛ. To his west, combining three squares, is Vivasvat. To the west of that, in a single square, is Vibudhādhipa. To the north of that, combining three squares, is Mitra. To the north of that, in a single square, is Rājayakṣman. To the east of that, combining three squares, is Pṛthvīdhara. To the east of that, in a single square, is Apavatsa. To the west of Parjanya, in a single square, is Apa. To the west of Ākāśa, in a single square, is Sāvitra. To the east of Dauvārika, in a single square, is Jaya. To the east of Pāpa, in a single square, is Rudra. Thus says Bṛhaspati.
"He who bestows upon Brahmins food seasoned with juices, along with household utensils,
his lineage shall not perish, and he attains eternal heaven.
Thus ends the gift of a house.
In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"The foremost among grains has been declared by the best of the twice-born;
even among grains, red rice (*raktaśāli*) is proclaimed to be the supreme grain."
By giving red śāli rice, a person is honored in the world of the Sun;
likewise, by the gift of wheat, one shall attain the world of the Vasus.
He who bestows *priyaṅgu* becomes beloved by the world;
but for him who gives *śyāmaka*, the deities are pleased.
A person who is devoted to the gift of other awned grains attains the heavenly world; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The giver of mung beans attains the world of Śakra, while the giver of māṣa beans attains the world of Yama;
likewise, O Brahmin, the giver of sesame seeds attains whatever world he desires.
By the gift of *mayu* beans, one indeed goes to the world of Nirṛti;
by giving *satīna* chickpeas, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
By giving lentils, black gram, and parched grain, one attains the world of Vāyu;
by the gift of other cultivated grains, one shall attain heaven.
By the gift of sugarcane and grapes, one shall attain supreme good fortune.
Thus concludes the gift of grain.
Now follows the gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*).
Regarding this, Viṣṇu states: "The gift of fearlessness is superior to the gift of food; by the giving of this, one attains the desired world. Saṃvarta says:
By granting safety to living beings, one shall obtain all desires;
one gains long life and shall always be of cheerful mind.
In the Nandipurāṇa:
"For the great ones, for those with subtle bodies, for those afflicted by disease,
and for those who are violent yet possess gentle forms, there is indeed constant happiness through fearlessness."
The protection of the life and fearlessness of a single sentient being is better than a thousand cows with their sacrificial fees given to a thousand Brahmins.
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*: "Fie on the life of that man who does not grant favor to one who is suffering and seeking refuge— even if that person belongs to the side of his enemies."
For one whose mind is not set upon protecting the distressed, sacrifices, gifts, and austerities do not lead to welfare either in this world or in the next.
In the Mahābhārata: "The wise declare that for one who, out of greed, hatred, or even fear, abandons one who has come for refuge, the sin is equal to the killing of a Brahmin."
Likewise,
the wise have said: "He who, though capable, looks on with indifference while living beings are being slain, goes to a terrible hell."

"He who might give this earth, bounded by the four oceans, to sentient beings, and he who grants them fearlessness— of these two, the giver of fearlessness is superior. Thus it is said in the *Rāmāyaṇa*.
If one who has come for refuge perishes while being watched over by a protector,
that unprotected person departs taking away all the merit of that protector.
Manu says:
Whatever may be asked for, it should be given by one who is free from malice;
for such a recipient will surely arise who delivers one from all [sins].
The giver of water obtains satisfaction; the giver of food, imperishable happiness;
the giver of sesame seeds, desired offspring; and the giver of a lamp, excellent vision.
The giver of land attains heaven; the giver of gold, long life;
the giver of a house, the finest dwellings; and the giver of silver, supreme beauty.
The giver of clothing attains the same world as Candra; the giver of horses attains the same world as the Aśvins;
the giver of a bull attains abundant prosperity; and the giver of a cow attains the realm of the Sun.
"One who gives a vehicle and a bed obtains a wife; one who grants fearlessness obtains sovereignty;
a giver of grain obtains eternal happiness; and a giver of the Veda obtains the eternal Brahman. Thus says Saṃvarta.
By giving sandals, shoes, umbrellas, beds, seats,
and various kinds of jewels, one becomes a lord of wealth.

Viṣṇu states: "By the gift of an umbrella one attains heaven; by the gift of sandals, a chariot yoked with mules. In the Mahābhārata: "He who bestows a pair of sandals upon a Brāhmaṇa with diligence shall cross over all the thorns and uneven terrain of Mount Mandara."
Indeed, a cart yoked with draft animals is given; likewise,
the giver of an umbrella obtains a house, and the giver of a house obtains a city.
By the gift of sandals, one obtains an unsurpassed chariot.
Bṛhaspati says: A man who gives an umbrella and sandals crosses the path of the Asipatravana forest, which is lined with razor edges,
and the intense heat of the sun.
In the Devīpurāṇa: "The gift of food, horses, cows, clothing, silver, umbrellas, and seats—
these eight gifts are especially praised in the world of the departed (pretaloka)."
He who bestows milk, curd, or even ghee, honey, oil, or likewise molasses upon brahmins, does not approach Yama.
Regarding the gift of a bed, in the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"By the gift of a bed, the best of Brahmins obtains a wife;
having given to a twice-born man a well-spread bed with a coverlet."
He obtains a wife who is born of a great family, endowed with beauty and wealth, possessed of influential kin, and likewise submissive to his will.
And by this very gift, a wife may obtain her husband.
Likewise,
by the gift of a canopy, one is liberated from all sins;
and so too for a brahmin who gives an umbrella— there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By giving an umbrella with a hundred ribs as a protection against the heat,
one is liberated from all sins and is honored in the heavenly world.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born,
by giving a pair of shoes that are smooth and well-oiled, one proceeds easily along the southern path.
Mounted upon a chariot yoked with mules, he ascends to the third heaven;
liberated from all sins, he shall travel happily along the path of Yama.
The giver of garlands attains prosperity; the giver of fruit finds his actions fruitful;
by the gift of ointment, one is liberated from all afflictions.
Likewise:
"A person becomes handsome by the gift of sandalwood;
and the gift of saffron is declared to be a bringer of good fortune."
Likewise, by the gift of camphor, one shall obtain all desires;
by the gift of musk, one shines with glory upon the earth.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "Those who give gifts of sandalwood, conch shells,
and pearls rescue their ancestors— even those who have committed sins— just as the Śruti declares."
The Gift of Trees in the Mahābhārata:
"He who offers a tree that bears flowers or one that bears fruit to a twice-born man indeed attains a home that arrives without effort, abounding in women and filled with many jewels."
Yama said: By offering flowers to the deities, one is born endowed with prosperity;
and that man who offers incense attains an upward rebirth.
He who gives a womb-purifying herb, an ointment, honey,
or salt to a Brahmin attains good fortune.
Through the gift of food, one obtains whatever desires are wished for by the mind;
through the gift of water, one finds eternal satisfaction.
Viṣṇu: Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear in one's home—
that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
In the *Bhaviṣyottara*, regarding the gift of a bed:
Śrī Kṛṣṇa said,
"O scion of the Pāṇḍu lineage, I shall describe to you the gift of a bed."
Having given which, one shall partake in happiness both in this world and in the next.
Since life is impermanent, who else will provide for you later? O Bhārata, one is a kinsman and a father only as long as he lives.
[388] Thinking, "He is dead, he is dead," affection ceases in an instant;
therefore, one should diligently give food, fruit, and so forth with one's own hand.
Reflecting in one's mind that "the self alone is indeed the friend of the self," if the self does not honor the self through the practice of giving and virtue;
Who else is a benefactor like him, who will pay homage later?
Therefore, having obtained a firm bed made of solid wood, [one should act].
It was adorned with arrangements of well-polished leaves and decorated with golden bands;
it was covered with swan-down pillows and provided with auspicious side-cushions.
Upon that [altar], which is provided with a concealing cloth and perfumed with the scent of incense,
one should place a golden image of Hari accompanied by Lakṣmī.
One should place a jar filled with ghee upon its head;
O Pāṇḍava, that should always be known by the wise as the Sleep Jar.
Betel, powdered saffron, camphor, agallochum, and sandalwood;
a lamp, sandals, an umbrella, a fly-whisk, a seat, and a vessel.
One should devoutly place seven kinds of grain at the sides,
as well as whatever else may be useful to one lying upon the bed.
Having prepared a bed equipped with musical instruments that produce amorous sounds and a canopy of five colors, one should present it to a Brāhmaṇa.
On an auspicious day, according to the prescribed rites, [give her] to a Brahmin accompanied by his wife,
O Kṛṣṇa, so that the daughter of the ocean may not remain empty for you.
"May my bed also not be empty, likewise in birth after birth.
Having spoken thus, he should offer the pure couch, prostrate, and dismiss [the deity].
This same rule is proclaimed for the eleventh day as well,
if a kinsman gives [an offering] for the sake of the Dharma when a kinsman has died.
And listen, O Indra among kings, as I describe the distinction here:
whatever object was previously enjoyed by him while he was living in his home.
Whatever was clinging to her body, as well as her clothing, vehicle, and vessels—
whatever she held dear— all that one should provide for her.
In that same manner, one should then place a golden man upon it;
having honored him, the death-bed (mṛtaśayyā) should be given away as prescribed,
[granting residence] in heaven, in the abode of Indra, and likewise in the dwelling of the Son of the Sun (Yama).
That person dwells in happiness by the power of the gift of a bed;
the terrifying messengers of Yama do not torment that man.
That man is never afflicted by heat or cold;
even if he is joined with evil deeds, he goes to the heavenly world.
Mounted upon a supreme celestial chariot and served by hosts of apsarases,
he shall remain there, freed from all sin, until the dissolution of all beings.

O son of Pāṇḍu, the stainless gift of a bed has been proclaimed by you as a treasury of all happiness. He who himself bestows it according to the prescribed rite shines with happiness for an eon in heaven, free from all conceptual constructs.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of a bed from the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa. 1.211.
Furthermore: Since Brahman, which consists of all dharmas, is superior to all gifts, one who gives that attains the world of Brahmā without falling away. 1.212

The *brahma* is the Veda; by teaching it, one reaches the world of Brahmā without falling away and without being corrupted. The reason for this is that, because the *brahma* consists of all dharmas, it is superior to other things that might be given. The suffix *-maya* is used here in the sense of abundance (*prācurya*), as in "Magadha is full of rice" (*śālimayā magadhāḥ*) or "the sacrifice is full of food" (*annamayo yajñaḥ*). Alternatively, it may be used in the sense of non-difference (*abheda*), as in "Brahmā is full of bliss" (*ānandamayaṃ brahma*). In this case, the non-difference between the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is expressed through metaphorical identification (*upacāra*). Bṛhaspati says: "A thousand cows and a hundred oxen are equal."
A vehicle is equal to a hundred oxen; a horse is equal to ten vehicles.
A maiden equal to ten horses and the gift of land are equal;
there is nothing equal to the gift of land, and the gift of knowledge is superior to that.
Yama said:
One might give this entire earth adorned with all kinds of jewels, and one might give the scripture to the Brahmins; that [gift of the scripture] is equal to those [other gifts].

In connection with the gift of the Veda (*brahmadāna*), the procedure for the gift of other branches of knowledge is now stated. Regarding this, the *Bhaviṣyottara* says: "O descendant of Yadu, I shall now describe to you accurately the procedure for the gift of knowledge, as well as the fruit that is truly yielded by its giving."
On an auspicious day as declared by the Brahmins, one should have a beautiful,
divine, and square mandala prepared with cow dung on all sides.
Having placed the book there upon a surface strewn with heaps of flowers and adorned with svastikas and other auspicious signs, one should worship it with perfumes and flowers.
A golden pen should be made, and the ink-pot should be of silver;
the ink should be produced from the soot arising from the flame of a lamp.
Having worshipped the scribe, the wise person should cause the commencement of the work, using a mixture of the juice of *bola* rubbed upon an *audumbara* leaf with the palm of the hand.
From that time forth, the scribe was disciplined and vigilant,
writing with the correct measures and nasal consonants, and accompanied by the proper division of words.
He who knows that [the letters] are equal, level-headed, circular, and dense, and are properly bound by their measures (mātrās), is a true scribe.
With his inner self absorbed in that, he should cause the letters to be written here—
either five books, or ten, or even twenty.
Whether thirty, forty, or at most fifty years of age,
the wise man should be a knower of grammar, logic, and epistemology, eating sweet and unctuous food, and remaining pure.
When the members of the assembly were satisfied and delighted,
he gradually completed the composition of the true scripture, whether it be Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava.
Once it has been completed, the scribe should be honored with garments and ornaments;
having thus worshipped him, that scripture should likewise be given to one who possesses virtuous qualities.
One should present the book, accompanied by a pair of garments, to the learned reciter who honors the scriptures and speaks with pleasant words.
Or else, one should establish it as common property for all people in a monastery;
the fruit that a man obtains by giving according to this rule—[that he shall attain].
Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall declare that to you; learn from me what fruit is gained from a pilgrimage to sacred fords and what merit belongs to those who perform sacrifices.
Whatever fruit is obtained by the proper gift of a thousand tawny cows,
that same fruit one attains from the gift of a single book.
O Pārtha, who could possibly describe the fruit that one obtains by giving away the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, or even the Rāmāyaṇa?
He who, having risen at dawn, diligently teaches his disciples, has truly studied the Vedas and Shastras; he has achieved fame and performed a deed worthy of himself.
What has not been given by him who, having provided a livelihood for his preceptor, teaches the twice-born? For he is one who perceives the goals of dharma, kama, and artha.
By giving students food, anointing oil, clothing, or even alms,
a person undoubtedly attains all their desires.
Discrimination is a long life and the fulfillment of all desires and goals;
by providing food to students, everything becomes as if given as a gift.
O Pārtha, one should always set one's mind upon performing service for anyone who desires to acquire weapons, scriptures, arts, or crafts.
Whatever fruit results from a thousand Vājapeya sacrifices properly performed, that same fruit one obtains from the gift of knowledge; of this there is no doubt.
The righteous-souled one who always causes the recitation of books to be performed in a temple of Śiva, a house of Viṣṇu, or likewise in a sanctuary of the Sun;
O bull among men, by that [act], cows, land, gold, garments, beds, and seats are given by him every single day.
A man devoid of knowledge does not discern dharma and adharma;
therefore, one whose soul is devoted to dharma should everywhere be intent on the gift of knowledge.
The three worlds, the four castes, and the four stages of life individually,
as well as all the deities beginning with Brahmā, are established upon the gift of knowledge.
O Indra among kings, for seventy-one cycles of four yugas,
he shall remain in the city of Viṣṇu, being honored by the highest of the gods.
Returning to the earth at the end of time, he becomes a righteous king,
rich in elephants, horses, chariots, and vehicles— a donor, an enjoyer, and one free from envy.
Endowed with beauty and good fortune, he shall be long-lived and free from disease;
surrounded by sons and grandsons, he shall live for a hundred autumns.
In this world, there is no gift that yields such distinguished fruit as knowledge—which dwells within the lotus of the mouth—excepting none other.
O Pārtha, what is there in this world that would not be considered given by one who bestows that [knowledge], including all things such as cattle, land, gold, elephants, horses, and chariots?
[392] Thus ends the procedure for the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna) according to the Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa;
[it is also found] in the Matsya Purāṇa.
Matsya said:
The Purāṇa is remembered by Brahmā as the first of all scriptures,
and from his mouths the Vedas subsequently issued forth.
In that period as well, there was only one Purāṇa,
a meritorious means for achieving the three aims of life, with an extent of one hundred crores [of verses].
Its meaning has been shown here in brief through four hundred thousand [verses];
now, those eighteen Purāṇas are being described here.
O best of sages, listen as I shall declare their names according to what was previously told by Brahmā to Marīci.
That Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of ten thousand verses;
and whoever, having written it, should give it away together with a water-cow (jaladhenu), [attains great merit].
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, however, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

The *Brahmapurāṇa* consists of 10,000 verses; this is the rule for its donation. (1) When this very world became a golden lotus (*padma*), that [Purāṇa], which likewise takes as its basis the conclusion of that narrative, is called the *Pādma* by the wise.
That Padma Purāṇa is recited here as consisting of fifty-five thousand verses;
and whoever should give that Purāṇa accompanied by a golden lotus, [attains the supreme goal].
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, one who offers [food] combined with sesame seeds shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.

The *Padmapurāṇa* consists of 55,000 verses; this is the rule for its gift. (2) That which Parāśara spoke concerning the events of the Vārāha-kalpa, setting forth all duties—that they know to be the Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa.
He who, having purified his soul, gives this [gift] accompanied by a cow of ghee on the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, goes to the abode of Varuṇa.
The wise know that Purāṇa to consist of twenty-three thousand verses.

The Viṣṇupurāṇa consists of 23,000 verses; this is the rule for its gift. (3) In connection with the Śrutikalpa, Vāyu here proclaimed the dharmas, wherein that which pertains to Vāyu is found, joined with the majesty of Rudra.
That Purāṇa, consisting of twenty-four thousand verses, is declared here;
on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, it should be accompanied by a cow made of molasses.
The man who gives curd mixed with other substances to a Brahmin who maintains a family shall dwell for one kalpa in the world of Śiva, his soul purified.

The Vāyu Purāṇa states that its extent is 24,000 verses; this is the rule for the gift of the Vāyu Purāṇa. (4) That work in which the expansion of Dharma is described with reference to the Gāyatrī, and which includes the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra, is called the Bhāgavata.
And whoever, having written this, should give it away on the full moon day of the month of Prauṣṭhapada together with a golden lion, goes to the supreme state.
That Purāṇa is proclaimed to consist of eighteen thousand verses;
the text is 18,000 [verses]. This is the procedure for the gift of the Bhāgavata Purāṇa, wherein Nārada here expounds the dharmas based upon the Bṛhatkalpa.
Twenty-five thousand [verses] are said to constitute that Nāradīya.
He who gives this, together with a cow, on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight,
attains supreme perfection from which rebirth is difficult to obtain.

The gift of the Nārada Purāṇa consists of 25,000 verses. (6) That Purāṇa which, having taken omens as its subject matter, investigates dharma and adharma, is here called the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa; it comprises nine thousand verses.
And whoever should give [this] after having it drawn, together with a golden karṣa,
shall partake in the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice on the full moon day of Kārttika.
The Mārkaṇḍeya-dānavidhi consists of 9,000 verses. (7) That which was told by Agni to Vasiṣṭha concerning the events of the Īśāna-kalpa is called the Āgneya-purāṇa.
And having had it written out, he who should give it on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa according to the prescribed rite, together with a golden lotus and likewise a cow made of sesame seeds—
that [manuscript], consisting of sixteen thousand [verses], bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
The Āgneya Purāṇa consists of 16,000 verses; this is the section on the rules for making gifts.
(8) In this work, the Four-faced One [Brahmā], having taken as his subject the majesty of the Sun, explains the stability of the world through the context of the events of the Aghora Kalpa.
He related to Manu the characteristics of the multitude of beings,
numbering fourteen thousand and five hundred.
[394] That which is primarily concerned with future conduct is here called "the future.
One who should especially give that on the full moon day in the month of Pauṣa—
One who gives [this work] together with a jar of molasses shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
[The extent is] 14,500 verses. Thus ends the procedure for the gift of the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa. (9) And concerning the narrative of the Rathantara-kalpa:
Savarṇi recounted to Nārada the supreme majesty of Kṛṣṇa.
That in which the great deeds of Brahmā-Varāha are described,
consisting of eighteen thousand verses, is called the Brahmavaivarta.
O Blessed One, he who gives the Purāṇa Brahmavaivarta in the month of Māgha on the full moon day is glorified in the world of Brahmā.

The Brahmavaivarta-dānavidhi consists of 18,000 verses. (10) Therein, the Lord Maheśvara, residing within the center of the fiery liṅga, spoke concerning the Āgneya [Purāṇa] for the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
This Purāṇa, consisting of eleven thousand verses, was spoken by Brahmā himself as the *Liṅga-kalpa*; he who bestows it upon Phālguna [attains its fruit].
Endowed with the gift of a sesame-cow, he attains identity with Śiva.

The *Liṅgapurāṇa* consists of 11,000 verses; this is the section on the rules for giving gifts. (11) Furthermore, that which was spoken by Viṣṇu to the Earth concerning the majesty of Mahāvarāha is here called the *Varāhapurāṇa*.
O best of sages, that Purāṇa which was spoken in connection with Mānava at the beginning of the Kalpa is here said to consist of twenty-four thousand verses.
Having fashioned a golden Garuḍa together with a sesame-cow,
he who gives it to a Brahmin householder on the full moon day [attains great merit].
By the gift of the *Varāha* [Purāṇa], one attains the station of Viṣṇu.
The rule for the gift of the *Vārāhapurāṇa* consists of 24,000 verses. (12) In it, Ṣaṇmukha [expounds] the dharma concerning Maheśvara.
In that eon, he was adorned among men by his conduct and deeds.
The Purāṇa named Skānda is said to consist of eighty-one thousand verses;
it should be recited with diligence, including one hundred and one [additional] verses.
And he who should give a painted image accompanied by a golden trident when the sun has entered the sign of Pisces attains the state of Śiva.

The Skanda Purāṇa consists of 81,100 verses; this concludes the procedure for its donation. (13) In that [work], the four-faced Brahmā, concerning the majesty of Trivikrama, expounded the three aims of life, wherein Vāmana is fully glorified.
One who gives away the auspicious Purāṇa, renowned as consisting of ten thousand verses and following the Kalpas,
during the equinox, goes to the abode of Viṣṇu.

The *Vāmana Purāṇa*, consisting of ten thousand verses, contains the rules for its gift. (14) In it, Janārdana, in the form of a tortoise, recounted the majesty of Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa in the netherworld (Rasātala).
In connection with Indradhūmna, seventeen thousand verses concerning the Lakṣmī-kalpa were spoken by the sages in the presence of Śakra.
The man who gives a tortoise made of gold, complete with a tortoise, during the solstice (ayana),
shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows.

The *Kūrmapurāṇa* consists of 17,000 verses; this is the procedure for its gift. (15) It contains the description of Janārdana in the form of a fish, who appeared at the beginning of the kalpa for the sake of setting the Vedas in motion, as well as the account of Narasiṃha given to Manu.
Concerning those who observe the vows of the sages for seven kalpas, he spoke;
know that this is the Mātsya [Purāṇa], consisting of thirteen thousand verses.
Whoever gives [this gift] at the equinox, accompanied by a golden fish and a cow,
by him the entire earth is given.

The Matsya Purāṇa states that the Dānavidhi consists of 13,000 verses. (16) Furthermore, when the world had become overgrown at the end of the Viśva Kalpa, Kṛṣṇa spoke concerning it; that is here called the Gāruḍa.
That collection of eighteen thousand verses is recited here;
whoever gives it, adorned with a golden swan, on an auspicious day.
He attains the primary accomplishment and a firm station in the world of Śiva.

The *Garuḍapurāṇa* consists of 18,000 verses; this is the procedure for its gift. (17) [396] Furthermore, Brahmā spoke concerning the majesty of the *Brahmāṇḍa*; that *Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa* consists of twelve thousand verses and two hundred more.
That Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa, wherein the detailed account of future kalpas is heard, was proclaimed by Brahmā himself.
The person who gives that, together with a pair of silk garments, during the Vyatīpāta yoga,
obtains the fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
The procedure for the gift of the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* consists of 12,200 verses. (18) Thus ends the section on the gift of knowledge (*vidyādāna*) in the *Mātsya Purāṇa*.
[In] the *Nandī Purāṇa*:
Since the entire world, along with all that is auspicious and inauspicious, is dependent upon the scripture,
therefore the scripture should be bestowed with effort by one who performs virtuous deeds.
The fourteen branches of knowledge have been declared in their proper order as they exist:
the six auxiliary sciences (ṣaḍaṅga), the four Vedas, the Dharmaśāstra, and the Purāṇa.
Mīmāṃsā and Tarka—these are proclaimed as the sciences (vidyās);
Āyurveda and the Sāmaveda are proclaimed with many divisions.
And the science of the self is the most excellent of all; it destroys the fear of saṃsāra, brings an end to all suffering, and annihilates all evil.
These sciences have been fully described according to their many divisions and subdivisions;
likewise, there are the arts (kalā-vidyās), as well as other sciences, and furthermore, the supreme sciences of craftsmanship (śilpa-vidyās).
O highly fortunate one, all of them indeed always accomplish every purpose;
yet, according to their relative degrees of intensity, they bring about distinguished results.
But that which has self-knowledge as its primary focus is known as Āyurveda;
these arts, which promote righteousness, accomplish all goals.
The science of agriculture and these other sciences are far-reaching and yield great fruits;
for indeed, by means of one or another of them, a living being survives somewhere or other.
By bestowing the knowledge of the arts, whether according to the prescribed rule or otherwise, a man grants inexhaustible worlds; indeed, by giving such knowledge, he attains the realm of Viṣṇu.
By giving a treatise on Dharma, a man shall dwell in heaven for three kalpas;
but for one who gives the knowledge of the Self, there is no measure of the reward.
[397] Even in ten thousand years, it is not possible to fully describe this merit; yet this much can be said: that for ten thousand supreme eons, it remains unsurpassed.
A mortal may dwell in Satyaloka, where the Lord Brahmā resides,
even after having restored to health a single living being, whoever that creature may be.
What on earth would not be given by the gift of Āyurveda,
for one whose rice crops are rendered abundant by the gift of the Sasyaveda?
What eternal merit indeed has not been performed there by one who,
through the majesty of the Mīmāṃsā-śāstra, has understood the definitive conclusions of the Vedas?
What auspicious gift indeed has not been bestowed by the performance of sacrificial rites—
the ancient knowledge of the self and that which consists of the treatises on dharma?
Having understood this primary triad of sciences from the treatise on Dharma, whatever dharma a man may resort to, he shall obtain the fruits of all acts of giving.
To him who imparts the Dharma-śāstra, the merit is indeed tenfold;
those learned in the Purāṇas and Ākhyānas are devoted to the worship of the ancestors and the gods.
They go to all the worlds filled with desires and the arising of every auspiciousness;
indeed, those who give according to the ancient injunctions partake in infinite fruit.
Those men who take refuge in the Dharma and bestow the knowledge of the Self do not enter again the womb or the hell that is so difficult to escape.
Having crossed over all evils, together with their sons, cattle, and kinsmen,
they are liberated from countless, terrible hells characterized by agonizing torment.
Likewise:
"By giving a verse, a riddle, a stanza, or any other well-spoken word that brings joy, one goes to the auspicious world of the apsarases."
This merit which has just been described as resulting from the gift of knowledge is of such a nature due to the conjunction of place, time, ritual procedure, faith, and the recipient.
A man who bestows this knowledge obtains a fruit multiplied ten millionfold—
especially that mortal who is devoted to merit, desirous of victory, and seeking to achieve renown.
He should indeed bestow the knowledge that grants various desires according to the prescribed rite;
thus, by the gift of knowledge, [he attains] that which is endowed with the qualities of all desires.
[398] This supreme secret must indeed be given with effort to a worthy recipient;
for wherever an offering is made, it is as if given to the deity with that person in mind.
For one whose merit is not yet exhausted, by what means can that merit be measured?
One by whom merit is not yet completed is "one whose merit is incomplete.
Having propitiated the guru— who has reached the further shore of explaining the sciences—
with effort, through power, devotion, prostration, all forms of wealth, and likewise with all virtuous qualities;
Just as the king of jewels, though possessing great radiance, becomes useless when covered by a jar,
so too are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
But without a wise Guru who provides perfect awakening, there is no attainment of the fruit of knowledge; therefore, one should worship the Guru.
Whoever constantly worships the Guru—whether he is standing still or setting out—just as one would worship the god Pinākin, adorned with garlands and ornaments; |||
Since it is through his grace that one may attain all prosperity,
one should therefore worship the Guru with effort, as if he were Mahādeva himself.
Indeed, through devotion, affection, diligence, and faith at all times,
he is truly one’s mother and father, and he alone is one’s kinsman.
He is indeed a wish-fulfilling gem, and he alone is my friend;
thus, a wise person, ever devoted with faith, should propitiate the guru.
The pacification of the suffering of ignorance and likewise the deliverance from hell—where else can this be found? Neither mother, nor father, nor even a highly virtuous kinsman [can provide it].
One should bring about such exaltation as the Guru brings about;
for who else could deliver one from the flood of suffering and the bondage of existence through knowledge?
One should worship like Mahādeva a person who correctly understands the meaning of the treatises and who presents knowledge in the form of the scriptures through the mere essence of reality.
He who worships the specific meaning known as the intended purport of the scripture should be honored with devotion like Śiva himself, for he removes the fear of worldly existence.
Because the treatise is correctly set forth through the understanding of the meanings of words and sentences,
and because the definitive meaning of the whole is established by the connection between the preceding and succeeding topics.
He who truly understands, according to reality, the words favored by his own scriptures—
he indeed is the omniscient one of great intelligence, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara himself in this world.
One should always worship him with every aspect of one's being through the yoga of devotion;
for just as the world is perceived as blind without the sun, so too is it without him.
Without the word of the Guru, everything is indeed composed of darkness;
therefore, one should always regard the Guru exactly as one regards Mahādeva.
He who sees thus is a person who shall attain all dharmas;
furthermore, among all gifts, knowledge from the guru is the foremost, according to its prescribed method.
Having heard this injunction duly with a mind purified by faith,
one should give that [gift] to them, especially to those who possess excellent qualities.
And whatever is suitable for whom, that one should present to him,
in all the temples of the gods, with extensive displays according to one's wealth.
These should indeed be bestowed with effort by those seeking the fruit of great merit;
having given the book there, one should dedicate the merit to the ancestors.
Desiring infinite fruit for his beloved kinsmen,
he should then bestow that knowledge according to the prescribed rite in a temple of Śiva.
Then one should feed Brahmins and men who are devotees of Rudra;
and according to one's capacity, a festival should be celebrated in one's own homes.
The king should hold a festival in the city, likewise the village headmen in the villages,
and householders together with their kinsmen should perform the celebration in their homes.
Then, by those who have bathed, eaten, anointed themselves, and are wearing garlands— being well-composed, attentive, and endowed with faith— the scripture should be proclaimed.
There, the wise one should honor the reciter with extensive offerings according to his means, and he should honor the guru with devotion according to his ability, and not with deceit.
Then, with flowers and incense, one should thoroughly honor the disciples;
the reciter should be a wise Brahmin, learned in the scriptures and of great majesty.
One who has practiced the arrangement of syllables, is proficient in the treatises on prosody,
knows the meaning of words, is eloquent, modest, and endowed with intelligence.
One who knows song, is skilled in speech, possesses a pleasant voice, speaks clearly,
is a teacher endowed with righteousness, wise, learned in the scriptures, and free from envy.
[400] A Brahmin who is naturally pure, whose mouth is always the Vedas and the Smṛtis,
who is of good conduct, learned in the science of logic, and proficient in the treatises on Dharma.
One who has thoroughly mastered the multitude of scriptures, who proceeds toward the subject at hand,
who does not offer an explanation that deviates from the context, and whose intellect is fixed upon the meaning of the preceding and following passages— [such a person is qualified].

"Viṣṭadhīḥ" means one whose intellect is preeminent; in the reading "paurvāparyaviṣiṣṭadhīḥ," the sense is that he is one whose intellect is distinguished (*viśiṣṭā*)—that is, specific (*saviśeṣā*)—regarding the sequence of prior and subsequent [words], and whose nature consists in establishing their connection.

He is the one who effects the division of the meaning through the chapters and sections, [teaching] refined knowledge (*vidyā*) by means of refined linguistic conventions (*saṃskāra*), as well as the vernacular knowledge (*prākṛtāṃ*) by means of vernacular conventions.
That teacher who awakens his disciples through mere conversations and explanations, and also awakens them by means of the arrangement of regional names and designations; |||

He is the guru, he is the father, he is the mother; he is remembered as the wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi)—he who, having explained the means prescribed in the scriptures, delivers one from the hells.
Who in this world on earth is a kinsman equal to him,
by whose gathering of the rays of speech the darkness residing in the heart is destroyed?
One should not be distressed by the harshness of that one of great splendor regarding the grief born of the night of great saṃsāra, nor indeed should one be offended when he questions.
One should not cause distress during his illnesses or when purifying his impurities;
rather, one should pacify his anger and rescue him when he is submerged in suffering.
One should protect oneself diligently from diseases and not be distressed;
thus, having heard this auspicious exposition from the mouth of the Guru, the best of men [should act].
One should diligently contemplate that which is to be practiced for the sake of one's welfare in the next world;
endowed with faith and bowed in reverence, one should listen to what is esteemed by the guru.
The word of physicians and that of high-souled elders must be carried out;
one should not perform it oneself, for they would be as poisonous as a blazing fire.
He who interrupts the teacher with irrelevant talk in his presence incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin, due to his lack of certainty regarding the teacher’s words.
And he who, having heard a scripture from another or having received auspicious refinement,
should cause the fame of that [scripture or refinement] to accrue to someone else, he would be a slayer of a Brahmin.
And he who, out of delusion, causes even the supreme scripture to be forgotten,
goes to a terrible, inexhaustible hell of fearsome appearance.
But whatever auspicious or inauspicious act a man performs after having understood the scripture,
that indeed becomes a hundredfold for one who is devoted to knowledge.
In this manner, the wise speaker should describe that which consists of austerity and tranquility, which brings about the fruits such as enjoyments and heaven.

One should speak slowly, explaining whatever pertains to the inner self (*adhyātma*) and so forth; one should cause [the disciple] to recite with a continuous flow, avoiding anger, agitation, or the turmoil of battle.
In the company of elders, one should recite with words charming through passion;
one should recite with a gracefulness that conforms to various meters.
At the conclusion of a chapter on creation, or at the very end of a narrative,
one should make a pause when there is a conjunction with words of praise.
When the recitation is completed, the wise one should praise his desired object;
having thus brought peace to the world, he should touch the water of pacification at the end.
May the *Suśruta* remain embodied; may there be constancy in its exposition;
may the world proceed according to Dharma; and may the king always be victorious.
"May he be endowed with kinsmen in the Dharma, and may the Guru be free from ailment.
Having spoken thus, they should reflect upon how they came and how they should depart.
The wise disciples should contemplate the scripture among themselves,
through the occasion of discussing its subject matter and by means of various explanations and realizations.
One should recollect the exposition through logical arguments and also by means of the marks one has made oneself;
thus, a self-controlled man should listen to the exposition day after day.
Through hearing all the scriptures, the minds of men here become dominated by faith;
they attain an inclination toward the nature of the scriptures, and all defects go to utter destruction.

In whatever way one might listen to the scripture, having heard the collection of Dharma as it was proclaimed, yet lacking faith— then, upon the completion of the composition of the scripture, or even at the commencement of the discourse, his intellect remains undisciplined.
One who seeks the three aims of life should worship the preeminent reciter with offerings according to one's ability, and likewise honor the Guru with devotion as if he were a father.
The triad consists of dharma, artha, and kāma;
this is declared to be the primary rule for the bestowing of knowledge. By this very procedure, [it should be given] to a Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtuous conduct.
One who is endowed with intelligence, skilled in reasoning, and a knower of the Vedas should awaken [the disciple] and impart the auspicious scripture with the desire to attain great merit.
"Vedavedin" means one who has acquired the Vedas.
Or, having gratified the teacher with abundant wealth so that he is well-satisfied,
one should cause auspicious, well-born, and intelligent disciples to study [the Vedas].
Thus, the gift of knowledge is remembered as the highest of all gifts;
at all times, for all social classes, it is the supreme boat for crossing over hell.

The *plava* is the means of crossing over. By bestowing knowledge according to this rule, a man devoted to merit swiftly obtains that fruit which belongs to a hundred horse-sacrifices (*aśvamedha*) duly performed.
Whatever fruit results from a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices properly performed,
that same fruit a fortunate mortal obtains through the gift of knowledge.
Having given to the Brahmins land filled with all kinds of crops and adorned with all manner of jewels during an eclipse of the moon or the sun.
Whatever fruit a mortal obtains through the gift of knowledge,
that same fruit belongs to him for as many syllables as exist within the body of the scripture.
The giver of knowledge shall dwell in heaven for as many thousands of years as there are lines in that book, measured by its syllables.

Having extracted as many kinsmen from hell as there are leaves counted in the book, he leads them to heaven; "kinsmen" (kulyāḥ) refers to those of one's lineage. And for as long as the counting of leaves exists in the book, so long does the man [remain in heaven].
For so many thousands of years, he rejoices in heaven together with his kin.
Whatever sin has been committed by that embodied being, even throughout hundreds of lifetimes,
all of it is destroyed by the gift of this knowledge.
[403] That person born in this world is truly blessed and possessed of fame,
who is a supreme being devoted to the practice of bestowing the gift of knowledge.
Free from deceit, one should acquire knowledge according to one's means;
such a person goes to the merit-filled worlds that are imperishable and adorned with enjoyments.
Those who give even paper, ink, a case for pens, or other such writing materials to one intent upon the scriptures, they too [attain the same merit] as those who bestow knowledge.
Mortals of great intelligence, possessing worlds of merit, go to auspicious realms;
thus is proclaimed the great glory of the gift of knowledge.
Having heard this, one is certainly liberated from the sins born of seven lifetimes.
Thus ends the procedure for the gift of knowledge (*vidyādāna*) in the *Nandipurāṇa*.
Now, in the *Matsyapurāṇa*, follows the gift of the Kalpas (*kalpadāna*).
I shall describe the recitation of the Kalpas, which destroys all sins.
By the mere recitation of which one is endowed with heroic merit.
The first is the Śvetakalpa, the second is the Nīlalohita,
the third is Vāmadeva, and after that is another, the Rāthaṃtara.
The fifth is declared to be Raurava, and the sixth is remembered as Prāṇa;
the seventh is Bṛhatkalpa, and the eighth is called Kandarpa.
Then Satya is declared the ninth, and Īśāna is remembered as the tenth;
Vyāna is declared the eleventh, and likewise Sārasvata is the next.
The thirteenth is indeed the Udāna, and then the fourteenth is the Gāruḍa;
the fifteenth is declared to be the Kaurma, [and] the sixteenth is that of Prajāpati.
The sixteenth is the Nārasiṃha Kalpa, and the next after that is the Samāna;
the eighteenth is declared to be the Āgneya, and after that follows the Somakalpa.
The one is called Mīnakalpa, another is Puman,
another is Vaikuṇṭha, and likewise another is Lakṣmīkalpa.
The twenty-fourth is said to be that known as the Sāvitrī-kalpa;
the twenty-fifth is the Ghora, and after that is another, the Vārāha.
The twenty-seventh is the Vairāja; after that follows the Gaurī-kalpa;
then the Māheśvara is proclaimed, wherein Tripura was destroyed.
Likewise, at the end, that new moon day which is remembered as the "Pitṛkalpa" of Brahmā—
this is the month of Brāhmaṇa, which destroys all sins.
Indeed, in the very beginning, Brahmā assigned the name of each respective Kalpa according to the greatness that was ordained within it.
But he who, having fashioned these [images] out of gold, should give them on every festival day,
dwells for a kalpa in the city of Brahmā and Viṣṇu, honored by sages in heaven.
Therefore, the gift of the Kalpas brings about the destruction of all sins;
having fashioned them in the form of sages, the wise man should then bestow the Kalpas.
Thus ends the Matsya-kalpa-dāna. Now, regarding things that should not be accepted; on this matter, Dakṣa says:
Common property, what has been requested, a pledge, one's wife,
her wealth, a deposit, a sealed deposit, and one's entire estate [cannot be alienated] when there is a lineage [of heirs].
Even in times of distress, the wise should not give away nine things;
the man who gives them is a fool and must undergo penance.

*Samānyam* means common property. *Yācitakam* refers to something belonging to another that has been brought over for the sake of accomplishing a task. The distinction between *nyasta* (placed) and *nikṣipta* (deposited) will be explained in the second chapter. *Dārāḥ* means wife; *taddhanam* means a woman’s property (*strīdhana*). *Anvāhitam* is that which has been entrusted by one person to another to be given to someone else. Kātyāyana states: "Neither sale nor gift [should be made] of those who are unwilling;
however, one may personally employ [the authority over] one's wife, sons, and all one's property."
"Should join" means "should reconcile.
However, in times of distress, giving away or even selling [the property] may be performed;
otherwise, it must never be done—such is the certainty of the scripture.
Śātātapa says: Wealth acquired through the sale of the Vedas, that which is earned from women,
and that which is received from a eunuch— these are not to be given to the ancestors or the gods.

"Nirviṣṭam" means obtained; the phrase "when women have been sold" is the ellipsis. From "klībān" means from eunuchs. Likewise: "He who performs funeral rites for the deceased with wealth acquired by improper means does not obtain the fruit thereof, because that wealth was ill-gotten."
Yama said:
He who bestows gold, silver, or copper upon ascetics does not obtain the fruit thereof; it merely turns back to that very place.
[405] Cooked food belongs to the householder, and milk products belong to the forest-dweller;
one who desires merit should not give these to those whose livelihood is by begging.
Livelihood consists of [the cultivation of] fields and so forth; however, students (*brahmacārin*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) subsist on alms.
One should not give sacrificial oblations (*havis*), blessings (*svasti*), milk, sesame seeds, or honey to a Śūdra;
nor should one accept gifts from a Śūdra, though one may offer them other things.
The meaning is that one should not say "svasti" [to them]. And this applies before the formal salutation (*praṇāma*). Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"One should never utter 'svasti' to a Śūdra who has not performed a salutation.
One should present some other object to the Śūdra for the purpose of purchasing those items, such as milk and the like. Thus says Aṅgiras.
A cow, a house, a bed, and women should not be given to many;
for when these sacrificial fees are distributed [among many], they indeed rescue the giver.
"Vibhaktaḥ" means divided or separate—that is, "one [who has been separated]. "Vibhaktadakṣiṇāḥ" refers to sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) belonging to such a person. There is a reading in some texts:
"For these recipients of vibhaktadakṣiṇā do not attend upon the giver.
Its meaning is as follows: these recipients, having already divided the sacrificial fee among themselves, do not attend upon the giver by way of being the cause for the fruit of the gift.
For a single [daughter] should be given to one man, by no means to many;
but she, once she has fallen into sale, burns the family down to the seventh generation.

A single cow given to two or more persons falls into a state of being sold; in that case, this is the fault of the giver. Merit should be bestowed with effort upon the deities, the teachers, and likewise upon one's mother and father; it is never enjoined that demerit should be given.

The meaning is that sin has never been ordained by a deity. Now, one might object: merit cannot be given to another, because it is impossible for another to establish a relationship of owner and owned with it; nor can it be said that, like the "gift of Brahman" (*brahmadāna*) or the "gift of fearlessness" (*abhayadāna*), that gift is merely some kind of connection. For it is impossible [to establish] a mere connection between the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the merit. This is not so. On the authority of the scriptural injunction, a relationship between the thing to be given and the recipient is postulated such that "the merit gives the fruit" and "the recipient enjoys that fruit. Since this would otherwise be inexplicable, it is postulated that from the merit being given, a further merit arises in the recipient, corresponding to the enjoyment of the fruit. As for what those learned in logic have stated—that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer"—that refers to the initial arising of merit. However, the production of subsequent dharmas is indeed postulated even for one who is not the original performer, on the authority of the scriptural injunction.

The giving of evil is not only unenjoined, it is also prohibited. Thus says Yama: "A Brāhmaṇa who gives a defiled gift goes to an inauspicious state, like a lordly serpent that has been wounded and is completely deprived of its slough."
In the *Nandipurāṇa*:
"A man who gives what is sinful always obtains sin multiplied a hundred-thousandfold;
one who gives merit obtains merit by the hundreds and thousands."
Likewise, a gift may become increasingly superior according to the excellence of the recipient;
for that which is given to teachers, mothers, fathers, and those who speak of Brahman, [becomes ever more meritorious].
One should know that the merit or even the demerit is multiplied a hundred-thousandfold.
Śātātapa says: "But he who gives a gift to a Brāhmaṇa preceded by a formal question..."
That Brahmin first goes to hell, and immediately thereafter [the other follows].
The command "Recite this! constitutes a question.
He who says "Do not give" regarding cows, fire, or Brahmins, having passed through a hundred births as animals, is reborn among Brahmins. (1.212)
Now he states the means for attaining the fruit of giving even for one who does not give:
"He who, though capable of receiving, does not accept a gift, attains those abundant worlds which belong to those whose nature is generosity. (1.213)

Even though he is capable of receiving gifts and is a worthy recipient, he who does not accept cows, land, gold, and so forth, attains those abundant and complete worlds that belong to those whose character is to give cows and other such things. || 1.213 ||
Since it might follow that one must refuse everything, he states an exception in certain cases:
"Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water—these should not be refused. (1.214)
One must not refuse kuśa grass or similar items when they are being offered. "Grains" refers to parched barley. Manu says:
"A bed, a house, kuśa grass, perfumes, water, flowers, jewels, curd, fish, parched grains, milk, meat, and even vegetables—one should not reject these."
Likewise:
"One may accept from anyone fuel, water, roots, fruits, food that has been set aside for guests, honey, and the gift of safety."
"Abhayadakṣiṇā" means the gift of fearlessness. Aṅgiras says:
"Grain found in a threshing floor or a field, water found in a pond or a well, and milk found in a cow-pen—these may be taken even from one whose food is otherwise unfit to be consumed."
[407] Now, when the sacrificial portions (*pakṣas*) and the *āgrayaṇa* oblations have been interrupted,
one should perform the sacrifice that has been prescribed and must not let the merit already performed fall into ruin.

By the word *pakṣa*, the rites prescribed for the end of the fortnight (*pakṣānta*) are indicated. "One should perform the sacrifice authorized" means that one should request [the food] with reference to the sacrifice. And in this way, the merit of the good deed is not lost. One may accept from a Brāhmaṇa all cooked food except for [certain items]; from a Kṣatriya, the gift of a cow; from a Vaiśya, all kinds of grain; but from a Śūdra, nothing at all should be accepted.
This refers to the case of Brahmins and others whose food is not to be eaten.
However, as for grain located in a field, or in a threshing floor, or outside the house—
it is the opinion of Aṅgiras that this may be taken at all times even from Śūdras.
For grain is purified by such processing; therefore, it is traditionally held to be pure.
Consequently, one may accept raw grain even during periods of death or birth-impurity.
Thus, that refers to a situation of distress. 1.214.
One may accept food brought unasked even from a person of evil deeds, except in the case of an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy. (1.215)

That which is unasked for and unsolicited, brought forward to be given to oneself, may be accepted even from a wrongdoer who is otherwise avoided—such as an unchaste woman (*kulaṭā*). An *kulaṭā* is a wanton woman. Manu says: "Prajāpati considered that alms brought forward and offered before one, without being previously solicited, may be accepted even from a man of evil deeds."
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblation, if he approaches such a woman.
One should avoid even food offered by a physician, an ungrateful person, a remover of arrows, a usurer, a eunuch, and an unchaste woman, even if it is being served.
In this context, the word "alms" (bhikṣā) indicates cooked food. Yama says:
One should avoid accepting alms offered by a physician, a hunter, a prostitute, a hypocrite, a eunuch, and a dancer.
Vasiṣṭha says: Weapons, poison, and liquor are things that must not be accepted as gifts. 1.215.
[408] He states that a Brahmin may accept gifts from anyone for a specific reason:
"For the sake of honoring gods and guests, and specifically for the purpose of supporting one's teacher and dependents."
One may accept gifts from anyone for the sake of one's own livelihood alone. 1.216
Thus ends the section on generosity. || 8 ||

For the purpose of worshipping the gods and other such duties, he may accept [wealth] from all sources, even from Kṣatriyas and others. This is an illustration for all necessary rites. His own livelihood (*ātmavṛtti*) consists merely in sustaining the body, not in personal gratification. As Viṣṇu says:
"Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to worship the deities and guests, he may accept gifts from all sources; however, he himself should not find satisfaction therein."
Even when capable of receiving gifts for these purposes,
one should not accept them from unchaste women, eunuchs, outcasts, or enemies.
Aṅgiras said:
For the sake of his teacher, or especially for guests and dependents,
one may accept the food of a Śūdra, but he must not eat it himself.
Yama says: One who constructs wells, gardens, and water-stations, as well as one who plants trees,
one who gives away a daughter in marriage, and one who builds a bridge, attains heaven without a doubt.
He whose pond always contains water indeed attains the realm of heaven; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
For those who possess beautiful ponds, water-stations, groves, wells, and shelters,
and who practice the giving of food and sweet speech— for them belong both this world and the world beyond.

Viṣṇu: "Now, for the maker of a well, when water flows from it, half of his evil deeds perishes. The one who releases [the water] becomes eternally satisfied and attains the world of Varuṇa. The giver of a water-channel is always satisfied. For the planter of trees, the trees become sons in the next world. The trees of the giver of trees please the gods with their flowers and the ancestors with their fruits; they satisfy guests with their fruit and travelers with their shade, and when it rains, they satisfy the ancestors with water. The builder of a bridge attains heaven. Likewise: "In wells, groves, tanks, and temples..."
And the one who performs the re-consecration obtains the fundamental fruit.
In the Nandīpurāṇa: "That man who digs a pond or a well in a place devoid of water goes [to heaven] for a hundred years for every drop [of water]."
Having attained incomparable oneness with the gods and being likewise freed from thirst and hunger,
the builder of a pond dwells in heaven for four yugas.
Wherever a Brahmin or even a single cow might drink water from a pond,
by having such a reservoir constructed, one shall dwell in heaven for ten yugas.
Likewise:
"Or he who should duly bestow a pond in the presence of the fire,
having worshipped with faith the oceans stationed in water-pots at the corners."
By him, the earth bounded by its four oceans would be considered as having been given,
provided that he has honored the twice-born in his presence according to the rules with food and drink.
He goes to the world of Varuṇa, endowed with divine objects of desire.
In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The Fish [incarnation] said:
Listen, O King of mighty arms, to the procedure regarding tanks and other such works."
Having reached the auspicious bright fortnight, when the northern course of the sun has passed.
When an auspicious day has been declared by the Brahmins, having performed the *brāhmaṇavācana* rite,
[he should proceed] in a region sloping toward the east or north, near the pond.
The auspicious altar should be four cubits in size, square, and four-faced;
likewise, the pavilion should be sixteen cubits and four-faced.
And around the altar, O King, there should be pits one cubit deep with three tiers,
numbering nine, seven, or five, provided with a womb and a mouth.
The sacrificial pit (yoni) should be one vitasti in measure and extend seven aṅgulas toward the east;
there should be pits (gartas) measuring one cubit, with triple-tiered raised rims (mekhalās).
On all sides, there should be banners of every color,
joined with flags and made from the branches of the Aśvattha, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees.
One should cause these doors to be made for each direction of the pavilion;
there shall be eight auspicious Hotṛ priests and likewise eight door-keepers.
Eight reciters should be appointed, Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas,
endowed with all auspicious marks, possessed of the sacred mantras, and having their senses subdued.
The most excellent of the twice-born, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct, shall be the installers;
and in each pit, there should be those of noble family as well as the sacrificial implements.
A white fly-whisk, a chowrie, and a very large copper vessel;
thereafter, there should be sacrificial offerings (balis) of many colors for each respective deity.
The wise preceptor, having consecrated it with mantras, should cast it upon the ground;
the sacrificial post (yūpa) should be three *aratnis* in height and fashioned from a tree that yields milky sap.
Or, by one desiring prosperity, it should be established according to the height of the sacrificer;
twenty-five officiating priests (ṛtvij) adorned with golden ornaments should be appointed.
And golden earrings, as well as armlets and bracelets,
finger-rings, sacred threads, and various kinds of garments.
One should honor all [the officiants] equally, but the preceptor (ācārya) again with double [the fee];
one should give him a bed as well as whatever is dear to oneself.
The tortoise and the crocodile are made of gold; the fish and the *duṇḍubha* are made of silver;
the crab and the frog are made of copper; and the crow and the porpoise are [made of iron].
Having thus approached them all at the very outset, O lord of the people, he,
wearing white garlands and garments and anointed with white unguents, [should proceed].
Having bathed with water containing all medicinal herbs, and having been sprinkled by the foremost of Veda-knowers,
the sacrificer, together with his wife and accompanied by his sons and grandsons, [should proceed].
Taking recourse to the western door, one should enter the sacrificial pavilion;
then, with auspicious sounds and the resonance of kettledrums.
The knower of reality should draw a mandala with five-colored powders;
it should be a sixteen-spoked wheel, containing a lotus at its center and possessing four faces.
Having fashioned that [altar] square on all sides, circular in the middle, and very beautiful,
and having placed it upon the sacrificial mound (vedi), he then [worshipped] the Lord of the World of the Planets.
The wise one should place all [the deities] according to the mantras in every direction;
he should bathe Jhaṣa and the others in the center, relying upon the Varuṇa mantra.
The wise man should likewise install Brahmā, Śiva, and Viṣṇu right there,
having also placed Vināyaka, Kamalā, and Ambikā.
Then, for the sake of the peace of all worlds, one should arrange the assembly of spirits;
having thus provided them with flowers, food, and fruits, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
And having wrapped water-jars filled with jewels in cloths,
