and having adorned them all around with flowers and perfumes, [he appointed] door-keepers at every entrance.
The teacher should say to them, "Recite! and he should honor them;
two masters of the Ṛgveda should be stationed to the east, and two knowers of the Yajurveda to the south.
The two Sāman-chanters should be stationed in the west, while the two Atharvan-priests are to the north;
the sacrificer, facing north, should sit down to the south.
He should say "Sacrifice! to those who are the Hotṛs and likewise again;
and he should say "Remain [engaged] in the recitation of the supreme mantra" to the Jāpakas.
Having thus addressed them all and sprinkled water around the fire,
the knower of mantras should offer oblations of clarified butter and sacrificial fuel sticks with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa.
The officiating priests must likewise offer oblations with all the Vāruṇa mantras;
having offered according to the rules to the planets, as well as to Indra and Īśvara.
He should offer oblations according to the rules to the Maruts, the World-Guardians, and Viśvakarman;
and he should recite the Rātrisūkta, the Raudrasūkta, the Pāvamānī hymns, and auspicious mantras.
To the east, the Bahvṛcas shall each separately recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta,
as well as the Śārṅga, Raudra, Saumya, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Jātavedasa hymns.
Those who know the Yajurveda should recite the Saura Sūkta with their right hand,
as well as the Vairāja, Pauruṣa, and Sauparṇa Sūktas, and the Raudra-saṃhitā.
The Śaiśava, the Pañcanidhana, the Gāyatra, and the Jyeṣṭhasāman;
the Vāmadevya, the Bṛhatsāman, the Raurava, and the Rathantara.
O King, the Sāma-singers, stationed at the western gate, chant the *Gavām Vrata*, the *Vikīrṇa*, the *Rakṣoghna*, and likewise the *Yaśas*.
And to the north, those of the Atharvaveda should recite the Śāntika and Pauṣṭika hymns,
mentally taking refuge in the Lord Varuṇa, the deity.
Having performed the consecration (adhivāsana) in this manner on the previous day throughout the night,
[one should take earth] from an elephant, a horse, a chariot, an anthill, a confluence, a lake, or a herd of cows.
Having taken earth from a crossroads, one should likewise cast it into jars,
along with yellow pigment (rocanā), white mustard seeds, perfumes, and guggulu resin.
Having first performed this for the officiant according to the ritual procedure with the great mantras, one should then perform his ceremonial bath (snapana) accompanied by the five jewels.
Having thus passed the night with rites performed according to the rules,
when the clear dawn had arisen, [he gave] a hundred cows.
It should be given to the Brahmins, either sixty-eight,
or fifty, or thirty-six, or even twenty-five.
Then, when an auspicious and pure moment had been declared by the astrologers,
[the ceremony was performed] with the sounds of the Vedas, accompanied by Gandharvas and various kinds of auspicious musical instruments.
Having adorned a cow with gold ornaments, one should cause it to descend into the water; O Lord of the People, she should be given to a Brahmin who chants the Sāman hymns.
Then, having taken a golden vessel endowed with the five jewels,
he placed within it a sea-monster and all those fish and other creatures on every side.
It was carried by four Brahmins who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and it was provided with the water of a great river and adorned with curd and unbroken grains of rice.
One should have it placed face down in the middle of the water, facing north,
with the Atharvaṇa Sāman and the verse beginning "punar mām etu."
Having cast [the water] with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and returned to the pavilion,
one should worship the members of the assembly and offer oblations on all sides.
Furthermore, O Best of Sages, one should offer oblations for four more days;
on the fourth day, the ritual (caturthī-karma) must be performed, and there too, gifts should be given according to one's ability.
O tiger among kings, having prepared the sacrificial vessels and the implements for the sacrifice, one should then remember Varuṇa while giving the sacrificial fee.
Having given equal portions to the officiating priests, he should then divide the pavilion;
he should present a golden vessel and a bed to the *sthāpaka*.
Then, according to his ability, he should feed one thousand Brahmins, or likewise eight hundred, or fifty, or even twenty.
In this very way, the procedure for tanks is declared in the Purāṇas,
as well as for all wells, step-wells, and lotus-pools.
This very same procedure is prescribed for consecrations as well;
however, there may be a distinction based on the mantra in the case of temples, gardens, and grounds.
But for one who is unable [to perform the full rite], this rule was seen by the Self-born One:
even when the means are very small, the rite should be performed like that of the fire-altar by men, provided there is no stinginess regarding wealth.
Water remaining during the rainy season is considered equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice;
that which remains during the autumn season yields the fruit of the latter.
Remaining during the late winter and early spring seasons is said to be equal to the Vājapeya and Atirātra sacrifices;
remaining during the spring season is declared to be equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice.

Even water that remains in the summer is superior to the Rājasūya sacrifice. O Great King, he who performs these specific duties with a foremost, stainless, and pure intellect goes swiftly purified to the abode of Rudra and rejoices in heaven for many kalpas.
Having enjoyed many worlds where his hands and feet are equal in size, together with women for two parārdhas,
he subsequently attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu through the power of yoga.
The definition of the higher units has been stated:
one, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten thousand,
a lakh, a niyuta, a crore, an arbuda, and a vṛndaka.
Kharva, nikharva, śaṅkha, padma, and sāgara,
as well as antya, madhya, and parārdha, are proclaimed in their respective order.
"A man should count these eighteen sites by tens.
Thus ends the procedure for the consecration of a pond according to the *Mātsya-purāṇa*.
[This is from] the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*.

Now, therefore, follows the ritual for Varuṇa. We shall explain the sacrifice for the construction of a large pond, a well, a tank, or a dam. On an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable *karana*, and under a propitious asterism (*nakṣatra*), one should go toward the eastern direction; having established the fire on ground sloping toward the east near the north, and having cooked a *caru* offering for Varuṇa, one should perform the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings and then offer oblations of clarified butter. One should offer with the three verses beginning with *samudrajyeṣṭhāḥ* (RV 5.4.16), verse by verse; then, with the eight verses of the *havir* offering; then five verses beginning with *tat tvā yāmi brahmaṇā vandamānaḥ* (RV 1.2.15); then two verses beginning with *tvaṃ no agne varuṇasya vidvān* (RV 4.1.4); and the verse *imaṃ me varuṇa śrudhi* (RV 1.2.19). The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is the ninth. There are indeed nine vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and water is indeed the vital breaths; therefore, one offers to the waters with nine verses. At the end of the sprinkling (*mārjana*), one should cause a cow to descend into the water. As she is descending, one should address her with this mantra: "O purifying water, make this place pure; may the ancestors be eternally purified and immortal. Saving those who are consecrated at the holy ford (*tīrtha*), she crosses over the world of light and darkness. Having herself climbed onto the tip of the tail and held on, and having ascended [the bank], one should cause her to rise in the north-eastern direction (*aparājitā*) with the verse *apo asmān mātaraḥ śundhayantu* (RV 7.6.24). Then, with the verse *sūyavasād bhagavatī hi bhūyāḥ* (RV 2.3.21), and if she has made the sound *hiṃ*, with the verse *hiṃ kṛtaṃ ced dhiṃ kṛṇvatī vasupatnī vasūnām*. One should give to a Brahmin a cow that has gold on her horns, offspring that are bulls, silver on her hooves, and a bronze milking vessel, or another gift according to one's means. Then one should perform the formal release (*utsarga*) with the words: "May the gods, ancestors, and men be pleased. Or, as Śaunaka says, "Release her! After feeding the Brahmins, one should have them recite a prayer for well-being (*svastyayana*).
Now follows the procedure for planting trees.
Regarding this, the Matsya Purāṇa states:
"I shall describe the rite for trees as well as for garden grounds."
Having prepared everything according to the rules for constructing a tank, O Lord of the World.
The officiating priest and the preceptor, likewise equipped with the necessary materials for the sacrificial pavilion,
should similarly honor the Brahmins with gold, garments, and unguents.
Having sprinkled the trees with water containing all medicinal herbs and decorated them with fragrant powders, one should adorn them with garlands and wrap them in cloths.
It should be performed with a golden needle, or likewise with a gold probe;
one should have seven or eight points made of refined silver.
"Polished by time" means made of silver.
One should consecrate the altars at the base of each of all the trees.
Guggulu is the best incense here, and they should be placed upon copper vessels.
Having filled all the jars with every kind of grain and adorned them with cloths, perfumes, and ointments,
the lord of men placed them at the base of all the trees.

Having made offerings to Indra and the other guardians of the world according to the prescribed rites and one's capacity, he should present all those [offerings], including gold, as a tribute to the deities.
The twice-born should thus prepare the upper garment for the tree;
thereafter, [the image] should be dressed in white garments and adorned with a crest made of gold.
One should release a milch cow, adorned with bronze for her udder and gold for her two horns, standing amidst trees, facing northward.
Then, with the consecration mantra, accompanied by musical instruments and auspicious songs, or with the mantras of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and with Vāsuṇa hymns on all sides; at that time—
With those very jars, the preeminent Brahmins should perform the ceremonial bath;
having bathed and wearing white garments, the patron should offer worship.
With a composed mind, he bestowed upon all those officiating priests cows,
golden threads, bracelets, rings, and sacred grass rings.
With garments, beds, as well as household utensils and trees,
they should offer the milk-ablution for a period of four days.
A fire sacrifice (homa) should be performed with ghee, barley, and black sesame seeds;
sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) of the Palāśa tree are recommended, and likewise, a festival should be held on the fourth day.
Furthermore, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should likewise be given there according to one's ability;
whatever is most dear to oneself, that very thing one should give without stinginess.
Having given double the fee to the preceptor and prostrating, one should ask for his forgiveness;
the wise person who performs the tree festival according to this rite [attains the fruit].
O King of the Raghus, that wise man who establishes even a single tree attains all desires and enjoys the infinite state.
O King, he too shall dwell in heaven for as long as thirty thousand Indras,
and he shall deliver from suffering all men of the past and the future, as many as there are hairs on his body.
One attains the supreme perfection from which rebirth is difficult to encounter again.
Viṣṇu: One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice, or releases a dark-colored bull.
Now follows the ritual procedure for the release of a bull.

On the full moon day of Kārttika or Āśvayuja, one should first examine a bull. It should be the son of a cow that has living calves and is full of milk; it must possess all auspicious marks, be either dark-blue or red, with its face, tail, feet, and entire body white, and be capable of protecting the herd. Then, having strewn grass around a well-kindled fire in the midst of the cows, one should cook a *caru* offering for Pūṣan with milk. Having offered oblations with the verses, "May Pūṣan follow our cows" (*pūṣā gā anvetu naḥ*) and "May there be prosperity here" (*iha raḍiḥ*), the smith shall brand the bull—marking one flank with a discus and the other with a trident. One should bathe it with the four verses beginning with "Golden-hued" (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*) and with the verse "The Goddesses who are auspicious to us" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*). Once bathed and adorned, having brought it together with four similarly adorned heifers, one should mutter the Rudra hymns, the *Puruṣasūkta*, and the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras. And one should recite the mantra "Father, O calf" (*pitā vatsa*) into the right ear of the bull, as well as this: [416] "Golden-hued... (four verses) and "The Goddesses who are auspicious to us... For the Blessed One, Dharma, is proclaimed as a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion; may he protect me on all sides.
I give this youth to you; sporting with him as your beloved, go forth. O King Soma, may we not be abandoned by our offspring nor by our bodies, and may we not fall into the power of our enemy.
One should have a bull yoked with a heifer placed in the northeastern direction;
one should give the officiating priest a pair of garments, as well as gold and bell-metal.
The blacksmith should be given his wages as he desires;
one should provide him with food containing abundant ghee and feed the Brahmins there as well.
In whatever reservoir a bull has been released and drinks its water,
it stands by that person, having gratified all the gods and the ancestors.
Wherever an elephant, filled with pride, scratches the earth with its tusk,
that constitutes a bountiful offering of food for the ancestors.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"I shall declare the fruit of the bull; listen as I speak.
A bull set free purifies ten ancestors and ten descendants."
Whatever water a bull drinks after descending into a river is declared to be inexhaustible for the ancestors once it has been touched by the bull.
Whatever water he touches with his tail or other parts, even down to the very end, all of that becomes inexhaustible for his ancestors; of this there is no doubt.
When a bull constantly scratches the earth with its horns and hooves,
those [scratches] become inexhaustible offerings of honey for the ancestors.
The satisfaction that is obtained by the ancestors through a pond measuring a thousand nalvas according to the prescribed rite is said to be attained by means of a bull.

Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Topic of Gifts, in this legal compendium (*nibandha*) on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra*, composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the glorious Vidyādhara race. || 8 ||
Now, in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary, [417] the section on Śrāddha (9).

Since *śrāddha* consists of the relinquishing of one’s own wealth, it is similar to *dāna* (giving); thus, as it arises in the mind immediately after the rules for giving, the author begins the section on the ritual of *śrāddha* following the section on giving. In this context, even though time is a subsidiary element (*aṅga*), it is not something to be "taken up" (*anupādeya*) [as a specific detail]; rather, it is a cause for entitlement (*adhikārahetu*) by its very nature. For a performer existing at one time cannot perform an action qualified by another time which is a subsidiary element. Rather, it must be performed at that very time; thus, it is logical that time is a cause for entitlement. However, in the case of subsidiaries like the *viṣṇukrama* steps, which are things to be "taken up," their very form is not the cause for entitlement, but rather the capacity regarding them. Therefore, because time is a cause for entitlement and because performance depends upon entitlement, he first states the times for *śrāddha*.

The new moon day, the Aṣṭakās, the occasion of prosperity, the dark fortnight, the two solstices, the abundance of materials and Brahmins, the equinoxes, and the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign. (1.217)
Vyatīpāta, Gajacchāyā, the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
and a personal inclination toward performing a śrāddha— these are proclaimed as the times for śrāddha.

The times for the *śrāddha*, beginning with the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), have been proclaimed by Manu and others as its constituent parts (*aṅga*). Here, the new moon is the fifteenth lunar day (*tithi*) of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). It is of two kinds: *sinīvālī* and *kuhū*. "Sinīvālī is that in which the moon is visible; likewise, *kuhū* is that in which the moon has disappeared. Among these, the *śrāddha* should be performed on *sinīvālī* by those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), and on *kuhū* by others. Thus says Vyāsa:
The *snīvālī* (the day when the moon is visible) should be observed by Brahmins who maintain sacred fires;
the *kuhū* (the day when the moon has vanished) should be observed by Śūdras and by Brahmins who do not maintain sacred fires.
This should be applied as "by Śūdras, by those without fires, and by Brahmins. As for that which was stated by Prajāpati:
Since Sinīvālī and Kuhū are mentioned in the Śruti as pertaining to rites for the ancestors,
if these two [lunar phases] fall during the midday fire-ritual, how then could the Śrāddha and other such ceremonies be performed?
"Sinīvālī is considered to occur when there is a decrease in the lunar day (tithi), and Kuhū when there is an increase;
even when there is equality, it should be known as Kuhū by those who know the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.

This [statement] should be understood as referring to cases where the *pitṛyajña* (ancestral sacrifice) falls on Sinīvālī due to a decrease. However, when the *pitṛyajña* falls on Kuhū, then that very [lunar day] must be accepted even by those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), because the *śrāddha* is prescribed to follow immediately after the *pitṛyajña*. As Manu says:

"Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month at the waning of the moon. Because of the repetitive expression (*vīpsā*), it is understood that the Amāvāsyā-Śrāddha is obligatory. And so says Laugākṣi:

"One whose father has died must personally perform the *śrāddha* ceremony necessarily every month on the new moon day, as well as at the time of a lunar increase (*vṛddhi*) and annually. And this [rite] should be performed even by one who maintains no sacred fires (*niragni*). Thus says Uśanas:

"A twice-born man whose father has died should perform the *śrāddha* ceremony day by day, whether he maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) or does not (*anagnika*), as well as monthly and annual rites. From the expression "whose father has died," it is understood that there is no such obligation for one whose father is still living. And so says Hārīta:
While his father is still living, a son should indeed avoid performing the Śrāddha rite;
or rather, some authorities declare that he should offer it to those same ancestors to whom his father offers them.
The position that "to those very same [ancestors]" applies only to one who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*). As Sumantu says:
"A twice-born man whose father is living shall not perform a *śrāddha* without the sacred fire;
however, one who maintains the sacred fire should offer it to those very same ancestors to whom his father would have offered."
In this regard, there is a specific rule from the Maitrāyaṇīya-praiṣa:
"At a wedding, at the birth of a son, at a sacrifice to the ancestors, at a Soma sacrifice, at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
and when a Brahmin arrives— these six occasions [are for offering] while the father is still alive."

The meaning is that these six are the times for *śrāddha* for one whose father is living. At the *pitryeṣṭi* within the *cāturmāsya* sacrifices and at the *saumika* sacrifice, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is made from the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*). And here, the mention of the "father" is intended as an illustration; as Viṣṇu says: "He who performs a *śrāddha* while his father is living should perform it for those whom his father would [perform it for]. While his grandfather is living, he should perform it for those whom his grandfather would [perform it for]. While his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are all living, he should not perform it at all. Thus, it has been stated that whether one whose father is living or another, if he maintains the sacred fires (*sāgni*), he should perform the *śrāddha* on the day of *sinīvālī*. In that regard, those prohibitions concerning *sinīvālī* should be understood as referring either to those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*niragni*) or to the *sinīvālī* day that is unsuitable for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*. Those [prohibitions] are now cited. Among them, Baudhāyana says:
[419] That day on which only the fourteenth lunar day remains after midday is to be known as Sinīvālī; however, it is fruitless for rites dedicated to the ancestors.
Kārṣṇājini says:
Those who perform śrāddha rites on the new moon day that has been pierced by the [preceding] lunar day (bhūta), whether out of delusion or even through ignorance, their lifespan is diminished.
And so forth. As for that which was stated by Pracetas:
"The sixth [lunar day] pierced by the [fifth] Nāga, as well as the eighth pierced by the seventh;
the eleventh pierced by the tenth, and the fourteenth by the thirteenth."
"An amāvāsyā pierced by [the previous lunar day] is not to be accepted by the best of sages"—this [rule] is to be understood as applying to occasions other than śrāddha. Hārīta says:
"In the signs of Libra, Capricorn, and Aries, as well as in Virgo and Gemini..."
However, an Amāvāsyā that is pierced by a lunar mansion should be diligently honored.
This also refers to the subject of vows, fasts, and the like. Baudhāyana states:

"If even a single *ghaṭikā* of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) does not extend into the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipat*), then it should be observed—even if pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta*)—for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors."

The meaning is that even by those who do not maintain the sacred fires (*anagni*), the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) must be observed as pierced by the first lunar day (*pratipad*) for the *śrāddha* rite. "Even for a single *ghaṭikā*" means it must pervade the time of the ritual. Therefore, a *kuhu* (new moon) that pervades the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) must be avoided by everyone for the performance of the *śrāddha*. Thus says Jābāla:

"Even if the new moon falls on the first lunar day (*pratipat*), if it pervades the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), it should always be taken as pierced by the preceding day for the ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*)."
Hārīta states that the *amāvāsyā* śrāddha is mandatory, and specifies a particular remedy for cases of incapacity:
"The *aṣṭakā*, the *anvaṣṭakā*, the *abhyudaya* (prosperity rites), the *tīrtha* (pilgrimage), and the attainment of worthy recipients—
these are indeed considered the constant monthly offerings for the ancestors."

"Even with roots, fruits, or likewise with water-libations, one should perform [the rite] when [proper materials] are unavailable; however, one must not neglect what has been obtained. Here, "monthly matter" refers to the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. On this very point, Devala says:
Whatever libation a maintainer of the sacred fires offers with water day by day,
by that very act he obtains the fruit of the annual and other ancestral rites.
Only a funeral ball (piṇḍa) should be offered in the absence of wealth and provisions;
however, when the day of the śrāddha has arrived, one may even remain without food.
Thus, in the event that the offering of the funeral ball is impossible, there shall be fasting. Furthermore:
In the absence of a vessel, a man should perform the ritual for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) by designating another object as the vessel;
having set aside the food, it goes to that place where the vessel is located.
The meaning is that, having performed the ritual procedure for the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña), one should take that food to where a Brāhmaṇa is and give it to that Brāhmaṇa. Likewise:
"Or, having placed the darbha-grass mats upon the seats with a concentrated mind, he proceeds to the placement accompanied by the primary and secondary injunctions (praiṣa-anupraisa)."
In the absence of all [recipients], one should cast [the offering] into the fire, or give it to a cow, or likewise into the water;
for there is no omission of what has been obtained, especially that which pertains to the ancestors.
For even with a single Brahmin, one should perform the Śrāddha consisting of six pindas;
there, one should cause the six arghya-offerings to be given and likewise provide seats for the six.
The father eats from the hand of the twice-born; the grandfather eats from the mouth;
the great-grandfather is said to reside on the palate, and the maternal grandfather in the throat.
O great sage, one should likewise perform the Śrāddha dedicated to the six deities;
he who causes it to be omitted becomes a slayer of his ancestors.
The elder is the great-grandfather. Manu says:
"By this rule, one should offer the Śrāddha three times a year—in the winter, summer, and rainy seasons—and the Pañcayajña daily."
Devala says:
According to this rule, one should perform the śrāddha once a year,
or three or four times, or as the śrāddha is prescribed— month by month or day by day.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
But one who is unable [to give much] should give something to a twice-born man, such as a water-pot;
or he should give grass to a cow, or otherwise offer funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Or one should satisfy the ancestors with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass following a ritual bath;
or, when the time for the *śrāddha* has arrived, one may burn dry wood in the fire;
or one may fast on that day, or recite the *Śrāddhasaṃhitā*.

In the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "One who is incapable of giving cooked food shall, according to his ability, give uncooked grain to the foremost of the twice-born, even if it be a very small amount, along with a meager sacrificial fee."
Even there, O King, being devoid of the necessary strength, he will bow down and give some sesame seeds resting on the very tips of his fingers to some eminent brahmin.
Bowing with devotion, he will offer upon the ground a handful of water mixed with seven or eight sesame seeds, specifically intended for us.
Having obtained it from anyone at all, or even from cows for their daily fodder,
one who is pure and endowed with faith shall give it when [the proper substance] is unavailable.
If all else fails, having gone to the forest, displaying his armpits,
he shall recite this aloud to the Sun and the other world-protectors:
[As it was said by the Yoginī Madālasā in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"I have no wealth, no riches, nor anything else suitable for a śrāddha; I bow to my ancestors. May my ancestors be satisfied through my devotion as I raise these two arms onto the path of the wind."
Thus have the ancestors sung regarding the purpose of existence and non-existence;
O King, he who performs this has thereby completed the Śrāddha.
Another Smṛti states:
"When one is unable to perform the constituent parts of the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña),
he should then cause Brahmins to recite, 'May there be success through completeness.'"

The *pitṛyajña* is the *śrāddha*. Thus, because the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha* is obligatory (*nitya*), its purpose is either the destruction of previously accumulated demerit (*durita*), the avoidance of the transgression caused by non-performance, or the fulfillment of the injunction (*niyoga*). For one who possesses knowledge of Brahman (*brahmajñāna*), however, liberation (*mukti*) is the result. For it will be stated: "The performer of the *śrāddha* who is established in the knowledge of reality is liberated. This same purpose should be understood to apply to other obligatory rites as well. Nor is it the case that the monthly *śrāddha* is said to be merely a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*);
for this [monthly rite] occurs subsequently, since it involves the use of excellent meat.

From this statement in the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*, it is understood that the *amāvāsyā-śrāddha* (new moon śrāddha) is an ancillary (*aṅga*) [of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña]. It should not be said that it has no separate purpose; for its meaning is that the time called the new moon, which is an ancillary of the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, is "that which has occurred" (*bhūta*) therein—that is, it is an ancillary to it. However, it does not mean that it is an ancillary to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña itself; for if that were the case, the *śrāddha* for one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagni*) would not be prescribed.

The *aṣṭakās* are the eighth days of the dark fortnights of the three months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa. Although the word *aṣṭakā* is the name of a specific ritual, it here indicates by metonymy the time that constitutes its constituent part; otherwise, it would not be appropriate for it to be stated that "the times for the *śrāddha* have been proclaimed. Regarding this, the author of the *Gṛhyasūtra*, Śaunaka, states: "The *aṣṭakās* occur on the eighth days of the four dark fortnights of the Hemanta and Śiśira seasons. [422]

Saying this, he declares the four eighth days (*aṣṭamī*) as being constituent parts of the *aṣṭakā* rites. Viṣṇu, however, mentions only three: "The new moon day, the three *aṣṭakās*, the three *anvaṣṭakās*, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Proṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following [the latter], and the ripening of rice and barley—Prajāpati has declared these to be the obligatory times for *śrāddha*.
One who does not perform *śrāddha* on these occasions falls into hell. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, the permanence of the *aṣṭakā* śrāddha is established. Furthermore, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, there are four *aṣṭakās*:
"In the first, pertaining to Indra (*aindrī*), one should satisfy the ancestors with vegetables;
in the second, pertaining to Prajāpati (*prājāpatyā*), one should satisfy them with pure meats."
On the third lunar day dedicated to Viśvedevas, one should offer cakes according to the prescribed order;
during the rainy season, however, on the fourth day, one should always offer pure vegetables.

The four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa constitute the rainy season (*varṣā*). According to the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of the Mādhyandina branch, that fourth [fortnight] in the middle of the rainy season is the *Śākāṣṭakā*. Likewise, there are the offerings to Indra, to the Viśvedevas, to Prajāpati, and to the ancestors (*pitrya*). An "increase" (*vṛddhi*) refers to marriage and other such occasions; it is a category of Vedic rites, including the birth of a son and so forth. Because it serves as a causal occasion (*nimitta*), it is not something to be undertaken for its own sake; and because it is equivalent to a specific time, it is proclaimed as a "time for *śrāddha*" (*śrāddhakāla*) and can thus be included under the term "time. Consequently, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is mandatory due to its being occasional (*naimittika*). For this very reason, Vṛddha-Śātātapa states:
"Those householders by whom the deities were not gratified at the time of the *vṛddhi* [śrāddha], all the fruit of their giving belongs to that; it is indeed an asuric rite. Thus it is said.

The dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) is well known. Its status as a time for *śrāddha* is established by way of defining the lunar days (*tithi*), beginning with the first day (*pratipad*), which serve as the delimiters for the afternoon that constitutes a constituent part of the *śrāddha*. This is mandatory, because of the statement of Kātyāyana: "One should not let the latter fortnight pass even with mere vegetables; 'Month after month, food [is offered] to you,' so says the Śruti. And this is optional with respect to the *śrāddha* on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), because of the statement of Gautama: "Now, one should offer the *śrāddha* to the ancestors on the new moon, or from the fifth day onwards of the latter fortnight. Nor is the rule of starting from the fifth day fixed, since he himself says: "Or on every [day]. Furthermore, one should not suspect that the *śrāddha* is to be performed every single day, for Kātyāyana says: "One should perform the *śrāddha* in the latter fortnight, beginning from the fourth day, on whichever day it happens to fall. But Manu, however, says:
In the dark fortnight, from the tenth day onwards—excluding the fourteenth—the lunar days are commended for the Śrāddha rite;
other days are not so praised.

Thus he has also stated the alternative beginning with the tenth day. By the very rule for the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) prescribed for every month, the latter half of the month of Proṣṭhapada is also obtained. Furthermore, regarding this, a separate rule is established by Yama:
"Taking Āṣāḍhī as the limit, whichever fortnight becomes the fifth, one should perform the Śrāddha therein, whether the Sun is situated in Virgo (Kanyā) or not."

Thus, this [particle] "iti" serves the purpose of conjunction with the *amāvāsyā* (new moon) *śrāddha*, and it also serves the purpose of ensuring that the *śrāddha* is performed there every day. For this very reason, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"In the dark fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, the *śrāddha* should be performed day after day;
or for three-quarters of the fortnight, or for one-third, or even for half."

Here, with the intention of referring to a month ending in the full moon (paurṇamāsyanta), the "latter fortnight of Proṣṭhapadī" is stated to be the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) of Āśvayuja. Even in the case of a fortnight reduced by one-third, the *śrāddha* must be performed every day; for from the accusative case in the word "pakṣam," there is understood an uninterrupted connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Likewise in the subsequent [passages]: "Or, in the latter fortnight of the fortnight reduced by one-third, beginning from the fifth day," according to the statement of Gautama. In the alternative of beginning from the fifth day, the first four lunar days (*tithi*) are omitted, and the fourteenth day is also omitted; thus, through the omission of five lunar days, the fortnight becomes reduced by one-third. In the case of a reduction by one-quarter (*tribhāga*), the commencement is on the tenth day; and it is called "one-quarter" because of the exclusion of the fourteenth day. In the case of a half-fortnight (*ardhapakṣa*), however, the commencement is on the eighth day; and it is called "half" because of the avoidance of the fourteenth day. This option depends upon the capacity of the performer. Furthermore, even in the latter fortnight of an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), the latter fortnight of Proṣṭhapadī may occasionally occur. To exclude that [case], Śāṭyāyani says:

"That which is the sixteenth day of the latter fortnight of the month of Nabhasya, if it should be joined with the sun's passage into Virgo (Kanyā), that time is suitable for the performance of Śrāddha rites.

The number sixteen is to be completed by including the first day of the bright fortnight (Śukla-pratipad). "Nabhasya" refers to the month of Proṣṭhapada. Regarding the specific requirement of its being joined with the sun's passage into Virgo, Kārṣṇājini says:
"Whether at the beginning or in the middle, whichever fortnight the sun enters [the sign], that fifth fortnight is to be honored for the sake of the sixteen *śrāddhas*.
Thus, when the sun is situated in Leo (*siṃha*), there is the commencement of the sixteen *śrāddhas*. And so says Jātūkarṇya:

"Taking the full moon of Āṣāḍha as the limit, whichever month constitutes the fifth fortnight should be known as the time for Śrāddha, whether the sun enters Virgo (Kanyā) or not. This statement has the commencement of the fortnight in mind. However, by virtue of its connection with the sun's entry into Virgo, the fortnight must indeed be associated with that; for there is the scriptural declaration: "If it should be accompanied by the sun's entry into Virgo. Consequently, whether in the first or the second fortnight following the full moon of Proṣṭhapadī, when the sun's transit into Virgo occurs, the subsequent fortnight is the time for Śrāddha. As for that which is stated in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
Those sixteen days when the sun has entered Virgo are equal to sacrificial rites; what is given there yields great fruit.
This refers to the intention of the superiority of its fruit. Regarding this, Śāṭyāyani said:
"The month when the sun is in Virgo is meritorious, as is the fifth fortnight;
the month when the sun is in Virgo and the fifth fortnight—that is called exceedingly meritorious."

Consequently, when the sun has entered the sign of Virgo (Kanyā), there is a distinct time for the Śrāddha rite. For this reason, Kārṣṇājini says again: "When the sun has entered Virgo, the ancestors indeed go toward their sons;
the city of the dead remains empty only as long as the scorpion [the sign of Scorpio] is not seen."
The *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"As long as the sun remains in the signs of Virgo and Libra in succession, that is the time for the *śrāddha*; at other times, the city of the departed spirits remains empty."
The *śrāddha* on the fifth day of the lunar fortnight is obligatory. As Jātūkarṇya said:
"For this is indeed a mandatory rule prescribed for the fifth fortnight;
an offering given on that day becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors."
It is mandatory and obligatory; for this very reason Vyāsa says:

"When the sun is in Leo, during the rainy season, even if one dwells at home on mere vegetables, one should, when the moon is between the two [asterisms] of Āśleṣā and Maghā, discharge the debt to both lineages."

Because a debt must necessarily be paid; "of both lineages" means of the maternal and paternal lineages. "Of the two fifth [days]" means on the fifth days of the dark and bright fortnights. Regarding this, Sumantu states the favorable conditions: "If a householder does not perform the *śrāddha* while the Sun is situated in Virgo, how can he have wealth or sons? For he suffers from the sighs of his ancestors."
O King, if one does not give [offerings] to the ancestors on this fifteenth day known as Dīpānvitā, it is as if nothing at all has been given during the Mahālaya festival.
In the Mahālaya rite, during the period when the sun is in Virgo; furthermore, another Smṛti states:
"One should offer the Śrāddha for all kinsmen as well when the sun is in Virgo, following the order of seniority, based on the anniversary of their death."
Thus, that [rule] refers to those who have neither offspring nor kinsmen.

The two solstices (*ayana*) are the transits of the sun into Capricorn (*makara*) and Cancer (*karkaṭa*); the time characterized by these is the time for *śrāddha*. Since the inclusion of the solstices is already established by the phrase "the transit of the sun," the separate mention of the solstice-śrāddha indicates its obligatory nature or its great fruitfulness. And so says Jātūkarṇya:
"At an eclipse of a planet, when one's own son is born, during the *maghā* asterism, and at the two solstices..."
Whatever is given daily in a conch shell or likewise in a lotus becomes equal to a thousand gold coins.

The *ayana-śrāddha* is mandatory because of the hearing of the word "constant" (*nitya*) and its association with the *uparāga-śrāddha* and others; its superior fruit is equal to the gift of a thousand *niṣkas*. Regarding the phrase "in the *pitrya* [fortnight] on the day of the ancestors' destruction": the meaning is that it refers to the *maghā* asterism occurring during the dark fortnight of the month of *nabhasya* (Bhādrapada). The *Śaṅkha* [Smṛti] says: "O best of the twice-born, the new moon when the moon has waned is called *amāvāsyā*;
the *aṣṭakā* is the *padma*, and what is given there is indeed inexhaustible."
In the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"The third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, the ninth of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the thirteenth of the dark fortnight of the month of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), and the fifteenth of Māgha."

These four lunar days—the beginnings of the Yugas—make whatever is given or offered as sacrifice immediately infinite. So too do an eclipse of the moon or sun, the three Aṣṭakās, and the two solstices.
A self-controlled man should offer even water mixed with sesame seeds here to the ancestors;
by him a Śrāddha has been performed for a thousand years—this is a secret that the sages declare.

From the statement, "Water is milk here," the necessity of these *śrāddhas* is determined. Some maintain that the phrase "in the dark fortnight" (*kṛṣṇapakṣe*) is a qualification of both the thirteenth and the fifteenth days; however, that is not correct, because it is seen otherwise in another scripture. Thus, it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "The Kṛta Yuga was established on the third day of the bright fortnight of Vaiśākha, and the Tretā Yuga on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Kārtika."
Then, on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, the Dvāpara age begins;
and likewise, on the full moon day of Māgha, the terrible Kali Yuga begins.
"The lunar days that mark the beginning of the Yugas are therefore renowned as Yugādis.
By this [it is meant]:
"Two [days] in the bright fortnight and likewise two in the dark fortnight are proclaimed as the beginnings of the Yugas."
Thus, the explanation of a certain [author] has been refuted. Yama says:
"On the full moon day of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, or Māgha, one should satiate three or five twice-born men, beginning with the ancestors; that too is said to be inexhaustible."

Gautama states: "One should offer to the ancestors on the full moon days of Śrāvaṇa and Āgrahāyaṇa, on the Anvaṣṭakās, and on the full moon days of Māgha and Vaiśākha. As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: "The transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), the two equinoxes (viṣuva), especially the two solstices (ayana), the Vyatīpāta yoga, one's own birth-star (janmarkṣa), and a time of prosperity (abhyudaya)—Prajāpati has declared these to be the optional times for Śrāddha;
whatever Śrāddha is given on these occasions conduces to infinity."

Thus, this [text] prescribes the rite for one desiring the infinite fruit consisting of the satisfaction of the ancestors; therefore, it does not negate the obligatory nature (*nityatā*) of the *ayana-śrāddha*. For it is understood from the force of such scriptural statements as “every *śrāddha* indeed grants satisfaction to the ancestors” and “one should satiate the ancestors,” that every *śrāddha* provides satisfaction to the ancestors. Alternatively, by the force of two [different] scriptural statements, let the *ayana-śrāddha* and others possess both an obligatory and a optional character, like the *agnihotra* and similar rites. Or rather, the two solstices (*ayana*) are denoted by the very word “two solstices”; however, these are distinct from the two movements of the sun toward the northern and southern directions [which occur at the equinoxes].

The "attainment of the substance and the Brāhmaṇa" refers to the time when there is the attainment—that is, the acquisition—of either the substance suitable for the *śrāddha* or of a Brāhmaṇa who purifies the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*). Because this is an occasional (*naimittika*) obligation, it is mandatory. As Hārīta says: "But when a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) or the requisite substance is available, one need not wait for the [specific] time; having found a worthy Brāhmaṇa recipient, the *śrāddha* is ordained to be performed immediately."

A *tīrtha* refers to Puṣkara and other such sacred sites. The *viṣuva* is the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*) at the signs of Aries and Libra. The purpose for mentioning this separately, like the solstices (*ayana*), is as follows; here is the specific rule stated by Pulastya: "The *śrāddha* should be performed during the two solstices, likewise during the two equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and on all the *yugādi* days, except for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa*)."

*Sūryasaṃkrama* is the Sun’s transition from one zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) to another. *Vyatīpāta* is a specific astrological conjunction (*yoga*) or a technical term. Regarding this, Vṛddhamanu states: "If the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) occurs on a Sunday under the asterisms of Śravaṇā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Ārdrā, or the head of Āśleṣā, it is called *vyatīpāta*."
*Nāgadaivata* refers to Āśleṣā; the meaning is that if the moon is in its first quarter (pada), [it is auspicious]. In the *Varāhapurāṇa*:

"When one perceives that a substance suitable for a *śrāddha* has arrived, or likewise a distinguished twice-born guest, one should perform the *śrāddha* during a *vyatīpāta* yoga or at the solstice (*ayana*)."
O best of Brahmins, when the equinox has arrived, as well as during the eclipses of the moon and the sun,
it occurs whenever the sun enters any of the zodiacal signs.

One should perform voluntary *śrāddhas* during the affliction of constellations by planets, upon seeing an evil dream, and likewise at the arrival of new grain. "Elephant-shadow" (*gajacchāyā*) means "shadow of an elephant"; thus says the *Kāṭhaka-śruti*.
For this shadow of the elephant is indeed the path of the gods and the ancestors.
Likewise: "One should offer the *śrāddha* during the 'elephant's shadow' (*hasticchāyā*). This refers to a verse concerning the ancestors in the *Mahābhārata*:

"With this [offering] made of all metals, one who is firm in his vow during the rainy season should perform the rite according to rule during the elephant's shadows, while being fanned with ear-fans."

The ellipsis is "one should offer the *śrāddha*. Because of the expression "fanned by the ear-fan," this statement refers specifically to the shadow of a visible elephant. Furthermore, "elephant-shadow" (*gajacchāyā*) is a technical term, and it is defined in another *Smṛti*:

"When the moon is in the constellation sacred to the ancestors (Maghā), and the sun is situated in the hand (Hasta), and the lunar day belongs to Vaiśravaṇa (the third day of the dark fortnight), that is remembered as 'elephant-shadow'."

Maghā is sacred to the ancestors (pitṛ-devatya). Haṃsa is the Sun (Āditya). Kara is the lunar mansion Hasta. The thirteenth day belongs to Vaiśravaṇa. The conjunction of these three is known as Gajacchāyā. Uparāga means an eclipse. And here, the Śrāddha is desired even at the beginning of the night. As Viṣṇu says:
"A wise man should certainly not perform a Śrāddha during the two twilights or at night;
yet it may be performed even during those times if there is the sight of Rāhu [an eclipse]."

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at death, and upon the birth of a son—even during an intercalary month—a gift should be given; what is given then produces inexhaustible merit."
In this context, something else regarding the subject of eclipses is also stated as a digression. On that point, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"When the moon or the sun is seen eclipsed by Rāhu, the great planet, the merit [of a gift] is said to be inexhaustible; and it is especially so when the sun is involved."
"Seen" means fit to be seen. Vyāsa says:
"When the sun is seized by Rāhu, every gift is equal to [the gift of] land, all twice-born men are equal to Brahmā, and all water is equal to the Gaṅgā."
The term "Divākara" (the Sun) is also an elliptical designation for the Moon, because it is said:
"The merit [of bathing] at the Moon is a hundred-thousandfold; that of the Sun is ten times more than that;
but when the waters of the Gaṅgā are present, the merit is ten millionfold for the Moon and ten times that for the Sun."
Whatever fruit results from the proper gift of ten million cows,
that same fruit is obtained by bathing in the Jāhnavī when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu.
Likewise, it has been declared that on the day of the sun [the merit] is tenfold;
and whoever bathes in the Jāhnavī during an eclipse of the moon or the sun [obtains the same].
[428] Having bathed in all the sacred fords, why does he wander the earth?
On Sundays there is an eclipse of the sun, and likewise on Mondays, an eclipse of the moon.
In that [case], the merit would be infinite; it is known as the "Cūḍāmaṇi" [gift], and whatever merit is gained on other weekdays is obtained during an eclipse of the moon or sun.
The merit that is said to be multiplied ten millionfold from a single morsel [of food] given to Cūḍāmaṇi is declared in the Liṅga Purāṇa:
"One should bathe during an eclipse of the moon or sun, even during the impurity caused by birth or death."
One who does not bathe meets with death; one who bathes incurs no sin.
In both birth-impurity and death-impurity, there is no fault during an eclipse of Rāhu;
purification shall remain in effect only so long as the release [of the moon or sun] is not seen.
This refers to the subject of bathing; therefore, even during an eclipse of Rāhu or periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*), the bath must be performed accompanied by mantras. Likewise:
"Having fasted for three nights in this manner during an eclipse of the moon or sun, and having bathed and given gifts according to the rule, one rejoices together with Brahmā."
Having fasted for one night in this manner, and having bathed and given according to one's ability,
there is a complete expiation from the sheath of sin, as if from a garment.
Kātyāyana states: At the Upākarma ceremony, at the Utsarga, at the ritual bathing for the deceased,
and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, the defect of menstrual impurity does not exist.

In the Devīpurāṇa: "An eclipse in the month of Kārttika at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā is most excellent; but an eclipse in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa at the Devikā, O great sage, is meritorious."
In Pauṣa, the Narmadā is meritorious; in Māgha, the Śubhā is present.
"The Śubhā is present" means that the Narmadā is situated in the middle of Kurukṣetra.
In Phālguna, the Varuṇā is meritorious; in Caitra, the Sarasvatī is meritorious.
In the month of Vaiśākha, however, the excellent river Candrabhāgā is exceedingly meritorious.
In Jyeṣṭha, the Kauśikī is meritorious; in Āṣāḍha, the river Tāpikā;
in Śrāvaṇa, the one named Sindhu; and in Proṣṭhapada, the excellent Gaṇḍakī.
In the month of Āśvina, the Sarayū is the most excellent; the Narmadā is even more meritorious;
and the Godāvarī is greatly meritorious when the moon is joined with Rāhu.

O high-minded one, when the sun is eclipsed by the moon—that form of darkness—a man becomes one who has accomplished his purpose through contact with the waters of the Narmadā. In this same way, the Gaṅgā is to be regarded, as well as the goddess Sarasvatī. [429]
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Gaṅgā at Kanakhala, the meritorious Prayāga, Puṣkara, Gayā,
and likewise Kurukṣetra, are meritorious when the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu."
Ṛṣyaśṛṅga said: When the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, whoever performs a śrāddha ceremony,
by that very act the entire earth is placed into the hand of the brāhmaṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Bhārgava, on whichever day there may be an eclipse of either the moon or the sun,
one should not perform the act of eating beforehand.
One should not practice that gathering when it has likewise set;
indeed, one should not eat at all until its rising occurs again.

This being the case, during an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat; rather, one should eat after bathing once they have been released. If they have not been released when they set, one should bathe and eat on the following day.

In this context, the words *candra* (moon), *sūrya* (sun), and *graha* (eclipse) indicate the day-and-night period (*ahorātra*) as previously described; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the statement, "One should not eat before [the eclipse]. The phrase "one may eat after bathing when the two are released" is stated as an exception (*pratiprasava*) to the general prohibition of eating throughout both day and night. The rest is well known. The word "having seen" (*dṛṣṭvā*) is intended to indicate the rising [of the moon], because of the scriptural injunction: "as long as its rising has not occurred. Likewise: "And if there should be an eclipse of the moon after the first watch..."
One should eat before the turning [of the shadow] in the west, and after the first [turning] in the east.

The meaning is "after the first watch. *Āvartana* refers to the middle of the day. However, if an eclipse occurs during the last watch of the night—that is, in the fourth *prahara* of the night—then one should eat before the first *prahara* of that very night. Likewise: "If [an eclipse] occurs in the afternoon, at midday, at midday, or in the *saṃgava* period, one should eat during the *saṃgava*; there should be no act of eating prior to that."

This [penance] pertains to one who is utterly incapable [of fasting]. However, for one who is capable, Kātyāyana has stated the following expiation regarding eating during an eclipse of the moon or sun:
"Having eaten during an eclipse of the moon or sun, one is purified by a Prājāpatya penance;
having eaten on that very same day, one is purified by a three-night fast."
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"Upon the sighting of Rāhu (an eclipse), there is birth-impurity for all castes alike;
having bathed, one should perform one's rites, but one should avoid cooked food."
Having eaten the remnants of a *navaśrāddha*, that which has been left over from a [deity] offering,
or what remains after a husband and wife have eaten, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
If there is a solar eclipse at night or a lunar eclipse during the day,
one should not perform an ablution therein, nor should one ever give a gift.
This refers to the case where an eclipse is not visible to those situated on a particular part of the earth. Devala says:
"Just as bathing and giving gifts are prescribed for the sun during its daytime eclipse, so too are bathing and giving gifts ordained for the moon during its nighttime eclipse."

Where the eclipsed moon sets after sunrise, there the bathing, giving of gifts, and other rites for the occasion of seeing Rāhu must be performed *before* sunrise, and not afterwards; this is the meaning. Furthermore, a *śrāddha* ceremony on account of an eclipse is mandatory. Thus, it is said in the *Liṅgapurāṇa*:
"A *śrāddha* must indeed be performed even at the cost of one's entire wealth during the appearance of Rāhu;
he who does not perform that *śrāddha* sinks like a cow in the mud."
Śātātapa says:

In times of distress, when there is no sacred fire, at a holy bathing place, and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, a twice-born man may perform an *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with uncooked food); however, a Śūdra may always perform it in this manner.
Bathing, giving gifts, austerity, and ancestral rites yield infinite merit during an eclipse of Rāhu;
at other times it is a demonic night, therefore one should avoid it.

"And likewise, a desire for the *śrāddha*. Here, "desire" (*ruci*) means intention (*icchā*). And that [intention] must always concern the performance of the *śrāddha*; only then should one perform the *śrāddha*. Since it is equivalent to time by virtue of being a specific occasion (*nimitta*), its status as the "time for the *śrāddha*" is figurative. Thus, the rule regarding the time for the *śrāddha* has been stated. Āpastamba also states the essential nature of the *śrāddha*: "Now, Manu has declared this ritual act under the name *śrāddha* for the ultimate welfare of progeny; therein the ancestors (*pitaraḥ*) are the deities, while the Brahmins serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire. By this, the meaning of the term *śrāddha* is defined as consisting of an oblation (*homa*). The Brahmins serve the purpose of the *āhavanīya*, that is, they function in the role of holding the oblation being poured into the *āhavanīya*. Since they cannot fulfill that function without eating, it follows that the *śrāddha* extends up to the feeding of the Brahmins; this is what is stated by him. Therefore, he will say later:
"Thereafter, they should eat while remaining restrained in speech, speaking as is appropriate.
For this very reason, Śaunaka, the author of the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, says: "One should feed at least nine *śrotriyas*, or an odd number. Manu also [says the same].

By the word *pitṛ* (ancestors) here, there is an inclusion of everyone—such as maternal grandfathers and others—who are prescribed as deities by other scriptural authorities; for it is only when this is so that the plural number is justified. Furthermore, by the word *pitṛ* here, even those who have not yet undergone the *asapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite are included, in order to establish the status of these as *śrāddha* rites, such as the *navaśrāddha* and others. Since in the case of *āmaśrāddha* and similar rites, the status of being a *śrāddha* exists primarily because they ultimately culminate in the feeding of Brahmins, albeit indirectly, the term *śrāddha* applies in its primary sense. However, because the constituent parts such as the cooking and serving of food are not performed, it is described there as being used in a secondary sense. Therefore, it is established that the *śrāddha* has the nature of a *homa* (an oblation). In this matter, the son and others possess the entitlement (*adhikāra*), because he is recorded in tradition as the performer (*kartṛ*) therein. For whoever is the performer of a particular ritual is the one entitled to it, just as a king is the entitled agent in the *Rājasūya*, which is performed by a king. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"The father's rites of offering funeral cakes (piṇḍa) and water must be performed by the son;
in the absence of a son, it shall be the wife; and in the absence of a wife, it shall be the uterine brother.
Here, the mention of the "father" is for the sake of illustration; therefore, the post-mortem rites for the mother must also be performed by the son. As for that which was stated by Śātātapa:
On the Anvaṣṭakā days, at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi), and likewise annually;
on these occasions, there is a separate śrāddha for the mother, whereas on other occasions she shares it with her husband.

Thus, that [rule] refers to the period subsequent to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite. For the sake of liberating her from the state of being a *preta*, the entire collection of *śrāddhas* must be performed separately for the mother. As Śaṅkha says: "The *anvaṣṭakā*, the *mātṛśrāddha*, and the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the anniversary of death—having partaken of these, there is no other [rite] for women that should be separate."

And here, by the term *ekoddiṣṭa*, every *śrāddha* that effects liberation from the state of being a *preta* is denoted; furthermore, it is stated that the *anvaṣṭakā* and other such *śrāddhas* must indeed be performed as *ekoddiṣṭas*. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says: "Having performed the *śrāddha* on the *anvaṣṭakās* preceded by the deities with vegetables, meat, and cakes, and having offered oblations into the fire on the *anvaṣṭakās* as in the *aṣṭakā* rites, one should feed the Brahmins for the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother—preceded by the deities—as before; then, having honored them with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), one should follow them [out] and bid them farewell. For this same reason, Śaṅkha prescribes only the *pārvaṇa* procedure for the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
"O twice-born ones, among the wives of the triad beginning with the father, the mothers are to be fed;

for that [offering] belongs to women alone, since it is here called the *mātṛśrāddha*. Some establish the statement "together with the husband" as applying to a mother who has been *sapiṇḍīkṛta* with the father, and they cite a verse by Śātātapa as their authority:
"When the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed, she attains a single form with her husband's ancestors; therefore, the wife is a sharer in their portions. Thus says Bṛhaspati as well.
The mother eats the śrāddha food, which is like nectar, together with her own husband;
likewise the paternal grandmother with her own, and the great-paternal grandmother with her own.

This is incorrect; for in neither of these two statements is the *sapiṇḍana* of the mother with the father understood, such that the former statement could serve as an authority for its application to that case. As for what was said—that upon the performance of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, there is "unity of form" (*ekamūrtitva*)—that indicates a unity of form characterized by the wife’s participation alongside her husband in a *śrāddha* dedicated to the deities beginning with the father; it does not, however, indicate identity. For there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) to suggest that one who is *sapiṇḍīkṛta* with another becomes identical to them, or that they experience the status of a deity through participation in a *śrāddha* dedicated to that other deity. Therefore, this statement remains valid even when the mother has been *sapiṇḍīkṛta* with the paternal grandmother. This is because that [statement] is intended solely to enjoin that from the time immediately following *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, the mothers possess the status of deities through participation in the *śrāddha* dedicated to the father and others. For this very reason, in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, the woman’s status as a single *piṇḍa* together with her husband is proclaimed by way of association with the terms *gotra* and *sūtaka*.
"She has attained oneness with her husband regarding the funeral ball (*piṇḍa*), the lineage (*gotra*), and the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*);
therefore, no separate offering of a funeral ball exists for wives.

Consequently, there is no separate *śrāddha* for a mother who has been made a *sapiṇḍa* with either the paternal grandmother or the paternal grandfather. And it is understood from the *Caturviṃśatimata* that this [separate performance] is not mandatory.
"Except for the anniversary of death (kṣayāha), there is no separate rite for women;
however, some great sages maintain that women should have a separate Śrāddha.

Consequently, it is established that in the three rites beginning with Anvaṣṭakā, the Śrāddha for women is performed separately; whereas at Gayā, Mahālaya, and other such occasions, it may be performed either separately or together with their own husbands.

"The offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and the performance of water-libations (*udaka-kriyā*) must be performed by the son for the father. Here, the mention of the "offering of funeral cakes" is intended as an indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all post-mortem rites (*aurdhvadehika*). Although the word "son" (*putra*) is primary (*mukhya*) in reference to the legitimate son of the body (*aurasa*) and secondary (*gauṇa*) in reference to the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) and others, it nevertheless applies to both the primary and secondary types in the rule: "In the absence of a son, the wife shall [perform the rites]. Otherwise, regarding the appointment of a daughter (*putrikā*), it has been stated:
"Among these, the one who offers the funeral cake and inherits the share is each subsequent one in the absence of each preceding one."

This contradicts the following: "In the absence of a wife, however, the uterine brother. The mention of the "uterine brother" is intended as an indicator for whoever is the heir in the absence of a wife; consequently, it is thereby stated that daughters and others are entitled to offer the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, in this context, the word "wife" (*patnī*) refers to a spouse who has entered into the bond of marriage and sacrifice. As for what Kātyāyana says: "At the *Aṣṭakā* rite, the husband should give for a woman who has no son, but never otherwise.
Likewise, the father does not [give] for his son, nor the elder brother for his younger brother. [433]

Thus, this [rule] should be understood to apply to the father and others when they do not inherit a share; however, even if they do inherit a share, the father and others must certainly perform it. Baudhāyana states:
"The son must perform [the rites] for the father, but the father should not perform them for the son.
Yet, out of excessive affection, he may perform them, provided he omits the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."

Viṣṇu states: "He who takes the wealth is the son who offers the *piṇḍa*; even in the absence of paternal property, he should offer the *piṇḍa*. The word *piṇḍa* is intended to indicate the *śrāddha* ceremony. Sons, brothers' sons, sons of co-wives, and younger brothers—even when they receive the inheritance—should perform the *śrāddha*. And so says Manu: "Of brothers born of the same father, if even one should have a son, Manu has declared them all to be possessed of a son through that one son."
If among all the wives who have but one husband, one should have a son,
Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son.
Likewise:
"The elder brother should protect his younger brothers like his own sons. And likewise:
The first birth is from the mother, the second at the tying of the girdle of muñja grass;
there, the Sāvitrī is said to be his mother, while the teacher is called his father.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, however, a different order is stated:
"O King, the son, the grandson, or the great-grandson, as well as the lineage beginning with the brother,
or even the lineage of the *sapiṇḍas*, becomes eligible to perform the rites."
In the absence of all these,
the sapinda of the maternal side— whether connected by the funeral cake (piṇḍa) or by water— is the recipient of the rites for all of them.
O King, when both families have perished, the rites should be performed by women;
or else, all the rites are considered to be performed by those who belong to the community of that [deceased] person.
Or, if his kinsmen have perished, the lord of the earth may cause [the rites] to be performed from blood;
likewise, he should perform the preliminary, intermediate, and subsequent rites.
These ritual acts are indeed of three kinds; hear from me their distinctions.

Those acts beginning with the cremation and ending with the touching of weapons and other implements, as well as those consisting of the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) that occur during the period of impurity (*aśauca*), are the first. The middle ones are those performed month after month, known as the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites.
These take place once the deceased has attained the status of an ancestor (*pitṛtva*), following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony.
Those rites performed for the ancestors are called the "northern" rites, O best of kings.
[434] But by the father’s and mother’s sapindas, as well as by those who share the same water,
by those included within the same lineage, or by the king who takes away the wealth;
The preliminary rites must be performed by the sons and others, while the subsequent ones,
O best of men, should be performed by the daughters' sons or likewise by their own sons.
"O King, the subsequent rites for women must also be performed on the anniversary of their death every year, according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* [offering]. Thus says another Smṛti.

The son, the brother, and likewise the disciple, as well as those who share in the same lineage (gotra) or the water offering (udaka), are ordained for the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa); and so too is a kinsman who has sought refuge.

Gautama says: "In the absence of a son, the sapinda relatives, the mother's sapindas, and the disciples should offer [the oblation]; in their absence, the officiating priest and the teacher. This is the Dharma. Furthermore: the maternal uncle for the sister’s son, the sister’s son for the maternal uncle, and likewise the father-in-law for the teacher, the friend for the maternal grandfather.
And for these very persons, as well as for one's wife, sister, mother, and father,
the offering of the śrāddha must be performed by their names in that same manner.
From the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "In the absence of a son, a sapinda shall perform the rite; in his absence, a sahodaka;
or those who are the mother’s sapindas, or those who are the mother’s sahodakas."
In the absence of all these, women should perform [the rites] for their husbands without mantras;
in their absence, however, the king should cause them to be performed as if for his own family.
All the rites, such as cremation and the rest, should be properly performed by men of the same caste;
for the king is the kinsman of all social classes.

In this context, the word "woman" (*strī*) refers to female slaves, women of the harem, and other women who have not been formally married. Consequently, there is no contradiction with the rule: "In the absence of a wife, however, the uterine brother [shall perform the rite].
The Śrāddha should be performed out of affection by all those belonging to the various castes and orders of life.
By performing it correctly in this manner, a man shall attain great prosperity.
Those who bear sectarian marks (*liṅgin*) belong to the stages of life (*āśramin*). Regarding this matter, Pāraskara states an exception by means of specific qualifications:
"A Brāhmaṇa must not perform the funeral rites (*aurdhvadaihika*) for a Śūdra, nor should a Śūdra perform them for a Brāhmaṇa, except in the case of a *pāraśava* son. [435]

A *pāraśava* is one born from a *brāhmaṇa* father and a *śūdra* mother who has been wedded. He is entitled [to perform the rites] in the absence of other sons, such as those born of *brāhmaṇa* wives and so forth. Kārṣṇājini states: "The son, the pupil, or else the wife, the father, the brother, the daughter-in-law, the teacher, the woman’s husband, or the heir to the wealth—these shall perform the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) and the water-libation."

The *Brahma Purāṇa* states: "A Brāhmaṇa never performs [services] for those of other castes out of desire, delusion, fear, or greed; having done so, he shall descend to the status of that [other] caste."
Sons born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes perform [funeral rites] for a Brahmin;
he, however, never performs them for such sons.
Their mother performs [services] for them, and they also perform [services] for her.
Another Smṛti states:
"The Śrāddha for women and for the son of a Śūdra woman is to be performed without mantras;
prior to the initiation of vows for the twice-born, they too should perform it in that very same manner."
Now, the section concerning the son of two fathers (*dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa*) is defined. Regarding this, Yama states:
"The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāsuta*) must perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather as a rule;
moreover, being connected to both [fathers], he should perform it for both."

The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*) is of two kinds: one who is related to the maternal grandfather alone, and another who is related to both the father and the maternal grandfather. Among these, the first should perform the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather as a rule, while the *śrāddha* for the father may be performed optionally. However, he who is related to both must perform the *śrāddha* for both as a rule. Regarding the inquiry as to whether the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* for him should be an *ekoddiṣṭa* or for three generations (*tripuruṣa*), Kātyāyana says:
"For a maternal grandfather who has no [other] son, the *śrāddha* and other rites should be performed like those for the father.
But for relatives, kinsmen, and others, it is always the *ekoddiṣṭa*."

And this [rule] applies to all daughters' sons (*dauhitra*) without distinction; it does not apply exclusively to the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*). However, regarding that son of an appointed daughter whose mother was herself formally accepted as a son by her maternal grandfather, Manu says:
"The son of an appointed daughter should first offer the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to his mother;
the second to his mother's father, and the third to his maternal grandfather."
But as for the daughter's son who is not the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā), rather, "whether she has been formally appointed or not,
the grandfather becomes the father of a grandson through the son whom she bears from a suitable husband; by him he shall offer the funeral cake and inherit the wealth."

By the force of this statement of Manu, the one who inherits the wealth of his maternal grandfather must invariably perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfather. As Skanda said: "A daughter's son who takes the inheritance must always perform the *śrāddha* for his maternal grandfathers according to the rules, as a means of discharging his debt."
Regarding this, he states the justification: "That which is proclaimed as wealth is the impurity of human beings;
by accepting it, one takes up impurity that is difficult even for the wise to break through."
"The sages have prescribed for him a supreme expiation that purifies:
until the fall of the body, he should perform the *piṇḍa* and water-offering rites for him. Thus it is said.

Now, as for a daughter's son (*dauhitra*) who is not the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) and does not inherit the wealth of his maternal grandfather—if he performs the *śrāddha* for that [grandfather] who has no other son, he is joined with the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*); however, by not performing it, he does not incur sin. Regarding the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*) who belongs to two lineages (*dvāmuṣyāyaṇa*) and is connected to both fathers—the father of the wife and the biological father—Devala says:
Those who belong to two lineages (dvyāmuṣyāyaṇas) should offer the rice-balls and water separately to both fathers;
indeed, one who offers six rice-balls to both does not err.

The meaning is "by two paternal groups. The same applies to the feeding of Brahmins. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says concerning one who is incapable [of performing the rites for both]: "There should be the offering of rice balls for two fathers; each rice ball should bear two names.
Three rice balls should be given to the two [fathers]; by doing thus, one does not err."
Regarding this, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga states the specific sequence:
"First, one should offer the rice-ball and water to the father who is the owner of the field;
afterwards, one should offer handfuls of water to those by whom [the deceased] was begotten."
Marīci:

Whether he be of the same lineage or of a different lineage, the son of a widow should first offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the performance of the Śrāddha rite to the owner of the field (kṣetrin).

If, after that, the owner of the field should survive while the owner of the seed has died, they shall first give [the share] to the owner of the seed; it is given later when [the owner of the field] has died.
If both have died, then one should first give [the inheritance] to the progenitor (bījī);
if it was not first given to the owner of the field (kṣetrī), it does not accrue to the progenitor.
Nārada says: Those who are born of a woman not authorized [to bear children], whether by one man or by many, are all non-partakers of the inheritance;
they are the sons of the seed-givers alone.
If the mother was taken through the payment of a bride-price, they shall give the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to the biological father;
but for one who was obtained without a bride-price, the giving of the cake belongs to the husband alone.
*Śulka* means the price. [437] Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: One should perform the offering according to the *gotra* of the first husband of women;
however, if she is a virgin (*akṣatayoni*) who has taken refuge with another family, [the offering is made according to that other's *gotra*].
In that same manner, the funeral cake (piṇḍa), the śrāddha offering, and the water should be given by one of that lineage.
He describes the Brahmins who are the cause for the perfection of the *śrāddha* in three verses:

"The foremost among all those learned in the Vedas, a *śrotriya*, a knower of Brahman, and young; one who knows the meaning of the Veda, a singer of the *Jyeṣṭhasāmans*, one who knows the *Trimadhu*, and one who knows the *Trisuparṇa*. (1.219)

A sister’s son, an officiating priest, a son-in-law, a person for whom one sacrifices, a father-in-law, a maternal uncle, one who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice, a daughter’s son, a pupil, a relative by marriage, and a kinsman; || 1.220 ||

Those Brahmins who are established in knowledge, established in austerity, who maintain the five fires, who are lifelong students, and who are devoted to their fathers and mothers, are the means for the perfection of the Śrāddha.

The foremost among students is the preeminent one; [the *śrotriya*] is one who has studied even a single branch (*śākhā*) of all four Vedas according to the rules. The knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*) is one who knows the Person of the Upaniṣads. "Young" means being in middle age. A knower of the meaning of the Veda is one who understands the meaning of the Vedic sentences. One who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman* is one who, having performed the vow called the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, studies the *Sāman* named *Jyeṣṭha*. One who, having performed the vow called *Trimadhu*, studies that very portion of the Veda is a *trimadhu*. Likewise for the *trisuparṇa*. One who, preceded by the *Trināciketa* vow, studies that portion of the Veda is a *trināciketa*. Relatives (*saṃbandhin*) are those connected through marriage; kinsmen (*bāndhava*) are those beginning with the maternal grandfather and so forth. Those established in knowledge (*jñānaniṣṭhā*) are knowers of the supreme self (*adhyātmavidaḥ*). In the reading "those established in action" (*karmaniṣṭhā*), they are those intent on the performance of prescribed duties. Likewise for those established in austerity (*taponiṣṭhā*). One who maintains the five fires—the *sabhya*, *āvasathya*, and the three fires of the *tretā*—is a "five-fire man" (*pañcāgni*). The plural "students" (*brahmacāriṇaḥ*) in the singular sense is intended to refer to the class. Others are well known. These Brāhmaṇas, when fed, lead to the success and prosperity of the *śrāddha*. On this point, Manu says:
Sacrificial offerings to the gods and the ancestors must be given by donors only to one learned in the Vedas;
what is given to such a most worthy Brahmin yields great fruit.
One should feed even a single learned man at a rite for the gods or the ancestors;
one obtains abundant fruit, but not by feeding many who are ignorant of the mantras.
One should seek out from afar a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
he is considered a worthy recipient for offerings to the gods and ancestors, and he is regarded as a guest.

Examination from afar consists of investigating many generations of men, beginning with one's ancestors. A *tīrtha* is a path for obtaining water; just as water is obtained by such a path, so too are the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) obtained by the gods and ancestors through such a Brahmin-path. A guest is an exceedingly great benefactor to the giver.
