"But where a thousand who do not know the *ṛc* verses eat, a single person who knows the mantras, being pleased, is worth all of them according to the Dharma."

The meaning is that even he alone is equal to all; he is worthy of everything. Some twice-born ones are devoted to knowledge, others likewise are devoted to austerity, some are devoted to austerity and Vedic study, and others are likewise devoted to ritual action.
The word *niṣṭhā* means intentness.
Offerings for the ancestors (*kavyāni*) should be established with effort among those preeminent in knowledge;
and offerings to the gods (*havyāni*) should be presented according to rule among all four [classes] alike.

The meaning is: "in the four [stages], beginning with the culmination of knowledge. One should honor those who are learned in the Vedas, who have completed their Vedic studies, who are śrotriyas, and who are householders, by offering them *havya* and *kavya*; but one should avoid those who are the opposite.
The Veda alone is knowledge; thus it is "Vedic knowledge. Householders are those who maintain a domestic fire.
This indeed is the primary rule for the offering of oblations to the gods and the ancestors;
but this secondary rule should also be known as that which is always practiced by the virtuous.

One should feed the maternal grandfather, the maternal uncle, the sister’s son, the father-in-law, the teacher, the daughter’s son, the wife’s brother, a kinsman, as well as the officiating priest and the person for whom one sacrifices.
The husband of a sister is a son-in-law.
One should diligently feed even a daughter’s son who is observing a vow at a śrāddha ceremony;
one should provide a kutapa blanket as a seat and strew the ground with sesame seeds.
Learn now in their entirety those foremost of the twice-born who purify the row that has been defiled by unworthy persons— those best of the twice-born who are the sanctifiers of the assembly.
Those who are foremost in all the Vedas and in all the expository sciences,
and who are born into a lineage of Vedic scholars, should be known as purifiers of the assembly.
The auxiliary sciences of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), such as the *Nirukta* and others, are called "explanations" (*pravacana*) because the meaning of the Vedas is proclaimed by them.

One who has mastered the three *Nāciketa* fires, one who knows the five fires, one who knows the *Triṣuparṇa*, one who is learned in the six auxiliary sciences, one born from a lineage where the gift of a daughter in marriage (*brahmadeyā*) was maintained, and likewise one who chants the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*.
The offspring of a woman wedded by the Brahma rite, born of a lineage established by a Brahman-gift,
who knows the meaning of the Vedas, is an expounder, observes celibacy, bestows a thousand [cows], and lives for a hundred years— such a one is to be known as a Brāhmaṇa who purifies the assembly.

A *pravaktṛ* is one who teaches for the sake of the Dharma; a *sahasrada* is one who gives much. Gautama states: "One should invite those who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and endowed with speech, beauty, age, and character"—this is the syntactical connection—"some say that the gift should first go to the young, as in the case of the ancestors. This means that the Brahmins representing the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are the eldest, the older, and the oldest respectively. Vasiṣṭha says: "One should feed ascetics or virtuous householders who are advanced in age, established in good deeds, learned in the Vedas, and not [acting as] students (*aśiṣya*). One may also feed lifelong celibates (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*) who are students, provided they are possessed of good qualities."
"But if one who knows the mantras is afflicted with bodily defects that defile the company, Yama declares him to be undefiled; indeed, he is a purifier of the company.
"Bodily" refers to leucoderma and the like. "Yama" [is the speaker].
Having drunk the Soma, they were free from passion, knowers of the Dharma, and possessed of tranquil intellects;
they were observers of vows, established in their religious observances, and approached their wives only during the proper season.

Free from passion and devoid of desire, observant of vows, established in restraints, celibate, and self-controlled; even one who maintains the five fires, a student of the Yajurveda, or one who is a scholar of the Ṛgveda and knows the *Trisauparṇa* or the *Trimadhu*— [these are worthy of the gift].

One who studies the knowledge known as the Pañcāgnividyā, which is recited in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad; one who has performed the Triṇāciketa sacrifice; one who is free from passion (viraja); a singer of the Sāmans according to the Chandoga school;
and a student of the Atharvaśiras—these four are purifiers of the company at a meal.

The *viraja* is a specific mantra; one becomes free from passion (*viraja*) through its study. The *Atharvaśiras* is a portion of the *Atharvaveda*. A householder, a student (*brahmacārī*), and one who knows the *Yajurveda*—these Brahmins, having bathed after completing their Vedic studies and vows, are purifiers of the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*).
Those ministers who abide by their vows, those Brahmins who are well-versed in the Vedas,
and those twice-born ones who have desisted from harming living beings— they are the purifiers of the assembly.

The ministers are those devoted to the practice of mantras such as the Rudra-mantra; they are "consonant with the Vedas" (śrutisaṃgatāḥ), meaning they are approved by the Vedas, that is to say, they are practitioners of the Vedic injunctions. Those who are truthful, wise, ever-devoted to giving, and endowed with auspicious conduct—those twice-born ones are purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvanāḥ).
Those twice-born who are devoted to the Agnihotra sacrifice, who are tranquil, patient, free from envy, and devoid of attachment to receiving gifts— they are the purifiers of the assembly.

Those who are free from envy and devoid of malice; one who wears the skin of the black antelope; one who is the offspring of a woman given in marriage according to the *brahmadeya* rite; one who does not sell what was given as a *brahmadeya*; and the husband of a woman given in marriage according to the *brahmadeya* rite—these Brāhmaṇas are purifiers of the assembly.
May there be such a person in that family who would diligently feed a yogi—a brahmin—at a śrāddha; by him we are satisfied.

Viṣṇu: "Now, those who purify the company (*paṅktipāvana*): one who has mastered even a single auxiliary of the Veda (*vedāṅga*), one who has mastered the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and grammar, one who has mastered even a single treatise on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*); one purified by sacred fords (*tīrtha*), one purified by sacrifice (*yajña*), one purified by austerity (*tapas*), one purified by truth (*satya*), one devoted to the recitation of the *Gāyatrī*, as well as a son-in-law and a daughter's son; and, according to specific distinctions of worthy recipients, yogis. From the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:

"But to those who are always established in right conduct, who possess knowledge, and likewise meditate—one should give to those with topknots (*śikhin*), to those whose garments are dyed with mineral pigments (*dhāturakta*), and to those who carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍin*)."
If no meditating monks (dhyānabhikṣu) are available, one should feed a celibate student (brahmacārin);
if even he is not available, one should feed a detached householder as well.

In this context, the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) is referred to by the word "meditation" (*dhyāna*) because of his application to meditation; the mendicant (*bhikṣu*) is one who has gone forth (*pravrajita*); and the indifferent one (*udāsīna*) is one free from passion and other such afflictions.
For perfected beings (*siddhas*) wander this earth in the form of Brahmins;
therefore, one should approach a guest who has arrived with palms joined in reverence.
The masters of yoga always worship the earth, bounded by the oceans, with offerings of water for the guest and the feet, with foot-ointments, and with food, day after day.
These practitioners of yoga move about in various forms according to the law of living beings;
therefore, a man should always offer the ancestral oblation (*śrāddha*) to a brahmin guest.

The *siddhas* are those who have realized the true nature of the self. According to the law of progeny (*prajādharma*), that is, in their natural form, [one should give] to him who is thirsty, weary, fully awakened, and hungry;
to him it should be given with due honor by one desiring the fruit of sacrifice.
To the Fully Awakened One, who possesses full consciousness:

one should always feed at the *śrāddha* ceremonies one who has not prepared food himself, who is free from aversion, exhausted by asceticism, of meager livelihood, who does not beg, who is solitary in virtue, and possessed of a sense of shame.

One who eats unprepared food, one whose meal is unprepared, one exhausted by heat, and one distressed by the sun's glare— these, along with those learned in the six limbs [of the Veda], practitioners of yoga, and masters of all tantras, as well as the Yāyāvara; these five are to be known as the purifiers of the row.

The *sarvatantra* is the householder known as the *śālīna*; the *yāyāvara* is a specific type of householder. He who recites the *Śrāddhakalpa* is always a sanctifier of the row (*paṅktipāvana*), as is one who has mastered even a single one of the fourteen branches of knowledge.
And all those who act according to the law are purifiers of the assembly—
those who are knowers of the Bhāṣya, and whoever are devoted to grammar.
Those who study the Purāṇas or the treatises on Dharma,
and those who have performed their ablutions at sacred fords and exerted themselves in spiritual practice;
Those who have performed the ritual ablutions at the conclusion of all sacrifices,
those who are ever devoted to the vow of truth, and those who are constantly intent upon their own duty;
One should invite to the śrāddha those who are free from anger and devoted to forbearance;
for he who bypasses a nearby twice-born man who is studying [the Vedas] commits a transgression.
In both eating and giving, he destroys the lineage for three generations.
Devala says:

One who is established in the highest stage of life (āśrama), one who lives a hundred years, one who chants the Jyeṣṭha-sāman, one who maintains the sacred fires, and one who has drunk the Soma juice— such a Brāhmaṇa is a purifier of the assembly (paṅktipāvana).

The "eldest stage" (jyeṣṭhāśrama) is the householder stage (gṛhasthāśrama). An "Agnicit" is one who has performed the piling of the Śākvara fire-altar; if the term were intended to include other types of piling, the mention of a "Soma-drinker" (somapa) would be redundant. In the *Matsya Purāṇa* it is said: "He who expounds the Veda, he who investigates the sacrificial ritual (adhvara), and he who knows the rules for the melodies of the Sāman—these are the purifiers of the row of guests (paṅktipāvana-pāvanas)."
A girl of eight years who is given in marriage to one endowed with learning and virtuous conduct is Gaurī; her son is Gaura, and he indeed is a sanctifier of the row.
Manu says: What do you ask about the father of a Brahmin, or what do you ask about the mother?
If there is anything to be known that has been heard, that is remembered as being the mother and the father.
Yama says: One who maintains the five fires, one learned in the Yajurveda, an Atharvan, one who knows the head of the Veda (the Upanishads),
one who knows the Self, one who knows the limbs [of the Veda], and likewise the son of a woman married according to the Brahma rite.
If one is a student of the Yajurveda who has studied the Pañcāgnividyā, or a student of the Atharvaveda who has studied the Brahmaśīrṣa; according to the Matsya Purāṇa:
"Having seen those who know the Maṇḍalabrāhmaṇa and those who know the Puruṣasūkta, a man is quickly liberated from all sins."
Yama says:
Whether they be elders, ascetics, self-controlled, learned, or otherwise,
one should feed all of them at the śrāddha and invite them with virtuous men.
Having first acquired wealth through harsh agricultural labors, one should afterwards become a host to all; such a person, O King, is worthy of being invited to a feast.
"Others" means those who are not elders (*asthavira*). "Ketana" means an invitation. Atri says:
"But those of the same lineage (*gotrin*) who are within six generations are unworthy of being invited to a *śrāddha*;
however, beyond six generations, even those born of the same lineage may be fed at a *śrāddha*."

Even when [qualified guests] are unavailable, those beyond the third degree may be fed. As Gautama says: "One should feed a virtuous person beyond the three. The mention of "six" or "three" refers to the enumeration of male *sapiṇḍa* relatives. Atri states:

"The father, grandfather, brother, or son who is a *sapiṇḍa*—these are not to receive the *arghya* offering from one another; likewise, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are not [to receive it] at a *śrāddha*."
These officiating priests, sons, and others who are kinsmen and twice-born Brahmins should also be appointed at the Vaiśvadeva rite, provided they are more distinguished by their virtues.
Women of the same lineage (sagotrā) must not be appointed [as wives], especially so. Vyāsa states, following the context of those who purify the row (*paṅktipāvana*):
"He whose maternal and paternal ancestors for ten generations have been learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*)."
And he who always approaches his lawful wives during their fertile seasons.
Chāgaleya said:
One should perform the entire Śrāddha rite with those who possess all auspicious marks, are endowed with learning, beauty, and virtue, and are renowned among three generations of their lineage.
The phrase "renowned among the three types of persons" refers to cases where those previously mentioned are unavailable. Devala states:

"A Brahmin who has studied one Vedic branch together with its ritual manuals (kalpa) or the six auxiliary sciences (aṅgas), who is devoted to the six duties, is called a Śrotriya and a knower of dharma."
One who knows the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, whose self is pure and who is free from sin,
and who has acquired the remainder [of the qualities] like a *śrotriya*, is traditionally known as an *anūcāna*.
One who is endowed with the qualities of a learned teacher, who knows the sacrifice, the Vedic study, and the mantras,
who eats only the remnants of the meal, and whose senses are subdued, is called a *bhrūṇa* by the wise.
He who, having attained all knowledge— both Vedic and worldly—
remains eternally self-controlled while established in his stage of life, is called one who is like a seer.
With vital energy drawn upward, devoted to fierce austerity, moderate in diet, self-controlled,
capable of both cursing and bestowing grace, and true to his word, he shall become a seer (ṛṣi).
He is steadfast, a knower of all reality, free from desire and anger;
established in meditation, inactive, self-controlled, and regarding clay and gold as equal—a sage.

Among these, each subsequent one is superior; even though they may possess greater learning, those who have observed their vows and are endowed with virtues are the best, as are those who are diligent cultivators.
O King, those who know the Sāvitrī and are observant of their ritual duties are worthy of being invited;
one should invite even a twice-born man of noble birth who follows the dharma of a Kṣatriya in battle.
But one should never, my dear, designate a merchant for the ancestral Śrāddha rites.
Vṛddha Manu says: He who explains the sacred word, he who investigates the sacrifice,
and he who possesses knowledge of the absolute self— he is the purifier of those who purify the assembly.
Yama said: He should be upright, compassionate, patient, self-controlled, tranquil, devoted to truth, pure, a knower of the Vedas,
a knower of all the scriptures, and dedicated to fasting.
Likewise:
"In a *śrāddha* and in the *vaiśvadeva* rite, one should feed a follower of the Ṛgveda;
in rites for prosperity (*puṣṭikarma*), a Yajurvedin; and in rites for pacification (*śāntikarma*), a follower of the Atharvaveda."

Āpastamba says: "Even among those of equal qualities, one who is advanced in age is superior; so too is one who is emaciated by [the pursuit of] sacred objects, provided he desires [to serve]. In the Matsya Purāṇa:

"One who knows the meaning [of the scriptures], a knower of the Vedas, a counselor, one whose lineage is known, endowed with noble birth, a knower of the Purāṇas, all-knowing, and devoted to Vedic study and the recitation of prayers."
Devoted to Śiva, intent on his ancestors, a devotee of the Sun, or a Vaiṣṇava;
one who honors Brahmins, a knower of yoga, tranquil, self-conquered, and possessed of virtuous conduct.
In the Skanda Purāṇa: One who is free from greed is superior to those endowed with noble lineage and Vedic learning;
and even over those two types of Brahmins, one who has resided [there] for a long time is superior.

The meaning is that he is either one who has lived [with him] for a long time and whose character is well known, or one who has long served in the teacher’s household (*gurukula*). Āpastamba says: "One should feed Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda, provided they are not related by birth, lineage, mantra, or pupilage; however, if others possess superior qualities, even a uterine brother (*sodarya*) may be engaged [to eat] despite his lack of such qualities. That is to say, among those unrelated by birth, lineage, mantra, or pupilage—among these outsiders—if they are devoid of good qualities, then even a uterine brother endowed with good qualities should be fed. How much more so, then, one who is only distantly related? (1.219, 220, 221)
[444] He states in three verses that even Brahmins who possess the aforementioned qualities may be censurable due to causes such as illness:
"One who is diseased, one with deficient or redundant limbs, one who is blind in one eye, and likewise one born of a remarried woman..."
One who has spilled his semen, one born from a pot or a skull, one with deformed nails, and one with black teeth. || 1.222 ||
One who teaches for hire, a eunuch, a defiler of maidens, one accused of a heinous crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, and one who marries before his elder brother; 1.223.

One who abandons his mother, father, or teacher; one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* (the son of an adulteress); the son of a low-caste woman; the husband of a woman previously married to another; a thief; and those whose actions are corrupt—these are censured.

The meaning is that those who are censured, such as the sick and others, are to be excluded from the *śrāddha*. "Sick" refers to one suffering from a chronic illness. Accordingly, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:
"Those whose minds are afflicted by fate do not deserve to eat at *śrāddhas*:
the eunuch, the mute, the one with deformed nails, the bald-headed, and the one with dental disease."
One with black teeth, one with a putrid nose, one with a missing limb, one with an extra finger,
one suffering from throat disease, one with a goiter, one with cracked limbs, and one afflicted with fever.
Lame, with crippled feet, or dull-witted, as well as others who are chronically ill;

one deficient in a limb (*hīnāṅga*) or lacking a limb (*ūnāṅga*), whether by enumeration or by measure—likewise one with an extra limb. A "limb" (*aṅga*) refers to the fingers and so forth. "One-eyed" (*kāṇa*) means having only one eye. Since the eye is not a "limb" but rather a sense organ (*indriya*), the one-eyed person is mentioned separately from those deficient in a limb. A "remarried woman" (*punarbhū*) is one who has been married again; her husband or her son is a *paunarbhava*. In reality, however, it is the son alone [who is meant]. For this very reason, Hārīta says: "The wanton woman, the remarried woman, the seed-bearer, and the woman who acts according to her own will."
And these five born of Śūdra wombs should be known as eaters of all things.

"Whatever offspring may ever be born of these women, one should not admit them into the rows [of guests at a meal]; they are recorded as being unworthy of the row. The *retodhā* is the son of a woman who has borne a child by another man; the *kāmacāriṇī* is one who goes to other men according to her own will; the *sarvabhakṣā* is a drinker of liquor. Devala speaks of the *avakīrṇin*:

One who is a "hidden-sign" (*gūḍhaliṅgin*) is an *avakīrṇin*, as is one whose vow has been broken (*bhagnavrata*). A "hidden-sign" is one devoid of the outward marks of his stage of life (*āśrama*), such as the staff and so forth. One whose vow is broken is one whose celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has been violated. Yama also says:
"A practitioner of vows who approaches a woman is designated as an *avakīrṇin*."
The *vratī* is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*). Regarding the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, Manu says:
"Two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others;
the *kuṇḍa* is he who is born while the husband is alive, and the *golaka* is he who is born when the husband is dead."

This refers to the son born of the field (*kṣetraja*). For anyone else, there is no possibility [of this status] because they are not Brahmins. One with deformed nails (*kunakhī*) is one whose nails are naturally fallen-off. One with black teeth (*śyāvadanta*) is one whose teeth are naturally black. A hired teacher (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*) is one who is a hired laborer (*bhṛtaka*) and is also a teacher; or alternatively, one for whom the teacher is a hired laborer is a hired teacher. On this point, Devala says: "The one who teaches for hire and the one who is taught for hire—both these Brahmins are fallen due to the buying and selling of their own Vedic study."

A *klība* is a eunuch. One who renders a maiden’s womb defiled by means of a finger or other such object is a defiler of maidens (*kanyādūṣī*), or one who causes a defect in a maiden. One who is accused of having committed a sin due to an unverified truth is an accursed person (*abhiśasta*). A betrayer of friends (*mitradhruk*) is one who acts with malice toward friends. A slanderer (*piśuna*) is one who points out the faults of others. A seller of *soma* (*somavikrayī*) is a seller of the *soma* creeper or of the *soma* sacrifice. A *parivindaka* is a superseder (*parivettā*). Regarding this, Manu says:

"He who enters into marriage and the consecration of the *agnihotra* while his elder brother remains [unmarried] is to be known as a superseder (*parivettā*); the elder brother is the superseded (*parivitti*)."
Śātātapa says:
"In the case of a eunuch, one who has gone to another country, an outcast, a renunciant,
or one devoted to the Yoga-śāstra, there is no fault in taking another wife."
There is no fault in superseding the sons of a paternal uncle, the sons of a co-wife, or the sons of another man's wife, provided one is united with a wife and the sacred fires.

Sons born of another man’s wife are brothers such as those adopted (*dattaka*) and others. Vasiṣṭha states: "If one does not wait for his elder brother for eight, ten, or twelve years while he remains unmarried (*aniviṣṭa*), he becomes liable to penance. "Unmarried" (*aniviṣṭa*) means one who has neither performed the marriage ceremony nor established the *agnihotra* fire. On this matter, there are two verses: "But if the elder brother has departed for the sake of dharma or wealth, it is proper to wait for him for twelve years; however, if he is heard from again and again, [one must wait]."
One who is insane, a sinner, a leper, an outcast, or even a eunuch,
as well as one afflicted by pulmonary consumption or disease, should not be waited for in a formal reception.
"There is no fault in lamenting for those who are lame, dwarfs, hunchbacked, stammerers, and the dull-witted; nor for those born blind, deaf, or mute. — Vṛddhavasiṣṭha.
And when the elder brother has not established the sacred fires, how may the younger brother act?
Having obtained the permission of the elder brother, he may perform the Agnihotra according to the rule.

And this should be understood to apply when the eldest brother, who is qualified for the rites, does not perform the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*); it does not apply when he is unqualified. Hārīta says:
"Among all uterine brothers, how can one become a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder)? They are superseded by means of wives, but not by the *agnihotra* or by sacrifice."

The meaning is that even if permitted by one entitled to give him in marriage, he should not marry [another]. Uśanas says: "If a man's father, paternal grandfather, or elder brother is [alive], there is no fault in his marrying before them, provided they are engaged in austerity, the Agnihotra sacrifice, or the study of mantras."

The meaning is that for one who has a father or other elders, and who acts with their permission, penances such as the *agnihotra* do not become causes for supersession (*parivedana*). Sumantu states:
"If a father has not performed the *ādheya* (establishment of the sacred fires), how may a son cause it to be done?
He has the right to perform the *agnihotra*, according to the statement of Śaṅkha."
The word "of one who has been authorized" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Whether the elder brother is addicted to vice, or even an atheist,
the younger brother, desiring to perform his duty, may then have the consecration (ādhāna) performed.
Disqualification due to addiction and other such causes is indicated here; therefore, only with the permission of that [elder] may the younger brother perform the consecration (*ādheya*).
"As long as the elder brother remains, one should not cause the consecration to be performed;
but having obtained his permission, one may do so—such is the word of Śaṅkha."
Śātātapa says:
"Neither sacred fires, nor the Vedas, nor austerities, nor a śrāddha rite can supersede [the marriage of] a younger brother; and so too [is forbidden] a girl who is deformed."

The phrase "the elder brother" (*jyeṣṭha*) is to be understood as the subject, even when he is not authorized [to perform the rite]. Even while the elder brother is the one entitled to perform the *śrāddha*, the younger brother who performs it is not considered a *parivettṛ* (one who marries before his elder). There is no fault in the marriage of a younger sister if the elder sister is deformed or remains unmarried. Yājñavalkya says:
"He who proceeds with the *tretā* fires without having first established the *āvasathya* fire becomes one who has not maintained the sacred fires; he is likewise called a *parivettṛ*."

Gārgya says that the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathyādhāna*) is also like the other types of fire-establishment. "While a full brother who is the elder remains, one should not take a wife, nor perform the establishment of the domestic fire; otherwise, he becomes fallen."
Brahmagarbha says:
Through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, receiving gifts, and by means of wealth from blameless persons,
one should maintain the *aupāsana* fire, tending to it at its proper time.

The subject at hand is now stated: one who abandons his mother, father, teacher, and so forth, for reasons other than grounds such as loss of caste (*pātitya*), is a "deserter of mother and others. And so says Manu: "One who, without cause, has abandoned his mother, father, or likewise his guru... Here, the "guru" refers to the teacher (*ācārya*) and not the father, because the father is mentioned separately. A "consumer of *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* food" is one who eats the food of a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*. And so, after defining the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, Manu says:
He who eats the food of those two is called a *kuṇḍāśin* by the wise; according to the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"A *kuṇḍa* consists of sixty-four pure *palas*, which is four *prasthas*."
Whoever should swallow that would become a consumer of food from a pit and fall to a low state.
One devoid of dharma is a *vṛṣala*. Regarding this, Manu says:
"For the Blessed Dharma is indeed a bull (*vṛṣan*);
those who act against him, the gods know as a *vṛṣala*, one who is excluded from all dharma."

His son is a *vṛṣalātmaja*. Alternatively, a *vṛṣala* is a Śūdra; he whose son is such is a *vṛṣalātmaja*. A woman who has previously belonged to another (*parapūrvā*) is one who was previously given to another man; her husband is a *parapūrvāpati*. A *stena* is a thief. Those who perform forbidden acts are "corrupt in action" (*karmaduṣṭa*); they, along with others not mentioned here—such as physicians, temple-priests (*devalaka*), and so forth—are to be understood from other scriptures. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Those who are thieves, outcasts (*patita*), or impotent, and those who follow the lifestyle of atheists..."
Manu declared those Brahmins to be unworthy of offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

One who holds the view that "there is no destiny" (daiva) is an atheist (*nāstika*). One whose livelihood is based on explaining the treatises of atheists and so forth is one who lives by that [atheistic] profession. Yama says:
"The gods do not eat the food of a slanderer, nor do they eat the food of a speaker of untruth;
they do not eat the food of one conquered by his wife, nor of one in whose house there is a paramour."
The ancestors do not partake of the sacrificial oblation from one who approaches with harsh words, nor from one dressed in red garments, nor from one whose ears extend beyond two finger-breadths.
One should not sit in a row with those who are endowed with these characteristics.
Śaṅkha says:
Those Brāhmaṇas who study on forbidden days, who are devoid of purity and proper conduct,
and whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of Śūdras, are defilers of the assembly.
Yama says:
Thieves, usurers, the wicked, those who destroy the property of others,
and those excluded from the four stages of life (āśramas) should be known as defilers of the row.
Those who have strayed from their own duties are proclaimed to be thieves;
whatever ancestral offering one gives to them perishes for him after death.
But those of small intelligence who knowingly bestow [food] upon them,
all of them eat excrement for a hundred years in the next world.
Therefore, one who desires to give should, in every respect, offer divine rites and ancestral śrāddhas to those who are tranquil; never, under any circumstances, to those who are not tranquil.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"He who subsists on air while remaining outside the four stages of life (āśrama),
and he who is a non-exerting proponent of liberation— both of these are defilers of the row."
In the Mahābhārata:
"O Bhārata, those whose lineage is unknown, those who belong to a *gaṇa*,
and those who are the sons of appointed daughters (*putrikā*), do not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha*."

*Ketana* means an invitation. *Gaṇaputra* refers to one who belongs to a group; "group" (*gaṇa*) here denotes a community of accountants, monastic residents, Brahmins, and so forth. Manu says: "One should not feed a friend at a *śrāddha*; his friendship should be cultivated through [other] wealth.
One should feed at a *śrāddha* that twice-born man whom one knows to be neither an enemy nor a friend."
In the absence of any other Brahmins, he himself has said:
"One may, if one wishes, honor a friend at a *śrāddha*, but never an enemy;
for an oblation consumed by one who hates it becomes fruitless after death."
From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
There is no questioning of the Vedas; he who questions them is a doer of evil. Such a person falls away from the fruit of the Veda as a recipient, and likewise from the fruit of the gift as a giver.
Anuyoga is a question for the purpose of examination, such as "What is he reciting? Kaśyapa says:
One should carefully avoid these Brāhmaṇas in all rites: those who kill those who trust them, those who are physically deformed, and those who point out the stars [for nefarious purposes].
Those who are one-eyed, those with leprosy, eunuchs, and those without skin— those who are hairless, meaning they are bald—
none of these should be associated with those who have mastered the Vedas at a *śrāddha* ceremony.
In the *Mahābhārata*, "those without skin" refers to those afflicted with *śipiviṣṭa* (leprosy), and "hairless" means those who are bald.
Even one who is vow-less, a gambler, a thief, or a seller of living beings,
if he has subsequently drunk the Soma juice, he too is worthy of the sacrificial feast.
In this context, "vow" refers to the Vedic vow. Manu says:
"As many morsels as one who is ignorant of the mantras swallows during offerings to the gods and ancestors, so many glowing lamps, spikes, and iron balls shall he swallow after death."

The *śūla* (spear) and the *ṛṣṭi* (lance) are specific types of weapons. An *ayoguḍa* is an iron ball. Devala states: "Those who give false testimony; those who harm men; those conquered by women; those who destroy bridges; those who subsist on the playing of the *tāla* (cymbals/clapping); those who recite heterodox scriptures (*vidharmapāṭhaka*); perpetual beggars; rogues who live off the pretext of performing penances; violent criminals (*sāhasika*); hunters; atheists; backbiters; the deceitful; merchants; those born of a remarried woman (*punarbhava*); those who are self-indulgent (*ātmambhari*); *pukkasa*s; those who travel by sea; those who perform sorcery (*kṛtyābhicāra*); those who frequent brothels (*melaka*); physicians; hired laborers (*bhṛtaka*); defilers of virgins; ungrateful persons (*kṛtaghna*); rogues (*kuhika*); cruel people; betrayers of friends; those who squander what has been given; those who break agreements; those of foul speech (*vāgduṣṭa*); those who speak harshly; artisans (*kāru*); craftsmen (*śilpika*); elephant-riders; and horse-binders—these are to be avoided. A *tālāvadhāraṇa* is one who lives by the playing of the *tāla*. *Vidharmapāṭhakas* are those who recite the scriptures of heretics (*pāṣaṇḍa*). A *pukkasa* is one who lives by killing deer. A *dattāpavyayin* is one who misappropriates what has been given. An *aśvabandhaka* is one who ties up horses for the purpose of selling them. Vasiṣṭha [states as follows].
Those kingdoms in which ignorant people consume foods that should be eaten by the learned desire drought, or a great danger arises.
Hārīta says:
Even those endowed with learning and noble lineage, if they are of base conduct and lowest among men,
and are constantly devoted to honey-based intoxicants, are proclaimed to be Yātudhānas.
The meaning is: "in actions that cause suffering to others, such as those involving honey.
Those who kill birds, fish, and deer; those who slay snakes and tortoises;
and those intent on the slaughter of various creatures—these indeed are outcasts among Brahmins.

Likewise: "A servant of a Śūdra, one supported by the king, a Vṛṣala who performs sacrifices for a village, and one who subsists by killing or imprisoning— these six are mere Brahmins in name (brahmabandhus)."
Yama said:
He whose Veda and sacrificial altar have been lost for three generations is indeed called a "wicked Brāhmaṇa," as is he who is the husband of a Vṛṣalī. [450]
Uśanas says: A barren woman is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*, and one whose children have died is also a *vṛṣalī*;
furthermore, a maiden who has reached puberty is to be known as another kind of *vṛṣalī*.
But that Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, should marry such a girl,
one should know him to be the husband of a Vṛṣalī, unworthy of receiving Śrāddha offerings and excluded from the row of diners.
Manu has declared that those who fall away from their purpose by means of teaching for a fee are indeed sellers of the Veda; one should not feed them at śrāddha ceremonies.
"Those who teach the unrefined and those who teach for a fee enter into terrible darkness," so said Vaivasvata.

Therefore, the meaning is that these persons are not to be fed. Manu says: "One should avoid at a śrāddha those who wear matted hair but do not study the Vedas, those who are weak, gamblers, and those who officiate as priests for guilds."
One with matted hair who is a celibate student, one who is weak, and one who is bald— these, as well as physicians, temple-priests, meat-sellers,
and those who live by trade, should be avoided at offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
A physician practices for the sake of livelihood, not for the sake of dharma. Devala says: One who subsists on the treasury of the gods shall be known by the name *devalaka*;
he is to be understood as one excluded from the row (*apāṅkteya*) in all rites at all times.
Likewise:
"A Brahmin who is devoted to the worship of [images of] gods for three years while seeking wealth is called a *devalaka*; he is censured in rites for the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*)."

*Vipaṇa* means trade. Although the seller of meat is already prohibited by the general rule against those who live by trade, he is mentioned separately in order to demonstrate that he must be avoided above all else. By this, it is understood that even those who live by trade may be accepted in times of distress if they possess the aforementioned qualities. In this way, other specific prohibitions should also be understood as intended for absolute avoidance, once the general prohibition has been established. A village servant, a servant of the king, one with deformed nails, one with black teeth, one who opposes his teacher, one who has abandoned the sacred fires, and likewise a usurer;

An "opponent" (*pratiroddhā*) is one who acts contrarily. "One who has abandoned the sacred fires" (*tyaktāgni*) means without a cause for abandonment prescribed by the scriptures; this is the understood sense. A "usurer" (*vārdhuṣi*) is one who subsists on prohibited interest. And the prohibition is as follows: "He who, having taken goods at a low price, sells them at a high price—he is indeed called a usurer, and is censured among those who discourse upon the Veda."

One afflicted with consumption, a cattle-herder, one who marries before his elder brother, one who has been cast out, a hater of Brahmins, one who is superseded in marriage by a younger brother, and one who belongs to a communal group (gaṇa)— these are indeed [excluded].
A *yakṣmī* is one afflicted with consumption (*rājayakṣman*). Devala describes the *nirākṛti*:
"A Brahmin who has forgotten the Veda after having studied it becomes a *nirākṛti*.
Kātyāyana, however, describes the *nirākṛti* differently.

But he who, having established the sacred fires, fails out of laziness to worship the gods and others with these [offerings], and thus rejects the deities and so forth, is to be known as a *nirākṛti*.
One who hates Brahmins is a hater of the Veda; one who is within a *gaṇa* is one who stays in the midst of a group—a *gaṇa* being a community of Brahmins and others residing in a monastery (*maṭha*).
Furthermore: "The man of bad character, the one who has broken his vow of chastity, the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, the son of a remarried woman, the one-eyed man, and he in whose house lives a paramour."
"Kuśīlava" refers to actors and the like. Likewise, [the text mentions] one who has entered into association with outcasts through spiritual or matrimonial connections.

The separate mention of this person from "outcasts" (patita) is for the purpose of showing favor toward one who has already performed penance, or for the purpose of showing favor toward one associated with those guilty of minor offenses (upapātaka).
One who sets fire to a house, a poisoner, one who eats from a vessel [given by a low-caste], a seller of Soma,
one who travels by sea, a bard, an oil-presser, and a forger;
A poisoner, a slanderer, a bard (one who recites auspicious verses), a forger (one who fabricates scales, measures, or testimony),
and one who disputes with his father; likewise, one who is squint-eyed,
a drunkard, one afflicted by a foul disease, one accused of a crime, a hypocrite, and a seller of liquids (or adulterators of substances).

A *kekara* is one with a squint or half-closed eyes. *Madya* refers to grape juice and the like, but not *surā* (distilled liquor), because the drinker of the latter is already prohibited on account of being an outcast (*patita*). Devala states the "eight diseases of sin": "Insanity, skin diseases, consumption, asthma, diabetes, fistula-in-ano, dropsy, and urinary stones—these are the eight diseases of sin. *Rasa* means poison, mercury, or sugarcane juice and so forth. [The following are also excluded from inheritance]:

the maker of bows and arrows, he who marries a younger sister while her elder sister remains unmarried (*agredidhiṣūpati*), a betrayer of friends, one who lives by gambling, and likewise one who is both son and teacher.
Devala says regarding the *agredidhiṣū*:
"If a younger sister is married while the elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as the *agredidhiṣū*, and the elder sister is considered the *didhiṣū*. [452]
Manu, however, describes the *didhiṣūpati* differently:
"He who, out of lust, should take pleasure in the wife of his deceased brother—even though she has been authorized [to remarry] according to the law—he is to be known as a *didhiṣūpati*. (MDh 3.172)
From the very mention of these characteristics, it should be understood that the husband of a *didhiṣū* woman is also to be avoided.
Furthermore, those afflicted with epilepsy, scrofula, or leprosy, as well as a slanderer,
one who is insane, blind, and a reviler of the Vedas— these too are to be avoided.
One who suffers from epilepsy; one with white leprosy (śvitrī), that is, one with white skin; one who trains elephants, horses, cattle, or camels; one who lives by the stars (an astrologer);
one who is a breeder of birds; and likewise, one who is a teacher of warfare.

One who divides watercourses and those who delight in obstructing them; a watercourse is a flow of water, and its divider is one who tears it apart. Obstruction is the blocking of that flow by means of embankments and the like.
Furthermore, one who builds houses, a messenger, and one who plants trees.
One who plays with dogs, one who lives by falcons, and one who defiles a maiden;

One who lays the foundation of a house, one who builds a house, a messenger, a minister of peace and war, one who plants trees for the sake of profit, a cruel person, one who lives the life of a low-born (vṛṣala), one who performs sacrifices for guilds (gaṇas), one devoid of proper conduct, a eunuch, and likewise one who is constantly begging; [these are excluded].

One whose livelihood is that of a *vṛṣala* (an outcaste) is a "vṛṣalavṛtti. Here, "gaṇas" refers to many people gathered together who perform a single task; a priest for each of these many individuals is a "pūgayājaka," and thus there is no redundancy. A "klība" is one lacking enthusiasm. One who lives by agriculture, one with elephantiasis (*ślīpadin*), and one who is censured by the virtuous;
likewise, a shepherd (*aurabhrika*), a buffalo-herder (*māhiṣika*), and the husband of a woman previously married to another.

*Ślīpada* is a specific disease. Even apart from those already mentioned, one who is censured by the virtuous is also included. An *aurabhrika* is one who lives off sheep; likewise, a *māhiṣika* is one who lives off buffaloes or the son of an unchaste woman. As Devala says: "The wife is called *mahiṣī*, and she who is unchaste is also [so called]; he who is born from her womb is indeed known as a *māhiṣika*."
One who carries out the removal of corpses should be avoided with great effort;
however, there is no fault if one does so for the sake of the Dharma by means of payment.
These lowest of the twice-born, who have abandoned proper conduct and are unworthy of the company at a meal—[453]—[should be excluded].
The most excellent among the twice-born should avoid Brahmins in both cases.

In both cases—those pertaining to the gods (*daiva*) and those pertaining to the ancestors (*pitrya*)—Gautama states: "One should not feed: a thief, an outcast (*patita*), an atheist (*nāstika*), one who lives as such, one who has killed his hero (his husband), an *agredidhiṣū*, the husband of an *agredidhiṣū* (an *agredidhiṣūpati*), one who officiates for a group of women (*strīgrāmayājaka*), a non-reciter (*ajapāla*), one who has abandoned the sacred fires (*utsṛṣṭāgni*), a drinker of liquor (*madyapa*), a man of evil conduct (*kucāra*), a false witness (*kūṭasākṣin*), a juggler (*prātihārika*), one whose wife has a paramour, a *kuṇḍa*-eater, a seller of boundary land, an arsonist, a poisoner, an *avakīrṇin*, a servant of a multitude (*gaṇapreṣya*), one who approaches forbidden women (*agamyāgāmin*), an elder brother whose younger brother marries first (*parivitti*), a younger brother who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), one for whom the elder brother has married after him (*paryāhita*), one who causes the elder to marry after him (*paryādhātṛ*), one who has abandoned himself (*tyaktātmā*), one with deformed nails (*durnakhi*), one with black teeth (*śyāvadanta*), the son of a remarried woman (*paunarbhava*), a gambler (*kitava*), one defeated at dice (*ajita*), a servant (*preṣya*), a pretender (*prātirūpika*), the husband of a Śūdra woman (*śūdrāpati*), one who has renounced the Vedas (*nirākṛti*), one suffering from consumption (*kilāsin*), a usurer (*kusīdin*), a merchant (*vaṇik*), one who lives by a craft (*śilpopajīvin*), and those whose character is devoted to gambling, instrumental music, clapping, dancing, and singing. Also, those divided against their father's will, and according to some, disciples and those of the same lineage (*sagotra*). A *vīrahā* is one who kills a person other than a Brāhmaṇa. The term "slayer of a Brāhmaṇa" (*brahmahā*) is already included under the category of the outcast (*patita*). The word "husband" (*pati*) is connected individually with both the terms *agredidhiṣū* and *didhiṣū*. The word "officiating priest" (*yājaka*) is connected individually with both the words *strī* and *grāma*. "Kucāra" means one of reprehensible conduct. "Prātihārika" means a magician. One should not feed a paramour; the meaning is that one should not feed the man who has a paramour, nor the paramour herself. Regarding the terms *paryāhita* and *paryādhātṛ*, Laugākṣi says: [Laugākṣi’s definition follows... *(Note: The provided Sanskrit text contains a repetition of the phrase "yājakaśabdaś ca strīgrāmaśabdābhyāṃ pratyekaṃ saṃbadhyate". This has been translated once for clarity.)* *(Note: The final sentence regarding Laugākṣi’s definition was cut off in the source text.)*
If an elder brother remains [unmarried] while a younger brother establishes the sacred fires,
then the elder is called the *paryāhita* and the younger the *paryādhātṛ*.

One who has abandoned his soul is a reckless person. A *prātirūpika* is one who deals with false weights, measures, and so forth, or is a deceiver by other means. A *kilāsin* is a leper, or one who seizes land. A *kusīdin* is one who lives on usury. One whose habit is the bow (*jyāśīla*) is one who lives by the science of archery; likewise those whose habits are instrumental music and so forth. *Sagotra* refers to those of the same lineage, and *sapiṇḍa* to those of the same ancestral offerings. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "A liar, a thief, one hostile to the king, a servant, one who lives by planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, a buffalo-keeper, a goat-herder, a Śūdra teacher, a bard, a bell-ringer, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, one who lives by predicting the stars and so forth, a Brahmin’s servant, a seller of offspring, a gambler, and those who forge documents or sell humans and animals—these are excluded from the company at a meal. Hārīta says: "In rites for the gods and ancestors, one should avoid a physician, a servant of a low-caste man, an artisan, a gambler, one who plays with dogs, one who lives by birds, a fisherman, a killer of living beings, a brick-maker, a harlot, a usurer, a snake-charmer, one who has fallen from his caste, a teacher for hire, one taught by a teacher for hire, a spy, a mediator, a professional actor, and others. Manu says: *(Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence regarding Manu; the translation reflects the available portion.)*
For one who sells Soma, [the gift] becomes excrement; for a physician, pus and blood;
for a usurer, it is without foundation; and for a temple-attendant, it is lost.
Whatever is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;
it is like an oblation poured onto ashes, so too when given to a twice-born man who has returned to the life of a householder.
But regarding other unworthy persons who are unfit to sit in the company (apāṅktya), as previously specified,
the wise declare that their food is fat, blood, flesh, marrow, and bone.
As many worthy recipients as an unworthy person looks upon while they are eating,
for that many the foolish giver receives no fruit from that act.
As many Brahmins as one who performs sacrifices for Śūdras may touch with his limbs,
for that many [Brahmins] the donor shall not obtain the fruit of the material gift.
A blind man, upon seeing [the gift], destroys the merit of ninety; one with a squint, that of sixty; one with leprosy, that of a hundred;
but one afflicted by a foul disease destroys the fruit of a thousand for the donor.

In this context, the intended meaning is "fitness" (yogyatā) as expressed by the word "blind" (andha). Therefore, the sense is that a blind person standing in a location from which he is capable of observing the Brahmins eating destroys the fruit of the feeding of ninety Brahmins. As stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:

"One who does not belong to an āśrama, one who performs penance [for other reasons], one who does not invite that [proper] Brahmin, a Śākya, an atheist, and a reviler of the Vedas [are likewise excluded]."
And those who revile one who practices meditation—all of them are defilers of the assembly.

*Upapatti* means "arising"; one who relies on mere logic is a "dry logician" (*śuṣkatārkika*), so called because of his association with the Śākyas. A logician who follows the sacred tradition (*āgama*) is indeed praiseworthy.
One should avoid at a *śrāddha* all those who are shaven-headed in vain, those with matted hair, all such hypocrites, as well as those who are merciless and of corrupt conduct.
He who recites the Vedas, he who maintains the Vedas, and he who subsists on the Vedas— both of these,
as well as the husband of a daughter, are not worthy of the śrāddha offering.

A *vedabhṛt* is one who has been hired for the purpose of acquiring the Vedas. Livelihood from the Veda refers to such things as officiating at sacrifices or teaching them. "And he who would approach wives in vain, or who would officiate at a sacrifice for one unqualified for the rite—those two, as well as the twice-born man who is an atheist, do not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha*."
He who cooks food for his own sake, and not for the sake of the gods or guests— such a fallen man, a Brahmarākṣasa, is not worthy even of the Śrāddha rite.
Hārīta says:
He who, having cast his own family behind him, goes instead to another's family, becomes a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* by that evil conduct; of this there is no doubt.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"Those who are ungrateful, atheists, and obstinate; those dwelling in the lands of the Mlecchas;
the Triśaṅkus, Barbaras, Āndhras, Bakas, Draviḍas, and Kuṅkuṇas."
One should avoid the Karṇāṭakas, the Bāhlīkas, and the Kaliṅgas.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, Īśvara said:
"The Śrāddha should be given after examination; this is the Vedic revelation."
And through examination, O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, straightforwardness is seen to be the superior quality.
But he who, abiding in sincerity, gives a śrāddha without making investigations—for him the ancestors and the deities are satisfied; of this there is no doubt. (1.222, 223, 224)
On the day before the *śrāddha*, one who is self-possessed and pure should invite the *brāhmaṇas*.

On the day prior to the *śrāddha* day, he should invite those *brāhmaṇas* who purify the assembly (*paṅktipāvana*); in their absence, his maternal grandfather and others. "Self-possessed" means having conquered the senses; "pure" means restrained and purified; he should invite them. An invitation is a command that must not be refused. Devala says:
"Free from anger, composed, healthy, full of faith, unhurried, and pure."
And here, one should always and repeatedly have a concentrated mind during the performance of the ritual action.
Being modest and soft-spoken, composed and established in his natural state, with a concentrated mind and intent upon that task,
the donor— having resolved, "I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow"— should invite the Brahmins after having eaten once, without meat, in a house where all the people have already eaten.
If it is not possible on that day, he should invite those Brahmins on the following day—
those who are not his relatives, who do not share his interests, and an odd number according to his own capacity.

"In the event of impossibility" means when it is impossible to invite them on the previous day. Even in the case of inviting them on that very day, they should be invited only after they have abandoned sexual intercourse with women on the preceding day. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"One should invite on the previous day the best of the twice-born mentioned above;
or, if that is not possible, on that very day, having excluded those who are attached to women."

With a restrained mind, he should propitiate by prostrations and other means the Brahmins who have arrived at the proper time for alms, as well as self-controlled ascetics; "self-controlled" (saṃyaminaḥ) refers to those practicing celibacy (brahmacāriṇaḥ), according to Pracetas.

He should send a trustworthy person of the same caste to invite the twice-born; this applies when he himself is unable to invite them. Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (kṛtāpasavya), on the previous day he should invite the ancestors who came before him.
"You must perform our ancestral rites for us; please be gracious."
Having prostrated with the left hand for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should invite [the guests].

Manu, however, desires the invitation of the Vaiśvadevika Brahmins to take place first; as he says: "Whatever rite one might desire that begins and ends with the gods, it should not begin and end with the ancestors;
for one who performs a rite beginning and ending with the ancestors quickly perishes along with his lineage."
And then follows the deliberation:

"One should invite Brahmins who are endowed with qualities such as noble birth, ritual action, and learning, who are free from greed, who have eaten their meal at the end of the afternoon, and who have been made to lie down [for the night]."
On the morrow, at our śrāddha ceremony, you must be free from all exertion and devoid of desire and anger.
If they say "So be it," then, provided this night passes without obstacle,
they should wait vigilantly for the time of the ancestral offering (śrāddha) according to what has been heard.
The remainder [of the sentence] is that they should say, "So be it. In the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Having touched his right knee, [the wise man] should invite him thus: 'You are invited by me today.
Having invited him in this manner, the wise man should cause him to hear the ancestral observances (*niyama*)."
In the performance of the Śrāddha rite, you all and I must remain free from anger, devoted to purity, and constantly observant of celibacy.
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
One who knows that "I shall perform [the rite] tomorrow" must perform the cleansing of the garments and so forth;
having smeared the ground and prepared the site, he should invite the Brahmins.
The student should discard his tooth-stick and become pure.
And they too must remain restrained in their actions of mind, speech, and body. || 1.225 ||

Once invited, they must remain with their mental, vocal, and physical activities fully restrained; likewise, the performer of the rite must also be so. Manu says: "A twice-born man invited to a *pitrya* rite should always remain self-controlled;
he should not recite the Vedas, and that indeed shall be his *śrāddha*. [457]
Devala says:
If one who has been previously invited by another should accept a gift,
or if he eats again even after having already eaten his meal, his merit perishes.
Manu says: "But that best of the twice-born who, having been invited according to the rule for offerings to the gods and ancestors,
somehow neglects his duty, being a sinner, shall go to the state of a pig."
This refers to one who has accepted an invitation. Āpastamba states: "Once [the rite] has begun, there shall be no eating until its completion. Yama says:
"Even after having caused an invitation to be made, the twice-born man who causes it to be neglected incurs the sin of killing a Brahmin and is born into the womb of a Śūdra."

Having invited a Brahmin, if one causes him to fall away—that is, if one lets him pass by—then he is not to be fed; this is the meaning. But that foolish man who, having been invited to a *śrāddha*, accepts an invitation from another, his merit accumulated over a year is destroyed.
But he who, having invited a Brahmin, does not honor him according to the rule,
is born among the terrible animal wombs that are most difficult to endure.
Hārīta says:
Whether at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, if one has invited a Brāhmaṇa but does not satisfy him according to the rule, he takes away the fruit of that [offering].
Knowing that [the merit] has been forgotten due to a lack of faith, one should diligently propitiate him;
by especially gratifying him, one shall obtain the full fruit of all that.
Manu says: But he who, having been invited to a śrāddha, rejoices with a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī),
incurs all whatever evil deed has been committed by the giver.

A *vṛṣalī* is a *śūdrā*. Manu says: "Whether the *śrāddha* is preceded by a rite for the gods or whether it is without the gods, one should remain celibate there; however, after eating at a regular (*nityaka*) *śrāddha*, one may eat."

Kātyāyana states: "On that day, one should be pure, free from anger, unhurried, vigilant, and truthful in speech. One should avoid sexual intercourse, physical exertion, and Vedic study. From the invocation until the ritual rinsing (upasparśana), one should remain restrained in speech; and the same applies when invited. The meaning is that *upasparśana* refers to sipping water (*ācamana*); one should remain silent until the end of the rite or until that specific point. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"For the sake of purification, having risen in the morning, one should clean one's teeth."

And this applies to the eater, not the giver, according to the Vedic injunction: "One whose teeth are moist should sacrifice to the ancestors. Hārīta says: "Then, when the next day has dawned, having gone toward the direction sloping toward the south, one should fetch *darbha* grass with its roots, inclining toward the south. Also, water that is not enclosed by others. Those who have performed the rites for Viśvakarman, together with women, children, and the elderly, shall bathe with fragrant substances, be well-anointed, and wear clean garments. "Bathing with fragrant substances" means bathing with materials such as scented oils and the like. Yama says: "In the *śrāddha* rite for the ancestors, the *darbha* grass should be with its roots."
By means of the root-mantra of the great-souled Śakra, one conquers the worlds.
Darbha grass protects against Asuras, sesame seeds protect against Rākṣasas;
but one who knows the Vedas protects the food given to an ascetic, which becomes inexhaustible.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The blades of grass should indeed be green, with their roots intact, glossy, and lush on all sides;
they should be a span (*ratni*) in measure and consecrated by means of the *pitṛ-tīrtha*."
They are provided with their tufts and have uncut tips. A cubit measured from the wrist is a *ratni*. They are consecrated and purified.

Likewise, *śyāmāka*, *nīvāra*, and *dūrvā* grasses are prescribed; this should be understood to apply when *kuśa* grass is unavailable. Thus Viṣṇu states: "In the absence of *kuśa*, one should offer *kāśa* and *dūrvā* in place of *kuśa*. Gobhila says: "Outside [the sacrificial ground], grass cut near its base is for the ancestors; in their absence, all kinds of grass may be used, excluding *śūkatṛṇa*, *śara*, *sūryasuta*, *nala*, and *ṣaṇḍha* (or *ṣaṇḍa*). *Śūkatṛṇa* refers to grass from awned grain. Kātyāyana [states]: [text follows].
Green Darbha grass is fit for sacrifice; yellow Darbha is fit for the five sacrifices;
roots with their bases are for the ancestors; and variegated Darbha is for the Viśvedevas.
Those things collected for the sake of a food-offering (piṇḍa) and likewise for the sake of libations (tarpaṇa),
their excrement and urine are prescribed to be discarded from one side only.
From the Purāṇa:
Whatever rites for the ancestors there may be, such as the libations (tarpaṇa) and others,
those should be performed with double-folded darbha grasses, especially for the purpose of spreading them out.
Until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the ancestral rites (*pitṛkriyā*) are performed with straight *darbha* grass;
after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, they should be performed according to rule with double the amount of grass.
The mantra for grasping the *kuśa* grass: "O you who were born together with Viriñci, O Supreme Lord, innate to creation! Drive away all evils and be the bringer of well-being to me. [459]
Thus [are the rules for] the *kuśa* grasses. Now, regarding the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*): on this matter, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:

"Having sipped water outside, near a river or similar body of water, being well-restrained and accompanied by water, a wise man—provided he is not of a single caste (i.e., not an outcaste) and is not lacking in vows—should fetch the water for sprinkling."
A wise person should not perform the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) with moss, grass, leaves, and the like; nor with unpurified water vessels, sand, cloth, or [impure] water.

A *śūdra* is of a single birth. The meaning is that one should not sprinkle with water that is mixed with *śaivala* (aquatic moss) and the like, contained in unrefined vessels, or water that has seeped through sandy ground or emerged from beneath clothing. Āpastamba says: "A wise man should not perform sprinkling with a hollow tube, nor with a broken vessel, nor indeed with a bell-metal vessel, nor even with water produced from the hands or body parts."

A *nālikā* is made of bamboo; a "broken vessel" is one made of clay; that which is born from the limbs of a living being refers to conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like; and that which is born from fruit refers to vessels made of coconut, *bilva*, and so forth.

Or, having properly performed the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) at home, a wise man, using water mixed with gold for the sake of purification, should not take up water with a portion of his lower garment.
If it has been brought with the left hand, one should sprinkle it with the right;
the first [sprinkling] is said to be for Agni, and the second from the hand of the Brahmin.
The third is from the water-jar, and the fourth is traditionally taught as being from the water-pot.

That which is contained in a vessel joined with fire is *āgneya*. A water-jar (*maṇika*) is a vessel for water. Having taken these, O wise one, one should go toward the house for the purpose of sprinkling, wearing one's sandals;
having reached the house without removing them, one should sip water from an attendant.
The vessel for sprinkling water should not be placed anywhere until the sipping of water (ācamana) has been offered and the water-dripper (galantikā) has been consecrated with sprinkling (prokṣita).
A *galantikā* is a water-drawing vessel. Viṣṇu states: "One should not perform the *śrāddha* rite with water taken at night. In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Water that is foul-smelling or frothy, as well as water from a pond, should be avoided; likewise, one should not use water where a cow does not find satisfaction, nor that which is taken at night."
Thus ends the sprinkling. Now, regarding the Vaiśvadeva and subsequent rites, Laugākṣi says:
"One should prepare cooked food for the sake of the ancestors and likewise for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva.
The Vaiśvadeva rite is not for the sake of the ancestors, nor is the Darśa rite for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva. [460]

The Vaiśvadeva rite is for the purpose of the sacrifice to the gods; the Darśa-śrāddha is that performed on the new moon day (*darśa*). This [term] is intended as an illustration for all *śrāddhas* in general. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"He who performs the Vaiśvadeva rite after having set aside a separate portion for the ancestral offering (*pitṛpāka*), that *śrāddha* becomes demonic (*āsura*); it does not reach the ancestors."
Laukāxi says: Having completed the rites at the end of the fortnight and the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, one who maintains the sacred fires should then perform the Piṇḍayajña;
thereafter, the wise man should perform the Anvāhāryaka.
The ritual of adding fuel to the sacred fire (*agnyanvādhāna*) occurs at the end of the fortnight. The *darśa-śrāddha* is the *anvāhāryaka*.
However, if the *vaiśvadeva* has not been performed, the *sthālīpāka* is prescribed;
except for the *piṇḍayajña*, that [offering] is ordained for the afternoon.
The meaning is that the Vaiśvadeva rite should be performed prior to the Piṇḍayajña and the Sthālīpāka. However, in the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa, a different sequence is given:
"O mighty-armed one, O lord of men, having performed the Śrāddha and having dismissed the Brāhmaṇas, one should thereafter perform the Vaiśvadeva and other rites."
Likewise: Having gratified the ancestors according to the rule, one should offer the bali-oblation according to the injunction;
then, having performed the recitation by the Brahmins, one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite.
O hero, know that whatever a wise man places upon the ground with the mantra for those consumed by fire is always considered a *bali* offering in the rite of *śrāddha*.

Thus, there are three times for the Vaiśvadeva: one after another cooking, another after the offering of the bali-oblation, and the third after the completion of the śrāddha. Now follows the subsequent procedure. Regarding this, the Purāṇa states:
"In the śrāddha, the ground smeared with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) should be purified with firebrands;
it should be covered with white clay and strewn with sesame and mustard seeds."
Uśanas: "One should perform the purification of the ground, the vessels, and the utensils with cow-dung and water. Devala:

"In that same manner, the donor, being self-restrained, having bathed in the morning and wearing his garments, should begin the preparation of the food with new vessels and in the company of his kinsmen."
[461] One should scatter sesame seeds there and perfume it on all sides with goats;
everything defiled by Asuras is purified by sesame seeds and by the goat.
Then, one should prepare food with many preparations, consisting of various condiments and edibles, and enriched with things to be sucked and drunk, according to one's ability.
Then, when midday has passed, he should approach the twice-born whose hair and nails have been trimmed and provide them with a tooth-stick according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oil, unguents for rubbing the body, bathing water, and various kinds of bath-powders using vessels made of udumbara wood, preceded by the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Then, having bathed and returned, he should rise to meet them with palms joined in reverence and offer water for the feet and water for sipping in the proper order.
Audumbara is copper. Viṣṇu says:
"One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, as well as for purificatory acts, the recitation of prayers, and giving according to the injunctions."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
During recitation, burnt offerings, and fasting, one should always wear clean garments;
at śrāddhas and similar rites, one should be adorned, pure, silent, and have the senses fully subdued.
Pracetas states: "The performer of a śrāddha should wear white garments. Baudhāyana declares the prohibition against wearing saffron-dyed clothing:

"If one performs recitations (japa), burnt offerings (homa), or accepts gifts while wearing saffron robes, that does not reach the gods; likewise, the sacrificial oblation (havis) offered among the offerings to gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) [is ineffective]."
Yogayājñavalkya states: During recitation, fire-offerings, giving, and in rites pertaining to the gods or ancestors, one should not wear a lower garment made of animal hide;
at other times, one may wear it as one desires.
For a girdle tied outside the undergarment is indeed demonic.
Bhṛgu says:
One is naked if one wears soiled clothes; one is naked if one possesses only a loincloth;
likewise, one is naked if one has two arm-straps but no upper garment, or if one lacks the arm-strap entirely and is without clothing.
One who is naked should wear saffron-colored robes; one who is half-clothed is likewise considered naked.
Śātātapa says: A man wearing only a single garment should not eat, nor should he perform the worship of the deities;
nor should he honor the twice-born while naked; a man in such a state should indeed act in this manner.

One should know that he whose garment has somehow slipped from the left shoulder so that his body is partially exposed, being clad in but a single cloth, must be excluded from rites for the gods and the ancestors. —
Vṛddha-Manu.
A wise man should perform his religious rites with cloth washed by himself;
he should never do so with cloth washed by a washerman, nor ever with unwashed cloth.
Kaśyapa says it is "unbeaten" (*ahata*):
"The Self-Existent One has declared that a garment which is free from the loom is called 'unbeaten';
it is recommended for auspicious occasions, but only for that specific time, not at all times."
A *māṅgalikya* garment is one used for weddings and similar auspicious occasions. Regarding other instances, Pracetas states that it is "unbeaten" (*ahata*) if it has been washed only once.
[He further says: "One should know that which is slightly washed, new, white, with its fringes intact, and not yet worn as 'unbeaten' (*ahata*); it is purifying in all ritual acts."

Vyāsa says: That cloth which has its fringes uncut, that which has been washed with clay, and that which is unwashed or dyed with mineral pigments— this is indeed the established rule regarding what is pure.
Śāṭyāyani says:
Then, having worshipped the sun and properly performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he himself,
taking up the sprinkling water and with his mind restrained, should go home.
Wearing sandals, holding darbha grass, carrying a vessel, and possessing a superior garment.

One who possesses an upper garment (*uttarīya*) with its fringe intact is called *sadaśottara*. The "worship of the sun" (*sūryopasthāna*) is intended as an illustration for the *brahmayajña* and other such rites. According to the *Yogayājñavalkya*:
"Having sprinkled the vessels with that water and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) again at home, one should take up with the left hand the water remaining in the vessel."
One should not perform sprinkling with that [water], nor with the water used for washing clothes.
In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
One should not touch anything that has not been sprinkled with water during rites for the gods or for the ancestors.
One should bring [the materials] from the north of the altar and dismiss them from the south.

The *vedi* is the ground for the *śrāddha* rite. Gobhila states: "One should not perform giving, sipping water (*ācamana*), fire-oblation (*homa*), eating, worship of the deities, Vedic study, or libations to the ancestors with one's feet raised."
He who has his feet placed upon a seat, or likewise upon his knees or shanks,
and who has applied ointment to his limbs, is called *prauḍhapāda*.
Baudhāyana says: "One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel. Likewise:

"During both twilights, while reciting prayers, while eating, while cleansing the teeth, during rites for the ancestors (pitr-kārya) and for the gods (daiva), and likewise after voiding urine or excrement—"
In the presence of gurus, especially when giving gifts or practicing yoga, one should maintain silence; by doing so, a human being attains heaven. — *Yogayājñavalkya* [463].
If there should be any lapse in the restraint of speech during the recitation of prayers and the like,
one should utter a Vaiṣṇava mantra or remember the imperishable Viṣṇu.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When six muhūrtas of the day had passed, he then sent each of those twice-born men as messengers for the purpose of bathing in pure water.
Having bathed, he should honor each of the invited guests who have also bathed with a welcome,
as they stand in a secluded place strewn with sesame seeds and sacrificial grass.
In the afternoon, having honored the arrived twice-born with a welcome,
he— holding the purifier (pavitra) in his hand and having offered them water for sipping (ācamana)— should seat them upon their seats.
One should invite an even number of Brahmins for the rite to the gods according to one's ability, and likewise an odd number for the rite to the ancestors;
this should be done in a secluded, pure place that slopes toward the south.
Two [seats] for the gods to the east, but three for the ancestors to the north, or even one for each.

When those invited Brahmins have arrived in the afternoon—that is, in the latter part of the day—and have been honored with words of welcome (*svāgata*) and have sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), he should seat them upon seats in a clean, pure, and enclosed space (enclosed by curtains or similar screens) on a southern plot of ground that slopes gradually downward. For the *daiva* rite (the Vaiśvadeva offering), he should seat an even number according to his capacity, facing east; for the *pitrya* rite (the ancestral offering), he should seat an odd number according to his capacity—or rather, according to the reading "an odd number" (*ayugmān*)—facing north. Alternatively, he may seat only two for the Vaiśvadeva and three for the Pitrya; or else one for each of the two. An "even number" refers to counts such as two, four, and so forth; an "odd number" refers to counts such as one, five, and so forth. This rule for a smaller number applies to one who is unable to provide a large number. As for that which was stated by Manu:
One should feed two at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one at each;
even if very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large assembly.
Hospitality, proper time and place, purity, and the excellence of the Brahmins—these five things are destroyed by prolixity; therefore, one should not seek prolixity.

Thus, this is for the purpose of praising a smaller number and not for the purpose of prohibiting a larger number. If that were the case, a larger number would not be prescribed; yet Gautama prescribes: "One should feed at least nine, or an odd number according to one's capacity. The author of the *Gṛhyasūtra*, Śaunaka, states: "Now, therefore, in the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, the optional (*kāmya*), the *ābhyudayika*, or the *ekoddiṣṭa*, having informed the Brāhmaṇas—who are endowed with learning, good character, conduct, and wealth—either individually or all together at the proper time, and having had them bathe and perform their purifications, one should seat them facing north like the ancestors (the *pitṛs*). One should seat one for each ancestor, two for each, or three for each; in the case of an increase [in the number of ancestors], there is a greater abundance of merit. But one should never seat only one Brāhmaṇa for all [ancestors]. This is explained by the rules regarding the *piṇḍas*. At will, this applies except in the *anādya* [case]. The meaning of this is as follows: In the four types of śrāddhas beginning with the *pārvaṇa*, one should seat Brāhmaṇas endowed with qualities such as learning, or those possessed of even a single quality such as learning, who have been informed and invited at the proper time on the previous day, and who have bathed—whether having returned from studentship (*samāvṛtta*) or having performed a ritual bath (*āpluta*)—and on that day have performed the purification of their feet. They should be like the ancestors, meaning equal in age to the *pitṛs*; the sense is that they are older, older still, or oldest. For the position of each individual ancestor, such as the father, one should seat one Brāhmaṇa, two Brāhmaṇas, or three Brāhmaṇas. By increasing the number of Brāhmaṇas, there is a greater abundance of merit; however, one must not seat only a single Brāhmaṇa for the positions of all the ancestors, such as the father and so forth. "At will, except in the *anādya*" means: the *ādya* is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, and other than that is the *anādya*; or, *ādya* refers to food, and its absence is *anādya*; or, *anādya* refers to raw food (*āmam*). [In the] *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Due to the absence of place, time, or wealth, one may feed each individual at both locations or at either one;
the remaining guests should be fed at another house according to one's means.
"In both cases" means in the rites for the gods (*daiva*) and for the ancestors (*pitrya*). Śaṅkha says:
"Or else, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who purifies the company;
having first presented the food offering (*naivedya*) to the deity, one should afterwards offer it to him."
From the Purāṇa:
"When there is only one Brahmin and a second is not available,
a Brahmin should be appointed for the ancestors, but one should appoint Agni for the gods."
Vasiṣṭha says: Or else, one may feed a single Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas,
who is endowed with learning, good character, and other virtues, and who is free from all inauspicious marks.
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha, how should the rite for the gods (daiva) be performed?
Having set aside a portion of all the food prepared, it should be placed in a vessel.
Having performed [the rites] in a temple of the deities, one should then proceed with the śrāddha;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin).
Bṛhaspati:
If one should feed only a single person at a śrāddha because the rite is small in scale,
one should take small portions from each [of the three] and offer that food to him.

The meaning is that one should mentally set aside a small third portion of the food sufficient for the satisfaction of the Brahmins and offer it to each of those ancestors, beginning with the father. [465]

Regarding the phrase "having worshipped in the afternoon," there is a doubt: does "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) refer to the latter part of the day divided into two parts, or does it refer to the fourth part of the day divided into five? On this point, some say that the afternoon is the fourth part of the day divided into five.
