For thus says the Śruti: "The sun, indeed, is all the seasons: when he rises, it is spring; when it is the time of the cows being gathered (*saṃgava*), it is summer; when it is midday, it is the rainy season; when it is the afternoon, it is autumn; and when he sets, it is winter. Smṛti also [confirms this], as Vyāsa has said:
The morning consists of three muhūrtas, and the saṅgava period is of the same duration;
midday shall consist of three muhūrtas, and the afternoon is likewise.
"The evening consists of three muhūrtas, during which all ritual actions are excluded. Thus it is said.

Therefore, based on such Vedic usage, the fourth division of the day—divided into five parts—is what is denoted by the term *aparāhṇa*. Others do not accept this; for they maintain that a restriction regarding the denotation [of the word] cannot be determined from such usage alone. Indeed, even in the Śruti, the term *aparāhṇa* is employed for other divisions of the day. For example: "The forenoon belongs to the gods, midday to humans, and the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) to the ancestors. Here, indeed, the third part of the day divided into three is used as the denotation of the term *aparāhṇa*. Likewise, in passages such as, "Therefore, one should proceed with the first *upasad* in the very early forenoon, and with the latter in the afternoon (*aparāhṇe*)," there is usage for the final *muhūrta* of the day—that is, the second part of the day when divided into two. As Manu says:
"Just as the latter fortnight excels the former fortnight,
so does the afternoon excel the forenoon for the performance of a śrāddha."

Therefore, it is not established that the term *aparāhṇa* (afternoon) is applied only to the fourth part of a day divided into five parts. And since that is not established, that [fourth part] alone is not what is denoted by the word *aparāhṇa*. For if it were so, then—due to the assumption of being either *yogarūḍha* (conventional based on etymology) or similar to words like *paṅkaja* (lotus), *kuśala* (skilled), or *pravīṇa* (proficient)—in a sentence such as "one should worship in the *aparāhṇa*," only the middle portion of the day would be connected with the meaning of the sentence, just as in the case of the midday and evening portions. But this is not the case. Therefore, by the etymological derivation "the latter part of the day" (*ahno 'paraḥ bhāgaḥ*), this word is purely etymological (*yaugika*). For this very reason, Jābāli states that the *amāvāsyā* Śrāddha should be performed on an *amāvāsyā* that extends through the *kutapa* period.

"But when the new moon day is pierced by the [preceding] lunar day, or when it is mixed with the first day [of the next fortnight], then for the rites for the ancestors, that which occurs during the *kutapa* period of those two days should be accepted. [466]

By this, it is ordained that the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha must be performed during the *kutapa* period; otherwise, the rule for performing [the rite] when the [lunar day] extends across the *kutapa* would be for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, the injunction that the śrāddha prescribed for the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) should be performed during the *kutapa* implies that the *kutapa* is included within the afternoon. Furthermore, the second half of the *kutapa* falls within the afternoon. For the day consists of fifteen *muhūrtas*, and the *kutapa* is the eighth *muhūrta*; thus, its second half constitutes the afternoon. If the afternoon were only the three *muhūrtas* preceding the evening (*sāyāhna*), then the rule "that which occurs at the time of *kutapa* is to be accepted" would set aside the afternoon—which is prescribed as a constant requirement—by prescribing the *kutapa*. And such a setting aside is improper when no contradiction exists. For this very reason, from the prescription of the *kutapa*, it is determined that the term "afternoon" does not apply to the third part of the day. As was stated by Gautama:
Having begun the śrāddha during the Kutapa period, a wise man should perform it until the Rauhina;
one who knows the ritual, adhering to the rule, must not let the Rauhina pass.

This [rule] also refers to *śrāddhas* such as the *kuhv-ādi*, which occupy only the *kutapa* period; it does not, however, refer to an *ekoddiṣṭa* performed on a lunar day (*tithi*) that extends throughout the entire midday. For if that were the case, one would have to postulate an unseen basis (*adṛṣṭa-mūla*) for the injunction regarding the non-transgression of the *rauhiṇa* period, whereas no such basis exists for another rule. For instance, when a *śrāddha* has begun during the *rauhiṇa* portion within the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), even if the lunar day (which is an auxiliary of the *śrāddha*) should expire, the completion of the commenced rite is implied by the injunction and is carried out immediately in the next lunar day. A *śrāddha* begun in the latter half of the *kutapa* and continued into the *rauhiṇa* is completed despite the transgression of the *rauhiṇa* limit due to human error; thus, the traditional rule (*smṛti*) against transgressing the *rauhiṇa* has a visible basis (*dṛṣṭa-mūla*). Therefore, the aforementioned scope alone is appropriate for this statement. As for the fact that Vyāsa and others employ the term "afternoon" (*aparāhṇa*) for the three *muhūrtas* following midday (*madhyandina*), that is because that portion cannot be designated by any other specific term; it is not, however, because that very portion is what is primarily denoted by the word "afternoon. Indeed, its usage is shown to apply to both late afternoon (*sāyāhna*) and the latter part of midday. Now, if the second half of the day is the "afternoon," then whatever is prescribed for the "afternoon" should be performed in the fourth division of the day divided into five parts. As Parāśara says: [text follows].
Whatever is prescribed for these [castes], that a wise man should perform.

The meaning of this is as follows: whatever ritual act—such as bathing, giving gifts, or performing *śrāddha*—is prescribed for times such as the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) and so forth, that should be performed during these five parts of the day consisting of three *muhūrta*s each, beginning with morning (*prātaḥ*). That is not correct; for by this sentence, it is not being restricted that the *śrāddha* prescribed for the afternoon must be performed specifically in the fourth part of the day divided into five. Rather, it restates what is established by propriety: that the *piṇḍānvāhāryaka-śrāddha* should be performed in the three *muhūrta*s following midday. For that [performance] has been stated [in the scriptures]: "It should be done after having performed the *pitṛyajña*; indeed, having completed the *pitṛyajña*. Since this is not a restrictive rule, for that very reason the *Matsyapurāṇa* states [the following] in the section on the *darśa-śrāddha*:
"From one muhūrta after the *kutapa* until four or even five muhūrtas thereafter, the recitation of the *svadhā* is prescribed. [467]

And this [statement] is appropriate only if the statement of Parāśara is non-restrictive (*aniyāmaka*). If, however, it were restrictive (*niyāmaka*), then the muhūrta named Rauhiṇa, which follows the eighth muhūrta named Kutapa, could not be enjoined as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*. For by Parāśara, only the three muhūrtas beginning with the tenth would be restricted, but not the ninth. Thus, if it were restrictive, the injunction that the five muhūrtas—specifically the thirteenth muhūrta, which falls within the late afternoon (*sāyāhna*)—are a constituent part would be untenable. Furthermore, because this [thirteenth muhūrta] falls within the fourth watch of the day, its status as a constituent part of the *śrāddha* is prohibited. Accordingly, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
If a man performs a śrāddha when the fourth watch of the day has arrived,
that śrāddha becomes asuric, and the giver shall go to hell.

For this very reason, because it is both prescribed and prohibited, an option (*vikalpa*) is stated: "or five *muhūrtas*. And this [option] is fixed (*vyavasthita*). When, prior to the fourth watch of the day, the lunar day (*tithi*) that serves as the constituent part of the *śrāddha* for the new moon and so forth is capable of accomplishing the entire performance of the *śrāddha*, then there is a prohibition; if not, then there is the injunction. Vyāghrapāt clarifies the lack of restriction in the views of Parāśara and Vasiṣṭha: "One who knows the rules, is endowed with faith, and properly employs worthy recipients, attains unsurpassed excellence by performing [the rite] at any time other than during the night."

Precisely because the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) is the second half of the day, it is heard in the *Bahvṛca-Brāhmaṇa*: "He says, 'The Āhavanīya fire is to be drawn out,' during the afternoon. For this very reason, the *Āśvalāyana-Sūtra* states: "At the time of the *utsarga*, having kindled the Gārhapatya fire in the afternoon," and so forth. Since the drawing out of the fire (*uddharaṇa*) is an ancillary (*aṅga*) to the Agnihotra prescribed for the evening, it must be performed in the evening itself, according to the rule: "The time [of the primary] is indeed the quality (*guṇa*) of that [ancillary]. Therefore, this term "afternoon" refers specifically to the evening (*sāyāhna*). Consequently, it is established that the afternoon is the second part of the day divided into two. In that regard, when performing a *śrāddha* on any day other than the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), this rite should be performed during the first portion of the afternoon, as there is no reason for delay. On the new moon day, however, it should be performed at whichever portion of the afternoon coincides with the new moon, in accordance with the requirements of the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Pitṛyajña. But for annual (*sāṃvatsara*) and other such *śrāddhas*, it may be performed at any point within the afternoon that is joined with the specific *śrāddha* lunar day. If that [lunar day] should extend only through the evening (*sāyāhna*), then the *śrāddha* must be performed during the evening itself by the force of the statement of Vyāghrapād; it is not to be performed when [the lunar day] extends until the end of the afternoon while beginning at sunrise. Thus, another Smṛti text says:

"One who does not perform the *darśa* (new moon), the *paurṇamāsa* (full moon), and the father’s annual anniversary (*sāṃvatsara*) when they are overlapped by the preceding day, falls into hell. In this passage, the mention of "the new moon," "at sunset," and "of the father" is for the sake of illustration. As for the statement that "it should be accepted at the time of *kutapa*," it should be understood as prescribing a specific time for the *amāvāsyā* śrāddha of one who maintains no sacred fires (*anagni*), and not for other types of śrāddhas. Regarding a particular type of śrāddha, Śātātapa states another time distinct from the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*).

"The *āmaśrāddha* is in the forenoon, the *ekoddiṣṭa* at midday, the *pārvaṇa* in the afternoon, and that occasioned by prosperity (*vṛddhinimittaka*) in the morning. Here, the *āmaśrāddha* for the twice-born (*dvija*) is non-obligatory (*anitya*), as it is prescribed on the occasion of their inability to prepare cooked food (*pāka*). For a *śūdra*, however, it is obligatory (*nitya*) since it occurs regardless of such an occasion. In this regard, this rule prescribing the forenoon does not apply to either type of *āmaśrāddha*, due to the contradiction of joining what is obligatory with what is non-obligatory. In that context, the rules for the *āmaśrāddha* of the twice-born are cited; among them, Saṃvarta says:
O mighty-armed one, it is declared that the entitlement of the twice-born to perform the fire-sacrifice exists even in the absence of their wives, due to such circumstances as traveling abroad.
And the wise know that for Śūdras, the funeral rite (śrāddha) should always consist of uncooked food.
Uśanas says: When a disturbance of place or time has arisen for oneself,
the twice-born should perform an *āma-śrāddha* (a rite with raw food), whereas a *śūdra* may do so at all times.
Pracetas says:

In times of distress, when there is no fire, at a sacred ford (tīrtha), and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun, the twice-born (dvijas) should perform the *āmaśrāddha*; indeed, it should always be performed by Śūdras.
When there is an inability to cook at a sacred site (tīrtha), during an eclipse of the moon or sun, in the absence of an eater,
or during the birth-rite (jātakarman) for a woman, a Śūdra, or a Svapaca,
one should then perform an Āmaśrāddha according to the Pārvaṇa rite.
One who cooks for himself or one who cooks by himself— such as Jamadagni— whether the fire has ceased to be joined with fuel or has even been extinguished,
he should always perform the *āmaśrāddha* (a śrāddha with raw food); the *agnaukaraṇa* (the ritual offering into the fire) shall take place in his hand.
Hārīta says: "In the event of an obstacle to a Śrāddha for the twice-born, an Āmaśrāddha (a rite with raw food) is prescribed;
this applies to obligatory rites such as those on the new moon day, except for those performed monthly or annually."

The meaning is that this rule applies with the exception of the monthly (*māsika*) and annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) *śrāddha*. This prohibition of the monthly and annual *śrāddha* performed with raw grain (*āmānnāśrāddha*) refers to occasions other than an eclipse. The implication is that when there is a lunar or solar eclipse, the monthly and annual *śrāddha* must be performed with raw grain alone. Through such statements, a specific procedure for the performance of the *śrāddha* using raw grain is prescribed as an occasional (*naimittika*) rite to restore eligibility when the right to perform the rite has been suspended due to an inability to prepare cooked food. Now, one might ask: why is a specific occasional procedure not likewise prescribed on the basis of being a Śūdra—as in the statement, "A Śūdra should indeed always perform it"—just as in the previous case? It is replied: since the Śūdra is already established by the rule "there is no *śrāddha* for a Śūdra," he would merely be restated (*anuvādya*) rather than something newly enjoined (*vidheya*). For instance, feeding Brāhmaṇas is prohibited for a Śūdra. As Sumantu says: [He continues: "The Śūdra is not entitled to the *śrāddha*, nor to the *tarpaṇa*, nor to the *pārvaṇa*. He may, however, perform the *śrāddha* with raw grain, provided he does not feed Brāhmaṇas. Thus, the Śūdra’s entitlement is restricted to the *śrāddha* with raw grain alone; therefore, the aforementioned rule regarding the suspension of eligibility based on the inability to cook food is what is intended here. Furthermore, the term "always" (*sadaiva*) in the verse "A Śūdra should always perform it" is used to indicate that the Śūdra is permitted to perform the *śrāddha* at all times, even during forbidden periods such as the *parvan* days or the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites. It does not mean that he must perform it constantly. Consequently, the occasional nature of the rite is established through the suspension of eligibility caused by the inability to provide cooked food. Thus, the occasional character of the procedure is determined by the context of the suspension of the primary entitlement. Therefore, the occasional rule is established precisely as described above. Even a Śūdra of good conduct should never feed Brāhmaṇas with uncooked food;
by feeding them thus, he incurs sin and shall obtain no fruit from his deed.
"For whatever sin may accrue to a wicked-minded Brahmin from eating [the food of a Śūdra], by that the fool who, being a Śūdra, feeds the twice-born is defiled. Thus it is said.

It should not be argued that in this context, only the feeding of Brahmins for the sake of personal pleasure (*saṃprīti*) and the like is prohibited, but not that which is prescribed by law (*vaidha*). For the supplementary statement, "He does not obtain the fruit thereof," is appropriate only in reference to the feeding of Brahmins as prescribed by law. Furthermore, it cannot be said that this prohibition does not concern the feeding of Brahmins who serve as the condition (*upādhi*) for the *śrāddha*, because there is no reason [for such a claim]. Moreover, when the feeding of Brahmins is prohibited, the very eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the *śrāddha* is undermined. This is because the ritual manuals on *śrāddha* (*śrāddhakalpa*) show injunctions regarding the invitation of Brahmins and so forth; likewise, they show injunctions such as "one should cook the sacrificial food (*havis*)," "one should bring it to the *śrāddha* site," "one should serve it," and "one should feed the Brahmins. From these injunctions, it is determined that the *śrāddha*-sacrifice culminates in the form of the feeding of Brahmins as its constituent condition. Nor can it be argued that an obstruction to the capacity to produce the condition occurs in the conditioned act itself, for in that case there would be no obstruction to the capacity [of the act]. As for what is stated by those learned in logic—that even in the *abhyuditeṣṭi* sacrifice, the *upāṃśuyāja* (the silent offering) is to be performed even though it lacks the dedication to a deity—that is indeed correct. For it is not a cognition of eligibility (*adhikārabuddhi*) that prompts the performance of the *abhyuditeṣṭi*, but rather a delusion of eligibility (*adhikārabhrama*). Indeed, due to the error regarding the prescribed time, a delusion of eligibility concerning another time is produced there. Therefore, even in the absence of the capacity for the dedication to a deity—which serves as the condition—the performance of the *upāṃśuyāja* is not improper. For in that case, the performance prompted by the delusion of eligibility is precisely what constitutes the cause for the completion of that modified (*vikṛta*) rite. Thus, the completion of the performance of the *upāṃśuyāja*—even though it lacks the dedication to a deity—once it has been commenced as a contingent rite (*naimittika*) upon the occurrence of the contingency, is justified by the force of the scriptural statement. In the *śrāddha*, however, it is not a delusion of eligibility that is the cause for performance, but rather the failure of that [eligibility]. Consequently, when there is an obstruction to the capacity to perform the primary rite consisting of the *śrāddha* as conditioned by the feeding of Brahmins, the Śūdra’s eligibility is destroyed. Nor should it be argued that the Śūdra is simply ineligible for the *śrāddha*; for... [text continues]
Delighting in his wife, pure, a supporter of his dependents, and devoted to the performance of ancestral rites. [470]

By such statements, the *śrāddha* is prescribed for the Śūdra by way of direct injunction (*śṛṅgagrāhitayā*). Consequently, since the *śrāddha* exists for the Śūdra along with all its constituent conditions (*upādhi*), the injunction, being in close proximity to that very rite, applies itself even to the *śrāddha*. In this context, for the sake of favoring the prohibition against feeding Brāhmaṇas, the *śrāddha* performed by the twice-born (*dvijāti*) does not directly employ the feeding of Brāhmaṇas; yet, it certainly employs it through an indirect channel (*praṇāḍyā*). Indeed, otherwise, it would be impossible to effect a lack of contradiction between the injunction and the prohibition regarding the feeding of Brāhmaṇas as they apply to the Śūdra. Furthermore, it is possible to effect the feeding of Brāhmaṇas indirectly by means of a request: "Having set aside this raw food (*āmanna*) intended for the ancestors, you may eat it," which the Śūdra makes toward the Brāhmaṇas. This being the case, the *āma-śrāddha* (raw-food *śrāddha*) obtained by the Śūdra independently of any specific occasion (*nimitta*) is restated (*anūdyate*) by such texts as: "The Śūdra should indeed always perform [it]. Now, one might object: "If the twice-born are likewise unable to cook the sacrificial oblation (*havir*) or feed the Brāhmaṇas, then—just like the Śūdra—the performance of the *śrāddha* with raw food, independent of any occasion, would constitute their entitlement (*adhikāra*) in the absence of cooked food. This is true, provided that the twice-born lack the capacity for the direct feeding of Brāhmaṇas as required by the injunction's propriety when performing the constituent parts (*aṅga*) such as cooking exactly as prescribed. And if there is no capacity for those parts, there is likewise no capacity for the primary act (*pradhāna*) of the *śrāddha* itself. When such a failure of entitlement (*adhikāra-bhaṅga*) occurs, a specific occasional (*naimittika*) performance of the *śrāddha* achievable through raw materials is enjoined for the sake of subsistence. This being so, it is impossible to designate the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) for both the permanent (*nitya*) *āma-śrāddha* performed by the Śūdra and the occasional (*anitya*) one performed by the twice-born, due to the contradiction of joining the permanent and the occasional. In that regard, it cannot be enjoined for the permanent rite, because that would lead to an undesirable option (*vikalpa*) with the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) prescribed by the original instruction (*aupadeśika*). However, the *āma-śrāddha* performed by the twice-born is a modification (*vikṛti*) because it is occasional. In that case, the afternoon is obtained through extension (*atideśika*), while the forenoon is obtained through the original instruction. There can be no option between what is obtained by extension and what is obtained by direct instruction; therefore, the injunction for the forenoon applies only there (in the case of the twice-born), and not to the *āma-śrāddha* performed by the Śūdra. Rather, in that case (for the Śūdra), only the afternoon injunction applies. For this very reason, this statement of Śātātapa is [consistent]: [Text follows...]
That period which is declared as Kutapa after midday—
whatever is given to the ancestors at that very time, even with mere uncooked food, becomes inexhaustible.

Thus, this refers to the *śūdra* subject; moreover, it is merely a restatement (*anuvādaka*), because the afternoon time is already established for the *āmaśrāddha* of a *śūdra* by the general instruction regarding the afternoon. Therefore, it is established that the *āmaśrāddha* performed by a *śūdra* must be conducted specifically in the afternoon.
Incidentally, some rules for the *āmaśrāddha* are recorded here. Regarding this, Vyāsa says:
"O son of Kuntī, one giving raw food (*āma*) should indeed give four times as much cooked food (*anna*)."
Whatever procedure applies to a śrāddha with cooked food, that same procedure applies to a śrāddha with uncooked food.
O Bhārata, all rites beginning with the invocation, as well as the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), should be performed;
and one should give to the twice-born either cooked food or uncooked food.
With that [uncooked food], one should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite and offer the rice balls (*piṇḍas*) with that very same substance.

In this context, the fourfold increase [of the offerings] is relative to the amount of food required for a man; the extension of the rule beginning with "with cooked food" (*siddhānnena*) and so forth applies specifically to the *āmaśrāddha* (funeral rite with uncooked food) for the twice-born, according to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"When one performs an *āmaśrāddha*, how should the offering of the rice balls be performed?"
Having taken [a portion] from the household cooking, [he should offer it] with roasted flour or with milk-rice.

The phrase "the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) should take place" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Likewise: "When the knower of the rules performs an *āmaśrāddha*, the giver of the śrāddha should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite in the hand of the Brāhmaṇa according to the injunction."
In the *āmaśrāddha* (the rite with raw food), there is an omission of those acts connected with eating, such as the inquiry regarding satisfaction (*tṛpti*).
Thus, the *śrāddha* should always be performed by a Śūdra using only raw food;
all of this is prescribed for the Śūdra, but excluding the sacred mantras (*mantra*).
From the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa:
"If Śūdras, desiring merit and knowing the dharma, perform [the rites],
the mantra for the *agnaukaraṇa* is prescribed as a simple salutation (*namaskāra*)."
Vyāsa speaks regarding the *hemaśrāddha* (gold śrāddha) for one who is unable to perform the *āmaśrāddha* (raw-food śrāddha):
"In the absence of materials, in the absence of twice-born [guests], during travel, upon the birth of a son,
or when one's wife is in her menses, one should perform the *hemaśrāddha*."
In this context, "substance" (dravya) refers to the food intended for consumption, and the "twice-born" (dvija) is the eater. Manu says:
"One should smear a clean and secluded place with cow dung, and one should diligently ensure that it slopes toward the south."
"Secluded" means uninhabited. Even for a clean place, the smearing with cow dung should be performed according to the injunction to ensure an excellence of refinement. Likewise:
"The ancestors are always satisfied by what is given in open spaces, on pure riverbanks, and indeed in secluded places."
The *cokṣas* are those pure by nature. Regarding Yama:
"If one should perform the ancestral offering (*nirvapet*) in places belonging to others, the *śrāddha* rite is obstructed by the ancestors of the owner of that land."
Forests, sacred mountains, and whatever riverbanks there may be—
all these are said to be without an owner, for in them there is no private possession.
Therefore,
one should diligently offer funeral oblations at sacred sites, on the banks of rivers, at holy fords, and upon auspicious ground.

In the slopes and thickets, as well as on the mountain ridges—[472] "slope" (*upahvara*) refers to the vicinity of a mountain; "thicket" (*nikuñja*) refers to a cave. [Ground that is] harsh, infested with worms, damp, crowded, and foul-smelling.
Furthermore, one should avoid a place that has an unpleasant sound during the performance of a śrāddha rite.

Rūkṣa means dry and lacking oiliness; klinna means muddy with mire; aniṣṭaśabda means having unpleasant or painful sounds. [One should not perform a śrāddha] at a conch-shell [sound], nor in a land of barbarians (mleccha), nor at night, and especially not during the twilight (saṃdhyā).
A wise man should not perform a śrāddha [in such places], nor should he go to a land of barbarians.
The *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states: "To the north of the river Manā and to the south of Kīkaṭa— this region,
known as Traiśaṅkava, is excluded from the rite of *śrāddha*."
The Pāraskaras, the Kaliṅgas, and those regions north of the Indus—
these lands, where the performance of śrāddha rites has perished, should be avoided with great effort.
One should not perform the libation for the ancestors on the backs of elephants, oxen, horses, and the like, nor on artificial ground, even in times of dire distress.
Now, those who are to be avoided: regarding this, Yama says— The cock, the village pig, the crow, the dog, and the cat;
the husband of a low-caste woman, the low-caste man himself, the eunuch, and a menstruating woman.
These, indeed, must be diligently avoided at the time of a śrāddha ceremony. Manu says:
"The Caṇḍāla, the boar, the cock, and likewise the dog..."
Neither a menstruating woman nor a eunuch should look at twice-born men while they are eating.
Whatever is looked upon by these when giving a house or at a meal,
whether in a rite for the gods or in a rite for the ancestors— whatever is looked upon by them.
In rites for the gods or for the ancestors, that [offering] goes to its destination improperly.
The pig destroys by means of its sense of smell, the cock by its flapping of wings,
the dog by the casting of its gaze, and one born of the lowest caste by physical touch.
Whether he be of low caste, a Śūdra, lame, or even one-eyed, or if he be the servant of the donor,
or one with deficient or redundant limbs— one should remove him from there as well.
One who is lame, one who is crippled, Devala,
one who is loathsome, impure, naked, intoxicated, a rogue, a woman in her menses,
one wearing blue or saffron garments, and one with severed ears— one should avoid these.
One should avoid weapons, iron, lead, those dressed in soiled garments,
and even stale food at śrāddha ceremonies.
Whether at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors, if even a woman who drinks liquor should touch the sacrificial ground,
or one who is menstruating, or an unchaste woman, then the Rakshasas indeed take possession of it.
Vyāsa states: When the time for the funeral offering has arrived, one should exclude the Caṇḍāla and the Śvapaca;
likewise, one who wears saffron robes, a leper, an outcast, or even a killer of an embryo.
A Brahmin of mixed birth and one who is a relative of an outcast—
these must be avoided by the wise even when the time for the funeral rites has arrived.

*Nirvāpa* refers to the *śrāddha* rite. One of mixed origin includes the *kṣetraja* son and others. Because of the word "present" (*upasthita*), these persons are to be avoided from the commencement of the rite onwards.

"A drinker of intoxicants, an unchaste woman, and likewise one whose husband has been previously taken by another—these should never look upon the *śrāddha* from the time of the pouring of the water oblation (*āvāpa*) onwards."
*Āvāpa* refers to the commencement of the *śrāddha*. In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Naked persons and others should never look upon this *śrāddha*;
for if they see it, the fathers and grandfathers depart."
Since the Triple Veda is the covering for all beings,
those fools who indeed abandon it are remembered as the naked ones and the like.
One should avoid at sight both the robber and the cruel man;
one should avoid all others who perform evil deeds.
A *dasyu* is a thief; a *nṛśaṃsa* is one who is cruel. Regarding the vital breath as Vāyu:

that man who wears matted hair in vain, who is shaven in vain, and who is naked in vain—those men who are perpetrators of great sins (*mahāpātakin*) are indeed the ones referred to as "the naked" and so forth.
If these [outcastes] should indeed cook food for offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya),
that food must be discarded for the sake of the primary purpose, or else it must undergo purification as prescribed by tradition.

It should be discarded or abandoned; however, in times of distress, it may be consecrated for the sake of the primary rite consisting of the *śrāddha*. And the consecration is described in the *Brahma-purāṇa*:
"But for sacrificial offerings that have already been prepared, their disposal is prescribed beforehand;
furthermore, sprinkling with water mixed with clay is enjoined."
One should also perform the scattering of *siddhārthaka* (white mustard seeds) and black sesame seeds,
and one should diligently seek the sight of a preceptor, the sun, fire, and sacred objects.

The *avaparjana*—the discarding or abandonment—of cooked sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*) that have been looked upon by dogs and the like is the first [rule]. [474] However, in times of distress, the sacrificial offerings may be used after performing the purification (*saṃskāra*) beginning with "with water mixed with clay," and so forth; thus they become acceptable. Regarding this, the *Brahma Purāṇa* states:
"The ascetic (*yati*) carries a triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), possesses compassion, and likewise uses a silver vessel."
A daughter's son, the Kutapa period, a black goat, and likewise a black antelope skin.
The eighth muhūrta of the day is the time known as *kutapa*. Furthermore, there are three kinds of sesame seeds— white, black, and wild—
and these ten were created by Brahmā himself for the satisfaction of the ancestors.
An offering given with *darbha* grass, mantras, sesame seeds, and gold or silver—even without water—destroys the *rakṣasas*; therefore, one should not give it alone.

The meaning is that what is given without *darbha* grass and so forth, or without water, is taken away by *rakṣas* demons; or rather, they take away even the water alone if it is given devoid of *darbha*, mantras, and the like. Manu says:

"The afternoon, as well as *darbha* grass, the preparation of the site, sesame seeds, abundance, purification, and eminent twice-born men—these are the perfections in the performance of *śrāddha* rites."
*Sṛṣṭi* means abundance; *mṛṣṭi* means deliciousness. Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds.
And three things they praise here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
Devala says: Darbha grass, sesame seeds, the shadow of an elephant, a daughter’s son, honey and clarified butter,
a woolen blanket (kutapa), and blue sapphire— these are the purifiers in rites for the ancestors.

A blue-colored vessel and a blue bull [are the offerings]. From another Smṛti: "The offspring of a daughter, as well as a rhinoceros-horn vessel, ghee from a Kapilā cow, and the daughter's son (dauhitra)—these are proclaimed [as the five]."

[A daughter’s son is to be honored at a *śrāddha* only in matters such as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), but not in the capacity of being the performer of the *śrāddha*. On this point, the definitive ruling is to be taken from the *Manusmṛti*. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"The daughter’s son is like the horn of a rhinoceros; that which is called the forehead is his [the horn's] tip.
That vessel which belongs to that horn is celebrated as the 'daughter’s son' (*dauhitra*)."
[This concludes the section on] mindfulness.
A Brahmin, a woolen blanket, cows, the sun, fire, and likewise the lunar day, sesame seeds, *darbha* grass, and time—these nine are traditionally known as *kutapa*. [475]
And from the Matsyas: the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), water, sesame seeds, the left side of the body, barley, wild rice,
mung beans, white flowers, and clarified butter.
These are always dear and praiseworthy for the ancestors here in this world.
Āpastamba says: Those sesame seeds that grow wild in the forest, ripening without being ploughed—they alone are pure for the *śrāddha*; those [cultivated] are not sesame, they are not sesame.
The meaning is that village-grown sesame seeds do not perform the function of [sacrificial] sesame. From the Purāṇa:
"Large udumbara fruits, garments, silver, and even a sword, as well as fruits and sacrificial fuel, are great purifiers at a śrāddha."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "The proximity to, the sight of, and the gift of a black antelope skin destroy demons, bestow Vedic luster, and grant cattle and sons."
Manu says: One should diligently feed even a daughter's son who is observing a vow at a Śrāddha;
one should provide him with a Kutapa blanket as a seat and scatter sesame seeds upon the ground.
*Kutapa* here refers to a woolen blanket (*kambala*). The *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
"He should slowly bring from the south, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), a water-pot, a bronze vessel, a stirring-stick, sacrificial fuel, and *kuśa* grass."
Having thus obtained all of that, on the ground in front of the house,
one should prepare a mandala smeared with cow dung and cow urine.
Having honored him with unbroken grains and flowers, he should offer water for washing;
then, repeatedly expressing his joy, he should wash the feet of the Brahmins.
Another Smṛti states:
"Two mandalas should be made sloping toward the south.
On the northern one, one should place kuśa grass, uncut and with their tips pointing eastward."
To the south, the twice-born should place [the offerings] with their tips pointing southward, together with sesame seeds.
Śambhu says: Having swept and smeared the ground, one should prepare two mandalas at the door;
the northern one should slope toward the north, and the southern one should slope toward the south.
In the *Brahmanirukti*:

"One should first cause the water for the feet (*pādya*) and likewise the water of honor (*arghya*) to be offered to the deities. One should cause the water for the feet to be offered with the mantra beginning 'śaṃ no devī'."

Āmbarīṣa, Sindhudvīpa, and the Ṛṣi; the Waters are the deity; Gāyatrī is the meter. [476] Yama himself should perform the washing of the feet with humility; then, saying "Success! (Siddhi), he should [sit] upon the prepared seats.
He should say to them, "Be seated," even while touching the seat;
and by engaging in conversations concerning the Veda, he fulfills this desire of the ancestors.

After washing their feet, he should address the Brahmins, saying, "May you declare the success of the Śrāddha rite," and then, touching the seat with the words "Be seated" (*samādhvam*), he should cause them to sit; this is the meaning. Regarding the ritual duty: having first caused the gods to sit and then the ancestors, he should cause them to be seated upon their seats while reciting all the *vyāhṛtis* together.
The *vyāhṛtis* are recited only at the time of seating the Brahmins representing the ancestors. Manu says: "One should first present the offering to the gods as a protection for them;
for the *rākṣasas* plunder a *śrāddha* that is devoid of protection."

"Guarding" means protection; this is another traditional teaching (*smṛtyantara*). One should say to them, "Be seated," even while merely touching the seat. When seats have been spread out, they should sit down, but they should not touch one another.

The command "Be seated" (*āsyatām*) is an alternative to "Sit yourselves" (*svadhvam*). Viṣṇu states: "One should have them sit upon seats covered with *kuśa* grass according to the order of seniority based on age;
however, for those superior in learning and austerity, the first seat is prescribed."
But for those distinguished guests seated in the eastern row, the food, including its fragrance and other qualities, should be equal.
Hārīta says:
When worthy persons are present, he who is unworthy yet occupies the seat of honor takes on the impurity of the row and is deprived of his life-span.
A Brāhmaṇa who creates an obstacle destroys the fourfold sin of the one who desires food,
the Lord of Food, and the row of diners.
The root *han* here has the sense of "going" (*gati*). The meaning is that one should exclude them and take [the others] for oneself. Gārgya says:
"Sin would accrue at every touch in the act of seating [them] in a single row;
therefore, discrimination is appropriate regarding rows containing those of low conduct and the like."
Bṛhaspati:
Those who sit in a single row and do not touch one another,
having established a boundary with ashes— among them there shall be no confusion of castes.
"By means of fire, or ashes, or even by a pillar, or by water,
or even by the shifting of the doorway— this is proclaimed as a breach of the row," says Pracetās. [477]
There he should place kusha grass cut once together with their roots,
barley, sesame seeds, a seat (brisi), a bronze vessel, and water, all of which have been brought by himself.
The vessels should be made of leaves, silver, or copper;
there should be sacrificial fuel, honey, flowers, incense, fragrant scents, a linen thread, and an alms-bowl.

Viṣṇu states: "The kutapa, the black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard, and unbroken grains are purifiers and destroyers of demons. The meaning is that one should sprinkle these [substances] [upon the site]. (1.226, 227)
Regarding the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather, he states the extension [of the rules] and the optionality of the *vaiśvadeva* ritual:
"The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; or else, the *vaiśvadeva* ritual may be performed as a single common procedure (*tantra*). (1.228)

The *śrāddha* for maternal grandfathers should also be performed in this same manner as the *śrāddha* for paternal ancestors. Regarding the feeding of the *vaiśvadeva* Brahmins, since it would logically follow that they should be invited separately for each *śrāddha*, this statement—"the *vaiśvadeva* rite may be performed as a single unit (*tantra*)"—is intended to provide an option. The specific arrangement here depends on one's capacity. For this very reason, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha says: "One who intends to perform two *śrāddhas* should invite ten, or four, or three Brahmins, or even a single knower of the Veda."

In this regard, the number ten is stated by relying on the position that there should be two for the gods (*daiva*) and three for the ancestral rite (*pitṛkṛtya*), as well as the alternative position regarding the division of the *vaiśvadeva* offerings. According to the position that there should be only one for each, the number four is stated. Within this very *vaiśvadeva* ritual framework, the number three is mentioned. Furthermore, in times of extreme distress, it is stated that there should be only one. Yājñavalkya says: "Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), having recited a Vaiṣṇava mantra, the Gāyatrī, and the Praṇava, one should then commence the Śrāddha."
With a concentrated mind, he should ask the Brahmins, "I shall perform the śrāddha. When they reply, "Do so," he should then offer seats of darbha grass.
Kātyāyana states: "In all inquiries, he asks the head of the row, or he asks everyone. The Brahmapurāṇa states:
Having sat down, the wise one should, with her permission, recite the Gāyatrī mantra,
which removes sins, is purifying, and likewise yields the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Therefore, I shall declare the mantra, the nectar fashioned by Brahmā,
for the sake of the deities, the ancestors, and the great yogis.
"Salutation to Svadhā, svāhā to Svāhā; may this always be so here. One should always recite this three times at the beginning and the end of the Śrāddha."
One should also recite this with a concentrated mind during the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa);
having heard this being recited when the time for the śrāddha ceremony has arrived.
The ancestors arrive quickly, and the Rākṣasas flee.

In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*: "There, the knower of dharma should scatter white mustard seeds on the ground for the warding off of obstructive spirits (*rakṣas*), and in all directions he should scatter sesame seeds with this mantra."
Oṃ! I destroy everything that is impure, as well as all the *dhātās*, *asuras*, and *dānavas*.
The *rākṣasas*, *yakṣas*, along with the *piśācas* and *guhyakas*, and all the *yātudhānas* have been slain by me.
With this mantra, one whose self is well-restrained should scatter sesame seeds in the cardinal directions as well as in the intermediate directions.

The traditional text (*nigama*) states: "One should scatter sesame seeds [with the mantra] 'Struck down are the Asuras and Rākṣasas'. This sacrifice (*yajña*) belongs to the Asuras; it was seen by Prajāpati Parameṣṭhin. 1.228.
Having provided water for washing the hands and also *kuśa* grass for the seats, he should, being authorized, invoke [the ancestors] with the verse beginning "O Viśvedevas... (RV 7.35.1).

Having given water for washing the hands into their hands, and having given *kuśa* grass for seats (*viṣṭara*) into their hands, and being authorized by the Brahmins invited for the *vaiśvadeva* rite, he should invoke the Viśvedevas with the verse "O Viśvedevas, come! (*viśve devāsa āgata*), which belongs to the *vaiśvadeva* [group], is in the *gāyatrī* meter, and was seen by Prajāpati. Because of the expression "being authorized," it is established by implication that there must be a request for authorization, saying "I shall invoke the Viśvedevas," and the granting of authorization, saying "Invoke them. Furthermore, at the end of this mantra, one should say during the recitation: "The gods named Purūravas and Ārdrava, come! However, in other *śrāddha* rites, the names are different. As Bṛhaspati has said:
In the *iṣṭi-śrāddha*, Kratu and Dakṣa; in the *nāndīmukha*, Satya and Vasu; in the *naimittika*, Kāla and Kāma; and in the *kāmya*, Dhuni and Rocana.
Purūravas and Āyus are likewise proclaimed in the Pāvaṇa; those twice-born ones who do not know their origin and names [are deficient].
This verse should be recited by those endowed with faith:
"May the illustrious Viśvedevas of great power come hither!"
May those who have been appointed to this śrāddha ceremony remain attentive.
The preceptors say: one should provide *darbha* grass for the seat, but never upon the hand;
in this way, there shall be eternal satisfaction for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings.
[479] For the rite for the gods, however, straight darbha grass should be offered individually;
and they should take up those kuśa blades with the mantra: "Thou art Dharma."
Bṛhaspati says: Having arranged straight darbha grasses with the left hand for the rite of the gods (daiva), one should offer them turned clockwise;
for the rite of the ancestors (pitrya), one should offer them doubled with the right hand (apasavya) in the manner of the apasavya rite.

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin), he places darbha grass to the south of the seat for the deities; it is established that on the other side, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he places them to the west. Baudhāyana says: "For the deities, it is clockwise; for the ancestors, it is counter-clockwise.
For the deities, the darbha grass is mixed with barley; for the ancestors, it is doubled and mixed with sesame seeds."

The circumambulation is clockwise (pradakṣiṇa) when directed toward the north, and counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇa) when directed toward the east. The doubling of the *darbha* grass should be performed until they are bent. As Śaunaka says: "Having offered water and having placed on the seat double-folded, bent *darbha* blades. Śātātapa states:
"Facing north for the gods and facing south for the ancestors, one should offer [the oblation] in the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha according to the rule, beginning with the rites for the gods."
Bṛhaspati: At the time of sitting, the offering of water for the feet (arghya), the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and the ritual washing (avanejana),
one should announce the relationship, the lineage (gotra), and the name as is appropriate.
Kātyāyana says:
One should always bend the right knee when attending upon the gods;
one should always bend the other knee when attending upon the ancestors.

Having spread darbha grass upon the seats, he asks, "Shall I invoke the Viśvedevas? Being permitted with the words, "Invoke them," he invokes them with "O Viśvedevas, come hither! Having recited "O Viśvedevas, hear this," he performs the scattering of unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) with the verse "The plants... (RV 10.97.1). 1.229.
Then, having scattered barley grains over a vessel containing a purifier (*pavitra*),
he should pour water while reciting *śaṃ no devīḥ*, and likewise scatter barley grains while reciting *yavo 'si*.
One should pour the *arghya* water into their hands with the mantra beginning "yā divyā."

Having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*), one should scatter barley grains into two vessels containing *pavitra* grass; having cast the barley into the two vessels, one should pour water into both vessels with the verse beginning "śaṃ no devīḥ. Then, having thrown barley into the water with the *yajus* formula "yavo 'si," one should, with the mantra "yā divyāḥ," place the *arghya* water contained in one vessel into the hands of the Vaiśvadeva Brāhmaṇas, and the water from the other vessel into the hands of the second Brāhmaṇa. For each offering of *arghya*, the mantra is repeated. Likewise, for the pouring of the water and the throwing of the barley, the mantra is repeated. [480] Prajāpati.
A wise person should fill with water for the *arghya* offering a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, iron, or even crystal, or likewise a sacrificial cup (*camasa*).

Kātyāyana says: A *pavitra* (purifier) should be known wherever it may be used as being made of *kauśa* grass, without an inner core, with its tips intact, consisting of two blades, and measuring one *prādeśa* in length.
The *Yogayājñavalkya* states:
"With the mantra 'pavitre sthaḥ' (you two are purifiers), one should prepare two purifiers (*pavitra*),
which are made of *kuśa* grass, covered within by [other] *kuśa*, made of *kauśa* fiber, and measuring a span (*prādeśa*) in length."
Yajñapārśva says:
Having placed herbs between the thumb and the finger-joint, one should cut the *pavitra*— which is a span in length and has Viṣṇu as its deity— to the measure of a *prādeśa*.
Not with the fingernail, nor with wood, nor with iron, nor from an earthen vessel.
According to the Caturviṃśatimata:
having placed two sticks each in the vessels of the gods, one should pour water [into them] with the mantra "śaṃ no devīḥ"; then one should also pour barley-grains with the mantra "yavo 'si."

Having performed worship with flowers, incense, and other offerings upon the leaves, a person should place sesame seeds into the vessel for the ancestors with the mantra "Tilo 'si" (Thou art sesame). In the *pārvaṇa* rite, however, one should place three stalks of grass into each of the vessels for the ancestors.
In an Ekoddiṣṭa rite, having placed a single blade of grass, one should pour out water.
The *śalākā* is the tip of a *darbha* blade. The wise man should prepare the two strainers (*pavitra*) with the mantra "Precetāḥ pavitre.
Having placed them into the vessels for the honored guests, he should pour water into them with the mantra "Śaṃ no devī."

The mantra "pavitre sthaḥ," ending in the dual number, should be employed for all three stalks. Even when there is only one vessel, the plural form "pātreṣu" is used because of the plurality of substances such as gold that may be placed within it. As stated in the *Matsya Purāṇa*:
"Having first honored the Viśvedevas with barley and flowers, and having established two vessels upon *darbha* grass purifiers, one should fill them."
Pracetas says: One should pour the *arghya* water for each individual Brahmin into a vessel;
having thrown barley grains into it with the mantra "Thou art barley" (*yavo 'si*), it should be well-honored with fragrant flowers.
Gārgya says: Having placed the *pavitra* in the hand and performed the worship according to the prescribed rule,
one should pour the *arghya* into the hands with the mantra beginning "yā divyā."
The Preceptors say: "From the feet up to the head is the flower-worship for the gods;
from the head down to the feet with the words 'Obeisance to you' is for the ancestors. [481]
Gārgya says: At the end of the mantra, one should utter "svadhā" when addressing the ancestors,
and "svāhā" when performing the oblation for the gods.
And here, the offerings of *arghya* and so forth are expressed by the word "oblation" (*homa*).
Having offered water, perfumes, garlands, and the presentation of incense together with lamps.

The offerings of perfumes, garlands, and so forth should be performed by first pouring water for each one. And thus says Gautama: "The offering of alms is 'appūrva'; one should give in this same manner for those things pertaining to the Dharma. Because water comes first (pūrva), it is called *appūrva*. On this point, Manu says: "One should honor [the guest] with fragrant perfumes and garlands, beginning with those intended for the gods."

Śaunaka further mentions the gift of clothing as well: "At this time, there is the offering of perfumes, garlands, incense, lamps, and clothing. The meaning of "at this time" is after the offering of the *arghya* water. The mantras for the perfumes and other items will be stated in the section on the worship of the ancestors (*pitṛ-pūjā*); they should be understood here as well, since there is no contradiction. In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "I shall invoke the gods," they say; then [the performer] says, "Invoke them! Having taken the thumb of the Brahmins, he should then summon the Viśvedevas.
Then, observing silence, one should mutter the mantra: "O All-Gods, come hither!
And for a second time, one should mutter the mantra: "O All-Gods, listen!"
One should recite the third mantra, which is ancient and increases merit:
"May the highly fortunate Viśvedevas of great power come hither!"
May those who are invited to this śrāddha ceremony be attentive;
and here for you is water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), flowers, incense, and unguents.
And this lamp-light is offered to the Viśvedevas.

And by this [verse], the ritual procedure for the mantras is established for the offering of water for the feet and so forth. Consequently—"This is the water for the feet for you, O Viśvedevas; this is the respectful offering (arghya) for you, O Viśvedevas"—in this manner it should be applied everywhere. For incense and the light of a lamp, the mantra begins with "This is for you" (ayaṃ vaḥ). And thus, there is an option between these [mantras] and other mantras. 1.231.

Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) and circumambulating the ancestors counter-clockwise, he should offer double-folded kuśa grass to the ancestors with the verse beginning "uśantas tvā. (1.232)
Having invoked them, he should recite the mantra "May they come to us" (Āyantu naḥ) with their permission;
however, the purpose served by barley should be fulfilled with sesame seeds, and he should perform the offering of water (argha) and so forth as before.

[482] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks!”—“Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a heap of filth; the person who is like a jewel casket; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. “And how, monks, is a person like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust, overwhelmed by sensual lust, and unable to escape from it. He does not understand as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a heap of filth. “And how, monks, is a person like a jewel casket? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust, undisturbed by sensual lust, and able to escape from it. He understands as it really is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, monks, is called a person like a jewel casket. “And how, monks, is a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust, undisturbed by sensual lust, and able to escape from it. Furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters and is one who will reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna, without ever returning from that world. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus. “And how, monks, is a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust, undisturbed by sensual lust, and able to escape from it. Furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters and is one who will attain Parinibbāna in this very life. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: “Friend Ānanda, just now the Blessed One spoke in brief about the person like a heap of filth, the person like a jewel casket, the person like a blue lotus, and the person like a white lotus, and then rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. It would be good, friend Ānanda, if you could explain the detailed meaning of this to me. “Listen, friend, and pay close attention; I shall speak.”—“Yes, friend,” the monk replied. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friend, when the Blessed One spoke in brief about the person like a heap of filth, he meant this: Here, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual lust... [as above] ...he does not understand as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friend, is called a person like a heap of filth. “When the Blessed One spoke in brief about the person like a jewel casket, he meant this: Here, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust... [as above] ...he understands as it really is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering. This, friend, is called a person like a jewel casket. “When the Blessed One spoke in brief about the person like a blue lotus, he meant this: Here, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust... [as above] ...furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters and is one who will reappear spontaneously and there attain final Nibbāna. This, friend, is called a person like a blue lotus. “When the Blessed One spoke in brief about the person like a white lotus, he meant this: Here, a certain person dwells with a mind free from sensual lust... [as above] ...furthermore, he has abandoned the five lower fetters and is one who will attain Parinibbāna in this very life. This, friend, is called a person like a white lotus. “This, friend, is the detailed meaning of what the Blessed One spoke in brief. Then that monk, having delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Ānanda, rose from his seat and went to the Blessed One. After paying homage to the Blessed One, he sat down at one side and reported to the Blessed One his entire conversation with the Venerable Ānanda. “Well done, well done, monk! Ānanda is wise, the monk Ānanda has great understanding. If you had asked me the meaning of this, I would have explained it to you in exactly the same way as Ānanda has explained it to you. Such indeed is the meaning of this, and so you should remember it. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, that monk rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. [482] Thus have I heard. Ānanda is wise, the monk Ānanda

Then, after the section of ritual items beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*) and ending with the offering of the lamp in the *vaiśvadeva* rite, he should place the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) and perform the rites counter-clockwise (*apradakṣiṇa*). Having offered double-folded *kuśa* grass for the seats (*viṣṭara*), directed toward the east, he says, "I shall invoke the ancestors," referring to the Pitṛs, Pitāmahas, Prapitāmahas, and so forth. Without seeking permission from the Brahmins, he performs the invocation. Being permitted by them, he invokes the ancestors, beginning with the father, with the *anuṣṭubh* verse "uśantas tvā" seen by Daman, dedicated to the Pitṛ-deities. Then he should mutter the *triṣṭubh* verse "āyantu naḥ," seen by Śaṅkha, dedicated to the Pitṛ-deities. Here, the functions of barley (*yava*) are to be performed with sesame seeds (*tila*). He should perform the *arghya* offerings and other rites as in the *vaiśvadeva*. This is according to the *Purāṇa*.
Then, having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder and taking sesame seeds while remaining self-controlled,
he should ask the north-facing Brahmins, "I shall invoke the ancestors."
Having been authorized, he should invoke the ancestors with the verse "uśantas tvā," scattering sesame seeds counter-clockwise while remaining composed and meditating upon the ancestors.
For the sake of protecting the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛsatra), he should correctly and completely recite the mantra beginning with "āyantu naḥ" three times in every direction.
One should scatter sesame seeds while reciting the mantra beginning with "apahatāḥ";
[the vessel] may be made of gold, silver, lotus, or precious gems.
He indeed prepares the water for the guest-offering (arghya) using a vessel made of auspicious leaves and the like.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "I shall invoke the ancestors," he should then say to the remaining Brahmins;
being told by them, "Invoke them," he should say, "Be attentive."
The performer should say, "Be attentive. He should offer the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the respectful offering (*arghya*), addressing them with their names in the dative case, saying:
"I shall worship the fathers and grandfathers with food in due order."
He should then mutter the verse "uśantas tvā" and invoke all his great-grandfathers, his grandfathers, and his fathers in their proper order.
"May the Somadattas, the Barhiṣads, and those others who are the Agniṣvāttas—
may all our ancestors of meritorious fame come to us."
Then, endowed with supreme faith, one should scatter sesame seeds in that house in a counter-clockwise direction and recite the mantra: "apahatās tv iti."
Then, taking water and purifiers (pavitra) in vessels made from sacrificial wood together with kuśa grass, one should pour them out while reciting the verse "śaṃ no devīḥ."
One should scatter sesame seeds over them while reciting "tilo 'si" in sequence;
they should be worshipped according to the scriptures with water for the hands (arghya), flowers, and perfumes.
Then, having taken the cups in order with his left hand,
he should pour that water with his right hand using the *pitṛ-tīrtha*.
Having placed darbha grass and water in the hands of each of the Brahmins individually,
he should then give [the offerings] while reciting the mantra, "yā divyā āpaḥ," and so forth.
"O you of such-and-such lineage, may this water with sesame seeds be for you;
this is your *argha*," having thus spoken, he should offer it to them as the *svadhā*.
Having offered water, milk, curd, ghee, sesame seeds, rice grains, mustard seeds, and auspicious tips of kuśa grass, he himself should then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having said, "This flower is for you," one should offer the flowers;
then, having said, "This incense is for you," one should burn it before them.
Having said, "This is your lamp," one should present a lamp while holding it;
as for the garment, if available, it should be a pair of auspicious cloths that have not been worn on the body.
One should offer white sandalwood, camphor, saffron, and other auspicious substances for the purpose of anointing, or whatever else is dear to the ancestors.
Kātyāyana says: One should pour [water] into the vessels for the ancestors with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, as before;
then, one should offer sesame seeds with the mantra "Tilo 'si," as well as perfumes and flowers.

As before, the meaning is that one should [proceed] with the verse beginning "chaṃ no devīḥ. Dakṣa says: Having placed the *pavitra* in his hand and performed worship starting from the feet, he should pour the *arghya* into their hands with the mantra beginning "yā divyā."
Having placed a threefold purifier (pavitraka) of the length of a span in his hand and having worshipped it,
he should indeed offer the arghya water toward the east while facing the direction of the ancestors.
Ślokagautama says:
Having properly worshipped [the deity] with water or even with foot-water while self-restrained,
one should worship each [deity] individually and separately, one by one, in sequence as before.
One should honor each individual Brahmin with a separate offering of arghya.
Pracetas says: One should offer these [libations] counter-clockwise, one by one in the order of the ancestors;
having addressed them by their lineage and name, one should say, "This is your *argha*."

Consequently, even if one were to seat two or three Brahmins for each individual [guest], nevertheless, only one Brahmin per person would be entitled to the *arghya* offering, not all of them. For this very reason, Śaunaka states that there should be exactly three *arghya* vessels: "In three vessels, whether containing a single substance or multiple substances. Another Smṛti text says:
"But that which is offered to the ancestors and deities joined with case-endings reaches inexhaustibility; otherwise, it is useless."
In the *Bahvṛca-Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:
"In all cases, one should use the *gotra* name ending in a vowel during the rite of offering inexhaustible merit (*akṣayya-karman*);
however, for the libation (*tarpaṇa*), one should use the *gotra* name; thus the giver does not err."
In all cases, the father is declared to be the one to whom the libation is offered during the rite of *tarpaṇa*;
however, for one desiring satisfaction, the libation for the father must be performed with the *akṣayya* water.
One should use the name ending in *śarman* for the offering of the *arghya* and other rites, and for the rite of making [the merit] inexhaustible;
however, one should use *śarmā* for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). Acting in this way, one does not go astray.

Then, one should employ the formula: "O [Name] Śarman of the [Name] Gotra, this is your *arghya*. The same applies to the grandfather and the others. In the *tarpaṇa*, however, the formula is: "May [Name] Śarman of the [Name] Gotra be satisfied. The same applies to the grandfather and the others. In the offering of the inexhaustible water (*akṣayyodaka*), the formula is: "May there be inexhaustibility for the father [Name] Śarman of the [Name] Gotra. The same applies to the grandfather and the others. || 1.232, 233 ||
Having offered the arghya water and having placed their remnants in a vessel according to the rule, he turns the vessel face down below with the words, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors. (1.234)

Having offered the *arghya* water, he collects the remaining *saṃsrava*—the remnants of water remaining in the *saṃsrāva* vessel—into a single vessel. According to the prescribed rule, he turns that vessel face down with the mantra, "Thou art the seat for the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*). "Face down on the ground" means on the earth itself, not on a wooden plank or similar surface. As Pracetās states: "Having collected all the *saṃsrava* into the first vessel, which belongs to the ancestors, and having said, 'Thou art the seat for the ancestors,' he should place it face down upon the ground."
One should touch the vessel for the overflow of the *arghya* water with the mantra "May they be purified" (*śundhantām*).
Then, one should turn it face down, along with the purifiers (*pavitra*), with the mantra "Thou art the seat for the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ sthānam asi*).
Having placed *kuśa* grass upon that, one should offer perfumes, flowers, incense, and a lamp, beginning with the deities, in their proper order.

By this, it is stated that the offering of fragrance (gandhadāna) should likewise be performed for the Brahmins; by implication, the offerings of flowers and so forth are also included. Consequently, this is an alternative to the sequence previously mentioned in the rule: "having offered water, fragrance, and garlands. Kātyāyana states: "Having poured the remnants from all the paternal vessels into a single vessel, one who desires a son anoints his face. Then, having sprinkled a portion [of the water] with the mantra, 'May the worlds, the seats of the ancestors, be purified,' he turns the vessel upside down with the mantra, 'Thou art the seat of the ancestors. He should place it face-down on the ground strewn with *kuśa* grass. Upon that [vessel], there are the offerings of *kuśa* grass, flowers, fragrance, incense, lamps, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), and garments. The offering of fragrance and so forth is upon that vessel because of its association with the *kuśa* grass. Others, however, hold the view that after stating that the offering of fragrance and so forth is for the paternal Brahmins, the offering of *kuśa* grass alone is upon the vessel; they also read the word *kuśa* in the accusative case. This is Śloka-Kātyāyana.
Having uttered "arghyaṃ svadhā yā," one should consecrate the remnants of the oblation;
desiring a son, one should touch the mouth with the mantra beginning with "ye devāḥ."
Yama says: One should place the paternal vessel first;
upon it, one should place that of the grandfather, and then having placed that of the great-grandfather, one must not remove it nor move it.
Upon seeing a vessel that has been touched, lifted, moved elsewhere, or opened,
the ancestors depart quickly and utter curses.
From the Matsya Purāṇa:
Having offered the *arghya* with the verse beginning "yā divyā," one should then present the sandalwood paste and other offerings;
thereafter, having given the garments in successive order, one should offer the remnants of the water from the beginning.
Then, having placed it in the vessel for the ancestors, one should set it upside down to the north.

The meaning of this is as follows: having offered the *arghya* with the words "those who are divine," one should first place the remainder of the *arghya*—the water poured from the vessel for the ancestors (*pitṛpātra*)—into that same vessel; immediately thereafter, one should set it down face-down to the north of the site of the *śrāddha*. Then, one should offer everything from perfumes (*gandha*) up to clothing (*vastra*). Viṣṇu states: "Sandalwood, saffron, and camphor are for anointing. Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"One should cause sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron to be given; by anointing the ancestors, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice."
Vyāsa says: Holding the *vipavitra* in his hand, he should worship with fragrances, reciting "gandhadvārām";
and having said "dhūr asi," he should offer incense; and the lamp [is offered] with "jyotir idaṃ ca te."

In this regard: the Viśvedevas saw the *anuṣṭubh* verse beginning with "gandhadvārām," which has the goddesses as its deity. Parameṣṭhin, the son of Prajāpati, saw the *yajus* formula beginning with "dhūr asi," which has the incense as its deity. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If one, having placed the purifier (*pavitra*) in his hand, touches a twice-born [guest], that *śrāddha* becomes demonic, as the ancestors depart disappointed."
Anointing with perfumes means applying them as an ointment. Devala states:

"One must not remove the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from the shoulders of Brahmins during rites for the gods or the ancestors, for the sake of accomplishing worship with perfumes and other offerings. [486]
Śaṅkha says: Having placed the sacred thread around the waist, one should apply ointment to the body;
if one eats while wearing only a single garment, the ancestors depart disappointed.
Vṛddha-Manu says:
One should not apply perfumes as an ointment during a Śrāddha ceremony without wearing the sacred thread (upavīta).
And being so enjoined, one should place a garland upon the head, excluding the topknot (śikhā).
Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"All varieties of jasmine, as well as mallikās and white yūthikās, should be offered.
[In the] Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
White jasmine flowers are excellent, as are lotuses and water-crystals,
along with all other varieties endowed with fragrance and beauty.
The *japā* flower and others, as well as the *bhāṇḍī*, *rūṣikā*,
and *kuraṇḍikā* flowers, should always be avoided in the performance of *śrāddha* rites.
Śaṅkha says:
Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, those growing from sacred trees (caityavṛkṣa),
and those that are red in color should be avoided.
The divine [gems] born of water are especially red.

A *caityavṛkṣa* is a tree standing in a cemetery. Viṣṇu continues [the rule] with the injunction: "One should avoid flowers that have a pungent odor, those produced from thorny plants, and red flowers. Likewise, one may offer white flowers even if they are from thorny plants, and also water-born flowers, even if they are red. This is the middle portion (*pratīka*) of the verse beginning with *oṣadhīḥ pratimodadhvam*. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"One should burn both sandalwood and agallochum, as well as uśīra and padmaka, along with turuṣka and guggulu, all simultaneously, anointed with clarified butter."
One should not give mere ghee, nor even spoiled *tṛṇaguggulu*.
Śaṅkha says:
One should offer guggulu mixed with ghee and abundant honey for the purpose of incense;
[this is] from the Purāṇa.
This divine incense, the essence of the lord of the forest, rich in fragrance and most enchanting, is the invocation for all the gods; may it be accepted.
Śātātapa says:
"If the best of the twice-born inhale incense that has been struck by the breath from their hands, that śrāddha becomes futile; therefore, one should avoid doing so."
Devala said:
One should unweariedly offer flowers with the mantra "puṣpavatī," as well as with "idaṃ jyotiḥ" and "sujyotir asi. [487]
Kratu said:
Seeing the sectarian mark on the forehead, as well as a garland on the neck,
and seeing the husband of a low-caste woman (vṛṣalī), the ancestors depart in despair.
And here, a circular *puṇḍraka* is prescribed, but not one that is vertical. Marīci states:
"A lamp should be fed with either ghee or sesame oil, but not with anything else."
Atri says:
One should give garments according to one's ability with the verse beginning, "You two [bestow] garments."
From the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"For clothing is sacred to all the deities and is praised by all the gods;
in the absence of clothing, rites such as sacrifices and gifts would never take place anywhere."
Therefore, garments should especially be given at the time of a Śrāddha;
by giving them, one indeed obtains the merits of sacrifice, charity, and austerity.
Likewise,
he who gives unbleached clothing during the performance of a Śrāddha rite obtains long life, the fulfillment of desires, sovereignty, and auspicious beauty.
Whoever gives these— silk, linen, cotton, and likewise unwashed fine cloth— at śrāddha ceremonies, obtains abundant fulfillment of his desires.
Śātātapa says: "One should give a garment with the mantra 'yuvā suvāsāḥ'; in its absence, a sacred thread. Likewise:
"Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to oneself—all that should be given to the ancestors by one who desires that it become inexhaustible."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"One should especially give sandals to the Brāhmaṇas at Śrāddha rites;
thus one obtains divine vision as well as chariots yoked with horses."
He who, knowing the Dharma, gives a sacred thread at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
obtains the fruit of a gift of the Veda, which is a purifier for all brāhmaṇas.
If a Brahmin should give a water-pot at the time of a śrāddha ceremony,
he obtains a divine cow that yields milk from a jar.
He who gives sandals filled with cotton during the performance of a śrāddha rite obtains a splendid vehicle as well as comfort for his feet.
By giving a fan and a palm-leaf whisk to a Brahmin with due honor,
one shall obtain things that are pleasant to the touch, fragrant, and soft.
Whoever should give an excellent parasol adorned with flower garlands,
an exquisite palace indeed follows him as he goes.
One should give a sacred thread (*pavitra*) to the yogis for the traveler to wear while crossing water;
then that person obtains the fruit of a thousand *niṣkas*.
Likewise: "At a śrāddha, one should cause vessels filled with salt to be given;
flavors, as well as food and good fortune, attend upon him."
One should indeed give a beautiful vessel made of metal at the Śrāddha meal;
such a vessel becomes the source of all desires, of sacred knowledge, and of wealth.
That man who gives silver and gold in śrāddha ceremonies,
having given them, the donor obtains the fulfillment of his desires as well as wealth.
From the Purāṇa:
"A vessel for the ancestors should indeed be made of silver or coated with silver;
even a conversation about silver, its sight, or the gift of it [is meritorious]."
The gift of silver is said to lead to infinite, inexhaustible heaven;
by this gift, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors.
Manu says:
Even water, when given with faith using silver vessels or those adorned with silver, conduces to imperishability for them.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"He who feeds the ancestors at a Śrāddha ceremony using an earthen vessel—
the giver of the food, the officiating priest, and the eater alike shall go to hell."
Atri:
For the meal at rites for the gods and the ancestors, one should use vessels of gold and silver respectively;
one should not use earthenware vessels for meals at rites for the gods or the ancestors.
Without leaves of the Palāśa tree, there would be no leaf-plates for eating.

Viṣṇu states: "One should give vessels made of metal, especially those of silver; for the offering of ghee and other substances, vessels of metal or vessels of *phalgu* wood [are appropriate]. *Phalgu* is a specific type of tree. This is from the *Matsya Purāṇa*.

"He who performs the feeding of the assembly (*paṅktibhojana*) without having established the boundary of ashes (*bhasmamaryādā*)—that *śrāddha* becomes demonic (*āsura*) and does not reach the ancestors."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"The mandalas should be prepared with auspicious flour-powders made from *naivāra* grain,
or else with white clay, or even with consecrated ashes."
One should avoid taking [water] from there that has been brought back mixed with stone powder.

In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Having washed his hands, vessels, and so forth, the knower of the rules should thereafter cast the washing-water, mixed with darbha grass and sesame seeds, into pure water. [489]
Viṣṇu:
"O best of the twice-born, may this śrāddha—devoid of mantras, devoid of ritual acts, and devoid of material wealth—attain completeness through your grace. (1.234)
Saying, "I shall offer in the fire," he takes food soaked in ghee and asks for permission;
being authorized with the words, "Do so," he makes an oblation in the fire as in the Pitṛyajña.
With a concentrated mind, he should offer the remnants of the oblation into vessels,
especially those made of silver, as they may be available.

Having taken the food that has been abundantly sprinkled with water and saying, "I shall offer this into the fire," he should request permission from those eating at the *śrāddha* with the mantra [beginning] "Do so. Being permitted by them with the words "Do so," he should offer a portion of that food into the fire according to the procedure for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña-homa* prescribed in his own *sūtra*. Then, with a concentrated mind and focused attention, he should place the remainder of the offering into the vessels for the Brahmins' meal—preferably those made of silver; in its absence, into whatever vessels are available, provided they are not of a prohibited kind. From the mention of silver vessels, it is understood that he intends the remainder of the offering to be given specifically into the vessels of the Brahmins invited for the ancestors (*pitṛ*). Regarding this, Manu states that the granting of permission must be voiced simultaneously by all the Brahmins.
Having been authorized by the Brahmins, the Brahmin should perform [the rite] in the fire together with the Brahmins.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"Having carefully brought forth the *dakṣiṇāgni* for the purpose of the *homa*, while uttering:
'To Agni Kavyavāha, svadhā! Obeisance!'"
