Saying, "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, svadhā! Adoration! and saying, "To Yama, the lord of the Aṅgirases, svadhā! Adoration!"
These are the oblation mantras for the three [deities] in their proper sequence:
always to the south for Agni, and likewise to the north for Soma.
Between these two, one should constantly offer oblations to Vivasvat in a fire that is especially well-kindled with abundant dry fuel.

One should offer oblations into a fire that is smokeless and flickering for the successful completion of the rite; he who offers oblations into a fire that is either unkindled or smoky [futilely sacrifices].
"We have heard that the sacrificer would become blind in the next world;
therefore, one should offer the oblation into the carrier of the *kavya* (Kavyavāhana) after placing a fuel-stick inside [the fire]."
Palāśa, phalguna, nyagrodha, plakṣa, aśvattha, vikaṅkata, udumbara, as well as bilva, candana, and those trees that are fit for sacrifice.
The *sarala*, the *devadāru*, the *sāla*, and the *khadira*—
these trees are especially recommended for the purpose of sacrificial fuel (*samidh*).
Those trees that have thorns, those that are fit for sacrifice, and whatever others are honored for the purpose of sacrificial fuel— these are to be taken, according to the word of the ancestors.
The śleṣmāntaka, the raktamāla, the kapittha, as well as the śālmalī,
the nīpa, and the vibhītaka are censured for use in śrāddha rites.
The *cirabilva*, the *ṭaṅka*, the *tinduka*,
the *āmrātaka*, the *bilvaka*, and the *kovidāra*— these are censured at a *śrāddha*.
Those trees that are the dwelling places of insects should be considered contemptible and unfit for sacrifice,
as well as those that are surrounded by thickets or encircled on all sides by creepers.
The best of the twice-born should avoid the dwellings of birds,
as well as all other such places that are unfit for sacrifice.
Having diligently set aside the first portion of all flowers, fruits, and foods, one should offer them into the fire for Jātavedas.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One who has maintained the sacred fires should offer oblations in the southern fire with a concentrated mind;
one who has not maintained the sacred fires should offer them in the *aupāsana* fire, or likewise in water in the absence of fire.

The *aupāsada* fire is the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). For one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the procedure for the *dakṣiṇāgni* is to be understood as applying in the absence of the *aupāsada* fire; however, when the *aupāsada* fire exists, [the offering] should be made in that very fire. And so says the *Vāyupurāṇa*:

"Having brought the *dakṣiṇāgni* with effort for the purpose of the *homa*, or even a common worldly fire for the sake of the fire-ritual, one should offer oblations for the successful completion of the rite."

In this sentence, the word *agni* refers to the fire under discussion (*prakṛta*). And in the injunction for the performance of the *śrāddha*, the domestic fire (*gṛhya agni*) is the subject under discussion, because the performance of the *śrāddha* is prescribed by the *Gṛhya-śāstras*. Since the *Gṛhya-śāstras* proceed on the basis of the domestic fire, it is only when that [domestic fire] is absent that the injunction for the *dakṣiṇāgni* (southern fire) or the common worldly fire (*laukika agni*) for its function is appropriate. But if that [domestic fire] is present, since its own function is accomplished by it alone, what is the use of prescribing another fire? Furthermore, the injunction for the performance of the *śrāddha* found in the *Dharma-śāstras* and the *Purāṇas* is not different from that stated in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, as it is recognized as such; therefore, even in the *Dharma-śāstras*, the domestic fire is the subject under discussion. Thus, it is logical that in the phrase "for the sake of the fire" (*agnyartha*), the word *agni* refers to the domestic fire because it is the subject under discussion. As for the statement, "And one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) [should perform it] with the *aupāsana* fire," that is intended to dispel the doubt that one who has not maintained the sacred fires has no entitlement to the *śrāddha*, because the *agnaukaraṇa* rite is prescribed in the *dakṣiṇāgni*. Consequently, one who has not maintained the sacred fires should indeed perform it with the *aupāsana* fire; the meaning is not that only one who has not maintained the sacred fires uses the *aupāsana* fire. Manu says: "But one who is without fire should perform the *agnaukaraṇa-homa* in the hand of a Brahmin."
In the absence of fire, however, one should place [the offering] directly into the hand of the Brahmin.
As for that which was stated by Jātūkarṇya: "In the absence of fire, one should give into the right hand of the Brahmin."
The absence of the sacred fires is traditionally taught to last as long as one has not found a wife.

Thus, the intention is that there is a certainty of the absence of the sacred fires (*agni*) prior to the giving away of the wife, but not that there is an absence of fires even before that [marriage]. Even one who has obtained a wife may be without the sacred fires prior to the division of the inheritance. By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "he should place [the fire] in her hand," worldly fire (*laukika-agni*) is excluded;
for he himself says in the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The oblation pertaining to the ancestral sacrifice (*paitṛyajñiya-homa*) is not prescribed to be performed in a worldly fire."
In the absence of fire, however, for a Brahmin it may be performed in the hand, or even in water, or on the ear of a goat,
or on the ear of a horse, or in a cow-pen, or near a Śiva-liṅga.
Śaṅkha says: Kātyāyana has declared that one may place the fire in the right ear of an unborn calf, in the right hand of a Brahmin, in water, or in a clump of *kuśa* grass.
The purifying fire dwells eternally in both silver and gold.

Kātyāyana says: Having offered into the hand of the one who heads the row at the ancestral rite (pitrya) with the appropriate mantra, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should silently deposit [the oblation] into the vessels of the others.
Even if there is a division regarding the maternal grandfather, one who maintains the sacred fires should perform the rite according to the *tantra* method.

The meaning is that for the Brāhmaṇa who represents the maternal grandfather, the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire) must be performed separately within the *vaiśvadevika* ritual framework and at a separate fire. As stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:

"In the rite for the gods (*daiva*), one who lacks a sacred fire should perform [the offering]; he should announce the remainder (*śeṣa*) to those for the ancestors (*pitrya*). For the Viśvedevas are not recorded by the authors of the Purāṇas as partakers of the remainder."
Yama says:
When the Brahmins have been served by divine food, the twice-born man who does not maintain a sacred fire should perform the *agnaukaraṇa* rite in the [guest] fire;
having offered it to the ancestors, he should then set aside the remainder for the sake of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*).
From the Vāyu Purāṇa:
If two or more twice-born men should be present at a single Vaiśvadeva rite, then the offering should be given with one hand; otherwise, the rule would be violated.

The meaning of this is as follows: when, in a single *śrāddha* rite dedicated to the Viśvedevas, there are two, four, or six Brahmins and so forth, then once the oblation (*homa*) has been performed into the hand of one, the ritual requirement is fulfilled; therefore, it need not be performed into the hands of the other Brahmins. The performance of the oblation into the hand of the one representing the Viśvedevas is an optional alternative for one who does not maintain a sacred fire (*anagni*). And when the oblation is performed into the hand, then the request for permission from the Brahmins is: "In you indeed shall the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) take place. The response is: "So be it. Regarding this, Śaunaka says: "If he is without a sacred fire, having taken clarified butter, he should say, 'In you indeed shall the offering into the fire take place,' as before; [the reply is] 'So be it. Thus says Yama.
Then, after having offered [the oblation] into the fire according to this rite, the knower of mantras,
having taken the remainder of the sacrificial offering and having gazed upon it, should say "Svadhā."

Having gazed at the remnant of the oblation while reciting the mantra "svadhā," and having taken it and offered it to the ancestors, he should set aside a portion for the sake of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas). || 1.235, 236 ||
Having offered the food, one should consecrate the vessel with the mantra, "The earth is the vessel";
then, having recited "Idam Viṣṇuḥ," one should cause the thumb of the twice-born to enter the food.

Having set aside for the purpose of eating various kinds of food prepared other than the remnants of the *huta* offering, and having offered portions to the gods and the ancestors and performed the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should perform the consecration of the vessel with the formula, "The earth is your vessel. Then, with the verse "Viṣṇu strode across this," seen by Medhātithi and addressed to Viṣṇu, one should place the thumb of the twice-born guest into that food. Śaunaka says: "Having brought all the cooked food forward and having presented each item individually, one should begin the serving according to the rule, starting with the deities."
The meaning is: having caused it to be perceived by the eaters, that is, having made it known to them. Uśanas says:
"Having given the remains of the oblation to the ancestors, one should serve the food;
[this includes] sacrificial offerings, honey, meats, milk-rice, and cakes."
Śaṅkha says:
A wise man should devoutly offer warm food to the twice-born,
with the exception of fruits, flowers, and beverages.
The meaning is that fruits and other such items should be served while they are not hot. This is the rule of dharma:
for the satisfaction of the ancestors, the serving of food by the wife is desired;
and it is declared that when she serves it herself, the fruit of the offering becomes infinite.

It is prescribed that one should first offer the remnants of the oblation (*hutaśeṣa*) and then personally perform the serving of food. Śaunaka, however, states that the offering of the remnants of the oblation occurs after the serving of food: "Food given upon food that has already been served brings prosperity. The meaning is that when the food remaining from the oblation is placed upon the food already set out in the vessel for eating, it becomes *samṛdhnuka*, which means it causes prosperity. Manu says: Having personally taken the increased portion of food with both hands, and intending to offer it to the ancestors in the presence of the Brahmins, he should place it down slowly. [493]

Then, from the place where the Brahmins are being fed, one should take a portion of food (*vardhita*) with both hands in another spot and, while meditating upon the ancestors such as the father in the presence of the Brahmins, slowly set it down by oneself alone. A "portion of food" (*vardhita*) is that part of the food prepared for the sake of each individual eater. Likewise: "The Asuras, evil-minded, suddenly seize that food which is brought forth while still held between both hands."
With self-restraint and concentrated mind, he should properly place on the ground itself the various side dishes such as soups and vegetables, as well as milk, curd, ghee, and honey.

The "condiments" (*guṇa*) consist of spices and the like, which are indicated by such words as "soup" (*sūpa*) and "vegetables" (*śāka*); these should be served in vessels placed upon a base, not in those situated on a wall or similar support. The elder Śātātapa states: "If food is brought in an iron vessel, the eater consumes what is equal to excrement, and the giver shall go to hell."
Likewise:
"But those fats, salts, condiments, and so forth, which are given directly from hand to hand, do not reach the giver; the eater partakes of the sin."
A gift given with vessels made of gold or silver, or with a sword, or with one made of udumbara wood,
or again with a vessel of phalgu wood, attains imperishability.
Audumbara is copper. Yama says: Having eaten molasses, treacle, vegetables, cow's milk products, or salt when they have been given by hand, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
Viṣṇu states: "One should not give salt directly. In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"Rock salt and likewise that produced from Lake Mānasa—these two are indeed supremely purifying, even when offered directly and constantly."
Hārīta states: To those seated in a row, one should offer equal portions of perfumes and other items for the meal;
one should not give unequally in the row, nor should one ask for more, nor cause it to be given.
The beggar, the instigator, and the giver—all go to hell.
Kārṣṇājini says:

"Rites for the ancestors (paitṛka) should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), especially everything except the offering of food; this same rule applies to the rites for maternal grandfathers as well."
But he who offers food to the Brahmins with his sacred thread over the right shoulder—
his ancestors and all those twice-born ones eat excrement.

But as for that *śrāddha* which is defiled by the performance of the rite or served out through ignorance—one who has eaten at such a meal should perform the *kṛcchra* penance or even the *cāndrāyaṇa*. [494] Here, "apasavya" means wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*). Yama says:
As long as there is sacrificial food, as long as prepared food is offered,
so long do the ancestors eat, until I say, "I give."
Whatever is cooked in the house, whether it be solid food or soft food,
one must never eat it without first offering it to the ancestors.
From the Purāṇa:

One should not serve food at a Śrāddha with an impure hand, nor with only one hand, nor without Kuśa grass; furthermore, one should not serve with a vessel made of iron, nor from an iron vessel itself.
The meaning is that one should not give [food] from an iron vessel using an iron ladle or similar implement.
Therefore, it should be given using an intermediary, such as a leaf or a blade of grass.

Paiṭhīnasi says: "The earth is your vessel, the sky is the lid; I offer the nectar into the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa; Svadhā! With the mantra 'idaṃ viṣṇur vi cakrame,' having pressed the thumb into both the food and the water, and having muttered the Gāyatrī preceded by the Vyāhṛtis, one should say, 'May it be palatable' (svadate). Yama says:
The blessed Viṣṇu, the size of a thumb, wanders the earth for the sake of slaying the Rākṣasas; who will strike me today?
Therefore, in all śrāddha rites, the grasping of the thumb is prescribed;
for any śrāddha performed without the thumb being grasped, or with the knee outside [the circle], is rendered void.
Whatever is eaten with the knees outside [the thighs] becomes entirely demonic;
one should say "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering to the gods (havya) and the offering to the ancestors (kavya)" in due order.
One should place that thumb into the waters that have been first offered.

Kātyāyana states: "Having dipped his thumb into the food with either the *vaiṣṇavī* verse or the *yajus* formula, and having scattered sesame seeds while reciting *apahatāḥ*, he should offer warm, well-prepared food. The *vaiṣṇavī* verse is "idaṃ viṣṇur vicakrame," and the *yajus* is "viṣṇo havyam. The phrase "he should give" implies giving to the gods and the ancestors. Viṣṇu says: "With the words *namo viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*, he should first present the food to the two [guests] facing east; to the father and grandfather, by name and lineage (*gotra*), to those facing north. From these stated sentences, the sequence is understood as placing the thumb first, followed by the formal dedication (*saṃkalpa*) of the food. Here, by the use of the locative case in "to the two facing east" and "to those facing north," the Brahmins are established as the locus for the offering (*āhavanīya*). By the use of the dative case in "to all the gods" (*viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ*) and "to the father" (*pitre*), the status of the All-Gods and the ancestors as deities (*devatā*) is indicated. Thus, that which was called *śrāddha* by Āpastamba in the passage beginning with "Now Manu proclaimed this rite under the name of *śrāddha*" is here expressed by the term "presentation" (*nivedana*) and so forth. [495] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
Then, having taken warm food mixed with sesame seeds and smeared with honey and clarified butter,
he should do so again with the *praṇava* (OM) using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the deities).
Having said, "This is your food," he should offer oblations to all the gods.

The meaning of this is as follows: for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins invited for the Vaiśvadeva rite, one should take a full vessel filled with food smeared with honey and ghee, along with water containing sesame seeds, with the tips of the hands, and announce: "Om! O Viśvedevas named so-and-so, this food is for you.
Then, one should offer food to the ancestors with an invocation:
"O [Name] of such-and-such lineage, this food is for you; Svadhā! Homage!"
Then, having given food in due order to the entire lineage,
one should perform the offering to all the gods.
Having taken hold of the twice-born’s thumb while restraining his speech and reciting the mantra, he should contemplate the food as nectar while reciting: "The earth is your vessel."
Proclaiming, "O Viṣṇu, protect this my offering," he should then respectfully take the thumb of each brahmin one by one.
"O you of such-and-such a lineage, this food is for you; svadhā! Homage!
And water mixed with sesame seeds and kuśa grass is also [offered] before them."
He should scatter [food] for the ancestors and the servants while reciting the mantra "apahatāḥ.
To them he should give the *apośāna* water, saying, "May you partake."

From this statement, it is understood that the insertion of the thumb comes first, and the mental resolve regarding the food follows. Consequently, there is an option regarding the sequence of the thumb-insertion and the resolve for the food. Atri says: "If one touches with both hands food that has not been mentally resolved upon, that which is given becomes unfit to be eaten; it does not reach the ancestors."
The formal resolve (saṃkalpa) consists of the offering of food to the gods and others.
If one should perform the resolve while the Brahmin has not yet sipped water for purification (apośāna),
that food is consumed by the Asuras and does not reach the ancestors.
Holding the food and drink in his hand, he should utter the word "anna" (food); then he should say "svadhā," thereby effecting the withdrawal of his own individual existence [into the universal].
[496] The names associated with the lineage connection: "This food, Svadhā!"—having thus uttered it according to the paternal line, one should withdraw one's own sense of self-identity.

One should form the mental resolve, "This is not mine," in order to relinquish one's own ownership. Then, having uttered, "O Father of such-and-such lineage, O [Name], this food is for you; Svadhā! Namaḥ! one should mentally resolve, "It is not mine. The same applies to the grandfather and the others. However, when only a single Brāhmaṇa is fed for many ancestors—such as the father and so forth—one should mentally divide the food into as many portions as there are ancestors and assign each portion to the father and the others respectively. Likewise: "Whether the offering has been given or not yet given, he who places the *bali* on the ground..."
That food goes to waste when the ancestors have departed disappointed.
Bharadvāja said:
That Brāhmaṇa who, having taken food intended for the ancestors, offers it as a bali-oblation, becomes a thief by that act and is considered a perpetrator of every kind of theft. (1.237)
Having recited the Gāyatrī with the Vyahṛtis and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā," they should eat while remaining silent, speaking only as much as is necessary for their comfort.

Having recited the *gāyatrī* verse accompanied by the three *vyāhṛtis*, and the three verses beginning with "madhu vātā" (which are in the *gāyatrī* meter, dedicated to the Viśvedevas, and composed by the seer Rāhūgaṇa Gautama), he should say to the Brahmins, "Enjoy [the food] as you please. Those Brahmins, restraining their speech, should eat. [As stated by] Pracetas: "Then, having offered the *apośāna* water, he should mutter the *sāvitrī* three times;
likewise, the three verses beginning with 'madhu vātā' and this triad beginning with 'madhu'."

The meaning is that one should utter "madhu" three times. Laghuyama states: "Having made the food consist of honey and consecrated it with the mantra 'madhu vātā,' whatever may be deficient in fire, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in mantra [is thereby perfected]."
Having said, "May everything be without flaw," one should then feed [the guests] with diligence.

"Consisting of honey" means abounding in *madhūka* flowers. Furthermore, the practice of speaking without interruption must be performed *before* the offering of the *apośāna* water, not afterwards. Regarding this, Pracetas says:

"Because of the speaking of those who have received the *apośāna* water and because of the speaking while there is an interruption, the ancestors depart disappointed along with the gods; of this there is no doubt."
Vyāsa says:
Having been told, "Enjoy [the meal]," they, with their faces properly composed and observing silence, should eat immediately after the *apośāna* rite. [497]
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One should not eat before [others] while seated on a superior seat; one should not give more [food] than is required, nor should one accept more. Baudhāyana says:
"One should say 'juṣasva' (be pleased) first, and at the end of the meal among the Brāhmaṇas, [one should say]:
'May there be no deficiency due to any error in the mantras or the ritual acts.'"
The *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa*:
"That which is placed in the palm of the hand and that food which has been prepared—these should be eaten as one; no distinction exists between them."

"Placed in the palm of the hand" means the food for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite. That food should be set aside separately before the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and subsequently mixed with the food intended for eating. Manu says:
"The twice-born should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering when asked by the giver, as long as there is steam in the food, and as long as they eat while remaining silent."
The ancestors eat only so long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described.
Pracetas says: Having performed the *āpośāna* rite, one should eat what has been placed in the vessel and is not forbidden;
likewise, one should restrain the restlessness of all the senses, as well as the feet and hands.
One should avoid biting off with the teeth, drinking from the hand, and eating to excess.

One should not drink water and other liquids using the hand. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Brāhmaṇas should not describe food in terms of its qualities or defects; they should not speak untruths; they should not praise one another; and they should not say that the food and drink are abundant. Except by means of a hand signal, the ancestors eat as long as there is food on the ground, as long as it is praised, and as long as it is warm—except for fruits, roots, and drinks. The meaning is that fruits and the like need not be kept warm. Yama says: "He who eats with the palm of his hand and he who releases wind [while eating]..."
His ancestors do not eat [the offering] if someone else praises it first.
In the Varāha Purāṇa: "If a Brāhmaṇa devoid of knowledge begs from a donor, his ancestors are satisfied by that gift; there is no doubt that they are satisfied for both the giver and the eater."
Hārīta says: Having raised his hand, laughing, filled with anger and wonder, he said:
"That which one eats at the time of a Śrāddha does not indeed please the ancestors."
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
When an excellent twice-born man places his foot upon a seat while eating,
he destroys the offerings to the gods and the ancestors, as well as his food, his offspring, and his cattle.
Devala said: That Brahmin who eats with a mind lacking serenity, or while wearing shoes, or who is prone to idle chatter, or who is angry—he is a defiler of the ancestors. [498]
Yama says: That which one eats after having already eaten, that which is smeared with oil,
and that which has been seen by women in their menses— verily, that goes to the Rākṣasas.

The plural number in the phrase "by those who are menstruating, etc. is to be explained as including others. Whatever is eaten or served by one who lacks the syllable *oṃ*, by one who is full of anger, or by one who is evil-minded—that indeed goes to the *rakṣas* demons.

"Without the syllable *oṃ* (*niroṃkāreṇa*)" means without the mantra for the meal beginning with *oṃ*. "Devoid of ritual" refers to food that has not been formally offered; "devoid of mantra" means without the recitation of sacred formulas; "without a sacrificial fee" (*adakṣiṇam*) means without the giving of a fee; and "offered or given without faith"—that indeed goes to the *rakṣas* demons.
If one who has been appointed to a *śrāddha* ceremony should omit anything whatsoever,
his ancestors will remain in a state of despair for that entire month.
Vasiṣṭha said:
When food has been offered to the ancestors from both branches [of the hand],
the evil-minded Asuras watch for that interval.
Therefore, O twice-born one, the hand should remain non-empty, lest it become parched.
Likewise:
"But one who is appointed to a *śrāddha* or a rite for the gods (*daiva*) and yet serves meat shall fall into hell for as many years as there are hairs on the animal's body."
In the Varāha Purāṇa:
"O Vasundharā, if a Brāhmaṇa who is weak in knowledge should offer a worthy recipient [of a gift],
the Rākṣasas seize his food as he eats it."
Śātātapa says: If a Brahmin who has partaken of the *argha* water drinks water from that same vessel,
one should know that what was eaten belongs to the ancestors, but the remainder belongs to the Asuras.
If a twice-born man, having eaten, always drinks water without first washing his hands,
that food is consumed by the Asuras, and the ancestors depart disappointed.
Manu says:
"That fool who, having eaten at a śrāddha, gives the leavings to a Śūdra,
goes head-first to the Kālasūtra hell."
Śātātapa says:
He who eats with a broken back, or likewise with his knees outside [the thighs],
or who constantly speaks while holding food in his hand, should be known as a slayer of his ancestors.
While eating food, one should never touch it with the left hand;
nor should one touch one's feet, head, or bladder, nor should one touch the vessel with the foot. — Baudhāyana.
If a twice-born man eats while placing one foot upon another when not in a state of distress, he is not to be fed at a śrāddha; his ancestors depart disappointed.
In the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*:
"One should not cause the remnants of a *śrāddha* to be given to a Śūdra or to one who has not been initiated (*anupeta*).
If one should give it out of passion or delusion, that [offering] certainly does not reach the ancestors."
Therefore, no food that has been left over should be given during a śrāddha rite,
except for curd and clarified butter, and except to a disciple or a son.
Being pleased, he should gladden the Brahmins and feed them food slowly;
he should repeatedly encourage them with food and praise for their qualities.

One should urge and incite him. The Vedic tradition (nigama) states: "He who does not give what is required, though it has been set aside for the sake of a śrāddha, is born in the lower, miserable, and terrible wombs of animals."
One should not eat meat, cakes, fruits, sugarcane, and the like by biting them with the teeth;
nor should there be remnants of a morsel left in the bowl, nor should one drink what remains after one has already drunk from it.
Atri says: One who speaks even with a "hum" sound, or praises the qualities from his hand,
or lifts the vessel from the ground, or releases it with his hand, or drinks [from it]— [these are faults].
One who eats with his feet placed on a high seat, with his armpit exposed, or with his hands outside his knees;
or one who eats without using the thumb, or makes a noise with the mouth while eating.
One may drink again the water and so forth remaining after drinking, or having drawn it up once more;
or one may eat again the sweetmeats, fruits, and the like that were half-eaten.
If a twice-born man blows upon the food with his mouth, or spits into the vessel while eating,
he destroys the śrāddha by eating in such a manner and goes to a downward state.
If a Brahmin eats ghee or oil that has fallen on the ground due to his nails,
Yama declares that to be impure, equal to the eating of cow's flesh.
Śātātapa says:
One who is free from greed and has conquered anger should eat food that is very hot, mixed with sesame seeds, entirely unobstructed, not too hurried, and in moderate, wholesome quantities.
Kārṣṇājini says:
One should perform [the rite] without becoming weary, free from hypocrisy and egoism;
one should avoid anger, delusion, and likewise greed during the performance of the śrāddha ceremony.
"One should provide food"—this is the grammatical connection. Manu says:
"A Brahmin, or even a mendicant, who has arrived for the purpose of eating..."
Having been permitted by the Brahmins, he should honor them according to his ability.
Yama says:
A mendicant or a student who has arrived for the purpose of eating should be fed at will, even if he arrives after others have already taken their seats. 1.238.
One should give food that is desirable and fit for oblation, without anger and without haste.
"Food" refers to milk-rice and the like, which is desired by the Brahmins; that is worthy of being a portion of the oblation, and one should give it free from anger and haste. Śaṅkha says:
"The food with which one should sprinkle the remainder of the *agnaukaraṇa* [offering]..."
But when that has been consumed, one should give whatever else may be the primary substance.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Then, free from envy, one should offer abundant food according to one's preference—sesame, meat, vegetables, soups, *kṛsara*, milk-rice, cakes, parched grain, various edibles, drinks, honey, clarified butter, curd, and milk. Yama says:
"Then, having brought pure [food], the self-restrained host should feed the twice-born:
rice, soup, clarified butter, vegetables, meat, curd, milk, and honey."
Having gathered all this together, he should offer it as he pleases;
whatever may be pleasing to the Brahmins, that he should give without envy.
Nārāyaṇa said: Whatever is an offering to the gods, whatever is purifying, whatever is intended for the ancestors, and whatever brings happiness—
this is given by the hand of a woman of the same caste to the twice-born.
That food which is warm reaches the heart; therefore, that warmth is praised here.
Manu says: I shall explain in its entirety that oblation which, when offered to the ancestors according to the prescribed rule, serves for many nights and even for eternity.
When sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, or roots and fruits are offered according to the prescribed rule,
the ancestors of men are gratified for a month.

Viṣṇu: "With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, *priyaṅgu*, *nīvāra* millet, and wheat, [the ancestors] are gratified for one month. With the meat of a sheep or a goat, they are gratified for eleven months; but with milk or its derivatives, for a full year. Manu: "The foods of sages, milk, soma, meat that is not seasoned, and salt that is not processed—these are by nature called sacrificial oblations (*havis*)."
That which has not been offered to others and is not yet cooked for the purpose of another task is [the proper substance]. Bṛhaspati says:
"Because it is given with faith—being consecrated, rich in condiments, and mixed with milk, honey, and ghee—it is therefore called *śrāddha*."
Āpastamba states: "In the case of the obligatory *śrāddha*, one should offer food that contains fat; ghee and meat are the primary options, but in their absence, oil and vegetables. Kārṣṇājini says:
"One should diligently give whatever was the favorite [food] of the deceased while he was alive."
Yama says: By a twelve-night *kṛcchra* penance, one is liberated from that deed;
therefore, a wise man should neither give, nor beg, nor cause [another] to give.
But Vṛddha-Śātātapa has stated otherwise:
"One should request only what is needed from that which has been prepared for the sake of the Śrāddha;
the foolish twice-born man who does not request anything becomes a slayer of his ancestors."

"He who does not give what is required, even though it has been prepared for the sake of the śrāddha—that miser of dull intellect shall not obtain the fruit of the śrāddha. Thus, that which has been prepared for the sake of the śrāddha must be requested and must be given; however, that which has not been prepared should neither be requested nor given—such is the settled rule.
Having recited the purifying mantras until satiety, as well as the previously mentioned recitation, || 1.239 ||
Having taken food and being satisfied, and having obtained permission regarding the remainder, one should scatter that food upon the ground and offer water once for each [ancestor]. (2.240)

Having recited the purifying *sūktas*, *yajus* mantras, and *sāmans* until the Brahmins are satisfied, one should take a portion from each of the various foods consumed by the Brahmins, place it in a single vessel, and recite the aforementioned prayers. Then, having addressed the Brahmins with the words, “Are you satisfied? and being answered by them with “We are satisfied,” one should say, “As you wish regarding the remaining food,” and scatter the food contained in that vessel upon the ground. Afterward, one should offer water to the Brahmins once for each. The preliminary recitation—the *vyāhṛtis*, the *Sāvitrī*, and the three verses beginning with “*Madhu vātā ṛtāyate*”—must be performed while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*). As Jamadagni has said:

"All the śrāddha rites must be performed according to the rules with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apavīta), except for the recitation of sūktas, hymns, and prayers, and the dismissal of the Brahmins," so says [the tradition].

Kātyāyana states: "While they are eating, one should recite the Gāyatrī preceded by the Vyāhṛtis and accompanied by the Praṇava, either once or thrice; as well as the Rakṣoghna mantras, the Pitṛ-mantras, the Puruṣasūkta, the Apratiratha, and other purificatory (pavitra) texts. The Rakṣoghna mantras begin with *kṛṇuṣva pājaḥ* (RV 3.4.23). The Pitṛ-mantras begin with *udīratām avaraḥ* (RV 7.6.17). Baudhāyana [says]:
He should softly cause those whose hopes are fixed to hear the *sāmans* that destroy demons, the *yajus* formulas containing the word "svadhā," the honey-verses, and the purificatory texts.
Manu says: At a rite for the ancestors, one should indeed cause [the guests] to hear the Vedic study, the treatises on Dharma,
the narrative legends, the histories, the Purāṇas, and the supplementary texts.
One should recite, according to one's ability, various hymns to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Arka, and Rudra,
as well as those addressed to Indra, Īśa, and Soma, and the Pāvamānī verses.
Likewise, the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans], as well as the Jyeṣṭhasāman and the Raurava;
similarly, the Śāntikādhyāya and the Madhubrāhmaṇa.
Likewise, he should recite the Maṇḍala-brāhmaṇa and whatever else brings joy to the Brahmins and to himself; all that he should utter.
In the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
Having recited mantras that destroy demons and having spread the ground with sesame seeds,
those very best of the twice-born ancestors should be meditated upon.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather,
abiding within the bodies of Brahmins, attain supreme satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise great-grandfather,
their forms nourished by the fire-oblation, attain satisfaction.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this rice-ball (piṇḍa) offered by me upon the earth.
May my father, grandfather, and likewise my great-grandfather attain satisfaction through this which has been uttered by me with devotion.
May his maternal grandfather attain satisfaction, as well as his father and his other paternal ancestors;
may the Viśvedevas reach supreme satisfaction, and may the malevolent spirits perish.
Lord Hari, the Lord of Sacrifice, the imperishable enjoyer of all sacrificial offerings, is present here as the Sovereign;
by his presence, may all demons and all Asuras immediately depart.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "I shall proclaim the auspicious Saptārcis [rite], which bestows all desires,
serves as a staircase to heaven and liberation, and brings about the deliverance of the ancestors."
I always pay homage to those ancestors of radiant splendor, both formless and embodied, who are meditative and possess the eye of yoga.
I bow to Dakṣa and Mārīca, the progenitors of Indra and the others, as well as to the Seven Sages and other such bestowers of desires.
I bow to all those ancestors who are the progenitors of Manu and the others, as well as of the Sun and the Moon, and likewise to the Pitṛs who dwell in the waters.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to the constellations and the planets, to wind and fire, to the ancestors, and to heaven and earth.
I bow down to those grandfathers, the progenitors of the celestial sages, who are honored by all the gods and who are the brothers of all living beings.
With palms joined in reverence, I always pay homage to Prajāpati, Kaśyapa, Soma, Varuṇa, and the lords of yogis.
Homage to the seven Gaṇas likewise in the seven worlds;
I pay homage to the Self-Existent Brahmā, who possesses the eye of yoga.
Thus has been spoken this [mantra] of seven flames, worshipped by the hosts of Brahman-sages;
for it is supremely purifying, glorious, and the destroyer of Rākṣasas. Thus [it is said].

Śaunaka states the specific procedure for requesting permission regarding the remainder (*śeṣānujñāpana*): "Having known them to be satiated, one should cause them to hear the three verses beginning with *madhu vātā ṛtāyate* and the single verse *akṣann amīmadanta*, which was seen by Rāhūgaṇa Gautama and has Indra as its deity; having asked the Brāhmaṇas, 'Is it complete? and being answered by them, 'It is complete,' one should set aside from each portion of food eaten by those Brāhmaṇas a part for the sake of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) together with the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice), and then request permission regarding the remainder, saying, 'What should be done with the rest? Then, if that food is accepted (*abhimata*) or permitted (*anumata*) by the Brāhmaṇas, it should be sent to the house of the Brāhmaṇas. Alternatively, if they agree, 'Let it be eaten together with our kinsmen,' then one should do exactly so. [504] Manu: The meaning of this is as follows: Having recognized that the eaters at the *śrāddha* are satiated, one should recite the three-verse hymn beginning with *madhu vātā ṛtāyate* and the single verse *akṣann amīmadanta*—the latter being a *pañkti* meter verse seen by Rāhūgaṇa Gautama and dedicated to the deity Indra. After reciting these, one asks the Brāhmaṇas, "Is it complete? When they reply, "It is complete," one takes a portion from each of the various foods eaten by those Brāhmaṇas and, together with the *sthālīpāka* used for the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, places it in another vessel for the purpose of the rice-balls. One then requests permission from the Brāhmaṇas, asking, "What should be done with the remaining food? Thereafter, if that food is accepted (*abhimata*) by the Brāhmaṇas, it should be delivered to the Brāhmaṇas' homes. Or, if they consent, saying, "Let it be eaten together with our kinsmen," then one should act accordingly.
Then, once they have finished eating, he should present the remains of the food;
he should act according to what those twice-born guests say, having been authorized by them.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"The Brahmins should be questioned with devotion while one kneels upon the ground: 'Are you satisfied? Has anything been provided for you? "
Manu says: Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
one should cast it away before those who have finished eating and scatter it upon the ground.
"Combining" means taking [the portions] together into a single vessel. For women who died before being consecrated for marriage, for those who have abandoned their families,
and for those who have left their husbands, the food-leavings upon the *darbha* grass and whatever *vikira* (scattered food) there may be shall constitute their share.
The drying up of that which has entered the earth belongs to one who is straightforward and free from deceit;
they declare this to be the ancestral share of the class of slaves.

*Bhāgadheya* means a share. Consequently, the meaning established is that both of these must be offered separately: first, the food remaining in the Brahmins' bowls intended for those deceased who were not initiated (*anupanīta*), as well as for other beings born in one's own family; and second, the food scattered upon the *darbha* grass intended for those who abandoned women of the family and others who should not have been abandoned. Furthermore, whatever remains on the ground as the leavings of the Brahmins should be assigned to the group of servants who are straightforward and free from deceit. Vasiṣṭha, however, says:
"One should offer parched grain, earth-dust, scattered grains, ointments, and sweetmeats to those who have followed in death—those in one's own family who died childless or lived short lives.

Thus, one should give parched grain and the other offerings intended for those deceased ancestors and others who have followed in death, as well as for those in one's own lineage who died without offspring or had brief lifespans. Likewise:
The Vedic revelation states that for those who have died before their consecration, along with their servants,
Manu has declared both the residue of food and the dregs of the liquor to be their allotted share.

That which has fallen into the vessel is *ucchiṣṭa* (remnant); that which has fallen on the ground is *ucchoṣaṇa* (scattering). Consequently, it is established that the formal assignment (*uddeśa*) must be performed for those who have died without having been consecrated (*asaṃskṛta*), together with their servants. The mantra for the scattering (*vikira*) for the Vaiśvadeva Brahmins, as stated by Gobhila, is: "To those gods who do not drink Soma and who are excluded from sacrificial portions, I shall give this food, the Vaiśvadeva scattering."
Regarding the scattering of food (vikiro) for the ancestors, the Brahmins, and the relatives, Bṛhaspati says:
"In front of the Brahmins who have sipped water,
he should scatter food with water and recite this mantra:"

May those living beings of my lineage who have not been consumed by fire, as well as those who have been consumed, be satisfied by what is given upon the earth; being satisfied, may they go to the supreme goal.

Thus, according to the opinion of Bṛhaspati, the scattering [of rice] occurs after the sipping of water (ācamana); however, according to other opinions, it occurs prior to the sipping of water. Kātyāyana, moreover, recites this mantra:

"May those in my family who were cremated by fire and those who were not cremated by fire, as well as all living beings born therein, be satisfied by what is given upon the ground and attain the supreme goal."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having sprinkled the food along with the grass with the mantra "May you look upon me," he should then place it before the Brahmins who are facing north, together with water.
One should scatter food with devotion; that is traditionally remembered as the portion for servants.

In this context, the mantra is for the scattering of food (*annavikira*), but not for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Here, "grass" refers to *darbha* grass, because of the statement: "and that which is the scattering upon the *darbha* blades. Marīci says:
"If, after giving the scattering of food at the *śrāddhas*, one does not rinse his mouth due to a lapse of intellect, his ancestors shall remain eaters of leavings for six months. (1.239, 240)
Taking all the food together with sesame seeds, facing south,
he should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) near the remains of the meal, just as in the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña).

Having taken and set aside small portions of each kind of food prepared, one should offer balls (*piṇḍas*) made of food according to the procedure for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. The distinction from the *Pitṛyajña* is that [the offering] is accompanied by sesame seeds and performed while facing south. "In the vicinity of the leavings" means not in the vicinity of the fire. Atri says:
"In front of the Pitṛs who are seated on their seats, at a distance of three *aratnis*, is the vicinity of the leavings; it is not in the vicinity of the seats where the leavings are placed."
Jātūkarṇya says:
Having raised [the ground] to the measure of a fathom, one should cause the rice-balls (piṇḍas) to be offered there,
so that even when they are being touched for rinsing, no drops fall upon it.
In the Bhāskara-smṛti: "The offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for Brahmins is prescribed at a distance of one cubit (bāhu)."
Manu says:
On a clean, smeared spot, one should prepare a large site made of sand,
either circular or square, sloping toward the south.
With a single *darbha* blade, he should scratch the center of that [spot] three times and discard it.
Then, in that place, he should spread many *darbha* blades—each having a single root and tip—evenly, with their tips pointing south and their bases toward the north. [506]

Kātyāyana states: "Having ascertained that they are satiated, having scattered food and having given water once each, he should mutter the Gāyatrī as before, [recite] the Madhumatī verses and 'madhu madhu madhu,' and ask, 'Are you satisfied? Being authorized by the reply, 'We are satisfied,' and having obtained permission regarding the remaining food, he should take all the food together, place it near the leavings upon Darbha grass, and offer three balls (piṇḍas). Some say this should be done after they have sipped water. The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa states:
"A twice-born man should perform the scraping with his left hand and his right hand [placed over it]."
Then, one should diligently perform the act of rubbing [the hands] during the śrāddha rite.
The wise man should perform the breaking, the grinding, and likewise the scraping for the ancestors only once; for the gods, it is said, it should be done three times.
*Ullekhana* is the drawing of lines on the spot where the rice balls (*piṇḍa*) are to be offered; this is according to the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Facing south, being pure, one should spread darbha grass once for the sake of the rice balls, with their tips pointing east and south, and immediately thereafter offer the rice balls."
Likewise, the wise man, devoted to the ancestors, should offer three balls of food mixed with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, having placed his left knee upon the ground.
Jātūkarṇya says:
Having spread Darbha grass near the roots at the place where the remnants [of the food] are kept,
and having performed the ritual rinsing (avanejana), one should offer the three pindas according to the prescribed rule.
Sumantu says: "At the time of performing the Śrāddha, [the offering] is given with one hand;
however, for the libation (tarpaṇa), one should use both hands—this indeed is the prescribed rule."

Bṛhaspati says: From all the prepared food, one should offer rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) mixed with honey and sesame seeds to the paternal ancestors, maternal grandfathers, and others, according to the rules of the *Gṛhya-sūtras*.
Marīci: The offering of the funeral ball (piṇḍa) for the vessels is prescribed to be made with a sword-vessel,
or else with one of silver or udumbara wood, or even again with the hand alone.
The *udumbara* [ladle] is made of copper. Pāraskara says:

"In the offering of the *arghya*, in the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), and likewise in the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) at the *akṣaya* [vessel], one should duly declare the lineage, the relationship, and the names."

The author of the *Gṛhyasūtra* states: "If one does not know the names [of the ancestors], one should offer the first *piṇḍa*, saying: 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling on earth. The second, saying: 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in the intermediate space. The third, saying: 'Svadhā to the fathers dwelling in heaven. In the *Viṣṇudharmottara*:
"Wise men should perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* using *kāśa* grass in the absence of *kuśa*. O King, *dūrvā* grass is also remembered as a supreme purifier."
Vyāsa says:
At the śrāddha rites, one who is composed should recite the Sāvitrī at each individual piṇḍa;
likewise, the words "to Soma" and "who possesses the ancestors" (pitṛmat) should be uttered.
Marīci says: At a pārvaṇa rite, one should fashion balls of food the size of a fresh āmalaka fruit;
at an ekoddiṣṭa rite, however, one should offer a single ball the size of a bilva fruit.
In the *navaśrāddha*, one should offer an even more substantial portion than that.
One should offer an even larger portion at the *navaśrāddha* than that;
and during the period of impurity (*aśauca*), one should offer an even larger portion every day.
Manu says:
Having offered the rice-balls (piṇḍa) to the ancestors according to the rule while remaining self-restrained,
he should wipe that hand upon those rice-balls for the sake of the partakers of the scrapings (lepabhāgin).
The Matsya Purāṇa states regarding those who partake of the lepa (the smearings):
"The fourth and subsequent ancestors are the sharers of the lepa; the fathers and others are the sharers of the piṇḍas.
The giver of the piṇḍas is the seventh among them; such is the sapinda relationship extending through seven generations."
Viṣṇu: "At this point, one should rub the hands at the base of the *darbha* grass with the words, 'O ancestors, rejoice here. Vyāghra:
"With a concentrated mind, one should wipe the residue from the hands upon the bases of the *darbha* grass;
then, having washed that vessel with water, one should [wipe it] for each *piṇḍa* as before."
Having performed the ritual washing, one should place the vessel for the funeral cakes face down.
Manu says:
Having sipped water, turned toward the north, and slowly restrained his breath three times,
one who knows the mantras should pay homage to the six seasons and to the ancestors.
From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Oil extracted from black sesame seeds and carefully preserved should be given by the wise as an unguent for the ancestors, using a vessel made of bilva wood."
The singular number in "tilāt" (from sesame) is intended to denote the genus. Likewise:
"One should offer the finest collyrium to the ancestors in the *apasavya* manner;
having pronounced the names of all, one should also give thread for the sake of clothing."
One should give a new thread of linen, or likewise one of cotton;
one should also offer silk thread, woven cloth thread, and silken thread.

*Kṣauma* is that which originates from *atasī* (linseed). *Pattorṇa* is washed silk (*dhautakauśeya*). *Paṭṭasūtra* is well known. *Kauśeya* is silk thread (*trasarīsūtra*). [508] A conch shell, woolen thread, or even new cotton thread should be offered;
a wise person should avoid a fringe, even if it is made from unwashed cloth.
Āśvalāyana states: "One should give a garment, or a fringe, or a tuft of wool. Consequently, because the fringe is both prescribed and prohibited, there is an option between them. Vyāghra says:
"One should offer perfumes, flowers, and the like, as well as incense and a lamp.
O ancestors, this garment and fringe [I] offer to you individually."
Bṛhaspati says: Having worshipped them with incense, lamps, garlands, perfumes, as well as garments, ornaments, and so forth,
one should place a water-vessel upon them.
From the *Brahma Purāṇa*: One should offer honey, clarified butter, water, the *argha* oblation, flowers, incense, ointment,
and the sacrificial cake (*bali*) according to the prescribed rule, so that it becomes an eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) offering.
From the Purāṇa:
Whatever food, whether fit to be chewed or swallowed, that is cooked in the house and is not forbidden,
must never be eaten at the base of the *piṇḍas* without first being offered there.

Viṣṇu: "Having made a scattering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should present water for the guest-offering (argha), flowers, incense, ointments, and various kinds of food—both edible and non-edible—and also a vessel of water mixed with honey, ghee, and sesame seeds. Manu:
"And with a concentrated mind, one should smell those rice-balls as they have been placed [on the ground].
(1.241) "In the same manner, one should offer this to the maternal grandfathers; thereafter, one should offer water for sipping (ācamana)."

In the same manner, one should offer the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the maternal grandfathers just as for the paternal ancestors. Then, one should cause the Brahmins to perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*). Viṣṇu states: "Having given the water for rinsing the mouth to those facing north, one should then give it to those facing east. Furthermore, having sprinkled the site of the *śrāddha* with the words "Well-sprinkled! (*suprokṣitam*), one should perform everything while holding *darbha* grass in the hand. Nārāyaṇa says:
"If those twice-born ones perform the rite of 'well-being' (*svasti*) without moving that vessel, that food is consumed by the Asuras, while the ancestors depart disappointed."
Bṛhaspati says: But those twice-born who pronounce blessings while the vessels remain [unemptied],
their ancestors depart as they came, having uttered a curse and being left without hope.
Jātūkarṇya says:
At a śrāddha, the vessels should be moved by oneself, a disciple, or a son;
never by women, nor by a child, nor by a member of one's own caste.
Then he should perform the recitation of the benediction (svastivācana) and likewise the offering of imperishable water (akṣayyodaka).
Having given the sacrificial fee according to his ability, he should utter the word *svadhā*.
Being authorized with the words "Let it be spoken," he should say, "Let *svadhā* be uttered for the ancestors. (1.243)
When they have said, "Let there be svadhā," one should then pour water upon the ground.

Then, after the *viprācamana* (the sipping of water by the Brahmins), one should perform the *svastivācana*. The meaning is that one should cause the Brahmins to say, "May you pronounce *svasti*. When they have said "Svasti," one should offer the *akṣayyodaka* (imperishable water). The meaning is that, immediately after pronouncing the name together with the gotra and relationship in the genitive case, one should say "May it be imperishable" (*akṣayyam astu*) and pour water upon those [pindas] for their satisfaction. Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, one should cause the utterance of *svadhā*; the meaning is that one should request permission from the Brahmins by saying, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be pronounced. When they have granted permission by saying "Let it be pronounced," and the request has been made to the Brahmins, "Let *svadhā* be pronounced for the ancestors, the fathers, and so forth," and they have replied, "Let there be *svadhā*," one should pour water on the ground. Śātātapa says:
For the sake of accomplishing one's intended purpose, one should cause [the sacrificer] to recite his desired prayers:
"Long are the sun’s horses; the rivers; and the three steps of Viṣṇu."
Thus, by bowing down to them, one shall obtain long life;
the gods abide in the midst of the waters, and everything is established in the waters.
May the auspicious waters placed in the hand of the Brahmin be for our well-being;
Lakṣmī dwells in flowers, and Lakṣmī dwells in the lotus.
May Lakṣmī dwell forever in the Soma; may there always be serenity for me.
May my merit be undiminished, and may there be peace, nourishment, and fortitude for me.
Whatever brings about the highest good in this world, may that always be mine;
and in every case regarding sacrificial fees, may we likewise have much to give.
They should say, "So be it," and he should accept that with his head bowed.
From the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
Once they have sipped water (*ācānta*), one should offer water, flowers, and barley,
while reciting the mantra "yavo 'si" (Thou art barley), endowed with faith and devotion.
One should likewise offer inexhaustible water mixed with sesame seeds, clarified butter, and honey;
having spread upon the ground kusha grass together with pavitras and likewise with sesame seeds.
From the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa:
"Golden and silver vessels, beautiful and auspicious;
elephants, horses, chariots, vehicles, and prosperous houses."
One should always consider that sandals, shoes, umbrellas, chowries, and antelope skins are meritorious as sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) in sacrifices.
The meaning is that one should form the understanding: "This very thing is the sacrificial fee (yajñadakṣiṇā).
Even a poor person should give a sacrificial fee to the Brahmins according to his ability;
in that manner.
Whatever is most excellent in the world and whatever is dear to one's own mind—
all that should be given to the ancestors by one who desires for them imperishable merit.
The gift of silver is said to lead to infinite, inexhaustible heaven;
by that gift, virtuous sons indeed deliver their ancestors.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Could there be some preeminent man in our lineage who would give a cow while she is being born as a gift to an eminent Brāhmaṇa?"
"Perhaps there might be someone in our family, that best of men, who would duly give a black antelope skin along with gold-horned [cattle] and hooves."
Pāraskara states:
"To Brahmins seated in a single row during a Śrāddha rite, food to be chewed and food to be swallowed should be given equally; however, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) may be according to one's means."
The meaning is "according to the [status of the] recipient. Vṛddha-Gautama says:
"One should first give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the 'pitṛ-devas,' and then to the two.

Those for whom the ancestors are their gods are the *pitṛ-devas*; that is to say, those who partake in the *śrāddha* as the ancestral deities. To them one should first give the fee, and then to the two—the two Brahmins of the Vaiśvadeva rite; such is the meaning. The locative case in "to the two" (*dvayoḥ*) is used in the sense of the dative. Consequently, the fee is to be given only to the Brahmins, not to the ancestors and others. And so Devala says:
Then, after the twice-born have sipped water, he should bestow upon them a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of gold,
gems, objects of enjoyment, and other things, according to his own ability.

This being the case, the term *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee) maintains its consistency. Furthermore, as for the statement, "The *dakṣiṇā* should be given to the ancestors," that refers specifically to the connection with Brahmins who have the ancestors as their presiding deities (*pitṛdevatya*). Otherwise, the Brahmins would not possess ownership over the sacrificial fees. [Regarding] Jamadagni:
all ritual action is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*), with the exception of the giving of the *dakṣiṇā*.

The Blessed One Matsya also considered that [the rite] should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya). Kātyāyana states: "Having spread out *kuśa* grass with *pavitra* blades upon which the *svadhā* is to be pronounced, he asks, 'I shall cause the *svadhā* to be pronounced. When [the Brahmins] have replied, 'Let it be pronounced,' and they have been authorized by saying, 'Let the *svadhā* be pronounced for the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers,' while the Brahmins are saying, 'May there be *svadhā*,' he should pour water with the mantra 'ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ' onto the *kuśa* grass together with the *pavitra* blades. (1.242, 243)
"May all the gods be pleased," and when this has been spoken by the Brahmins, he should mutter it.
"May our donors increase, as well as our Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. [1.245]

When the performer and the Brahmins have said, "May all the gods be pleased," the giver should mutter the verse: "May our donors increase. From the Purāṇa: While holding barley-water with the left hand using the divine *tīrtha*, he should recite: "And may all the gods be pleased in this sacrifice."
In the Matsya Purāṇa: Then, having offered the recitation of *svadhā* and water for the Viśvedevas, the wise man, facing eastward, should receive blessings from the twice-born.
When the twice-born have said, "May the ancestors be non-terrible," and "May they be so," and he has likewise been told by them in return, "May our lineage increase," and "So be it."
May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give.
And when they said again, "May these true blessings come to pass," he replied, "So be it."
In this regard, Baudhāyana [states] after the verse "May our givers increase": "May our food be abundant, may we receive guests;
may there be those who ask of us, and may we not have to ask anyone."
Thus the mantra is traditionally handed down. 1.244, 245.
Having spoken these affectionate words and having prostrated,
he should dismiss them with the words "Vāja-vāja," being joyful, beginning the dismissal with the ancestors.

Having recited the mantra previously mentioned and having spoken pleasant words to the Brahmins, he should bow to them and, being pleased, dismiss them with this *triṣṭubh* verse beginning with "vāje vāje," revealed by Vasiṣṭha and addressed to the *pippṛ* deities. In this context, the dismissal of the ancestors (*pitṛvisarjana*) occurs first. Regarding this, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states: "Then, standing before them and receiving the water-vessel, he should dismiss them with the tip of a *kuśa* blade while muttering 'vāje vāje'."

The dismissal of the Brahmins (*vipravisarjana*) must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), according to the statement of Śaunaka: "Having placed the thread over the left shoulder, he should dismiss them with the words *svadhā*; or he should dismiss them with *astu svadhā*; or with *astu svadhā*. The mantra is to be repeated for each individual Brahmin, because it is impossible to perform the dismissal—consisting of touching the tips of the *kuśa* grass—at all the Brahmins simultaneously. Bṛhaspati says: "Today my birth has become fruitful through the salutation of your feet;
today, by your grace, all those born in my lineage have gone to heaven."
"Those such as these who have been distressed by me through the giving of vegetables and other things—having forgotten that accumulation of distress with my mind, you ought to forgive them. (1.246)
Having turned face upwards that vessel for the ancestors into which you previously placed the remnants in the arghya-vessel, one should dismiss the Brahmins. 1.247.

That *arghya* vessel into which the remnants of the *arghya* offerings were previously poured should first be turned face-up; thereafter, the dismissal of the Brahmins mentioned earlier should be performed. Regarding those who maintain that the *pitṛ-pātra* in their home should be placed face-up and covered with another vessel, following that opinion, it is stated in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* after the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*):
"Then, having taken water from the vessels containing the remnants and reciting the *ūrjaṃ vahantī* verses, he sprinkles the *piṇḍas*. (1.247)
Having circumambulated [the vessel] clockwise, he should eat what has been served to the ancestors;
he should remain celibate for that night together with the Brahmins.

Having circumambulated those Brahmins and followed them as they depart, one should eat only the food remaining from the *śrāddha*, which was served to the ancestors. Both the performer of the *śrāddha* and the guests should observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for that night. From the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should perform a circumambulation outside and follow [the Brahmins] for eight steps, accompanied by one's circle of kinsmen and together with one's sons and wife."
Having returned and prostrated, and having sprinkled water around the fire,
he who knows the mantras should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite as well as the regular bali offering.

"Outside the house" means outside [the village]. Kātyāyana says: "Having dismissed [the guests] with the mantra *vāje vāje*, having followed them [a short distance] with *amā vājasya*, and having circumambulated them clockwise, one should enter. Manu says:
"Having washed his hands and sipped water (*ācamya*), he should provide for his kinsmen;
having given to his kinsmen according to his ability, he should also honor his relatives."
"Therefore, one should perform the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*); such is the established dharma.

[513] "Relatives" (*jñātayaḥ*) are those on the father’s side; "kinsmen" (*bāndhavāḥ*) are those on the mother’s side. By the term "domestic offering," the entire ritual cycle beginning with the *vaiśvadeva* is indicated, according to the *Purāṇa*:
"Then, having prostrated with devotion, one should dismiss the Brahmins."
And he should follow him as far as the gate, and return only after having expressed his approval.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Then one should perform the daily rites and likewise feed the guest;
some men, however, desire that the daily rite for the ancestors (śrāddha) also be performed.
For the ancestors, it is not the same as for others; one should perform the remainder as previously described.
Others say that it should be done with a separate cooking, while some say it should be as before.
Then that man should eat that food together with his servants and others.
The daily rites (*nityakriyā*) consist of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and others. Another Smṛti states:
"A *śrāddha* performed without hospitality for guests is demonic (*āsura*), provided that [guests] are available.
When one ought to say 'Give! Give!', if it be otherwise, the fault falls upon the eater."
Devala says: Having completed the ancestral rite (pitṛmedha) and having extinguished the lamp with his hand,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), wash his hands, and satisfy his kinsmen with the remnants.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Sisters and kinsmen are indeed always to be honored at *śrāddha* ceremonies."
Likewise: "Bards, panegyrists, and heralds, as well as those skilled in the triple symphony of song, dance, and instrumental music,
if they receive no gain at the ancestral rites (śrāddha), destroy one's great fame."
Therefore, those too must be separated, both individually and as a whole.

Singing, dancing, and instrumental music constitute the triple symphony (*tauryatrika*). Devala says: "If a Brahmin, having given a *śrāddha*, does not eat at any time thereafter, the gods do not accept the sacrificial offerings (*havis*), nor do the ancestors accept the ancestral oblations (*kavya*)."

Āpastamba states: "Having taken portions from all [the food], he eats a mouthful slightly less than half a *grāsa* with the subsequent *yajus*: 'Established in the vital breath, I offer the nectar; may my self enter into Brahman for the sake of immortality. This refers to the case of fasting on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*) and other such occasions as previously resolved, as well as cases where eating is prohibited due to disease. The subsequent *yajus* is: "Established in the vital breath, I offer the nectar; may my self enter into Brahman for the sake of immortality. Consequently, by the rule "one should eat what has been partaken of by the ancestors," eating is indeed enjoined as a duty. In that regard, even if meat and similar items have been partaken of by the ancestors, they must not be consumed by one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) on the day of the fast (*aupavasathya*), according to the Vedic injunction: "One should observe the vow without beans and without meat. However, one who does not maintain the sacred fires may certainly consume them. Furthermore, regarding that which...
"The fourteenth day destroys one's lineage up to the seventh generation through the anointing of the head;

the fifteenth day [destroys it] through eating meat; likewise, the eighth day [destroys it] through sexual desire. By such statements, the avoidance of meat on the fifteenth day precludes the consumption of meat as prompted by passion (*rāga*); it does not [preclude it] as prescribed by rule (*vidhi*). Furthermore, since the injunction for the food to be consumed during ancestral rites (*pitṛ-sevita-bhojana*) is fulfilled by a single act of eating, its repetition is purely motivated by passion. As stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
One who, having been appointed to a *śrāddha*, engages in sexual intercourse after eating, or after feeding others, or after appointing others,
causes his own ancestors to sink into the semen within the womb.

*Vyavāya* means sexual intercourse. Śātātapa says: "Those crooked men who, having performed a *śrāddha*, eat at another *śrāddha*, their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water."
Likewise:

"Furthermore, after eating, one should avoid these eight: eating again, traveling on a journey, carrying a load, Vedic study, sexual intercourse, giving a gift, accepting a gift, and performing a fire sacrifice or a funeral rite."
Yama says: A twice-born man who has partaken in a śrāddha feast should drink water ten times while reciting the Gāyatrī;
thereafter, he should perform the sandhyā worship, recite prayers, and also offer oblations.

In this case, the mantra is recited only once, because there is no difference in the purpose (*kārya*). For where the function of a mantra is specifically enjoined, the mantra also repeats with each performance of the action (*karmavṛtti*). This is the case, for example, with the mantras for pouring out (*nirvāpa*), taking the clarified butter (*ājyagrahaṇa*), and cutting the sacrificial grass (*dhūpacchedana*). Since these mantras reveal the substance (*dravya*) that is to be consecrated through actions such as pouring out, it is logical that the mantra should repeat according to the distinction of those acts. From the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"One should always avoid eating again, traveling on a journey, gambling, physical exertion, sexual intercourse, Vedic study, quarreling, and sleeping during the day."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "And when the sun has set, having become purified, one should place all the vessels used by the Brahmins into water with their openings facing downwards."
And on the second day, there shall be the washing of all the vessels in that manner. || 1.248 ||
Having prescribed the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha, which serves as the archetype for all śrāddhas, he now speaks in order to prescribe the *ābhyudayika* śrāddha, which is its modification:
"Thus, having performed the circumambulation clockwise, one should worship the *nāndīmukha* ancestors at a rite of prosperity (*vṛddhi*).
The rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) should be mixed with curd and jujube fruits (*karkandhu*), and the ritual acts should be performed with barley. (1.249)

In rites for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), such as marriages and the like, one should worship the ancestors known as the *nāndīmukha* in the manner prescribed for the *pārvaṇa* śrāddha. "Having performed circumambulation" means while performing circumambulation; here, the sequence of actions is not intended to be significant, just as in the expression "closing the eyes and laughing. Here there is another specific detail: the ritual acts should be performed with rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) mixed with *karkandhu* fruits, barley, and sesame seeds. *Karkandhu* is the jujube fruit (*badara*). Regarding this, the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* states:
"At the weddings of daughters and sons, upon entering a new house, at the naming ceremony of children, and likewise at the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍākarma*) and others..."
At the parting of the hair ceremony and upon seeing the face of a son or other offspring,
the self-restrained householder should worship the Nāndīmukha class of ancestors.
O lord of men, one should feed an even number of Brahmins facing the east.
The Matsya Purāṇa states:
"In a continuous flow of festivals and joys, during sacrifices, marriages, and other auspicious ceremonies,
the Mothers are to be worshipped first, and the Fathers immediately thereafter."
Then the maternal grandfathers and likewise the Viśvedevas are to be honored.
Śātātapa says:
One should not perform any Vedic rite without first having offered Śrāddha to the ancestors;
likewise, all three mothers must be worshipped with great care beforehand.
If one serves the śrāddha meal without having performed the Mātṛ-yāga,
the Mothers, possessed by anger, will indeed inflict harm upon him.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Now, regarding rites for prosperity that are auspicious and beautiful— such as a birth, the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), a marriage, or [the birth] of a son..."
One should satisfy the ancestors known as the Nāndīmukhas according to the prescribed ritual.
Śātātapa says: "The Śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed by that for the paternal ancestors, and then for the maternal grandfathers;
thus, at a Vṛddhi ceremony, three Śrāddhas are prescribed."
Bhāskara says: At the time of the *niṣeka* rite, during the *soma* sacrifice, likewise at the *sīmantonnayana*, and at the *puṃsavana*,
the *śrāddha* should be understood as performed as an ancillary part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*), like a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*.
Kātyāyana says: Regarding the group of rites beginning with marriage, of which we have heard that Garbhādhāna is at the end—
here, one should perform the Śrāddha only once at the beginning of marriage, not at the start of each individual rite.
Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires, the two oblations, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the offering of bali, the new-moon sacrifice, the full-moon sacrifice,
and the first-fruits sacrifice— thus do the wise who know the sacrifice declare.
In this very way, the Śrāddha should be performed for these [ancestors] collectively, not separately;
there should be no Śrāddha on the Aṣṭakā days, nor is a Śrāddha within another Śrāddha desired.
From the Purāṇa: Some men maintain that it should be devoid of the Vaiśvadeva offering;
in that case, an even number of twice-born men should be invited, and they should be honored by circumambulating them from left to right. [516]
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
One should perform the Śrāddha for the maternal ancestors on the day before, that for the paternal ancestors on the day of the rite,
and that for the group of maternal grandfathers on the following day.
Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"If [the performer] is unable [to perform them] on separate days, they perform the three Śrāddhas on a single day, or [employ] a single Vaiśvadeva ritual for all."
Śātātapa says:
"The Śrāddha for the maternal ancestors is prescribed for the forenoon, and that for the paternal ancestors for midday;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers, three Śrāddhas are prescribed on the occasion of a Vṛddhi (prosperity) ceremony."
Vasiṣṭha says: One should perform three Śrāddhas, or [perform] the Vaiśvadeva rite as a single ritual procedure (tantra).
One should first make the offerings for the mothers, and immediately thereafter for the fathers.
Then, one should offer the rice-balls (piṇḍas) for the maternal grandfathers in due order.
Kātyāyana says: Those rites which are to be performed repeatedly by those who perform rituals—
these [specific days] should not be used for over-frequent practice, nor for the Śrāddha.
When the rites for the Mothers are being performed in groups, the worship of the Mothers should be done only once;
likewise, the śrāddha should be performed only once at the beginning, not separately for each group.

And this entire restoration (*pratyuddhāra*) has been explained by the birth of a son; thus, it pertains to this subject. This is its meaning: the restoration of one who has fallen [from his caste] after having performed penance—that is, his readmission (*jñātiparigraha*)—is explained by the birth of a son. All those sacraments (*saṃskāra*), such as the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) and others, which are performed when a son is born, must be performed for him as well. And in this way, because the sacraments such as the birth-rite and others are performed simultaneously, they constitute a performance "in groups" (*gaṇaśaḥ*). "The father should give [offerings] to his own ancestors on account of the sacramental rite of his son."
Until the carrying away of the funeral cakes for them; but in the absence of that [son], it is according to their order.

At an *abhyudaya-śrāddha* (prosperity rite), the father should offer the funeral balls (*piṇḍas*) to his own ancestors until the marriage of those sons—that is, up to their wedding. In the absence of that father, [the duty falls] according to the order of succession. Here, by the word "order" (*krama*), the brother or others immediately following the father are indicated. Regarding the father’s obligation to perform the *śrāddha* and other rites at the son’s marriage, it has been stated by the phrase "at the marriages of daughters and sons"; however, the separate entitlement of the groom himself has also been stated by the phrase "without having sacrificed to the ancestors, one should not perform the *śrāddha*. Therefore, at the marriage of a son, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* must be performed separately both by the father and by the son. And by the son...

"One who possesses the sacred fire (agnimān) should offer [the śrāddha] to those same persons to whom his father would have offered it"—relying on this injunction, the rite should be performed. And here, the mention of "one possessing the fire" is intended as an indicator for any qualified person in general. For this very reason, at the *samāvartana* ceremony, a student whose father is still living offers the śrāddha to his grandfather and others. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
"But in the case of a mother’s śrāddha, if Brahmins are not available, one may indeed perform the worship."
Accompanied by their sons, these eight fortunate women were filled with joy.
From the Caturviṃśatimata:
Now, when an occasion for prosperity (abhyudayika) has arisen, the installation of deities is prescribed;
it is the cause of increase for castes, duties, families, guilds, and the world.
Three are to be honored on the father’s side, and likewise three on the maternal grandfather’s side;
these are declared to be the mothers, with the paternal and maternal aunts as the eighth.
