On the paternal side, there are three: mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother. On the maternal side, there are three: maternal grandmother, maternal paternal grandmother, and maternal paternal great-grandmother. Likewise, there are eight mothers: [the above six] plus maternal aunt and paternal aunt.

Having worshipped Brahmāṇī and the other seven [goddesses], as well as Durgā, Kṣetrapāla, and Gaṇādhipa, at the beginning of rites for prosperity (vṛddhi) and so forth, one should thereafter worship the Nāndīmukha ancestors.

Having honored the paternal ancestors beginning with the mother, and then the maternal grandfathers as well, some [teachers] say that the maternal grandmothers should then be honored; thereafter, an even number of twice-born men should be fed.

Kātyāyana says: In all rites and other ceremonies, the Mothers together with their troop-leaders must be worshipped with diligence; when they are worshipped, they in turn bestow worship [upon the worshipper].
And upon bright images, or those depicted on cloth and the like,
or even upon heaps of unbroken grains, with various kinds of food offerings.
One should cause five streams of clarified butter to flow against the wall, or seven streams; they should be neither too low nor too high.
And having recited the life-prolonging mantras for the sake of peace, he remained there with a concentrated mind.
Additional verses provided in the edition: "Lalitā, Umā, Gaurī, Ambikā, Salilāśrayā, Bhagāhī, and Bhagākṣī— these are proclaimed as the seven streams."
Anumati, Rākā, Sinīvālī, and likewise Kuhū;
Dhātrī, Sarveśvarī, and also Annaiśvarī.
These deities, who are always the presiding deities of the devotee's body,
are indeed to be worshipped on the branch of the walnut tree, dwelling there eternally in solitude.
"The omnipresent Mahāgaṇapati is to be worshipped in a clay ball;
the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) smeared with ghee is the first [offering], and honey and meat is the second. Thus [it is said].
The *āyuṣyāṇi* [hymns] are those beginning with the *ā no bhadra* verses. As for the Mothers:
Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, and Aindrī— these seven are considered the Mothers (Mātṛs) in their respective order.
Or alternatively:
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā, Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, the Mothers, the Mothers of the World.
One should offer Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi, together with the Self-deity;
one should present water, the Arghya offering, fragrance, flowers, incense, and a lamp.
From the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"A wise person seeking prosperity should perform the *śrāddha* for the gods in the forenoon,
using the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*savya*), and with straight blades of *darbha* grass."
[He should circumambulate] to the left [and then] to the right; likewise, being self-restrained and pure, he should feed an even number of Brāhmaṇas at a rite for prosperity (vṛddhi).
He should cause them to recite: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be satisfied."
Atri says:
An increase [in prosperity] may indeed occur in the forenoon, except for that occasioned by a birth.
Upon the birth of a son, a wise man should perform a śrāddha at that very moment.

Kātyāyana states: "In rites for prosperity (*ābhyudayika*), the ritual procedure is performed from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*); the recitation of mantras is performed excluding those dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*); the *darbha* grasses are straight; barley serves the purpose of sesame seeds; the question regarding satisfaction is 'Is it prepared? (*saṃpannam*?); the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) are mixed with curd, jujube fruits, and unhusked rice; he asks, 'Shall I invoke the Nāndīmukha ancestors?'; in place of the word 'imperishable' (*akṣaya*), he says, 'May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased'; he asks, 'Shall I cause the Nāndīmukha ancestors to pronounce the benediction?'; and he should employ the formula 'svadhā' as: 'May the Nāndīmukha fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers be pleased. He should feed an even number of guests. Thus it is said.
Hereafter I shall explain the specific detail that occurs here:
the Brahmins invited in the morning, both in even numbers on both sides.
"Having seated [the guest], one should give the *kuśa* grass with the right hand alone.
The syntactical connection is "having seated [him] in the morning. The invitation (*āmantraṇa*) takes place on the preceding day itself. Likewise:
"For there is never any bending down of the left knee."
One should always serve even one's ancestors here with devotion, just as one would the gods.

Having seated them upon kusha grass after they have been offered [the invitation] with the words "To the ancestors," one should cause the arghya water to be presented to the ancestors, addressing them by their lineage names and personal names.

In this [rite for the gods], the practice of circumambulation with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya) is not performed, nor is the *pitrya* tīrtha (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) prescribed;
indeed, one should not perform the filling of the vessels and other such acts in the manner used for the ancestors.

Having placed the pairs of hands with the right hand uppermost and the tips of the fingers joined by the pavitra grass, the arghya should be offered; it is not given here to each individual separately.

The offering of *arghya* should be performed by joining the hands of two pairs of Brahmins; in that case, the hand of the elder Brahmin should be placed on top. Likewise, the three-fold recitation of "madhu, madhu, madhu" intended for those wishing to eat, which follows the *Gāyatrī*, is to be performed here excluding the *Madhumatī* mantras.
While they are eating, one should never recite the *Pitṛsaṃhitā*;
instead, another auspicious recitation, such as the *Soma-sāman* and so forth, should be performed.
Whatever portion of that food there may be, even as much as a sesame seed or a barley grain,
which remains in proximity to the leavings when the [guests] are satiated, it becomes the opposite in this case.
When [the guests] say "It is well-prepared," they are satisfied; this is prescribed as the point for inquiry. When it is replied, "It is very well-prepared," one should offer the remaining food.

But upon the darbha grass with its tips pointing eastward, having addressed the first [ancestor] as before, one should pour water without sesame seeds at the root-end, saying: "Ava nenikṣva" (Be purified).
The first is a Brahmin who is the foremost of those belonging to the Paṅkti group;
in the second and third [seats], in the central region and the foremost region respectively,
one should place the maternal grandfather and the others to the left of these very [paternal ancestors].
Having set aside a portion of all the food, having sprinkled it with condiments,
and having mixed it with unbroken grains, jujube fruits, and curd, he should then face the east.
Having offered rice balls the size of bilva fruits like those used for the foot-washing,
one should then again perform the foot-washing with the water used for washing that vessel.

In the rites of ancestral offerings (śrāddha), by offering successive balls of rice (piṇḍa) one after another, each subsequent one becomes superior; and by performing the ritual actions from bottom to top, each preceding one becomes inferior.
Therefore, in all *śrāddha* rites— whether those performed on auspicious occasions (*vṛddhimat*) or others—
one should offer the rice grains so that they are slightly attached at the base, middle, and top portions [of the blades].
One should silently cast perfumes and other offerings, and thereafter cause the twice-born to sip water (ācamana).
This same procedure, excluding the barley and other grains, should apply in other cases as well.
In a region sloping toward the south, for one facing the south,
upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south— this is recorded as the rule for other [rites].
Then one should sprinkle the first [seat] with the words,
"May it be well-sprinkled," and likewise the even-numbered seats with water, saying, "May the waters be auspicious."
Immediately after the offering of flowers, one should say, "May there be joy," and then present the unbroken grains (akṣata), saying, "May there be well-being and freedom from misfortune."
The offering of imperishable water (akṣayyodaka) is prescribed to be performed in the same manner as the offering of the guest-water (arghya).
One should always perform it with the dative case-ending alone, and never with the dative-accusative ending (caturthī).
When all the prayers have been responded to by the best of the twice-born,
one who has placed the vessels face upwards should sprinkle water over the rice-balls covered by the sacred grass.
Having caused the auspicious benediction to be recited by an even number of Brahmins, and having always grasped the thumb of the leading Brahmin, he should then bow down and follow after him.

The *dhurya* is the leader at the head of the row. The *Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* states: "In the *ābhyudayika* (rite for prosperity), an even number of Brahmins [are invited]; the *darbha* grasses are rootless. Facing north, one should give [the offerings] to those facing east; or, facing east, to those facing north. There are two *darbha* blades as purifiers (*pavitra*), and four vessels with handles (*sopayāma*). Having consecrated them with the mantra *śaṃ no devīḥ*, he pours barley (*yava*) into them with the formula: 'Barley you are! Soma is your deity; you are the essence of cows, created by the gods. Like the ancients, through the satisfaction of the Lord, gladden the worlds of the Nāndīmukha ancestors for us, *svāhā*! 'The ancestors be pleased'—this is the formula for their acceptance and dismissal. The same applies to the father and grandfather in the subsequent rites, and the fire-oblation (*agnaukaraṇa*) is mandatory. The oblation is performed with the utterance of *svāhā*. The grasping of the thumb is done with the mantra *ato devā avantu naḥ*. At the verse *idaṃ viṣṇur vi cakrame*, one should cause [the Brahmins] to hear the *pāvamānī* hymns, the *śaṃvatī* verses, the *aindrī* verses, and the *apratiratha* hymn. After they have eaten, having smeared the places where the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are to be offered with cow dung, having spread *kuśa* grass with tips pointing eastward upon them, and having adorned them, there is an offering of rice mixed with ghee and jaggery (*guḍaudana*) separately in each case. With half of that, one should offer two oblations of ghee in each instance. One should dismiss them with the formula: 'May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased. The ritual procedure is performed clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*). Barley takes the place of sesame seeds; everything is done twice, twice. Thus says the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*.
O lord of men, O mighty-armed one, in this world one regards dharma when performing the *vṛddhiśrāddha*; the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) may be performed or not performed.
Thus ends the procedure for the Nāndīmukha Śrāddha. 1.249.
Now he states the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite:
"The *ekoddiṣṭa* is devoid of the deities; it has a single *argha* offering and a single purifying blade of grass (*pavitraka*).
It is indeed devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*) and the *agnaukaraṇa* oblation, and is performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). (1.250)
At the point where the word "akṣayya" (imperishable) occurs, he should say "upatiṣṭhatām" (may it attend) during the dismissal of the Brahmins;
he should say "abhiramyatām" (may you take pleasure), and they should reply, "We have taken pleasure."

The *śrāddha* performed with reference to a single person is called *ekoddiṣṭa*. It is devoid of the *daiva* portion, meaning it is without the *viśvedevas*. In that rite, there is only one *arghya* offering and one *pavitra*; it is also devoid of the invocation (*āvāhana*) mantra and the *agnaukaraṇa* (offering into the fire). Whatever ritual action is performed in the *pārvaṇa* with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*), here it should be done with the thread over the right shoulder (*apasavya*). *Apasavya* means *prācīnāvīta*. The mantra "upatiṣṭhatām" should be used in place of the mantra "akṣayyam astu" for the dismissal of the Brahmins; one should say "abhiramyatām" instead of "vāje vāje. The Brahmins should reply, "We have been gratified" (*abhiratāḥ smaḥ*). If many Brahmins are appointed for the single dedication to one person, the plural form is used. Kātyāyana says: "Now, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa*: there is one *arghya*, one *pavitra*, and one *piṇḍa*; there is no invocation, no *agnaukaraṇa*, and no *viśvedevas*. The question regarding satisfaction is 'svadhitaṃ' [is it well-prepared?], and the response is 'susvadhitaṃ' [it is well-prepared]. In place of 'akṣaya', one uses 'upatiṣṭhatām'; the dismissal is 'abhiramyatām', and others say the reply is 'abhiratāḥ smaḥ'. Śātātapa says:
The *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha that is mentioned here as being occasional (*naimittika*) should also be performed without [an offering to] the gods; one should feed an odd number of twice-born men.

The *ekoddiṣṭa* has been described, and it is of three kinds: the new (*nava*), the mixed (*miśra*), and the old (*purāṇa*). Among these, that which ends with the eleventh day is the new; from then until the end of the year is the mixed; and after that is the old. Regarding this, the rules concerning the new and the mixed are now stated. On this point, Vyāghra says: "On the eleventh day, in the fourth month, every month for a year, and likewise annually on the anniversary of death—the *ekoddiṣṭa* [is performed]."
*Addition in the manuscripts: "By the phrase 'and thus every year,' it is understood that in the fourth year, a pure *śrāddha* for three ancestors (*tripauruṣa*) should be performed," says Kātyāyana.
The *śrāddha* for one who maintains the sacred fire (*agnimant*) should be performed on the eleventh day after the cremation.
However, one should always perform the *dhruva* rites on the anniversary of the day of death.
Those [rites] after three fortnights are fixed. For this very reason Jātūkarṇya said:
"The śrāddha which occurs after three fortnights should take place on the anniversary of the day of death;
however, for a twice-born who maintains the sacred fires, one should perform it before the cremation. [522]
Likewise: "The twelve monthly rites, the first six-month rite,
and likewise the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*— these constitute the sixteen *śrāddhas*."
In order to define the two *śrāddhas* prescribed by the term "six-monthly," he says:
"When six months are completed by a single day, or when a year is deficient by three days,
then those two [śrāddhas] shall be considered 'six-monthly'."

The meaning is that when six months are deficient by one day or three days, and the year is likewise deficient by that same number [of days], then the *ṣāṇmāsika* (six-monthly) *śrāddha* should be performed. As stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*: "Without performing these sixteen [rites], even after performing them ten million times for a hundred years, one is not released from the state of a *preta*; so said the Lord Śiva."
For one who has died within a year, there are thirteen months;
for him as well, the śrāddha must be performed every month for a full year.
Likewise: "On the anniversary of death, one who desires the welfare of the deceased should give [offerings];
by what is given on the anniversary of death, the deceased is liberated from unwholesome karma."
The *śrāddha* for the collection of bones, the one at the end of three fortnights, the monthly *śrāddhas*,
those on the two empty lunar days (*riktatithi*), and likewise the sixteen *preta-śrāddhas*.
The meaning is that when two lunar days (*tithi*) are deficient by one day, [the rites] occur on the sixth and twelfth days of the month respectively. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi:
"In the case of the six-monthly and annual *śrāddha* ceremonies, these two should take place on the preceding day;
however, the monthly rites should be performed on their own respective day and also on the twelfth."
Likewise: "One should perform the sixteen śrāddhas prior to the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa;
all of them should indeed be performed according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa."
The funeral rites for the deceased and the sixteen ancestral offerings (śrāddhas) must be performed at their proper times; otherwise, one is not liberated from that [debt].

By this it is stated: even when the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed on the twelfth day or other such occasions, the monthly rites (*māsika*) must still be performed every month. Although these are *ekoddiṣṭa* rites intended for the liberation from the state of being a *preta*, they nevertheless include mantras; they are not mantra-less like the *navaśrāddha*. As Paiṭhīnasi says:
"Having passed the *navaśrāddha*, the son should offer the monthly rites on the anniversary of death, addressing the *preta* with mantras, for a year. [523]
"Having passed over" means "having completed. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"For men who have abandoned their bodies, the sixteen *śrāddhas* should always be performed on the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh [days]."

Then, for twelve months, the Śrāddha rites should be performed twelve times according to the number [of ancestors], as prescribed by the Śruti; therein, one should satisfy the Brahmins with offerings.
And from this it is understood that the monthly rite must be performed at the completion of each month. Śaṅkha says:
"One may perform the first *śrāddha* on the eleventh day even if he is impure;
his purity for that occasion is temporary, but he remains impure thereafter."
Paiṭhīnasi:
Even when immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) occurs, the offering for the deceased must be made on the eleventh day;
that very day is prescribed for his *śrāddha*, the funeral couch, and the final rites.
[The word *api* here implies "even though impurity (*aśauca*) exists.
The *Matsyapurāṇa*:
"Likewise, on the eleventh day, one should [feed] exactly eleven Brahmins."
At the end of the period of impurity (sūtaka), however, the son or others should feed an odd number of twice-born men.
On the second day, one should again perform the ekoddiṣṭa rite in the same manner.
[The phrase "at the end of the birth-impurity" refers specifically to the Brāhmaṇa; however, for the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras: Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states:
"In the seventh and the third, as well as in the first and the ninth [months]."
The śrāddha performed on the eleventh day is declared to be common to all.

The meaning is that [impurity] is common to the four castes (*varṇa*). Anticipating the objection that, "in that case, the period of impurity has been offered as a libation of sesame seeds," he says the same author: "But for all four castes, the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) is indeed distinct for each."
*Sūtaka* means impurity (*aśauca*). Among these, Yama speaks of the *navaśrāddhas*:
"That which is given here for a living being on the fourth, the fifth, the ninth, and likewise the eleventh day is called *navaśrāddha*."
Likewise: "For that twice-born who has maintained the sacred fires, but prior to the performance of the *saṃcayana* rite, one should feed an odd number of Brahmins; that is called the *navaśrāddha*."
Atri says:
For the sake of the deceased, one should feed ten Brahmins at the end of the period of impurity;
however, for the purpose of the *navaśrāddha*, one should feed a single Brahmin on the eleventh day.

This being the case, the feeding of Brahmins at the conclusion of the period of impurity (*āśaucāntakārya*) on the eleventh day is a separate ritual act from the nine-day *navāha-śrāddha*. Vyāsa states: "That which is given to a living being on the first, seventh, ninth, and likewise the eleventh [days] is called *navāha-śrāddha*."

In the *Bahvṛca-Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "They should offer the *navaśrāddha* together," meaning not individually. The mention of *navaśrāddha* is for the sake of illustration. For this very reason, Pracetas states: "The rites beginning with the eleventh day should be performed according to rule by the eldest [brother] in succession; they should not perform the *śrāddha* one by one, but the annual (*ābdika*) rite should be performed separately."
Within one year, however, all should perform the śrāddha together;
but when the year has passed, they should perform the śrāddha separately.
Uśanas says:
The *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and even the sixteen *śrāddhas* must indeed be performed by one [heir] alone,
even among those whose wealth has been divided.
The meaning is "by the eldest alone. Śātātapa states:
"The śrāddha which is offered on the eleventh day for one's mother and father must be performed by them together;
and the previous [funeral rites] must likewise be performed separately."
Regarding the ancestral rites of a year ago and so forth: Marīci states, "Whatever has been performed by the eldest alone with the consent of all,
or with undivided wealth, shall be considered as performed by all."
A tiger; one who seizes the wealth of a deceased person without having performed the funeral rites for that dead man;
and one who commits the murder of those belonging to the [four] castes—such a person shall diligently perform the penance prescribed for the killing of each respective caste.
Likewise: "For the sake of purifying the dwelling, nine *śrāddhas* should be diligently offered;
thereafter, for the sake of purifying the deceased, [one should perform them] on the anniversary of death for one year."

"For the sake of purifying the house" means for the purpose of satisfying the servants who have entered the house. Regarding purification, however, if there should be birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) at the end of the night, then likewise the nine *śrāddhas* should be offered at the proper time and in the proper order.
For him to whom these sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites are not offered,
his state as a *piśāca* remains fixed, even if hundreds of other *śrāddhas* are performed for him.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
But if one does not obtain the *navaśrāddha*, one is not released from the state of a preta;
however, by obtaining it before the completion of twelve days, one overcomes one's evil deeds.
In the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa: "The ancestors of that son who does not perform the Navaśrāddha, the Tri-pakṣa, the six-monthly, and the monthly rites have fallen into sin."
Vyāsa says: "The wise have recorded these sixteen Śrāddhas: those performed on the twelfth day, at the three-fortnight mark, at six months, monthly, and at the end of the year."
In the case of the six-monthly and annual śrāddhas, those two [the invitation and the preparation] should take place on the very day before.
The Āśvalāyana-Pariśiṣṭa states:
"The *navaśrāddha* lasts for ten days, while the *navamiśra* lasts for six seasons; beyond that, it is called *purāṇa*. Thus, the *śrāddha* is said to be of three kinds."

Nor does this [text] exclude the status of the eleventh-day rite as a *navaśrāddha* (new funeral rite), because its existence is ordained by other scriptural statements. In the *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa*: "He for whom the *navaśrāddha* and other such rites have not been performed has no entitlement to the monthly, six-monthly, or annual rites."
From the *Śaunaka-gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "In all funeral rites for the deceased, one should not say 'svadhā' nor 'abhiramyatām';
instead, one should dismiss [the guests] by saying 'may there be well-being' (*svasti astu*), omitting the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) and doing so only once."
In the *piṇḍa* of the *ekoddiṣṭa*, however, the word "after" (*anu*) is not appropriate;
one should not use the word "father" (*pitṛ*), for otherwise one becomes a slayer of one's father.
This refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites performed prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. In the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣ�ṭa*:

"Whether he be of a different lineage (*asagotra*) or the same lineage (*sagotra*), whether a woman or a man, whoever offers [the first oblation] on the first day shall complete it throughout the ten-day period."

The first funeral rite (navaśrāddha) is performed without water, without incense, and devoid of perfumes and garlands; it is without mantras and is devoid of both rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water libations.
[The offering] is without water and is priceless. [It consists of] the funeral cake (piṇḍa), water, and the ritual washing (avanejana). In the Varāha Purāṇa:
"Having understood that he will perform [the rite] tomorrow, one performs the act of inviting the Brāhmaṇas:
'You have gone to the divine world by the path ordained by Kṛtānta.'"
"O Brahmin, I appoint you with my mind, which has become like the wind;
I shall honor you with enjoyments. In this manner, one should invite the Brahmin.
When the sun had set, he went to the brahmin’s residence,
offered water for his feet according to the rules, and paid homage to that best of the twice-born.
Having washed the feet of the deceased with oil out of a desire for his welfare,
when the night has turned to dawn and the sun has risen;
Having had the shaving of the beard performed and the clipping of the nails thereafter,
one should provide the Brahmin with a bath and anointing according to the prescribed rite.
One should take a portion of ground and, immediately thereafter, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
having selected a place for the water-supply, a large sacrificial mound should be prepared.
One should designate a cremation ground on the bank of a river;
however, those who have departed and do not prepare a portion of the ground have failed to do so.
O auspicious lady, the world would be rendered as leftover food by him on that path;
neither the gods nor the ancestors ever accept anything from him here in this world.
By that leavings, O beautiful one, they fall into a terrible hell;
therefore, having bathed with oil and gone to a great river, [one should perform the rite].
Having meditated upon the sacred fords with his mind, the wise man should sprinkle himself with their waters;
having thus performed purification, he should then quickly summon a Brāhmaṇa.
O Mādhavī, seeing that the twice-born has arrived, you should perform the rites of hospitality;
having then offered the water for honor and the water for the feet, you should do so with a joyful and contented heart.
And one should prepare a seat according to the ritual procedure, accompanied by the mantra.
Likewise:
Having seated him upon an auspicious seat, one should provide an umbrella there.
An umbrella is given to the brahmin for the purpose of protection;
afterwards, one should give a pair of auspicious sandals that provide comfort to the feet,
[as well as] the ground with its scorching sands and its sharp thorns.
By giving a pair of sandals to a brahmin who is self-restrained and having performed the offering of sesame seeds, one enables the deceased to cross over difficult passages.
Having uttered the name and lineage of the preta immediately thereafter,
one who holds darbha grass in his hand should quickly summon him to the ground upon the earth.
The mantra:
"Having abandoned this world, you have gone to the supreme destination.
Having thus invoked him, one should offer perfumes, flowers, and incense.
Devala says: In all *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, one should offer the food to the Brahmins;
thereafter, one may eat at will oneself during the auspicious meal.

The phrase "in all *ekoddiṣṭa* rites" refers to the *navaśrāddha* (the nine-day funeral rites). In those cases, the remaining food should be given only to the eaters. The "auspicious meal" (*maṅgalabhojana*) consists of the remnants from the annual *ekoddiṣṭa*. For this very reason, Aṅgiras states:
"One should never eat what remains from the *navaśrāddhas*, nor that which has been kept overnight for the [deceased] planet, nor the food left over after being eaten by a married couple."
Bṛhaspati says: On the fourth day, food should indeed be given to the Brahmins by the kinsmen,
as well as cows, gold, and wealth, according to their capacity, for the sake of the deceased.
The meaning is that on the fourth day, [one should perform] the collection of the bones;
one should diligently give whatever was desired by the person while they were alive.

The grammatical connection is: "while he is still living. Satyavrata states: "Having risen in the morning and invited eleven Brāhmaṇas representing the deceased, one should perform the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) according to the rules in the afternoon, designating each one individually with various kinds of food, snacks, and savory dishes. The sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) consist of clothing, gold, a female slave, sandals, an umbrella, and a water-pot. Then, the gift of a bed to a virtuous recipient follows, after which rites such as the recitation of auspicious prayers (*svastyayana*) proceed. When the tenth day has passed, one should feed them one by one, designating each for that [deceased]; or, a bed may be given to a single virtuous person among them. Viṣṇu says: "Having performed the *śrāddha* for twelve days, one should perform it on the thirteenth day. Vyāsa [says]:
The son and the wife should perform the shaving of the head at the conclusion according to the prescribed rule;
any other person who is entitled to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) should likewise do so with a concentrated mind.
Likewise:

"On the day the period of impurity ends, one should undergo shaving for the mother and likewise for the Guru. This means that when the mother has passed away, or when the Guru has passed away, [one should shave]. Another Smṛti states:
On the day of the Bārhaspatya [Thursday], on the fourteenth lunar day, and at Tripuṣkara,
a householder should not perform the *navaśrāddha*, for fear of the loss of sons and wealth.
On the eleventh day of the moon, on Nandā, on Sinīvālī, on the day of Bhṛgu (Friday),
on the fourteenth day of the month of Nabhasya, and under the asterism Kṛttikā— these are the Tripuṣkara occasions.

The prohibition regarding the *Nandā* applies specifically to the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*); regarding *Śukra*, it applies specifically to the new moon; regarding the fourteenth, it applies specifically to the fourteenth day of the month of Bhādrapada; and regarding the *tripuṣkara*, it applies specifically to the *kṛttikā* constellation. Baudhāyana states: "The widow of a deceased person shall avoid honey, meat, and salt for one year; she shall sleep on the ground for six months—so says Maudgalya. This refers to the case of a non-Brāhmaṇa wife; however, a Brāhmaṇa wife must avoid honey and such things at all times. Pracetas states: "Food should always be given to the deceased for one year, according to the rules for their livelihood."
All sons should diligently perform [the rite] according to the procedure for the ekoddiṣṭa.
Having first poured [the water] onto a stone, one should then perform the śrāddha;
afterwards, one should pour [the remaining water] onto that very same stone according to the prescribed rule.

Hārīta says: "They do not accept blessings; they do not scatter food; they do not offer the *svadhā* call. While [the guests] are eating, one should mutter prayers, excluding those mantras addressed to the ancestors (*pitṛmantra*).
One should bestow sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) upon all of them in due order.
And likewise, according to one's ability, one should give gifts such as cows, land, gold, and so forth."
"One should give new vessels—in which the food is prepared and in which it is eaten—to those who have eaten. Likewise:

"There are no mantras for the *agnaukaraṇa* rite, and there is only a single offering of water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*). Until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony is completed, one should say 'Svasti' and then dispose of the offerings in the new vessels."
For indeed, without specifying [anyone else], everything is given right there for the sake of the preta.
Now he describes the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite:
"One should prepare four vessels joined with scented water and sesame seeds;
for the purpose of the *arghya* offering, one should pour the vessel of the deceased (*preta*) into the vessels of the ancestors (*pitṛ*). (1.252)
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," he should perform the remainder as previously described;
this Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite for a woman is likewise performed as an Ekoddiṣṭa.

One should prepare four vessels containing water mixed with perfumes such as sandalwood, as well as sesame seeds, in order to offer the *arghya* (water of honor) to the *preta*s and others. Having offered the *arghya* to the *preta*, one should pour the water from that vessel into the three vessels belonging to the grandfather (*pitāmaha*) and the other ancestors, using the two *anuṣṭubh* verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ," which were seen by Prajāpati, in due order for the ancestral deities and the living deities. As for the remaining rites, such as the invitation of the Brahmins and so forth, one should perform them according to the *pārvaṇa* ritual. This aforementioned procedure—consisting of the *pārvaṇa* rite dedicated to the grandfather and other deities, and the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite dedicated to the *preta*—is to be understood as the rite known as *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. This must be performed for a woman as well, and not for a man alone. On this point, the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* states: [529]
Having prepared four vessels and filled them with sesame seeds and water,
one should pour the contents of one vessel into the three vessels for the ancestors, pronouncing their names and lineages.

Śaunaka says: "Now, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, there are four water-vessels: one for the deceased (*preta*) and three for the others. One should join the first vessel to the [other] three vessels with the mantra, 'Our intention is indeed common' (*samānī va ākūtiḥ*). In this very same manner, one should join the first funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to the three [others]. By means of the two verses beginning with 'He unites with those rich in honey' (*madhumatībhiḥ saṃgacchate*), the fourth [deceased] becomes authorized. Thus says the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Having taken one of the four *arghya*-vessels with the left hand, and [pouring] water with sesame seeds (*tilodaka*) with the right hand alone..."
Recalling the mantra, "May the earth unite you with those who are equal," one should pour a fourth part of water into the hand of the deceased Brahmin.
Then, with the respective mantras for the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others,
one should offer that water individually with the two verses beginning with "ye samānāḥ."
According to that same procedure, as before, he should offer the *arghya* from the vessel for the deceased;
having presented the *arghya* to them, he himself should afterwards perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Because of the statement "to the grandfather and the others," the word *preta* refers to one who has recently passed away; it is not understood to mean "the father of the great-grandfather. Then, by that same procedure, having offered the water-libation (*avanejana*) at the base of the *darbha* grass for the father, he should offer the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) with devotion as before.
Having formed the *piṇḍa* and meditated upon it as having eight limbs and the luster of the Vasus,
one should then [place] gold, silver, and *darbha* grass upon that *piṇḍa* in three ways.
Having prepared this according to the rules, he should offer it to the Grandfather (Brahmā) and the others, saying:
"May the Earth, Vāyu, Agni, and Prajāpati unite with you."
One should recite this mantra with devotion, repeating it an equal number of times.
With the two verses beginning "ye samānāḥ," one should offer the deceased to the ancestors.
Then, having fashioned those three rice-balls (piṇḍas) into perfectly round shapes, one should worship them.
With water for the guest-offering (*argha*), flowers, incense, lamps, garlands, and ointments,
having first honored the principal ancestor, one should then honor the others in their proper order.

In this context, one should first perform the primary offering of the vessel and the *piṇḍa* for the father; thus it is understood that the term "deceased" (*preta*) is applied to the father. It is further understood that the vessel and *piṇḍa* of the father are to be cast into the vessels and *piṇḍas* of the grandfather and the others. Consequently, whatever is said by certain [authorities]—namely, that the vessel and *piṇḍa* belonging to the father’s great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*) should be divided into three parts and placed into the vessels and *piṇḍas* of the father and the others—that must be disregarded, as it contradicts the scriptural injunctions and conflicts with the statement of Śātātapa. For instance:
Among the hungry ghosts here who were bound by means of mantras,
they have indeed achieved their purpose once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed.

"Having crossed over from the state of a *preta* here, they have reached the company of the ancestors (*pitṛgaṇa*). Thus, the great-grandfather does not attain the status of a *pitṛ* at the time the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is being performed; rather, he had already attained that status previously. Therefore, for the father alone, the attainment of the status of a *pitṛ*, preceded by liberation from the state of a *preta*, is accomplished through the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Furthermore, the purpose of attaining the status of a *pitṛ* is stated in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa*:
"Then, O King, when that deceased one has attained the status of a *pitṛ*..."
With all the rites of the śrāddha, one should honor the ancestors who preceded him.

Furthermore, those headed by the fourth ancestor (the *caturtha-puruṣa*) have no entitlement to worship in the *śrāddha* rites, because they lack such entitlement beyond that point. This is due to prohibitions such as: "The funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) does not go to the fourth," and so forth. Viṣṇu states:
"Until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed, the deceased is indeed a *preta*. To him who has gone to the world of *pretas*, one should offer food along with a water-pot."
For one who has gone to the world of the ancestors, a śrāddha performed with faith [is beneficial];
therefore, offer a śrāddha even for one who has gone to the world of the ancestors.

By reflecting on the meaning of such statements as these, it is understood that prior to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, the deceased exists in a particular state characterized by the application of the term "preta" (*preta*). After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, however, a certain excellence (*atiśaya*) produced by that rite arises therein, which serves as the basis for the application of the term "pitṛ" (*pitṛ*). Furthermore, Śātātapa has stated:
"Having offered four *piṇḍas* according to the names of each, the giver of the *piṇḍas* should divide the first one into three parts with the two verses beginning with 'ye samānāḥ'."

Thus, as for the statement of Laugākṣi: "Having set aside the fourth *piṇḍa*, one should divide it into three parts and place them upon the *piṇḍas*," both of these refer specifically to the *piṇḍa* of a father or others who have not long passed away. The offering of that *piṇḍa* is prescribed either before or after the three *piṇḍas* of the grandfather and the rest. In that regard, when it is offered first, it is the "first" (*ādya*); when it is offered later, it is the "fourth. Consequently, statements such as "one should divide the first into three" and "having set aside the fourth *piṇḍa*, having divided it into three parts," refer precisely to that case. Even there, with the intention that the *piṇḍa* arises first for one who has passed a long time, the Purāṇic statement beginning with "but making the father the primary one" is the authoritative source. For this very reason, Viṣṇu stated: "At the end of a year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, preceded by the gods, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather. Śātātapa, however, states that the *piṇḍa* of the deceased is to be offered afterwards.
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* śrāddha preceded by the deities; one should feed the ancestors there, and furthermore, designate the deceased (*preta*) as well. Thus [says] Uśanas.
At the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, one should feed the Brahmins as in the Pārvaṇa ceremony;
however, one should separately prepare food according to the procedure for the Ekoddiṣṭa.
Thus it has been stated. Also in the Purāṇa:
"Having passed over two Śrāddhas, one should perform the Sahapiṇḍatā (the offering of the rice-balls together).
For those two, first there is the rite for three ancestors, and after that, the Ekoddiṣṭa."

The *tripuruṣa* rite has the three ancestors beginning with the grandfather as its deities; the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite has the deceased alone as its deity. Now, the person entitled to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is defined. Regarding this, the *Purāṇa* states: "Only a son—whether legitimate (*aurasa*) or born of the wife (*kṣetraja*)—should perform the *sapiṇḍatva* for his parents; this is indeed the eternal law."
This is the primary meaning of the scripture. In the absence of a son, others also have the right [to perform the rite]. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi states:
"A brother, or a brother's son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple, shall perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* when one has died without a son."
For one who is bereft of all kinsmen, the wife shall perform the sapindikarana;
or she may have it performed by a sacrificial priest (rtvij) or even by a family priest (purohita).
As for that which was stated by Sumantu:
"For one who is deprived of all kinsmen, a blameless wife shall perform [the rites];
or else, [they may be performed] by disciples, fellow-students, officiating priests, servants, or family chaplains."
"One should perform all rites except for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*;

it is certain that the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed by the sons and not by others"—this [rule] should be understood as applying when there is a son who is unable to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* due to being abroad or other such reasons. However, once the capacity is regained, even if the time has elapsed, it must be performed by the son alone. This has been stated in the *Vāyupurāṇa*:
"Having performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*, the son who knows the ritual procedure should perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for his father; so the experts of the Purāṇas know."
A son who has returned from a long absence should not perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite until he has performed the sixteen *śrāddha* ceremonies, even if a very long period of time has elapsed.

When one who has been away from home returns at the end of his journey, the son should not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite even after the lapse of time unless he has first performed the sixteen *śrāddhas*; rather, the meaning is that he must perform it only after having given them. If those [śrāddhas] have already been performed by a brother or another relative, then he should perform only the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Likewise: "If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* was not performed due to ignorance or delusion, it should nevertheless be performed according to the rules, even after a very long period of time."

Ignorance and delusion are intended to indicate all forms of incapacity. Sumantu says: "If a son, out of delusion, does not perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite while his father is still living, he shall suffer misery; once dead, he shall fall into hell."
The mention of "hearing" (the Veda) is intended as an illustration for any person qualified [to perform the rites]. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"The *navaśrāddha*, the *sapiṇḍana*, and the sixteen *śrāddhas*—all these should be performed by one alone, even among those whose wealth has been divided."
When divided, each individual must perform the annual rites and so forth separately;
when undivided, what is performed by one alone is performed by all.
Kātyāyana says:
If the grandfather passes away after the father,
the grandson must perform the sixteen śrāddhas, beginning with the eleventh-day rite.
If the grandfather has a son, it should not be performed by his grandson;
having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father, he should perform the monthly rites (*māsānumāsika*).
The two ancestors who have not yet been consecrated are not to be consecrated by the grandson or great-grandson;
rather, one should consecrate the father in that case—so said Kātyāyana.
It is the settled rule that one should consecrate one's father with the pure Pitāmaha, even if he is most sinful, or with the performer of evil deeds, provided he himself is pure.

The meaning is that the grandfather and great-grandfather, being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and not yet united with the *sapiṇḍas*, are neither to be consecrated by the grandson nor the great-grandson, nor are they to be made *sapiṇḍa*. This should be understood to apply when a closer relative capable of performing the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is present; however, in his absence, the grandson or others must indeed perform it because of the [required] *sapiṇḍatva*. Regarding the rule "even the most sinful [is purified] by one who is pure," this refers to cases other than those involving outcasts (*patita*) and the like. Thus, in the section following the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, Baijavāpa states: "One should not extend [the rites] to those cursed, outcasts, killers of embryos, or women who practice sorcery; 'extension' here means *sapiṇḍana*. Gautama says: "Those who perform evil deeds and women who practice sorcery should not be reunited. Then, concerning outcasts, Vṛddhayājñavalkya says:
One should not perform a śrāddha for those killed by snakes, or by horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles, nor for those who have committed suicide.
Regarding the *śrāddha* and other rites for the deceased, Chāgaleya says:
[Death occurs] from a Caṇḍāla, from water, from a serpent, from a Brāhmaṇa, or even from lightning.
And for those who have committed evil deeds, death comes at the hands of fanged beasts and wild animals.
Whatever water and offerings of rice balls are given to the departed spirits, none of that remains; it perishes in mid-air.
Therefore, he states the means for liberation from the state of a preta and for obtaining the offering of rice-balls (*udapiṇḍa*) and so forth:
"Out of fear of public reproach, men should perform the Nārāyaṇa-bali;
then food, along with ritual fees (*dakṣiṇā*), should be given even to them."
The word "tataḥ" (then) means immediately after the performance of the Nārāyaṇa-bali. Vṛddha-Yājñavalkya says:
"Whatever is offered with reference to Nārāyaṇa or Śiva for the sake of purification, that shall indeed be mine; otherwise, it shall not be so."
Because of the principle of inclusion:

whatever rite one performs for the sake of a deceased person, such as the offering of water, the *śrāddha*, or the presentation of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), that should be performed for Nārāyaṇa or for Śiva.
Yama says: "For those who have been killed by Caṇḍālas, or by horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles,
as well as for those killed by the rod of a Brahmin’s curse, a Śrāddha must not be performed."
For those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) as well as for those who have committed suicide,
the offering of water, the giving of funeral cakes (piṇḍa), and whatever Śrāddha rite has been performed [are likewise fruitless].
All that does not remain; it is plundered by Rākṣasas.
Another Smṛti states:
"Those killed by lightning, bulls, kings, Brahmins, water, horned animals, fanged beasts, or fire..."
Those who observe the vow of a great eunuch born in vain are not vessels for spiritual excellence.
"Vessels for water" means vessels for the water used in the *arghya* offering. Likewise:

"When one's father has been killed by a Brāhmaṇa or others, or has fallen from his caste, or has abandoned all attachments, or has died out of the natural order of succession, the offering should be given to those very persons to whom he himself would have given."
A monk who is free from attachments [should not seek death], according to another Smṛti: "O Brahmin, death by one's own will through horned animals, fanged beasts, or reptiles,
or by means of the lowest castes, poison, hanging, or even by self-inflicted blows [is forbidden]."
Or by extracting poison from those whose limbs are fully affected,
or likewise by means of falling into water, fire, or chasms, as well as through fasting and other such methods.
Those who would [commit such acts] are indeed said to be performers of evil deeds;
likewise, those who have taken refuge in heresy are great sinners.
And women who are unchaste, as well as those who have fallen from their status after being elevated,
for them there is no ritual bathing, no consecration, no Śrāddha, and no Sapiṇḍana rite.
The sixteen śrāddhas have been declared; indeed, there are no others.
In this case, fasting results from the power of anger toward the sinful person, and not from a state of poverty. Women who have fallen from their status after being elevated die within ten days;
one should cast the Vaitāna fire into water and the Gṛhya fire at a crossroads.
One should burn the sacrificial vessels in the fire when the sacrificer has died in vain.
The reading is "sāgnike pāpakarmāṇi. Then, when a full year has passed, those who are compassionate should perform the rite for them,
having reached the eleventh lunar day (ekādaśī) of the bright fortnight.
Having likewise worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should place ten rice-balls (piṇḍas) smeared with ghee and mixed with honey upon darbha grass.
Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, facing south, he should silently offer each of those [portions] mixed with sesame seeds to Viṣṇu and likewise to Yama.
Having taken up the funeral cakes with self-restraint, one should cast them into the water at a sacred ford or similar place;
while casting them, one should proclaim the name and the lineage of the deceased.
Furthermore, one should worship Viṣṇu and Yama with flowers and sandalwood paste,
as well as with incense, lamps, and food offerings consisting of various kinds of eatables and delicacies.
[535] Then one should fast during the day and invite Brahmins who are endowed with noble lineage, learning, and austerity, and who are possessed of beauty and good character.
Nine, seven, or five [times], according to one's own capacity;
when the following day has arrived at midday, being well-composed.
Having performed the worship of Viṣṇu, he should seat those Brahmins facing north according to their seniority, while recollecting them as being of the nature of the ancestors (pitṛs).
Having fixed the mind upon Viṣṇu, one should perform everything without weariness;
whatever has been prescribed beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) should be performed starting with the deities.
Then, having ascertained that the Brahmins were satisfied and having asked them about their satiety according to the prescribed rite,
[he should offer] sacrificial food together with side dishes and sesame seeds and so forth.
In this manner, one should indeed offer the morsels of food while recollecting the divine form;
first, one should offer them to Viṣṇu, and to Brahmā and Śiva as well.
One should offer the fourth ball of rice to Yama together with his retinue,
having mentally mentioned the deceased by name preceded by their lineage.
Having thus uttered the name of Viṣṇu, one should cast the fifth [offering] as before;
then, having caused the Brahmins to sip water (ācamana), one should honor them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
One should honor a most venerable Brahmin with gold,
a cow, clothing, and land, while mentally recollecting the deceased.
Then the Brahmins, with *darbha* grass in their hands, should scatter sesame-water while pronouncing the name and keeping the lineage in mind.
Having gone outside, one should, with a concentrated mind, offer sesame seeds and water to him;
afterwards, remaining restrained in speech, one should eat together with friends and kinsmen.
Thus, abiding by the doctrine of Viṣṇu, whoever gives [liberation] to one who has committed suicide quickly rescues that person; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
In the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"One should perform the Śrāddha for a year on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight;
or one may perform it on the twelfth day [after death], or on the first day of the bright fortnight."
Another Smṛti states:
"The moment the Nārāyaṇa-bali is performed, the deceased becomes pure;
at that very moment, being liberated from sin, he becomes fit for the performance of rites."
On the very day he becomes pure through the offering of food by his sons, according to the procedure for the ritual union with Viṣṇu, there occurs the remembrance of Him.
If a son offers a funeral rice-ball (*kriyāpiṇḍa*) to that deceased ancestor, the period of impurity prescribed for him is indeed three days; of this there is no doubt.
Upon the completion of the Viṣṇu-śrāddha on the thirteenth day, the offerer of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) shall observe impurity for three days, but not his relatives or those born of the same lineage.

And thus, among those for whom *śrāddha* is prohibited, the *Nārāyaṇabali* has been prescribed for certain individuals, such as those who commit suicide. In that regard, for those who cause their own death according to scriptural injunction (*vidhi*), there is neither a prohibition of *śrāddha* nor an injunction for the *Nārāyaṇabali*. This is because a contradiction between an injunction and a prohibition [does not apply here], and because that which is not prohibited does not entail sin (*pratyavāya*). It is the act of dying—which brings about sin—that serves as the occasion for the prohibition of *śrāddha* and so forth. Thus says Brahmagarbha: "He who, afflicted by a great disease, is unable to live..."
Thus, one who performs great rites with fire or water does not incur fault in the hereafter.
Vivasvān said:
For one who is detached from all the senses, aged, who has fulfilled his duties,
and who is afflicted by disease, death at a sacred ford by one's own will is superior to asceticism.
Likewise, Gārgya also spoke with reference to the householder:
"One should not desire life in vain through embarking on the Great Journey, entering fire or water, or even leaping from a precipice."
Bhṛgu says that [the mountain] Parvataka is the peak. "In vain" means devoid of the performance of dharma. Manu, however, speaking with reference to the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), says:
"Having taken his stand in the unconquered [northeastern] direction, he should proceed straight forward until the fall of his body, disciplined, subsisting on water and air."

The north-eastern direction is Aparājita; facing that, until the fall of the body, one should proceed with a concentrated mind, consuming only water, air, or food, without crookedness. Having cast off the body by means of any one of these practices of the great seers, a Brahmin, freed from sorrow and fear, becomes fit for absorption into Brahman.
Regarding one killed by a *nāga* or a serpent, a specific ritual act is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"Whether by negligence or intentionally, one who has died from a *nāga* or a serpent should worship the *nāgas* on both fortnights, specifically on the fifth lunar days."
One should fashion an image of a serpent out of flour on the ground;
one should worship it with white flowers, fragrant scents, and sandalwood paste.
One should offer incense and lamps, and scatter white rice grains;
likewise, one should present raw grain, desired food, and milk as an offering.
Having approached him, one should speak thus: "Release, release such-and-such a person here.
On that day, one should give sweet food; in this manner, one should practice for a year.
Then, according to one's means, one should give a golden serpent to a twice-born man;
thereafter, one should give a cow with its calf—such is the injunction of the Gāruḍa Purāṇa.

Having diligently performed the rites according to their respective divisions for the sake of the Nāgas, and having caused the twice-born to be released, [one should say]: "May the serpents be well-pleased."
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"A son must perform [the rites] for his father, but a father should not perform them for his son;
out of excessive affection, he may do so, provided it is without the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*."
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"If the father has died but the grandfather is still living,
he [the grandson] should offer three rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) beginning with the great-grandfather."
To them, however, the ancestral rice-ball (piṇḍa) should be offered as before;
and if the mother has died while the paternal grandmother is still living, [the offering is made to her].
In that case as well, this same procedure should be performed, beginning with the great-grandmother.
As for the statement:
"And because they have died out of their proper order, the sapinda-relationship must certainly not be performed."
This statement refers to deceased persons other than one's mother and father. Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*:
"One should not give [offerings] separately to women, except on the anniversary of their death;
for it is recorded in tradition that their satisfaction comes solely from the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered to their own husbands."
Likewise:
"If the grandfather passes away after the father,
the grandson must perform the rites beginning with the eleventh day, including the sixteen-fold śrāddha."
This should not be performed by a grandson if the grandfather has sons;
having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father, he should perform the monthly rites.
The two ancestors who have not yet been consecrated should not be consecrated by the grandson or great-grandson;
rather, one should consecrate the father in that case—so said Kātyāyana.

It is the settled rule that one should consecrate one's father with the funeral rites performed by the grandfather— even if the grandfather is most wicked or himself a doer of evil— provided he is pure.

In a case where the two paternal grandfathers have not been consecrated by anyone for some reason—that is, their *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has not been performed—one should perform the consecration (the meaning being that one should effect the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*) of the father together with them. Thus says Vājasaneya Yajñapārśva:
"For one who knows [the rule], the *pitṛyajña* should end with the *homa* while the father is alive;
or, having fed the father, he should offer two rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the two ancestors beyond him."
To those for whom the father would offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa), to them the son should also cause it to be given;
while the father lives, one should not offer it—this is the Vedic revelation (naigamī śrutiḥ).
The wise have declared that if the grandfather lives while the father is deceased,
the offering should be made to the father alone.
If two [ancestors] have died while the great-grandfather is still living,
one should offer two pindas to the two ancestors who preceded him and feed the great-grandfather.
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"A father should by no means perform the *śrāddha* for his sons,
nor should a brother ever perform it for his younger brothers."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says:
Ascetics must never engage in social contact with their sons in this world;
by the mere taking up of the triple staff (tridaṇḍa), the state of being a ghost (pretatva) does not occur.

This should be understood by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikānyāya*): for one who does not possess the state of a *preta*, how could there even be a suspicion of impurity (*aśauca*) upon his death? Prajāpati says:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite never occurs for ascetics (*yatis*);
rather, when the eleventh day has arrived, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed."
Bṛhaspati: For an ascetic (yati), there shall be no *navaśrāddha* nor *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*;
when the eleventh day has arrived, one should perform the *pārvaṇa* for him.

In this context, the mention of the *navaśrāddha* (the nine-day funeral rites) is intended as an illustration for all rituals performed for the purpose of liberating one from the state of being a preta. Thus says Śātātapa: "One should not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa*, water offerings, rice-balls, impurity periods, or the post-mortem rites for a mendicant who has become one with Brahman, other than the *pārvaṇa* [rites]."

The lay follower (upāsaka) who has become one with Brahman meditates: "I am Brahman. Now, regarding the times [for rites]: therein is the *Bhaviṣyat-purāṇa*: "A sacrificer who is without a sacred fire (*anagniman*) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a deceased person who maintained no consecrated fire (*anāhitāgni*), O bull among men, when the full year has elapsed."

One who maintains no sacred fire should, according to the law, perform the rite of offering the rice-ball for both his father and mother when a full year has elapsed, or on whatever day an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) occurs. [539]

When the performer and the intended recipient are both without sacred fires (*niragni*), the time is here prescribed as a restrictive rule, because it is enjoined as an integral part (*aṅga*) of that rite. As for the statement of those learned in the *nyāya* that "the rite is enjoined with respect to time, not time with respect to the rite," that intends to convey that [time] is not something to be adopted (*anupādeya*); it does not, however, mean that it is not an injunction (*avidheya*). For if that were the case, it would not possess the status of an integral part; indeed, that which is not enjoined cannot be an integral part. *Vṛddhi* means prosperity. *Uśanā*:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father should take place on the anniversary of his death;
upon the arrival of the installation of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and other such rites, this may even be performed before the year has elapsed."
Laghuhārīta: A brother, or a brother’s son, or a sapinda, or even a disciple,
having performed the sapindikarana rite, should thereafter perform the prosperity-rite (abhyudaya).
Sumantu said: O hero, when a householder is without the sacred fire, he should perform [the rite] at that time;
however, if the deceased possessed the sacred fire, the *sapiṇḍana* must indeed take place after three fortnights.

In this case as well, the restriction regarding time is as before. The grammatical connection is: "when the householder is without fire. The performer of the *śrāddha* is the householder. Likewise: "O King, when the sacrificer possesses the sacred fire but the deceased is without fire, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should be performed by the sons on the twelfth day."
Jābāli says: A son who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on the first new moon after the ten-day period;
another [son] may do so when the full year has elapsed.
The mention of "ten nights" is intended as an indication for the entire period of impurity. Kātyāyana states:

"Having performed the rites on the eleventh day prior to the new moon according to the prescribed rule, a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍana* ceremony for his mother and father."
Hārīta states: "If the new moon occurs before the tenth day from the date of death,
the son who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* on that very [new moon]."
A son who maintains the sacred fire but has not yet performed the sapindikarana rite should not perform the ancestral sacrifice (pitr-yajña);
by performing neither the parvana nor the abhyudaya rites, he does not obtain the fruit [of his actions].

For indeed, in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, the mother holds the status of a deity for the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*), according to such scriptural statements as: "The son of an appointed daughter should first offer a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to his mother. It is understood that for the other [son] as well, the mother attains satisfaction in the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and other rites just like the father. For it has been said:
The mother eats the śrāddha food, which is equal to the svadhā offering, together with her own husband;
likewise the paternal grandmother with her own husband, and the great-grandmother with her own. [540]

And since that [status of being a deity] is not possible for one who is not designated as such, she too must be designated. And in the designation, she enters only by way of association (*sahabhāva*), not as the primary object. Therefore, even though the status of the father and others as deities is established by the original injunction (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*), the status of women as deities is not contradictory. Consequently, the performance of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the mother before the *darśa* sacrifice is logical. Thus, it is also established that in the *śrāddhas*, the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are to be designated together with their wives. Viṣṇu, following the rule that "the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must be performed," states: "For Śūdras, [it is performed] on the twelfth day, excluding the mantras. This refers to the *śrāddha* performed on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). By the force of this statement, the performance of the *śrāddha* occurs even during the period of impurity (*aśauca*). And thus, for a performer who maintains the sacred fires (*sāgnika*), three times for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* are stated: the twelfth day; any day between the end of the impurity and the first new moon; and the first new moon immediately after the impurity. For one without sacred fires (*anagni*), however, there are four times. As Gobhila says: "When a year has passed, or six months, or three fortnights, or on whatever day an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) occurs. Paiṭhīnasi [says]: [The same].
A son who maintains the sacred fires should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for his father;
however, for one who does not maintain the fires, no other rite is ever prescribed except the *ekoddiṣṭa*.

This refers to the *śrāddhas* performed during the first year for one who, not maintaining the sacred fires (*anagni*), intends to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* at the end of the year. Vṛddhavasiṣṭha states:

"One must not perform the *sapiṇḍana* without having offered the sixteen *śrāddhas*. If those are omitted, even when the *sapiṇḍana* is performed, the deceased does not attain the status of an ancestor (*pitṛ*)."

This also has the same scope as the preceding [rule]. However, regarding a different case, Laugākṣi said: "For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* occurs before the completion of a year, the monthly rites and the water-pot offering must also be performed for that person for the duration of the year."

As for that which was stated by Hārīta: "The primary *śrāddha* is monthly; in the event of inability, it may be performed every twelve days, or all twelve on a single day," this refers to the case of one who lacks the capacity. Regarding the continuation [of the rule] with the word "having postponed," Uśanas says:
"But he who performs the *preta-śrāddhas* while omitting the *vṛddhi-śrāddha* is a performer of *śrāddhas* who is cooked in a terrible hell together with his ancestors."

The meaning is that one who would postpone the *preta-śrāddhas* when prosperity has not yet arisen; and this refers to a case where one is capable [of performing them]. Śāṭyāyani says: "A twice-born man, in order to perform the *nāndīmukha* rite, may even postpone all the *preta-śrāddhas* as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. [541]
Now follows the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the mother. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"How should the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother be performed by her sons?
It is traditionally taught that her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is to be performed together with the paternal grandmother."
Gārgya says: The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a woman must be performed by her husband alone;
for even when she has died, she has attained oneness with him through mantras, oblations, and vows.
Sumantu said: "The father should be joined with the grandfather by his sons when a full year has passed;
likewise the mother with the maternal grandfather—so spoke the blessed Śiva."
Yama says: One whose father is living should perform the *sapiṇḍana* for his mother with his paternal grandmother;
one whose father is deceased should do so with his father; and the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) should do so with her father’s father.

"By his father" means by the mother's father. Śātātapa states the rule for the case when both the father and the paternal grandmother are absent: "A woman who dies having followed her husband attains, together with him, the status of a single funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and residence in heaven as long as the dissolution of the earth. Thus it is said.

This being the case, when the subject is one who has ascended the funeral pyre (anvārūḍhā), the *sapiṇḍana* of the mother must be performed together with the father, whether the paternal grandmother is living or deceased. Otherwise, however, it is established that it should be performed with her own father or paternal grandmother. If, on the other hand, the *sapiṇḍana* were to take place with the father alone even when the father is deceased, then the rule concerning the woman who has ascended the pyre would be rendered meaningless. Since that rule—stating that "she is to be *sapiṇḍita* with her husband"—is meaningful as a restrictive injunction (*niyāmaka*), the statement "one whose father is dead [should perform it] with the father" cannot be said to be intended as a restriction; thus, there is no fixed rule. As for that which... [text ends].
When the father has died, one should not perform the *sapiṇḍana* rite for the mother separately;
by performing the *sapiṇḍana* for the father alone, it is as if it has been performed for her as well.
Thus, if that [text] were to be taken literally, it would have to be interpreted as referring to a state of distress (*āpad*). Laghuhārīta states:
"The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for a woman must be performed by her son alone;
however, for a man, others such as brothers' sons and so forth may also perform it."
In the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"For women as well, this same *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed;
however, in the absence of a son, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for them is not performed."
This applies in the absence of a husband. As Paiṭhīnasi says:
"When a woman dies without a son, the husband shall perform the *sapiṇḍana*;
her *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* shall take place together with her mother-in-law and the others. [542]
Śātātapa says:
"The *sapiṇḍana* rite for women married through the Āsura and other such forms of marriage is prescribed with their maternal grandfather, their paternal grandmother, and their mother-in-law."
*Tanmātrā* means "the mother’s mother. *Pitāmahī* refers specifically to the mother’s mother. Now follows the determination of the mother’s lineage (*gotra*). Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"One should perform the *sapiṇḍana* for the mother by means of the husband’s *gotra* and name;
one should [perform it] silently, interposing the ancestors with *kuśa* grass between the two *piṇḍas* of the couple."
Obstructing [the path] and concealing it— Śātātapa says:
"The daughter's son should perform the washing with the [mother's] family name,
as well as the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) for his mother and for his maternal grandfather."
*Avanejanam* is the offering of water. As Laugākṣi says:
"One should perform the rite of the rice-balls and the water-offering for the maternal grandfather by means of his *gotra*;
thus said Prajāpati regarding the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*)."
Mārkaṇḍeya says: In marriages such as the Brāhma and others, whatever maiden has been wedded,
the rites of offering rice-balls (piṇḍa) and water (udaka) for her must be performed using the gotra of her husband.
In marriages such as the Āsura and others, one who knows the Dharma [should perform the rite] by means of the father's gotra.
The meaning is "by the paternal *gotra* of the mother. Vyāsa states:
"Oneness with the husband lasts only so long as a son is not born;
upon the birth of a son for an appointed daughter (*putrikā*), that oneness ceases. (1.252, 253)
For one whose sapindikarana has taken place before the completion of a year,
one should provide food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of a year.

The connection is "within a year. The accusative case in *varṣam* is used to denote uninterrupted duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). Even for that deceased person for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite occurs before the completion of a year—such as on the twelfth day or similar occasions—one should give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born (*dvija*) for the duration of a year. In the phrase *tasya*, the genitive is used in the sense of the dative; in *dvijanmane*, the dative is used in its proper sense of the recipient. In the reading *dadyāt saṃvatsaraṃ dvijaḥ*, the locative is used in its literal sense, since the Brāhmaṇa serves the purpose of the *āhavanīya* fire in the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, the accusative in *saṃvatsaram* denotes uninterrupted duration. Therefore, food must be given every single day for the duration of a year. And so says Āpastamba:
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should offer a water-pot filled with food every day for the duration of that year.
As Laghu-Hārīta said:
Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, separate status is no longer possible;
however, if separation has already been effected, the *sapiṇḍatā* must be performed again.
Śātātapa says:
"After the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, in whatever [occasion] a [śrāddha] is offered,
that śrāddha should be known as being like the Pārvaṇa, except for the Abhyudaya (prosperity) śrāddha."

This is an exception to that rule; for even in the case of such a person, the offering of food together with a water-pot is prescribed, as indicated by the use of the singular number. By the force of the word "api" (even/also), this should be performed even at the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite at the end of the year. 1.254.
He states another exception as well:
"But on the anniversary of death, it should be performed every month for a year;
and likewise every year thereafter, while the first [rite] is performed on the eleventh day. (1.255)

The *śrāddha* that is performed every month for one year from the day of death, as well as that which is performed on that same day each subsequent year, and the first [śrāddha], and that which is performed on the eleventh day—all this should be performed in this manner; that is to say, according to the procedure of the *ekoddiṣṭa*. By the word "first," the *navaśrāddhas* (the nine preliminary śrāddhas) are meant. The fact that the monthly and annual *śrāddhas* are *ekoddiṣṭa* in form is not absolute, because there is also a rule prescribing them as being like the *pārvaṇa*. As Jātūkarṇya says: "A son should perform the *śrāddha* for his father who has entered the company of the ancestors according to the *pārvaṇa* rite, both annually and monthly; this is to be known as the eternal rule."

One who has been united with the ancestors (sapiṇḍita) is included among the group of ancestors. Regarding the monthly rites (māsika), there is no fixed option because there is an absence of an authoritative rule for such a determination. For this very reason, Kātyāyana says:
"After the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, one should not offer the monthly oblations.
Śaunaka says: "One should offer them according to the procedure for the Ekoddiṣṭa rite."

In this regard, one rule stated is that one should offer the monthly *māsika* rite according to the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa*; another rule states that one should not offer it. However, regarding the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) Śrāddha, there is a settled option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*). In that context, the possession of the sacred fire (*agnimattva*) by the *kṣetraja*, *aurasa*, or *putrikāputra* sons is the determining factor for the performance of the *pārvaṇa* rite. Likewise, the fact that the person intended for the Śrāddha died on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) or during the fortnight of the departed (*pretapakṣa*), or that he was an ascetic (*yati*), serves as the determining factor for the *pārvaṇa* nature of the Śrāddha performed by anyone at all. For a Śrāddha for one killed by a weapon, the fact that it is performed on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight determines the *ekoddiṣṭa* nature for every performer. Similarly, the lack of sacred fire for either the performer or the intended recipient, or the performer’s lack of the *aurasa*, *kṣetraja*, or *putrikāputra* types of sons even if he possesses the sacred fire, determines the *ekoddiṣṭa* nature. Any Śrāddha other than that performed on the anniversary of death—such as those prescribed for specific times like the sun's passage into a zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*), eclipses, or the *mahālaya* period—is governed by the rule that no injunction for the *ekoddiṣṭa* form exists; therefore, it must be performed exactly like the *pārvaṇa*. The sages have declared this settled rule. Among them, Jātūkarṇya says: [The text continues with the citation of Jātūkarṇya.]
Every year, the *kṣetraja* and *aurasa* sons should perform the rite according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure alone;
the other ten types of sons should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite.
Kārṣṇājini says:
The Kṣetraja and the Aurasa sons should perform [the rite] primarily with fire according to the very procedure of the Pārvaṇa;
the other ten types of sons should perform the Ekoddiṣṭa.
Kārṣṇājini says:
For all [members of the household], the performance of rites in the householder stage of life has the fire as its primary element.
Because of that connection, one who has provided assistance is entitled to perform the pārvaṇa rite everywhere.
For one who died without the sacred fires, the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is prescribed on the anniversary of death;
for one who maintained the fires, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed every year. For others, however, the *pārvaṇa* rite is not performed.
As for another Smṛti text:
"But those Brahmins who maintain many sacred fires, as well as those who maintain only one fire—
for them, after the Sapiṇḍana rite, the Ekoddiṣṭa is performed and not the Pārvaṇa."

Thus, that [rule] refers to subjects other than the *kṣetraja* and so forth, or it refers to the *śrāddha* for one who has no son. The son of an appointed daughter (*putrikā-putra*) should also perform [the rites] like a legitimate son (*aurasa*), because he is equal to him. And so Vyāsa says:
"The primary son alone should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the father;
the legitimate son is the primary, while the son of an appointed daughter is equal to him."
Śaṅkha says:
"If one's new moon day (amāvāsyā) coincides with the end of the month, or if it occurs during the fortnight of the ancestors (pretapakṣa), then for such a person,
the Pārvaṇa rite is prescribed after the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been performed."

The "Preta-pakṣa" is the second fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada. Śātātapa states: "One should not perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the water offering, the rice-ball offering (*piṇḍa*), the period of impurity, or the funeral rites for a deceased person—other than the *pārvaṇa* rite—for a mendicant who has attained the state of Brahman."
Garga says:
"The śrāddha performed on the fourteenth day for one slain by a weapon, after the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa has been completed, must be performed according to the ekoddiṣṭa rite."
Likewise:
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, for one who has died on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
