the annual rite performed each year— other than that— is the *ekoddiṣṭa*, not the *pārvaṇa*.
Prajāpati says:

On the day of the sun's passage into a new sign (saṃkrānti), during an eclipse, on the full and new moon days, at festivals, and during the Mahālaya rites, one should offer three rice-balls (piṇḍas) here; however, on the anniversary of the death, one should offer them all together.
Kātyāyana says: Among those [shares] beginning with the fifteenth, as well as the others for one who has no son,
only one share is to be given here to the one who is childless, and always to a woman without a son.
Āpastamba: For those who have died without sons— whether they be women or men— an *ekoddiṣṭa* rite should be performed for them, and not a *pārvaṇa*.

Now, the statements concerning cases where the day of death is unknown are stated. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says: "If the day of death is not known when someone has died while away on a journey, but the month is known, then the rite should be performed on the day of the new moon (darśa) corresponding to that month."
The meaning is that whatever rite is to be performed on the anniversary of death (mṛtāha) should be performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) when those [details] are unknown.
When the month is not known but the day alone is known,
then that day should fall in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or Māgha.
"When the day and month of death are not known, however, the day and month of departure should be taken according to the previously mentioned method. Thus it is said.

In this context, the word *dina* (day) refers to the lunar day (*tithi*). The meaning of the phrase "in the manner previously stated" is as follows: when there is knowledge of the month but no knowledge of the specific lunar day of death in the case of a person who has died while away from home, the time of his death is to be taken as that of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) of the known month. Likewise, when there is knowledge of the lunar day of death but no knowledge of the month, the time of his death is to be taken as that of the known lunar day in either the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or the month of Māgha. Similarly, when neither the lunar day nor the month of death is known, the day and month of departure are to be taken; the time of his death is then considered to be the very same lunar day and month in which he departed. In the absence even of that, the time of his death is the day on which news of his death was heard. As Pracetas states: "When the day of death is unknown, [it is observed] on the new moon day or the day one hears the news. Thus says Jātūkarṇya.
If a father has gone abroad and there is neither news of him nor any means of communication,
after fifteen years have passed, one should create a representative image of him.
Then, one should perform his consecration according to the prescribed rule;
thereafter, one should carry out all the remaining rites beginning with that very [consecration].
Another Smṛti states:
"If the body is not found, but the bones are found,
then one should pour clarified butter over them and perform the funeral rites for the deceased according to the prescribed rule."
Having obtained the burnt bones, one should soak them in milk;
if even those are not available, [one should use] three hundred leaves of the *palāśa* tree.
Taking sixty-two [units] more, one should fashion its counterpart;
therein, thirty-two [units] at the head, and sixty thereafter at the throat.
There are eighty [hair-pores] on the chest, twenty on the hips, twenty on each of the two arms,
ten on the fingers, and six on the testicles in the process of accomplishment.
There are sixty in the two thighs, twenty in the knees,
then twenty in the two shanks, and finally ten in the toes of the feet.
One should place [the images] made of *palāśa* wood and wrap them with woolen thread;
one should then smear them with barley flour and consecrate them according to the prescribed rite.
At the conclusion of the consecration, one should pour a stream of water from all sides.
Vṛddha-Manu: If he should return alive, one should immerse him in a vat of clarified butter,
lift him out, bathe him, and perform for him the birth-rite and other ceremonies.
Having observed the vow for twelve days, or else for three nights,
he should bathe and marry that woman as his wife, or another in her absence.

Having established the sacred fires according to the rules, he should either perform the Vrātyastoma sacrifice or, having gone to a mountain, perform a sacrifice with an animal dedicated to Indra and Agni. There, indeed, he—
Then he should perform the long-life sacrifice (āyuṣmatīṣṭi) and the desired rites.

The term *āyuṣmatīṣṭi* means a sacrifice for long life (*āyuṣkāmeṣṭi*). It has been stated that the monthly and annual rites are to be performed on the anniversary of death; in this context, by the word "day" (*ahaḥ*), a full day and night (*ahorātra*) is indicated. That [day] is of three kinds: *sāvana*, *saura*, and *aindava*. As it is said in the *Brahmasiddhānta*: "A *sāvana* day is from sunrise to sunrise;
the *saura* [day] consists of one-thirtieth of a zodiacal sign; and the *aindava* [day] is the duration of a lunar phase (*tithi*)."

The solar day (*saura ahorātra*) is the duration of time that the sun takes to traverse thirty degrees of the sign Aries. The lunar day (*aindava*), however, is measured by the *tithis* beginning with the first (*pratipad*). It is this very [lunar day] that is intended here by the term "day of death" (*mṛtāhani*). As it has been said:
"On whichever day of a month, fortnight, or *tithi* a person dies, they know that corresponding day to be his *kṣayāha* (anniversary of death) every year."
The month, as before, is also of three kinds. This is stated in the *Brahmasiddhānta* itself:
"The lunar month is from new moon to new moon; the solar month consists of thirty days;
and the solar month is defined by the sign of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti) by those who know it."

Likewise: the lunar month begins with the bright fortnight and ends with the new moon; the solar month is the period during which the sun remains in a single zodiac sign, consisting of thirty civil days (sāvana).

For rites for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*), the lunar month alone is to be accepted. For they record: "The solar month is prescribed for marriage and the like; the *sāvana* month is prescribed for sacrifices and the like;
but for annual ancestral rites, the lunar month is prescribed. [547]
Laghuhārīta says:
Since the sun revolves like a wheel by the power of time,
therefore the annual Śrāddha should be performed, marked by the [specific] month.
The mark of the month must indeed be made starting from Pauṣa, Māgha, and so forth;
therefore, by this lunar arrangement, that [lunar] month is proclaimed.

The designations *pauṣa* and so forth belong exclusively to the lunar month. For instance: that night which is joined with the asterism Puṣya is called *pauṣī*; the month in which that occurs is the *pauṣa* month. The same applies to *māgha* and the others. Even though the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) may occur on the second or third day [of the lunar fortnight], that month is nevertheless not designated as *pauṣa* and so on. The designation *pauṣa* and so forth applies only to the month, the half-month, and the year, and not to the two-day period and so forth; thus says Pāṇini: "In the sense of a name, [the suffix *aṇ* is used] when [the word] means 'that full moon occurs in this [month]' (Pāṇ 4.2.21). Furthermore, such a rule regarding the full moon does not apply to the solar or the *sāvana* months. Therefore, for monthly and annual rites, only the lunar month is to be accepted. As for what has been stated in another Smṛti:
In whichever zodiac sign the sun has entered when a man meets his end,
in that very sign the ancestral rites (pitṛkārya) should be performed on the anniversary of his death.
This concerns the case of death occurring during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). As that same author states: "If death occurs in an intercalary month, one should rely upon the solar month;
that very day [of the solar month] is the [correct] day for his *śrāddha*, rice-balls, water offerings, and so forth."

Furthermore, regarding one who has died during an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), this should be understood to apply when another such intercalary month occurs. And so says Bhṛgu: "But for those who have died during an intercalary month, the annual *śrāddha* must be performed specifically in an intercalary month, and never for any others."

[Regarding others who have not died during an intercalary month: the annual Śrāddha should not be performed during an intercalary month; rather, it should be done upon its departure—this is the meaning. In response to the question, "What, then, is called an *adhimāsa* (intercalary month)? Garga says:
"When the sun enters Aries and the other signs during the lunar months, those are called Caitra and so forth; in the absence of that [regular sequence], there is an *adhimāsaka*."
Laghuhārīta also says:
"Where Indra and Agni are offered, that is proclaimed as the beginning of the month;
Agni and Soma are remembered for the middle, and Pitṛsoma for the conclusion."
But when the sun ever passes beyond that [lunar month],
the first is to be known as the *malimluca* (intercalary) month, and the second is recorded as the *prakṛta* (natural) month.

The phrase "where Indra and Agni are invoked" is an indicator for the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*). "Agni and Soma" indicates the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*). "Pitṛs and Soma" indicates the new moon (*darśa*). By this, the lunar month is indicated. When the sun, having passed that month, enters another zodiac sign (*rāśi*) in the following month, then the former is the *malimluca* (intercalary) month, and the latter is the *prakṛta* (regular) month. Śātātapa says: "When the sun transits [the next sign] after passing over Sinīvālī, that is declared to be the *malamāsa*; the ritual acts should be performed in the latter [month]."

The phrase "Sinīvālī" refers to the intention of including all months ending with Sinīvālī; this is according to the *Kāṭhaka-gṛhyasūtra*. That month in which there is no solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), or where there are two transits, should be known as an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), occurring in the thirtieth month.
Regarding this, Kuthumi states that even during an intercalary month (malimluca), the monthly *śrāddha* must be performed:
"One should offer a water-pot for a year, as well as food accompanied by meat;
even when the year has increased [by an intercalary month], the monthly *śrāddha* is to be performed every month."
Hārīta says: Even if the sun has not entered a new zodiac sign (saṃkrānti), the first annual śrāddha must be performed by the twice-born;
likewise, the monthly śrāddhas and the sapindīkaraṇa rite should be performed first.
The monthly rite (*māsika*) prescribed for the first year is intended here; it does not refer to the *darśa-śrāddha*, for R̥ṣyaśr̥ṅga states an exception to that:
"If there should be an extra month beyond the year, which is the thirteenth, one should not perform the thirteenth *śrāddha* on the occasion of the new moon."
As for that which was stated by Śātātapa:
"When two months having the same name should occur at any time within a year,
the rites for the ancestors are to be performed in the first, and the rites for the gods in the latter."

Thus, this refers to the ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) up to the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* ceremony. For this very reason, Laghuhārīta states: "Whatever śrāddha-related rite there may be after the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—whether it be an *iṣṭa* (sacrificial) or a *pūrta* (charitable) one—one should perform it during the intercalary month (*malimluca*)."
As for that which Satyavrata stated:
"The śrāddha performed every year on the anniversary of the death of one's mother and father should not be performed in an intercalary month; such is the word of Vyāghra."

Thus, this [prohibition] refers to rites other than the *prathamābdika-śrāddha* for one who has died at a time other than an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*). As for the statement of Gabhasti: "A ritualist should not perform any rite whatsoever during an intercalary month, with the exception of the occasional (*naimittika*) *śrāddha*; for that [occasional *śrāddha*] is prescribed for that very occasion."

"For that *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha which is performed on a specific occasion is called *naimittika*. It should be performed according to the previous measurement [of time], even if there is an excess of time, in accordance with dharma. (549) This refers to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rites preceding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. And as for that which was stated by Vṛddhavasiṣṭha:
If an intercalary month should occur when the day for the ancestral rite (śrāddha) has arrived, one should perform two śrāddhas;
by acting thus, one does not err.
Thus, that [rule] pertains to the monthly [rites]. Regarding the annual [rite], however, Laghuhārīta says:
"The wise should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) every year in the twelfth month;
in some cases, it may even be in the thirteenth, except for the first year."

The meaning of this is as follows: when the twelfth month has always concluded and the thirteenth has arrived, the annual rite (*sāṃvatsarika*) is to be performed; however, if an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) occurs, the offering of the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍakriyā*) is to be performed once the thirteenth month has passed and the fourteenth has begun. But in the first year [of the deceased], even if there is an intercalary month, the annual rite is to be performed in the thirteenth month itself. Incidentally, something else regarding the intercalary month is also stated. On this point, Bṛhaspati says: "One should perform obligatory and occasional rites with self-restraint during the intercalary month, as well as ritual bathing at sacred fords (*tīrthasnāna*), the 'elephant's shadow' rite (*gajacchāyā*), and likewise the *śrāddha* for the deceased."

In the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "During an eclipse of the moon or sun, at the time of death, and upon the birth of a son—even during an intercalary month—a gift should be given; what is given then produces inexhaustible merit."
Vṛddha-Manu: The establishment of the sacred fires, the installation [of deities], sacrifices, gifts, and vows;
Vedic observances, the release of a bull, the tonsure ceremony, and the girdle ceremony.
One should avoid auspicious rites and consecrations during the intercalary month.

And there is no prohibition against the rite of releasing a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) performed on the eleventh day, because it has a fixed time and provides benefit to the deceased. Whether one is young or old, or when Venus has set,
one should avoid visiting a deity, just as during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*).
One should not perform the consecration of ponds, wells, tanks, and the like, nor sacrificial rites,
nor great gifts and vows during an intercalary month.
"Visiting the gods" refers to visiting deities such as Someśvara and others, and that is intended here first. According to the *Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa*:

"Sacrifices not accompanied by the *vaṣaṭ*-call, oblations, the full-moon and new-moon festivals, and likewise the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice—these should be performed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*), but one should avoid optional (*kāmya*) sacrifices."

Parāśara states: "The Upākarma, the Utsarga, the birth ceremonies, festivals, and the Aṣṭakās should be performed on the later [tithis] when there is an increase in the month, with the exception of rites for the ancestors."
The birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other such ceremonies must certainly be performed for the sake of the child's welfare. For this very reason, Satyavrata says:
"The *śrāddha* performed at the birth-rite, as well as the *navaśrāddha*, and the annual *śrāddha*—these are prescribed even during an intercalary month (*malamāsa*)."

For this very reason, it is precisely another festival occasioned by childbirth—prescribed by the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*)—that is prohibited here. The term *paitṛka* refers to ancestral rites such as the *śrāddha* performed during lunar and solar eclipses, the "elephant-shade" (*gajacchāyā*), and so forth, for which there is no other alternative time. Therefore, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:
"During a lunar or solar eclipse, at death, and upon the birth of a son, [the rite] should be offered even in an intercalary month (*malamāsa*); what is given then produces inexhaustible merit."
This is true:
when performing the consecration of deities, groves, ponds, and so forth, if one acts while the sun is facing north,
or facing south, one shall not obtain the fruit thereof.
Having concluded this incidental discussion, let us return to the subject at hand. || 1.255 ||
One should give the morsels of food to cows, horses, or Brahmins, or else cast them into fire or water;
while worthy Brahmins are present, one must not clear away the remnants of the twice-born's meal.

The meaning is that one should give the *piṇḍas* associated with the *pārvaṇa* and other types of *śrāddha* to any one among a cow, a goat, or a Brahmin, or feed any one of them. Alternatively, one may cast them into fire or even into water. Furthermore, while the Brahmins have not yet risen from their own seats, one should not wipe or clear away those remnants. The plural number in the word *piṇḍān* (the *piṇḍas*) is not intended to be restrictive; therefore, when the wife eats the middle *piṇḍa*, the disposal of both *piṇḍas* must be performed. Regarding this, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states: "One should give the *piṇḍas* to a cow, a goat, or a Brahmin, or [dispose of them] in fire or even in water."
Or he should have it drunk by Brahmins according to the rules, or otherwise by birds.
Or he may offer the middle *piṇḍa* to his wife, who is endowed with modesty, saying:
"O ancestors, bestow within her a fetus that shall increase our lineage."
"Vayas" refers to birds. Manu says: "A devoted wife, the lawful consort, intent on the worship of the ancestors, should then properly eat the middle *piṇḍa* if she desires a son."
She gives birth to a long-lived son, endowed with fame and intelligence,
wealthy, possessed of progeny, virtuous, righteous, and pure.
Bṛhaspati says: If the wife is staying in another place, or is ill, or likewise pregnant,
then that aged bull or goat deserves to eat [the sacrificial cake].

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Having thus requested the boons and paid obeisance, one should place the *piṇḍas* in water or cast them into the fire. Or, the wife—having bathed after her menses and not being pregnant—should eat the middle *piṇḍa*. By 'having bathed after her menses' is meant one who is not pregnant. Yama states: "One should cause one *piṇḍa* to float in water, present one to the wife, and offer one as an oblation into the fire; these are declared to be the three *piṇḍas*."
In the Vāyu Purāṇa: "A man desiring enjoyment should always offer the rice-ball (piṇḍa) into the fire;
one desiring offspring should indeed offer it to his wife, preceded by the recitation of mantras."
Seeking the highest state, one should always give [the remains] to cows;
one should cause the funeral ball (piṇḍa) to be placed in water for the sake of command, wisdom, glory, and fame.
Desiring long life, he offers [food] to the crows;
standing in water or facing south, he may cause them to go into the sky.
The abode of the ancestors is space, as well as the southern direction.
Regarding the wiping away of the leavings of the twice-born, Vasiṣṭha has stated otherwise:
"At a Śrāddha, the leavings must not be removed until the end of the day;
for streams of *svadhā* flow [from them], which those who have not yet performed their water-libations drink. (1.256)
He states what degree of satisfaction for the ancestors is produced by which substance:
"By sacrificial food (haviṣya) indeed [they are satisfied] for a month, but by milk-rice (pāyasa) for a year;
likewise by fish, deer, sheep, birds, goat, and the meat of the spotted deer. (1.257)
The ancestors are indeed satisfied for increasing periods of months by the offering of the flesh of the human, the ruru deer, the boar, and the hare, respectively. (1.258)

When food fit for oblation (*haviṣya*) is offered, the ancestors beginning with the father and grandfather remain satisfied for a month. Regarding what constitutes *haviṣya*, Manu says: "The foods of sages, milk, Soma, meat that is not seasoned, and salt that is not alkaline—these are by nature called *havis*."

*Rice cooked in milk* (*pāyasa*) is rice boiled in milk. By giving that, the ancestors and others are satisfied for the duration of a year. As it was stated by Manu: "For a year, however, [they are satisfied] with cow's milk and *pāyasa*. And in this context, *pāyasa* should be understood as milk that is not prohibited. Regarding that, Mārkaṇḍeya states the prohibition of specific types of milk:
Sheep, goats, camels, and all animals with uncloven hoofs,
as well as buffaloes, yaks, and even a cow that has not yet calved.
Having said, "Give this for the sake of my ancestors," whatever has been brought forth must always be avoided by the virtuous during the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.

This is the meat of a fish (*matsya*); it is called *mātsya*. When given by him, the ancestors and others remain satisfied for two months. In this context, the fish intended for consumption should be understood as the *pāṭīna* and similar species. This is the meat of a deer (*hariṇa*); it is called *hāriṇa*. In the same way, an increase in the number of months [of satisfaction] should be observed for the meat of sheep (*aurabhra*) and others. An *urabhra* is a ram; its meat is *aurabhra*. Likewise, there are also the meats of the *śvāvidh* (porcupine) and others. A *śakuni* is a bird; here too, only those fit to be eaten by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) are to be accepted. A *chāga* is well known [as a goat]. A *pṛṣata* is a spotted deer. An *eṇa* is a black deer. A *lohita*, however, is a deer (*hariṇa*). This has been stated in the *Āyurveda*: [text follows].
The black antelope (*eṇa*) among these two is to be known as such; the ruddy one is called the *hariṇa*.

The *ruru* is a specific species of deer. Here, the "boar" (*varāha*) refers to the wild one and not the domestic one, because the latter is absolutely unfit to be eaten. "Śāśam" means pertaining to the hare (*śaśa*). On this point, Manu says:
"With sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, or fruits..."
By what is given according to the prescribed rule, the ancestors of men are gratified for a month.
Likewise,
with the meat of the vādhrīṇasa, there is satisfaction for twelve years.

Viṣṇu: "With sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, *syāmaka* grains, *priyaṅgu*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), mung beans, and wheat, [the ancestors] are gratified for one month. With the meat of a *gavaya* (wild ox), they are gratified for nine months; with the meat of a hornless goat (*tūpara*), for eleven months. *Gāvaya* means belonging to the *gavaya*; by that [meat], they are gratified for nine months. *Tūpara* means hornless. Śaṅkha: "One should diligently offer parched grain mixed with honey, as well as groats with sugar, and *śṛṅgāṭaka* and *gavedhuka* in the *śrāddha* ceremony."
Śṛṅgāṭaka is a water-born plant with three thorns; gavedhuka is the fruit of a specific grass that has the shape of a conch shell. 1.257, 258.
The flesh of the rhinoceros, large-scaled fish, honey, and the food of sages; the flesh of iron, kālaśāka greens, and the meat of the vādhrīṇasa crane.

Whatever one who stays at Gayā gives, all that attains infinity. *Khaḍga* is a specific kind of deer named Gaṇḍaka; its flesh is meant here. *Mahāśalka* is a specific kind of fish; by this term, its meat is indicated. *Madhu* is honey. *Munyanna* is wild grain such as *nīvāra* and other crops. *Loha* is a red goat; its flesh is meant here. *Kālaśāka* is well known. *Vādhrīṇasa* is described in the *Nigama*: "The *tripiba* is a white, aged goat, lord of goats, whose senses have declined."
The ritualists call that [animal] a *vādhrīṇasa* in the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.

It is so called by way of etymology: "one who drinks with three," because while drinking, its two ears touch the water as it drinks through its mouth and its two ears. [It refers to] the meat of that "Lord of Goats" (*ajāpati*), meaning a goat whose sensory faculties are diminished and incapable of sexual enjoyment. Likewise:
"The bird with a black neck, red head, and white wings."
"He is indeed called the *vādhrīṇasa*"; such is this Vedic scripture from the *naigama* section.

His flesh, or likewise whatever he gives while staying at Gayā—all this attains infinity; that is, it reaches a state of inexhaustibility. The intended meaning is that the satisfaction produced by this becomes infinite. The mention of Gayā is for the sake of illustration. Therefore it has been said: "At Gaṅgādvāra, at Prayāga, at Naimiṣa, at Puṣkara, at Arbuda, at Saṃnihitī, and at Gayā, a Śrāddha offering shall attain inexhaustibility."
On this point, the Vāyu Purāṇa states:
"He who performs the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice for the ancestors at all times with śyāmāka grains and sugarcane shall quickly attain success."
Know that those called *śyāmāka* and *hastina*, which have emerged from sacrificial rites,
as well as *praśāntika* and *priyaṅgu*, should be accepted in the performance of the *śrāddha* ceremony.
These also would always be equal to śyāmāka grains in their qualities;
black beans, sesame seeds, barley, and rice would likewise be excellent.
Large barley, rice, and likewise *madhūlikā*—
whether black, white, or red— should be accepted for the performance of the *śrāddha* rite.
Bilva, āmalaka, mṛdvīkā, panasa, āmra, ātoda, dāḍima, bhavya, pālevata, akṣoṭa, kharjūra, and āmalaka.
Kaśeru, kovidāra, tālakanda, as well as bisa,
tamāla, śatakanda, madhyālu, and śītakandaka.
Kidney beans, black pot-herbs, suniṣaṇṇaka, and suvarcalā;
meat, vegetables, curd, milk, cañcu, and likewise the sprouts of vetra.
Kaṭphala, kaṅkaṇī, grapes, lakuca, and mocā;
karkandhu, cumin, āra, tinduka, and that which is called madhu.
Vaikaṅkata, nāgarika, śṛṅgāṭaka,
parūṣaka, pippalī, marica, paṭola, and the fruit of bṛhatī.
Fragrant fish and meat, all kinds of peas,
and other such items that are savory and sweet.
And in this case, garlic and long radish should indeed be given.
In the Āditya Purāṇa:
Madhuka, asafoetida, camphor, black pepper,
jaggery, rock salt, and cucumber are likewise commended for the performance of śrāddha rites.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa: "Barley, rice, wheat, sesame, mung beans, mustard seeds, millet, kovidāra, and flat beans— these are auspicious here."
In the Vāyupurāṇa: "Eatables such as cakes, flour-mash, brick-shaped offerings, ghee-filled pastries,
kṛsarā, honey, clarified butter, milk, and milk-rice."
He who gives unctuous and warm food, as well as cow's curd unmixed with anything else and various kinds of edibles, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having given at a śrāddha during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism, one does not grieve;
one should feed the Brahmins with ghee and pour ghee upon the ground.
Pṛthuka grains mixed with sugar and milk, offered daily, shall remain inexhaustible for a year; likewise, [the ancestors] will be satisfied by means of dogs, rams, and deer.
One should feed him barley meal, parched grain, cakes, and boiled grains with their condiments—
all of them moistened with ghee and prepared with curd.
The ancestors gratify him who offers these things during the ancestral rites (śrāddha).
In the Matsya Purāṇa: "Whatever is mixed with honey, cow’s milk, ghee, and milk-rice— this, when offered, the ancestors, who are the five deities, declare to be inexhaustible."
In the Brahma Purāṇa: "The bottle-gourd, the narrow-necked jar, the water-pot, the cucumber,
as well as the madhūka, the coconut, the lakuca, and the harītakī."
One should offer mārkava, curd-vegetable, the vegetable known as utpala,
bhṛṅgarāja, and non-spoiled wild forest products.
Then the roots should be offered: ginger, fresh ginger, lotus stalks, tamāla, śatakanda, bahusūcī, and kaṇṭakī.
Kūrcālaka, piṇḍāla, dīrghamūla,
and varūṭaka should be given along with fresh buttermilk that has not been separated from its butter.
Cooked products of the cow should be given immediately after cooked ghee;
likewise, the milk of a faultless cow, boiled and mixed with sugar, [is to be offered].
Wild buffalo milk combined with sugar and ginger,
sprinkled with honey and served cold, is indeed like nectar itself.
Sour curd (dadhiśukta) produced from curds should be offered everywhere;
one should cause it to be given seasoned with black pepper and also combined with honey and jaggery.
Pulastya said: "The food of sages is prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; meat for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya;
the gift of honey for the Śūdra; and whatever is not in conflict with any of these."
Likewise, during the rainy season on the thirteenth day, and under the asterism of Maghā, there is no doubt [of success]. || 1.260 ||

Whatever one gives to the ancestors on the thirteenth day during the rainy season, and on those [occasions] when the moon is in the Maghā constellation, that too attains an infinity of results characterized by satisfaction; the meaning is that it accomplishes infinite satisfaction for the ancestors. And here, only the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada) and those [occasions] when the moon is in Maghā are intended. Manu says: "Whatever, even if joined with honey, one may offer on the thirteenth day during the rains and under the Maghā asterisms—that indeed shall be inexhaustible."
"Regarding the phrase 'on the thirteenth day' (trayodaśīm), the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative. This is a verse from the *Pitṛgāthā*:
'May there be born in our lineage one who would offer us milk-rice mixed with honey and clarified butter on the thirteenth day, during the rainy season, and under the Maghā asterism.'"
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather,
wait upon the son who is born, just as birds wait upon the peepal tree."
"With honey, meat, vegetables, milk, and milk-rice—
this man will offer us the śrāddha during the rainy season and under the asterism Maghā."
Paiṭhīnasi states:
"Whether it be a son or a grandson, whoever among us should give [a cow] made of all metals on the thirteenth lunar day during the rainy season and under the Maghā asterism."
In the verses addressed to the ancestors: "May there arise in our family someone, a supreme among men, who,
being composed in mind, [offers] during the rainy season, in the dark fortnight, on the thirteenth day..."

He who performs a *śrāddha* with honey-sweetened milk-rice (*pāyasa*) throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or on the day when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east, [attains the highest merit].
As for that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"The man who performs a śrāddha on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight should know for certain that his eldest son will meet his death."
Thus, as stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"A householder who has sons should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day,
nor should he observe a fast on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or during an eclipse of the moon or sun."
A householder who has sons should not perform a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth lunar day; nor is fasting desired by anyone during either of the two solstices (*ayana*).

Regarding this, the following must be considered: Is this a prohibition of that which was prescribed by the rule, "In all the dark fortnights (aparapakṣa), one desiring the preeminence of kinsmen and so forth should perform the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight"? Or is it a prohibition of what is obtained from the injunction, "One should perform the *śrāddha* on the *yugādi* days," as it applies to the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada? Or rather, is it a prohibition of that *śrāddha* which is performed on the three *aṣṭakās*, the three *anvaṣṭakās*, the day after the full moon of Proṣṭhapadī, and on the days of the ripening of rice and barley, as indicated by this [text]? If this were a prohibition of the obligatory (*nitya*) *śrāddha* occasioned by its being a *yugādi* day or by its being the thirteenth day after the full moon of Proṣṭhapadī, then because it would be both enjoined and prohibited, an option (*vikalpa*) would result, just like the choice regarding the performance or non-performance of the *ṣoḍaśin* cup in the *atirātra* sacrifice. Nor should it be argued that the prohibition, having a specific scope—namely, the householder with sons—is stronger than the general injunction, and thus there is no option; for a prohibition requires the prior existence of the possibility of the prohibited act. Consequently, the fact that the performance of the *trayodaśī-śrāddha* exists for the householder with sons is understood precisely from the prohibition itself. Therefore, the option is unavoidable. Now, it might be argued: "This is not a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), but rather an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). Thus, this injunction for the *śrāddha* applies only to those other than the householder with sons; hence, there is no option. This is not correct. For if that were the case, the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) would not be "one should not perform it" (*na kuryāt*), but rather "neither a householder nor one with sons" (*na gṛhī na putravān*). Furthermore, one should not alter the sequence of words and their meanings without justification. Moreover, a negative particle (*nañ*) joined with an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) does not connect with the meaning of the verb (*karoti*), but rather with a noun or another verbal root. Therefore, this prohibition does not concern the obligatory *trayodaśī-śrāddha*, but only the optional (*kāmya*) one. For an option does not arise in the case of something obtained through natural inclination (*rāga*), such as the eating of *kalañja* (a forbidden plant), which is not sanctioned by scripture. [Objection: But the eating of *kalañja* is unscriptural, whereas its prohibition is scriptural; therefore, there is no option. [Reply: However, the *trayodaśī-śrāddha*, though optional, is indeed enjoined by scripture. Therefore, an option with a scriptural prohibition is appropriate. [Objection: True, it is enjoined, but only as a means toward a fruit, not as something to be performed for its own sake. Its performance is based solely on a desire for the fruit; thus, its similarity to the eating of *kalañja* is logical. Even in the view of those who hold that where an injunction impels a person, the fact that the object is a means to a fruit is understood from the scripture, even in that view, the impelling power of the injunction is seen to be directed solely toward making known the object's status as a means to a fruit, and not for the sake of establishing the person's activity, since that is established by the desire for the fruit itself. An injunction is meaningful only when there is a lack of prior engagement across the three times (past, present, future). Hence they say: "An injunction is that which impels one who has not yet acted, and makes known what was unknown. Therefore, this prohibition concerns the optional *trayodaśī-śrāddha*, and not the obligatory one. For this very reason, Āpastamba speaks of the censure of this [optional rite] only as optional: "When performed on any day of the dark fortnight, it pleases the ancestors; however, due to the restriction of time and other factors, there is a distinction in the fruit for the performer. If performed on the first day, offspring will be mostly female. On the second, thieves; on the third, those endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcas*); on the fourth, one possessing small cattle; on the fifth, many males, many offspring, and he does not die childless; on the sixth, one devoted to travel and gambling; on the seventh, increase in agriculture; on the eighth, nourishment; on the ninth, single-hoofed animals; on the tenth, success in business; on the eleventh, iron, tin, and lead; on the twelfth, cattle; on the thirteenth, many sons, many friends, and handsome offspring, but they die young; on the fourteenth, success in weapons; on the fifteenth, nourishment. By the phrase "when performed on any day of the dark fortnight," he states the obligatory nature of the *aparapakṣika-śrāddha*. By the phrase "however, due to the restriction of time... there is a distinction in the fruit," he states that when performed specifically on the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and so forth, it bestows particular fruits. Therefore, this is a prohibition of the optional *trayodaśī-śrāddha* alone. As for the censure of the *maghā-śrāddha* found in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: [The text continues with the citation.]
For one performing a śrāddha under the Maghā asterism, the eldest son perishes;
likewise, there should be fasting on the occasion of a saṃkrānti as well as during lunar and solar eclipses.

Thus, this [text] does not establish a prohibition, because that [prohibition] has already been established. And so, in the section concerning the latter fortnight (aparapakṣa) relating to virgins, the Devīpurāṇa states:
"In that regard, a great worship should be performed for the ancestors and the deities;
however, one who has an eldest son should avoid the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) during the asterism."

The constellation presided over by the ancestors is Maghā. "Worship" refers to the *śrāddha*; therefore, the *śrāddha* performed during the Maghā asterism in the dark fortnight of Bhādrapada, when accompanied by the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), is censured. This does not refer to the *śrāddha* rite in general, because it is specifically the offering of the *piṇḍas* that is prohibited. Furthermore, in the prohibitory statement, the word "offering of *piṇḍas*" (*piṇḍadāna*) is not an indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) for the *śrāddha*, as there is no reason for such an indirect application. Thus, it has been stated that the *Maghā-śrāddha* is devoid of the offering of *piṇḍas*; likewise, other *śrāddhas* devoid of the offering of *piṇḍas* are mentioned in the Matsya Purāṇa:
"The *śrāddha* on the two solstices (*ayana*), and likewise on the two equinoxes (*viṣuvat*)."
And on all the days of the sun's transit (saṃkrānti), except for the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa).
On the third day of Vaiśākha and on the ninth day of Kārttika,
as well as on the [ninth] day of the bright fortnight, Śrāddha should be performed by men according to the rules for the Saṃkrānti.
In the Mahābhārata:
"One should not perform [the rite] under the lunar mansion under which a man was born;
nor, O Bhārata, should it be done under the two Proṣṭhapadas or under the Āgneya (Kṛttikā)."
One should avoid all harsh and inferior [omens],
and one should avoid all those things which have been declared in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa).

The Kṛttikās belong to Agni. The harsh [nakṣatras] are Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūla. The fifth, fourteenth, and twenty-third from one's birth asterism are the *pratyara*. This prohibition regarding the Śrāddha refers specifically to the Śrāddha of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). For that [Śrāddha] is to be performed on any single lunar day without restriction; thus, since it can be performed elsewhere by abandoning what is prohibited, there is no absolute contradiction even in the case of this prohibition. However, if it were intended for other [Śrāddhas], an absolute contradiction of the injunction for the Śrāddha would result. [Thus ends] the section on astrology (*jyotiṣa*).

The funeral rites for humans are not recommended at all during the Sādhāraṇa, Dhruva, or Ugra yogas, nor even during Maitra; likewise, they are not recommended in any way during the Tripuṣkara yoga or when the moon is in the Yamala asterisms.

The *Kṛttikās* and *Viśākhā* are common [to all]. The three *Uttarās* and *Rohiṇī* are fixed (*dhruva*). The three *Pūrvās*, *Bharaṇī*, and *Maghā* are fierce (*ugra*). *Anurādhā* is friendly (*maitra*). The *Tripuṣkara* consists of three feet; the *Yamala* consists of two feet. On the basis of the authority of the scriptures, it must be accepted that even a *śrāddha* performed by a son or others achieves for his father and ancestors the fruit characterized by satisfaction. Likewise, a sacrifice to Vaiśvānara performed by a father accomplishes for his son spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) and other such qualities. This being the case, it can be understood from the scripture that the excellence resulting from the satisfaction of the ancestors arises from specific offerings, specific times, and specific places. (1.260)
It has been stated that the *śrāddha* on the dark fortnight should be performed on a single lunar day; he now explains which result is attained when it is performed on which day:
"A daughter and those who seek a daughter, cattle, excellent sons, as well as gambling, agriculture, trade, and likewise animals with cloven and uncloven hoofs. (1.261)
The giver of the Śrāddha always obtains sons endowed with Vedic luster, gold, silver, and base metals, preeminence among kinsmen, and all desired objects. (1.262)
On the days beginning with the first lunar day, excluding the fourteenth,
offerings are indeed presented there for those who have been slain by weapons.

On every dark fortnight, one who performs the *śrāddha* on the first day (*pratipad*) always obtains a daughter. Likewise, on the second day, by means of a daughter, one obtains sons-in-law; on the third, cattle; on the fourth, excellent sons; on the fifth, success in gambling; on the sixth, agriculture; on the seventh, trade; on the eighth, animals with cloven hooves such as cows; on the ninth, animals with uncloven hooves such as horses; on the tenth, sons endowed with Vedic luster (*brahmavarcas*); on the eleventh, gold and silver; on the twelfth, base metals such as tin and lead; on the thirteenth, preeminence among one’s kinsmen; and on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), all the aforementioned desires. However, the fourteenth day is to be avoided here; on that day, the *śrāddha* should be offered specifically for those killed by weapons. The mention of "those killed by weapons" is intended to illustrate the various types of "bad deaths" (*durmaraṇa*) mentioned in other scriptures. Regarding this, the *Brahmapurāṇa* states:

For those who have died by fasting, starvation, weapons, fire, poison, or hanging, the offering should likewise be performed on the fourteenth lunar day for the sake of their satisfaction; this is the settled rule.
From the Vāyu Purāṇa:
One should cause [the Śrāddha] to be offered for those whose youth died in the house;
indeed, one should give it on the fourteenth day for those who were slain by a weapon.

Marīci states: "For those who have killed a Brahmin, or for those who have killed a snake, a venomous creature, a weapon, a wild beast, or an animal, the rites should be performed on the fourteenth day; for others, however, they are censured."

From this statement, it is determined that the ritual for those killed by weapons and others occurs specifically on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), but not that they must occur only on that day. Therefore, it is appropriate to perform their *śrāddha* on other times as well, such as the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). For this very reason, the *Devīpurāṇa* states: "For those who perished in battles, and for those who fell into water, fire, or from a precipice—on the fourteenth day there should be worship; indeed, the new moon is [the time] according to one's desire."
Garga says:
However, the śrāddha performed on the fourteenth day for one who has been slain by a weapon, once the sapindīkaraṇa has been completed, should be performed according to the ekoddiṣṭa rite.
Likewise:
After the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, except on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight and other annual occasions,
the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is performed and not the *pārvaṇa*.

And in this case, the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* (offering for a single deceased person) applies when only one person has a weapon in hand, but not when three do; in that latter situation, the *pārvaṇa* (ancestral rite) alone is performed. 1.261, 262, 263.

He states the specific results according to the specific lunar mansions: "Indeed, heaven, offspring, vigor, heroism, land, strength, as well as preeminence among kinsmen, great good fortune, prosperity, and excellence of sons. (1.264)
The turning of the wheel [of sovereignty], as well as sons, trade and other such pursuits, freedom from disease, fame, freedom from sorrow, and the supreme goal—these he bestowed. (1.265)
He who duly bestows a Śrāddha offering grants wealth, knowledge, success in medicine, base metals, cattle, goats and sheep, horses, and long life. [560] 1.266.
From Kṛttikā to Bharaṇī, he who is a believer, full of faith, and free from pride and envy shall obtain these desires. (1.267)

A believer who possesses faith and is free from envy, offering the *śrāddha* according to the prescribed rules to the ancestors during the lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Bharaṇī, shall obtain his desired objects—such as heaven and the like—in accordance with the sequence of those constellations. Consequently, one desiring heaven should perform the *śrāddha* under Kṛttikā; one desiring offspring under Rohiṇī; one desiring splendor under Mṛgaśiras; one desiring heroism under Ārdrā; one desiring land under the two Punarvasus; one desiring strength under Puṣya; one desiring a son under Aśleṣā; one desiring preeminence under Maghās; one desiring good fortune under the Pūrva-phalgunīs; one desiring prosperity under the Uttara-phalgunīs; one desiring leadership under Hasta; one desiring a daughter under Citrā; one desiring the turning of a wheel (sovereignty) under Svāti; one desiring a son under Viśākhā; one desiring success in trade under Anurādhā; one desiring freedom from disease under Jyeṣṭhā; one desiring fame under Mūla; one desiring freedom from sorrow under the Pūrva-āṣāḍhās; one desiring liberation under the Uttara-āṣāḍhās; one desiring wealth under Śravaṇa; one desiring knowledge under Dhaniṣṭhā; one desiring success as a physician under Śatabhiṣaj; one desiring base metals under the two Pūrva-bhadrapadās; one desiring cattle under the two Uttara-bhadrapadās; one desiring goats and sheep under Revatī; one desiring horses under Aśvinī; and one desiring long life under Bharaṇī. The *śrāddha* should be performed under the lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā until the attainment of the fruit. For this very reason, it is stated in the Vāyu Purāṇa:
"The man who constantly performs the *śrāddha* during the conjunction of Kṛttikā," and so forth, has been stated [in verses 1.264, 265, 266, and 267].
The Vasus, Rudras, and sons of Aditi are the ancestors who are the deities of the śrāddha;
when the ancestors of men are gratified by the śrāddha, they in turn satisfy [the higher deities].

It has been stated that the *śrāddha* is to be offered to the deceased who are related to oneself; in that regard, this [verse] prescribes that one should cultivate the notion of the Vasus and others toward the ancestors—the fathers and so forth—who have become the deities of the *śrāddha*. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: those fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers who are designated as the deities of the *śrāddha* in the scriptures are to be understood, respectively, as the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. When those Vasus and others, having been established as deities in the *śrāddhas*, are gratified by the *śrāddha*, they in turn gratify the fathers and other ancestors of human beings. The meaning is that when they are meditated upon in the form of the Vasus and others, they attain satisfaction through the *śrāddha*. For this very reason, Manu says:
[561] For they declare the Vasus to be the fathers, the Rudras the grandfathers, and likewise the Ādityas the great-grandfathers; such is this ancient Vedic revelation. 1.268.
When pleased, the ancestors bestow upon men longevity, progeny, wealth, knowledge, heaven, liberation, and happiness, as well as sovereignty. (1.269)

It is the ancestors who bestow fruits such as long life upon those who perform the *śrāddha*, and not the Vasus and other deities. However, one who takes the literal meaning of the previous verse might conceive the notion that the entire *śrāddha* has the Vasus and others as its deities, rather than the ancestors (fathers and so forth). This verse is intended to establish that the *śrāddha* yields fruits such as longevity by means of dispelling that misconception. Furthermore, the mention of the "grandfather" (*pitāmaha*) here is intended to include the father and the rest by implication. Thus, it is stated that the ancestors—beginning with the father—who are connected to the *śrāddha* as its deities for the human performers, become the givers of fruits such as longevity. Although a deity does not directly bestow a transcendental result (*apūrva*), nevertheless, because the arising of the result-bestowing *apūrva* follows from the performance of the rite complete in all its constituent parts (*aṅga*), it is logical to state that the deities—the fathers and others who constitute these constituent parts—are the cause of the fruit. Moreover, the fact that longevity and the other items are each individual fruits is indicated by the use of the accusative case for each one. In this way, it should be understood that *śrāddhas* performed on the new moon day, during the *aṣṭakā* festivals, and so forth, are both obligatory (*nitya*) and optional (*kāmya*). Alternatively, through the performance of the obligatory *śrāddha* itself, the performer attains longevity and other results; just as in the case of the two obligatory sacrifices, the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, the attainment of fruits such as longevity is indicated by the *sūktavāka* formula.

In this regard, that which is to be done when the time for the *śrāddha* has passed is now stated. On this point, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says: "If impurity (*āśauca*) should arise when a *śrāddha* for the ancestors is about to be offered, then once that impurity has elapsed, the *śrāddha* is offered to them."
If an obstacle should arise when the Ekoddiṣṭa has arrived,
one should diligently perform the Śrāddha on that same lunar day in another month.

This refers to the monthly [śrāddha]. Marīci says: When an obstacle to the śrāddha arises and the day of death is unknown, it should be performed on the eleventh day, especially during the dark fortnight.
From the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:

"When the annual rite (*māsika*) is due, but an impurity (*sūtaka*) from a death occurs in the interim, the wise declare that the rite should be performed at the time of purification or on the new moon day."
That which is performed every month on the anniversary of the day of death is here called the *māsika*.

Thus ends the ninth chapter, on Śrāddha, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which itself originated from the lineage of the Vidyādharas. 9.
[562] Now begins the tenth chapter, on the procedure for the worship of Vināyaka, in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti with its commentary.
Now he states the means for avoiding obstacles in the attainment of the fruits of desired actions:
"Vināyaka was appointed by Rudra and likewise by Brahmā to the lordship over the Gaṇas for the sake of accomplishing the obstacles to [worldly] actions. (1.270)

The specific deity known as Vināyaka has been appointed by Rudra and the Four-faced One (Brahmā) to create obstacles for the actions of all performers and to preside over the hosts of attendants, such as Puṣpadanta and others, for the sake of accomplishing those actions; therefore, since he can be warded off only through prescribed means, the procedure for those means is now commenced. 1.270.
In that regard, since there is a section concerning the pacification of obstacles caused by Vināyakas, he first states the characteristics of those obstacles:
"Learn now the symptoms of one who is afflicted by him:
in a dream, he plunges excessively into water and sees shaven-headed men. (1.271)
He wears saffron-colored garments and mounts carnivorous beasts;
he dwells together with outcastes, donkeys, and camels. (1.272)
And as he walks, he likewise imagines himself followed by others.

O sages, listen to the signs that will be described for that man who is afflicted and oppressed by that *vināyaka*: in his dreams, he excessively plunges into water—the meaning is that he sees himself submerged in water; he sees men with shaven heads or those wearing saffron-colored robes (*kāṣāya*); likewise, he climbs upon carnivorous beasts such as tigers and so forth, and he stays in one place together with people of the lowest castes (*antyajātis*). Furthermore, he imagines that others are following him from behind as he walks. Those who eat raw flesh (*kravya*)—that is, uncooked meat—are called *kravyādas* in the context of dreams. (1.271, 272)
Now, regarding wakefulness: one becomes despondent, with undertakings rendered fruitless, and sinks down without apparent cause. (1.273)
Afflicted by that, the prince does not obtain a kingdom;
the maiden does not find a husband, nor does the woman conceive offspring.

The teacher does not obtain the status of an ācārya, nor does the learned disciple obtain his studies; likewise, the merchant does not obtain profit, and the farmer does not obtain the fruits of his cultivation. [563] 1.275

Dejected, anxious in mind, with his undertakings fruitless and his efforts unsuccessful, he sinks down and desponds due to the absence of auspicious signs (*animittataḥ*), that is, the non-appearance of visible omens. O King, the prince does not obtain the kingdom; the maiden, though possessed of good qualities, does not obtain a husband; and the woman, even when she has given birth, does not give birth to a long-lived child. The Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) does not obtain the status of a teacher (*ācāryatva*), nor does the student (*śiṣya*) obtain his studies, nor does the merchant obtain the accumulation of wealth for the sake of his livelihood, nor does the farmer obtain success in agriculture. These are the characteristics of one afflicted by the *vināyakas*. In this regard, the *Baijavāpagṛhya* states: "Now, concerning the *vināyakas*: there are indeed four *vināyakas*, namely Mita, Saṃmita, Śālakaṭaṅka, and Kūṣmāṇḍarājaputra. Afflicted by these *vināyakas*, Brāhmaṇas do not obtain the status of teachers even though they are learned in the Vedas (*svādhyāyavantaḥ*). Princes, though endowed with the marks of royalty, do not obtain the kingdom. Maidens, though possessed of auspicious marks, do not obtain husbands. Even the children of women who are well-behaved die. Indeed, the characteristic of being afflicted by the *vināyakas* is as follows: in a dream, one sees everything [as distorted]; one plunges excessively into water; one leaps into the air and sinks in dust and mud; one thinks, 'Someone is chasing me from behind'; one sees camels, donkeys, dogs, Cāṇḍālas, and other impure beings; and in the act of creation, one sees oneself hidden, internally soiled, while others appear pure. The *Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa* says:
O King, he saw himself deluded regarding his own actions, with his inner self defiled,
covered by the four [elements], and departing toward the vicinity of a cremation ground.
O tiger among kings, he sees him; there is no doubt in this.
O Lord, his limbs are moist with oil and he is adorned with oleander flowers.

His ceremonial bath (snāpana) should be performed according to the prescribed rules on an auspicious day for the sake of pacifying the affliction caused by Vināyaka. On an auspicious day, the bath must be carried out according to the procedure that will be described hereafter. As for what is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"On the fourth lunar day of the bright fortnight, and on the day of Jupiter (Dhiṣaṇa)..."
And during the Tiṣya and Vīra constellations, O King, right before him.

Thus it is said; however, that should be understood as referring to the ritual bathing of Śrī-Kāmavināyaka. As for the injunction regarding the *puṇyāha* (auspicious day) ceremony, it pertains to those cases involving the ritual bathing of one who has been possessed (*upasṛṣṭa*), because for one who is possessed, a long delay is not appropriate. *Dhiṣaṇa* is Bṛhaspati; the meaning is "of that very Vināyaka."
He states the procedure for the ritual bathing:
"And for one who has been anointed with a paste of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter... (1.276).
Likewise, with his head anointed with all medicinal herbs and all fragrant substances,
while he is seated upon an auspicious throne, the auspicious twice-born ones should recite benedictions.

He should be rubbed with a powder of white mustard seeds mixed with clarified butter. Then, having smeared his head with all medicinal herbs and fragrant substances ground together with water, he should be seated upon a *bhadrāsana*. Thereafter, the auspicious Brahmins and twice-born priests should be addressed: "May you, sirs, pronounce a blessing (*svasti*)," whereby they should be made to utter words of well-being and prosperity. Here, the genitive case is used in the sense of the agent; thus, the meaning is that they are to be addressed by him. Furthermore, it is stated in the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa* that after performing the worship of the deities beginning with Śiva, the rites such as the offering of the seat (*sādana*) and so forth should be carried out.
Having worshipped Vyomakeśa, Pārvatī, and likewise Bhīmaja, O dear one,
as well as Kṛṣṇa’s father, Araka, Āra, and Sita;
O Bhārata, [he saw] Dhiṣaṇa, Kledaputra, Koṇa, Lakṣma,
Vidhuntuda, Bāhuleya, and the bearer of Nandaka.

Vyomakeśa is Śiva; Bhīmaja is Gaṇeśa; Kṛṣṇa’s father is Vasudeva; Āra is Mars (Bhauma); Sita is Venus (Śukra); Kledaputra is Mercury (Budha); Koṇa is Saturn (Śaneśvara). Lakṣma refers to the one possessing marks, namely the Moon (Candra), meaning "full"; Vidhuntuda is Rāhu; Ketu, though not explicitly mentioned here, should be understood by association; Bāhuleya is Skanda; Nandakadhārī is Viṣṇu; and "all medicinal herbs" refers to Sahadevī and others. Thus, the Matsyapurāṇa states: "Sahadevī, Vacā, Vyāghrī, Balā, and likewise Atibalā..."
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, likewise Siṃhī, and Suvarcalā as the eighth.
One should indeed employ this group of eight great medicinal herbs during the great ritual ablutions.
Or [one may take] *brāhmī*, *suvarcalā*, and so forth. Thus says the *Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa*:
"Brāhmī, *suvarcalā*, *mustā*, *viṣṇukrāntā*, *śatāvarī*, *durlabhā*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *priyaṅgu*, *rajanī*, and *vacā*."

Or *surā* and so forth. Likewise, the *Smṛti* states: "Sura, māṃsī, vacā, kuṣṭha, the two types of *rajanī*, *satī*, *caṇyaka*, and *musta*—this is known as the group of all medicinal herbs (*sarvauṣadhigaṇa*). [565]

*Surā* is well known as *tābhora*. The "two nights" (*rajanīdvayam*) refers to *haridrā* and *dāruharidrā*. *Satī* is a specific type of camphor, or alternatively, substances such as sand (*vālukā*). Thus Vasiṣṭha says:
"Sand, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *kuṣṭha*, as well as *vacā*, and the powder of *nāgakesara*—this is the group of all medicinal herbs according to Bhṛgu. (1.276, 277)
Moreover:

One should cast in clay from the foot of an Aśvattha tree, from the footprint of an elephant, from an anthill, from a confluence, and from a lake, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā), fragrant substances, and guggulu resin. || 1.278 ||
Regarding the waters brought from a lake in four pitchers of a single color:

having fetched water with four pitchers of a single color, one should cast into that water earth collected from the horse's footprint and other such sites, as well as fragrances consisting of *gorocanā*, *aguru*, musk, camphor, sandalwood, and saffron, and *guggulu*. On this point, the *Baijavāpa-gṛhya* states: "Having brought four jars from four springs, one should [place] all medicinal herbs, all fragrances, gold, rice and barley, *guggulu*, earth, and molehills into them. The word "one should cast" (*prakṣipet*) is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. (1.278)
Then, a blessed seat (bhadrāsana) should be placed upon a red bull-hide.

The ox (*anadvān*) is the draft-ox that pulls the cart (*śakaṭa*). Upon its hide, which is red, the auspicious seat (*bhadrāsana*) is established according to the ritual manual. Thereafter, it is to be placed after the casting of earth and other materials into the water. (1.279)
With that which has a thousand eyes and a hundred streams, purified by the seers—I sprinkle you with it; may the purifying verses cleanse you.
King Varuṇa gave you fortune; Sūrya and Bṛhaspati gave you fortune;
Indra and Vāyu gave you fortune; and the Seven Seers bestowed fortune upon you. (1.281)
Whatever misfortune is in your hair, whatever is in your parting, or whatever is upon your head;
may the waters always destroy that [misfortune] on your forehead, ears, and eyes. 1.282

With each of the three mantras beginning with "sahasrākṣam," the preceptor performs the ritual bathing of the one possessed by Vināyaka using each water-pot individually; the three mantras are repeated for each pot. (1.280, 281, 282)
[566] Having bathed, one should offer mustard oil with a ladle made of udumbara wood into the head,
while grasping kusha grass with the left hand.
Mitā, Saṃmita, Śālakaṭaṅkaṭa, and Kūṣmāṇḍarājaputra—these names, ending with the word *svāhā*, [are to be recited]. (1.284)
Accompanied by their names and bali-mantras joined with salutations,
one who is firm in his vows should place a winnowing basket at a crossroads after having spread kuśa grass upon it.
Rice that has been husked and rice that has not, as well as rice mixed with minced meat, cooked fish and likewise raw fish, and meat—these alone [are the offerings]. (1.286)
Variegated and fragrant flowers, as well as various kinds of liquor, radishes, fried cakes, pastries, and likewise garlands of *uṇḍeraka*— these he offered.
Curd-rice, milk-porridge, and food mixed with molasses along with water-offerings (modaka).

In the manner previously described, the Guru should offer oblations upon the head of the *snātaka* with his left hand holding *kuśa* grass and his right hand holding a ladle (*sruva*) made of *udumbara* wood, using mustard oil, while reciting: "Svāhā to Mitāya! Svāhā to Saṃmitāya! Svāhā to Śālakaṭaṅkaṭāya! Svāhā to Kūṣmāṇḍarājaputrāya! Then, at a crossroads, he should place a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) and spread *kuśa* grass over it with its tips pointing in all directions. There, he should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*), consisting of rice that has been partially husked and partially unhusked, and so forth. Because of the specific instruction regarding the names and the mantras for the offering, it is understood that the offering should be presented using the names beginning with "Mitā," in the dative case, accompanied by the word of salutation (*namaḥ*), thereby transforming them into mantras for the offering. Rice grains whose state as husked grain has begun through threshing and other processes but is not yet completed are called "partially prepared" (*kṛtākṛta*) rice. Rice mixed with sesame paste is *palalaudana*. *Mūlaka* is a specific type of vegetable. Fried cakes are *lopikāḥ* and *pūrikāḥ*. Small cakes are *tūṇḍerakāḥ*. The rest is well known. Having placed all these items in a single vessel, he should offer them all at once. 1.283, 284, 285, 286, 287.
Then one should worship Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka.
Having offered an *arghya* of *dūrvā* grass and mustard flowers in a full *añjali*, one should say:
"Grant me beauty; grant me fame; grant me fortune. [567] 1.289
"Give me sons, give me wealth, and grant me all my desires.

Having prepared a full *añjali* as an *arghya* offering consisting of *dūrvā* grass, mustard seeds, flowers, and water, and having presented it to Ambikā, the mother of Vināyaka, he should worship her with the mantra: "Grant me [good] form. (1.288, 189)
Then, wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, [he appeared].
One should feed the Brahmins and give a pair of garments even to the Guru.

Having approached Ambikā, having put on two white garments, and having adorned oneself with white garlands and unguents, one should feed the Brahmins. And one should give a pair of garments to the Guru. By the use of the word "Guru," it is implied that the performer of the ritual bath is to be honored like a Guru. (1.290)
Having thus worshipped Vināyaka and the planets according to the prescribed rule, || 1.291 ||
One obtains the fruit of one's actions and attains unsurpassed prosperity.

By worshipping Vināyaka and the planets in the manner described, and according to the procedure to be explained, one obtains the fruit of actions already performed and those yet to be performed through the pacification of obstacles. One also attains unsurpassed prosperity—that which has nothing superior to it. The repetition of the word "obtains" (*āpnoti*) is for the purpose of prescribing the worship of Vināyaka and the others as a distinct rite for one who desires prosperity. 1.291.
One should always perform worship of the Sun and likewise apply the *tilaka* of one's Lord.
By performing [this worship] for Mahāgaṇapati as well, one shall attain success.
Thus ends the section on the procedure for the worship of Vināyaka. 10.

By performing worship at all times for Āditya the Lord, Skanda, and Mahāgaṇapati, and by applying a sectarian mark (tilaka) made of gold or other materials, one shall attain the fulfillment of the fruits of one's actions. || 1.292 ||

Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the procedure for the worship of Vināyaka, in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which itself originated from the line of the venerable Vidyādharas. || 9 ||

Now begins the section on the procedure for the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajña*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary. (11) Now he states the procedure for the sacrifice to the planets.

One who desires peace (*śānti*) and so forth, or one practicing sorcery (*abhicāra*), should perform—that is, carry out—the *grahayaṣṭi* (sacrifice to the planets) whose nature will be described below. Peace is the warding off of misfortunes that are about to yield their fruit. Prosperity (*puṣṭi*) is the augmentation of the body and other factors. Sorcery is the obstruction of the merit that bestows long life. The rest is well known. The connection of "desire" (*kāma*) is with each of these—rain, long life, and prosperity—individually, not with them combined together, because they are mentioned as objects of desire while being established by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the qualification of such an object of desire is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Previously, the *grahayaṣṭi*, accompanied by the ritual bath for Vināyaka, was prescribed for the sake of prosperity; now, it is prescribed alone for other fruits—this is the distinction between the rules (*vidhi*). In the word "practicing sorcery" (*abhicaran*), the present participle suffix (*śatṛ-pratyaya*) expresses that sorcery is the cause (*hetu*) for the *grahayaṣṭi*. Since sorcery is not yet accomplished, it cannot be a cause in its own form; rather, it is the desire for it that is the cause, because through that desire, sorcery becomes connected to the action as its result. (1.293)
He speaks of the planets: the Sun, the Moon, the Son of the Earth (Mars), the Son of the Moon (Mercury), and Bṛhaspati (Jupiter). || 1.294 ||
Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu are known as the planets (grahas).

These are the deities of the planetary sacrifice (*grahayajña*). Although the terms *sūrya* and so forth are used here due to the requirements of the meter, in the actual performance of the sacrifice, the offerings must be designated using the terms *āditya* and so forth. Thus, the *Bahvṛca-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa* states: "Jaggery-rice for Āditya; milk-porridge with ghee for Soma; sacrificial food for Aṅgāraka (Mars); rice with sesame for Budha (Mercury); sixty-day rice for Bṛhaspati (Jupiter); curd-rice for Śukra (Venus); bean-rice mixed with sesame flour and ghee for Śanaiścara (Saturn); meat-rice for Rāhu; and variegated rice for Ketu. There is no reason to disregard the words as they are heard in this prose text [of the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti*]. (1.294)
He states the materials for the images of the planets, beginning with the Sun:
"From copper, from crystal, from red sandalwood, and from gold, [should be made] both. (1.295)
The planetary deities should be fashioned in order from silver, iron, lead, and bell-metal;
or they may be drawn on a cloth with their respective colors, or even upon a fragrant mandala or [other suitable surfaces]. [1.296]

*Tāmra* itself is *tāmraka*; therefore, an image of the Sun should be made from it. [An image] of the Moon from crystal; of Mars from red sandalwood; of Mercury and Jupiter from gold; of Venus from silver; of Saturn from black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*); of Rāhu from lead; and of Ketu from bell-metal (*kāṃsya*). However, one who is unable to fashion these images should paint the planets on a cloth using pigments of colors corresponding to those of the planets. If he is unable even for that, he should delineate the planets upon circular mandalas of fragrant substances such as sandalwood, which are of colors corresponding to those of the planets. On this point, the *Matsyapurāṇa* states:

The Sun should always be depicted with two arms, seated upon a chariot drawn by seven horses, in the lotus posture (padmāsana), with hands like lotuses, and possessing a splendor equal to the interior of a lotus.
Śaśin should be depicted as white, wearing white garments, possessing ten arms, with white horses and white ornaments;
he has two primary hands holding a mace and is bestowing boons.
Wearing red garlands and garments, holding a spear, a trident, and a mace in his hands,
the son of the Earth (Mars) should be four-armed, mounted upon a ram, and granting boons.
Wearing yellow garlands and garments, with the luster of the petals of the Karṇikāra flower,
holding a sword, shield, and mace in his hands, the wise Budha (Mercury) stands upon a lion and grants boons.
Likewise, the preceptors of the gods and the Daityas should be depicted as yellow and white respectively, each with four arms,
holding a staff, granting boons, and carrying a rosary and a water-pot.

The son of the Sun (Saturn) should always be depicted as having the luster of sapphire, holding a trident and a bow, granting boons, and mounted upon a vulture, with his hands bearing an arrow and a bow.
With a formidable face, bearing a sword, shield, and trident, and bestowing boons,
Rāhu is praised there as being seated upon a blue lion-throne.
All smoke-colored, two-armed, wielding maces, and having distorted faces;
seated eternally upon vultures, these banners shall be granters of boons.
All the planets that bestow welfare upon the world should be depicted wearing crowns;
they should all always be one hundred and eight in number, each raised [in height] by one's own finger-breadth.
The Sun and Mars are red; Venus and the Moon are white;
and both Mercury and Jupiter are traditionally held to be yellow.
One should know Kṛṣṇa as Śanaiścara (Saturn), and likewise Rāhu and Ketu.
This has been explained by the preceding statement. [Now, the specific section on Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha: In the Devīpurāṇa:
"O twice-born ones, now hear concerning the image of Prabhākara.
One should have the god made seated upon a chariot, with a lotus in his hand and beautiful eyes."
One should fashion for him a chariot with seven horses and a single face,
adorned with a variegated crown and possessing a splendor like the interior of a lotus.
With hands adorned with various ornaments,
he always held the lotus, and the lotus was likewise held effortlessly upon his shoulder.
In some paintings, one should depict his body covered by a tunic,
provided with a pair of garments, and his feet enveloped in splendor.
Two doorkeepers, Daṇḍa and Piṅgala, should be placed at the two sides;
and two male figures, both holding staffs in their hands, should be made at the two sides.
And one should likewise depict the imperishable Creator (Dhātṛ) at his side with hand raised as if holding a pen, accompanied by various hosts of gods; thus one should fashion the Sun-god.
His charioteer Anūru was like a lotus leaf,
and his two horses stood at his sides with necks turned back, exuding fragrance.
Bound with serpent-ropes and joined with a chariot of seven horses,
one should likewise fashion [an image] upon that [chariot], standing on the seven horses and holding a lotus in hand.
In the Padma Purāṇa: "For this very reason, no one should ever cause the feet of the Sun to be drawn anywhere;
he who does so attains a most sinful and censured state."
One obtains the form of leprosy in this world, which is designated as suffering.
In this context, the characteristics of Vahni and the others are stated. I shall now describe the characteristic of Vahni, which is marked by all defining features:
he is radiant, possesses a golden body, sits upon a half-moon seat, and is all-pervading.
One should have his garment made here resembling the rising sun;
one should likewise represent him wearing a sacred thread and having long beard and eyebrows.
He holds a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) in his left hand and a rosary (akṣasūtra) in his right;
he is joined with a canopy of flames, mounted upon a goat, and resplendent.
Or one should fashion her seated in a vessel, endowed with seven crests upon her head;
I shall now describe the form of Kātyāyanī, who likewise possesses ten arms.
She imitated the appearance of all three gods,
was endowed with a mass of matted hair, and was marked by the crescent moon.
She is endowed with three eyes, her face resembles the full moon,
she has the luster of an *atasī* flower, and she is well-established with beautiful eyes.
Endowed with fresh youth, adorned in all her limbs,
possessing very beautiful teeth, and likewise having full and elevated breasts.
One should depict Mahiṣāsuramardinī standing in the tribhaṅga posture;
one should give her a trident in her right hand, and likewise a sword and a discus.
Likewise, understand that on the left side there is a sharp-edged spear,
as well as a shield, a full-drawn bow, a noose, and a goad.
One should place either a bell or an axe on the left side;
likewise, one should depict a two-headed buffalo below it.
Likewise, one should place the Dānava with a sword in hand upon the severed head;
[one should also place him] pierced by a trident in the heart, adorned both horizontally and vertically.
His limbs were stained crimson, his eyes flashed with red light,
he was encircled by a serpent-noose, and his face was terrifying with a frown.
One should depict the lion of the Goddess as having a face dripping with blood;
the Goddess’s right foot is placed evenly upon the lion.
One should visualize that form standing slightly above and to the left upon a buffalo, with its thumb raised,
and being praised by the immortals.
I shall describe Vināyaka, who has the face of an elephant, three eyes,
a protruding belly, four arms, and wears a serpent as his sacred thread.
With stiff ears, a large snout, a single tusk, and a broad belly,
he held his own tooth in his right hand and likewise a blue lotus in the other.
One should visualize a sweetmeat (modaka) and an axe (paraśu) on the left side;
[the deity] has a large, dense, and thick trunk, with stout shoulders, feet, and hands,
endowed with both wisdom and folly, and accompanied by a mouse below.
Brahmā, holding a water-pot, should be depicted with four faces.
In some instances he should be depicted as mounted upon a swan, and in others as seated upon a lotus;
he is lotus-colored in hue, with four arms and auspicious eyes.
One should visualize a water-pot in the left hand and a sacred thread in the right hand;
likewise, one should imagine him holding a staff in the left [hand] and also the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles.
The Lord, clad in white garments, was being praised on all sides by sages, gods, and gandharvas, as if he were creating the three worlds anew.
He was clad in a deer skin and wore a divine sacred thread;
a vessel of clarified butter was at his side, and a sacrificial oblation (caru) was before him.
Sāvitrī is on the left side and Sarasvatī on the right;
likewise, the sages should be placed in front in the position belonging to Pitāmaha.

Such is the specific detail found in the manuscript of Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha. Having stated this incidental matter, the subject at hand is now discussed. These planets, having had the sacred fire (agni) led forward, are to be worshipped in the north-eastern region of the sacrificial ground (agnyāyatana). And so says the Matsya Purāṇa: "To the north-east of the pit (garta), one should prepare an altar (vedi) two vitastis in width, provided with three ridges (vapra), and measuring one vitasti in height."
For the establishment of the gods, [he made] a square [altar] that floats upon the water.
The word "should do" (*kuryāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. A *garta* is a dug-out pit serving as the site for the fire; a *vapra* is a surrounding embankment or moat.
Having performed the ritual bringing forward of the fire (*agnipraṇayana*), one should invoke the gods upon it.
Upon that [altar], three rows of square cells (*koṣṭhaka*) are to be made, with three cells in each row.
Saturn, Venus, Moon,
Jupiter,
Mars, Rahu, Ketu, Mercury, Sun.
In that regard: one should know Bhāskara (the Sun) to be in the center, Lohita (Mars) to the south,
Guru (Jupiter) to the north, and Budha (Mercury) to the northeast.
One should know Bhārgava (Venus) to be in the east, Soma (the Moon) in the southeast;
one should know Śani (Saturn) to be in the west, and Rāhu in the southwest.
One should place the banner in the north-western direction with white rice grains.
And these should be placed facing the sun. || 1.296 ||
He states the worship of the planets:
"Garments and flowers should be offered according to their respective colors."
Scents, offerings, and incense made of guggulu should also be presented. || 1.297 ||

Whatever be the color of a planet, garments and other items of that same color should be offered to it. For incense, *guggulu* resin should be given. Here, due to the constraints of the meter, the sequence is not intended to be definitive; it should be understood from elsewhere that the offerings of perfume, flowers, incense, garments, and food-oblations (*bali*) are to be given in their proper order. In this regard, perfumes and flowers are to be offered to all the planets, as are the incense and so forth; one should not, however, offer everything from the perfume down to the oblation to a single planet and then proceed to give them to another. (1.297)
He states the procedure for the oblation:
"And sacrificial porridges accompanied by mantras must be prepared for each respective deity."
