Not only should worship be performed for the Sun and the other [planets], but also for each of them, *caru* oblations must be offered. These should be prepared with their respective mantras. A *caru* is a rice porridge that has not been drained, is pure, and is cooked internally by its own heat. Regarding the reading *tantravantaḥ*, the *tantra* refers to the ritual procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the *pākayajña*. And here, because all nine planetary sacrifices (*grahayāga*) occur at the same time, there is no distinction in the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) and other such elements. As Śaunaka says: "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*), the fuel (*idhma*), the clarified butter (*ājya*), and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should be common to all, as they occur at the same time. Thus, this [procedure] is sung as the portion belonging to the sacrifice.

"Having performed the *pākayajñas*, one should perform them with a single portion of clarified butter (*ājya*), a single sacrificial grass mat (*barhis*), and a single *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, even though the deities may be different. Thus [it is said].
He now states the mantras for the oblations (*homa*).
"Ā kṛṣṇena," "imaṃ devāḥ," "agnir mūrdhā divaḥ kakut. 1.298.
The verses beginning with "uḍbudhyasva" are proclaimed according to their respective order;
likewise, "bṛhaspate atiyadaryaḥ" corresponds to the *parisrut* offering.
"May the goddesses be auspicious to us," and likewise "From the section," and "Making a banner," and these [verses] as well.

Since the Blessed One is a master of yoga and a Vājasaneyin, the mantras recited in the *Vājasaneyaka* (the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa) are precisely those to be adopted here. It should be understood that the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details for these are exactly those found therein. The nine mantras beginning with "With the black one" (*ākṛṣṇena*) are prescribed and proclaimed to be used respectively in the nine oblations (*homa*) dedicated to deities such as Āditya and the others. In that context, since only one offering per sacrificial pap (*caru*) is obtained by extension from the *pākayajña* rules, each offering must be performed with a single mantra, as no other number of offerings is prescribed. "Ākṛṣṇena": Hiraṇyastūpa Āṅgirasa is the seer; Āditya is the deity; Triṣṭubh is the meter. "Imaṃ devāḥ": The deities; Soma; Yajus (prose). "Agnir mūrdhā": Viśvarūpa Āṅgirasa; Aṅgāraka (Mars); Gāyatrī. "Udbudhyasva": Parameṣṭhin; Budha (Mercury); Triṣṭubh. "Annāt parisrutaḥ": The Aśvins, Sarasvatī, and Indra; Śukra (Venus); Atijagatī. "Saṃ no devīḥ": Sindhudvīpa; Śanaiścara (Saturn); Gāyatrī. "Kāṇḍāt kāṇḍāt": Agni; Rāhu; Anuṣṭubh. "Ketuṃ kṛṇvan": Madhucchandas; Ketu (the Comet); Gāyatrī. [1.298, 299]
Following the *caru* oblation, he describes the fire-oblation (*homa*) preceded by an exposition of the nature of the sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*):
"The *arka*, the *palāśa*, the *khadira*, the *apāmārga*, and then the *pippala*. (1.300)
Udumbara, śamī, dūrvā, and kuśa are the sacrificial fuels (samidh) respectively; for each, there should be one hundred and eight or twenty-eight [pieces]. 1.301.
They should be offered as oblations with honey and clarified butter, combined with curd and milk.

One hundred and eight or twenty-eight fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of *arka* and other trees, smeared with honey and clarified butter, or with curd and milk, should be offered for each [deity] with the previously mentioned mantras. The genitive case in "for each one" (*ekaikasya*) is used in the sense of the dative. This number refers specifically to the fuel-sticks, as they form a single syntactical unit [with the rest of the passage]. Furthermore, the fuel-sticks should not be cast into the fire all at once after reciting the mantra once for the sake of a single deity; rather, they should be offered one by one, with the mantra repeated for each individual stick. Thus it is stated in the *Matsyapurāṇa*:
The fuel-sticks (samidh) should be offered separately with their respective mantras; likewise,
they should be a span (prādeśa) in length, possessed of their tips, and split from branches and leaves.
A wise person should always prepare the sacrificial fuel for all ritual acts.
He states the two types of food for feeding Brahmins:
"Jaggery-rice and milk-rice, sacrificial food, and milk-rice made with ṣaṣṭika rice. (1.302)
A wise person should give these foods to the twice-born in the order of the planets: curd-rice, rice with ghee, kṛsara, meat, and variegated dishes. 1.303.

According to one's capacity or as available, one should respectfully offer food such as rice mixed with molasses (*guḍaudana*) and so forth to the twice-born (*dvija*) in accordance with the prescribed ritual and the order of the planets. By the etymology "that which is eaten" (*bhujyate*), the term *bhojana* refers specifically to edible food. If one is unable to give rice mixed with molasses, then one should give common food according to one's means and as it is obtained, following the prescribed ritual. Rice mixed with molasses is *guḍaudana*. Sixty-day rice (*ṣaṣṭikānna*) mixed with milk is *kṣīraṣāṣṭika*. *Ṣaṣṭika* is a specific variety of grain. In this context, all of the rice mixed with molasses is considered variegated (*citraka*). (1.302, 303)
The sacrificial fee is said to be, in order: a cow, a conch shell, a bull, gold, a garment, and a horse. (1.304)
A black cow, a white cow, iron, and a goat—these are indeed recorded as the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

The sacrificial fees should be given according to the sequence of the planets. A "cow" (*gauḥ*) refers to a milch-cow that has recently calved; an "ox" (*anaḍvān*) is a bull capable of drawing a cart. "Iron" (*āyasa*) means made of metal. The rest is well known. And these sacrificial fees must be given specifically to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Thus says the *Matsyapurāṇa*: "The sacrificer, together with his wife, and the composed officiating priests..."
Free from pride, one should worship with effort by means of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās).
One should give a tawny cow to the Sun, and likewise a conch shell to the Moon;
to Mars, one should give a red, draft-ox endowed with a hump.
One should give gold to Budha, yellow garments to Guru,
a white horse to the preceptor of the Daityas (Śukra), and a black cow to the son of the Sun (Maṅgala).
One should give an iron image to Rāhu and an excellent goat to Ketu;
the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be made equal in value to gold by the sacrificer.
Alternatively, cows adorned with gold should be given to all;
or else one should give gold, or whatever else by which the Guru is pleased.
And whoever is in a difficult situation for another at any time, that person should honor them with effort. || 1.305 ||
Brahmā granted them this boon: "When worshipped, you shall worship [the person].

Whichever planet of a man is ill-placed—standing in a heap of suffering such as being situated in the eighth house from the natal ascendant (janmarāśi)—he, being unable to worship that planet along with the other planets, should worship that one alone with effort and devotion according to the prescribed rite. For when worshipped, it does not cause suffering. Because Brahmā Prajāpati granted this boon: 'You shall worship the worshipper of these planets and shall endow him with his desired fruit. (1.305)
On this very point, he states another reason:
"The rises and falls of kings depend upon the planets. (1.306)
Since both the existence and non-existence of the world depend upon them, the planets are most worthy of worship.

Even for kings who possess an accumulation of merit earned over many lifetimes, their exaltations—consisting of extraordinary prosperity—and their falls—which take the form of extreme misfortune—are dependent upon the planets. Likewise, the existence and non-existence, the rise and dissolution, of the world are entirely dependent on the planets. Therefore, the planets are to be worshipped with even greater distinction than other more venerable beings, according to the manner described. Although merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are the causes for the experience of pleasure and pain, they do not become such causes without depending on specific times. Furthermore, a specific time cannot be determined without the particular movements of the planets; thus, the exaltation of kings and so forth is dependent on the planets. Consequently, having observed an unfavorable planetary position, one should perform a *grahayaṣṭi* (planetary sacrifice) to ward off the mass of future suffering indicated by it. For that [sacrifice] is prescribed for one desiring peace (*śānti*); this is the intended meaning. 1.306.

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on the procedure for the sacrifice to the planets (*grahayajñavidhiprakaraṇa*), in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, born of the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the lineage of the venerable Vidyādharas. || 11 ||
Now begins the section on the Duties of Kings (*rājadharmaprakaraṇa*) in the *Yājñavalkyasmṛti* with its commentary.

(12) The duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) and the duties of the student (*brahmacārin*) and the householder (*gṛhastha*) have been stated. Now, in order to declare the duties of the king—who is also a householder—such as the protection of the realm and so forth, [the author] first states those qualities endowed with which he becomes fit for the protection of the subjects.
Possessing great energy, liberal, grateful, and a servant of the elderly. || 1.307 ||
He is disciplined, endowed with goodness, of noble birth, truthful in speech, pure, not procrastinating, mindful, and likewise neither mean nor harsh. (1.308)

He should be righteous, free from vices, wise, brave, and a knower of secrets; likewise, he should be a protector of his own vulnerabilities, proficient in both the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī) and the science of government (daṇḍanīti).
Then, O lord of men, that king was disciplined both in the science of economics and in the triple Veda.

A king who possesses qualities such as great energy (*mahotsāha*) becomes capable of establishing the Brāhmaṇas and others in their respective duties; this is the meaning. "Great energy" means great exertion. The greatness of energy consists in its vast scope and its being unimpeded. "Generous" (*sthūlalakṣa*) means one who gives much. One who remembers a benefactor for the sake of returning the favor is "grateful" (*kṛtajña*). A "servant of the elders" (*vṛddhasevaka*) is one who attends upon persons advanced in knowledge and other virtues. "Humble" (*vinīta*) means modest toward teachers and others. One who does not deviate from justice even when fallen into misfortune is "virtuous" (*sāttvika*). "Noble-born" (*kulīna*) means born of a pure lineage. "Truthful in speech" (*satyavāk*) means one whose promise is true. "Pure" (*śuci*) means possessing external and internal purity. "Not procrastinating" (*adīrghasūtrī*) means one who is free from hesitation regarding a limited matter. "Possessing memory" (*smṛtimān*) means having excellent recollection. "Not mean" (*akṣudra*) means having a noble heart. One who becomes angry at a slight injury or pleased by a small benefit is "mean-hearted. "Gentle" (*aparuṣa*) means one whose speech is not harsh. "Virtuous" (*dhārmika*) is well-known. "Free from vice" (*avyasana*) means devoid of vices such as gambling that distract from the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). "Wise and brave" (*prājñaśūra*) are well-known terms. "Knower of secrets" (*rahasyavid*) means one who knows himself, or knows counsel, or knows the vulnerabilities of enemies. "Guardian of his own weaknesses" (*svarandhragoptā*): a "weakness" (*randhra*) is that deficiency in the constituents of sovereignty through which an enemy may enter; he is the protector or guardian thereof. "Trained" (*vinīta*) means educated in *ānvīkṣikī*, *daṇḍanīti*, *vārtā*, and the *trayī*. *Ānvīkṣikī* is the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*) not contradictory to the Vedas and other scriptures. *Daṇḍanīti* is the science of statecraft (*arthaśāstra*). *Vārtā* is the science of agriculture and so forth. The *trayī* consists of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas. By the mention of the *trayī*, its auxiliary branches (*aṅga*) such as grammar, as well as Mīmāṃsā, the Purāṇas, and the Dharmaśāstras, are included. (1.307, 308, 309)
He should appoint as ministers those who are wise, hereditary, steadfast, and pure. (1.310)
He should deliberate on the kingdom together with them, and thereafter with a Brahmin, and finally by himself.

That king, possessing the aforementioned qualities, should diligently appoint—meaning, he should take as his ministers—those who know what ought and ought not to be done, who are wise and capable of reasoning and refutation (*ūhāpoha*), who are hereditary (*maula*) having come down through a lineage of fathers, who are steadfast and unswerving in their master’s welfare, and who are pure, having passed the tests of integrity (*śuddhopadhā*). Then, together with them, he should deliberate upon the kingdom—the royal business consisting of the sixfold policy (*ṣāḍguṇya*) and its constituent elements, such as sovereignty (*svāmya*) and so forth; that is to say, he should investigate them in terms of what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted. Furthermore, he should deliberate again with a Brahmin who knows the sixfold policy, and finally, he himself should determine that very matter by means of the presence of corroborating and subverting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*). (1.310)
And he should appoint as his domestic priest one who is an astrologer and of highly exalted birth.

One should appoint as domestic priest (purohita) a Brāhmaṇa who is skilled in the science of government (daṇḍanīti) as well as in the Atharvāṅgirasa, and who is endowed with qualities such as being an astrologer (daivajña). An astrologer is one who knows the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra); for by that science, the destiny (daiva) of living beings—that is, the ripening of their karma—is known. One whose aforementioned qualities—such as wisdom and so forth, which have been described for ministers—are "risen" (uditāḥ), meaning manifested in him, is called "one whose qualities are risen" (uditoditaḥ). One should appoint, that is, choose, such a person as domestic priest; for the office of domestic priest arises through formal selection (varaṇa), just like the office of the Adhvaryu priest and others. (1.311)
For the sake of performing rites prescribed by the Śruti and the Smṛti, he should certainly choose officiating priests. || 312 ||
One should also perform sacrifices according to the prescribed rules with abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

For that purpose—the performance of rites such as the *agnihotra* enjoined by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*—one should select (*vṛṇuyāt*) priests (*ṛtvij*), beginning with the Brahman, and appoint them through the act of selection, just as one appoints the *āhavanīya* and other fires through the rite of fire-consecration (*adhāna*). Likewise, one should perform sacrifices such as those consisting of oblations (*havir-yajña*) and those consisting of Soma (*soma-saṃsthā*), providing them with abundant sacrificial fees, that is, accompanied by the giving of the fees originally intended. || 312 ||
And he should give enjoyments and various kinds of wealth to the Brahmins.
That which is bestowed upon Brahmins is an inexhaustible treasure for kings;
it is never spilled, it causes no distress, and it remains untainted by the need for expiatory rites.
It is said here that what is offered into the fire by a Brahmin is superior to [the offering] made from the presence of Agni.

A king should give to Brahmins enjoyments—specific kinds of food—as well as riches and wealth, such as cattle, land, gold, and so forth. Herein lies the praise: because it serves his own interests and is like a treasure-store, that which is bestowed upon or given to Brahmins is a "treasure" (*nidhi*) for kings. A worldly treasure may sometimes be exhausted before it can be enjoyed due to thieves and the like, but what is given is not so; this is the distinction intended by the word "indestructible" (*akṣaya*). A treasure is gold and other valuables buried in the earth. This gift is superior not only to a treasure, but even to the *agnihotra* and other rites. For in a gift, there is no spilling or injury of any sacrificial oblation (*havis*) by which it might become defective and fruitless like the *agnihotra*. Furthermore, it is untainted by expiations or other defects that cause the need for them. Therefore, what is offered into the fire of the Brahmin’s self—that is, what is given—is more excellent and more highly praised than an oblation poured into the *āhavanīya* and other ritual fires. (1.313, 314)
Since wealth given in this manner becomes an ultimate benefit, he explains how its acquisition and so forth should be carried out:
"One should seek what is not yet obtained through righteous means, and one should protect with effort what has been obtained. (1.315)
One should increase what has been protected through policy; what has increased, one should bestow upon worthy recipients.

One should strive to obtain what has not yet been acquired or reached by means of righteousness. That which has been made one's own with effort, one should protect and guard through resolute application. And what has been protected, one should increase and cause to grow through policy—that is, by the method taught in the scriptures. And once it has grown, one should bestow it upon worthy recipients who are endowed with learning, austerity, and virtuous conduct. || 1.315 ||
Having given land or having established a permanent endowment, one should cause a written deed to be made. [579] 1.316

For the sake of informing future virtuous kings, the monarch—having bestowed land consisting of fields, gardens, villages, and so forth upon a Brahmin, or having established a fixed endowment (*nibandhana*)—should cause a written document to be executed in the manner to be described hereafter, for the information and certain determination of future virtuous kings who act according to the meaning of the scriptures. A "fixed endowment" (*nibandha*) is a regulation such as: "In this village, for each field, this amount of wealth must be given by the owner of the field to him every year or every month," and so on. (1.316)
He states the rule for writing [the document]:
"On a cloth or on a copper plate, marked with one's own seal. (1.317)
Having inscribed his own lineage, himself, the measure of the gift, and a description of the boundaries of the donation, the lord of the earth [should record this]. (1.318)
One should cause a firm edict to be issued, complete with one's own hand and the date.

On a cloth made of cotton or similar material, or on a copper plate, one should have the ancestors of oneself—such as the father, grandfather, and so forth—inscribed as being endowed with qualities such as learning, valor, and righteousness, recording that "this is his son" and "this is his grandson. Having thus caused himself also to be inscribed, the king should cause a royal edict (*śāsana*) to be issued. A "grant" (*pratigraha*) consists of land or a fixed endowment (*nibandha*); the "severance" (*cheda*) or confiscation thereof is described by the scripture as giving rise to sin. Therefore, having caused [the document] to be written, he should cause it to be completed with his own hand, including the statement "This is the approval (*mata*) of King So-and-so, son of So-and-so," together with the date of the grant, such as the year and other details. An "edict" (*śāsana*) is that by which future kings and others are instructed to cease the seizure of gifts; it should be caused to be made marked and stamped with his own seal—the insignia of his own lineage, such as Garuḍa or another symbol—to endure for a long time. For without it, neither the recipient nor his descendants would be able to enjoy the land or the endowment. On this point, Bṛhaspati says: [The text continues with the verse of Bṛhaspati.]
Having bestowed land and other gifts, the king should then cause a righteous edict to be made upon a copper plate or a cloth, containing the details of the location, his lineage, and so forth.
Inviolable, unseizable, and free from all that is subject to change,
it lasts as long as the moon and sun and is inherited by sons and grandsons.
He who severs the gift shall write down the fruit of that act as sixty thousand years in hell for the giver and protector, and likewise in heaven for the taker.
Accompanied by its own seal, the year, the month, the fortnight, the day, and the presiding letter—
such is declared to be a royal edict.
Vyāsa says:
But the scribe of peace and war, personally commanded by the king,
shall inscribe the royal edict either on a copper plate or on cloth.
One should record the place, the lineage succession, the country, and the village reached,
as well as the Brahmins and other venerable persons who were present, and the officials in charge.
Then, awakening all his household members, as well as the scribes, messengers, physicians, and chief officials, down to the fat merchants and the caṇḍālas, he spoke thus:
For the merit of my mother, father, and myself,
I have today given this gift to [Name], the son of [Name], who is a fellow practitioner of the holy life.
Coextensive with the sun and moon, following the lineage of sons and grandsons,
unseizable, irremovable, and free from all future liabilities.
He who severs the gift [of land] shall write down the fruit of that act as follows: for sixty thousand years, he shall experience heaven for the giver and protector, and hell for the taker.
"Known by me"— thus it is written, accompanied by the donor's own hand-lettering,
and likewise marked with the king's seal, along with the year, month, fortnight, and day.
By this procedure, one should write the royal edict. || 1.317, 318 ||
Since it is required to consider which specific region one should inhabit to perform this task, he says:
"One should dwell in a region that is pleasant, suitable for cattle, providing a livelihood, and of the *jāṅgala* type. (1.319)

In that [region], he should construct fortresses for the protection of his subjects, his treasury, and himself. It should be pleasant and charming; beneficial for cattle (*paśavya*); providing a livelihood (*ājīvya*), meaning it possesses on all sides medicinal herbs, forests, trees, grasses, wood, and so forth; and it should be of the *jāṅgala* type—having few trees, water, or mountains, abounding in birds and wild animals, and characterized by abundant rain and sunshine. A king should dwell in such a land. And there, for the sake of protecting his people, his wealth, and himself, he should establish fortresses, such as mountain forts (*giridurga*) and others. (1.319)
And in each of those places, he appointed supervisors who were expert, skilled, and pure.

He should diligently appoint supervisors and officials over the activities of income and expenditure—those who are skilled and proficient in various tasks pertaining to the goals of *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma*; who are learned in the treatises on *dharma* (*dharmaśāstra*), adept in their duties, pure, and intent upon wealth; and who are industrious in the matters of revenue, the inner apartments, and disbursements. The essential meaning is that he should appoint capable supervisors. Their qualifications have already been described.
Wisdom, purity in one's inner disposition, vigilance, application,
freedom from addiction to worldly affairs, and devotion to the master constitute fitness.
Manu says:
Among them, he should appoint those who are brave, capable, and of noble birth to financial affairs;
those who are pure to the management of mines and works; and those who are timid to the duties within the inner apartments.

Viṣṇu: "He should appoint trustworthy persons over mines, factories, tolls, ferries, and elephant forests; righteous men for religious duties; experts for financial matters; heroes for military operations; fierce men for fierce tasks; and eunuchs for women. Manu: "He should appoint various learned supervisors in their respective places;
they shall oversee all the affairs of the people as they carry out their work."
Actions refer to deeds that are well-done or ill-done. || 1.320 ||
There is no dharma higher than this for kings: that which is acquired through battle.

Wealth is given to the Brahmins and constant fearlessness to the subjects. There is no other duty for kings superior to this: the granting of wealth to the Brahmins acquired in battle and the granting of fearlessness to the subjects. This is also the means for conquering enemies; therefore, one should engage in battle for its accomplishment—this is the essential meaning. (1.321)
Now, one might object that because of the suspicion of potential misfortune, the engagement of prudent people in battle is irrational; thus, this injunction is not tenable. To this, he says:
"Those who fight in battles for the sake of land, without turning their backs... (1.322).
With non-deceptive weapons they go to heaven, just like yogins.

Those Kṣatriyas who fight with non-deceitful weapons to protect their own land and conquer that of others, and who do not turn their backs toward their enemies, go to heaven like yogins when slain by their foes; the meaning is that having enjoyed heaven, they are liberated. *Āhavāḥ* means battles. *Kūṭāni* refers to poisoned weapons; those other than these are *akūṭāni*. *Akūṭaiḥ* means with those free from poison. This being the case, there is no ground for the suspicion of harm, as this world or the next is invariably conquered. (1.322)
The words of those who do not retreat when broken are equal to sacrifices. [582] 1.323
The king takes the merit of those who were slain while fleeing.

When one's own royal soldiers have broken and are intent on flight out of fear of the enemy, those who do not turn back but instead advance toward the foe—their footprints are equal to sacrifices; the meaning is that they obtain the fruit of sacrifice at every step. But as for those intent on flight who are slain by the enemy, the lord takes their merit. (1.323)
I am one who speaks of "you," impotent, weaponless, and dependent on another.
One should not kill one who has desisted from combat, nor one who is watching the battle, and so forth;

nor one who says, "I am yours," nor a eunuch, nor one who is terrified, nor one who is weaponless, nor one who is unarmed, nor one who has joined another's side, nor one who is fighting with someone else, nor one who has turned back, nor one who is fleeing, nor those who are merely spectators of the battle and the like. (1.324)
Furthermore:
Having performed the protective rites, he should rise and personally inspect income and expenditure. (1.325)
Then, having observed the legal proceedings, he should bathe and eat according to his desire.

Having ensured the protection of himself and his subjects, and having exerted effort, he should personally inspect the income and expenditure being carried out by the officials. The mention of "personally" is for the sake of showing due respect. Immediately thereafter, having observed other legal matters such as the non-payment of debts and so forth, he should bathe and eat according to his desire. The mention of bathing is indicative of the entire midday ritual (mādhyāhnika). "According to his desire" means when there is a feeling of hunger. (1.325)
Then, the gold brought by the attendants should be deposited in the treasury.

He should see his spies, and then, accompanied by his ministers, he should dispatch messengers. He should deposit into the treasury—the storehouse for the accumulation of wealth—the gold and other riches brought in by officials appointed to collect taxes and duties. Then, he should see the spies who have returned from secret missions to report on the activities of enemies and others, so that he may hear their reports. Thereafter, having deliberated upon the multitude of affairs with his ministers, he should send forth messengers to achieve their successful accomplishment. (1.326)
Then he may move about at his own will, either alone or in the company of his ministers. || 1.327 ||
Having inspected the forces, he should deliberate with the commander-in-chief;

having eaten as much as he desires, he may sport with women. Or, due to business, he may assemble with his ministers. Then, having inspected the elephant, horse, and other forces, he should deliberate on matters concerning the army together with the commander-in-chief and the general. 1.327.
Having performed the twilight devotions, he should listen to the secret speech of his spies.
He should eat while accompanied by song and dance, and he should also recite his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*).
Having performed the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*), and having heard secret words, he should spend some time with song and dance and then recite the Veda. (1.328)
He should go to sleep to the sound of musical instruments, and likewise awaken in that same manner. || 1.329 ||
Having understood the scriptures as well as all that ought to be done, one should reflect upon them.

For the sake of sleep, one should enter [the bed] to the sound of musical instruments—such as the resonance of lutes, flutes, and drums—and likewise awaken by the sound of musical instruments alone. Having awakened during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should reflect upon the scriptures—the words of the Śruti and Smṛti—as well as the means for comprehending their meaning, such as the Nigama and Nirukta, and all other duties. (1.329)
And then he should respectfully dispatch spies among his own people and among others. || 1.330 ||
Greeted with blessings by the officiating priests, the family chaplain, and the teachers,
he should see the astrologers and physicians and bestow cows, gold, and land.
And likewise, the houses of those who have not yet taken wives, as well as the homes of those learned in the Vedas.

Having performed his twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) and remained in seclusion, he should respectfully dispatch secret agents—disguised as merchants, physicians, wandering mendicants (parivrājaka), Buddhists, or Digambaras—who can discern the movements of others, toward his own feudatories and officials, as well as toward other kings, such as his enemies. Then, having been greeted with blessings concerning long life, health, victory, sovereignty, and so forth by the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and others, and having seen the astrologers and physicians who have arrived, and having deliberated with them on matters dependent upon them, he should bestow cows, gold, land, and household goods upon those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya). "Household goods" (naiveśika) refers to articles for marriage or for the household. In the phrase "of the śrotriyas," the genitive case is used in the sense of the dative. (1.330, 331)
He was patient toward brahmins, straightforward toward his loved ones, and wrathful toward his enemies.
A king should be like a father toward his circle of servants and toward his subjects;

he should exercise forgiveness toward affectionate Brahmins, straightforwardness toward enemies, and anger [toward the wicked], respectively. He should protect his servants and his subjects like a father. (1.332)
[584] He states the fruit of protecting the subjects: "By protecting them according to justice, he takes a sixth part of their merit. (1.333)
Because the protection of subjects is superior to all forms of giving:

since the king protects his subjects according to justice and in the manner prescribed by the scriptures, whatever merit those subjects perform, the king obtains a sixth part of that merit. Because the protection of subjects—which consists essentially of the gift of fearlessness—is superior to all other gifts, it is therefore logical that he receives this sixth share of merit. Thus, the protection of subjects is a cause for the acquisition of wealth, just as receiving gifts and so forth is for a Brāhmaṇa. (1.333)
Furthermore:
[The king should protect his subjects] from flatterers, thieves, evildoers, violent criminals, and the like. || 334 ||

He should protect the subjects from those who cause them suffering, and especially from the scribes (kāyastha). He should protect the subjects from extortioners (cāṭa) and others who inflict pain. By the preceding verses, it was implied that he himself should not oppress them; here, however, it is stated that he should act in such a way that others do not oppress them. An *cāṭa* is a slanderer (*piśuna*). A *taskara* is a well-known thief. A *durvṛtta* is one who carries off the wives of others and so forth. A *mahāsāhasika* is one who commits acts such as killing humans or taking prisoners. By the word "and others" (*ādi*), those who employ false weights and measures or counterfeit gold and so on are indicated. The *kāyasthas* are those appointed to collect taxes. (1.334)
Regarding the protection of subjects, he speaks of the gravity of the fault:
"Whatever sin the subjects commit when they are not protected," (1.335).
Therefore, half of that [sin] belongs to the king because he receives taxes from them.

Since subjects—when unprotected by the king, unguarded, and not restrained from unrighteousness—commit sins such as theft, adultery, and the like, half of that sin falls upon the king; the meaning is that the king takes up half [of it]. This is because he collects taxes for the sake of their protection. In this case too, it should be understood that a sin equal to half of the sin [committed by the subjects] accrues to the king. For what is unseen (adṛṣṭa) performed by one does not belong to another. (1.335)
Having learned through spies the conduct of those who hold office over the kingdom, || 1.336 ||
The king should honor the virtuous, but he should execute those who act contrarily; having stripped those who live by bribery of their wealth, he should banish them. (1.337)
He should always provide housing for those learned in the Vedas (śrotriya) who offer him gifts, alms, honor, and respect.

Having ascertained from the reports of spies the various activities and the multitude of undertakings of those appointed and authorized to collect taxes and protect the subjects in the kingdom, he should honor the virtuous who act as prescribed with gifts and other rewards. He should have the wicked who act contrary to this executed or punished according to their offense. Those whose livelihood depends on bribery he should deprive of wealth and banish from the country; "bribery" (utkoca) is the taking of money from a litigant for the sake of a legal case. Having provided for the Vedic scholars with gifts, honors, and hospitality, he should cause them to dwell [in his realm] at all times; "honor" (māna) refers to worship, respectful treatment, and activities that proclaim one's goodness. (1.336, 337)
The king who, by unjust means, seeks to protect his own treasury from the kingdom [is acting wrongly]. || 1.338 ||

Such a king, having taken wealth from his own realm by unjust means and forbidden paths, increases his treasury with those accumulations of riches; yet, before long, he is stripped of his fortune and perishes along with his kinsmen. (1.338)
The fire that arises from the suffering and oppression of the subjects [consumes the king]. || 1.339 ||
Without burning away the king’s fortune, family, and life, it does not cease.

That mass of unrighteousness (*adharma*), which is a cause of suffering like a fire, having arisen from the excessive pain—the suffering resulting from the oppression of subjects and the unjust seizure of their wealth—does not turn back, nor does it desist, until it has consumed and brought to destruction the king’s fortune and the rest. 1.339.
Whatever indeed is the duty of a king in the protection of his own kingdom, [that same duty applies to others].
He incurs that very hardship while bringing another kingdom under his control; this has been explained by the words themselves. 1.340.
He states a specific rule regarding the territory of a foreign kingdom: "However, whatever custom, legal practice, or family tradition exists in a particular place... (1.341).

In the same way, when a foreign kingdom has come under one's control, it must be protected according to its own customs; that is, whatever local practice exists in that foreign realm—such as the *holākā* sacrifice and the like—and whatever legal procedure is based on currency and so forth, and whatever family custom there may be, such as "this much wealth must be given to the king by this family"—that kingdom, having come under control, must be protected endowed with those very same customs and practices. (1.341)
Since the kingdom has its root in counsel, therefore counsel must be well-guarded.
He should act in such a way that others do not know his actions until the emergence of their results.

Since it has been determined that rituals are to be performed with mantras, he should keep them well-guarded so that others do not know the mantra until the mantra’s result has emerged from the performance of the previous ritual; for the kingdom has its root in a well-guarded mantra. (1.342)
The enemy, the friend, and the neutral are respectively the immediate neighbor, the one beyond him, and the one beyond that. || 1.343 ||
The maṇḍala should be visualized in due order through the means of conciliation and the other [stratagems].

The kings situated immediately adjacent, separated by one, or separated by two [territories] in the four directions should be known respectively as the enemy (*ari*), the friend (*mitra*), and the neutral (*udāsīna*). This circle of twelve kings (*dvādaśarājaka-maṇḍala*) should be considered for accomplishment through the means (*upāya*) to be described hereafter—conciliation (*sāma*) and so forth. Among them, one who is inferior should be won over by force (*daṇḍa*), one who is equal by conciliation (*sāman*), one slightly superior by gifts (*dāna*), and one even more superior than that by sowing dissension (*bheda*). Alternatively, the enemy may be won over by force, the friend by conciliation, and the neutral by gifts; yet all may also be won over by sowing dissension. (1.343)
The expedients are conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and likewise, force. || 1.344 ||

When properly applied, these means succeed; however, force (*daṇḍa*) is a resort only when there is no other way. One should understand that for the aforementioned enemies and others, there are four means of subjugation, beginning with conciliation (*sāma*). These, when correctly and appropriately employed, would succeed—meaning they would become capable of accomplishing the task. Among these, force is the resort only in the absence of any other alternative; the meaning is that force is the final expedient when no other means exists. *Dāna* (giving) is well known. *Bheda* (sowing dissension) is the creation of discord between a master and his servants. *Daṇḍa* (force) is the infliction of pain upon wealth or the body. (1.344)
And [he understands] peace, war, marching, halting, and likewise seeking refuge. || 1.345 ||

One should properly determine these qualities; one should determine and employ the six qualities—beginning with peace (*saṃdhi*)—according to principle and according to their respective spheres. Peace (*saṃdhi*) is the undertaking of an agreement that neither of us two shall harm the other. Hostility (*vigraha*) is enmity. Marching (*yāna*) is an expedition. Halting (*āsana*) is indifference. Seeking refuge (*saṃśraya*) is for one oppressed by another to seek shelter with a more powerful king. Double-dealing (*dvaidhībhāva*) is the dividing of one's own forces into two parts. (1.345)
He states the time for the expedition: "When the enemy's kingdom is endowed with the excellence of crops, then one should march. (1.346)
When the enemy is weak while one’s own self possesses spirited mounts and men;

when the kingdom of the other enemy is endowed with crops and other qualities such as gold, yet that enemy himself is destitute of mounts and the like, while one’s own elephants, horses, and so forth are spirited and one’s own men are spirited—then one should march against the enemy's kingdom. (1.346)
And he states the reason why a person should not engage in an undertaking whose fruit is uncertain:
"The accomplishment of action is established in both destiny and human effort. (1.347)
In that regard, destiny is manifested as the result of human action performed in a previous life.

When both destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*) are present, the accomplishment of an action and its fruit is established as certain; however, even if human effort exists, the fruit is not achieved in the absence of destiny. Nor is it possible to determine the absence of destiny prior to the commencement of an undertaking. Therefore, the intention is that engagement in activities such as a military expedition is justified due to this uncertainty regarding the result. In this context, "destiny" refers to that which originates from a previous body, while "human effort" is the person's activity consisting of exertion culminating in *apūrva* (unseen merit). Therein, the term "pertaining to a previous body" implies a predominance [of that factor], because during the performance of rites such as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and the enjoyment of their fruits, there is an identity of the body. (1.347)
If that is so, then let fate alone—which depends upon human effort—be the achiever of the result; what is the use of human effort? To this he says:
"Some [results arise] from fate, some by force, and some from human effort. (1.348)
The goals of human beings are accomplished; their source, however, is human effort.

Rain, great portents, lightning strikes, and so forth, occur by fate (*daiva*) as either beneficial or harmful to living beings such as humans. Some occur through the forceful human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of another; for example, a mother makes her son drink milk even against his will, a father teaches him, or a tiger or a snake kills a living being. On the other hand, some matters are accomplished solely through one's own exertion, such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the like, or violence, theft, and the like. For all of these, human effort (*pauruṣa*) is the source, the cause. In some cases, the causality of effort is understood precisely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, regarding those things whose cause—such as lightning strikes—is not understood from other means of knowledge, their understanding comes from the Veda alone. The effort involved in rites such as the *kārīrī* is established by verbal testimony (*vacana*) as the cause of rain. Lightning strikes and the like, however, are understood generally from the scriptures themselves as causes of suffering, produced by the effort of unrighteousness (*adharma*). Therefore, one must certainly strive in matters such as one’s livelihood. (1.348)
[588] Now he explains the mutual dependence of destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*):
"For just as there can be no movement of a chariot with only a single wheel," (1.349).
Thus, without human effort, destiny does not succeed.

Just as a wheel of a chariot or similar object, though recognized as the cause for the movement of a chariot, cannot by itself—being solitary and devoid of other wheels—cause the chariot to move; so too, destiny (daiva), though recognized as the producer of effects consisting in the experience of pleasure and pain, is not established in its final form as an effect without human effort (puruṣakāra) as a cooperative cause. Even in the case of one who brings about a lightning strike or the like, human effort that causes a person to be situated in a specific location certainly serves as a cooperative cause for destiny. Therefore, one who desires a result should not rely solely on destiny. (1.349)

Regarding the consequence that the various means, such as conciliation and the rest, might produce many mutually contradictory results, he states what should be accepted: "Among the acquisitions of gold, land, and friends, the acquisition of friends is superior. (1.350)
Therefore, one should strive to attain that, and with a concentrated mind, one should protect the truth.

Among the gains of gold, land, and friends—which stand as the goals to be attained through the means (upāya) such as conciliation (sāma)—the acquisition of a friend is the best and most excellent; therefore, one should exert effort toward the attainment of friends. At the time of establishing friendship, if the truth (satya) previously made is not protected, even a friend may become an enemy; therefore, one must apply oneself to the preservation of truth. This should be understood as being for the sake of acquiring a friend, which is the cause of a gain superior to the acquisition of gold and land achieved through conciliation and other means; otherwise, however, the acquisition of gold alone is more powerful. (1.350)
He states the constituent elements of sovereignty: the sovereign, the minister, the people, the fort, the treasury, and likewise the army. (1.351)
These subjects are friends; the kingdom is said to have seven constituent parts.

The king’s task is the protection of the realm; that is sovereignty (*rājya*), which consists of seven limbs. When it is asked what those seven limbs are, their specific nature is indicated by the passage beginning with "the master" and ending with "the allies. When the question arises as to why these constitute limbs, it is stated: "These are the constituents (*prakṛti*). That from which an effect originates, persists, and necessarily comes into being is a constituent, just as gold is the constituent of an earring. Sovereignty does not originate without the master and the others, nor does it persist for long once originated without them. Therefore, the master and the rest are the limbs of sovereignty. The master is a distinguished person endowed with qualities such as great energy (*mahotsāha*). The ministers are the counselors and so forth. The people are the subjects to be protected. The fortress is well known. Accumulated wealth is the treasury. The army is the force. Allies are kings who provide assistance. (1.351)
Regarding what must be done by one who has attained sovereignty, he says:
"Having obtained that [kingdom], the king should inflict punishment upon the wicked. (1.352)

For Dharma was created in the past by Brahmā in the form of the rod (*daṇḍa*). Having attained that [Dharma] as his duty—that is, having obtained the authority of sovereignty—the king should inflict the rod, which consists of the infliction of punishment upon the body or wealth, upon the wicked who transgress the scriptures; he should employ it. Furthermore, one should not suspect the king who employs the rod of sin (*pratyavāya*), because Dharma itself was created and ordained by the blessed Brahmā according to the ritual injunctions in the form of the rod. Since it was ordained for the king, the meaning is that the rod does not constitute unrighteousness (*adharma*). (1.352)
He can be led by one who is free from greed and possessed of a disciplined intellect, according to what is right.

That rod [of punishment] can be guided and administered according to justice and in accordance with the scriptures only by one who is true to his word, pure, possessed of good assistants, wise, free from greed, one who dispenses wealth and resources justly, resolute, whose intellect has been sharpened by service to the elders and the acquisition of knowledge, who is truthful in his resolve, pure, possessing internal and external purity, accompanied by good assistants such as ministers endowed with the multitude of qualities prescribed in the treatises, and who is intelligent, reflecting upon the matters he has mastered; it cannot be done by anyone else. 1.353.
He states that for one who inflicts punishment correctly there is prosperity, whereas otherwise there is transgression:
"When applied according to the scriptures, [the king] [overcomes] the world including the gods, asuras, and humans. (1.358)

It would gladden the entire world, whereas otherwise it would provoke its anger. Punishment applied without transgressing the scriptures would gladden the world, including the gods and others; consequently, there is the attainment of happiness for oneself. But if it is applied improperly, that very same punishment would provoke their anger; consequently, there is the attainment of suffering for oneself. (1.354)
He states another result as well:
"Unjust punishment destroys heaven, fame, and the world. (1.355)

Proper punishment by a king brings about heaven, fame, and victory. [590] The improper application of punishment destroys the heaven earned through previously practiced dharma, as well as fame and this world; however, proper application brings about heaven, fame, and victory earned through other forms of dharma by way of removing obstacles. Therefore, punishment must be applied only properly. 1.355.
He states who is subject to punishment:
"Even a brother, a son worthy of honor, a father-in-law, or even a maternal uncle. (1.356)
There is no one who should not be punished by the king for deviating from his own dharma.

One who fails to perform the duties pertaining to their own caste (*varṇa*), stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth, is subject to punishment. There is no exemption from punishability on account of a person's specific relationship [to the offender] or their high status. *Arghya* means worthy of worship. The rest is well known. As for the other Smṛti text which states: "The mother and father are not to be punished; the *snātaka*, the family priest (*purohita*), the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and those possessed of learning, good character, purity, and right conduct—these are indeed authorities on *dharma*," that refers to cases of minor offenses. It does not intend to mean an absolute absence of punishment in all circumstances. For this very reason, Dakṣa says:
But having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, he who does not abide by his own duty,
the king should swiftly brand him with the mark of a dog's foot and banish him.

It is said that for a king who punishes those deserving of punishment and duly executes those deserving of death, there is not only an absence of sin, but indeed a special spiritual prosperity as well:
"The king who punishes those who deserve punishment and causes those who deserve execution to be slain properly... (1.357)

By him, sacrifices would have been performed with the excellent sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) completed through punishments such as fines and the like, while punishing those deserving of punishment and executing those deserving of death. By those [sacrifices] wherein excellent sacrificial fees were properly obtained and received, sacrifices would have been performed. One should not, however, suspect that the infliction of punishment is for the sake of desire (*kāmyatva*), because Vasiṣṭha states that there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its non-infliction: "Upon the release of one deserving of punishment, the king shall fast for one night, and the domestic priest (*purohita*) for three nights; upon the punishing of one undeserving of punishment, the priest shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance and the king for three nights. Likewise:
The king incurs guilt by releasing such a man;
if the king causes him to be slain, he does not incur sin by acting according to dharma. || 1.357 ||
Having reflected thus, the king [performed] separately [rites] whose fruit was equal to that of a sacrifice.
[591] Surrounded by his councilors, the king should personally examine legal cases every day.

Thus, having reflected upon and thoroughly considered how the infliction of punishment upon those deserving of it yields a fruit equal to that of a sacrifice, the monarch—surrounded by councilors possessing the characteristics to be described hereafter for the purpose of distinguishing between those who deserve punishment and those who do not—should daily inspect and investigate legal disputes (*vyavahāra*), ensuring they are not confused with other separate matters. 1.358.
Families, castes, guilds, assemblies, and even countries. || 1.359 ||
The king, having disciplined those who have strayed from their own duty (*svadharma*), shall establish them on the path.

Families (*kula*) refers to households and the like; castes (*jāti*) refers to Brahmins and so forth; guilds (*śreṇī*) refers to goldsmiths and the like; corporations (*gaṇa*) refers to monasteries, Brahmin communities, and the like; and districts (*janapada*) refers to kingdoms (*rāṣṭra*). Having disciplined—that is, punished—those who have departed from their own duty, he shall establish them on the path, which is their own duty. Since a punishment for a single individual was prescribed previously, whereas here it concerns many, there is no tautology. (1.359)
He states the definition of the *kṛṣṇala* and other units useful for the application of punishment:
"The mote of dust seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*. (1.360)
Eight of those [atoms] make one *likṣā*; three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*.

That which is seen as an extremely subtle particle entering the rays of the sun through a window-lattice, composed of three *dvyaṇukas* according to the system of the Vaiśeṣikas—that is remembered by Manu and others as a *trasareṇu*. Eight of those *trasareṇus* make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa*. (1.360)
Three of those [gauras] are one te; six of those [te] are one yava; three of those [yavas] are one madhya.
Five *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen of those *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*.

Three of those black mustard seeds (*rājasarṣapa*) make one white mustard seed (*gaurasarṣapa*). Six of those constitute one middle-sized barley grain (*yava*), three barley grains make one *kṛṣṇala*, five such *kṛṣṇalas* make one *māṣa*, and sixteen *māṣas* make one *suvarṇa*. (1.361)
A pala is proclaimed to be four or even five suvarṇas. || 1.362 ||
It has been stated that four or even five *suvaras* are proclaimed to be one *pala*; the determination of the *pala* should be made according to the local custom.
The measure of gold has been stated; now he states the measure of silver:
two *kṛṣṇalas* are a silver *māṣa*, and sixteen of those are a *dharaṇa*.
Ten *dharaṇas* are a *śatamāna*, and that indeed is a *pala*. (1.363)

[592] Four *suvarṇas* constitute a *niṣka*. A *māṣa* of silver is measured at two *kṛṣṇalas*. Sixteen such *māṣas* of silver make one *dharaṇa*. Ten *dharaṇas* constitute the silver measure known as a *śatamāna*, which is also called a *pala*. Four *suvarṇas* of silver constitute a *niṣka*. (1.363)
He states the measure of copper:
a *kārṣika* copper *paṇa*. A *karṣa* is a fourth part of a *suvarṇa* or a *pala*; that which is equal to it is *kārṣika*. That [coin] made of copper is a *tāmrika paṇa*. This is the copper [coin].
A fine of eighty thousand paṇas is the highest amercement (uttamasāhasa).
Half of that is declared the middle [fine], and half of that is remembered as the lowest.

A fine consisting of one thousand and eighty *paṇas* is called the highest *sāhasa*; a fine consisting of five hundred and forty *paṇas* is called the middle *sāhasa*; and a fine consisting of two hundred and seventy *paṇas* is called the lowest *sāhasa*, which is referred to in other treatises as the first *sāhasa*. As for that which was stated by Manu:
"Two hundred and fifty *paṇas* are recorded as the first *sāhasa*."
The middling [offering] is to be known as five hundred, while the best is indeed one thousand.
Thus, that refers to the case of a minor offense. 1.364.
Furthermore, there is the punishment of exile, the punishment of speech, the punishment of fines, and likewise the punishment of death.

These [punishments] may be applied individually or collectively, depending on the nature of the offense: "Fie! Punishment! Fie upon you, a coward! and so forth, constitutes verbal punishment (*vāgdaṇḍa*). Harsh speech such as "I seize all your property" or "I banish you from the country" is also included. Monetary punishment (*dhanadaṇḍa*) ranges from the seizure of a *kṛṣṇala* up to the confiscation of everything. Corporal punishment (*vadhadaṇḍa*) consists of beating the body or the taking of life. These punishments—individually, or collectively two, three, or four at a time—should be employed according to the gravity of the offense. (1.365)
Having ascertained the offense, the place, the time, and also the strength [of the offender],
as well as their age, their deed, and their wealth, he should inflict punishment upon those deserving of punishment.
Thus ends the section on the Duties of Kings (Rājadharma). 12.

[593] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”—“Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, bhikkhus, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, who consumes these four nutriments? “Bhikkhu, it is craving that consumes these four nutriments. Craving has its origin in feeling; feeling has its origin in contact; contact has its origin in the six sense bases; the six sense bases have their origin in name-and-form; name-and-form has its origin in consciousness; consciousness has its origin in kamma-formations; and kamma-formations have their origin in ignorance. But with the remainderless fading away and cessation of ignorance comes the cessation of kamma-formations; with the cessation of kamma-formations comes the cessation of consciousness; with the cessation of consciousness comes the cessation of name-and-form; with the cessation of name-and-form comes the cessation of the six sense bases; with the cessation of the six sense bases comes the cessation of contact; with the cessation of contact comes the cessation of feeling; with the cessation of feeling comes the cessation of craving; with the cessation of craving comes the cessation of clinging; with the cessation of clinging comes the cessation of existence; with the cessation of existence comes the cessation of birth; with the cessation of birth, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this whole mass of suffering. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those bhikkhus delighted in the Blessed One’s words. [593]

Having ascertained the offense and other relevant factors, one should inflict punishment upon those deserving of it; that is, one should apply it. In this context, the knowledge of the offense is restated (*anūdyate*) because it was already established by the preceding statement, whereas the knowledge of the place and other factors is prescribed (*vidhīyate*). For in some regions, even a slight cold or heat, or a brief deprivation of food, causes excessive suffering, while in others, even a great deal does not cause such [suffering]. Likewise regarding time, such as the autumn season and so forth. Similarly, having understood the strength of the person to be punished, the punishment of beating and the like should be administered. So too regarding age, occupation, and wealth. Otherwise, there would be the destruction of their physical form, the abandonment of duties such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice, and the failure to acquire wealth. However, when punishment is meted out after understanding the place and other factors, security (*yoga-kṣema*) is maintained. All of this is ordained for a Kṣatriya exercising sovereignty. But when a non-Kṣatriya performs the duties of a Kṣatriya, he too must perform all of this, according to the maxim: "By assuming his office, one acquires his duties," and because the protection of subjects is contingent upon the collection of taxes. For everyone who gives wealth aims at a purpose inherent to themselves. And there is no purpose for the payment of taxes other than self-protection. Therefore, it is established that one who collects taxes must provide protection for the subjects. (1.366)

Thus ends the section on Royal Policy (*rājanīti*) in the *Aparārka*, a commentary on the *Yājñavalkīya-dharmaśāstra* composed by the illustrious Aparādityadeva, who was born in the lineage of King Jīmūtavāhana of the Śilāhāra dynasty, which originated from the noble Vidyādhara clan. 12.
And this first chapter on conduct is completed.
